en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Sutta Nipāta in the Khuddaka Nikāya.
(First Part) Introduction to the Composition:
Having paid homage to the Three Jewels, who are most worthy of veneration;
We shall provide a commentary on the meaning of that *Suttanipāta*,
which was taught by the Lord of the World— who sought the world’s transcendence—
for those who abandon minor conduct within the *Khuddakanikāya*.
This Sutta Nipāta is included within the Khuddaka Nikāya itself;
therefore, we shall provide a commentary on its meaning as well.
It is filled with hundreds of verses and marked by both Geyya and Vyākaraṇa.
If it is asked why it is called the *Suttanipāta*, it is because this has reached its culmination (*saṅkhama*).
Because it is well-spoken (*suvutta*), because it is heard (*savana*), and because it provides excellent protection (*suṭṭhu tāṇa*) for the meanings;
because of its indication (*sūcanā*) and its bringing forth (*sūdanā*), it is therefore called a "thread" (*sutta*).
Having extracted such discourses from here and there, this [compilation] was therefore brought together; thus it has come to be known as the Saṅkhā.
And all these discourses are authoritative for one who is such (a Tathāgata).
Because there is no other designation or mark for specific distinctions among these words and their groupings,
it has thus attained the name "Sutta Nipāta" (Collection of Discourses).
1. Uragavagga. 1. Commentary on the Uragasutta.

Thus, this section, having been thus determined as a collection (*saṅkhā*), is called the Uragavagga (Snake Chapter), the Cūḷavagga (Minor Chapter), the Mahāvagga (Major Chapter), and the Aṭṭhakavagga (Chapter of Eights).
The *Pārāyanavagga* consists of five chapters (*vagga*). Among them, the *Uragavagga* is the first.

By way of suttas, there are twelve suttas in the *Uragavagga*, fourteen in the *Cūḷavagga*, twelve in the *Mahāvagga*, sixteen in the *Aṭṭhakavagga*, and sixteen in the *Pārāyanavagga*, making seventy suttas in total.
Of these, the *Uragasutta* is the first. By measure of the textual recitation (*pariyatti*), it comprises eight recitation units (*bhāṇavāra*).
Furthermore, for one who possesses the measure of the Vagga Suttas and the Pariyatti,
it is said: “He who restrains arisen anger with medicines, as one would [neutralize] the spreading venom of a snake with antidotes—
that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, like a serpent casting off its old, worn-out skin.”
This verse is the beginning. Therefore, in order to provide a commentary on its meaning from this point forward, the following is said:
“Having explained the method by whom, where, when, and why this verse was spoken, we shall provide a commentary on its meaning.”
By whom was this verse spoken, where, when, and for what reason was it spoken? It is said:
That Blessed One, who had received his prophecy in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas and fulfilled the perfections (*pāramitā*) until the *Vessantara-jātaka*, was reborn in the Tusita heaven;
having passed away from there, he took birth in the royal family of the Sakyas, and in due course...

What is the Great Departure? Having attained perfect self-enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree and having set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, he taught the Dhamma for the welfare of gods and humans; this was spoken by that Blessed One, the Self-Become, the Teacherless, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
And that [teaching] took place at Āḷavī, at the time when the training rule regarding the destruction of living plants was laid down.
Thus it was spoken for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those who had approached there. This is the summary of the answer here.
In detail, however, it should be understood by way of the distant cause (*dūrenidāna*), the not-so-distant cause (*avidūrenidāna*), and the proximate cause (*santikenidāna*).

Therein, the "distant cause" refers to the account from the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha down to the present subject matter; the "not-so-distant cause" refers to [the account] from the Tusita heaven down to...
The discourse on the present basis (*paccuppannavatthukathā*)—from the "proximate cause" (*santikenidānaṃ*) up to the discourse on the present basis—is as follows.

In this context, since both the "not-far-off cause" (*avidūrenidānaṃ*) and the "proximate cause" (*santikenidānaṃ*) converge within the "far-off cause" (*dūrenidānaṃ*) itself, the detailed exposition here should be understood by way of the far-off cause alone. Furthermore, this [exposition] is found in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*.
"Vutta" (spoken) here means not detailed; therefore, it should be understood according to the method detailed in that [other] place. However, this is the distinction:
there, the occasion for the first verse arose at Sāvatthī, whereas here it is at Āḷavī. As it is said:
"At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine. Now at that time..."
The monks of Āḷavī, while performing construction work, were cutting down trees and having them cut down.
One particular monk from Āḷavī was cutting down a tree. A deity dwelling in that tree said this to the monk:
“Venerable sir, do not cut down my abode out of a desire to build your own abode. That monk, paying no heed, continued on.
“Let me cut it off! She struck the arm of that deity’s child. Then it occurred to that deity:
“What if I were to deprive this monk of life right here? Then it occurred to that deity:
“It would not be fitting for me to deprive this monk of life right here.”
"What if I were now to report this matter to the Blessed One? Then that deity approached the Blessed One;
having approached, she reported this matter to the Blessed One. "Excellent, excellent, deity!
It was indeed well of you, deity, that you did not deprive that bhikkhu of life. If today, deity, you had deprived that bhikkhu of life..."
“You would commit a transgression, and you, goddess, would produce much demerit.
Go, goddess, to that secluded tree in such-and-such a place; approach it.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One further addressed that goddess in order to subdue the anger that had arisen within her:
“Whoever restrains an arisen anger, as one would a runaway chariot”—this verse he spoke.
Then, people thought: “How indeed can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, cut down trees and have them cut down?
These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are harming a living being that possesses but a single faculty. Thus [they spoke].
Having heard the complaints, the Blessed One was informed by the bhikkhus.
After laying down this training rule: “It is an offense entailing expiation for the destruction of vegetation,” he then delivered a teaching on the Dhamma for those who had gathered there:
“He who restrains arisen anger...”
"Like the spread poison of a snake, [overcome it] with medicines"—thus he spoke this verse.

In this way, this single subject is included in three places: in the Vinaya, the Dhammapada, and the Sutta Nipāta. And to this extent, that summary (mātikā) which was established—"By whom, where, when, and because of what this verse was spoken; this..."—[is fulfilled].
"Having thus explained the method, we shall provide a commentary on the meaning"—thus it has been explained both in brief and in detail, setting aside the commentary on the meaning. 1.
Now, here is that commentary on the meaning: "He who" refers to whoever, of whatever sort, has gone forth from a kṣatriya family or a brāhmaṇa family.
Whether he be a layperson or one gone forth, whether young, middle-aged, or an elder. "Uppatitaṃ" means fallen upwards and upwards, gone;

the meaning is "proceeding," which is what is meant by "arisen" (*uppanna*). And this "arisen" is of many varieties according to its status as present, past, having passed away, having made room, or having gained a footing.
In that regard, all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*) possessing the state of arising and so forth are called "presently arisen."
It is with reference to this that it was said: “phenomena arisen, phenomena not yet arisen, phenomena bound to arise.
Wholesome and unwholesome states that have ceased after having experienced the flavor of their object are called “ceased after having been experienced.
All other conditioned states that have ceased after having reached the three stages beginning with arising are called “arisen after having been experienced. This is what is meant by such [states].

This should be seen in such Suttantas as: “An evil course of view has arisen,” and “And how there comes to be the fulfillment of the development of the mindfulness enlightenment factor that has arisen.
As for the karma described by the method beginning with, “Those karmas which were performed by him in the past,” although it is past, it prevents the ripening of another [karma].
It is called "arisen by making room" because it remains having made room for its own result;

and since the result, even though not yet arisen, will necessarily arise when such room has been made, it is thus termed "arisen by making room. Unwholesome states that have not been eradicated in their respective planes are called "arisen by way of the plane obtained."
And here, the distinction between the "plane" (bhūmi) and that which is "obtained on the plane" (bhūmiladdha) should be understood.

To explain: the "plane" refers to the five aggregates belonging to the three planes, which serve as the object of insight (vipassanā). That which is "obtained on the plane" refers to the class of defilements (kilesa) capable of arising within them;
for it is by means of these that the plane is said to be "obtained. Therefore, it is called "obtained on the plane."

Furthermore, this is not by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*). For even when all aggregates (*khandha*)—whether past and so forth—are fully understood, defilements still arise in those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), taking as their object the aggregates of others, such as Mahākaccāyana and Uppalavaṇṇā, just as they arose for Soreyya’s son, the merchant’s son, Nanda, and others, taking the aggregates [of the former] as their object.
And if this were called "attained to the plane" (*bhūmiladdha*), [it would follow that it is not yet abandoned].

If that were not abandonable, no one would ever be able to abandon the root of existence. However, it should be understood as "ground-acquired" (*bhūmiladdha*) by way of its objective basis (*vatthu*).

For wherever aggregates arise that have not been fully understood through insight, the defilements that are the root of the round of existence (*vaṭṭamūla*) underlie them from the moment of their arising. In the sense of being unabandoned, these are called "arisen as ground-acquired."

This is how it should be understood. In this regard, for one whose underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have not been abandoned within the aggregates, those very aggregates are the basis (*vatthu*) for those defilements, and not the other aggregates.
Furthermore, for those defilements with underlying tendencies that have not been abandoned in past aggregates, only the past aggregates are the basis, and not the others.
The same principle applies to future aggregates and so forth. Likewise, regarding the aggregates of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

For those whose underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have not been abandoned, the aggregates (*khandha*) of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) alone are the basis (*vatthu*), and not the others. This same principle applies to the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

Furthermore, for Stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and other noble persons (*ariya-puggala*), whichever class of defilements that are the root of cyclic existence has been abandoned from their aggregates by whichever respective path, those specific aggregates are the basis for those respective abandoned root-defilements of cyclic existence.
Because they lack a fixed foundation, these states do not receive the designation of "planes.

However, because an ordinary person has not entirely abandoned the defilements that are the root of the round of existence, whatever action he performs—whether wholesome or unwholesome—his round of existence increases due to those defilements as its condition.
This root of the round for him exists only in the aggregate of material form, and not in the aggregates of feeling and so forth... [and so on].
Nor should it be said that [the underlying tendencies] reside only in the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) and not in the aggregates of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth. Why?
Because they lie latent in all five aggregates without distinction. How so? Like the sap of the earth in a tree.

For just as in a great tree, depending upon the surface of the earth and relying on the essence of the earth and the essence of water, and conditioned by those, [the tree grows] with roots, trunk, branches, twigs, leaves, shoots, foliage, flowers, and fruits;

Having grown and filled the sky, as long as the end of the eon lasts, while the lineage of trees remains as a succession of seeds, it cannot be said that "that essence of the earth exists only in the root and not in the trunk and so forth, or only in the fruit and not in the root and so forth. Why?
Because it pervades all parts without distinction—the root and the rest. Just so, in the case of that very tree...
Suppose a certain man, disgusted with flowers, fruits, and the like, were to apply a poison called *maṇḍūkakaṇṭaka* to a tree in each of the four directions;
then that tree, touched by that poison, having its essence of earth and water exhausted and becoming incapable of germination, would no longer be able to produce a new continuity. Even so...

The clansman, having become disillusioned with the process of the aggregates (*khandha*), undertakes the cultivation of the four paths within his own continuum, just as that man [administers] a poison-plant four *yojanas* in extent to trees in the four directions.
Then, through the contact of that poison of the four paths, his continuum of aggregates—

since all defilements rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) have been completely exhausted— consists of every variety of action, such as bodily karma and the rest, which has attained the state of mere functional activity (*kiriyabhāva*).
Due to the fact that it no longer possesses the nature of producing renewed existence in the future, it is incapable of generating a continuity of existence in another life.
Rather, with the cessation of the final consciousness, it attains final Nibbāna without fuel, like a fire without a source of kindling, being without any further clinging.
In this way, the distinction between the plane and what is obtained on that plane should be understood.
Furthermore, there is another fourfold classification of what has arisen (*uppanna*), according to whether it is manifested, its object is grasped, it is suppressed, or it is not eradicated.

Among these, that which is currently occurring is precisely "arisen as manifestation. However, regarding the defilements that have not yet arisen in the prior stage when an object has come into the range of the eye and so forth, they arise at a later stage precisely because the object has been grasped.
Because it necessarily arises from an object, it is called "arisen by way of apprehending an object.
An example here is the arising of a class of defilements in the Elder Mahātissa while he was wandering for alms in the village of Kalyāṇī upon seeing a disagreeable form.
Its application is to be seen in such passages as, "a sensual thought has arisen," and so forth. By means of either serenity or insight...

That which has not been suppressed by the arising of defilements and has not entered into the mental continuum is called "unsuppressed and arisen" because of the absence of a cause that would prevent its occurrence.

Regarding this, it is said: "Monks, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is peaceful, sublime, refreshing, and blissful; it is a dwelling that [overcomes] evil states as they arise..."
This is to be seen in such passages as: “He makes unwholesome states disappear from their very basis.

Even though a mass of defilements has been suppressed by means of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), because it has not been eradicated by the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), it is said to be “arisen but not eradicated,” since it has not transcended the nature of arising.
[For example,] when a Thera who had attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) was traveling through the air, in a grove of trees in full bloom...

An illustration of this is the case of a person who, while gathering flowers and singing with a sweet voice, hears the sound of a woman’s song and gives rise to defilements. The application of this principle should be seen in such passages as:
“One who cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path causes arisen evil, unwholesome states to vanish right on the spot.
And all three types—namely, that which is suppressed by the apprehension of an object, that which is suppressed by suppression, and that which has not yet arisen—are included here.
It should be understood that it is included by way of what has already been acquired on the plane (*bhūmiladdha*).

Thus, when this [anger] has arisen in the aforementioned various modes, it should be understood as "arisen anger" by way of its being acquired on the plane, its having the object, its being grasped, its being un-suppressed, and its not being eradicated. Why? Because such a person is to be disciplined. For it is precisely such [a state] that has arisen.

It is possible to discipline [the mind] by whatever means necessary. However, regarding that which has arisen—namely, what is termed present conduct, past conduct, and conduct occurring in a given opportunity—effort here is both fruitless and impossible.
Effort is fruitless in the case of past conduct, because it has already ceased even without such effort.
Likewise, it is impossible in the case of conduct occurring in a given opportunity, because of the [simultaneous] presence of defilements and purification.
"Regarding 'having attained unity':
here, as for the term 'discipline' (*vinaya*), it is twofold; therein, each one is fivefold."
"Among these eightfold [methods], he is called a 'trainer' (vinetī).

This discipline (vinaya) is twofold: the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandonment (pahāna-vinaya). Furthermore, within this twofold discipline, each individual type of discipline is divided fivefold.
For the discipline of restraint consists of: restraint by virtue (sīla-saṃvara), restraint by mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), and restraint by knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara).

Restraint is fivefold: restraint by patience, and restraint by energy. Discipline through abandonment is also fivefold: abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*), abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*), abandonment by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*), and abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*).

Among these, in such passages as "He is endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint, fully endowed," it is restraint by virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*); in such passages as "He guards the eye faculty, he attains restraint over the eye faculty," it is restraint by mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*).
“Whatever streams there are in the world, Ajita,” said the Blessed One,
“mindfulness is their damming up;
I call this the restraint of the streams.”

In such passages as "they are covered by wisdom," restraint through knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*) is to be understood; in such passages as "he is patient with cold and heat," restraint through patience (*khantisaṃvara*) is to be understood;

and in such passages as "he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire, but abandons it and dispels it," restraint through energy (*vīriyasaṃvara*) is to be understood. And all this restraint...
It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it restrains bodily and verbal misconduct and so forth that ought to be restrained, and it is called "discipline" (*vinaya*) because it disciplines them;
thus, first of all, discipline as restraint should be understood as being fivefold.
Likewise, [the discipline of insight] is that which occurs through the factors of insight, such as the discernment of name-and-form, up to the point where one's own practice does not decline.

By means of each respective knowledge, there is the abandoning of each respective continuity of harm. That is to say: by the definition of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the abandoning of the personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*);

by the discernment of conditions (*paccaya*), the abandoning of the views of no-cause and false-cause; subsequently, by the overcoming of doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇa*), the abandoning of the state of indecisiveness;
by the comprehension of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*), the abandoning of the grasping "I" and "mine"; and by the definition of the path and the non-path...
By the perception of a path where there is no path; by the view of annihilation through the vision of arising;

by the view of eternalism through the vision of passing away; by the perception of safety in what is fearful through the vision of fear; by the perception of gratification through the vision of danger;

by the perception of delight through the contemplation of disenchantment; by the lack of desire for liberation through the knowledge of the desire for liberation; and by equanimity through the knowledge of equanimity.

The abandoning of the contrary state regarding the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhiti*) and Nibbāna by means of the *gotrabhū* [consciousness], which is the abandoning of the grasping at the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*),
is called "abandoning by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*). Furthermore, as long as the concentration— divided into access and absorption— continues without its own decline,
there is the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) struck down by it, as well as their respective opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.
Abandonment in the sense of non-arising is what is called suppression-abandonment (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*). However, that which occurs through the cultivation of the four noble paths—
by virtue of which, within the continuum of one who possesses each respective path,

the dense thicket of defilements belonging to the side of origination (as described in the method beginning with "for the abandoning of the various types of views") never arises again— is [abandonment by eradication].

Abandonment characterized as total eradication is called abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*). Furthermore, the abandonment of defilements at the moment of the fruition (*phala*) due to their subsiding is called abandonment by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*).
Moreover, Nibbāna, which has abandoned all conditioned phenomena because it is the escape from all that is conditioned, is called abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*). And all this abandonment—

Because it is abandonment in the sense of giving up (*yasmā cāgaṭṭhena pahānaṃ*) and discipline in the sense of disciplining (*vinayanaṭṭhena vinayo*), it is therefore called "discipline as abandonment" (*pahānavinayo*);
or alternatively, because each respective discipline arises for one who has abandoned this or that [defilement], it is called "discipline as abandonment.
Thus, discipline as abandonment should be understood to be divided fivefold. In this way, since each one is divided fivefold—
These are the ten kinds of discipline (*vinaya*).

Among them, setting aside *paṭippassaddhivinaya* (discipline by subsiding) and *nissaraṇavinaya* (discipline by escape), he is said to discipline [beings] by means of the remaining eightfold discipline in various ways.
How so? By means of restraint through virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), he disciplines misconduct of body and speech.

For even while subduing anger associated with that [state], one subdues anger; even while subduing covetousness, dejection, and so forth through mindfulness and the restraint of wisdom, one subdues anger associated with dejection;
even while enduring cold and so forth through the restraint of patience, one subdues anger arising from those respective grounds of resentment;
and even while subduing thoughts of ill will through the restraint of energy—

He removes the anger associated with that [state]. By generating within himself those states through which there is abandonment by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and eradication (*samuccheda*), he thus removes the anger that is to be abandoned by substitution of opposites, suppressed, and eradicated.
And here, indeed, "discipline" (*vinaya*) occurs in the sense of discipline as abandonment (*pahāna-vinaya*).

That is not possible. However, by means of those states through which abandonment occurs, one who disciplines [others] is also called, in a figurative sense, "one who disciplines by means of disciplinary abandonment.

But at the time of the abandonment consisting in subsidence, because there is no longer anything to be disciplined, and because the abandonment consisting in escape is not yet to be produced, it is said that he does not discipline anything by means of them. Thus, among those [types of discipline], the discipline of subsidence—
Excluding the discipline of renunciation (*nissaraṇavinaya*), he is said to discipline by means of that or that method through the remaining eightfold discipline. Or alternatively:
"Bhikkhus, there are these five ways of removing resentment, wherein the resentment arisen in a bhikkhu must be entirely removed."
Which five? Monks, toward whichever person anger might arise, loving-kindness should be cultivated toward that person...
[and so on] ...compassion...equanimity...or one should resort to non-attention and lack of mindfulness toward that person; in this way, anger toward that person is to be removed.
Or else, one should resolve upon the fact that that person is the owner of their own karma: "One is the owner of their own karma..."
"This venerable one... [and so on] ...will be an heir"—thus are the five ways of removing resentment spoken of. And those which are stated as:
"Friends, there are these five ways of removing resentment wherein the resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu should be entirely removed."
“What five? Here, friends, a certain person is impure in bodily conduct but pure in verbal conduct;
even toward such a person, friends, resentment must be removed.
In this manner, and by other such methods, five ways of removing resentment have been taught. By removing resentment through any one of these, one is said to “remove it. Furthermore, because—
“Monks, even if bandits and thieves were to hack away at your limbs one by one with a two-handled saw, whoever should harbor ill will in that situation would not be following my instruction.
Thus was the Teacher’s admonition:
“He who returns anger for anger makes his own condition worse.”
One who does not retaliate against an angry person wins a battle difficult to win.
He acts for the benefit of both himself and the other—
namely, one who, knowing the other is provoked, remains composed and mindful.
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven things that are pleasing to an enemy and cause harm to an enemy, which come upon a woman or a man who is prone to anger.
What are the seven? Here, bhikkhus, an enemy wishes for an enemy thus:
‘Oh, may this person be ugly! Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, an enemy does not desire an enemy’s beauty.”

He rejoices. Monks, when a person is prone to anger, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger, even though he may be well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and clothed in white garments, he is nonetheless ugly, being overcome by anger.
This, monks, is the first thing that is pleasing to an enemy and conducive to making one an enemy for one who is prone to anger.
He approaches a woman or a man.
"Furthermore, monks, an enemy desires this of his enemy: 'Oh, may he sleep in discomfort!'...
'May he not have abundant wealth!'... 'May he not be possessed of riches!'... 'May he not be possessed of fame!'..."
‘He would not have friends’... [and so on] ... ‘With the breakup of the body, after death, he might be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
For what reason? Because, monks, an enemy does not rejoice at the departure of an enemy to a good destination.
This person, monks, who is prone to anger, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger, engages in misconduct with the body...
“He engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind. Having engaged in misconduct by body... [and] having engaged in misconduct by speech...
[and] misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death... he is reborn in hell, overcome by anger. “An angry person does not know the goal;
an angry person does not see the Dhamma... [and so on].
“By whatever anger they are provoked, beings go to a state of misery;
having fully understood that anger, those who possess insight abandon it.
One should cast out anger and relinquish conceit; one should transcend every fetter.”
“Anger produces misfortune; anger agitates the mind.
Forgive one transgression, O one of vast wisdom; the wise do not become subject to the power of anger.
By reflecting on the danger of anger in such a manner, anger is subdued. Therefore, because he subdues anger by reflecting in this way, he is called a “subduer.”

"Anger" refers to the occurrence of any one of the nineteen bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*): namely, the nine stated in the Sutta according to the method beginning with "He has done me harm," and likewise the nine established as their opposites beginning with "He has not done me good," making eighteen;
together with the improper object such as a stump or thorn, there are nineteen. The arising of resentment from any one of these bases...
*Āghātaṃ*: "Visaṭanti" means spread out or expanded. "Sappavisanti" means the poison of a snake.
"Ivā" is a word used for comparison; by eliding the vowel *i*, it is simply stated as "iva. "Osadhehī" means by means of antidotes (*agada*). This is what is meant:

just as a physician who treats poison, [removes] the expanded snake-poison that has pervaded the entire body after being bitten by a snake—[using] roots, stalks, bark, leaves, flowers, and so forth...
Just as one might quickly cure [a disease] by administering various medicines or prepared drugs, even so, he who—
having pervaded the arisen continuum of consciousness with the meaning as previously described—
subdues anger that has arisen through any of the aforementioned methods of subduing, does not tolerate it, but abandons it, dispels it, and brings it to an end.

Thus the bhikkhu abandons this shore and the further shore. It should be understood that as this bhikkhu thus subdues anger, he abandons the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana), which are designated as "this shore" and "the further shore," because anger is entirely abandoned by means of the third path.
For "further shore" (pāra) is a general term for a bank; therefore, those [fetters] are "this shore" (ora) and they constitute the "further shore" (pāra) of the ocean of saṃsāra.

Having done this, it is called "this shore and the far shore" (*orapāra*). Alternatively: "Just as one might dispel spreading snake venom with medicines, so he who dispels arisen anger"—that bhikkhu, having completely dispelled anger through the third path and established in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), abandons "this shore and the far shore.

In this context, "this shore" (*ora*) is one's own individual existence (*sakattabhāva*), and "the far shore" (*pāra*) is the existence of others (*parattabhāva*). Or else, "this shore" refers to the six internal bases.
The sense bases: this shore is the six internal sense bases; the further shore is the six external sense bases. Likewise, this shore is the human world; the further shore is the deva world.

This shore is the realm of sensual desire; the further shore is the realm of form and the formless realm. This shore is existence in the realms of sensual desire and form; the further shore is existence in the formless realm. This shore is the personal self;
the further shore is the requisites for the happiness of that self. Thus, one abandons desire and lust for this "this-shore" and "further-shore" by means of the fourth path.

It is said, “He abandons this shore and the further shore. And here, although for a non-returner (anāgāmin) there is indeed no desire or lust for this present existence and so forth because sensual lust has been abandoned,
nevertheless— in order to illustrate the excellence of his state, as with the third path and the others—
all this division of this shore and the further shore is subsumed together, and it is said, “He abandons this shore and the further shore,” by virtue of the abandonment of desire and lust for them.
Now, in order to illustrate that meaning, he gives a simile: "Like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin.
In this context, it is called *uraga* because it moves by means of its belly (*ura*); this is a designation for a serpent. It is of two kinds:

those that change form at will (*kāmarūpī*) and those that do not change form at will (*akāmarūpī*). Those that change form at will are also of two kinds: those born in water and those born on land. One born in water obtains the power to change form only in water.
Not on dry land, like the Naga King Saṅkhapāla in the *Saṅkhapāla Jātaka*. "Land-dweller" means dwelling only on land, not in water.
It has come to be designated as "worn out" (*jiṇṇa*) due to its state of decay, and as "ancient" (*purāṇa*) due to its long duration. One who casts off the skin abandons it in four ways:
by remaining within its own species, by feeling disgust, by relying [on another], and by strength. "Own species" refers to the species of snakes.
A long-term existence. For snakes do not transcend their own species in five instances:
at birth, at death, when shedding their slough while asleep, when engaging in sexual intercourse with one of their own kind, and when casting off old skin.
Indeed, when a snake sheds its skin, it does so while remaining within its own species. And even while remaining within its own species, it does so out of disgust.
He abandons it. As for "feeling disgust": when he is released from half the area but remains unliberated from the other half and hangs there, then, being terrified, he abandons it.
Even while feeling such disgust, he abandons it by leaning against a space between poles, or a space between roots, or a space between rocks.
And even while abandoning it by leaning against something, he generates strength, exerts effort, and with energy straightens the crooked [body].
Having tucked its tail in, it casts off [the prey] while still watching, spreading its hood; having thus cast it off, it departs wherever it wishes.
In the same way, this bhikkhu, desiring to abandon both this shore and the far shore, abandons them in four ways:
by birth, by disgust, by support, and by power. "Birth" refers to the bhikkhu because of the statement, "born of noble birth."
Virtue. For this very reason it was said: "A wise man, established in virtue...

Thus, a bhikkhu standing firm in this same class [of virtue], feeling revulsion toward that near shore—divided into his own personal existence and so forth—which produces suffering like a worn-out, ancient hide, by seeing the danger therein at every turn, and relying on spiritual friends, develops the strength known as supreme exertion.

Having generated [this resolve], one should divide the day and night into six parts, according to the method described as: "By means of walking and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states.
Thus, striving and exerting oneself like a snake, one should sit cross-legged;
and like a snake exhaling its curved tail, one should likewise exert oneself with unremitting effort like a snake.
Having spread his hood, having likewise generated an expansion of knowledge, he casts off this shore and the further shore like a snake casting its skin.
And having cast it off, like a snake that has shed its skin, he—having laid down his burden—departs toward the realm of nirvana without remainder, just as he pleases.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He who subdues arisen anger, as one would neutralize the spreading venom of a snake with medicines—
that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, like a serpent casting off its old, worn-out skin.
Thus was this first verse taught by the Blessed One, culminating in the state of arahantship.
2. Now the turn has come for the commentary on the meaning of the second verse.
Regarding that as well: “Having first explained the method—by whom, where, when, and why this verse was spoken—we shall provide its commentary on the meaning.”

This alone is the table of contents (*mātikā*). Beyond this, however, in all the verses, I shall provide a commentary on the meaning by demonstrating the manner in which each arose, without setting forth a table of contents from this point onward for fear of excessive prolixity.
For example: "He who has cut off passion without remainder"—this is the second verse.
The Origin of the Discourse: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain son of a goldsmith, who was an attendant of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, had gone forth in the presence of the Elder.
Considering that "the meditation on the foul is suitable for the young," the Elder, for the purpose of subduing his lust, [instructed him].
He gave him the meditation subject of the foul (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*). His mind did not find even a mere inclination toward it.
He reported to the Elder, "This is of no benefit to me. The Elder, considering that this was suitable for young men, explained the very same thing to him again.
Thus four months passed, yet he did not attain even the slightest distinction. Then the Elder [reported] this to the Blessed One.
He led him into the presence [of the Blessed One]. The Blessed One said, "Sāriputta, this is not within your domain; you do not know what is suitable for him. He is to be converted by a Buddha.
Having spoken thus, he created a radiant-colored lotus by means of his psychic power and placed it in the man's hand, saying:
"Come now, monk, pierce this with a reed and place it on the sandy ground in the shade of the monastery, facing toward me."
“Sit cross-legged and attend to it, reflecting: ‘The blood is red, the blood is red. It is said that for five hundred births he had been a goldsmith;
therefore, knowing that the sign of the red lotus was suitable for him, the Blessed One gave him the meditation subject of the red lotus.
Having done so, in just a moment he attained all four jhānas there in due order, and by way of direct and reverse progression, etc.
He began his play with meditation according to his method. Then the Blessed One resolved, "Let that lotus wither.
Emerging from his meditation, he saw it withered and blackened in color; seeing this, he realized the perception of impermanence, thinking, "A radiant form has been crushed by old age.
He then applied this realization to himself as well. Thereupon, [he reflected]: "That which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering..."
"Thus it is non-self"—in this way she saw even the three realms of existence as if they were ablaze. As she was seeing thus, not far away there was a lotus lake.
There, children had descended and, having repeatedly plucked the lotuses, were making a heap of them.
To her, those lotuses in the water appeared like masses of flames in a reed-thicket; the falling petals seemed to enter into a precipice.
They appeared as if withered; the tips of the lotuses placed upon the dry land appeared like they had been scorched by fire.
Then, as he contemplated all phenomena according to that [insight], the three realms of existence appeared to him even more intensely than a burning house—utterly devoid of refuge.
Thereupon, while the Blessed One was seated in the Fragrant Chamber, he [perceived] his...
A bodily radiance issued forth from the monk’s upper body; it completely enveloped his face.
Then, reflecting, "What is this?", he saw the Blessed One as if standing near him. Rising from his seat, he extended his hands in reverential salutation.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, perceiving what was suitable for him, spoke this illuminating verse while teaching the Dhamma: "He who has cut off passion without remainder..."
In this context, *rāga* (lust) is so called by virtue of its coloring nature; it is a designation for lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
*Udacchidā* means he cuts off, breaks, and destroys. For grammarians accept that in Vedic usage, a present tense verb may be used even for past time.
*Aseṣaṃ* means together with its underlying tendencies (*sānusaya*). *Bhisapupphaṃ va saroruhaṃ* refers to a lotus flower grown in water.
"Having plunged" means having entered, having gone down into; the rest is exactly as before. What is meant?
Just as these boys, having descended into the lake, cut the lotus flowers and the water-lilies, even so, that bhikkhu who has plunged into this dwelling in the world of the three realms—
“There is no fire equal to lust”;
“I am burning with sensual lust; my mind is consumed by fever”;
“Those who are stained by lust fall back into the stream, like a spider returning to its own web.”
“Friends, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, and whose mind is consumed by it, even kills a living being”—
having followed this line of reasoning and so forth, by reflecting on the danger of lust and gradually severing lust through the aforementioned kinds of restraints such as the restraint of virtue,
and through the perception of foulness regarding animate and inanimate objects, he [proceeds].

By means of the path of non-returning he eliminates the remainder, and by means of the path of Arahantship he eliminates even that which remains without residue, in the very manner previously described.

Thus that bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore, like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin. In this way, this verse was taught by the Blessed One with Arahantship as its culminating point.
And at the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in Arahantship.
3. As for "He who has cut off craving"—what is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
A certain bhikkhu, while staying on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond, was entertaining unwholesome thoughts out of a tendency toward craving.
The Blessed One, having understood his inclination, spoke this illuminating verse.

In this context, "it flows" (*sarati*) means craving (*taṇhā*). The meaning is that it does not reach satiety with respect to sense objects. This is a designation for craving for sensual pleasure, for existence, and for non-existence.
"Flowing" (*saraṇta*) means gone or proceeding; what is meant is that it stands having overspread everything up to the peak of existence.
"Flowing swiftly" (*sīghasaraṇti*) means moving rapidly; disregarding the dangers pertaining to both the present life and the future life, in just a moment—
It means they are capable of reaching even another world-system or the peak of existence. Thus, this craving—which flows swiftly, flows rapidly, and exists in every form—is described as follows:
"Vast above, difficult to fill, desire spreads out in all directions."
“And those who long for it, they become the bearers of the wheel. “With craving as his companion, a person wanders through the long journey of saṃsāra;
from this state of being to another state of being, he does not transcend the cycle of existence.”
“‘The world is deficient, unsatisfied, a slave to craving,’ O Great King—
by reflecting on such dangers and by means of the aforementioned restraints of virtue and so forth,
that which has been gradually dried up is utterly cut off by the path of Arahantship; at that very moment, the bhikkhu abandons it in every respect.”
"From this shore to the further shore. At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in Arahatship.
4. As for the verse beginning "He who has crushed pride": What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
A certain bhikkhu, while dwelling on the bank of the Ganges during the summer season, [built] a reed bridge over the river whose waters were low; later, it was swept away by a great flood.
Seeing him being carried away, [the monk] stood there moved by a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking, "Conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Knowing his underlying intention, the Blessed One spoke this illuminating verse.
In that context, *māna* (conceit) is an inflation of the mind based on birth and other such factors. It is the conceit, "I am superior," or "I am equal."
The conceit “I am inferior” is one kind of conceit; thus it is threefold. Furthermore, one conceives:
“I am superior to the superior,” “equal to the superior,” “inferior to the superior”; “superior to the equal,” “equal to the equal,” “inferior to the equal”;
“superior to the inferior,” “equal to the inferior,” “inferior to the inferior. Thus it is ninefold. All these various types of conceit—
"By whatever conceit they are intoxicated, beings go to a miserable destination"—
by reflecting on the danger in this way according to such a method, and by means of the aforementioned restraints of virtue and so forth,

one who diminishes the defilements little by little— because the defilements are weak and feeble like a bridge of reeds, and because the supramundane states are exceedingly powerful— [should proceed].
By means of the path of arahantship, which is like a great flood, he has destroyed it without remainder;
that is to say, by way of abandoning it entirely, he cuts it off and causes its destruction. At that very moment, that bhikkhu abandons every aspect of both this shore and the far shore.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in arahantship.
5. How did this arise? This verse and the twelve that follow have a single origin.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, a certain brahmin, when the marriage of his daughter had been prepared, thought: "With flowers never before used by any outcaste..."
“Having adorned the girl, I shall send her to her husband’s family.
Searching throughout Sāvatthī, both inside and out, he did not see even a single blade of grass or a flower that had not already been used.
Then, seeing a number of young brahmins of a profligate nature gathered together, he thought, “I will ask them; surely someone among this group will know,” and so he approached them.
He asked. Mocking that brahmin, they said: "Brahmin, a fig flower has never before been enjoyed by anyone in the world.
Decorate your daughter with one and give her away.
On the following day, he rose early, performed his meal distribution, and went to a grove of fig trees on the bank of the river Aciravatī, [seeking] one by one...
While searching the tree, he did not see even as much as a stalk of a flower. Then, when midday had passed, he went to the second bank.
There, a certain bhikkhu was seated at the foot of a certain pleasant tree for his midday rest, attending to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
He approached him there, but without paying attention, sat down once.
Having once squatted and once stood, he grew weary searching for that fig tree among all its branches, twigs, and leaves.
Then that bhikkhu said to him: "Brāhmaṇa, what are you seeking? "The udumbara flower, sir.
"Brāhmaṇa, there is no such thing as an udumbara flower in the world; this statement is false. Do not grow weary."

Then the Blessed One, having understood that bhikkhu’s underlying intention, emitted a radiance and, for him who had developed great reverence through his focused attention, spoke these verses of illumination:
"He who did not find substance in states of existence"—all [the verses] beginning with this should be recited.
Therein, regarding the first verse: *nājjhagamā* means he did not attain, or does not attain; *bhavesu* means...
In the realms of existence consisting of one, four, or five aggregates—whether possessing perceptions of the sensual, fine-material, or immaterial spheres;
or being non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—he searches with wisdom, seeking the "essence," which is to say, permanence or a self-entity.

"Like flowers among *udumbara* trees" means that just as this brahmin did not find flowers while searching among *udumbara* trees, so too [he does not find it] even for a practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*).
Investigating with wisdom, he found no essence whatsoever in any states of existence.

Seeing those phenomena as impermanent and non-self by way of their lack of essence, and gradually attaining supramundane states, he abandons both this shore and the far shore, like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin—this is the meaning and the construction [of the verse]. As for the construction of the remaining verses:
Without entering into further detail, we shall state only the essential meaning:
“He within whom there are no internal agitations, who has transcended ‘it is’ and ‘it is not. — [Dhp 89]
In this context, first of all, this word *antara* [is used as follows]:
“On riverbanks, in dwellings, in assembly halls, and on streets, people gather and deliberate: ‘What is the difference between this and that?’”
“He attained a state of rest midway because of a minor degree of distinction”;
“Anger produces harm, anger agitates the mind;
fear born from within—people do not understand that.”
Thus it is seen in many senses, such as the intermediate state between causes and so forth; but here it refers to the mind (*citta*).
Therefore, "for whom there is no anger within" means that for whose mind there is no anger, because it has been eradicated by the third path.
Furthermore, since "existence" (*bhava*) is prosperity and "non-existence" (*vibhava*) is misfortune; likewise, "existence" is increase and "non-existence" is decrease. "Existence" is...

"Permanence" (*sassata*) refers to eternalism, while "non-becoming" (*vibhava*) refers to annihilationism (*uccheda*). "Becoming" (*bhava*) refers to merit (*puñña*), and "non-becoming" (*vibhava*) refers to demerit (*pāpa*).
Furthermore, "non-becoming" (*vibhava*) and "non-existence" (*abhava*) are identical in meaning. Therefore, regarding the phrase "one who has transcended this state of becoming and non-becoming":

here, that which is called the manifold state of becoming and non-becoming—characterized by success and failure, increase and decrease, permanence and annihilation, and merit and demerit—is [transcended] by means of each respective path as it arises.
By this method, the meaning should be understood as "he has transcended that state of being and non-being. Regarding the phrase "for whom there are no thoughts" (*yassa vitakkā*):
here, for whichever bhikkhu there are the three thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty;
the three thoughts of relatives, country, and immortality; and the three thoughts associated with compassion for others, gain, honor and fame, and not being despised—[these are absent].
These nine types of applied thought have been thoroughly shaken off, intensely scorched, and consumed— this is the meaning—

by means of the three lower paths, which are capable of abandoning each respective type through the discernment of its opposite after reflecting on its danger here and there in the manner described for Samantabhaddaka.
And having thus shaken them off, they are well-established within.

Without remainder means that they have been cut off entirely by the path of Arahantship, so that they will never arise again within one’s own continuity of aggregates—which constitutes the internal—and within the mind, which constitutes the internal-of-the-internal. For what has been cut off is called "fashioned" (*kappita*);
as it is said: “with hair and beard fashioned. This is how the meaning should be understood here.
8. Now, regarding the phrase "he who does not overstep": here, "he who does not overstep" means he who does not run too far forward.
"He does not retreat" means he does not lag behind. What is meant? For one who exerts energy too intensely falls into restlessness and thus oversteps;

one who is too lax falls into indolence and thus retreats. Likewise, one who exhausts himself through craving for existence oversteps, while [one who exhausts himself] through craving for sensual pleasure...
One who pursues sensual pleasure overreaches; one overreaches through the view of eternalism and underreaches through the view of annihilationism.
One overreaches by grieving for the past and underreaches by longing for the future.
One overreaches through views concerning the past and underreaches through views concerning the future. Therefore, having avoided these two extremes, [one follows] the Middle Way.
One who practices the way neither oversteps nor falls short—this is what is meant.

"He has transcended all this proliferation": by means of that Middle Way, which culminates in the path to Arahatship, he has transcended and gone beyond all this threefold proliferation consisting of craving, conceit, and views, which arises from feeling, perception, and thought.
The meaning is "having transcended. 9.
In the verse immediately following that, however, the only distinction is the phrase "knowing all this world to be false" (*vitatha*). Its meaning is as follows:
"all" (*sabba*) means without remainder; it is said to be complete and without deficiency. Even so, that which pertains to insight (*vipassanā*)—

Here, only the conditioned (saṅkhata), consisting of the classifications of worldly aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), is intended. "Unreal" (vitatha) means that which has departed from its true nature (vigata-tathabhāva).

It is called "unreal" because it exists in whatever way it is grasped by foolish people under the influence of defilements—whether as permanent, or as pleasant, or as beautiful, or as a self (attā)—since it does not exist in that manner.
"This" (idaṃ) refers to all of that very same [conditioned world] by way of direct perception.
He spoke while demonstrating. "Having known" means having understood by means of path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*); moreover, that is through non-delusion, not merely through the sense-object.
"In the world" refers to the world as a spatial realm; the connection is that he has known the entire collection of phenomena, such as the aggregates and so forth, as "this is false. 10–13.
Now, in the four verses following this, [the terms] "free from greed," "free from lust," "free from hatred," and "free from delusion" refer to these...

These are the distinctions. Here, greed (*lobha*) is by way of the act of coveting. This is a comprehensive designation for the first unwholesome root, or for improper greed (*visama-lobha*), regarding which it is said:
"Sometimes even toward one's mother's sister, greed-afflictions arise;
even toward one's paternal aunt, greed-afflictions arise; even toward one's daughter, greed-afflictions arise."
Thus it was said. Lust (*rāga*) is so called by way of being excited; this is a designation for lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Hatred (*dosa*) is so called by way of being corrupted; this is a designation for anger as previously described. Delusion (*moha*) is so called by way of being deluded;
this is a designation for ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths (*cattāri ariyasaccāni*). In that regard, because this bhikkhu, loathing greed, applies insight...
He began by thinking, "When indeed might I, having subdued greed, dwell free from greed?

Therefore, showing him the means for abandoning greed—which is the vision of the falsity of all conditioned phenomena—as well as the benefit of abandoning greed, which is the abandonment of this shore and the further shore, he spoke this verse.
This same method applies to the subsequent verses as well. However, some say: "By the very method already stated, these phenomena..."
“For each individual bhikkhu who, having felt revulsion, applied himself to insight (vipassanā), one single verse was spoken here.
One may take whichever [verse] is preferred. This same method applies to the four verses that follow.

14. Now, this is the commentary on the meaning: they are called *anusayas* because they lie latent (*sayanti*) within the continuum (*santāna*) in the sense of being unabandoned; namely, sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, lust for existence, and ignorance.
This is the designation. They are "roots" (*mūla*) in the sense that they conform to their own modes within associated states;

they are "unwholesome" (*akusala*) in the sense of being insecure; and they are "roots" also in the sense of being the foundation for states. They are "unwholesome" in the sense of having blame and painful fruition.
Both of these are designations for greed, hatred, and delusion. For it has been said: "Greed, monks, is both unwholesome and a root of the unwholesome," and so forth.
They are thus demonstrated by this method. In this way, because these underlying tendencies (anusaya) have been abandoned by their respective paths, they do not exist at all for anyone;

and these unwholesome roots (akusalamūla) have likewise been eradicated. "Samūhatā" means precisely "eradicated. For those skilled in the characteristics of language (saddalakkhaṇakovidā) maintain that the letter *s* is inserted [in the form] of the plural of the personal pronoun (*paccatta*).
However, the teachers of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathācariya) state: "The word *seti* is a particle (*nipāta*)."
They explain it thus. Whatever is pleasing may be accepted. However, although it is stated here:

“Even though such a bhikkhu is one whose taints are exhausted, and one whose taints are exhausted neither takes up nor abandons, but stands having abandoned,” nevertheless, by the grammatical characteristic of using the present tense for what is proximate to the present, it is said: “He abandons this shore and the further shore. Now...
Furthermore, when one attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue, one abandons what is comprised of one’s internal and external sense bases;
this should be understood as "crossing over from this shore to the far shore.

In that regard, the absence of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) should be understood in two ways: by way of the sequence of the defilements (*kilesa*) and by way of the sequence of the paths (*magga*).

For, according to the sequence of defilements (*kilesa*), there is the absence of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) by means of the third path;

of the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) by means of the fourth path; of the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) by means of the first path; and of the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) by means of the fourth path alone.
However, according to the sequence of paths (*magga*), the underlying tendency to views and the underlying tendency to doubt are [abandoned] by means of the first path.
There is non-existence. By the second path, there is the attenuation of the underlying tendencies of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and aversion (*paṭighānusaya*);

by the third path, their total non-existence; and by the fourth path, there is the non-existence of the underlying tendencies of conceit (*mānānusaya*), lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), and ignorance (*avijjānusaya*).

In this regard, not all underlying tendencies are unwholesome roots; for only the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and lust for existence [are so] by virtue of the unwholesome root of greed (*lobha*).

They are included [within the roots]. The underlying tendencies of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) and ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) are designated as "the root of unwholesomeness that is hatred" and "the root of unwholesomeness that is delusion," respectively;
however, the underlying tendencies of views, conceit, and doubt do not constitute any root of unwholesomeness.
Furthermore, because he established the abandoning of defilements by way of the absence of underlying tendencies and by way of the eradication of the roots of unwholesomeness, therefore—
“For whomsoever no underlying tendencies (anusaya) exist at all, and the roots of unwholesomeness have been utterly uprooted.”—Thus the Blessed One said. 15.

Regarding the phrase “for whomsoever there is the birth of distress” (darathajāti): here, the defilements (kilesa) that have first arisen are called “distresses” (daratha) in the sense of being a feverish burning (pariḷāha).
But because they arise from those various distresses (*daratha*), they are called "born of distress" (*darathajā*). "Oram" refers to identity-views (*sakkāya*). As it is said:
"Bhikkhu, 'this shore' is a designation for identity-views. "Āgamanāya" means for the sake of arising.
"Paccayāse" means simply conditions. What is meant? For one who [acts] for the sake of grasping the aggregates of clinging...
Because those defilements that serve as conditions have been abandoned by the Noble Path, certain defilements—synonyms for distress (*daratha*)—no longer exist;
in the manner previously described, that bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore.

16. Regarding the phrase *yassa vanathajāti*: here too, *vanathajā* should be understood just like *darathajā*. As for the etymological meaning (*vacanatthe*): [it refers to the arising of the forest-thicket].
This is the distinction: *vana* means "it is desired" (*vanute*) or "it desires" (*vanoti*); the meaning is that one asks for it, serves it, or cultivates it.

This is a designation for craving (*taṇhā*), for it is called "the forest" (*vana*) because of its longing for sense objects and its cultivation [of them]. Because it "spreads" (*tharati*) or "stretches out" (*tanoti*) the forest by way of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), it is "forest-thicket" (*vanatha*);
this is a designation for the underlying tendency of craving (*taṇhānusaya*). "Born from the forest-thicket" (*vanathajāta*) means born from the forest-thicket.
However, some say: "All defilements are called 'thicket' (*vanatha*) in the sense of being dense; but those that arise repeatedly are 'sprouts of the thicket' (*vanathaja*).
Here, this [latter] meaning alone is intended in the *Uragasutta*, while the other is intended in the *Dhammapada* verse.
"For the bondage of existence" means for the bondage to existence. Alternatively, it means for the bondage of the mind to sense objects.
The meaning is: "and for the sake of future arising. "Causes that are like causes" means they are simply causes.

17. Regarding the phrase "who [has abandoned] the hindrances": here, *nīvaraṇā* refers to the mind; or, they are called *nīvaraṇā* because they obstruct (*nīvaranti*) the practice of what is beneficial, which is to say, they conceal it.
"Having abandoned" means having cast off. "Five" is the numerical delimitation of them. Because of the absence of distress (*īghā*).
"Free from distress. Because he has crossed over all doubt, he is "one who has transcended doubt. Because he is free from the dart [of craving], he is "dartless.

What is meant? A bhikkhu who, having seen the danger in the five hindrances—such as sensual desire—in both their general and specific aspects according to the method explained in the *Samantapāsādikā*, abandons them by means of the respective paths, and because they have been abandoned...
He is "free from distress" (anīgha) due to the absence of the slightest suffering consisting of the defilements;

he is "one who has crossed over doubt" (tiṇṇakaṅkha) because he has transcended the state of perplexity that arises in the manner of the inquiry, "Did I indeed exist in the past? and so forth; and [he is free] from the five arrows mentioned thus:
"In this regard, what are the five arrows? The arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, the arrow of delusion, the arrow of conceit, and the arrow of views."
Because he is free from [defilements], he is "without dart. That bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore in the manner already described.
Here too, the abandonment of the hindrances should be understood in two ways: according to the sequence of defilements and according to the sequence of the paths.
For, according to the sequence of defilements, the abandonment of the hindrance of sensual desire and the hindrance of ill will occurs through the third path.
[It is abandoned] by the fourth path for the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor and the hindrance of restlessness;
by the first path for the hindrance of remorse—consisting of regret that occurs in the manner of "Alas, I have not done what is wholesome," etc.—and for the hindrance of doubt.
However, according to the sequence of the paths, [it is abandoned] for the hindrance of remorse and the hindrance of doubt...
Abandonment of the hindrance of sensual desire and the hindrance of ill will occurs through the first path;

their attenuation occurs through the second path; their complete abandonment occurs through the third; and the abandonment of the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor and the hindrance of restlessness occurs through the fourth path. Thus—

“He who, having abandoned the five hindrances, is free from distress, has crossed over doubt, and is without taints—that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin.
Thus the Blessed One concluded his teaching with the very pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu attained Arahantship.
“Established. Some say: “By whichever verse was taught to whichever of those monks, at the conclusion of that respective verse, each of those monks was established in Arahatship.
[From] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Uraga Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Dhaniya Sutta: 18.
“Well-cooked rice” refers to the Dhaniya Sutta. What is its origin? At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. At that time...
Dhaniya the cowherd lived on the bank of the Mahī River. This was his prior practice:
during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, for twenty thousand years, he gave twenty meal-tickets to the Saṅgha every single day.
Having passed away from there, he was reborn among the devas. Thus, having spent an entire interval between Buddhas in the world of the devas, [he was reborn] in the time of our Blessed One.
In the middle of the kingdom of Videha, there was a mountain district called Pabbataraṭṭha; in that place was a city named Dhammakoraṇḍa.
There he was reborn as the son of a merchant, living by means of a herd of cattle.
He possessed about thirty thousand cows, and twenty-seven thousand cows were being milked. The cowherds were his permanent residents.
They do not remain [there]. During the four months of the rains, they dwell on dry land;
for the remaining eight months, they dwell wherever grass and water are easily obtained—whether that be a riverbank or the shore of a lake.
Then, at the time of the rains, departing from their own village where they had lived, they search for a place for the cattle to dwell in comfort throughout the great earth.
Having split apart, Kālamahī went in one direction and Mahāmahī in the other; flowing on, they met again near the ocean and continued their course.
Entering the space that became the intermediate island (Antaradīpa), she established a dwelling for her calves and a residence for herself, and there she made her home.
She had seven sons, seven daughters, and seven daughters-in-law.
There were many laborers. Those known as the "Gopas" knew the signs of the rains.

When the birds built their nests at the tops of trees, and the crabs closed off the openings near the water and moved about through the openings near the land, they took it that there would be good rain.
But when the birds built their nests in low places on the surface of the water...
The crabs close the door near the land and frequent the door near the water;
when they do so, people take it as a sign that there will be a poor rainfall.
Then Dhaniya, having observed the signs of good rainfall, [went] from the middle of the island as the rainy season approached.
Having departed from Mahāmahī, even as it rained for seven days and seven nights on the opposite shore, he made a dwelling place for himself in a spot not submerged by the water;
having enclosed it on all sides and constructed cowsheds, he established his residence there.
Then, when the collection of wood, grass, and other materials had been arranged, and all his sons, wives, laborers, and servants were settled together, [he remained there].
When various kinds of food and delicacies had been prepared for those who had gathered from all four directions, clouds arose on every side like circles of mist.
He had the cows milked, settled the calves in their pens, caused smoke to be raised from the cattle-pens in all four directions,
fed his entire retinue, performed all necessary duties, and had lamps lit here and there.
Having himself eaten rice with milk and lying upon a great couch, he beheld his own glorious prosperity;
being filled with joy, as he lay there he heard the sound of thundering clouds in another direction and uttered this inspired utterance:
"I am one whose rice is cooked and whose milk is milked."
Herein, this is the commentary on the meaning: *pakkodana* means cooked rice; *duddhakhīra* means milk taken after milking cows. *Ahaṃ* indicates oneself;
*asmī* indicates one’s state of being so. The meaning is: “I am—*ahaṃ asmi*—one who possesses cooked rice and milk.
*Iti* means “thus he said. In the *Niddesa*, however, it says: “*Iti* is the junction of words, the connection of words...”

"The completion of the phrase, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of the phonemes, and the sequence of the words—this is what [the word *iti*] signifies. Thus its meaning has been described.
It should be understood that he too [used the word *iti*] with reference to this very thing.
For, while revealing the sense "whatever word was spoken by the preceding word, for each of those he said 'thus' (*iti*)," the word *iti* [is connected] with the subsequent word, Metteyyo.
The phrase "iti vā bhagavā" (thus indeed the Blessed One) and so forth constitutes a syntactical connection (*padasandhi*), and not otherwise.

"Dhaniyo gopo" is the name of that merchant’s son. For among these five kinds of wealth, beginning with immovable property (*thāvara*), he—setting aside the wealth that follows one [into future lives] such as generosity and virtue—is called "Dhaniya" even because of his immovable wealth consisting of fields, lands, groves, and so forth.

“Rich” (*dhaniyo*) means being endowed with that wealth consisting of cattle—which is distinguished by the statement, “there is no wealth equal to cattle”—in consideration of how it is of great benefit to the world by providing the five products of the cow;
this is so even when compared to mobile wealth such as silver and gold, or to wealth consisting of limbs through the various fields of craft. Thus, he is rich because he possesses that.
A *gopa* is one who protects cattle (*gunna*). For he who protects his own cows is called a "cowherd" (*gopa*), whereas he who works for others as a hired laborer is a "cow-keeper" (*gopālaka*).
But this one [protects] his own; therefore, he is called a *gopa*.
"On the bank" (*anutīre*) means near the riverbank. "In the Mahī" (*mahiyā*) refers to the river named Mahāmahī. "By one who is equal" means by one who acts in accordance with [the other].
One who dwells together with a retinue is a "co-resident" (*samānavāsa*), and he is of such a kind. Therefore, it is said: "a co-resident.
"Covered" (*channa*) means made rain-proof by coverings of grass and leaves. "Hut" (*kuṭī*) is a designation for a dwelling house.
"Set on fire" (*āhita*) means brought or ignited. "Forest fire" (*ginī*) means fire; in various places, fire is conventionally referred to as "forest fire."
"Atha ce patthayasi" means "if you now desire. "Pavassa" means "rain down," "pour forth," or "release water"—this is the meaning.
"Deva" is an address to the cloud. This, then, is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).
As for the commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*): thus Dhaniya the cowherd, while lying upon a great couch in his own bedchamber—

Having heard what was produced by the clouds, by saying, "I am one whose rice is cooked," he demonstrates his own possession of the means for the subsiding of bodily suffering and the cause of bodily happiness.
By saying, "I am one whose milk has been milked," he demonstrates the means for the subsiding of mental suffering and the cause of mental happiness.
By saying, "On the bank of the Mahī," he demonstrates the excellence of his dwelling place; by saying, "A fellow-dweller," [he refers] to such a person.
The absence of sorrow, which has the separation from loved ones as its proximate cause, even at that time; the warding off of bodily suffering by saying, "The hut is roofed";

and the phrase "the fire is kindled" refers to the fact that cowherds prepare three kinds of fires—by way of enclosures, smoke, and the heat of wood—and since all these have been prepared in his house, he says "the fire is kindled" with reference to the fire of the enclosure in every direction.
By speaking thus, he illustrates the prevention of wild beasts approaching;

by referring to smoke and fire from cow dung and the like in the midst of cattle, he illustrates the non-affliction of the cattle by gadflies, mosquitoes, and so forth; and by referring to wood fires at the sleeping places of cowherds, he illustrates the warding off of the affliction of cold for the cowherds.
By illustrating it in this way, he [protects] himself, the cattle, or his attendants against the conditions of rain.
Because he was free from any ailment, he became filled with rapture and joy and said: "But if you wish it, O God, pour down rain!

While Dhaniya was speaking this verse, the Blessed One—dwelling in the Perfumed Chamber of the Great Monastery of Jetavana—heard it with his purified divine ear-element, which surpasses that of humans. Having heard it, he [beheld him] with the Buddha-eye.
While surveying the world, he saw Dhaniya and his wife and thought: "Both of these are endowed with the necessary causes.
If I go and teach them the Dhamma, both will go forth and attain arahantship.
If I do not go, they will perish tomorrow in the flood of water. At that very moment, [the Buddha traveled] seven hundred yojanas from Sāvatthī to Dhaniya’s [dwelling].
Having traveled through the air to his dwelling place, he stood above Dhaniya’s hut. Dhaniya continued to recite that verse again and again;
he did not finish it, and even after the Blessed One had departed, he kept on reciting. Hearing this, the Blessed One said:
"They are not satisfied or confident with just this much; rather, they are like this"—and to demonstrate this, he spoke:
“I am free from anger, my stubbornness has vanished; I have spent one night on the bank of the Mahī.
My hut is open and the fire is extinguished;

so, O Deva, rain if you wish.”—He spoke this counter-verse, which was similar in phrasing but not in meaning. For “I am free from anger” (*akkodhano*) is not the same as “the rice is cooked” (*pakkodano*).
The words beginning with "ca" (and) coincide in meaning like the near and far shores of the great ocean;

however, because some of the phrasing here coincides with that [of the previous verse], they are called "similar in phrasing" (*byañjanasabhāga*). In this regard, the meaning of the words common to the preceding verse should be understood according to the method already explained.
This is the commentary on the specific term (*visesapadāna*) according to both its word-form and its meaning: "One who is not angry" (*akkodhana*) means one whose nature is free from anger.

For that anger—which arises from the previously mentioned bases of resentment and which, even when it occurs in someone to a very slight degree, subsides only after burning the heart—and that [anger] which, having arisen with greater force, causes another to merely distort his face...
One person does it; then another, with even greater force, merely moves his jaw, wishing to speak harshly;
another, with even greater force than that, utters harsh words;
another, with even greater force than that, looks around in all directions seeking a staff or a weapon; and another, with even greater force than that, seizes a staff or a weapon.
Then, one who is more powerful pursues him with clubs and other weapons; another, being even more powerful, inflicts one or two blows;
another, being even more powerful, deprives even a kinsman or blood relation of life;
and some, being even more powerful, later becoming remorseful, deprives even themselves of life, as did the resident of Kālagāma in the island of Siṃhala.
Like a servant. At this point, anger has reached its highest degree of intensity.

That [anger] was entirely abandoned by the Blessed One right at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), cut off at the root, and made like a palm stump; therefore, the Blessed One said, "I am one who is free from anger.
"Free from barrenness" means one from whom barrenness has departed. For those five mental barrennesses (*cetokhila*) were spoken of as being states that bind the mind.

For when the mind is like barren soil—just as crops do not grow even if it rains for four months on a plot of land that is barren—likewise, even if the rain of the causes of skillfulness, such as hearing the true Dharma, falls, skillfulness does not grow;
and those [barren states] have been entirely abandoned by the Blessed One right at the seat of enlightenment. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "I am one from whom the barrenness has departed."
“Ekarattivāso” means a stay for one night. For while Dhaniya had entered upon a fixed residence there for the four months of the rains, the Blessed One did not do so.
Rather, the Blessed One stayed there for that very night out of a desire for his welfare;
therefore, it is called “a stay for one night. “Vivaṭā” means with the covering removed. “Kuṭī” means...

The personal entity (*attabhāva*). Indeed, depending on various purposes, this personal entity is called the "body" (*kāya*), the "cave" (*guhā*), the "fleshly body" (*deha*), the "carrier of the body" (*sandeha*), the "ship" (*nāvā*), the "chariot" (*ratha*), the "wound" (*vaṇa*), the "banner" (*dhaja*), the "anthill" (*vammika*), the "hut" (*kuṭī*), or the "little hut" (*kuṭikā*).
Here, however, because it has come to be designated [as such] based on bones and so forth—just as a hut is named after its beams and other materials—it is [called the personal entity].
It is called a "hut. As it has been said:
