"Just as, friend, space enclosed by wood, creepers, clay, and grass comes to be reckoned simply as a 'house,' even so, friend, [the body] depending on bones..."
“Dependent upon the bones, dependent upon the sinews, dependent upon the flesh, and dependent upon the skin, the space enclosed therein comes to be reckoned simply as ‘form.
It is a hut because it is the dwelling place of the monkey of the mind. As it has been said:
“If that hut were a skeleton-framed house,
it would be a dwelling for a monkey; the monkey, having entered the five-doored hut,
wanders around from door to door, knocking again and again.”
That hut is so called because beings are covered by the roof of craving, conceit, and views, through which the rain of defilements such as lust pours down again and again. As it is said:
"The covered leaks, the uncovered does not leak;
therefore, uncover what is covered, and thus the rain will not leak upon you."
This verse is spoken in two places: in the *Khandhaka* and in the *Theragāthā*. In the *Khandhaka*, it was spoken with reference to this meaning:
“For one who conceals an offense, the defilements and offenses rain down upon him again and again; but for one who does not conceal them, they do not rain down.
In the *Theragāthā*, it is said: “For one whose covering of lust and so forth...”
There is [the case] where, because lust and other defilements arise again toward desirable objects and so forth, the rain overflows the roof.
Or, for one who tolerates arisen defilements, the hut of his own person—covered by the covering of those tolerated defilements—is repeatedly drenched by the rain of defilements.
However, for one whose covering of defilements has been destroyed by the wind of the knowledge of the path to Arahatship, [the rain no longer overflows].
"Open, it does not rain upon it. This is the meaning intended here.
For the covering described by the Blessed One has been demolished in the very manner already stated; therefore, he said, "the hut is open. "Nibbuto" means calmed.
"Gini" means fire—that elevenfold fire by which all this world is set ablaze. As it is said:
—"Set ablaze by the fire of passion," and so forth in detail. That fire was extinguished at the very foot of the Blessed One’s Bodhi tree by the sprinkling of the water of the Noble Path;
therefore, he said, "The fire is extinguished.
By speaking thus, he rebukes and instructs Dhaniya—who is satisfied with what is not to be satisfied—under the guise of referring to something else.
He instructs him. How so? Dhaniya, when you say, "I am free from anger," you are satisfied thinking, "I have cooked my rice.
Yet the cooking of rice must be performed at the expense of wealth for as long as one lives, and the depletion of wealth is the basis for suffering such as guarding it.

This being so, you are satisfied with nothing but suffering. I, however, am satisfied by the thought, "I am free from anger," because of the absence of suffering both in this life and in the life to come.

By saying, "I am satisfied," he illuminates this: while you are satisfied thinking, "I have milked the milk," and thus being pleased even though you have not yet finished your task, you imagine, "I have finished my task";
I, however, being satisfied by thinking, "The obduracy has been removed," am satisfied because I have indeed finished my task.
By saying, "A single night's stay on the bank of the Mahī," he illuminates this: [the rest follows].
"You are content with 'living on the same bank as Mahiya,' pleased by residing there for four months.
But such fixed residence arises from attachment to a dwelling place, and that is suffering; thus, while this is the case, you are content with nothing but suffering.
I, however, am content with 'staying for only one night,' pleased by an unfixed residence. And an unfixed residence exists because of the absence of attachment to a dwelling place."
By saying, "It is so, and the absence of attachment to one's dwelling is happiness," he demonstrates that he is satisfied with happiness itself.
By saying, "The hut is open," you are satisfied thinking, "The hut is covered"; thus you are satisfied with the state of having a covered house.
Yet, even though your house is covered, the rain of defilements pours over the hut of your own person; by means of this, the four [mental disturbances] are produced...
Being swept away by great floods, you would have met with misfortune and ruin; yet, such being the case, you are content with what is not enough.
But I, being satisfied that "the hut is open," am satisfied because of the absence of the covering of defilements within the hut of my own self.
And since the hut is thus open for me, that rain of defilements does not pour through it, by which [defilements] the four [fires] are produced.
He illustrates: "Being swept away by great floods, I might have met with misfortune and ruin; such being the case, I am content simply because I am content.
By saying, "The fire is extinguished," you are pleased thinking, "The fire was kindled," and thus you are satisfied while believing you have prevented a calamity that has not yet occurred.
But I, being pleased that "the fire is extinguished," am satisfied because of the absence of the eleven kinds of feverish fires.
He indicates that one is content simply by warding off harm caused by one's own actions.
By saying, "But if you wish, O God, rain down," this statement is appropriate for those like us who are free from suffering, have attained happiness, and have fulfilled all our duties;
"But if you wish, O God, rain down," for there is no increase for us whether you rain or do not rain.
This indicates: "There is indeed loss or gain; why then do you speak thus?
Therefore, what was stated—"And speaking thus, Dhaniya, being dissatisfied with mere dissatisfaction, rebukes, advises, and instructs under the guise of something else"—is correctly stated.
20. Even after hearing this verse spoken by the Blessed One, Dhaniya the cowherd did not say, "Who is this speaking the verse?
Instead, being satisfied with those well-spoken words and desiring to hear more of the same kind, he spoke another verse beginning with "Andhakamakasā.
In that context, "Andhakā" is a designation for black flies; it is also a designation for brown flies.
Some [commentators] say: "Gnats" means simply gnats. "Are not found" means they do not exist. "In a marsh" refers to two kinds of marshes—the river marsh and the mountain marsh;
here it is the river marsh. "With grown grass" means where grass has sprouted. "They roam" means they perform their feeding activities.
"Even rain" refers to various types of rain, such as wind-rain and so forth; these we shall explain in the Āḷavaka Sutta.
But here, it is said with reference to the rainy-season swarms. "They would endure" means they would forgive. The rest is clear.
In this regard, Dhaniya, there are gadflies and mosquitoes that, having gathered together and drunk the blood, bring cattle to ruin and disaster in a mere moment;
therefore, as soon as they have emerged, those cowherds kill them with dust and twigs. Of these—
By means of the absence of cattle, he spoke of safety, describing how there was no exhaustion from traveling on the road due to treading upon grass grown in the marshes,
and indicating the absence of hunger and fatigue: "Just as the cattle of others— exposed to the touch of flies and mosquitoes,
exhausted by the journey, and withered by hunger— would not endure even a single fall of rain, so it is not for me."
"Likewise, my cows—because they lack the aforementioned qualities—would endure even two or three rains.

Then the Blessed One [spoke], because Dhaniya, while living on the island in between, having seen danger, had bound a raft, crossed over the great Mahī river, and reached that marshy bank, thinking: "I have arrived safely; I am standing in a place free from fear."
Thinking thus, he spoke these words; yet he stood in a place of very great danger.

Therefore, praising his own place of arrival as superior and more excellent than the place from which he had come, he uttered this verse, "You have bound the raft," which is similar in meaning but not similar in phrasing.

In this context, "raft" (*bhisī*) refers in common worldly usage to a boat constructed by spreading out materials and binding them together to form a broad float. However, in the Noble Dhamma and Vinaya, it is a designation for the Noble Path.
For the Noble Path is described thus: "The path, the way, the road, the track, the direct route, the course, the vehicle, the ship, the ford, the raft, and the bridge."
“The origin of the journey has been explained here and there.
It should be understood that with this verse as well, the Blessed One spoke this meaning while exhorting him in the same manner as before:
“Dhaniya, having bound together a raft and crossed over the earth, you have come to this place; yet once again, your raft—”
"It must indeed be bound; yet the river must be crossed, and this place is not secure.
But by me, having unified the factors of the path within a single state of mind, a raft was bound with the bond of knowledge.

Because it has attained a state of single flavor through the fulfillment of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, and because they do not exceed one another, there is no further need for it to be bound."
And because it cannot be escaped by anyone among gods or humans, it is well-composed. By means of that [path], I have crossed over; I have reached the shore that was previously desired.
Furthermore, in going, I have not gone to some particular place like those who have attained the stage of stream-entry and so forth.
Rather, having gone to the further shore, I have reached the destruction of all taints, the further shore of all phenomena, the supreme security, Nibbāna.
"Gone" means having attained omniscience; "crossed over" means having attained Arahantship.

If one asks, "Having dispelled what has he gone to the further shore?"—it is by dispelling the flood, having crossed over and transcended the fourfold flood beginning with the flood of sensual desire, that he has gone to the further shore.
Furthermore, since for me there is no longer anything further to be crossed, there is no need for a raft; therefore, it is appropriate for me alone [to discard it].
He said, "Then if you desire it, O Deva, rain down.
Having heard that as well, Dhaniya spoke this verse, "Gopī is obedient to me," in the same manner as before.
In that context, "Gopī" refers to his wife. "Obedient" means she carries out his words and is compliant. "Not fickle" refers to a woman.

For she is fickle due to five kinds of fickleness: fickleness regarding food, fickleness regarding ornaments, fickleness regarding other men, fickleness regarding wealth, and fickleness regarding foot-fetters.

Thus, through fickleness regarding food—consisting of various kinds such as rice, cakes, and liquor—a woman consumes even the food of a person living in probation (pārivāsika) and eats even what is meant for warming the hands; and she does so even without providing double the amount of wealth.
He drinks liquor. Out of a craving for ornaments, when unable to obtain another ornament, he even smears his hair with a drop of water or oil and rubs it over his face.

Out of a craving for other men, even when called by her own son to such a place, she first thinks of unrighteous conduct. Out of a craving for wealth, [thinking] "Having captured the king of swans..."
“Do not let your gold go to ruin. By being fickle-footed—that is, having the habit of wandering about to monasteries and other such places—one destroys all one’s wealth.
In this context, Dhaniya said, “I am not fickle,” demonstrating that even a single instance of fickleness does not exist in his cowherd wife.
“One who has lived together for a long time” means she who has dwelt with him for a long duration, having grown up together from her childhood.
By this, he shows that she does not know other men. "Pleasing" means he shows that, not knowing other men in this way, she clings only to my mind.
"I hear nothing evil of her" means he shows that he hears nothing of her such as, "She laughed or conversed with someone named so-and-so," nor does he hear any fault of infidelity.

23. Then the Blessed One, being pleased with Dhaniya because of these qualities, spoke this verse—“My mind is obedient”—in the same manner as before, both in meaning and in phrasing. Therein, the words are clear in their literal sense.
However, this is the underlying intention: Dhaniya, you are pleased thinking, “Gopī is obedient to me,” but she...
They may be obedient or they may not; the minds of others are difficult to know, especially those of women.
For even while carrying a woman in their womb, men are unable to guard her;
because her mind is so difficult to restrain, it is impossible for people like you to know whether a woman is free from lust, or suitable for cohabitation, or pleasing, or free from evil. As for me—
But my mind is obedient, responsive to instruction, and functions under my control; I do not function under its control.
This state of obedience of his became manifest to all people during the Twin Miracle, when streams of fire and streams of water were issuing from the six colors.
For when creating fire, one must attain the fire-kasiṇa absorption.
In the creation of water, there is the water-kasiṇa; in the creation of blue and so forth, there are the blue and other kasiṇas. For even in the Buddhas, two thoughts do not arise simultaneously;
yet, by virtue of his single-minded nature, he possessed such mastery. Furthermore, that [mind] was liberated through the departure from all bonds of defilement;
because it was liberated, it alone was free from craving, unlike yours, O Gopī. From the time of Buddha Dīpaṅkara...
And because she has been cultivated for a long time through generosity, virtue, and so forth, she is well-acquainted; she is not yours, O cowherd.

Furthermore, because she has been tamed by the unsurpassed taming, she is well-tamed; and because she is well-tamed, having abandoned the pursuit of the six sense-doors according to her own will, she is pleasing because she follows only the inclination of my own mind; she is not yours, O cowherd.
But by the words "no evil exists in me," the Blessed One demonstrates the absence of evil in his own mind, just as Dhaniya did regarding Gopikā.

And this absence of evil in him is not to be understood only at the time of his Perfect Enlightenment; it should be known that it existed even while he was living in the midst of the household life for twenty-nine years, during which time he still possessed lust and other defilements. For even then, in accordance with his status as a householder—
Neither bodily misconduct, nor verbal misconduct, nor mental misconduct— things censured by the wise— had ever arisen in him before. After that,
Māra followed the Tathāgata for seven years— six years while he had not yet attained full enlightenment and one year after he had attained it—
thinking, "Perhaps I might find even something as small as the tip of a hair's worth of evil conduct in him."
“...might I see him. But not seeing him, he became disillusioned and uttered this verse:
“For seven years I followed the Blessed One, step by step;
yet I could find no opening in the mindful Sambuddha.”
Even during the time of the Buddha, the young man Uttara followed him for seven months, desiring to observe his conduct.
Seeing no fault whatsoever, he concluded, "The Blessed One is pure in his conduct.
For there are four things that a Tathāgata need not guard against. As it has been said:
“Monks, there are these four things that the Tathāgata need not guard against. What are the four? Monks, the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct is utterly pure;
there is no misconduct of body by the Tathāgata that he would need to guard against, thinking, ‘Lest another should find out about this of mine.
His verbal conduct is utterly pure… [as before] …His mental conduct is utterly pure… [as before] …”
“Monks, the Tathāgata’s livelihood is completely pure; there is no wrong livelihood in the Tathāgata that he would need to guard against, thinking, ‘Lest others should find this out about me.
Thus, because there was no evil in the mind of the Tathāgata not only at the time of his Perfect Enlightenment, but even before.”
Therefore, he said: "But no evil exists in me. The intention behind this was: "It is not possible for you to hear evil from my mind alone, nor from you, Gopikā.
Therefore, if one who is pleased by these virtues should say, 'Then rain, O God, if you so desire,' it is I who should say this."

24. Having heard that as well, Dhaniya, desiring to drink even more of the elixir of well-spoken words and demonstrating his own status as a free man, said: "I am supported by my own wages. In this context, "supported by my own wages" means supported solely by food and clothing belonging to myself;
I live by performing work for myself, not by taking wages from another to perform work for another.
He shows that he says, "I do. "Sons" refers to both daughters and sons; all of them are spoken of collectively as "sons.
"Together" means staying close by, not having departed. "Healthy" means free from affliction; he shows that they all possess strength in their thighs and arms.
"I hear nothing evil of them" means that I hear no evil concerning them, such as being thieves, adulterers, or immoral.
25. When this had been said, the Blessed One, exhorting Dhaniya in the same manner as before, spoke this verse:
“I am not a hireling. Here too, the words have their meaning plain on the surface. But the underlying intention is this: you are satisfied thinking, “I am a free man”;
yet in the ultimate sense, even though you live by performing your own work, you are indeed a slave because you are a slave to craving.
And you are not released from the doctrine of being a hireling. For it has been said: "The world is deficient, unsatisfied, a slave to craving.
But in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), I am not a hireling of anyone. Indeed, I am not a hireling of another or of myself. Why?

Because I move through the entire world by means of what has been accomplished [by my own effort]. For from the foot of Dīpaṅkara until the seat of enlightenment (*bodhi*), I have lived by my own exertion.
Until now, I have been a hireling for the sake of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). But having attained omniscience, I am like a royal servant who has received his wages;
I am free from debt and free from obligation. By means of that very attainment of omniscience which I have received, and by the supramundane bliss of concentration (*lokuttarasamādhi*), I live.
Since there is now no further task to be done for me, nor any further practice to be undertaken, for those who have not yet abandoned rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)—
No purpose whatsoever can be achieved by wages for those such as these; the reading "bhaṭiyā" (by wages) also exists.
Therefore, if one who is content with freedom from servitude should say, "Then rain, O God, if you so desire," it is I who should be told this. 26.
Having heard even that, Dhaniya, still unsatisfied by the nectar of the well-spoken words, [described] his own possession of a complete herd of cattle of five kinds.
Explaining this, he said: "There is fat. In that context, *vasā* refers to cows whose calves have been weaned and are grown.
*Dhenupā* refers to young calves who are still drinking from their mothers, or cows that are currently giving milk. *Godharaṇī* refers to pregnant cows.
*Paveṇī* refers to mature cows who, having reached sexual maturity, desire union with bulls. *Usabho pi gavampatī* refers to the bull who is the lord of the herd, [protected] by the cowherds.
Having bathed him early in the morning, fed him, given him five-fingerfuls of rice, and tied a garland around his head, he is sent with the command:

"Come, dear son, lead the cattle to the pasture, guard them, and bring them back. Thus sent, he avoids improper pastures, leads the cattle to the right grazing grounds, and brings them back after protecting them from the dangers of lions, tigers, and other predators; such a bull is also called a lord of cattle (*gavampati*).
"Here in my herd of cattle there is [melted fat]," he showed.
When this was said, the Blessed One, thus exhorting Dhaniya, spoke this counter-stanza: "There is no fat.
Herein, this is the intended meaning: in our teaching, in the sense of being unspoiled and in the sense of being mature...

Or, the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) known as "cows" (*vasā*), or the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) known as "milch-cows" (*dhenupā*) in the sense of being the source for young calves— referring to them in the sense of flowing— or the volitions of wholesome, unwholesome,

and imperturbable formative activities (*abhisaṅkhāra-cetanā*) known as "oxen" (*godharaṇi*) in the sense of linking rebirth and maintaining the womb, or the lineage (*paveṇi*) in the sense of a desire for union.

There is neither volitional consciousness reckoned as "Gavampati" nor "Usabha," whether it be aspiration or craving, in the sense of predominance, in the sense of being a precursor, or in the sense of excellence.
Therefore, I am satisfied with this non-existence which constitutes total security from bonds;
you, however, are satisfied with existence which serves as the basis for sorrow and the like. Thus, for one who is satisfied with total security from bonds—
"It is only fitting for me to say: 'If you wish it so, O Deva, rain!

Having heard that as well, Dhaniya, desiring to attain an even more excellent and well-spoken utterance—the taste of the Deathless—spoke these words, "The stakes are driven in," showing the excellence of the tethering-stakes of his own herd of cattle.
In this context, "stakes" (*khilā*) refers to the posts used for tying cattle.
*Nikhātā* means those that have been driven into the ground after being struck; they are small or large, having been dug out and set in place.
*Asampavedhī* means motionless or unshakable. *Dāmā* refers to specific types of rope-bindings made with knotted loops for the purpose of tethering calves.
*Muñjamayā* means made of *muñja* grass. *Navā* means recently made. *Susaṇṭhānā* means well-formed, having a perfectly rounded shape.
"Na hi sakkhinti" means "they will not at all be able. "Dhenupāpi chettuṃ" means even to cut down the young calves.

When this had been said, the Blessed One, knowing that the time for Dhaniya’s faculties to reach maturity had arrived, spoke this verse illuminating the Four Noble Truths as an exhortation to him in the same manner as before:
"Like a bull, having broken through... In this context, "usabho" means...
The protector is the leader of the herd, the lord of the cattle, the bull. However, some say: "The *usabha* is the eldest of a hundred cows;
the *vasabha* is the eldest of a thousand; the *nisabha* is the eldest of a hundred thousand. Others say: "The *usabha* is the eldest in one village field;
the *vasabha* is the eldest in two; the *nisabha* is unopposed everywhere. All these are merely elaborations (*papañca*).
Moreover, whether one calls him *usabha*, *vasabha*, or *nisabha*, all these terms should be understood in the sense of being peerless.
As it is said: "Truly, the ascetic Gotama is a *nisabha*. The letter *ra* is used here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
"Bonds" refers to bonds of rope and the bonds of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Elephant" refers to a *hatthī*. "Putrid creeper" refers to the *gaḷocī* creeper. Just as...
For even a body with a golden complexion is a putrid body; likewise, a dog or a puppy, even if born on that very day, is called an "old jackal" (*jarasiṅgāla*).
In the same way, though it be quite fresh, the *gaḷocī* creeper is called a "putrid creeper" (*pūtilatā*) because of its lack of essence.
"Having split open" means having cut open. "The womb and the bed" refers to the "womb-bed. Therein, by the mention of the "womb," the womb-born mode of birth (*jalābujayoni*) is indicated.
By the mention of "lying down," the remainder [of the postures] are included; or rather, it should be understood that all of them are stated by way of the "lying in the womb.
The rest here is clear from the literal meaning of the words.
However, this is the underlying intention: "Dhaniya, you are satisfied with bondage, but I, on the other hand, am distressed by bondage."

Endowed with the power and vigor of a great bull, having severed the five fetters belonging to the higher realm (*pañcuddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) by means of the power and vigor of the fourth noble path;

and like an elephant [breaking] a rotten creeper, having shattered the bonds of the five fetters belonging to the lower realm (*pañcorambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) by means of the power and vigor of the three lower paths;

or alternatively, like a bull [breaking] its bonds, [he has severed] the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), and like an elephant [breaking] a rotten creeper, [he has destroyed] the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
Having cut them and having loosened them, I stand firm. Therefore, I shall not enter a womb again.
Thus liberated from all sufferings rooted in the suffering of birth, I shine while saying: "If you wish, O Deva, then rain!
Therefore, if you too wish to speak like me, cut those bonds. And here, the "bonds" are...
The truth of origination is [the cause]; lying in the womb is the truth of suffering; "one shall not approach" here refers to non-approach by way of the state without residue (anupādisesa);
and "having cut and having shattered" here refers to cutting and shattering by way of the state with residue (saupādisesa)—this is the truth of cessation;
and that by which one cuts and shatters is the truth of the path.
Having heard this verse which illuminates the Four Noble Truths, at the conclusion of the verse, four people— Dhaniya, his wife, and their two daughters—
were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Then Dhaniya, through the application of verified confidence (*aveccappasāda*),
with faith rooted and firmly established in the Tathāgata, beheld the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One with the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).
With his heart stirred by the nature of things (*dhammatā*), he thought: "I have severed my bonds, and for me there is no more lying in a womb.
From the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), who else but the Blessed One would roar such a lion’s roar?
"Has my Teacher come? Then the Blessed One appeared, variegated with a network of six-colored rays and tawny as if sprinkled with liquid gold.
As if releasing the radiance of his body, he was released at the residence of Dhaniya with the words, “Now look upon it as you please.

Then Dhaniya, seeing his residence illuminated on all sides by thousands of lamps burning like the sun and moon that had entered within, gave rise to the thought, “The Blessed One has arrived! And at that very moment, a cloud also...

It rained. Therefore, the compilers of the collection said: "Filling both the lowlands and the highlands. In this context, "lowland" (*ninna*) means a marshy place; "highland" (*thala*) means a raised mound.
Thus, having made even that which was uneven—both the high and the low—the great cloud rained down, filling it all;
what is meant is that it began to rain. "At that very moment" (*tāvadeva*) refers to the instant the Blessed One [emitted] the bodily radiance...
Dhaniya released the radiance of his mind consisting of faith, thinking, "The Teacher has come to me," and at that very moment it rained.
Some, however, describe that even the rising of the sun occurred at that same moment.
Thus, at that moment when Dhaniya’s arising of faith pervaded the Tathāgata’s radiance and the sun rose—
Having heard the sound of the raining god, Dhaniya, filled with joy and gladness, spoke this matter;
the two verses beginning with “Great indeed is our gain” are to be recited.
Therein, because Dhaniya, together with his wife and children, had seen the Dhamma-body through the penetration of the Blessed One’s Noble Path, [he spoke thus].
Having seen the form-body with the supramundane eye, he obtained the acquisition of faith with the mundane eye. Therefore he said:
"Truly, it is no small gain for us that we have seen the Blessed One. In this context, *vata* is a particle used in the sense of wonder;
*no* means "for us"; *anappakā* means "abundant. The rest is self-evident. "I go to him for refuge."
In this context, although his going for refuge was already accomplished through the penetration of the Path, he had merely reached it by way of a definitive decision;
now, however, he makes a formal surrender of himself through speech.

Or rather, having attained the state of surrender and the state of immovable refuge by means of the Path, he proceeds to go for refuge through prostration, making that manifest to others by means of speech.
The Blessed One is "possessed of eyes" (*cakkhumā*) by virtue of the five eyes: the physical eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, and the all-encompassing Buddha-eye.
Addressing him thus, he said: "We go to you for refuge, O possessor of eyes.
Furthermore, the words "Be our teacher, O Great Sage" are spoken in order to fulfill the act of going for refuge by way of entering into discipleship; [this applies to] both Gopī and myself.
"Obedient, let us lead the holy life under the Sugata"—this is by way of undertaking.
In this context, "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) is a designation for abstinence from sexual intercourse, the path, the ascetic’s duty, the teaching, and contentment with one's own wife.
For in such passages as "one who leads the holy life" (*brahmacārī*), it is abstinence from sexual intercourse that is called the holy life. Furthermore, this...
In such passages as, "O Pañcasikha, the holy life is for the sake of utter disenchantment," it refers to the Path (*magga*).
In such passages as, "Indeed, Sāriputta, I recall having practiced the holy life endowed with four factors," it refers to the Dhamma of the recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
In such passages as, "This holy life is successful and flourishing," it refers to the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
“We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us;
we lead the holy life with none other than them. Therefore, among us, the young do not die.

In such passages as these, “contentment with one’s own wife” (sadārasantosa) is intended. But here, what is intended is the holy life of the higher paths, preceded by the holy life of the ascetic’s duty (samaṇadhamma).

"Sugatassa" means "in the presence of the Sugata. For the Blessed One is called the "Sugata" because he has gone well (*sugata*) by not falling into either of the two extremes, because he is endowed with the excellent journeying upon the Noble Path, and because he has gone to the beautiful state known as Nibbāna.
And here, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity; therefore, the meaning is "in the presence of the Sugata."
“Carāmase” means “let us go. For that which elsewhere is called “carāmasi” (we go) is here expressed as “carāmase.
However, the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā say that “se” is a particle (*nipāta*). For that very reason, with reference to the sense of supplication (*āyācana*), they also propose the reading “carema se.
One may accept whichever of these is preferred.
Thus Dhaniya, under the pretext of practicing the holy life (*brahmacariya*), requested the Blessed One for ordination (*pabbajjā*).
Explaining the purpose of his ordination, he said: "May we become those who have gone beyond birth and death, and who bring an end to suffering.

"Beyond birth and death" refers to Nibbāna; may we go there by means of the path of Arhatship. "Of suffering" means of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*). "Bringers of an end" means...
"Causing non-existence. "We shall exist" means *bhavāma*; or alternatively, "O, may we come to be!

The phrase "we move about" (*carāmase*) should be understood in the same manner as explained previously. Even after saying this, it is said that both of them again paid homage to the Blessed One and requested ordination, saying, "May the Blessed One let us go forth."
33. Then Māra the Evil One, seeing that both of them had thus paid homage and were requesting the going-forth, thought:
“These two desire to transcend my domain; come now, I shall create an obstacle for them. Approaching, he spoke this verse, showing the virtues of the household life:
“The possessor of sons rejoices in his sons,” and so forth. Therein, “rejoices” (nandati) means he is satisfied and gladdened. “In his sons” (puttehi) means...

In the sense of "together with" (*sahayoga*) or in the sense of the "instrumental case" (*karaṇattha*), the instrumental form is used: "he rejoices together with his sons" means it is said that he rejoices by means of his sons acting as the instrument.
"One who has sons" (*puttimā*) refers to a person possessing sons. "Thus" (*iti*) means he spoke in this way.
"Māra" is a certain *dāmarika* son of the gods in the realm of those who exercise power (*vasavatti*). For he [desires] one who wishes to transcend the six states...
He kills whoever he is able to; even for one whom he cannot kill, he desires death. For this reason, he is called "Māra.
"Pāpimā" means either a base person or one of evil conduct. This is the word of the compilers of the collection, and such terms occur throughout all the verses.
And just as a father rejoices because of his sons, so too does a cowherd rejoice because of his cows. He who has cows...
The meaning is that he too rejoices in the same way as the cowherds, together with the cows, or by means of the cows acting as instruments.
Having said this, he now points out the reason that establishes that meaning: “For the acquisitions (upadhī) are a man’s delight.

In that context, “acquisitions” refers to the four acquisitions: the acquisition of sensual pleasures (kāmūpadhi), the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesūpadhi), and the acquisition of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārūpadhi).

For sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) are called "clinging" (*upadhī*) in the sense that "pleasure is clung-to here," because they serve as the basis for the pleasure described thus: "Whatever happiness and gladness arise dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification of sensual pleasures.

The aggregates (*khandhā*) are also [called clinging] because they serve as the basis for the suffering rooted in the aggregates, and the defilements (*kilesā*) are also [called clinging] because they serve as the basis for the suffering of the states of deprivation.

Because of their nature as foundations; for even volitional formations are foundations for the suffering of existence. However, here it is the "clinging to sense-pleasures" (*kāmūpadhi*) that is intended.
That is twofold by way of the clinging to beings and the clinging to formations. Among these, that which is bound up with beings is primary;
showing this, [the author] says, "By children, by cattle," and states the reason: "For clinging is a man's delight. Its meaning is: because...
These bases of attachment are a man’s delights; they delight a man by bringing him joy and gladness.
Therefore, it should be understood: “One who has sons delights in his sons; likewise, one who has cows delights in his cows. You have sons and you have cows;
therefore, Nanda, do not expect to go forth into homelessness because of these. For these are the attachments of one who has gone forth.”
“They do not exist; such being the case, even though you long for the end of suffering, you will remain suffering.
Now he points out the reason that establishes this meaning: “For he does not rejoice who is without acquisitions (nirupadhi).
Its meaning is as follows: because he for whom these acquisitions do not exist is separated from beloved kinsmen and is devoid of enjoyments and requisites.
“He does not rejoice; therefore, having abandoned these acquisitions (*upadhi*), you who have gone forth will surely remain in suffering.

Then the Blessed One, perceiving that “this Evil Māra has come for the purpose of creating an obstacle,” like one striking fruit with fruit, shattered Māra’s argument by means of the very simile brought forward by Māra, and having reversed that same verse:
Showing that "possessions are the basis of sorrow," he said: "One who has children sorrows because of his children. In this regard, the meaning of every word is quite plain.
However, this is the intended meaning: "O Evil One, do not speak thus: 'One who has children rejoices because of his children.
For separation and parting from all things dear and pleasing is inevitable; this is a law that cannot be transcended, and of those [dear ones]..."

Through the separation from beloved and pleasing children, wives, cattle, horses, mares, goats, gold, silver, and so forth, beings—whose hearts are pierced by the sharp arrow of excessive sorrow—become insane, distracted in mind, or even meet death; they experience suffering equal to death itself.
Therefore, grasp it thus: "The father of children grieves because of his children; and as the father of children [grieves], so do cowherds because of their cows."
"In that same way he grieves. For what reason? "For acquisitions are a man's grief. Because acquisitions are a man's grief, therefore it is said:

"He does not grieve who is without acquisitions. He who, through the abandoning of attachment to acquisitions, becomes one without acquisitions, is content with robes for the body and almsfood for the belly.
Wherever he goes, he goes having taken up [the burden]. Just as a winged bird... [he understands] "there is nothing further beyond this state.
Thus, through the total eradication of all sorrow, [it is said]: "For he does not grieve who is without substrate (nirupadhi).
In this way, the Blessed One concluded his teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. Or alternatively: "He who is without substrate, who is free from defilement..."
Therefore he does not grieve. For as long as defilements exist, all acquisitions (upadhaya) necessarily result in grief;
but with the abandonment of defilements, there is no grief. Thus, the Blessed One concluded his teaching by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the discourse, both Dhaniya and Gopī went forth into homelessness. The Blessed One returned to Jetavana through the air. Having gone forth, they...
They realized arhatship. And at their place of residence, cowherds built a monastery for them;
even today, it is known simply as the Gopālakavihāra.
From the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Dhaniya Sutta in the Suttanipāta-ṭīkā is finished.
3. Commentary on the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta:
"Toward all beings... This is the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta. What is its origin? The origin of all suttas is fourfold.
—by way of one’s own inclination, by way of another’s inclination, by way of an occasion, and by way of a question.
For the *Dvayatānupassanā* and others arise from one’s own inclination; the *Mettasutta* and others from another’s inclination; the *Uragasutta* and others from an occasion;
and the *Dhammikasutta* and others from a question. Among these, the *Khaggavisāṇasutta* arises specifically by way of a question.
Regarding their origin: specifically, because some verses here were spoken by a Paccekabuddha when questioned,
while others were uttered as mere inspired utterances (*udāna*) by one who had not been questioned but was expressing in accordance with the method of the path he himself had realized,
the origin of some verses is based on a question, while the origin of others is from his own personal inclination.
In this regard, the origin of this inquiry, which is formulated without distinction, should be understood from the very beginning as follows:

At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then, while the Venerable Ānanda was alone in seclusion, there arose in his mind this reflection: "The aspiration and the resolve of the Buddhas..."
"...and it is seen [in them]; likewise for the disciples, but it is not seen in the paccekabuddhas.
What if I were to approach the Blessed One and ask him about this? Emerging from seclusion, he approached the Blessed One and asked about this matter in due order.
Then the Blessed One spoke to him the Pubbayogāvacara Sutta.
“Ānanda, there are these five benefits for one who has practiced the preliminary training. Either he attains final knowledge in this very life;
or, if he does not attain final knowledge in this very life, then he attains it at the time of death;
or, if he does not attain it at the time of death, then as a son of the gods he attains it; or else, [he becomes] a follower of the Buddhas.”
“When they are present, one becomes quick in direct knowledge; then, in the final period, one becomes a paccekabuddha.
Having said this, he spoke again:

“Ānanda, those called paccekabuddhas are endowed with resolute intention and have practiced their former yoga. Therefore, the aspiration and the resolute intention of all—whether Buddhas, paccekabuddhas, or disciples—must be desired.”
He asked: "Venerable sir, how long does the aspiration of the Buddhas endure?
"Ānanda, for the Buddhas, at the minimum limit it is four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons; at the medium limit, eight incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons;
and at the maximum limit, sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons."
These distinctions are to be understood according to whether one is predominant in wisdom (*paññā*), faith (*saddhā*), or energy (*vīriya*).

For those predominant in wisdom, faith is dull and wisdom is sharp. For those predominant in faith, wisdom is middling and faith is strong. For those predominant in energy, both faith and wisdom are dull, while energy is strong.
However, without having reached four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) and a hundred thousand aeons (*kappa-satasahassa*), [the fruit of Buddhahood is not attained].

Even if one were to give day after day a gift equal to the giving of Vessantara, and were to accumulate all the qualities of the perfections (pāramitā) such as virtue (sīla) corresponding to that, it is impossible for one to become a Buddha in the interim. Why?
Because wisdom does not conceive an embryo, does not reach fullness, and does not attain maturity. It is just as, for example, [after] the passing of three, four, or five months...

Even if one were to play with it, sprinkle it with water, and tend to it a thousand times every day, it is impossible for a crop that is yet to ripen to reach completion within half a fortnight or a month before its appointed time. Why?
Because the crop does not take root, does not attain fullness, and does not reach maturity. In the same way, [the mind]...
"Without having reached four incalculable eons... it is impossible that this could happen.
Therefore, for the sake of ripening one's knowledge, the fulfillment of the perfections must be carried out over exactly the time period thus described.
Furthermore, for one who aspires to Buddhahood within even such a duration of time, eight accomplishments must be sought when making the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*). For this—
“Human birth, possession of the [appropriate] gender, the cause, meeting with a Teacher,
going forth, possession of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal—
through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.”
"Abhinīhāra" (the resolution) is a designation for the original aspiration (*mūlapaṇidhāna*). In this context, "human state" (*manussatta*) means the human birth.
For apart from the human birth, even for one established in the remaining births, including the divine birth, the aspiration does not succeed.
However, by one established here who aspires to Buddhahood, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving and so forth, [one must attain] precisely the human state.
It should be aspired for. Standing upon that, a resolution (*paṇidhi*) should be made; for in this way it succeeds. "Possession of the marks" (*liṅgasampatti*) means the male state.
For those of the female sex, the neuter sex, or those with both sexual organs—even if they stand within the human species—their resolution does not succeed.
However, one standing upon that [male state] who aspires to Buddhahood, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving and so forth, [should maintain] the male state itself.
It should be aspired for; standing upon that, a resolution (paṇidhi) should be made. For in this way it succeeds.

"The cause" refers to the excellence of the proximate support (upanissaya-sampatti) for Arahantship. For it succeeds for one who, striving in that very existence, is capable of reaching Arahantship, but not for another, just as in the case of the wise Sumedha.
He, indeed, having gone forth at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha...
By means of that very existence, he became capable of attaining *arahantship*. "Seeing the Teacher" means seeing the Buddhas face to face.
For it is accomplished in this way and not otherwise, as was the case with the wise Sumedha. He indeed made his aspiration after seeing Dīpaṅkara face to face.

"Going forth" (*pabbajjā*) refers to the state of homelessness. And that occurs either within the Dispensation (*sāsana*) or among the orders of ascetics and wanderers who profess the doctrine of karma and the efficacy of action.

Or it is permissible as was the case with the wise Sumedha. For that one named Sumedha, having been an ascetic, made his aspiration. "Endowment with qualities" means the attainment of qualities such as the jhānas.
For even for one who has gone forth, success comes only to one endowed with qualities, not to another—as was the case with the wise Sumedha.
He, having become a possessor of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and an attainer of the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), made his aspiration. "Service" (*adhikāra*)...
*Adhikāra* means "renunciation" (*pariccāga*). For one who has made a renunciation of life and so forth, the aspiration succeeds only for that very person, not for another;
as was the case with the wise Sumedha. For he [said]:
"Let the Buddha, together with his disciples, step over me and go;”
"Do not step on this mud; it will be for my benefit.
Thus, having renounced his life, he made this aspiration. *Chandatā* means the desire to act.
That succeeds for one in whom it is powerful. And if someone were to say: "Who [could endure] four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand [more]?"...

Having been cooked in hell for an eon, he still desires Buddhahood. Upon hearing this, it should be understood that the aspiration of whoever dares to say, “I [do],” is powerful. Likewise, if someone were to say:

“Who desires Buddhahood while treading across and traversing an entire world-system filled with glowing embers? Who [desires it] while [treading] an entire world-system filled with spears and spikes?”...
Having heard, "Who desires Buddhahood after treading upon and stepping over that which is crowded?
Who desires Buddhahood after crossing over the entire Cakkavāḷa filled to the brim with water?
Who desires Buddhahood after crushing and stepping over the entire Cakkavāḷa covered without interval by a thicket of bamboo?"—whoever was able to say, "I [can]," [stood forth].
It should be understood that his [desire] was powerful. And it was endowed with such a desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) that the wise Sumedha made this aspiration.
Thus, having successfully accomplished his resolve, the Bodhisatta does not fall into these eighteen impossible states.
For from that time forth, he was never born blind, nor born deaf, nor insane, nor mentally dull, nor mute.
One who is a cripple does not arise among the mlecchas, nor is he reborn from the womb of a slave-girl;
he is not one whose wrong view is fixed, his gender does not change, he does not commit the five deeds of immediate retribution, he is not a leper,
he is not one whose final existence has been spent as a bird in the animal realm, nor is he among the hungry ghosts who suffer from hunger, thirst, and parched craving.
He is reborn neither among the Kālakañjika Asuras, nor in the Avīci Hell, nor in the Lokantariya realms;
among the sense-sphere deities he does not become Māra; among the fine-material sphere deities he is not reborn in the non-percipient realm, nor in the Pure Abodes;
he is not reborn in the immaterial realms, nor does he migrate to another world-system.
And he is endowed with these four stages of Buddhahood: zeal, ingenuity, steadfastness, and conduct for the welfare of others.
Regarding these: "Zeal is said to be energy; ingenuity is called wisdom;
steadfastness is resolve; and conduct for the welfare of others is the cultivation of loving-kindness."

These should be understood. Furthermore, these six inclinations—which lead to the maturation of enlightenment—should be known: the inclination toward renunciation, the inclination toward seclusion, the inclination toward non-greed, the inclination toward non-hatred, the inclination toward non-delusion, and the inclination toward escape.
It is because they possess these that Bodhisattvas, having an inclination toward renunciation, perceive the faults in sensual pleasures; and having an inclination toward seclusion...
And it is said that Bodhisattvas, seeing the fault in socializing, have a disposition toward non-attachment; Bodhisattvas, seeing the fault in greed, have a disposition toward non-greed;
Bodhisattvas, seeing the fault in hatred, have a disposition toward non-hatred; Bodhisattvas, seeing the fault in delusion, have a disposition toward non-delusion;
and Bodhisattvas, having a disposition toward renunciation, see the fault in all states of existence.
And he is endowed with those [qualities].
But for how long must the aspiration of Paccekabuddhas last? For Paccekabuddhas, it lasts for two incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) and one hundred thousand aeons (*kappa*).
It is not possible for it to be less than that. The reason for this should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
Furthermore, for one who makes the formal resolution (*abhinīhāra*) while aspiring to the state of a Paccekabuddha over such a period of time, five perfections must be fulfilled.
For them, these are: human birth, the perfection of gender, freedom from taints, vision, and hearing.
“Qualification” and “zeal”—these are the causes for the formal resolution (*abhinīhāra*).
In this context, “seeing that which is free from taints” means the vision of anyone among the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Now, how long is the aspiration of the disciples? For the two chief disciples, it lasts for one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*).

For one hundred thousand eons, for eighty thousand eons for the great disciples, and likewise for the Buddha’s mother, father, attendant, and son—it is not possible [to reach such a state] beyond that. The reason for this is exactly as stated above.
Furthermore, since the application of all these individuals is characterized by zeal (*chanda*), their resolution (*abhinīhāra*) is endowed with two factors.

Thus, by means of this aspiration and this resolve, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) over the aforementioned period of time, Buddhas arise in the world in either a khattiya or a brahmin family;
Paccekabuddhas arise in one of the families of khattiyas, brahmins, or householders;
whereas the Chief Disciples (aggasāvakas) arise only in khattiya or brahmin families.
Like all Buddhas, they do not appear during a contracting aeon (*saṃvaṭṭamāne kappe*), but appear during an expanding aeon (*vivaṭṭamāne kappe*).

Private Buddhas (*paccekabuddhā*) appear only at the time when Buddhas appear, but before a Buddha has arisen. Buddhas awaken by themselves and awaken others; private Buddhas awaken by themselves but do not awaken others.
They penetrate only the [eighteen] attributes, but not the flavor of the Dhamma. For they are unable to teach the supramundane Dhamma by applying it to conceptual designations;
their realization of the Dhamma is like a dream seen by a mute person, or like the taste of seasoned sauce experienced in a city by a forest-dweller.
They attain every variety of psychic power, meditative attainment, and analytical knowledge.
Due to their distinction in qualities, they stand below the Buddhas and above the disciples. Having ordained others, they instruct them in the training of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika*).
They observe the Uposatha by means of this summary: "The extraction of the arrow of the mind must be performed;
one must not fall into complacency," or simply by the words, "Today is the Uposatha. And while observing the Uposatha at the foot of the Mañjūsaka tree on Mount Gandhamādana...

"Having assembled in the Jewel Chamber, they perform [the rites]. Thus the Blessed One, having explained to the Venerable Ānanda the aspirations and the formal resolves (*abhinīhāra*) of the Paccekabuddhas in all their aspects, now, in order to describe those various Paccekabuddhas who had arisen through such aspirations and such resolves, said: "Having laid down [all violence] toward all beings..."
By way of the method beginning with "The staff," he spoke this Khaggavisāṇasutta. This, first of all, is the origin of the Khaggavisāṇasutta as established by a general inquiry.
Now, it must be explained in detail. In that regard, the origin of this very verse should be understood as follows:
It is said that this Paccekabuddha, while entering the stage of a Paccekabodhisatta, fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons;
having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, he lived as a forest-dweller and practiced the ascetic life, fulfilling the duty of going forth and returning.
It is said that those who attain Paccekabodhi do so without failing to fulfill this duty.
There is no such thing. But what is this so-called "practice of going and returning"?
It is "taking and bringing back. We shall explain how that comes about.
Here, a certain bhikkhu takes [an object] but does not bring it back; another brings it back but does not take [one]; yet another...
One neither goes out nor returns; another both goes out and returns.

In this regard, a certain bhikkhu rises early in the morning, performs the duties for the shrine terrace and the Bodhi-tree terrace, pours water at the Bodhi-tree, fills the water-jar, and places it in the water-shed;
he then performs the duties toward his teacher and his preceptor, as well as the eighty-two minor duties.
Having undertaken and practicing the fourteen great precepts, he attends to his bodily needs, enters his lodging,
and spends as much time as possible on a secluded seat until it is time for the alms-round. Knowing the time has come, he puts on his lower robe,
fastens his waistband, arranges his upper robe, and slings his bowl over his shoulder.
Mindful of his meditation subject, having reached the courtyard of the shrine and paid homage to the shrine and the Bodhi tree,
he puts on his robe near the village, takes his bowl, and enters the village for alms. Having thus entered, if the monk is fortunate and meritorious,
he returns either to the family that supports him or to the rest-house, where he is honored and respected by the lay devotees.
Being asked various questions by lay followers, he abandons that attention through answering their questions and by diverting himself with Dhamma teachings;
even when he has returned to the monastery, being questioned by the monks, he speaks, recites the Dhamma,
and engages in various activities, both after the meal and during the first watch of the night.
If, having thus engaged in idle chatter with the bhikkhus even during the middle watch, he is overcome by bodily indisposition and sleeps during the last watch as well,
and does not attend to his meditation subject, this is called "carrying away" but not "bringing back.
However, one who is frequently afflicted by illness, whose food eaten at the time of dawn does not properly digest, and who especially fails to rise [early]—
Being unable to perform the duties as prescribed or to attend to the meditation subject,
he enters the village at the very early hour, taking his bowl and robes, longing for nothing other than rice gruel or medicine.
Having obtained there rice gruel, medicine, or a meal, and having finished his meal, he sits down on a prepared seat.
Having attended to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), whether he has attained distinction or not, he returns to the monastery and dwells with that very same mental attention.

This is called "he brings back but does not take away. And such monks as these—having drunk the rice-gruel, having begun insight (*vipassanā*), and having attained *arahantship* in the Buddha’s teaching—are beyond counting. Even in the Island of Ceylon alone, among them...
In those villages, there was no seat in the assembly hall where a bhikkhu had not attained Arahantship after drinking rice-gruel.

However, one who dwells in negligence, having cast aside his burden and broken all the observances, whose mind remains bound by the five kinds of mental obstructions and fetters, and who, failing to apply himself to the attention of the meditation subject,
enters a village for alms while entangled in the diversions of householders— [The text continues with the description of such a person's state.]
When one who has been distracted by mental proliferation emerges empty-handed, this is called "neither taking nor bringing back.

However, he who rises early, fulfills all the duties in the manner previously described, and until the time for the alms-round sits cross-legged and attends to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)—for the meditation subject is of two kinds: [the internal and the external].
The universal and the protective. The "universal" consists of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*).
It is called "universal" because it is desired everywhere. Loving-kindness is indeed desired everywhere—in one's dwelling place and so forth.
For a bhikkhu who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to his fellow celibates in their dwellings; through that, he lives in comfort, free from conflict.
He dwells thus: dwelling with loving-kindness toward the deities, he dwells happily, protected and guarded by the deities.
Dwelling with loving-kindness toward kings, royal ministers, and others, he dwells happily, cherished by them.

Dwelling with loving-kindness toward villages, market towns, and so forth, he dwells happily, honored and respected by people everywhere during his alms-round and other activities. Through the cultivation of mindfulness of death...
Having abandoned attachment to life, he dwells diligently. Furthermore,
that which must always be maintained— whether it be one of the ten foulness subjects, the kasiṇas, or the recollections, because they are undertaken in accordance with one's temperament,
or else the analysis of the four elements itself— must be maintained, guarded, and developed at all times.
And this is called the "retention" (pārihāriya) meditation subject; it is also known as the "root meditation subject.
In this regard, we shall demonstrate that first universal meditation subject by way of the analysis of the four elements, after which one attends to the retention meditation subject.
For he reviews the body, however it is positioned and however it is disposed, according to its elements—whatever there is in this body:
Among the twenty components, that which is hard and solid is the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*).
That which performs the function of cohesion and is fluid is the water element (*āpodhātu*). That which performs the function of maturation and is heat is the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
Furthermore, that which performs the function of distension and is air-like is the air element (*vāyodhātu*). Now, as for that which [is derived] from these four great elements...
That which is untouched, without fissure or opening, is the space element (ākāsadhātu). The consciousness that cognizes it is the consciousness element (viññāṇadhātu).
Beyond that, there is no other being or person; there is only this mere heap of formations (saṅkhāra) moving along.
Having thus attended to the meditation subject from its beginning, middle, and end, and having recognized the proper time, he rises from his seat.
Having dressed, he goes for alms in the village in the manner previously described.

And while going, unlike the blind worldlings who are deluded regarding the acts of approaching and so forth—thinking either, "The self approaches; an approach has been produced by the self," or "I am approaching;
an approach has been produced by me"—he is not thus deluded, [but rather] with the thought, "I am approaching."
When that consciousness arises, simultaneously with it, the mind-originated sustaining wind-element arises.
This [wind-element] expands this collection of bones, which is conventionally designated as the "body" and constitutes the arrangement of the earth-element and so forth.
Then, by means of the expansion of the wind-element resulting from mental activity, this collection of bones conventionally designated as the "body" moves forward.
As he thus advances, with each lifting of a foot, the fire element accompanied by the air element arises predominantly among the four elements, while the others are weak.

However, during the phases of shifting forward, shifting back, and drawing back, the air element accompanied by the fire element arises predominantly, while the others are weak. But in descending, the water element accompanied by the earth element [arises predominantly].
The one arises in excess, while the other is weak. In the cases of placing down and pressing together, the earth element accompanied by the water element arises in excess, while the other is weak.
Thus these elements, together with the respective consciousness that produces them, disintegrate right there where they arose.
In this regard, who is it that goes forward? Or for whom is there going forward?
Thus, in each of the various modes such as the lifting of one foot and so forth, there are the elements arisen in each mode,
as well as the remaining material phenomena inseparable from them, the consciousness that originates them, and the remaining immaterial phenomena associated with it—
these are the material and immaterial phenomena. Beyond this, they do not reach any other mode, such as shifting forward or shifting backward.
They break up right there and then; therefore they are impermanent. And what is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is non-self.
Thus he goes along attending to the meditation subject in all its aspects as complete.
For sons of good family who have gone forth in the Dispensation out of desire for the goal—whether ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty [years]—[should practice thus].
Seventy or even a hundred [monks] living together, having made a formal agreement (*katikavatta*), dwell thus:
"Friends, you have not gone forth out of debt, nor out of fear, nor because you were driven by a livelihood; rather, you have gone forth here desiring to be freed from suffering.
Therefore, subdue any defilement that arises while walking right there while walking; [subdue it] while standing, while sitting, and while lying down."
“Restrain yourselves right on the way! Having made this agreement, when they went out for alms, there were stones at intervals of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gāvuta, and one gāvuta;
mindful of that sign, they went along attending to their meditation subject.
If defilement arose in anyone while walking, he restrained it right then and there. If he was unable to do so, he stood still. Then, from behind him...
Even one who is coming along stands still. He, having reproached himself—thinking, "This bhikkhu knows the thought that has arisen in you;
this is not suitable for you"—and having increased his insight (*vipassanā*), enters the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*) right there.
If he is unable to do so, he sits down. Then even one who is coming behind him sits down; the same method applies. The plane of the Noble Ones.
Even if he is unable to fall asleep, he goes along suppressing that defilement and attending only to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
He does not lift his foot with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject.
If he should so lift it, he turns back and returns to the previous spot, just like the Elder Mahāphussadeva, the resident of the Ālindaka in the island of Ceylon.
It is said that for nineteen years he lived fulfilling his practice of going and returning;
and people along the road—while plowing, sowing, threshing, and performing their labors—saw the Elder traveling in such a manner and thought:
"This Elder goes back again and again; has he perhaps lost his way, or what is it?"

"Have you forgotten something? they conversed. But he, disregarding them, practiced the duties of a recluse with a mind intent solely on his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and within twenty years he attained *arahantship*.
On the day he attained *arahantship*, a deity dwelling at the end of his walking path stood there having lit a lamp with her fingers. The Four Great Kings and Sakka [also appeared].
Sakka, lord of the gods, and Brahmā Sahampati came to attend upon him.
Seeing that radiance, the forest-dwelling Mahātissa Thera asked on the following day, "Venerable sir, there was a radiance in your presence during the night; what was that radiance?
The elder, seeking to avoid the matter, replied, "Radiance can be the light of a lamp, or it can be the light of a gem."
He spoke these and other such words. Being pressed with the command, "You must conceal [this]," he admitted, "Yes," and confessed it—just like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa.

It is said that he, while fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning, resolved for seven years to remain solely in the standing and walking postures, thinking, "First, I shall honor the Blessed One’s Great Struggle."
After fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning for sixteen years, he attained Arahatship.
Thus, lifting his foot with a mind intent on the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), but when returning after having lifted it with a mind dissociated from that subject, he went near a village;
standing in a place where there might be suspicion—thinking, "Is it a cow or a renunciant?"—he put on his outer robe and took up his bowl.

Having taken it and reached the village gate, he takes water from a streamlet, makes a mouthful, and enters the village thinking, "May there be no distraction from my meditation subject even by the mere words 'Long-lived one, may you live long! addressed to people who have come to give alms or pay homage.
However, if someone asks, "Venerable sir, is today the seventh or the eighth [of the lunar fortnight]?"...
If they ask about the day, he swallows some water and reports it.

If there are no such inquiries, at the time of departure he goes out after spitting at the village gate, just like the fifty bhikkhus who entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery on the island of Sri Lanka. It is said that on the Uposatha day of their entry into the rains retreat...
They made a formal agreement: “Until we have attained arahantship, we shall not speak to one another.

When entering a village for alms, they would rinse their mouths with water at the village gate before entering; when questioned during the day, they would swallow the water and report [their success];
when not questioned, they would spit it out at the village gate and return to the monastery. There, people [pointed out] the place where they had spat.
Having seen them, they recognized, "Today one has come; today two. And they thought: "Why is it that these do not converse with us, or perhaps even with each other?
If they do not converse with each other either, they must certainly have fallen into a dispute;
well then, let us go and reconcile them with one another. Thinking thus, they all went to the monastery.
When fifty bhikkhus had entered the rains retreat there, two bhikkhus did not see each other in any one place.
Then, a man among them who possessed sight spoke thus: "Sirs, such is not the dwelling place of those who create strife;
the terrace of the shrine and the terrace of the Bodhi tree are well-swept, the brooms are well-placed, and [the water] is well-set out."

"Water for drinking and water for washing. They turned back right there. Those bhikkhus, having begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*) within that very month, attained *arahantship* and performed the invitation of purity (*visuddhi-pavāraṇā*) at the Great Invitation ceremony (*mahā-pavāraṇā*).
Thus, like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kāḷavalli bower, [the bhikkhus] who had entered the rains retreat at the Kalambatittha monastery...
And just as one who lifts his foot with a mind intent on his meditation subject reaches the vicinity of a village,
rinses his mouth, observes the streets, and enters that street where there are no drunken libertines, gamblers, or others who cause quarrels,
nor any fierce elephants, horses, or the like; and while walking there for alms, he does not act in a hurried or restless manner.
He does not go with speed; indeed, there is no such thing as the "alms-collecting ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of rapid movement.
Rather, having reached uneven ground, he proceeds only after coming to a standstill, like a cart filled with water.
Having entered from house to house and waited for the appropriate time—observing whether the people are willing or unwilling to give—he takes alms and, in a suitable place...
Having sat down in a secluded place and attending to his meditation subject, he establishes the perception of repulsiveness toward food;
reflecting on it by way of the similes of axle-oil, wound-ointment, and an infant’s flesh, he partakes of food endowed with the eight factors, neither for sport nor for intoxication...
[as in the Sutta] ...and having finished eating, performed his duties with water, and allowed the fatigue from the meal to subside for a moment, he proceeds as before regarding the meal.
In this way, after the meal, he attends to the meditation subject during both the first watch and the last watch of the night.
This is called "carrying away and bringing back. Thus, this process of carrying away and bringing back is called the "practice of going and returning.
While fulfilling this, if one is endowed with a strong supporting condition (*upanissaya*), one attains Arahatship even in the first stage of life. If not, [one attains it later].
If he does not attain it in the first stage of life, then he attains it in the middle stage of life. If he does not attain it in the middle stage of life, then he attains it at the time of death.
If he does not attain it at the time of death, then having become a son of the gods, he attains it.
If he does not attain it as a son of the gods, then having become a paccekabuddha, he attains final nibbāna. If he does not become a paccekabuddha...

Having offered it, he attains final Nibbāna; or else, in the presence of the Buddhas, he becomes one of swift direct knowledge—just like the Elder Bāhiya—or he becomes one of great wisdom—just like the Elder Sāriputta.
This Paccekabodhisatta, however, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, became a forest-dweller.
Having fulfilled this practice of going forth and returning for twenty thousand years, she passed away and was reborn in the world of the gods of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
Falling from there, she took conception in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī.
Skilled women can discern the state of the embryo on that very day, and she was one among them; therefore, she [the queen] knew of that establishment of the embryo.
She informed the king. It is the natural law that when a meritorious being has been conceived, the woman receives special care regarding her pregnancy.
Therefore, the king granted her such care.
From then on, she was permitted to consume nothing that was too hot, nor too cold, nor too sour, nor too salty, nor too pungent, nor too bitter.

For when the embryo is swallowed by a mother who is excessively hot, it is as if dwelling in an iron cauldron; when she is too cold, it is as if dwelling in the intermediate space between worlds (*lokantarika*).

When she eats what is extremely sour, salty, pungent, or bitter, the limbs of the one lying in the womb experience intense pain, as if they were being split with a knife and sprinkled with those very acids and so forth. This is also the case from excessive walking, standing, sitting, or reclining.
They do not prevent it [from moving], thinking, "May there be no pain from the movement of what is within the womb.
Because of being spread with soft coverings, he is permitted to perform walking meditation and other activities on the ground in moderation;
he receives food and drink that are sweet, wholesome, and endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and so forth. They have him walk, sit, and stand only after having carefully attended to him.

While being cared for in this manner, when her pregnancy had reached maturity, she entered the birth chamber and gave birth at dawn to a son who resembled a lump of red arsenic smeared with clarified butter, endowed with the marks of merit and grain.
Then, on the fifth day, they presented him, adorned and prepared, to the king; the king was delighted and had him attended by sixty-six nurses.
Thus, increasing in all perfections, he attained the age of discretion before long.
When he was just sixteen years old, the king anointed him in the kingship and provided him with various theatrical performances.
Having been anointed, the prince ruled over the kingdom under the name Brahmadatta across twenty thousand cities throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
For formerly there were eighty-four thousand cities; as they declined, they became sixty thousand, and from that point, declining further, they became forty thousand.
At the time of their total decline, however, there were twenty thousand.
And this Brahmadatta arose at the time of their total decline; therefore, he had twenty thousand cities and twenty thousand palaces.
There were twenty thousand elephants, twenty thousand horses, twenty thousand chariots, twenty thousand foot soldiers,
twenty thousand women— consorts and dancing girls— and twenty thousand ministers. While exercising his great sovereignty,
he performed the preliminary work for the *kasiṇas* and realized the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments.

Since one who has been anointed king must necessarily sit in the court of justice, he therefore ate his morning meal early one day and sat in the place of judgment. There, they made a loud noise and a great clamor.
Thinking, "This noise is an obstacle to meditative attainment," he ascended to the palace roof and thought, "I shall enter into meditative attainment."
While sitting, he was unable to attain [absorption]; due to his preoccupation with kingship, his meditative attainment was lost.

Then he thought, "Which is better: kingship or the duty of a recluse? Thereupon, realizing that "the pleasure of kingship is limited and fraught with many dangers, whereas the pleasure of the recluse's duty is vast, possesses many benefits, and is practiced by the supreme beings," he commanded a certain minister:
"Rule this kingdom with righteousness and justice; do not act unrighteously.
Having thus handed over everything, he ascended the palace and dwelt in the bliss of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*);
no one was permitted to approach him, except for those who brought water for rinsing the mouth, tooth-sticks, or food.
When half a month had passed, the chief queen asked, "The king is not to be seen anywhere—at the garden excursions, the military parades, or the theatrical performances;
where has he gone? They reported the matter to her. She sent a message to the minister:
"Since the kingdom is concealed, I too am concealed; let him come and enjoy union with me. He...
Covering both his ears, he rejected it, saying, "This is not to be heard. She sent for him two or three more times, and when he still refused, she threatened him:
"If you do not comply, I shall remove you from your position and even take your life!
Terrified, he thought, "Women are indeed firm in their resolve; perhaps she will actually do this," and one day [he met her] in private.
Having gone there, he enjoyed her company upon a splendid couch. She was meritorious and possessed a pleasant touch.
Infatuated by his passion for her touch, he went there frequently, feeling increasingly apprehensive.
Gradually, however, he began to enter without hesitation, as if he were the master of the house himself.
Then the king’s men reported that matter to the king. The king did not believe it. They reported it a second time and a third time.
Then, having seen him for himself while he was hiding, he had all his ministers assembled and informed them. They said, "This man is an offender against the king;
he deserves the severing of his hands, he deserves the severing of his feet," and so on, up to being impaled on a stake.
They then pointed out all the various punishments. The king said, "If I were to inflict execution, imprisonment, or flogging upon him, cruelty would arise within me;
if I were to deprive him of life, it would be the taking of life; if I were to seize his wealth, it would be theft.
Enough with such deeds! Expel him from my kingdom. The ministers then deprived him of his position. He, [his own...]
Taking his wealth and his wife and children, he went to another kingdom. There, the king, having heard of him, asked, "Why have you come?
He replied, "Your Majesty, I wish to attend upon you. The king accepted him.
After a few days had passed and he had gained the king's confidence, the minister said this to the king: "Great King, I see honey free from flies; while eating it..."
“There is not. The king did not hear him, thinking, “What is he saying, wishing to mock me?
Finding an opportunity, the man praised it even more highly and reported it again. The king asked, “What is this? “The kingdom of Bārāṇasī, Your Majesty,” he replied.
The king said, “You wish to take me there and kill me! He said, “Do not speak thus, Your Majesty; if you do not believe me, [then listen].”
“Send men,” he said. He sent men. Having gone there, they dug through the city gate and rose up in the king’s bedchamber.
When the king saw them, he asked, “Why have you come? “We are thieves, Great King.
The king had wealth given to them, and after admonishing them, saying, “Do not do such a thing again,” he dismissed them. They returned and reported this to their own king.
Having thus tested him two or three times in the same manner and concluded, "The king is virtuous," he arrayed his fourfold army and approached a certain city on the border.
There, he sent a message to the minister: "Give me either the city or battle.
He reported that matter to Brahmadatta: "May Your Majesty command: shall I fight, or shall I [give] the city?"
"Do not fight," the king sent word, "hand over the city and come here. He did accordingly.
