The rival king, having seized that city, dispatched a messenger in the same manner to the remaining cities as well.
Those ministers also reported this to Brahmadatta; being told by him, "Do not fight, you must come here," they returned to Benares.
Then the ministers said to Brahmadatta, “Great King, let us fight with him. The king forbade them, saying, “There will be the taking of life on my part.
The ministers said, “Great King, we shall seize him alive and bring him right here,” and having persuaded the king through various means, they began to go forth, saying, “Come, Great King!”
The king said, "If you do not commit the act of killing, wounding, or plundering the seventh [person], I shall depart.
The ministers replied, "No, Your Majesty; we shall not do it. We will frighten them and cause them to flee.
Having arrayed the fourfold army and placed lamps inside jars, they set out at night. On that day, the opposing king captured a city near Bārāṇasī.
Now, having caused him to remove his armor at night, he fell asleep heedlessly along with his army.
Then the ministers seized the King of Bārāṇasī, went to the enemy king’s camp, had all the lamps removed from every pot, and made a noise with an army of total darkness.
Seeing Mahābala, the enemy king’s minister was terrified and [said] to himself—
Having approached the king, he raised a great shout, saying, "Arise! Eat honey free from flies! A second time, and a third time, he did so.
The rival king, awakened by that sound, fell into fear and terror. Hundreds of shouts of exultation arose.
He thought, "Trusting the words of another, I have fallen into the hands of my enemy," and [remained] throughout the entire night... him.
Having lamented thus, on the second day he thought, "The king is righteous; he will not harbor resentment. I shall go and ask for his forgiveness.
Approaching the king, he knelt on both knees and said, "Forgive me, Great King, for my transgression.
The king, having exhorted him, said, "Rise; I forgive you. As soon as the king had spoken these words, he [rose].
He attained supreme consolation and obtained the kingdom in the very province near the King of Bārāṇasī. They became friends with one another.
Then Brahmadatta, seeing both armies standing together in harmony, thought:
"In the protection of my single mind, not even a drop of blood the size of a tiny fly’s mouthful has been shed among this body of people. Oh, how wonderful!"
"Ah, how wonderful! May all beings be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction.

Having thus generated the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*), taking that very state as his foundation, he contemplated conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), realized the knowledge of private enlightenment (*paccekabodhi-ñāṇa*), and attained self-becomehood (*sayambhutā*).
Seated upon the back of an elephant, he was made happy by the bliss of the path and the bliss of the fruit.

The ministers, having prostrated themselves, said: "It is time for the departure, Great King; honor should be paid to the victorious army, and provisions for food should be given to the defeated army.
He replied: "I am not a king, sirs; I am one called a Paccekabuddha. "What does Your Majesty say?
Paccekabuddhas do not look like this. "What then, sirs, is the appearance of a Paccekabuddha?"
"Paccekabuddhas have hair and beard two finger-breadths long and are endowed with eight requisites. He stroked his head with his right hand;

immediately the marks of a householder disappeared, the appearance of a renunciant manifested, and he became like an elder of a hundred years, with hair and beard two finger-breadths long and possessed of the eight requisites. Having attained the fourth jhāna, he...
Having ascended into the air from the back of the elephant, he sat upon a lotus flower. The ministers, having paid homage, asked:

"Venerable sir, what is your meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and how did you attain it? Since his meditation subject had been the jhāna of loving-kindness (*mettā*), and he had attained it by practicing insight (*vipassanā*) upon that, he spoke this verse of exultation (*udāna-gāthā*) to demonstrate that matter:
And he spoke this very verse as a prophetic utterance: “Having laid aside the rod toward all beings. Herein, “toward all” means without exception.
“Beings” means sentient creatures. This is the summary; we shall explain the detailed exposition in the commentary on the *Ratana Sutta*.
“Having laid aside” means having set down. “The rod” refers to the rod of body, speech, and mind.
This is a designation for bodily misconduct and the rest. For bodily misconduct is called a "rod" (*daṇḍa*) because it punishes;
that is to say, it afflicts and brings about misfortune and ruin. The same applies to verbal misconduct and mental misconduct.

Alternatively, "rod" refers specifically to a weapon or staff; thus it is also said, "having laid aside that [rod]. "Without harming" means not causing injury. "Even one or another" means whichever it may be.

"Even one": "of them" means of all those beings. "One should not desire a son": among these four types of sons—the son born of one's own loins (*atraja*), the son born of the field (*khetraja*), the adopted son (*dinnaka*), and the pupil (*antevāsika*)—one should not desire any kind of son at all.
"How much less a companion?": as for desiring a companion, how could that even be possible?
He is "one" (eka) by way of being designated as one who has gone forth; he is "one" in the sense of being without a second; he is "one" by the abandoning of craving;
he is "one" because his defilements have been entirely removed; and he is "one" because he has fully awakened to the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.

For even while dwelling in the midst of a thousand recluses, he is "one" because the fetters of a householder have been severed—thus he is "one" by way of being designated as one who has gone forth. He stands alone; he walks alone.
One sits alone, one lies down alone, one moves about and conducts oneself alone—in this way, one is "one" in the sense of being without a second.
"A person with craving as his companion wanders through the long course of saṃsāra;
from this state of existence to another state of existence, he does not transcend the cycle of rebirth."
“Having thus understood this danger—that craving is the origin of suffering—the bhikkhu, free from craving and without grasping, should wander mindfully.
Thus, in the sense of the abandoning of craving, he is one. All his defilements have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, and rendered incapable of further arising.
"Subject to non-arising in the future"—thus he is "one who has entirely departed from the defilements," which is one [meaning of *eko*].

Having become teacherless, being self-become (*sayambhū*), he has personally awakened to the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha—thus he is "one who has awakened to the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha," which is one [meaning of *eko*].
He "conducts himself" (*carati*) in these eight modes of conduct (*cariyā*), namely: for those endowed with aspiration, in the four postures (*iriyāpatha*).
The conduct of the four postures; the conduct regarding the sense bases for those who guard the doors of the senses within the internal sense bases;
the conduct of mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness for those dwelling in heedfulness; the conduct of concentration in the four jhānas for those devoted to higher consciousness;
the conduct of knowledge in the four noble truths for those endowed with wisdom; and [the conduct] in the four noble paths for those who have practiced rightly.
The conduct of the path; the conduct of those who have attained the fruits regarding the four fruits of recluseship;
the world-benefiting conduct toward all beings of the three Buddhas, and therein, that of the Paccekabuddhas and disciples in a limited sense. As it is said:
"Conduct means the eight types of conduct, beginning with the conduct of the postures," and so forth in detail. One endowed with these conducts...

The meaning is "it would be. Alternatively, it refers to the "conduct of the bases" (*āyatanacariyā*), as it is said: "One who resolves conducts by means of faith; one who exerts conducts by means of energy;
one who establishes conducts by means of mindfulness; one who is undistracted conducts by means of concentration;
one who understands conducts by means of wisdom; one who cognizes conducts by means of consciousness. For one practicing in this way, wholesome states increase. Thus [it is called conduct].
"Practices; thus practicing, one attains distinction—therefore, one 'practices the practice of distinction. In this way, eight other practices are mentioned.
The meaning is that one should be endowed with those as well. Regarding the phrase "like the horn of a rhinoceros":
here, "rhinoceros horn" refers to the horn of the *khagga* deer. For a detailed explanation of the meaning of the word *kappa*, see the commentary on the *Maṅgala Sutta*.

We shall explain it. Here, however, this [term] should be understood as a metaphorical counterpart (*paṭibhāga*), as in such passages as: "Indeed, sir, we were conversing with a disciple who was like the Teacher himself.
"Like a rhinoceros horn" (*khaggavisāṇakappa*) means "resembling a rhinoceros horn.
This, then, is the commentary on the meaning according to the words.
According to the underlying intention (*adhippāyānusandhi*), it should be understood as follows: When the aforementioned kind of punishment is being exercised toward living beings, it is harmful;
therefore, by not exercising it toward them, and by promoting the welfare of others through loving-kindness (*mettā*) which is its opposite, one lays down the rod toward all beings.
And because of that very laying down of the rod, [one is like those] beings who have not laid down the rod.
Beings harass one another with sticks, or with weapons, or with their hands, or with clods of earth; yet, not harassing them in such a way, [one practices] toward at least some of them.

Having relied upon this meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*), and having practiced insight (*vipassanā*) into whatever there is therein belonging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as other conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) following that very sequence, [one thinks]: "I have attained this private enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*)."
This, first of all, is the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
This, however, is the connection (*anusandhi*): when this had been said, those ministers asked, "Now, venerable sir, where are you going?
Then, having reflected upon and understood where the former Paccekabuddhas dwell—namely, on Mount Gandhamādana—he replied.
When this was said, they spoke again: "Venerable sir, now abandon us; you do not wish [to keep us]. Then the Paccekabuddha said:
"One should not desire a son," and so forth. The intended meaning there is:
"I would not now desire even any kind of son among my own offspring, much less a companion such as you. Therefore, even regarding you who are with me..."
Whether he wishes to go [to another realm] or to remain like me, he should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Or, when they said, "Venerable sir, please abandon us now; we do not wish [for you to stay]," that Paccekabuddha replied, "One should not desire a son;
how much less a companion? Having spoken thus, and seeing the virtue of solitary wandering in the sense already described, he was filled with joy.
Born of rapture and joy, he uttered this inspired utterance: “Let one wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Having said this, even as the great multitude was looking on, he rose into the air and went to Mount Gandhamādana.
On the Himālayas, there is the mountain named Gandhamādana, which lies between Cūḷakāḷapabbata, Mahākāḷapabbata, and Nāgapaliveṭhana.

Having passed beyond seven mountains—Candagabbha, Sūriyagabbha, Suvaṇṇapassa, and Himavanta-pabbata—there is a mountain recess named Nandamūlaka, which is a dwelling place for paccekabuddhas. There are also three caves:
the Suvaṇṇaguha, the Maṇiguha, and the Rajataguha. At the entrance of the Maṇiguha stands a tree named Mañjūsaka.
It was one *yojana* in height and one *yojana* in width.
Whatever flowers there were, whether in the water or on land, they all blossomed there, especially on the day a *paccekabuddha* arrived. Above it was a pavilion made of every kind of jewel.
There, a "sweeping wind" cast away the refuse, and a "leveling wind" spread sand composed of every kind of jewel.
It levels the ground; the sprinkling wind brings water from Lake Anotatta and scatters it;
the fragrance-making wind brings the scents of all the fragrant trees from the Himalayas; the gathering wind plucks flowers and lets them fall;
the spreading wind spreads them everywhere. Furthermore, seats are always prepared there.
On the day a Paccekabuddha appears and on Uposatha days, all the Paccekabuddhas assemble and sit together; this is the custom there.
When a Paccekabuddha who has attained enlightenment goes there, he sits upon the seat prepared for him.
Then, if other Paccekabuddhas are present at that time, they too assemble at that very moment.
They sit on the prepared seats. Having sat down, they enter some meditative attainment (samāpatti) and emerge from it.
Then, for the purpose of giving thanks to everyone, the senior monk of the Saṅgha asks the recently arrived Paccekabuddha about his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), saying, "How was it attained?
At that time too, he recites that same verse of his own inspired utterance (udāna). Again...
The Blessed One, being questioned by the Venerable Ānanda, spoke that very same verse; and Ānanda [recited it] at the Council.
Thus, each single verse was spoken four times: at the place where he attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, in the Mañjūsaka grove, when questioned by Ānanda, and at the Council.
The commentary on the first verse is completed. 36.

As for the origin of the verse beginning with *saṃsaggajāta*: This Paccekabodhisatta, while practicing the duties of a recluse according to the aforementioned method for twenty thousand years under the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, performed the preliminary work of the kasiṇas.
Having attained the first jhāna, having discerned name-and-form, and having performed the contemplation of characteristics, he was reborn in the Brahma-world before attaining the Noble Path.
Passing away from there, he was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī;
and as he grew up in the same manner as before, from the time he first distinguished the difference between "this is a woman" and "this is a man,"...
Having understood this, he does not delight in the hands of women; he cannot endure even the mere act of being anointed, bathed, or adorned.
Men alone nourish him; at the time of suckling, nurses put on bodices and give him milk in the guise of men.
Upon smelling the scent of women or hearing their voices, he cries; and even when he has reached the age of discretion, [he remains thus].
He did not wish to see women; therefore, they recognized him as "Anitthigandha" (One Whose Fragrance is Not for Women).

When he reached the age of sixteen, the king, thinking, "I shall establish his family lineage," brought suitable maidens from various clans for him and commanded a certain minister, "Amuse the prince. The minister, by means of a stratagem...
Desiring to delight him, he had a fence of mats constructed not far from him and employed theatrical performances.
Hearing the sound of singing and instrumental music, the prince asked, "Whose sound is this? The minister replied, "This, Your Majesty, is the sound of your dancing girls;
such performances belong to those possessed of merit. Rejoice, Your Majesty, for you are one of great merit."
He said: "The prince had the minister flogged with a rod and had him expelled. He reported this to the king.
The king went together with the prince’s mother, asked the prince for forgiveness, and reinstated the minister.
Being excessively oppressed by those [officials], the prince gave them high-quality gold and commanded the goldsmiths, "Make a beautiful female form. They [were instructed] by Vissakamma—
They fashioned a female form resembling a celestial nymph (*nimmita*), adorned with every ornament, and presented it to him.
Upon seeing it, the prince nodded his head in wonder and sent word to his parents, saying, "If I may obtain such a woman, I shall take her.
His parents thought, "Our son possesses great merit; surely some maiden who has likewise performed meritorious deeds must have appeared in the world together with him."
Having placed that golden image upon a chariot, they gave it to the ministers, saying, "Go, search for such a girl as this.

Taking it with them, they wandered through the sixteen great provinces; going from village to village, wherever they saw a gathering of people—at river fords and other such places—they would set up the golden image like a deity and [adorn it] with various flowers, garments, and ornaments.
Having performed the worship and erected a canopy, they stood to one side, thinking: "If anyone has previously seen such a thing, how will he produce it?
By this means, having wandered through all other provinces except for the Madda kingdom, and disregarding that place as being "the little kingdom," they turned back without first going there.
Then it occurred to them, "Let us go even as far as the Madda country, lest the king send us back again once we have entered Bārāṇasī.
They went to the city of Sāgala in the Madda country. In the city of Sāgala there was a king named Maddava.
He had a daughter sixteen years of age who was beautiful. Her maids of honor were at a bathing place for the purpose of fetching water for her bath.

She had gone there. Seeing that golden image set up by the ministers from afar, they said, "The princess has come in person after sending us to fetch water," and as they approached, they said, "This is not the mistress;
our mistress is more beautiful than this. When the ministers heard this, they approached the king and [reported] in a fitting manner...
They requested the girl according to the proper custom, and he gave her. Then they sent word to the King of Bārāṇasī: “The girl has been obtained;
will she come of her own accord, or shall we bring her ourselves? He replied, “If I were to come myself, there would be oppression of the countryside;
you yourselves should bring her,” and so he sent them.
The ministers took the girl, departed from the city, and sent her to the prince, reporting: "A girl resembling a golden image has been found.
Upon hearing this, the prince was overcome by passion and fell away from the first jhāna. He dispatched a succession of messengers, saying:
"Bring her quickly! Bring her quickly! They traveled day and night, staying for only one night at each stage, and reached Benares.
Having arrived and standing outside the city, they sent word to the king: "Should she enter today, or not?

The king said, "This girl has been brought from a family of great wealth; having performed the auspicious rites, we shall have her enter with great honor. For now, lead her to the pleasure garden. They did accordingly.
She, being exceedingly delicate, was distressed by the jolting of the carriage and by the exhaustion of the journey.
Afflicted by a sudden onset of wind-disease, he became like a withered garland of *māla* flowers and passed away that very night. The ministers lamented, "We have been deprived of our honors.
The king and the citizens lamented, "The lineage of the family has perished. A great clamor arose throughout the city.
As soon as the prince heard of it, great sorrow arose within him. Thereupon, the prince began to dig up the very root of that grief.
He thought: “This thing called sorrow does not belong to one who is unborn; rather, it belongs to one who is born. Therefore, sorrow is dependent upon birth.
Then, [asking] “But what is birth dependent upon? he reflected thoroughly by means of the power of prior meditation, thinking: “Birth is dependent upon existence.
Having thus seen dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, and contemplating the formations right there, he—

Seated there, he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. Seeing him seated, his faculties stilled and his mind at peace, made happy by the bliss of the path and its fruit, the ministers prostrated themselves and said: "Do not grieve, O King! Jambudīpa is vast;
we shall bring you another even more beautiful than this. He replied: "I am not one who grieves; I am a Paccekabuddha, free from sorrow."
"So it is. From this point onward, everything is exactly like the previous verses, with the exception of the commentary on the verses.
In that commentary on the verses, however, "born of association" (*saṃsaggajāta*) means one who has arisen through association.
Therein, association is fivefold by way of seeing, hearing, physical contact, conversing, and sharing enjoyments. Among these, having seen one another...

Lust arising by way of the visual consciousness process is called "contact through seeing. In this regard, there was a young bhikkhu, a Dīgha-bhāṇaka residing at Kalyāṇavihāra, who was wandering for alms in the village of Kāḷadīghavāpī on the island of Ceylon.
A daughter of a householder, having fallen in love with him upon seeing him, died after failing to obtain him by some means; her fragment of a lower garment—
Having seen [her], and thinking, "He did not obtain cohabitation with one who wears such garments," he broke his heart and passed away.
And that very youth is the illustration.

Furthermore, having heard of the excellence of form and so forth being described by others, or having heard the sounds of his own laughing, talking, singing, or music, by way of the cognitive process of auditory consciousness—

The arising of lust is what is called "association with hearing. In that regard, the dweller of the Five-Door Cave, who had gone to a lotus pond with five young women—the daughter of a blacksmith living in a mountain village—bathed, offered a garland, and was traveling through the air when he heard the sound of her singing loudly;
having been particularly diminished by sensual lust, he met with ruin and disaster.
The young man Tissadaha is an illustration.
Sexual contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) refers to the passion that arises from touching each other’s limbs;
the young bhikkhu Dhammagāyana is an illustration of this here. It is said that in the Mahāvihāra, a young bhikkhu was preaching the Dhamma. There, among the great multitude...
When he arrived, the king also went there together with his harem.

Then, upon perceiving the prince’s form and voice, a powerful passion arose in the king’s daughter, as it did in that youth as well. Seeing this, the king took notice and had them enclosed by a screen of coarse cloth.
They touched one another and embraced. Again, having removed the screen of coarse cloth, they looked at each other.
"I saw that both had indeed died.
However, lust arising during mutual conversation and discourse is called "contact through discourse.
Lust arising when engaging in shared enjoyment with monks and nuns is called "contact through shared enjoyment. In both of these cases, one incurs an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

The monk and the nun serve as the illustration. It is said that during the festival of the great monastery named Maricavaṭṭi, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya prepared a great almsgiving and served both Saṅghas.
There, when hot rice-gruel was being distributed, a young novice nun (saṅghanavaka-sāmaṇerī) gave a tooth-bracelet to a young novice monk (saṅghanavaka-sāmaṇera) who had no support.
They conversed with one another. Having both received full ordination and reached sixty years of age, they went to the opposite shore;
through their mutual conversation, they regained their former recognition, and immediately developing affection for each other, they transgressed the training rules and became *pārājika*.
Thus, among the five kinds of association, through any such association, affection arises for one who has become associated, due to the condition of prior lust.
Strong passion arises. From that, this suffering following upon affection comes into being;

following after that very affection, this suffering consisting of various kinds such as sorrow and lamentation—both in the present life and in future lives—comes into being, is produced, occurs, and is born.
Others, however, say: "The release and attachment of the mind toward an object [is craving]. From that...
“Affection, and from affection comes suffering.
Having spoken this half-verse, which thus analyzes the meaning, that Paccekabuddha said:
“Indeed, by digging up the root of that suffering which arises as a consequence of affection—sorrow and the rest—I have attained Paccekabodhi.”
When this was said, those ministers asked: "Venerable sir, what should we do now? Then he said:
"Whether it be you or others, whoever desires to be liberated from this suffering, let everyone, perceiving the peril born of affection, wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
And here, that which was stated as "this suffering arises from affection" (snehanvayaṃ) [is to be understood].
"It was with reference to this that it was said: 'Beholding the danger born of affection'—this is how it should be understood. Or alternatively:
through the aforementioned association, affection arises for one who has formed an association; from that affection, this suffering originates.
Beholding this danger born of affection as it truly is, I have attained [this state]. Having connected the text in this way...
The fourth line, although stated by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*) according to the method previously explained, should also be understood in that same way.
Beyond that, everything is exactly as stated in the preceding verse.
The commentary on the verses concerning association is completed.

37. What is the origin of the *Suhajja*? This Paccekabodhisatta, having arisen in the same manner as described in the preceding verse, while ruling the kingdom in Bārāṇasī, attained the first *jhāna*.

Having investigated whether the ascetic life (*samaṇadhamma*) was superior or the kingship was superior, he entrusted the kingdom into the hands of his four ministers and [devoted himself to] the ascetic life.
He acted [unjustly]. Although the ministers were told, "Act according to the Dhamma and with equity," they accepted bribes and acted contrary to the Dhamma.
Having accepted bribes, while defeating the owners [of the property], they once defeated a certain royal favorite.
He entered [the court] together with the king’s food-bearer and reported everything. On the following day, the king himself went to the place of judgment.
He arrived. Then the great multitude of people, crying out in a great clamor, "The ministers are acting as if they were masters over their master!", made it like a great battle.
Then the king, having risen from the seat of justice and ascended to his palace, sat down intending to enter meditative absorption;
however, his mind being distracted by that noise, he was unable to attain absorption. He thought, "What..."

“The dhamma of a recluse is better than sovereignty,” he said. Abandoning the pleasures of kingship, he again attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and, practicing insight (*vipassanā*) in the manner previously described, realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha. When asked about his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he spoke this verse:
“Out of compassion for friends and dear ones, one whose mind is bound to them neglects their true welfare.”
“Perceiving this danger in intimacy, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

In this context, they are *mittā* by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*). They are *suhajjā* by virtue of having kind hearts. For some are indeed only *mittā* because of their desire for absolute welfare, but not *suhajjā*;
while others are *suhajjā* by producing happiness in the heart through walking, coming, standing, sitting, conversation, and so forth.
There are those who are good friends but not friends; some are both good friends and friends. These are of two kinds:
householders and those who have gone forth. Among them, householders are of three types: the benefactor, the one who shares in pleasure and pain, and the compassionate one.
Those who have gone forth are specifically those who explain the Dhamma. They are endowed with four factors, as it is said:
“Householder’s son, a helpful and kind friend is to be recognized by four grounds: he protects one when one is negligent;
he protects one’s property when one is negligent; he is a refuge when one is afraid;
and when duties and obligations arise, he provides twice as much wealth.”
Likewise:
“Householder’s son, a friend who is easy to please should be known by four grounds as one who shares in both happiness and suffering:
he reveals his secrets to you, he guards your secrets, he does not abandon you in times of misfortune, and he would even sacrifice his own life for your sake.”
Likewise:

“Householder’s son, a compassionate friend who is well-wishing is to be known by four grounds: he does not rejoice in one’s misfortune, he rejoices in one’s prosperity, he restrains one from speaking dispraise, and he commends one when praise is being spoken.
Likewise—

“Householder’s son, a friend who speaks for one’s welfare and is well-disposed should be known by four grounds: he restrains one from evil, establishes one in what is wholesome, makes one hear what has not been heard, and points out the path to heaven.

Here, those intended are householders; however, in terms of their essential meaning, all [types of friends] are applicable. Those are the friends and well-wishers. “Feeling compassion” means feeling sympathy; it means desiring to bestow happiness upon them and desiring to remove their suffering.
"Destroys the welfare" (*atthaṃ hāpeti*) is threefold according to the welfare of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*);
likewise, it is also threefold according to one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both. One "destroys" or "ruins" the welfare in two ways:

by the loss of what has been gained and by the non-arising of what has not yet been gained. "With a mind bound" (*paṭibaddhacitto*) means: "I cannot live without this; this is my resort, this is my final refuge. Thus...

Even when placing oneself in a low position, one has a mind bound [to others]. Even when placing oneself in a high position—thinking, "These cannot live without me; I am their refuge, I am their resort"—one has a mind bound.
But here, it is this kind of mind that is intended. "This fear" means this fear of losing one's purpose.

This was said with reference to the loss of one’s own meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). "Familiarity" (*santhava*) is threefold—by way of familiarity through craving (*taṇhā*), familiarity through views (*diṭṭhi*), and familiarity through friendship (*mitta*).
Among these, craving, even in its eight hundred divisions, is familiarity through craving; views, even in their sixty-two divisions, are familiarity through views;
and the compassion felt for friends due to a state of mind bound to them is familiarity through friendship. It is this last kind that is intended here, for by means of it, his attainment [is lost].
[They] have fallen away. Therefore he said: "Perceiving this danger in intimacy, I have attained [this state]. It should be understood that the rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses concerning friends and relatives is complete.
38. Regarding the origin of the verse beginning "The bamboo is broad": it is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there were three paccekabodhisattvas.
Having gone forth and fulfilled the practice of coming and going for twenty thousand years, they were reborn in the world of the devas.
Passing away from there, the eldest of them was reborn in the royal family of Bārāṇasī, while the others were reborn in the families of frontier kings.
Both of them, having mastered a meditation subject and renounced their kingdoms to go forth, eventually became Paccekabuddhas.

While dwelling in the Nandamūlaka cave, one day, having emerged from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), they reflected and examined themselves, thinking, "What deed did we perform to attain this supramundane bliss?
As they reviewed their past, they saw their own conduct during the time of Kassapa Buddha. Then, reflecting on where the third brother was, they saw him ruling as king in Bārāṇasī.
Recalling his virtues, they thought, "He was naturally endowed with qualities such as fewness of wishes;
he was our very instructor, one who exhorted us, patient in speech, and a censurer of evil. Come now, let us show him an object and release him.
Seeking an opportunity, they saw him one day going to the park adorned with all his ornaments, and arriving through the air, they said:
They stood at the gate of the pleasure garden at the base of a bamboo thicket. The great multitude, insatiable in their desire to see the king, gazed upon him.
Then the king, looking about to see if there was anyone who was not occupied with beholding him, saw the Paccekabuddhas.
At the mere sight of them, affection for them arose within him.
So, descending from the back of the elephant, he approached them with peaceful decorum and asked, "Venerable sirs, what is your name?
They replied, "Great King, we are named 'The Unattached' (Asajjamānā). "Venerable sirs, what is the meaning of 'The Unattached'?
"It means 'not clinging,' Great King. Then, pointing to that bamboo thicket, they said: "Just as, for example..."
"Great King, suppose this bamboo thicket were standing there completely interwoven with roots, trunks, branches, and twigs;
even a man with a sword in his hand, having cut it at the root and pulling it, would not be able to uproot it.
In the same way, you are entangled within and without by a tangle, clinging to it and attached to it. Or rather, even if one were in the very middle of it..."
"Just as this bamboo shoot, because it has not yet produced joints, stands unattached to anything and can be pulled out by cutting it at either the top or the root,
even so we, being unattached anywhere, go in all directions. Having said this,
they immediately entered the fourth jhāna and, while the king was still watching, they departed through the air for the Nandamūlaka Cavern.
Then the king thought: "When indeed might I also become thus unattached?
Sitting right there and practicing insight (vipassanā), he realized Pratyekabuddhahood. When asked about his meditation subject in the same manner as before, he uttered this verse:
"Just as one who is clinging to a wide-spreading bamboo thicket, so too is the longing for children and wives."
“Like the tip of a bamboo shoot, unattached, one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
In this context, *vaṃsa* means bamboo; *visāla* means broad. The letter *ca* has the sense of emphasis, or it is the particle *eva*;
here, by the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), the letter *e* has been dropped. It is connected with the following word; we shall join them later.
"Yathāti" means "in the counterpart image. "Visatto" means clinging, entangled, and bound. "In children and wives" refers to sons, daughters, and spouses.
"Whatever longing" refers to whatever craving or affection there is. "Like a bamboo shoot, not adhering" means not sticking, like a bamboo shoot.
What is meant? Just as a bamboo is broad and yet remains unattached, so too is the longing for children and wives [unattached].
She too, because she stands having thus woven those strands together, is indeed "clinging" (*visattā*). And I, through that longing, am "clinging" like a wide bamboo stalk;

thus, seeing the danger in longing, and cutting off that longing with the knowledge of the Path, [I am free] from these—whether they be the bamboo-shoot-like objects such as form and so forth, or greed and so forth, or sense-desire existence and so forth, or views and so forth.
Or, by not clinging through craving, conceit, or views, he attained Paccekabodhi. The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before.
The commentary on the *Vaṃsakaḷīra-gāthā* is complete. 39.
Regarding the origin of the verse beginning "The deer in the forest": It is said that there was once a monk who was a practitioner of yoga under the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Having passed away, he was reborn in Benares into a wealthy merchant family of great riches and vast enjoyments;
he was handsome. Then, having become an adulterer, he died there and was reborn in hell.
After being cooked there, by the remainder of the karmic result, he took conception as a female in the womb of a merchant’s wife. The limbs of those who have come from hell are warm.
Thus it was. Because her womb was burning with that [fire], the merchant’s wife carried the fetus with great difficulty and hardship, and in due time she gave birth to a girl.
From the day of her birth, she was beloved by her parents, her other relatives, and her attendants.
And when she reached maturity and was given to a family, there too she remained beloved by her husband, her mother-in-law, and her father-in-law.
She became unpleasant and disagreeable to him. Then, when the festival was proclaimed, the merchant’s son, unwilling to sport with her, brought a courtesan and sported with her.
Having heard of this from the female slaves, she approached the merchant’s son, enticed him in various ways, and said:
"Noble sir, as for women, even if one were the youngest sister of ten kings or of a universal monarch..."
“Whether she is a daughter-in-law or a daughter, she nevertheless performs the bidding of her husband.
When her husband does not speak to her, she experiences suffering as if she were impaled on a stake. If I am worthy of favor, let me be favored;
if not, I shall be dismissed and go to my own family. The merchant’s son said, “Enough, lady; do not grieve. You are ready for pleasure.”

"Come, let us play at the festival," he said. At that mere conversation, the merchant’s daughter became inspired with zeal and prepared much food and drink, thinking, "Tomorrow we shall play at the festival.
On the second day, the merchant’s son went to the place of amusement without having informed her.
She, thinking, "He will send word now; he will send word now," kept watching the road.
Sitting there, she saw that it was past noon and sent for her people. They returned and reported, "The merchant’s son has gone.
She took all that had been prepared, mounted a carriage, and set out for the park.
Then, on the seventh day, the Paccekabuddha in the Nandamūlaka cave emerged from cessation (*nirodha*) at Lake Anotatta.
Having washed his face and chewed a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā*, he reflected, "Where shall I go for alms today?
Seeing that merchant’s daughter, he realized, "If she offers me hospitality, this karma will reach its exhaustion.
Standing upon a sixty-yojana expanse of *manosilā* near the mountain slope, he put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and set out.
Having entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), he traveled through the air and descended on the path leading back toward Bārāṇasī.

Seeing him, the slave girls informed the merchant’s daughter. She descended from her carriage, paid him respectful homage, took his bowl, filled it with food consisting of all the finest flavors, and [offered] a lotus flower.
Having covered [the bowl] and placed a lotus flower underneath it, she took the bouquet of flowers in her hand, approached the Paccekabuddha,
gave the bowl into his hands, and after paying homage, with the bouquet of flowers still in her hand, she made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, just as this flower is,
may I be dear to the great multitude wherever I am reborn."
“May I be pleasing,” he thought. Having thus made his first aspiration, he made a second: “Venerable sir, the dwelling in a womb is suffering;
may I not enter that, but instead attain rebirth upon a lotus flower. He made a third aspiration as well: “Venerable sir, women are loathsome;
even the daughter of a wheel-turning monarch falls under the power of another. Therefore, may I not be born in the female state.”
“May a man not fall back into existence. For the fourth time he made this aspiration:
“Venerable sir, having transcended this suffering of saṃsāra, may I reach at the end that deathless state which you have attained.
Having thus made these four aspirations and having honored that cluster of lotus flowers with a five-limbed prostration before the Paccekabuddha, [he departed].
Having paid homage, he made this fifth aspiration: “May my fragrance and my complexion be just like that of a flower.
Then the Paccekabuddha, taking the bowl and the bouquet of flowers, stood in the air and said:
“May what you have desired and prayed for be fulfilled quickly!”
"May all my aspirations be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day.

Having offered this verse of thanksgiving, he resolved, "Let the merchant’s daughter see me as I depart," and went to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave. Upon seeing him, great joy arose within the merchant’s daughter.
Unwholesome karma committed in a previous existence had been exhausted due to a lack of opportunity;
she was born pure, like a copper vessel washed with tamarind vinegar.

At that very moment, everyone in her husband’s family and her own kin was delighted and sent affectionate words and gifts, asking, "What shall we do? The merchant's son sent men, saying, "Bring her back quickly, very quickly!"

“I have come to the garden having forgotten the merchant’s daughter. From that time forth, he cherished her as if she were sandalwood paste smeared upon his chest, a pearl necklace fastened around him, or a garland of flowers, and he attended to her.
Having experienced there the pleasures of sovereignty and wealth for as long as her life lasted, she passed away and [was reborn] in the world of the gods in male form.
He was reborn within a lotus flower. That son of the gods, when walking, walked only within the interior of a lotus flower;
when standing, sitting, or lying down, he lay only within the interior of a lotus flower. They gave him the name Mahāpaduma-devaputta.
Thus, by means of that power of psychic potency (iddhi), he wandered through the six celestial worlds in forward and reverse order.
At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī had twenty thousand women. Yet, the king did not obtain a son from the womb of even one of them.
The ministers petitioned the king: "Your Majesty, a son who will uphold the family lineage must be desired;
for when a biological son (*atrāja*) is absent, even a son born of another’s field (*khetraja*) can sustain the family lineage. The king said, "Excepting the chief queen, all the rest..."
“Let the female dancers perform a religious drama for seven days,” he commanded, and had them sent out as they pleased;
yet even so, he did not obtain a son. Again the ministers said, “Great King, the chief queen is indeed the foremost of all women in merit and wisdom;
perhaps Your Majesty might obtain a son from the womb of the chief queen. The king—
She reported this matter to the chief queen. She said, "Great King, only a woman who speaks the truth and is virtuous may obtain a son;

how can one who lacks shame and fear of wrongdoing have a son? Having ascended the palace, she undertook the five precepts and repeatedly reflected upon them. As the virtuous princess was thus reflecting on the five precepts,
As soon as the thought of aspiring for a son arose, Sakka’s seat became heated.
Then Sakka, reflecting on the cause of his seat being heated and understanding the matter, thought, "I shall grant a noble son to the virtuous princess.
Coming through the air and standing before the queen, he asked, "What do you aspire for, O Queen?"
“Your son, Great King,” [he replied]. Having said, “I give you your son, O Queen; do not worry,” he went to the world of the gods.
There, reflecting, “Is there anyone here whose lifespan has been exhausted? he perceived that Mahāpaduma was about to pass away from this world to be reborn in the higher celestial realms.
He went to his mansion and said, “Dear Mahāpaduma, go to the human world.”
He entreated him. He replied, “Great King, do not speak thus; the world of humans is loathsome.
“Dear son, you were reborn here after performing merit in the human world; you must fulfill the perfections while remaining right there.
Go, dear son. “The dwelling in a womb is painful, Great King; I am unable to dwell there. “What use have you for dwelling in a womb, dear son?”
"For indeed, you have performed such deeds that you shall be reborn right within the heart of a lotus; go now, dear one.
Though addressed thus again and again, he consented.
Then Mahāpaduma, passing away from the world of the gods, was reborn within the heart of a lotus in a stone-slab pond in the royal park of the King of Bārāṇasī.

He was reborn. And on that very night, at the time of dawn, the chief queen dreamed that she went to a park surrounded by twenty thousand women, and having reached a lotus pond with stone slabs, she felt as if she had obtained a son.
When the night had turned to day, while guarding her moral precepts, she went there just as before and saw a single lotus flower. She [could not] even...
It was on the bank, not in deep water. At the mere sight of it, maternal affection for her son arose within her.
She entered by herself and took hold of that flower. As soon as the flower was grasped, its petals unfolded.
There she saw the boy, like a golden image cast upon a plate. Upon seeing him, she cried out, "I have found my son! and raised a shout.
He caused [the child] to be proclaimed. The great multitude released thousands of shouts of "Sādhu!", and the king sent word to him.
Having heard this, the king asked, "Where was he found? and upon hearing where he had been found, he said, "Both the garden and the lotus in the pond are our very own property;
therefore, because he was born in our field, this son shall be named Khetraja (Field-born). Having said this, he brought him into the city.
He had twenty thousand women perform the duties of nurses. Whichever woman, having ascertained the prince’s preference, fed him with whatever delicacy he desired, received a thousand pieces of money.
All of Benares was stirred up, and every person sent thousands of gifts for the prince. As the prince was being led here and there and told, "Eat this! Consume that!"...
Oppressed by food and becoming despondent, he went to the city gate and played with a ball of lac.
At that time, a certain Paccekabuddha was dwelling at Isipatana near Bārāṇasī.
Having risen early, he performed all his duties—such as the observance of the duties regarding his lodging and the preparation of his body—and emerged from seclusion.
Reflecting, "Where shall I take alms today? and seeing the prince’s prosperity, he wondered, "What deed did this man perform in the past?
Investigating further, he thought, "Having given alms-food to one such as me, he made four aspirations;
three of them have been fulfilled, but one still remains unfulfilled. By some means, I shall show him the object [of his aspiration]. Thus, in the course of his alms-round, he...
He went into the presence of the prince. When the prince saw him, he said, "Ascetic, do not come here;
for these people might say to you, 'Eat this, consume that! At that single word, the ascetic turned back from there and entered his own lodging.
The prince said to his attendants, "This ascetic turned back as soon as he was addressed by me."
“Is this ascetic angry with me? Then, although they told him, “Your Majesty, those who have gone forth are not given over to anger;
they subsist on whatever is given by another with a mind of faith,” he thought, “This ascetic is indeed angry with me;
I shall ask his forgiveness. Having informed his parents, he mounted the elephant and, with great royal splendor, [proceeded].
Having gone to Isipatana and seeing a herd of deer, he asked, "What are these called? "Sir, these are called deer," they replied.
"Are there any who look after them, saying, 'Eat this, consume that, taste this'?
"No, sir; they dwell wherever grass and water are easily obtained."
The prince took that as his object of reflection: "Since these [ascetics] dwell wherever they wish even without being guarded, when indeed shall I too live in such a way?
The Paccekabuddha, knowing of his arrival, swept the lodging and the walking-path, made them smooth, and walked up and down the path once or twice.
Having shown the footprints for entering, and having swept and smoothed the area for the midday rest and the leaf-hut,
he showed the footprints for entering but did not show the footprints for exiting, and then departed elsewhere. The prince went there,
and seeing that place swept and smoothed, thought, "I believe someone is dwelling here."
Hearing what his attendants said—"He is a Paccekabuddha"—he replied: "That ascetic was angry even at dawn;
now, seeing his own quarters invaded by elephants, horses, and the like, he will be even more enraged. You stay right here.
Having dismounted from the elephant's back, he entered the lodging all alone, into a place that had been well-swept according to the rules of protocol.
Having seen the footprints, he thought with a clear mind, "This ascetic was walking here; he did not contemplate trade or other such work, but surely he must have been contemplating his own welfare.

With this conviction, he ascended the walkway, cleared away all worldly thoughts, went and sat upon a stone slab, became one-pointed in mind, entered the leaf-hut, and practiced insight meditation (vipassanā).
Having attained the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhiñāṇa), when his former priest questioned him about the subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) in the same manner as before,
he sat in the sky and spoke this verse:
"Just as a deer, unbound in the forest, goes wherever it wishes for its feeding ground;”
“A wise man, looking for safety, should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
Herein, “deer” refers to two kinds of deer: the *eṇi* deer and the *pasada* deer; moreover, it is a designation for all wild quadrupeds.
But here, the *pasada* deer is intended. “In the forest” means excluding both the village and its precincts.
The remainder is the forest (*arañña*); however, here a park (*uyyāna*) is intended, and therefore it is said "in a park.
"As he wishes" means in a reflected image (*paṭibhāga*). "Unbound" means unbound by ropes, ties, and so forth; by this, he illustrates his unrestrained movement.
"He goes wherever he desires for the sake of his range" means that in whichever direction he wishes to go, in that very direction he goes for the sake of his range.
He goes. And this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, just as a forest deer wandering in the forest thickets goes with confidence, stands with confidence, sits with confidence, and lies down with confidence—for what reason?"
“Monks, he has gone beyond the range of the hunter. In the same way, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as above] ...enters and dwells in the first jhāna. This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, rendered him trackless;
having struck down Māra’s eye, he has gone where the Evil One cannot see him. (The full passage follows.)
"A wise man" (*viññū naro*) means a learned person. "Freedom" (*seritaṃ*) refers to acting according to one's own will and not being dependent on others.
"Beholding" (*pekkhamāno*) means looking with the eye of wisdom. Alternatively, it refers to freedom from phenomena (*dhamma-serita*) and freedom from persons (*puggala-serita*).

For supramundane phenomena are "free" because they do not fall under the power of the defilements; and persons endowed with those [phenomena] are also free. The term "freedom" (*seritā*) is a designation for their state.
"Beholding that. What is meant? "Just as a deer in the forest, unbound, goes wherever it wishes for the sake of grazing—when indeed shall I too go thus?
Thus, while you stood surrounding me from here and there, I was bound and unable to go wherever I wished; because of that lack of freedom to go wherever I wished, [I thought:]...
Having seen the benefit in going wherever one desires, calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) gradually reached full perfection.
Thereafter, I attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha. Therefore, "another wise and learned man, looking for freedom from bondage, should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained.
The commentary on the Migarañña-gāthā is finished. 40.
As for the origin of the verse beginning "Āmantanā hoti": it is said that in the past there was a king named Ekavajjika-Brahmadatta, who was of a gentle disposition.
Whenever his ministers wished to deliberate with him on what was appropriate or inappropriate, at that time...

They led him away one by one to a private place. One day, when he had retired for his midday rest, a certain minister approached him and requested leave to go aside, saying, "Your Majesty, I have something to report. He rose and departed.
Again, while he was seated in the great assembly hall, one man requested a boon, another on the neck of an elephant, and another on the back of a horse.
One person requested him as he was going to the park seated in a golden chariot; the king descended from it and went aside.
Another requested him as he was traveling on a tour of the countryside; having heard his request as well, he dismounted from his elephant and went aside.
Thus, becoming disillusioned with them, he went forth into homelessness. The ministers [governed] by means of their authority.
They increased in number. One among them went and said to the king, "Great King, give me such-and-such a province. The king replied, "A certain person is already enjoying that.
Disregarding the king's words, he thought, "I shall go there myself, take that province, and enjoy it," and having gone there and started a quarrel, both of them [went] back to the king.

Having come into his presence, they reported each other's faults. The king, seeing the danger in their greed and thinking, "It is not possible to satisfy these men," realized Paccekabodhi through insight (vipassanā).
In the same manner as before, he uttered this verse of exultation (udānagāthā):

“There is conversation in the midst of companions—at rest, standing, walking, or on a journey—yet, beholding that which is uncraved and free from ownership, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Its meaning is as follows: for one standing in the midst of companions, whether at rest (during the daytime), or during the great attendance (of the community),...

In staying, in going—meaning the journey to the pleasure grove—and in wandering through the countryside, there is addressing one another in various ways such as, "Listen to this for me," or "Give this to me.

Therefore, having become disillusioned with that, [I seek] that which is practiced by the Noble Ones, which has many benefits and is exclusively blissful; even though it is so, [it is not attained] by those overcome by greed.
"Renunciation is not coveted nor longed for by any base men;

seeing that it is free from the influence of others because it is uncraved, and because it is a state of security through the nature of the Dhamma and of such persons, I applied myself to insight and gradually attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Āmantā verses is finished. 41.
As for the origin of the verse beginning "Play and delight": In Benares there was a king named Ekaputtaka-Brahmadatta.
He had an only son who was dear to him, pleasing, and as dear to him as his own life. In all his modes of conduct, he took his son with him.
This was the custom. One day, as he was going to the park, he left him behind and departed.
On that very same day, the prince died from an illness that had arisen. Fearing, "Out of affection for his son, the king’s heart might break," the ministers did not inform him and cremated him.
Intoxicated by liquor in the park, the king did not even remember his son; and so it was on the second day as well.
At the time of bathing and eating, he sat down after having finished his meal; then, remembering [his son], he said, "Bring my son.
They reported the matter to him according to the appropriate protocol. Then, overcome by grief, as he sat there, he reflected wisely:
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. Thus, in due course...
By contemplating dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in both forward and reverse order, he realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
The rest is exactly as stated in the verse on association (*saṃsaggagāthā*), with the exception of the commentary on the meaning of that verse.
In this commentary, however, "play" (*khiḍḍā*) means sporting. It is twofold: bodily and verbal. Therein—
"Bodily" means such things as playing with elephants, horses, chariots, bows, and javelins.
"Vocal" means such things as singing, reciting verses, and playing the mouth-drum. "Pleasure" refers to the pleasure of the five strands of sensual desire.
"Abundant" means pervading the entire physical existence down to the marrow by reaching it. The rest is self-evident.
Furthermore, the connection (*anusandhi*) here should be understood according to the same method stated for the verse on association; after that, [the word] "all.
The commentary on the verse on pleasure and delight is finished. 42.
As for "Cātuddisa," what is its origin? It is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there were five *paccekabodhisattas*.
Having gone forth and fulfilled the practice of going forth and returning for twenty thousand years, they were reborn in the world of the devas.
Passing away from there, the eldest of them became the king in Bārāṇasī, while the others became ordinary kings.
All four of them, having mastered a meditation subject, renounced their kingdoms, went forth, and eventually became paccekabuddhas.

While dwelling in the Nandamūlaka Cave, one day, having emerged from meditative attainment and reflected upon their own past deeds and those of their companion according to the method described in the *Vaṃsakaḷīra-gāthā*,
they understood the situation and sought an opportunity to show the king of Bārāṇasī the object [of his fear] through a stratagem.
That king was terrified three times during the night and, being afraid, let out a cry.
He ran about on the ground floor. Although the chaplain rose early and asked after his comfortable sleep, he replied, "Teacher, how could there be comfort for me?
and related the whole situation. The chaplain said, "This disease cannot be cured by any medicinal treatment such as upward purgatives; however, a means of food has occurred to me."
Having reflected, [the brahmin] thought, "Great King, this is a foretoken of the loss of your kingdom,
threats to your life, and other such calamities. Having thus greatly terrified the king, he incited him to perform a sacrifice for the sake of pacifying those misfortunes,
saying, "A sacrifice must be offered by giving as much dakṣiṇā as possible— so many elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, as well as silver and gold."
Then the Paccekabuddhas, seeing thousands of living beings being gathered for the sake of the sacrifice, thought:
"Once this deed is done, he will become difficult to convert; come now, let us go there beforehand and observe.
Arriving by the same method described in the *Vaṃsakaḷīra-gāthā*, they went in a procession through the royal courtyard while wandering for alms. The king was at the lion-window.
Standing there, he looked out over the royal courtyard and saw them; at the mere sight of them, affection arose within him.
Then, having summoned them and had them sit on seats prepared on the open terrace, he fed them with great care.
When they had finished their meal, he asked, "Who are you? "We are called the Cātuddisas, Great King. "Venerable sirs, as for this term 'Cātuddisa'..."
“What is the purpose? “Great King, we have no fear or mental terror from any quarter whatsoever in the four directions. “Venerable sir, for what reason does that fear not exist for you?
“Because, Great King, we cultivate loving-kindness, we cultivate compassion, we cultivate sympathetic joy, and we cultivate equanimity; therefore, that fear does not exist for us.”
Having said, "There is no [fear]," they rose from their seats and went to their own dwellings.
Then the king thought: "These recluses say that through the cultivation of loving-kindness and other such qualities there is no fear;
yet the brahmins praise the slaughter of many thousands of living beings. Whose word, then, is the truth? Thereupon, this thought occurred to him:
—“The recluses wash the impure with the pure, but the brahmins wash the impure with the impure.
It is not possible to wash the impure with the impure; the word of those who have gone forth alone is true.
Having thus developed the four divine abodes, beginning with loving-kindness, in the manner of “May all beings be happy,” etc., with a mind that radiates goodwill, he...
He commanded his ministers, “Release all living beings; let them drink cool water, eat green grass, and let a cool breeze blow upon them.
They did so. Then the king, thinking, “By the very word of my virtuous friends, I have been liberated from evil karma,” sat right there and attained insight (*vipassitvā*).

He realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha. When his ministers said at mealtime, "Eat, Great King, it is time," he replied, "I am not a king," and after saying everything according to the previous method, he uttered this verse of inspired utterance as a declaration:
"He is impartial toward the four quarters and free from resentment, content with whatever comes his way."
“Enduring hardships, fearless, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

In this context, *cātuddiso* means one who dwells at ease in the four directions; or, according to the method beginning with “he dwells pervading one direction,” it refers to one whose four directions are pervaded by the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). Among those [four directions]...
It is "unimpeded" (appaṭigha) because it is not struck by fear toward any beings or conditioned phenomena anywhere in the directions.
"Contented" means being satisfied by way of the twelve kinds of contentment; "with whatever [is available]" means with low or high requisites.
Regarding "enduring dangers and undaunted," here "dangers" (parissaya) are those which afflict the body and mind, or which cause their decline.
They are called *parissaya* because they either cause one to fall from prosperity or because one lies down (*sayati*) in dependence upon them;
this is a designation for external dangers such as lions and tigers, and internal afflictions of body and mind such as sensual desire.

One who "endures" (*sahati*) those dangers through patience characterized by forbearance and through qualities such as energy is "one who endures dangers" (*parissayānaṃ sahitā*). This is due to the absence of fear, which causes rigidity.

"Unafraid. What is meant by this? Just as those four ascetics were, so too, being content with various requisites and established in contentment here at the foundation of practice, he is "four-quarted" through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] toward the four directions, and "unrepelled" due to the absence of fear from resistance toward the seven conditioned formations. Because he is four-quarted, of the aforementioned kinds...
"Enduring hardships, being unassailable, and fearless"— having seen such qualities in the practice and having practiced accordingly,
I have attained Paccekabodhi. Alternatively, knowing that like those ascetics, by being content with whatever is available,
one becomes "four-faced" in the manner already described, and aspiring thus to this state of being four-faced, one practices with wise consideration.

"I have attained [this state]. Therefore, another who aspires to such a station should also wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, fearless, enduring the perils from all four quarters and remaining free from aversion. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the "Cātuddisa" verse is completed.
43. *Dussaṅgahā*: What is its origin? It is said that the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī passed away.
Then, when the days of mourning had elapsed, one day the ministers petitioned him, saying, "Sire, for kings it is necessary to have a chief queen for various affairs;
it would be well if Your Majesty were to bring another queen. The king replied, "In that case, my men, find out."
He said: "While they were searching, they learned that the king in a neighboring kingdom had died. His queen was ruling the kingdom, and she was pregnant.
The ministers, realizing that she was a suitable match for the king, requested her hand in marriage. She replied: 'A pregnant woman is generally unpleasant to people;
if you will wait until I have given birth, so be it. Otherwise, seek another.'"
He said: They reported this matter to the king as well. The king said, "Bring her even though she is pregnant. They brought her.
The king, having consecrated her, gave her all the wealth and status of a chief queen. He favored her retinue with various kinds of gifts.
In due time, she gave birth to a son. The king treated him in all his activities just like his own born son.
He dwelt there, holding [the prince] on his lap and against his chest. Then the queen’s attendants thought, “The king is excessively fond of the prince;
royal hearts are exceedingly trusting. Come now, let us cause a rift between them.
Thereupon they said to the prince, “Dear boy, you are the son of our king, not of this king. Do not place your trust in him here.”

They replied, “He has attained it. Then, although the prince was addressed by the king with the words, “Come, my son,” and though the king took him by the hand and pulled him toward him, he did not draw near to the king as he had done before.
The king, wondering, “What is this? and having understood the situation, thought, “Alas!
Even though they have been supported by me in this way, they still behave with such repugnance. Having become disillusioned, he abandoned his kingdom and went forth into homelessness.
When it was said, “The king has gone forth,” many of his ministers and attendants also went forth.
Thinking, “The king has gone forth together with his retinue,” people brought him excellent requisites. The king had these excellent requisites distributed according to seniority.
Among them, those who received fine things were satisfied, while others complained, “We [must do] the sweeping of the cells and so forth...”
“While performing all our duties, we receive only coarse food and worn-out robes.
Having learned of this as well, he thought, “Alas! Even while things are being given according to seniority, they still grumble; oh, how difficult it is to manage this assembly!
Taking his bowl and robe, he entered the forest alone, applied himself to insight (vipassanā), and realized Pratyekabuddhahood. In that regard—
And when asked for a meditation subject by those who had arrived, he spoke this verse:
“Some who have gone forth are difficult to support, as are householders living at home;
being unconcerned with the children of others, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”
This is evident in its meaning. However, the construction [of the verse] is as follows: “Some who have gone forth are difficult to restrain, being overcome by lack of contentment;
and likewise, those householders living in their homes are of the same nature.

It is out of loathing for this state of being difficult to restrain that I began insight meditation and attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
The commentary on the *Dussaṅgahagāthā* is completed. 44.
Regarding the phrase "having removed": what is its origin? It is said that in Benares, a king named Cātumāsika-Brahmadatta went to his pleasure garden during the first month of the summer.
There, upon a delightful stretch of ground, he saw a *koviḷāra* tree covered with thick, dark green foliage.
Having seen it, he said, "Prepare my couch at the foot of the *koviḷāra* tree," and after sporting in the park, he lay down there at eventide.
Again, in the middle month of summer, he went to the park; at that time the *koviḷāra* was in full bloom, and he acted exactly as before.
Again, in the last month of summer, he went; at that time the *koviḷāra* had its leaves fallen away.
It was like a withered tree. Even then, without having seen that tree, he ordered his bed to be prepared right there because of his prior familiarity with it.
Although the ministers knew [it was a withered tree], they spread out the bedding there out of fear, thinking, "It has been commanded by the king.
Having sported in the park, as he was lying down there in the evening time, he saw that tree and said, "Hey, this..."
Previously, with its leaves covered, it was beautiful to behold like one made of jewels.
Then, with flowers resembling coral sprouts placed among the branches that were the color of jewels, it became magnificent and lovely to look upon.
And its lower ground, strewn with sand like strands of pearls, was covered with loose flowers as if spread with a red woolen cloth.
It had become so that today it stands like a withered tree, with only its branches remaining. Thinking, "Alas!

The *koviḷāra* tree has been struck down by old age," he attained the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), reflecting: "If even that which is not clung to (*anupādinnam*) is thus destroyed by old age, how much more so that which is clung to (*upādinnam*)?
Following that very insight, he practiced insight (*vipassanā*) into all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) as suffering (*dukkha*) and as non-self (*anattā*).
“O, may I too become like a koviḷāra tree with its leaves fallen, having cast off the outward signs of a householder!
While thus aspiring, as he lay on his right side upon that very couch, he gradually realized pratyekabodhi.
Then, at the time of departure, when his ministers said, “It is time to go, Great King,” he replied, “I am no king,” and so forth.
In the same manner as before, he spoke this verse:
“Having cast off the marks of a householder, like a *koviḷāra* tree with its leaves stripped away;
having severed the bonds of household life, let the hero wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”

In this context, "having removed" means having taken away. "Householder's insignia" refers to hair and beard, clothing, ornaments, garlands, perfumes, ointments, women, sons, female slaves, male slaves, and so forth.
For these manifest the state of a householder; therefore, they are called "householder's insignia. "One whose bowl is broken" means one whose bowl has fallen [from the cycle of rebirth].
"Having cut off" means having severed by means of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*). "A hero" means one endowed with the heroism of the path. "Householder's bonds" refers to...
The fetters of sensual desire. For sensual desires are indeed the fetters of householders; this, first of all, is the literal meaning of the words.
This, however, is the underlying intention: "O, may I too, having cast off the insignia of a householder, become like a *koviḷāra* tree with its leaves completely stripped away.
While reflecting thus, I applied myself to insight and attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.
The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before.
The commentary on the *Koviḷāra* verses is completed. The first chapter is finished. 45–46.

As for the origin of the verse beginning "If one should obtain": it is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there were two individuals destined for solitary enlightenment (*paccekabodhisatta*).
Having gone forth and fulfilled the practice of going and returning for twenty thousand years, they were reborn in the world of the devas.
Passing away from there, the elder became the son of the king of Bārāṇasī, and the younger became the son of the royal chaplain.
Having conceived in the womb on the very same day and emerged from their mothers' wombs on the very same day, they became companions who played together in the dust.
They were [there]. The son of the family priest was wise. He said to the prince: "Friend, you will receive the kingdom upon your father’s passing;
I shall take the position of family priest. Since it is possible to govern a kingdom well when one is well-trained, come, let us learn our craft.
Thereafter, both of them, having accumulated merit in their past lives, [traveled] through villages, market towns, and so forth.
While wandering for alms, they went to a village in a border district. At that time, Paccekabuddhas were entering that village at the hour for alms-round.
Then, when the people saw the Paccekabuddhas, they became inspired;
they prepared seats, offered choice hard and soft food, honored them, and paid them homage. It occurred to them: "We are like them..."
"There is no such thing as a high-born family; yet these people give us alms if they wish, and do not give them if they do not wish.
But they show such honor to these renunciants—surely they must know some craft. Come, let us learn that craft from them."
When those men had withdrawn, they obtained an opportunity and requested, "Venerable sir, please teach us that craft which you know.
The Paccekabuddhas replied, "It is not possible to learn it without having gone forth into homelessness.
They then requested the going-forth and were ordained. Thereafter, the Paccekabuddhas instructed them: "You must dress yourselves in this manner..."

Having explained the rules of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika*) by way of such instructions as, "It should be worn thus," they assigned separate leaf-huts for them, saying, "The perfection of this craft consists in delighting in solitude;
therefore, one must sit alone, walk alone, stand alone, and lie down alone.
Thereupon, each entered his own leaf-hut and sat down.
From the moment the chaplain’s son sat down, he attained concentration of mind and achieved *jhāna*.
The prince, becoming restless after only a short while, came into his presence. Seeing him, the chaplain’s son asked, “What is it, friend?
He replied, “I am restless. “In that case, sit here,” he said. After sitting there for a moment, the prince spoke.
“Friend, it is said that the perfection of this craft consists in delighting in solitude,” said the chaplain’s son.
“Very well, friend; in that case, go back to your own seat. I shall master the perfection of this craft.
Having gone, he became weary again after only a moment and returned three times in the same manner as before.
Then the chaplain’s son, having dismissed him in that same manner, thought as he departed:
"This man is neglecting his own work, and he comes here to me so frequently. He left his leaf-hut and entered the forest.
The other remained sitting in his own leaf-hut, but after a mere moment, becoming weary once again, [he went] to his leaf-hut.

Having arrived and searched here and there, he did not see him and thought: "He who, in the time when I was a householder, could not even obtain a sight of me though he came bringing a gift—now that I have come, he has departed without wishing to grant me even a sight.
Oh, you wretched mind, are you not ashamed that you have brought me here four times? Now I shall no longer act under your control."

"Indeed, I shall bring him under my own control. Having entered his own lodging, he applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*), realized *paccekabodhi*, and traveled through the air to the Nandamūlaka cave.
The other also entered the forest, applied himself to insight meditation, realized *paccekabodhi*, and went to that very same place.
Both of them, having sat down upon the surface of the mindstone (*manosilātala*), each separately uttered these verses of inspired utterance (*udānagāthā*):
“If one should find a prudent companion, a wise man who lives righteously and walks with one,
then, having overcome all dangers, one may wander with him, joyful and mindful.

“If one does not find a prudent companion to walk with—one who is wise, steadfast, and lives a holy life—then like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom, one should wander alone like a mighty elephant in the forest.
In this context, *nipaka* means naturally clever, wise, and skilled in the preliminary exercises for the meditation subjects (*kasiṇa*) and so forth. *Sādhuvihārin* means...
It is endowed with either the state of absorption (*appanā*) or access (*upacāra*). "Steadfast" (*dhīra*) means possessed of steadfastness (*dhitisampanna*).

Therein, the perfection of steadfastness was stated by way of being prudent (*nipaka*); here, however, the meaning is simply "possessed of steadfastness. Steadfastness (*dhiti*) is the quality of unflagging exertion;

it is a designation for energy (*vīriya*) such as that which occurs in the thought, "Willingly, let skin and sinews [be torn away]. Furthermore, it is also that by which evil has been overcome (*dhikata-pāpa*).
“Steadfast. “Like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom”:
just as a rival king, realizing that a conquered kingdom brings no benefit, abandons his sovereignty and wanders alone, so too should one abandon companions who are foolish and wander alone.
Alternatively, “like a king [abandoning] a kingdom”: just as King Sutasoma abandoned his conquered kingdom and wandered alone, and as did Mahājanaka.
"Thus one should wander alone"—this is also its meaning. The remainder can be understood according to what has already been stated, and so it has not been elaborated upon.
The commentary on the verse regarding companions is finished. 47.
Regarding this verse, "Truly, I praise... [it refers to] the Pacceka Buddhas seated upon the thrones prepared in the expanse of the sky.
Regarding the sitting posture, the origin story is exactly the same as that of the Cātuddisa Gāthā. However, this is the distinction:
unlike that king who was terrified three times during the night, this king was not; nor was a sacrifice prepared for him.
Having had the Paccekabuddhas sit upon seats arranged on the surface of the sky, he asked, "Who are you? "We..."
“Great King, we are called those who eat blamelessly. “Venerable sir, what is the meaning of this term ‘those who eat blamelessly’?
“Great King, whether we receive something beautiful or unbeautiful, we eat it without making any facial expression.
Having heard this, the king thought to himself, “What if I were now to investigate whether they are indeed such or not? On that day, [he gave them] broken rice...
He served them with split pea porridge as a second course. The Paccekabuddhas ate without any change of expression, as if they were consuming the Deathless (amata).
