The king thought, "They may indeed remain without change of expression for one day because of their prior promise, but tomorrow I shall know," and so he invited them for the following day as well.
On the second day also, he acted in the same manner, and they likewise ate in that same way. Then the king—
Thinking, "Now, having given him Sundarī, I shall test him," he invited them once more;

for two days he provided great honors and served them with exquisite and most varied hard and soft foods. They too, eating in that same manner without any change of expression, pronounced auspicious blessings for the king and departed.
Not long after they had left, the king thought, "They are indeed eaters of blameless food..."
Thinking, "These are ascetics; oh, may I too become one who eats blameless food," he abandoned his great kingdom, undertook the going-forth, and began insight meditation.
Having become a Paccekabuddha, while clarifying his own meditative object in the midst of the Paccekabuddhas at the foot of the Mañjūsaka tree, he uttered this verse:
“Truly we praise the excellence of companions; companions who are equal and best should be cultivated.
Failing to find such, one who eats blameless food should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
This is plain in its literal sense. However, as for the phrase “excellence of companions,” here it refers to the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to those beyond training (*asekha*).
The perfection of companions should be understood as simply having accomplished companions. Here is the application of the meaning:
regarding this "perfection of companions" that has been mentioned, it is said that we certainly praise that perfection of companions; in one sense alone we extol it. How so?
Because companions who are excellent should be cultivated. Why? Because for one who cultivates those who are superior to oneself in virtue and the other [qualities], [there is great benefit].
The qualities beginning with virtue (sīla), when not yet arisen, come into being; once arisen, they reach growth, increase, and full maturity.
For one who associates with equals, through mutual support and the dispelling of remorse, these qualities—once attained—do not decline.
However, failing to find such excellent and equal companions, and having abandoned wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy (kuhana) and so forth, [one should practice] in accordance with the Dhamma...
Eating food obtained by fair means, and therein neither giving rise to aversion nor attachment, being one who eats blamelessly,
a clansman desiring his own welfare should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros. For it was by wandering in this very way that I too attained this success.
The commentary on the verse beginning with "Anavajjabhojī" is finished. 48.
As for the origin of the verse beginning with "Disvā suvaṇṇassa": A certain king of Bārāṇasī had gone to his daytime rest during the summer season.
Near him, a courtesan was grinding *gosīta* sandalwood. On one of her arms, there was a single golden bracelet.
On one arm there were two [bracelets], which struck against each other, while the other [arm] did not strike.
Seeing this, the king thought again and again, gazing at that maidservant: "In exactly this way, there is conflict in living in a group, but no conflict in living alone.
At that time, the queen, adorned with all her ornaments, was standing there fanning him. She [thought]: "This maidservant..."
Thinking, "I suspect the king’s heart is bound [to her]," she raised the slave girl and began to grind the grain herself.
On both of her arms were many golden bracelets, which, as they struck against one another, produced a great noise.
The king, becoming even more deeply disillusioned, remained lying on his right side and, applying insight (vipassanā), attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
He had realized the truth. As he lay there, made happy by that unsurpassed bliss, Queen Candanahatthā approached him and said, "I shall anoint you, Great King.
The king replied, "Go away; do not anoint me. She asked, "Why so, Great King?
He said, "I am no longer a king. Hearing this conversation between them, the ministers approached.
When addressed by them with the words "Great King," he said, "I am not a king, sirs. The rest is exactly as stated in the first verse.
This, however, is the commentary on the verse: *disvā* means having looked upon. *Suvaṇṇassa* means of gold (*kañcana*).
The word *valayāni* (bracelets) is to be supplied; for this reading is incomplete in meaning. *Pabhassarāni* means having the nature of shining, which is to say, they are radiant.
[The rest] is as stated. This, however, is the application [of the meaning]:

having seen the golden bracelets on his arm, and reflecting thus—"When living in a group there is contact, but when living alone there is no contact"—he undertook insight meditation and attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
The remainder is exactly according to the method already explained.
The commentary on the *Suvaṇṇavalaya-gāthā* is finished. 49.

As for the origin of the phrase "Thus by the second": a certain king of Bārāṇasī, while still young, desired to go forth into homelessness and commanded his ministers, "Take charge of the kingdom with the queen; I shall go forth. The ministers said, "No, Great King..."
"A kingdom without a king cannot be protected by us; neighboring kings will come and plunder it.
Wait until at least one son is born," they advised him. The king, being of gentle heart, consented. Then the queen conceived.
The king again commanded them: "The queen is pregnant; once a son is born, having consecrated him in the kingdom—"
“Renounce the kingdom; I shall go forth into homelessness. The ministers replied, “It is difficult to know, Great King, whether the queen will give birth to a son or a daughter;
please wait until the time of delivery has come. They thus persuaded him once more. Then she gave birth to a son.
Even then, the king commanded his ministers in the same manner. The ministers again addressed the king, saying, “Please wait...”
"O Great King, until he is capable," they said, persuading him with many reasons.
Then, when the prince had become capable, he summoned his ministers and, without giving them the opportunity to say, "This one is capable;

having consecrated him in the kingdom, proceed [with the coronation]," he had all the requisites, such as saffron robes and other items, brought from the marketplace and [placed] within the inner palace.
Having thus gone forth, he departed just like Mahājanaka. His entire retinue followed after the king, lamenting in various ways.
The king traveled as far as the boundary of his own kingdom, where he drew a line with a wooden staff and said, "This line must not be crossed.
The great multitude made the line their headrest and lay prostrate upon the ground, lamenting, "Now, dear father, yours..."
“The king’s command—what can it do? Thus he caused the prince to pass over the letter. The prince, crying out “Father! Father! ran and reached the king.
Upon seeing the prince, the king thought, “I have ruled the kingdom while protecting this great multitude;
why then should I not be able to protect this one child? Taking the prince with him, he entered the forest.
There, having seen a leaf-hut where previous paccekabuddhas had dwelt, he took up residence together with his son.
Then the prince, being unaccustomed to fine beds and such, would weep while lying on a spread of grass or a bed of ropes.
When struck by cold winds and the like, he would cry out, "It is cold, father! It is hot, father! Flies are biting me, father!"
“I am hungry, dear father; I am thirsty, dear father,” he would say. The king spent the night simply trying to console him.
By day, after wandering for alms, he would offer him food, which consisted of a mixed meal containing much *kaṅgu*, *varaka*, *mugga*, and other such grains.
Although the prince did not find it palatable, he ate it out of hunger, and in just a few days, [his body became like] a lotus placed in the heat.
[The others] ate with their mouths hanging down as if they were withered. But the Private Buddha, by the power of his reflective discernment, ate without any change of expression.
Then, seeking to persuade the prince, he said: "My dear son, excellent food is to be obtained in the city;
let us go there. The prince replied, "Yes, father. Thereupon, placing him in front, he turned back by the very same path they had come. The prince’s mother also—
The queen, thinking, "The king will not now take the prince and dwell long in the forest;
he will return in just a few days," had a fence constructed right where the king had marked the spot with his walking stick and took up residence there.
Then the king, standing not far from that fence, sent him off, saying, "My son, your mother is sitting here; go."
Until he reached that place, the prince stood watching, thinking, "May no one harm him.
The prince ran toward his mother. Seeing him, the guards informed the queen.
The queen, surrounded by twenty thousand female dancers, went out and received him, and asked for news of the king.
Then, hearing that [the prince] was coming from behind, he dispatched men. At that very moment, the king also returned to his own residence.
Not seeing the king, the men turned back. Thereupon, the queen, having become despondent, took her son, went to the city, and consecrated him in the kingdom.
The king, having reached his own residence and sitting there, attained insight (*vipassanā*).
Having realized private enlightenment, at the foot of the Mañjūsaka tree in the midst of the paccekabuddhas, he uttered this verse of inspired utterance: “Thus,
were there speech or even anger with a second person,
Foreseeing this danger in the future, One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”
This [passage] is plain in its literal sense (*padatthato*). However, the intended meaning (*adhippāyo*) here is as follows:

"If I do not renounce this verbal expression of mine—which arose through my dwelling together with this second prince who informs me of cold, heat, and so forth, and through my resentment born of affection for him—then in the future it will be just as it is now."
"Now, [if] there were such verbal exchange or provocation with this second person, both of these would be obstacles to the attainment of distinction.
Foreseeing this danger for the future, I abandoned that and practiced with wise attention, thereby attaining Pratyekabuddhahood.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verse beginning with "For sensual pleasures are variegated" is completed.
Regarding the origin of this verse: It is said that in Benares, the son of a merchant attained the position of a merchant while still a youth.
He possessed three palaces for the three seasons. There, with all his prosperity, he was like a young god.
He attended upon them like a servant. While still young, he requested his parents, saying, "I shall go forth into homelessness.
They tried to dissuade him. He persisted in the same way. Again, his parents tried to dissuade him in various ways, saying, "My dear son, you are delicate;
the life of renunciation is difficult, like walking upon the edge of a razor's blade. Yet he persisted in the same way.
They thought, “If he goes forth, we shall be grieved; if we prevent him, he will be grieved.
Rather, let us be grieved, but let him not be. Thus they gave their permission.
Then, disregarding his entire retinue who were lamenting, he went to Isipatana and approached the presence of the Paccekabuddhas.
He went forth. Since he did not obtain a magnificent dwelling, he spread out a mat upon a wooden bed and lay down.
Being accustomed to excellent couches, he suffered intensely throughout the entire night.
At dawn, having performed his bodily ablutions and taking his bowl and robe, he entered the town for alms together with the Paccekabuddhas. There, the elders [received] the seat of honor...
They received the first alms-food, while those who were junior received whatever seat and coarse food was available.

He became extremely distressed even by that coarse food. Within just a few days, having become emaciated and disfigured, he grew disillusioned because the practice of the ascetic life had not yet reached maturity.
Then, having sent a messenger to his parents, he left the order. After only a few days, he regained his strength.
Again he desired to go forth. Then, having gone forth in that very same manner, and having again left the order, and having gone forth for the third time,

practicing rightly and realizing private enlightenment (paccekabodhi), he uttered this verse of exultation (udānagāthā) and further recited this very verse of proclamation in the midst of the paccekabuddhas:
“Sensual pleasures are indeed variegated, sweet, and enchanting; they agitate the mind with their manifold forms.
Having seen the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In this context, “sensual pleasures” (*kāmā*) are twofold: sensual objects (*vatthukāmā*) and sensual defilements (*kilesakāmā*). Among these, sensual objects are agreeable forms and so forth.

Phenomena (*dhammā*) include all the various types of lust, such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth, which are defiled desires (*kilesakāma*). However, in this context, objective desires (*vatthukāma*) are intended.

They are "variegated" (*citrā*) by way of their many forms, such as visible forms (*rūpa*) and the rest. They are "sweet" (*madhurā*) by way of worldly gratification. They are "delightful to the mind" (*manoramā*) because they please the minds of foolish worldlings (*bālaputhujjana*).
The phrase "in manifold forms" (*virūparūpena*) means by way of diverse forms; that is, by way of various intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*), it is said.
They are indeed variegated by way of visible forms and so forth, and even within those visible forms and the rest, they possess diverse aspects by way of blue and so on.
Thus, by displaying gratification in such various and manifold ways, they agitate the mind and do not allow it to delight in the life of renunciation.
The remainder here is self-evident. The conclusion should also be understood by joining two or three phrases according to the method already stated in the preceding verses.
The commentary on the verses concerning sensual pleasures is finished.
51. As for the phrase "and calamities": what is their origin? It is said that in Benares, a boil arose on the king. Intense pains were occurring.
The physicians declared, "Without surgical treatment, there will be no relief. The king granted them immunity from punishment and [authorized] the surgical procedure.
He had them do so. Having split it open, they removed the pus and blood, made an incision, and bound the wound with a cloth.
They also gave him proper instructions regarding his diet and conduct. Due to eating coarse food, the king’s body became emaciated, and his abscess withered away.
Feeling at ease, he began to eat rich, succulent food. Consequently, his strength was restored, and he indulged in the pleasures of the realm.

His abscess returned once more to its original state. After having thus had the surgical treatment performed three times and being shunned by the physicians, he became disillusioned, renounced his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, entered the forest, and began the practice of insight (vipassanā).
Having realized the state of a Private Buddha (paccekabodhi) within seven years, he uttered this verse of exultation (udāna-gāthā) and went to the Nandamūlaka Cave.
“Famine, plague, and calamity, disease, the arrow, and fear—this is what they are.
Seeing this danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In this context, *eti* means famine; it is a designation for adventitious causes of misfortune that partake of the unwholesome.
Therefore, these strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are also a plague (*īti*) in the sense that they bring about manifold calamities and in the sense of being a severe affliction.

A boil (*gaṇḍa*) also oozes impurity; it becomes swollen, ripened, and burst open. Therefore, these [sensual pleasures] are a boil because they ooze the impurity of the defilements and because they exist in a state of being swollen, ripened, and burst open by way of arising, decay, and dissolution. It afflicts, thus it is an affliction (*upaddava*).
It overcomes by producing harm; the meaning is that it overwhelms. This is a designation for royal punishment and the like.

Therefore, even the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are a calamity, because they bring about the cause for not attaining the goal of Nibbāna and because they serve as the basis for all misfortunes.
Furthermore, since these [sensual pleasures] produce a state of illness through the defilements, or else, by giving rise to greed, they destroy the health known as virtue (*sīla*).
It robs one of health that is natural; therefore, in the sense of robbing one of health, it is "disease" (*roga*).

In the sense of having entered within, in the sense of being like a thorn within, and in the sense of being difficult to extract, it is a "dart" (*salla*). Because it brings fear pertaining to both the present life and the future life, it is "fear" (*bhaya*).
"Of me" is *me etaṃ*. The rest here is self-evident. The conclusion should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the Ītigāthā is completed. 52.
Regarding the verse beginning with "And cold": what is its origin? It is said that in Benares there was once a king named Sītālukabrahmadatta.
Having gone forth into the homeless life, he dwelt in a forest hut. In that place, it was cold when it was cold, and hot indeed when it was hot.
Because the area was open, it became [unpleasant]. In the village where he sought alms, he could not obtain enough food.
Even drinking water was difficult to find, and he was afflicted by wind, heat, gadflies, and reptiles. It occurred to him:
"At a distance of only half a *yojana* from here there is a well-provided region; there none of these dangers exist. What if I were to go there?"
"One who dwells in comfort is able to attain distinction. Then it occurred to him:
"Those who have gone forth are not slaves to their requisites; they bring such a mind under their control, rather than being controlled by the mind.
I will not go," and having reflected thus, he did not go. In this way, he reflected upon the arisen thought up to three times.
He turned back. Then, having stayed right there for seven years and practicing correctly, he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.
Having uttered this verse of exultation, he went to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave:
“Cold and heat, hunger and thirst, wind and sun, gadflies and snakes;”
"Having overcome all these, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In this context, "cold" (*sīta*) is twofold: that caused by internal disturbance of the elements and that caused by external disturbance of the elements;
likewise for "heat" (*uṇha*). "Gnats" (*ḍaṃsa*) refers to brown flies. "Crawling things" (*sarīsapā*) refers to any long-bodied creatures that move by crawling.
The remainder is self-evident. The conclusion should also be understood according to the method already stated.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Sītālukā* verses. 53.
What is the origin of the *Nāgova*? It is said that in Benares, a certain king, having ruled for twenty years, [passed away].
Having died and been cooked in hell for exactly twenty years, he was reborn in the Himalayan region in the womb of an elephant.
Once his trunk had grown, he became a magnificent leader of the herd, a great elephant whose entire body was the color of a lotus.
The female elephants ate the branches he had broken off, bending them down repeatedly; even when he plunged into the water, the female elephants smeared him with mud—everything.
It was just like the case of the elephant Pālileyyaka. Having become disillusioned with his herd, he departed.
Then the herd followed him by tracking his footprints. Thus, though he departed three times, they followed him each time.
Thereupon, he thought: "Now my grandson is ruling the kingdom in Bārāṇasī; what if I were to go to the pleasure garden from my previous birth? There—"
"He will protect me. Then, while the herd had fallen asleep during the night, he left one group and entered that very garden.
Seeing him, the park keeper informed the king. The king, thinking, "I shall capture the elephant," surrounded it with his army.
The elephant proceeded directly toward the king. Seeing that it was coming straight at him, the king fastened an arrow to his bow.
He stood there. Then the elephant, thinking, "He might even pierce me," spoke in human speech:
"Brahmadatta, do not pierce me; I am your grandfather. The king asked, "What are you saying? and questioned him about everything.
The elephant related the entire account of his conduct in the kingdom, in hell, and in his birth as an elephant. The king said, "Excellent! Do not fear; do not..."
And he commanded, "Do not frighten anyone," and he stationed elephant trainers, guards, and mahouts around the elephant.
Then one day, the king, mounted upon the elephant's back, thought: "This [being] ruled for twenty years and fell into hell;
by the remainder of the karmic result, he has been reborn in the animal realm. Even there, unable to endure the crowding and friction of living in a herd..."
Having arrived here, he thought, "Alas, living in a crowd is suffering; indeed, solitude alone is bliss.

Having reflected thus, he began insight meditation right there and realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha. When his ministers approached him while he was thus gladdened by supramundane happiness, they prostrated themselves and said, "It is time for the chariot, Great King.
Thereupon, saying, "I am not a king," he proceeded in the same manner as before.
He spoke this verse:
“Like a bull elephant who has left the herds behind, with his shoulders grown full and majestic,
dwelling in the forest as he pleases— let one wander alone like the single tusk of a rhinoceros.”
This is evident from the literal meaning itself. However, the intended application here is according to logical reasoning, not by way of mere hearsay.

Just as this elephant is called a "nāga" because it has been tamed (*danta*) regarding virtues dear to humans and thus does not reach the state of being untamed (*adanta*), or because of the greatness of its body, so too, when will I ever become a "nāga" in regard to the virtues dear to the Noble Ones?
I would be a *nāga* by virtue of being tamed— by not returning to the state of the untamed, by not returning again to this state of existence through non-doing,
and by the greatness of my body of qualities. And just as he, avoiding the herds,
dwells as he pleases in the forest with the happiness of solitary wandering, alone like the horn of a rhinoceros (*khaggavisāṇakappa*), when indeed shall I too, having avoided the crowd...
Dwelling in the forest according to his pleasure with the happiness of solitary abiding and the happiness of *jhāna*,
he should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros— meaning he should live in the forest for as long as he desires,
however much or however little that may be, in whatever way brings him ease. And just as this [rhinoceros] has grown its horn because its trunk is well-formed, when indeed shall I too...?
"May I become one whose aggregates have arisen through the greatness of the aggregate of the virtue of one beyond training (*asekha-sīlakkhandha*).

And just as he is called 'Lotus-like' (*padumī*) because his limbs resemble a lotus or because he was born in the family of the lotus, when indeed shall I too become 'Lotus-like' because my straight limbs resemble a lotus or because I am born in the noble birth-lotus? And just as he [is endowed] with strength, power, speed, and so forth..."
"Exalted! When indeed shall I too become exalted through such purity of bodily conduct and so forth, or through virtue, concentration, and penetrative wisdom?
Thinking thus, he applied himself to insight and attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
The commentary on the Nāga Verses is complete.
54. What is the origin of the Aṭṭhāna-tanti? It is said that the young son of the King of Bārāṇasī, while still a youth, desired to go forth and requested permission from his mother and father.
His parents tried to dissuade him, but even though he was being restrained, he persisted, saying, "I shall go forth.
Then, after telling him everything as previously related in the case of the merchant’s son, they finally gave their consent. Having gone forth, he remained right there in the pleasure grove.
They made him promise that he would dwell [there], and he did accordingly. His mother, accompanied by twenty thousand dancing women, went to the park early in the morning;
having had her son drink gruel and eaten various snacks in between, she conversed with him until midday and then entered the city. And his father, arriving at midday, fed him.
Having eaten himself and conversed with him throughout the day, he would station watchmen at evening time and enter the city.
In this way, he lived day and night without being secluded from him.
Now, at that time, a Paccekabuddha named Ādiccabandhu was dwelling in the Nandamūlaka cave; while reflecting, he saw him.
“This prince was able to go forth, but he cannot cut his matted locks. Thereafter, he reflected:

“Will he become disenchanted through his own natural disposition, or not? Then, knowing that if he were to become disenchanted through his natural disposition, it would take too long, [the deity] thought, “I shall provide him with an object of focus,” and arrived at the park from the surface of the rock of emerald in the same manner previously described.
He stood there. A royal official, seeing him, announced to the king, "A Paccekabuddha has arrived, Your Majesty.
The king, his heart filled with joy at the thought, "Now my son shall dwell without longing alongside this Paccekabuddha," attended upon the Paccekabuddha with great care.
Having requested that he remain right there, he had a leaf-hut and all other requisites constructed—including a dwelling place and a walking path—and settled him there.
While living there, one day having found an opportunity, he asked the youth, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a renunciant. [The other said], "Renunciants do not look like this. When [the youth] asked, "Then, venerable sir, what are they like?
Is it something unbecoming for me? [the other replied], "You do not perceive what is unbecoming to yourself; is it not so?"
His mother, together with twenty thousand women, would come in the morning and keep the park unoccupied;
his father, with a great army, would do so in the evening; and guards would remain throughout the entire night.
"Those who have gone forth are not like you," he said, "but rather they are like this," and while standing right there, by means of his psychic power (iddhi), [he appeared] in the Himalayas.

He showed him a certain monastery. There, seeing the Paccekabuddhas standing by the handrail of the balustrade, walking up and down, and performing tasks such as dyeing and sewing, he said: "Do not come here;
indeed, the going-forth (pabbajjā) has been forbidden to you. "Yes, the going-forth was forbidden; however, from the time we went forth..."
"Ascetics are permitted to seek their own liberation and to go to whatever place they desire;
this much alone is sufficient," he said, and standing in the air, he recited:
"It is impossible for one who delights in company to experience temporary liberation."
Having spoken this half-verse, he departed for the Nandamūlaka cave while his body was still visible.
When the Paccekabuddha had thus gone, the prince entered his own leaf-hut and lay down.
The guard, thinking, "The prince is asleep; where will he go now? fell into negligence and succumbed to sleep. Perceiving that he was negligent, [the Paccekabuddha...]
Taking his bowl and robes, he entered the forest. There, having practiced insight while secluded and having realized private enlightenment (paccekabodhi), he attained the state of a Paccekabuddha.
When questioned there by Ādiccabandhu as to how he had attained this, he spoke the half-verse that had been uttered [by him previously], completing it.
The meaning of this is as follows: “Aṭṭhāna” means “not a cause,” “not a reason”; thus it is said to be a *tanti* (a technical term).
The elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika-lopa*) has been made, as in such expressions as “ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ. “Saṅgaṇikārattassa” means “of one who delights in company.
“Yaṃ” is an instrumental case ending, as in such expressions as “yaṃ hirīyati hirīyitabbena. “Phassaye” means “one would attain.”
"Temporary liberation" refers to a mundane attainment (*lokīyasamāpatti*).
For that [attainment] is called "temporary liberation" because one is liberated from opposing states only at the very moment of absorption. That temporary liberation—that is the reason;
there exists no such cause by which one who delights in company could encounter the Paccekabuddha Ādiccabandhu.
Having heard these words, he abandoned his delight in social company and, practicing with proper method, said, "I have attained it. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Aṭṭhānagāthā* is finished.
The second chapter is concluded.
55. As for "the tangles of views," what is their origin? It is said that once, when a certain king in Benares was in seclusion, he thought:
"Just as there are things like heat that counteract cold and so forth, does there exist something that can counteract this cycle of existence (vaṭṭa), or not?
He asked his ministers: "Do you know the way out of the cycle (vivaṭṭa)? They replied: "We know it, Great King."
They said: "What is it? Then, by way of the method beginning with "Is the world finite," they spoke of eternalism and annihilationism.
Thereupon the king thought, "These do not know; all these are followers of speculative views.

Seeing for himself their contradiction and irrationality, he reflected, "There is the turning away from the cycle of existence that strikes down the round of rebirth; that must be sought," and having abandoned his kingdom—
Having gone forth and practicing insight, he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. And in the midst of the Paccekabuddhas, he uttered this inspired verse (*udāna*) as a declaration:
“Transcending the thorns of views, having reached the certainty of rightness and found the path, I have arisen with knowledge that is not to be led by others;
let me wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”

The meaning of this is as follows: "The snares of views" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*). For these are "snares" (*visūka*) in the sense that they obstruct, pierce, and run counter to right view of the Path (*magga-sammādiṭṭhi*).
Thus, they are snares for view, or the views themselves are the snares; hence, "snares of views.

"One who has transcended" means one who has passed beyond them by means of the path of vision (*dassana-magga*). "Attained to certainty" (*niyāma*) means having reached the state of being subject to non-falling into the lower realms.
And by being destined for full enlightenment, he has attained the state of certainty, namely the first path known as the "certainty of rightness" (*sammattaniyāma*).

Up to this point, both the accomplishment of the function of the first path and its acquisition have been described. Now, with the phrase "having acquired the path," he shows the acquisition of the remaining paths.
"I am one whose knowledge has arisen" means that I am one who has arisen to the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (individual enlightenment).
By this, he shows the fruit. "Not to be led by others" means that he cannot be led by others [to think], "This is the truth; this is the truth.
By this, he illuminates his self-become nature (*sayambhutā*); or, because there is an absence of being led once the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* has been attained, it is self-determined.
Or, he has transcended the thorns of views through serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), having entered the certainty (*niyāma*) reached by the first path, and by the remaining [paths]...
Having attained the path, he has arisen with the knowledge of the fruit; since all that has been realized by himself alone, he is not to be led by others.
The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the verse concerning the diversity of views is completed.
56. As for the origin of the story of *Nillolupa*: It is said that the king of Bārāṇasī had a cook who, having cooked an intermediate meal, presented it to him;
it was pleasing to behold and sweet in flavor. [The cook thought], "Perhaps the king might grant me some wealth.
That food, by its very fragrance, aroused the king's desire to eat, causing saliva to rise in his mouth. However, as soon as the first morsel was placed in his mouth—
The seventeen thousand palaces were as if filled with nectar. The cook thought, "Now he will give me [a reward], now he will give me [a reward].
The king also thought, "This cook is worthy of honor. However, he reflected:
"If I honor him after tasting the flavor, an evil reputation will spread about me, saying, 'This king is greedy and excessively fond of flavors.'"
He said nothing at all. In this manner, until the conclusion of the meal, the cook thought, "Now he will say something; now he will say something.
But the king, out of fear of disrepute, said nothing.
Then the cook, thinking, "This king has no sense of taste," served food devoid of flavor on the second day. As the king was eating, [he thought], "He deserves punishment..."
Even though he knew, "Today it is the cook," the king reflected as before and said nothing out of fear of ill repute.
Then the cook thought, "The king knows neither what is good nor what is bad," and taking all the profits for himself, he cooked anything at all and gave it to the king.
The king thought, "Alas, what greed! I, for one, possess twenty thousand cities..."
"Even while eating, through greed for this [food], I do not receive even a mere portion of a meal.

Having become disillusioned, he abandoned his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and while practicing insight (vipassanā), realized Pratyekabuddhahood. And in the same manner as before, he uttered this verse:
"Free from greed, free from deceit, free from thirst, free from hypocrisy, with defilements and delusion burnt away;
“Having become free from longing for the entire world, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In this context, *nillolupo* means free from greed (*alolupo*). For one who is overcome by craving for flavors is greatly plundered and plundered again and again;
therefore, he is called *lolupo*. Thus, rejecting that, he says, “free from greed” (*nillolupo*). *Nikkuho* means...

In this context, although one who lacks the three bases of hypocrisy is called "honest" (*nikkuho*), the intended meaning of this verse is that one is "honest" because of not falling into astonishment over pleasant food and such things. Regarding the term *nippipāso*:
here, "thirst" (*pipāsā*) is the desire to drink; by the absence of that, one is "thirstless," meaning free from the longing to eat out of greed for delicious flavors.
The meaning is as follows: "Free from malice" (*nimmakkho*): here, malice (*makkho*) is characterized by the destruction of the virtues of others; he is "free from malice" due to the absence of that.
He says this with reference to the absence of malice toward the cook’s virtues during his own time as a householder. "One who has blown out the stain of delusion" (*niddhantakasāvamoho*):
here, there are six factors—namely, the three beginning with lust and the three beginning with bodily misconduct—which, as the case may be, are in the sense of being unappealing.
It should be understood as "bitter" (kasāva) in the sense of causing one to abandon one's own nature and take on another nature, and in the sense of being dregs.

As it is said: "In this regard, what are the three bitter things? The bitterness of lust, the bitterness of hatred, and the bitterness of delusion—these are the three bitter things. In this regard, what are the other three bitter things? The bitterness of body, the bitterness of speech, and the bitterness of mind.
Because among these five bitter things, with the exception of delusion, all of them and the delusion that is their root have been blown away.

"Having cleansed the stain of delusion" means that because the stains of body, speech, and mind, as well as delusion itself, have been cleansed—therefore he is "one who has cleansed the stain of delusion.
In the case of the others, the state of having cleansed the stain of lust through non-greed and so forth, and the stain of hatred through non-malice, is already established.
"Free from expectation" means free from craving. "In the whole world" means in the entire world, within the three realms of existence.
The meaning is: having become free from craving for existence and non-existence regarding the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*). The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
Alternatively, after stating "three feet," one may also establish the connection here as: "one would be able to wander alone."
The commentary on the *Nillolupa* verses is complete. 57.

Regarding the origin of the verse beginning with "Evil companions": It is said that in Benares, a certain king, while performing a circumambulation of the city with great royal splendor, saw people carrying out old grain from the storehouse.
Seeing this, he asked his ministers, "What is this, sirs? They replied, "Your Majesty, new crops will soon arise;
these people are discarding their old grain and such in order to make room for them.
The king asked, "What, sirs, is the supply of the harem, the army, and so forth complete? "Yes, Your Majesty, it is complete," they said. "In that case—"
“Indeed, my friend, have a hall for gifts built; I shall give alms, lest these grains go to waste without being used.

Then a certain counselor holding wrong views stopped him, beginning with the argument, “Great King, there is nothing given,” and continuing until he said, “Both fools and the wise, having wandered and transmigrated, will make an end of suffering.”
Thus, seeing them plundering the storehouse for a second and even a third time, he gave the same command.
A third time, however, they restrained him, saying, "Great King, this so-called 'giving' is merely a pretext for what has already been given," and so forth.
He, becoming disillusioned, thinking, "Alas! I cannot even give away what belongs to me; what use have I for these evil companions?", abandoned his kingdom.
Having gone forth and practicing insight, he realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. And censuring that evil companion, he uttered this verse of exultation:
"One should avoid an evil companion, one who sees no harm and is established in the wrong path."
“One should not associate with one who is indolent and heedless; one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

This is the summary of its meaning: he who is “evil” because he is possessed of the tenfold evil view, who “sees harm” because he perceives harm even for others, and who is “established in the uneven” such as bodily misconduct and so forth—toward such a person, one who desires his welfare...
A son of good family should avoid an evil companion who sees no harm and is intent on what is uneven.
"He does not associate with him of his own accord" means he does not associate by his own volition; the implication is: if one is under the power of another, what can be done?
"Pasuta" means attached; the meaning is that they cling here and there due to their views. "Pamatta" means one whose mind is abandoned to the strands of sensual pleasure.
Or that which is devoid of the cultivation of wholesome states—one should not associate with, frequent, or attend upon such a person;
rather, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The commentary on the verses concerning evil companions is complete.

58. What is the origin of the term "bahussuta" (the learned)? It is said that formerly, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, eight paccekabodhisattas went forth, fulfilled the practice of "going and returning," and were reborn in the world of the gods;
all of this is exactly as stated in the verse on "eating blameless food. This, however, is the distinction: having seated the paccekabuddhas, the king asked, "Who are you?"
They said, “Great King, we are indeed known as ‘the very learned. The king thought, “I am named Sutabrahmadatta;
I never reach satiety with what is heard. Come now, I shall listen to a diverse method of teaching on the True Dhamma from them.
Being well-pleased, he gave the water of hospitality, served them, and at the conclusion of the meal, [he addressed] the Elder of the Saṅgha.
Taking his bowl and bowing, he sat down before him, saying, "Venerable sir, please give a discourse on the Dhamma.
The elder said, "May you be well, Great King; may there be the destruction of lust," and then rose up. The king thought, "This one is not very learned, but the second one will be;
tomorrow I shall hear a diverse teaching of the Dhamma," and so he invited him for the following day.
In this manner, he invited them all as they proceeded in order. They all likewise rose, each distinguishing one specific phrase—saying, "May there be the destruction of hatred;
may there be the destruction of delusion; may there be the destruction of rebirth; may there be the destruction of the cycle of existence; may there be the destruction of the substrata;
may there be the destruction of craving"—while the rest of their speech remained identical to that of the first.
Then the king thought, “These people say, ‘We are very learned,’ yet they have no varied discourse; what could these men possibly have said?

He began to examine the meaning of their words. Then, examining them with the thought, “May there be the destruction of lust,” he understood that when lust is destroyed, hatred and delusion—and indeed all other various defilements—are also destroyed. Thus, he was filled with joy.

He thought: “These recluses are learned in the non-figurative sense. For just as when a man points to the great earth or the sky with his finger, it is not merely the finger-tip that is pointed out, but rather the earth and the sky themselves;
even so, by these [recluses] pointing out each individual meaning, they have indicated what is immeasurable.”
“...the meanings have been demonstrated. Then, thinking, “When indeed shall I too become so very learned?

and aspiring to such a state of great learning, he renounced his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and through insight, having realized pratyekabodhi, uttered this verse of inspired utterance (udāna):
“One should associate with one who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, a sublime friend endowed with eloquence;
having understood the meanings and dispelled doubt, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: “Learned” refers to two kinds of those who are learned—one who has mastered the three Piṭakas in their entirety according to the letter, and... [the rest of the passage continues].

He is one who has heard much through the scriptures (*pariyatti*), and because he has realized the knowledge of the path, its fruits, and the higher knowledges (*vijjā-abhijñā*), he is one who has realized much (*paṭivedha-bahussuta*).
He is one who has mastered the traditional teachings and is a bearer of the Dhamma. Furthermore, he is "exalted" (*uḷāra*) because he is endowed with exalted bodily, verbal, and mental actions.

He is "possessed of presence of mind" (*paṭibhānavā*) because he possesses appropriate presence of mind, liberated presence of mind, and both appropriate and liberated presence of mind. This is by way of the scriptures, thorough inquiry, and realization.

Or, one who possesses ready wit should be understood as being threefold. For he to whom the scriptures appear readily is one who possesses ready wit regarding the scriptures (*pariyatti-paṭibhānavā*).

He to whom inquiry appears readily when he is inquiring about the meaning, the knowledge, the characteristics, and what is possible and impossible, is one who possesses ready wit regarding inquiry (*paripucchā-paṭibhānavā*).
He by whom the Path and so forth have been penetrated is one who possesses ready wit regarding realization (*adhigama-paṭibhānavā*).
One should associate with such a friend who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, sublime, and possessed of ready wit.

Then, through his influence, one comes to know various kinds of meanings—distinguished as one’s own welfare, another’s welfare, and the welfare of both, or distinguished as pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal.
Thereafter, regarding such questions as: "Did I exist in the past? and so forth...
Having removed doubt regarding points of uncertainty, having led away and destroyed all hesitation, and thus having performed all duties,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The commentary on the *Bahussuta* verses is complete.
59. What is the origin of delight in play (*khiddā-rati*)? In Benares there was a king named Vibhūsaka-Brahmadatta.
Early in the morning, having eaten either rice-gruel or a meal, he would have himself adorned with various kinds of ornaments.
Looking at his entire body in a large mirror, he would remove whatever he did not like and have himself adorned with other ornaments. Of him—
One day, as he was acting in this manner, the time for his meal arrived at midday. Then, without even adorning himself, he wrapped his head with a cloth, ate, and went to sleep during the day.
Again, having risen and acting in the same way, the sun set. It was the same on the second day and the third day. Thus, while he was thus intent on adornment—
A disease of the back arose in him. He thought: "Alas!
Although I was adorning myself with all my might, I became dissatisfied with this barber’s work of adornment and gave rise to greed. Now, greed is indeed a state that leads to the states of misery;
come now, I shall subdue this greed. Having thus renounced his kingdom and gone forth, he attained Pacceka-bodhi through insight.
Having realized this, he uttered this inspired verse:
“Without adorning himself with worldly play, delight, or sensual pleasure, and without looking back at them;
abstaining from all grounds for ornamentation, a speaker of truth—one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”

In this context, "play" (*khiḍḍā*) and "pleasure" (*rati*) have already been explained previously. "Sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukha*) refers to the sensual pleasure derived from objects (*vatthukāmasukha*).
For even the objects of desire are called "pleasure" by virtue of being the domain and so forth of pleasure. As it is said: "There is form that is pleasant, associated with pleasure.
Thus, having neither adorned nor deemed sufficient this world-sphere with such play, pleasure, and sensual enjoyment, [he renounced].

Without grasping at this as being "pleasing" or "essential. "Not looking back" means one whose nature is not to look back at that ornament—one who is without longing, free from craving, abstaining from the pursuit of adornment, truthful in speech, and who wanders alone.
In this context, adornment is twofold: the adornment of the householder and the adornment of the homeless one. Of these, the adornment of the householder...

"Adornments" refers to such things as garments, head-wraps, garlands, and perfumes; "adornment-places" refers to the embellishment of the bowl and so forth, which are the requisites of one who has gone forth into homelessness.

Since "adornment" itself is the "place of adornment," he is "abstinent from the three kinds of places of adornment. Because he speaks what is not false, he is a "speaker of truth"—thus should the meaning be understood.
The commentary on the verse concerning the places of adornment is complete.
60. What is the origin of the verse beginning with *puttañ ca dāraṃ*? It is said that the son of the King of Bārāṇasī was consecrated while still a youth and ruled the kingdom.
Like the Paccekabuddha mentioned in the first verse, he experienced the glory of sovereignty and one day reflected:
"While I rule the kingdom, I cause much suffering for many. What is the use of this kingdom for the sake of a single meal?"

“Alas! By means of this evil deed, let me now produce happiness! Having thus renounced his kingdom and gone forth, he attained insight, realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, and uttered this verse of exultation:
“Children and wife, father and mother, wealth and grain, and kinsmen;”
"Having abandoned sensual pleasures as they arise, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In this context, "wealths" refers to gems such as pearls, jewels, beryl, shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold.
"Grains" refers to the seven types of grain—rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, panic seed, and kudrūsa—as well as other remaining foods. "Relatives" refers to...

Regarding the four kinds of relatives—namely, those by birth, by kinship, by clan, by friendship, and by craft—the phrase "according to their respective spheres" (*yathodhikāni*) means they remain established according to their own particular domains.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verse concerning children and wives is complete.
61. What is the origin of the thought, "This is attachment"? It is said that in Benares there was once a king named Pādalola-Brahmadatta.
Having eaten either rice-gruel or solid food early in the morning, he would watch three kinds of theatrical performances in his three palaces.
These three kinds of performances, it is said, were those inherited from former kings, those inherited from the immediately preceding king, and those produced during his own time. One day...

Early in the morning, he went to the Lower Dance Hall. Those dancing girls, thinking, "We shall delight the king," performed dance, song, and instrumental music that was exceedingly captivating, like the celestial nymphs of Sakka, Lord of the Devas.
The king, feeling dissatisfied, thinking, "This is nothing extraordinary for young women," went to the Middle Dance Hall. Those dancing girls did likewise.
They did so. Still dissatisfied even with that, he went to the Mahānāṭaka-pāsāda (the Great Dance Hall). Those dancing girls also performed in the same manner.

After two or three royal cycles had passed, the king, seeing their dance—which, due to their old age, was like playing with bones—and hearing their singing, which was no longer sweet, went once more to the Dahara-nāṭaka-pāsāda (the Hall of Young Dancers), and then again to the Majjhima-nāṭaka-pāsāda (the Hall of Middle-aged Dancers).
Having reflected thus, being dissatisfied with everything, he thought:
"These dancing girls, desiring to delight me like the nymphs of Sakka, the lord of the gods, have exerted themselves to the utmost in dance, song, and instrumental music;
yet I, being dissatisfied with all this, only increase my greed. And this greed is a state of mind that leads to the states of misery. Come now, I shall [abandon] greed."
Thinking, "I shall restrain myself," he renounced his kingdom, went forth, and through insight realized pratyekabodhi, uttering this verse of exultation: "This is a fetter;
here the pleasure is trifling, the gratification slight, and suffering is greater."
"Knowing 'this is a snare,' the wise one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The meaning of this is as follows: "This is a snare" (saṅgo) refers to one's own enjoyment.

For living beings cling there, like an elephant sunk in the mud; thus it is a "snare" (saṅga). "The happiness here is trifling" (parittaṃ ettha sukhaṃ) refers to the time of enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Because it must be produced through perverted perception, or because it is included among the phenomena of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), pleasure is "inferior" in the sense of being base;
it is "limited," meaning it is short-lived, like the pleasure of watching a dance illuminated by the light of a flash of lightning—this is what is meant.
Regarding the statement, "There is little gratification, but suffering here is more," this refers to those five [aggregates] which, O monks... [as stated in the Sutta].
“Happiness and joy that arise dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure—this is the gratification in sensual pleasures,” it was said.
As for the danger in sensual pleasures, suffering is stated here by way of such passages as: “And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in sensual pleasures?
Here, bhikkhus, a clansman earns his living by some craft or trade, whether by calculation or accounting,” and so forth.
Compared to that, [the pleasure] is as little as a single drop of water. On the contrary, suffering alone is much more abundant, being like the water in the four oceans.
Therefore it is said: "The gratification here is slight; suffering is more. This is a hook:
having shown the gratification, these five strands of sensual pleasure are like a fishhook by way of their power to drag one in. Thus...
"Having known this, the wise and intelligent man, having understood thus, should abandon all this and wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
The commentary on the *Saṅgāmagāthā* is complete. 62.
Regarding the phrase "having torn away": what is its origin? It is said that in Benares there was once a king named Anivattabrahmadatta.
Having entered into battle, he does not turn back until he has conquered, nor does he desist from undertaking another task until it is completed;
therefore, they perceived him in this way. One day he went to a park. At that time, a forest fire broke out.
That fire, burning dry and green grass and other vegetation, proceeded without turning back. The king—
Seeing that, he produced a counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*):
"Just as this forest fire, even so does the elevenfold fire go on burning all beings without turning back, producing great suffering;
when indeed shall I, for the sake of turning back this suffering, burn away the defilements with the fire of the Noble Path-knowledge, just like this fire?"
“...might he go without turning back? Then, having gone for a short while, he saw fishermen catching fish in the river.
A large fish, having entered through the opening of their net, broke through the net and escaped. They cried out, “The fish has broken the net and gone!
Having heard those words as well, the king conceived a corresponding sign: “When indeed...”
“May I too, by means of the knowledge of the Noble Path, break through the net of craving and views and go forth unattached.
Having renounced his kingdom and gone forth, he applied himself to insight (vipassanā) and realized Pratyekabuddhahood, and uttered this verse of exultation:
“Having torn asunder the fetters, like a water-dweller breaking through a net, I have crossed over the flood.”
“Like a fire that has burned and does not turn back, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Regarding this, the word *jāla* in the second line refers to a net made of thread. *Ambu* means water;
one who moves therein is an *ambucārī*, which is a designation for a fish. A net in the water, moving in the water, is a *salilambucārī*; [it is cast] in that river-water.
"Having broken through, it moves through the water"—this is what is meant. Regarding the third line, "burnt" (daḍḍha) refers to the place that has been burnt.

Just as fire does not return to a place once burnt, nor does it come back to it again, so too the place of the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa), having been burnt by the fire of path-knowledge, is not returned to;
it does not come back to it again—this is what is meant. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the Sandālanagāthā is finished.

63. As for "with downcast eyes" (*okkhittacakkhu*): what is its origin? It is said that in Benares there was a king named Cakkhulola-Brahmadatta, who, like Pādalola-Brahmadatta, was devoted to watching theatrical performances. However, this is the distinction: he was dissatisfied.
He went here and there; having seen various plays, he wandered about greatly delighting in them, increasing his craving by watching the changing performances.
It is said that upon seeing a certain householder’s wife who had come to see a play, lust arose within him.
Thereafter, having attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he thought again: "If I continue to increase this craving, I shall fill the states of misery (*apāya*)."

“I shall become one; come now, I will restrain him. Having thus gone forth and attained *paccekabodhi* through insight (*vipassanā*), he censured his own former practice and uttered this verse of exultation (*udāna*) illustrating its opposite qualities:
“With downcast eyes and not fickle of foot, with sense-faculties guarded and mind protected;”
“Unflooded and unburning, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

In this context, “with downcast eyes” means with eyes cast downward; it is said that one should look only the distance of a yoke, having set the seven neck bones in a row, for the purpose of avoiding what is to be avoided and perceiving what is to be grasped. It does not mean [looking] with the jawbone...
Striking against the heart’s core. For such downcast eyes are not befitting a recluse.

And "not fidgeting with his feet" means not acting like one who scratches his feet out of a desire to enter the midst of a group—such as a second person for one, or a third for two—and thus being free from long journeys or unsettled wandering.
"Guarded in his faculties" refers to the six sense-faculties.

Here, he is one whose faculties are guarded by means of the remaining [restraints] practiced separately. "One who has a guarded mind" (*rakkhitamānasāno*): "mind" (*mānasa*) is the same as "mental" (*mānasāna*);
he is one for whom that [mind] is guarded, thus he is "one who has a guarded mind. What is meant is that his consciousness is guarded so that it is not plundered by the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Untainted" (*anavassuto*): by means of this practice, he is free from the influx of defilements toward various objects.
"Unburnt": thus, being free from the influxes (*anvāssava*), he is unburnt by the fires of the defilements (*kilesa*);
or, not leaking externally, he is unburnt internally. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verse beginning with "With downcast eyes" is complete.

64. Regarding the phrase "having caused to be removed": what is its origin? It is said that in Benares there was another king named Cātumāsika-Brahmadatta, who used to go for garden excursions every four months.
One day, during the middle month of summer, as he was entering the garden, he saw at the garden gate a *pāricchattaka* (coral tree) with branches adorned with flowers and covered in leaves.

Having seen this, he took one flower and entered the garden. Then, thinking, "The king has taken the finest flower," another minister, while still mounted on the neck of his elephant, took one flower. By this same means, the entire army took flowers;
those who could not find flowers even took the leaves. That tree was stripped of both leaves and flowers, remaining as a mere trunk.
It became so. Seeing it as he was departing from the garden in the evening, the king thought, "What has happened to this tree?
At the time of my arrival, its branches were the color of jewels and adorned with blossoms like coral; now it has become leafless and flowerless.
While reflecting thus, he saw nearby another tree that was not yet in bloom but was covered with dense foliage. Having seen it, he...

It occurred to him: "This tree was desirable to many people because it was laden with flowers, and for that reason it met its ruin in an instant; but this other tree, being undesirable, remains just as it was.
This kingship is like the flowering tree—desirable; but the state of a monk is like the non-flowering tree—undesirable."
"Therefore, as long as even this [kingdom] is not plundered like this tree, so long should one go forth,
being completely covered in the yellow robe just as the Pāricchattaka tree is covered with leaves. Having abandoned his kingdom and gone forth,
he practiced insight (vipassanā), realized Pratyekabuddhahood, and uttered this verse of exultation:
“Having cast off the marks of a householder, like a *pārichatta* tree with its leaves fully covered;
clad in saffron robes, having gone forth, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

Regarding this, the meaning of the line “clad in saffron robes, having gone forth” should be understood as: having gone forth from the home and being clad in saffron robes. The remainder can be understood according to the method already stated, and thus it is not elaborated here.
The commentary on the Pāricchattaka verses is completed.
The third chapter is finished. 65.
As for the verse beginning "In flavors" (rasesu): what is its origin? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī was once surrounded by the sons of his ministers in a pleasure grove.

He played in a lotus pond with stone slabs. His cook, having taken the essence of all kinds of meat, prepared an exceptionally well-prepared midday meal that was like the nectar of immortality and offered it to him.
Having become greedy for it, he ate it himself without giving anything to anyone else. And because he had emerged from his water-play very late, he ate very hurriedly.
He did not remember anyone with whom he had previously eaten; then, having developed reflective awareness, he thought:
"Alas, an evil deed has been done by me! Overcome by craving for flavors, I forgot all people and ate alone.
Come now, I shall subdue this craving for flavors. Abandoning his kingdom, he went forth into homelessness and, practicing insight, attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
Having realized this for himself and censuring his own former practice, he uttered this inspired verse (udāna-gāthā) which illuminates the qualities that are its opposite:
“Free from greed for flavors, not lustful, not supporting others,
wandering for alms from house to house with a mind unattached to family after family— one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”
In this context, "in tastes" (*rasesu*) refers to things to be savored, distinguished as sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, alkaline, astringent, and so forth.
"They do not crave" (*gedham akaruṃ*) means they do not become greedy; what is meant is that they do not give rise to craving.

"Not covetous" (*alolo*) means undisturbed by various specific tastes, thinking, "I shall taste this," or "I shall taste that. "Not supporting others" (*anaññaposī*) means being devoid of those who must be supported, such as co-resident disciples and others.
It means he is content with merely maintaining the body. Or, as previously in the pleasure grove he was greedy and longing for flavors, being one who lived off others;
not being so now, he has abandoned that craving by which, being greedy, he would create a grasping for flavors.
Having abandoned that craving, he is "not one who lives off others" because he does not produce another future personal existence rooted in craving.
[The Blessed One] shows this. Alternatively, "the other" (*añña*) refers to the defilements in the sense that they break up one's welfare (*atthabhañjanaka*).

By not nourishing them, he is "one who does not nourish the other"—this is also the meaning here. "One who goes from house to house" (*sapadānacārī*) means one who does not bypass [houses], one who goes in regular succession;
the meaning is that he enters for alms continuously, without skipping over either wealthy families or poor families. "With a mind unattached to family after family" (*kule kule appaṭibaddhacitto*).
With a mind that does not cling due to the defilements to any place whatsoever, such as among the kṣatriya clans and so forth— meaning, being like the moon,
ever-new— the rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verse concerning greed for flavors is complete.
66. Regarding the origin of the verse beginning “Having abandoned the five hindrances”: It is said that in Benares there was once a certain king who had attained the first *jhāna*.
For the sake of protecting his meditative absorption, he renounced his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and by practicing insight (*vipassanā*), realized *paccekabodhi* (private enlightenment).
While illustrating the perfection of his own practice, he uttered this verse of exultation (*udāna*).

“Having abandoned the five hindrances that defile the mind and having dispelled all secondary defilements, being independent and having severed the fault of attachment, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.

In this context, “hindrances” (*āvaraṇāni*) refers specifically to the mental obstructions (*nīvaraṇāni*). Their meaning is explained in detail in the *Uragasutta*. Furthermore, as for those [hindrances]...
Just as clouds and the like obscure the moon and sun, so do they obscure the mind; therefore, they are called "obstructions of the mind.
Having abandoned these either by means of access concentration (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*).

"Corruptions" (*upakkilesa*) refers to unwholesome states that, having approached, afflict the mind—namely, covetousness and the rest, as described in the *Vatthūpama Sutta* and other texts. "Having dispelled" means having driven away and destroyed them by way of the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*).

"Having abandoned"—this is the meaning. "All" means without remainder. Thus, one who is perfected in serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) is "independent" because the basis for views has been abandoned by the first path.
By the remaining paths, the fault of attachment to the three realms—the craving-fetter—is severed;
this is what is meant. For it is attachment itself that, being the opposite of virtue (guṇa), is called the "fault of attachment. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the *Āvaraṇagāthā* is completed. 67.
Regarding the phrase "having turned his back": what is its origin? It is said that in Benares there was a certain king who had attained the fourth *jhāna*.
For the sake of protecting that *jhāna*, he renounced his kingdom, went forth into homelessness, and through insight (*vipassanā*) attained *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment).
Having realized for himself the perfection of his own practice, he uttered this verse of exultation:
“Having turned one’s back on both pleasure and pain, and likewise on prior joy and grief;
having attained pure equanimity and tranquility—one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”

In that context, "having turned one's back" means having placed behind oneself; the sense is "having discarded" or "having abandoned. "Pleasure and pain" refers to bodily agreeable and disagreeable [feeling].
"Joy and grief" refers to mental agreeable and disagreeable [feeling]. "Equanimity" refers to the equanimity of the fourth jhāna.

"Tranquility" refers specifically to the tranquility of the fourth jhāna. "Purified" [means] by [being freed from] what are known as the five hindrances, initial application, sustained application, rapture, and pleasure.
It is "purified" because it is liberated from the nine opposing states; the meaning is that it is free from adventitious defilements, like refined gold.

This, however, is the construction: "having turned one's back upon pleasure and pain"—the intention being that "pain" [is turned away from] on the preliminary stage of the first jhāna, and "pleasure" on the preliminary stage of the third jhāna. Again, the word *ca* (and) mentioned at the beginning [should be understood here].
The governing phrase is: “Having turned one’s back on both joy (*somanassa*) and grief (*domanassa*), even before.
By this, it is indicated that joy [is abandoned] at the access to the fourth jhāna, and grief at the access to the second jhāna itself.
For these are, in a figurative sense (*pariyāyato*), the stages for their abandoning; but in a non-figurative sense (*nippariyāyato*), the first jhāna is for suffering, and [the second is] for grief.

The second jhāna is the place for the abandoning of pleasure; the third jhāna is the place for the abandoning of happiness; and the fourth jhāna is the place for the abandoning of mental joy. As it is said:
“Having attained and dwelling in the first jhāna, the arisen faculty of pain ceases there without remainder,” and so forth.
All of this is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. Since—
Having previously turned one's back on bodily pain, mental grief, and pleasure during the first three jhānas, and having now turned one's back on mental joy (*somanassa*) in this very fourth jhāna,
one "should wander alone" with the serenity (*samatha*) and purified equanimity obtained by this method.
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the verses has been concluded. 68.
As for the origin of the phrase "one who has aroused energy" (*āraddhavīriyo*): it is said that there was a certain frontier king whose military force consisted of a thousand warriors;
though small in terms of his kingdom, he was great in wisdom. One day, thinking, "Although I am small, because I am wise..."
Thinking, "But it is possible to seize the whole of Jambudīpa," he dispatched a messenger to the neighboring king, saying:
"Within seven days, either grant me your kingdom or give me battle. Thereupon, that king assembled his ministers and said:
"I have committed an act of rashness without even consulting you; such a message has been sent to a certain king—what should be done? They replied:
—“Is it possible, Great King, to turn that messenger back? —“It is not possible; he will have already gone.
—“If this is so, we have been ruined by you. Therefore, it would be better to die at the hands of another’s sword.
Come now, let us kill one another, or kill ourselves, or hang ourselves, or eat poison. Thus they spoke among themselves.
Each one of them praised only death. Then the king said, "What use have I for these? Tell me, do I have warriors?
Thereupon, that thousand of warriors stood up, each saying, "I am a warrior, O Great King! I am a warrior, O Great King!
The king, thinking, "I shall test these," had a funeral pyre prepared and said, "Tell me, this [which I am about to do]..."
“I have committed a rash act; my ministers reproach me for it. I shall enter the funeral pyre—who will enter with me?
Who has surrendered their life for mine? When this was said, five hundred warriors stood up and said, “We too, Great King, shall enter.
Then the king said to another five hundred warriors, “Now you—”
“Father, what will you do? They replied, “This is not a manly deed, O Great King; this is a woman’s work.
Nevertheless, a messenger has been sent by Your Majesty to the opposing king, and therefore we shall fight with that king and die.
Then the king, thinking, “You have surrendered my life,” arrayed his fourfold army and [proceeded] with him.
Surrounded by a thousand warriors, he went and sat at the border of his kingdom.
When that rival king heard the news, he became enraged, thinking, "Aha!
That petty king is not even fit to be my slave," and taking his entire army, he set out to do battle. The petty king [heard] of that expedition...
Seeing the army, he said: "Sirs, you are not numerous enough;
all of you, joining together and taking up swords and shields, go straight forward quickly before this king. They did exactly so.
Then that army split in two and made a way for them. They captured the king alive, while the other warriors fled.
The minor king ran forward, thinking, "I shall kill him," but the opposing king begged for his life.
Then, having granted him safety and made him swear an oath, he took him as his own man;
together with him, he marched against another king, stood at the boundary of that king's realm, and sent word: "Give me either the kingdom or battle."
Thus, thinking, "I cannot even endure a single combat," he surrendered his kingdom.
By this very means, having seized all the kings, he finally captured the King of Bārāṇasī as well.
Surrounded by one hundred and one kings, while ruling over the entire land of Jambudīpa, he thought: "Formerly, I was insignificant..."
"I have become so; indeed, through the perfection of my own knowledge, I have become the lord of the entire Jambudīpa.
Yet that knowledge of mine is associated with worldly effort; it leads neither to disenchantment nor to dispassion.
It would be well indeed if, by means of this knowledge, I were to seek the supramundane Dhamma. Then, having given the kingdom of Bārāṇasī to the king, [he departed].
Having sent away his wife and children as well as his own kinsmen and countrymen, he took up the life of renunciation, applied himself to insight meditation,
and having realized the state of a Paccekabuddha, he spoke this verse of exultation while demonstrating his own perfection of energy:
“With energy aroused for the attainment of the supreme goal, with a mind undaunted and conduct untiring;”
“With firm exertion, endowed with strength and power, one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
In this context, “one whose energy is aroused” means *āraddhaviriyo*. By this, he shows his own arousal of energy, which is the initial energy (*ādivīriya*).
The ultimate goal (*paramattha*) is said to be Nibbāna; for the sake of its attainment is *paramatthapattiyā*. By this arousal of energy...
It shows the fruit to be attained. By the term "unshaken in mind" (*alīnacitto*), he shows the non-languor of the mind and mental factors, which are supported by strength and energy.
By the term "not of indolent conduct" (*akusītavutti*), he shows the non-collapse of the body during standing, sitting, walking, and so forth.
By the term "firm exertion" (*daḷhanikkamo*), he shows the striving energy that proceeds thus: "Even if my skin and sinews [should waste away]."

That which is called "striving in the gradual trainings and so forth, whereby one realizes the supreme truth with the body and penetrates and sees it with wisdom"— or alternatively, by this he shows the energy associated with the Path;
for that is firm because it has reached the perfection of cultivation, and it is exertion because it has entirely emerged from its opposites.
Therefore, a person endowed with that [energy] is called "one of firm exertion" (*daḷhanikkama*) because he is firm and resolute.
"Endowed with the power of strength" (*thāmabalūpapanna*) means endowed with both bodily vigor and the power of knowledge at the moment of the Path;

or alternatively, "endowed with the power that has become strength," which is to say, endowed with the power of firm knowledge. By this, its association with insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*) is shown.
By illuminating this, he establishes the state of thorough exertion. Alternatively, all three feet may be connected by way of initial, intermediate, and intense energy.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verse beginning with "Aroused energy" is complete.
69. As for “seclusion” (*paṭisallāna*): what is its origin? Its origin is exactly like that of the introductory verse of this [chapter];

there is no difference whatsoever. However, in the commentary on the meaning of this term, "seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*) means turning away from those various conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), withdrawing and dwelling in solitude, being alone, and physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*). "Meditative absorption" (*jhāna*) is so called because it burns up (*jhāpana*) opposing states.
And mental seclusion is called such because of its close contemplation of the characteristic of the object (*ārammaṇa-lakkhaṇa-upanijjhāna*).

In that context, the eight attainments are called "meditation" (*jhāna*) because they burn away opposing factors such as the hindrances and because they closely contemplate the object; while insight, the path, and the fruits are so called because they burn away opposing factors such as the seven perceptions, and among these, the fruits are so called specifically because of their close contemplation of the characteristic.
However, here it is precisely the close contemplation of the object that is intended.

Thus, not neglecting, not abandoning, and not relinquishing both this seclusion and meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "Regarding phenomena" (*dhammesu*) means regarding the phenomena such as the five aggregates that have come under the scope of insight (*vipassanā*).
"Constantly" (*niccaṃ*) means continuously, uninterruptedly, and persistently.
"Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhammacārī*) means practicing the Dhamma of insight that has followed along by taking those very phenomena as its object.
Alternatively, "dhammas" refers to the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). "Anudhamma" is that which is in conformity with those states;

this is a designation for insight (*vipassanā*). In this context, although one should say "constantly practicing in accordance with the Dhamma among dhammas," it may have been stated as "among dhammas" (*dhammesu*) by means of a change in grammatical case for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse.
"Having comprehended the danger in states of existence" (*ādīnavaṃ sammasitā bhavesu*) refers to that [insight] characterized as the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
Perceiving through insight the defects such as impermanence in the three realms of existence,

one who does not abandon this physical seclusion and mental seclusion may be said to have attained the path known as insight that has reached its culmination; thus should the construction of the verse "One should wander alone" be understood.
The commentary on the verses for seclusion is finished. 70.
As for the origin of "The Destruction of Craving": It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī was circumambulating the city with the great majesty of royal power.
Beings, their hearts captivated by the beauty of his body, even those walking ahead turned back.
They gazed up at him even as they walked behind him and as they walked on both sides.
Indeed, by its very nature, the world is insatiable in its desire to see the Buddha and to behold the full moon and the ocean-king.
Then, a certain wife of a householder, having gone to the upper terrace of her palace, stood looking out after opening the lion-window. Upon seeing her, the king’s heart became bound to her.
Having offered the sacrifice, he commanded his minister: "Go, my man, and find out whether this woman has a husband or not.
He went and reported, "She has a husband. Then the king thought:
"These twenty thousand dancing girls delight me alone, just like celestial nymphs; now, since even they have not satisfied me, [what will happen] regarding another's wife?"
“I gave rise to craving; once arisen, it draws one only toward states of misery. Having seen this danger in craving, [the Bodhisatta] thought, “Come now, I shall subdue it!
