Abandoning his kingdom, he went forth into homelessness. While practicing insight (vipassanā), he realized pratyekabodhi and uttered this verse of inspired utterance (udāna):
“Striving for the destruction of craving, heedful, not dull-witted, learned, and mindful;
having discerned the Dhamma, resolute, and diligent in effort—one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In this context, “destruction of craving” refers to Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence of that very craving whose dangers have been thus seen. “Heedful” means...

"One who acts with persistence" means one who acts with diligence. "One who is not lisping" (*aneḷamūga*) means one whose speech is not indistinct; or alternatively, one who is both not lisping and not deaf, meaning he is wise and competent.
"One who is possessed of learning" (*sutavā*) means that he possesses the hearing of what brings about welfare and happiness;

it is said that he is endowed with the *āgama*. "One who is mindful" (*satimā*) means one who recollects things done long ago and so forth. "One who has scrutinized the Dhamma" (*saṅkhātadhamma*) [means] through the investigation of the Dhamma...

One who has fully understood the Dhamma. "Destined" means one who has entered the fixed course by means of the Noble Path. "Exerting" means endowed with the energy of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).
This reading should be construed in reverse order. Thus, being endowed with these qualities such as diligence and so forth, one is "exerting" through the exertion that brings about the fixed course;
because of having attained the fixed course by means of that exertion, one is "destined"; and from that, through the attainment of Arhatship—
"One who has fully understood the Dhamma" (*saṅkhātadhammo*). For an Arahant is called "one who has fully understood the Dhamma" because there is nothing further to be understood. As it is said:
"Those who have fully understood the Dhamma, and those many trainees here. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the Stanza on the Destruction of Craving is completed.
71. As for the origin of the story of the lion: It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī had a pleasure grove at a distance from his city.
Having risen early in the morning, he was going to the grove when, midway along the road, he alighted from his carriage and approached a body of water, thinking, "I shall wash my face.
In that place, a lioness had recently given birth to a cub and had gone out in search of food. Seeing it, the king’s man [said], "This is a lion cub..."
“Sire,” he reported. The king, thinking, “It is said that Sīha does not fear anyone,” had drums and other instruments beaten to test him.
Although the lion cub heard that sound, he remained lying down exactly as before. The king had them beaten a second and even a third time;
on the third occasion, he raised his head, looked at the entire assembly, and then lay down just as he was. Then the king [thought]: “As long as...”
Saying, "Let us go while our mother has not yet returned," he went along and thought: "On that day, even though he was but a lion cub, he did not tremble nor fear;
when indeed shall I too, having cut off the dread of craving and wrong views, neither tremble nor fear?
Taking that as his mental object, as he was going, he again saw fishermen catching fish.
Having tied it to branches and seeing that even when the net was cast out, the wind passed through it without clinging, he took that as a sign, thinking:
"When indeed shall I too, having rent asunder the net of craving and views or the net of delusion, proceed thus without being entangled?
Then, having gone to the park and sitting on the stone slab at the edge of the lotus pond, he saw the lotuses, struck by the wind, bending down.
Having touched the water and seen that when the wind had subsided they remained in their original places, unsullied by the water, he grasped that sign as well:
"When indeed shall I too, though born in the world, remain unsullied by the world, just as these things born in the water remain unsullied by the water? Again and again, [he thought]: "Just as..."
Thinking, "Just like the *sīhavāta* lotuses, one must be thus:

not trembling amidst what is not-trembling, unattached, and unsmeared," he renounced his kingdom, went forth, and while practicing insight (*vipassanā*), realized Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment and uttered this verse of exultation:
"Like a lion, not trembling at sounds; like the wind, unattached in a net."
“Like a lotus unsullied by water, one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
In this context, “lion” refers to four kinds of lions: the grass lion, the pale lion, the black lion, and the maned lion.

Of these, the maned lion is declared to be the foremost; it is this one that is intended here. The wind is of many kinds, according to its directions such as the east and so forth; [the word] *paduma*...
By way of the red, white, and so forth. Among these, any wind and any lotus whatsoever will do.

In this context, since terror arises from self-attachment (*attasineha*), and self-attachment is the smear of craving (*taṇhālepa*), and that [craving] occurs through greed associated with views or dissociated from views, it is indeed craving itself.
However, clinging there occurs through delusion (*moha*) for one who lacks investigation.
...and delusion is ignorance. Therein, craving is abandoned by serenity (*samatha*), and ignorance by insight (*vipassanā*).
Therefore, having abandoned self-attachment through serenity, one is not agitated by sounds—such as impermanence and so forth—just like a lion;

and having abandoned delusion through insight, one is unattached to the aggregates, bases, and so forth, just like the wind in a net. By serenity alone, greed and that which is associated with greed [are abandoned].
Thus, having abandoned such views, he remains unstained by greed for all the enjoyments of existence, just as a lotus is unstained by water.
Herein, virtue (*sīla*) is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of serenity (*samatha*), serenity is concentration (*samādhi*), and insight (*vipassanā*) is wisdom (*paññā*).
Thus, when these two qualities are established, the three aggregates (*khandha*) are also established. Among them, through the aggregate of virtue, one is "gentle" (*surata*).
Thus, like a lion, he does not tremble out of a desire to be angry at sounds that are grounds for resentment.
Having penetrated the true nature of things through the aggregate of wisdom, he is not caught in the various phenomena such as the aggregates, just as the wind is not caught in a net.

Being free from passion through the aggregate of concentration, he is not defiled by passion, just as a lotus is not stained by water. In this way, through serenity and insight, and through the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, according to their respective occurrence—
He should be understood as one who is not restless, does not cling, and is unsmeared by virtue of the abandoning of ignorance, craving, and the three unwholesome roots.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Thus ends the commentary on the "Asantasantā" verse.

72. What is the origin of the verse beginning "Just as a lion"? It is said that a certain king of Bārāṇasī, wishing to pacify a rebellion in the borderlands, set aside the road through the villages and proceeded with a great army by taking a direct forest path.
At that time, a certain lion was lying down on the foot of a mountain, basking in the heat of the rising sun.
Seeing him, the king’s man informed the king. Thinking, "It is said that the lion does not tremble at sound," the king had sounds made by means of drums, conchs, small drums, and so forth.
The lion lay down just as before. He had it done a second time; the lion lay down just as before. He had it done a third time.
The lion, thinking, "I have an adversary," planted all four feet firmly upon the ground.
He let out a lion’s roar. Upon hearing it, the elephant-riders and others descended from their elephants and other mounts and entered the thickets of grass;
the herds of elephants and horses fled in every direction. The king’s own elephant, seizing the king, fled while crushing him against the dense forest thickets.
Unable to support him, the elephant hung him from a tree branch, and [the king], falling to the ground, followed along a narrow footpath.
While traveling, he reached the dwelling place of the Paccekabuddhas and there asked them, "Venerable sirs, did you hear any sound?
"Yes, Great King," they replied. "Whose sound was it, venerable sirs? "First that of drums, conchs, and so forth;
afterwards, that of a lion. "Were you not afraid, venerable sirs? "We were not afraid, Great King."
“I am afraid of some sound. “But is it possible, venerable sir, for me to do the same?

“It is possible, Great King, if you go forth. “I shall go forth, venerable sir. Then, having ordained him, they instructed him in the training of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika*) according to the method previously described.
He too, practicing insight (*vipassanā*) according to the method previously described, realized the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
He uttered this verse of inspired utterance:
"Just as a lion, powerful with his fangs, moves having overcome [all] by force, so should a king among deer;
one should frequent remote lodgings and wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros."

In this context, he is a lion (*sīha*) because of his endurance, his killing, and his swift speed. Here, it is specifically the maned lion (*kesarasīha*) that is intended. "Possessing the strength of tusks" (*dāṭhabalī*) means one who has the power of tusks.
Regarding the terms "overpowering" (*pasayha*) and "conquering" (*abhibhuyya*), both should be connected with the word "roaming" (*cārī*):

namely, "one who roams overpowering" (*pasayhacārī*) and "one who roams conquering" (*abhibhuyyacārī*). Therein, "one who roams overpowering" refers to roaming by way of suppressing; "having conquered,"...

Having terrified them and brought them under his control, he moves having overcome them with his gait. He himself moves having forced his way by means of his bodily strength, moving having overcome them with his splendor.
In this regard, if someone were to ask, "What does he move having forced and having overcome?
then one should reply, "He moves having forced and having overcome the deer," making the genitive case "of the deer" (*migānaṃ*) into an accusative case.
"Pantāni" means remote places. "Senāsanāni" means dwelling-places. The remainder can be understood according to the method already explained;
therefore, it is not elaborated upon here. The commentary on the *Dāṭhabalī* verses is complete. 73.
As for the origin of the verses beginning with "Mettaṃ upekkhaṃ": It is said that a certain king was an attainer of the jhānas of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]. He...
Thinking, “Kingship is an obstacle to the bliss of jhāna,” he abandoned his kingdom for the sake of guarding his jhāna, went forth, and while practicing insight,
realized pratyekabodhi and uttered this verse of inspired utterance:
“Cultivating at the proper time loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, deliverance, and sympathetic joy;”
“Unopposed by the whole world, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In this context, *mettā* is the desire to bring about welfare and happiness according to the method beginning with, “May all beings be happy.
*Karuṇā* is the desire to remove harm and suffering according to the method beginning with, “Oh, may they be liberated from this suffering! “They rejoice...”
Muditā (appreciative joy) is the desire for the non-separation of beings from welfare and happiness, expressed in such passages as, "May these worthy beings rejoice; well done, very well done!
Upekkhā (equanimity) is the state of looking on with impartiality toward pleasure and pain, thinking, "They shall be known by their own karma.

However, for the sake of the ease of the verse composition, loving-kindness (mettā) was mentioned first and equanimity (upekkhā) stated afterwards, with appreciative joy (muditā) following. "Liberation" (vimutti) refers to all four [immeasurables].
For these are called "deliverances" (vimutti) because they are liberated from their own opposing states. Therefore it was said:
"Cultivating loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and sympathetic joy at the proper time.
In this context, "cultivating" means developing the three [immeasurables] by way of the third and fourth jhānas, and equanimity by way of the fourth jhāna.
Having cultivated loving-kindness at the proper time, he emerges from that and cultivates compassion; emerging from that, he cultivates gladness;

or, emerging from that or from any other jhāna devoid of rapture, he cultivates equanimity. One who does this is said to be “cultivating at the proper time,” or one who cultivates at a time when it is convenient to cultivate.
“Not obstructed by the whole world” means not being obstructed by the entire world of sentient beings in the ten directions.
For through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], beings become non-repulsive; and hostility, which consists in opposition toward beings, is pacified.
Therefore it is said: "not being obstructed by the whole world. This is the summary here;
however, the detailed discussion of loving-kindness and the rest is set forth in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Appamaññā-gāthā* is completed. 74.
As for the origin of the verse beginning "Lust and hatred": it is said that near Rājagaha, a Paccekabuddha named Mātaṅga was dwelling;
he was the very last of all the Paccekabuddhas. Then, when our Bodhisatta had been born, the deities...
Seeing him, those who had come to honor the Bodhisatta cried out, "O sirs, O sirs! A Buddha has appeared in the world!

Hearing that sound as he was emerging from cessation and perceiving his own end of life, he went through the air to the mountain in the Himalayas called Mahāpapāta, the place where the Paccekabuddhas attain final Nibbāna.
Having gone there and cast the skeletal remains of a Paccekabuddha who had previously attained Parinibbāna into a precipice,
he sat down upon a stone slab and uttered this verse of exultation:
“Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and having torn asunder the fetters;”
“Without fear during the dwindling of life, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In this context, lust, hatred, and delusion are as described in the *Uragasutta*. “Fetters” refers to the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Having torn these apart by means of the respective paths, [one should act] “without fear during the dwindling of life”; here, “the dwindling of life” refers to the consciousness of death (*cuticitta*).
There is disintegration; and because attachment to life has been abandoned at that exhaustion of life, there is no further becoming.
Having thus shown to himself the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining, at the conclusion of the verse he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
The commentary on the "Exhaustion of Life" verse is complete.
75. As for the origin of the verse beginning with "They serve": it is said that in Benares, a certain king was ruling over a prosperous kingdom exactly as described in the opening verse.
A severe illness befell him, and agonizing pains arose.
Twenty thousand women surrounded him, massaging his hands and feet and performing other services. His ministers said, "This king will no longer live; come now..."
Thinking, "Let us seek refuge for ourselves," they went into the presence of another king and requested service.

They remained there in attendance, yet they received nothing at all. When the king recovered from his illness, he asked, "Where are so-and-so and so-and-so? Upon hearing of their situation, he shook his head.
He remained silent. Those ministers, hearing that the king had emerged and finding nothing there, were overcome by supreme loss;
they returned once more, paid homage to the king, and stood to one side.
When the king asked them, "Where have you been, dear ones? they replied, "Having seen Your Majesty weak, we [left] out of fear for our livelihood."
“...has gone to such-and-such a country. The king, nodding his head, thought: “What if I were now to test them;

would they do the same again? As if previously afflicted by a debilitating disease, he manifested himself as being in intense pain and issued a proclamation of illness. The women surrounded him, and everything was exactly as it had been before.
They did so. Those ministers likewise departed again, taking even more people with them. In this manner, the king acted exactly as before for a third time, and they likewise departed.
Then, seeing that they had returned for a fourth time, he became disillusioned, thinking:
"Oh, these men have performed a difficult task, in that they have departed without concern, abandoning me while I was ill!"
Having renounced his kingdom and gone forth, and having realized private enlightenment (paccekabodhi) through insight (vipassanā), he uttered this verse of exultation:
“They associate and serve for the sake of some purpose; friends without a motive are rare these days.
People are impure, perceiving only their own self-interest; one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”
In this context, "they attend" means they wait upon him by remaining close to his person.
"They serve" means they attend to him with such acts as joining their palms in salutation and by promising to carry out whatever needs to be done.

"Those for whom the purpose is the cause" (*kāraṇatthā*) means that for these people there is no other cause for attending and serving than the purpose itself; the purpose alone is their cause. What is meant is that they serve for the sake of the purpose.

"Friends who are disinterested are rare today"—this means they are "disinterested" not for the sake of obtaining something for themselves, such as thinking, "We shall receive something from this person," but solely because:
"A friend who is helpful... [and so forth].
“He who is a friend in happiness and in suffering,
he who is a friend who speaks for one’s welfare, and he who is compassionate toward friends.”
Friends endowed with such noble friendship as has been described are rare to find today. Their wisdom is fixed upon themselves;

they look only to their own self and not to others—thus they are called "those whose wisdom is for their own sake" (*attaṭṭhapaññā*). Regarding the term *diṭṭhatthapaññā*, this too was indeed an ancient reading;
however, it is now explained thus: their wisdom concerns only the present object (*attha*), and they do not look toward the future.
"Unclean" means they are possessed of unclean, ignoble deeds of body, speech, and mind. The rest should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses concerning the sense of cause is completed.
The fourth chapter, consisting of eleven verses, is finished.
Thus, this *Khaggavisāṇasutta*, consisting of forty-one verses,
should be understood according to its meaning and its sequence by applying the method of interpretation as stated in some instances to all parts as appropriate.
However, for fear of excessive prolixity, we have not applied it in every case.
The commentary on the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya, is completed. 4.
Commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.
Thus have I heard: this is the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. What is its origin?

While the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Ekanālā, a brahmin village in Dakkhiṇāgiri, having completed the two duties of a Buddha—namely, the duty before the meal and the duty after the meal—and having concluded the duty after the meal, he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye.
Seeing that the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja was endowed with the necessary conditions for attaining *arahantship*,

and knowing that "when I go there, such-and-such will happen; then, at the conclusion of that discourse, having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, this brahmin will go forth and reach *arahantship*," he went there, initiated the conversation, and spoke this Sutta.
In this regard, it may be asked: "What is the duty of the Buddhas before the meal, and what is their duty after the meal? It is said:
The Blessed Buddha, having risen early in the morning, performed such bodily care as washing his face for the sake of refreshing his body and favoring his attendants;
then, until the time for the alms-round, he spent that interval in a secluded seat. At the time for the alms-round, he put on his lower robe.

Having fastened his waistband, donned his robe, and taken up his bowl, he would enter a village or town for almsfood—sometimes alone and sometimes surrounded by the community of monks; sometimes in his ordinary manner, and sometimes while performing many miracles.
For example, as the Lord of the World entered for alms, gentle beings would go ahead of him.
Winds cleanse the earth; clouds, releasing droplets of water, settle the dust on the road and remain above as a canopy.
Other winds gather flowers and scatter them upon the path;
elevated places of ground sink down, and depressed places rise up, so that at the moment of setting foot down, the ground becomes level.
Lotus flowers, as large as chariot wheels, receive his feet with pleasant contact;
as soon as his right foot is placed within the threshold, six-colored rays stream forth from his body, causing the palaces, gabled chambers,
and other structures to appear as if dappled with molten gold or draped in variegated cloths, as they flash hither and thither.
Elephants, horses, birds, and other creatures, remaining in their respective places, utter sounds in a sweet manner;
likewise do musical instruments such as drums and lutes, as well as the ornaments worn on the bodies of people.
By that sign, people know: "Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms. They, being well-clad and well-robed, [bring] perfumes, flowers, and so forth...

Having taken [the requisites], they went out from their homes, entered the street, and after respectfully honoring and bowing to the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, they requested:
"Venerable sir, give ten bhikkhus to us, twenty to us, a hundred bhikkhus to us.
Having also taken the Blessed One’s bowl, they prepared a seat and served him the alms-food with great care.
When the Blessed One had finished his meal, he surveyed their mental continuums and taught the Dhamma in such a way that some were established in the taking of refuge,
some in the five precepts, some in one of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning, and some,
having gone forth, attained the supreme fruit of arahantship. Having thus assisted the people in various ways, he departed.
Rising from his seat, he goes to the monastery. There, in the pavilion, he sits upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him, awaiting the conclusion of the monks' meal.
Then, at the conclusion of the monks' meal, the attendant informs the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One enters the Fragrant Chamber. This, first of all, is the duty before the meal.
Whatever has not been stated here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Brahmāyu Sutta*.

Then the Blessed One, having thus completed his meal and sitting in attendance within the fragrant chamber, washed his feet, stood upon the footstool, and exhorted the community of monks: “Monks, accomplish your task with diligence; the arising of a Buddha—”
“Rare in this world is the attainment of human birth; rare is the perfection of faith; rare is the going forth into homelessness;
rare in this world is the hearing of the True Dhamma. Then the bhikkhus, having paid homage to the Blessed One, asked for a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Thereupon the Blessed One gave a meditation subject to the bhikkhus according to their individual temperaments. They [received] the meditation subject...
Having received [the teachings] and having paid homage to the Blessed One, they each went to their own dwelling places:
some to the forest, some to the foot of a tree, some to one of the mountains and so forth, some to the realm of the Four Great Kings... and some to the realm of Vasavatti.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the Fragrant Chamber, if he so desired, with his right [hand]...
Mindful and clearly comprehending, he lies down for a short while in the lion’s posture.

Then, having steadied his body, he rises and surveys the world during the second watch. During the third watch, in whatever village or town he dwells near, the people there—having given their alms-food before the meal and being well-robed and well-dressed after the meal—[bring] perfumes, flowers, and so forth.

Having taken [the bowl], he gathers at the monastery. Then the Blessed One, having approached with a miracle suited to the assembled company, sits upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma Hall and teaches the Dhamma—timely and of appropriate measure.
Then, perceiving that it is time, he dismisses the assembly.
Then, if he wishes to bathe his limbs, he rises from the Buddha-seat and goes with his attendant to the place where water has been prepared.
Taking a bathing robe from the attendant's hand, he enters the bathhouse.

The attendant, having brought the Buddha-seat, arranges it in the courtyard surrounding the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭī). After the Blessed One has bathed his limbs, [he puts on] a well-dyed double-layered cloth...
Having dressed, fastened his waist-band, and arranged his upper robe, he went there and sat down alone for a moment in seclusion.
Then, monks coming from here and there approached the Blessed One to attend upon him.
There, some asked questions, some [asked for] a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and some [sought] a hearing of the Dhamma.
They made requests. The Blessed One, fulfilling their intention, spent the first watch of the night.

During the middle watch, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world system, finding an opportunity, approached the Blessed One and asked questions, even as few as four syllables, according to their specific preparations. The Blessed One [responded] to those deities...
Answering questions, he passes the middle watch of the night. Then, having divided the last watch into four parts, he devotes one part to walking meditation;

entering the fragrant chamber for the second part, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, mindful and clearly comprehending; he spends the third part in the attainment of fruition; and the fourth part—

Having entered the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*), he surveys the world with the Buddha-eye for the purpose of seeing beings—those with little dust in their eyes, those with much dust in their eyes, and so forth.
This is his duty after the meal.
Thus, at the conclusion of the fourth part of this post-meal duty, known as the surveying of the world, [he reflects] upon the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.

Surveying the world with his Buddha-eye to see beings—whether they had performed meritorious deeds such as giving, morality, and the observance of the Uposatha, or whether they had not; and whether they were endowed with the necessary conditions for spiritual progress (*upanissaya*) or not—he saw that the Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja was endowed with the conditions for attaining *arahantship*.
He thought: "When I have gone there, a conversation will arise; then, at the conclusion of that conversation..."
Having understood that "after hearing this teaching of the Dhamma, this brahmin will go forth and attain arahantship," [the Blessed One] went there,
initiated the conversation, and spoke this Sutta.
Regarding the words "Thus have I heard" and so forth, [they were spoken] by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council during the recitation of the Dhamma.
When the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa was questioned, he spoke regarding five hundred arahants;
Kasibhāradvāja spoke, saying, "I, O ascetic, both plough and sow"; and the Blessed One spoke, saying, "I too, O brahmin, both plough and sow," and so forth.
Having combined all of this together, it is called the "Kasibhāradvāja Sutta."
In this context, the word *evaṃ* has the sense of indicating a manner, a characteristic, and a restriction. By way of its meaning as "manner," it illustrates this point:

[the Dhamma] is skilled in various methods, originates from manifold inclinations, is perfect in both meaning and phrasing, possesses diverse miracles, is profound in its penetration of the teaching of the Dhamma and its meaning, and is characterized by a nature that can be perceived by all beings according to their respective languages.
Who is capable of understanding the word of that Blessed One in every aspect? Rather, [the phrase] "Thus have I heard" means, "I too have heard it in one particular way.

By way of indication, in order to exempt himself [from the charge of error], saying, "I am not self-become (sayambhū), nor have I realized this myself," he must now state: "Thus have I heard; by me it was thus heard."

He points to the entire Sutta. By way of emphasis, he demonstrates his own power of retention in accordance with the state of being praised by the Blessed One in such passages as: “Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are learned, Ānanda is foremost;
among those who possess insight, those who possess mindfulness, those who possess fortitude, and among attendants, Ānanda is foremost. Thus he shows his own power of retention.
It generates in beings a desire to hear [the teaching], thinking: "Thus have I heard; and that [teaching] is neither deficient nor redundant in meaning or in phrasing;

it is exactly thus and should not be viewed otherwise. Regarding the phrase *me sutaṃ* ("thus have I heard"): here, the word *me* has the sense of the pronoun *mayā* ("by me"), and the word *sutaṃ* has the sense of consciousness through the ear-door (*sotadvāraviññāṇa*).
Therefore, *evaṃ me sutaṃ* means "thus [was it heard] by me" by way of the cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*) preceded by auditory consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*).
"Upadhāritaṃ" means "it has been stated.
"Ekaṃ samayaṃ" means "at one time. "Bhagavā" means "the Fortunate One," "the Conqueror," or "the Possessor of Wealth"—thus it is stated.
"Viharati Magadhesu" means that there were princes of the realm named Magadha; their territory, though consisting of many districts, was a single kingdom.
By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsadda*), it is called "Magadha. In that Magadha country, some [explain] as follows:
"Because King Cetiyarāja, while entering the earth after speaking a falsehood, was told, 'Do not enter the pit (*mā gadhaṃ pavisā*)';
or because the men digging the earth while searching for that king were told, 'Do not make a pit (*mā gadhaṃ karothā*)'; therefore, [the land is] Magadha," and so forth.
They proliferate in many ways through various methods; one should accept whatever is pleasing.
"Dwells" (*viharati*) means that by interrupting one posture with another, one carries (*harati*) the personal existence (*attabhāva*) without it falling away; what is meant is that one maintains it.
Alternatively, he "dwells" because he brings about (*harati*) the manifold welfare of beings through the divine, brahma, and noble dwellings (*vihāra*). "Brings about" (*harati*)...
It brings together, leads toward, generates, and produces—this is what is meant.

For when beings behave wrongly regarding sensual pleasures, it is said that at that time the Blessed One dwells in a divine abiding for the purpose of generating the wholesome root of non-greed in them, thinking:
"Perhaps, having seen this practice and developed a liking for it, they might become dispassionate toward sensual pleasures."
But when they act wrongly toward living beings for the sake of power, he dwells in the divine abode (brahmavihāra) in order to arouse the root of non-hatred (adosa-kusalamūla) in them—
thinking, "Perhaps, having seen this practice and developed a liking for it,
they will pacify their hatred through non-hatred. But when those who have gone forth dispute over matters of the Dhamma, then...
He dwells in the noble abiding for the purpose of generating the wholesome root of non-delusion in them, thinking:
"Perhaps, having seen this practice and developed a liking for it, they might pacify their delusion by means of non-delusion.
However, he never fails to dwell in the abiding of the postures, because without that, there would be no maintaining of the physical body. This is the summary here.
The detailed explanation, however, we shall give in the commentary on the *Maṅgala Sutta*.
"In Dakkhiṇāgiri" refers to the country situated on the southern side of that mountain which stands surrounding Rājagaha;
it is said to be in that country. There, the name applies equally to the monastery as well.
"By name. "In the brahmin village of Ekanālā": *Ekanālā* is the name of that village.
Because many brahmins resided there, or because it was the domain of brahmins, it is called "the brahmin village.
"Now at that time": at the time when the Blessed One, having sat down cross-legged on the invincible throne (*aparājita-pallaṅka*), [attained] the unsurpassed...
Having fully awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment and having set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma,
he dwelt near the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa in the kingdom of Magadha at the Dakkhiṇāgiri Mahāvihāra, awaiting the ripening of the faculties of a certain brahmin—
at that time, acting as the instrumental cause— so it is said. Furthermore, the two particles *kho pana* here [function as follows].
It should be understood that [the word *matta*] is used merely for metrical completion, or for the purpose of indicating a change of subject. Regarding "of the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja":
that brahmin lived by means of plowing (*kasi*), and "Bhāradvāja" was his clan name; therefore, he is called thus. As for "five measures" (*pañca-mattāni*):
just as the word *matta* denotes "measure" in the phrase "one who knows the measure in food" (*bhojane mattaññū*), so it is here as well; therefore, it refers to five measures.

"Not deficient and not excessive" means five hundred ploughs; this is what is meant. "Yoked" means employed; the sense is that they have been placed upon the necks of the oxen and fastened with yokes and thongs. "At the time of sowing" means at the time of planting;
it is said to be the time for depositing the seed. In that regard, there are two kinds of sowing: sowing in mud and sowing on dry land.
And the sowing of seeds. What is intended here is the sowing of seeds. And that was the auspicious sowing on the first day.
In this regard, there was a perfection of requisites: three thousand oxen were stationed there, all with horns adorned with gold and hooves made of silver;
they were all garlanded with white flowers and perfumed with every kind of fragrant scent.
They were adorned with five-fingered ornaments, with all their limbs and members complete and endowed with every auspicious mark;
some were black, the color of collyrium; some were white, the color of crystal; some were red, the color of coral; and some were dark-brown, the color of emerald.
Five hundred farmers, all dressed in garments of black antelope skin and adorned with garlands, [accompanied them].

Ten ploughs at a time, each group of ten, proceeded along with flower-cushions placed upon their right shoulder-tips, their bodies radiant with markings of yellow orpiment and red arsenic. The heads, yokes, and goads of the ploughs were bound with gold.
On the first plough eight oxen were yoked; on the remaining ones, four each; as for the rest—
They were brought there for the purpose of tiring them out through the work of turning over the soil. In each clump, one man plows with a seed-cart and another sows.

But the brahmin, having had his beard trimmed early in the morning, bathed, anointed himself with fragrant perfumes, put on a garment worth five hundred pieces, draped a cloth worth a thousand pieces over one shoulder, and arranged two rings on each of his fingers— Please note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the brahmin's hand adornments. The translation reflects the portion available.
Having put on twenty finger-rings, lion-shaped earrings on his ears, and a Brahma-diadem upon his head,
and having placed a golden garland around his neck, he supervised the work while surrounded by a host of brahmins. Then his brahmin wife,
having caused milk-rice to be cooked in many hundreds of vessels and loaded onto large carts, bathed him with scented water.
Adorned with every ornament and surrounded by a company of brahmin women, she went to the field.
His house, too, was everywhere well-smeared with perfumes and well-provided with offerings of flowers; and in various places throughout the fields, banners were raised on high.
Together with his attendants and laborers, the assembly that had gathered at the field numbered two thousand five hundred. All—
They were dressed in new, unwashed garments, and a meal of milk-rice was prepared for everyone.
Then the brahmin had the golden bowl in which he himself ate washed, filled with milk-rice, and prepared with ghee, honey, molasses, and other ingredients;
he then had the ploughing ceremony performed. The brahmin’s wife [prepared] five...
Hundreds of farmers, carrying vessels made of gold, silver, bronze, and copper, were seated;

taking golden ladles, they went about serving him with milk-rice. Meanwhile, the brahmin, having had the ritual offerings performed, put on his red-gold sandals and, taking up his red-gold staff, said:
"Give the milk-rice here, the ghee there, and the sugar there."
“Eat,” he said, and wandered about feeling satisfied. Then the Blessed One, while remaining seated in the fragrant chamber, became aware that the brahmin’s meal distribution was underway.

Thinking, “This is the time to tame this brahmin,” he put on his lower robe, fastened his waistband, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, took up his bowl, and emerged from the fragrant chamber, just as the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed would do.
Therefore the Venerable Ānanda said: "Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning time...
In this context, *atha* is a particle used to introduce a new section; *kho* is for the purpose of completing the phrase. *Bhagavā* is exactly as previously explained.
*Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ* means the period of the early part of the day; the sense is *pubbaṇhasamaye*, or [it may mean] in the morning.
“At the time” means at the morning time; it is said that they were digging at one spot in the morning.

Thus, the accusative case is used to express continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). “Having dressed” means having put on [the robes]; this should be understood in terms of changing from the monastery robe to the outer robe.
For the Blessed One was not without clothes prior to that. “Taking bowl and robe” means taking the bowl with his hands.
"Having taken up the robe with the body" means having received it and worn it.

It is said that when the Blessed One was about to enter for alms, a stone bowl the color of an indranīla gem came between his two hands, like a bee coming into the center of a pair of blooming lotuses.
Therefore, having received the bowl that had thus come between his hands, [he took it].
"And having put on the robe properly rounded about the body"—this is how its meaning should be understood.
For one who takes [something] up in whatever manner is simply said to "take it," just as in the expression, "having taken it up, he departs.
"By which" means by whichever path. "To work" (*kammanta*) means the place where work is performed. "By that" means by that path. "Approached" (*upasaṅkami*).
"He went" means he went by the same path by which the brahmin Kassapa Bhāradvāja’s farm was reached.
Now, why did the monks not follow the Blessed One? It is said:
whenever the Blessed One desired to go somewhere alone, at the time for the alms-round, he would close the door and enter the inner fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi).
He enters. Then the bhikkhus, through that sign, know: "Today the Blessed One wishes to enter the village alone;
surely he has seen someone who ought to be trained. Taking their own bowls and robes, they circumambulate the Gandhakuṭī and go out for alms.
And at that time, the Blessed One acted in this way. Therefore, the bhikkhus...
“They did not follow after the Blessed One.
Now, at that time means: at the time when the Blessed One approached the place of work, at that same time the brahmin’s distribution of food was taking place;
the meaning is that the serving of the meal was underway. As for what we said previously:
“The brahmin’s wife is going along, carrying five hundred bowls made of gold, silver, bronze, and copper in which the five hundred farmers are seated;
she is serving them rice porridge with a golden spoon. Then the Blessed One went to where the serving was taking place.
For what reason? To show favor to the brahmin. Indeed, the Blessed One did not...
Like a wretched man, he approaches the food-distribution hall out of a desire to eat. For the Blessed One has two relatives, the Śākyas and Koliyas, numbering eighty thousand kings;
they are capable of providing regular meals according to their own prosperity.
Yet the Blessed One did not go forth for the sake of food; rather, it was for the sake of [realizing] "many incalculable five..."
Having gone forth with the resolve: "By relinquishing through the great renunciation, fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), being liberated, I shall liberate others; being tamed, I shall tame others;

being at peace, I shall bring others to peace; having attained final Nibbāna, I shall lead others to final Nibbāna," he wanders the world liberating others and leading them to final Nibbāna because of his own liberation...
[and so on] ...and because of his own attainment of final Nibbāna, for the sake of showing favor to the brahmin.
It should be understood that he approached the place where the serving was taking place.
Having approached, he stood to one side; thus, having approached, he stood at one side. "To one side" (*ekamantaṃ*) is a neuter locative designation;
it means to one spot or to one side. Alternatively, it is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative.
Within the range of his vision, at the place where he could hear the conversation—standing where the brahmin could see him—he took his stand on high ground.
Having stood there, he emitted from his body a radiance tawny like liquid gold, surpassing the brilliance of a thousand moons and suns, extending eighty cubits all around;
because it completely enveloped them, even the walls, trees, straw mats, and lumps of clay in the brahmin’s workshop [were illuminated].
They appeared as if made of gold. Then, having eaten the milk-rice, people beheld him whose body was adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two supreme major marks,
whose pair of arms was graced by a fathom-wide halo, whose beautiful appearance was radiant like a garland of banners, who was like a moving lotus pond,
like the vault of heaven with its clusters of stars blazing with networks of rays, and like the peak of the Golden Mountain set ablaze.
Seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One standing to one side, blazing with glory, the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja washed his hands and feet, raised his joined palms in salutation, and stood surrounding him.
Then the brahmin Kasībhāradvāja saw the Blessed One standing for alms, surrounded by them; having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One: "I, ascetic..."
“I am threshing and I am sowing.

But why did he speak thus? Was it because of a lack of faith in the Blessed One—who was serene in every limb, inspiring confidence, and had attained the highest self-control and tranquility—or rather, because despite having prepared milk-rice for two thousand five hundred people, he received not even a single spoonful as alms?

“Out of stinginess?”—it was neither. However, seeing that the people had abandoned their work and were not yet satiated with beholding the Blessed One, he felt displeasure, thinking, “He has come to bring about the ruin of my business. Therefore, he spoke thus.
And having seen the perfection of the Blessed One’s marks, he thought, “If this man were to employ himself in business, the people of the entire Jambudīpa [would...].”
"If he were like a crest-jewel upon his head, what purpose of his would not be accomplished?

Even so, by not engaging in manual labor due to laziness, but instead wandering for alms and eating during the auspicious times for sowing and so forth, he lives preoccupied with physical strength"—this was his thought.
Therefore he said: "I, ascetic, plow and I sow; having plowed and sown, I eat."
"My business does not fail, nor am I endowed with such marks as you are"—this is the intended meaning.
"You too, O ascetic... eat; what purpose of yours would not be accomplished being endowed with such marks?"—this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, he heard: "A prince has indeed been born in the Sakyan royal family; he, having renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch..."

“...has gone forth. Therefore, knowing “Now this is he,” and wishing to raise an objection by saying, “It seems you are wearying yourself after abandoning the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch,” he said, “I, however, am an ascetic.
Furthermore, this brahmin of sharp intelligence did not speak out of a desire to disparage the Blessed One;
rather, having seen the excellence of the Blessed One’s physical form, he was reflecting upon the excellence of his wisdom.

He spoke thus even for the purpose of initiating the conversation: "I, indeed, am a recluse. Then the Blessed One, showing himself to be the foremost ploughman and sower in the world with its devas according to those capable of being trained, said: "I, too, am a brahmin.
Thereupon, a thought arose in the brahmin: "This recluse says, 'I plough and I sow,' yet he possesses neither..."
"I see the coarse implements of a ploughman, such as the yoke and the plough; does he speak falsely, or not?

Thus, while scrutinizing the Blessed One from the soles of his feet up to the hair at the crown of his head, [the brahmin]—having performed his studies in the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*) and having recognized the perfection of his thirty-two excellent characteristics—thought, "It is impossible and out of the question that one such as this would speak falsely," and at that very moment, he conceived great reverence.
Abandoning his claim to be an ascetic and addressing the Blessed One by his clan name, he said,
"But we do not see anything [superior] in Master Gotama.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin of sharp wit thought, "He has said this with reference to a profound meaning."
Having understood [the matter] and having questioned [him], desiring to know that meaning, he addressed the Blessed One in verse.
Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda said: "Then the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja addressed the Blessed One in verse.
In this context, "in verse" means by means of speech regulated by syllables and phrases. "Addressed" means spoke.
76–77. In this context, the brahmin speaks of "plowing" as the conjunction of the implements of plowing, such as the yoke and the plow.

However, since it is the power of the Buddhas to speak by planting [a new term] through its similarity to a previous phenomenon, the Blessed One, illustrating that power of the Buddhas and planting [the new term] through its similarity to a previous phenomenon, said:
"Faith is the seed. What, then, is the similarity to the previous phenomenon here?

[Objection: But surely the Blessed One was asked by the brahmin about the equipment for plowing, such as the yoke and the plow, and yet he spoke of sowing seeds that were not asked about, saying, "Faith is the seed.
If this is so, does this discourse not become incoherent? [Reply: It is said: There is no such thing as an incoherent discourse for the Buddhas, nor indeed do the Buddhas...
They speak without introducing a preliminary subject-matter (*pubbadhamma*). In this regard, the connection (*anusandhi*) should be understood as follows:
For the Blessed One was questioned by this brahmin concerning plowing by way of the basic requisites such as the yoke and the plow;
out of compassion for him, and not omitting the fact that "this was not asked," [the Blessed One] explained plowing together with its root, its benefit, its requisites, and its fruit.

Showing the field starting from its very root, he said: "Faith is the seed. For the seed is the root of farming, because when it exists, [farming] must be done, and when it does not exist, it need not be done;
and because it must be done in proportion to that [seed]. Indeed, when the seed exists, they farm;
when it does not exist, they do not. And skilled farmers plow the field according to the measure of the seed, not less.
“May our crop not fail,” he thought, and not more than that, “may our effort not be in vain.

And because the seed itself is the root, the Blessed One, showing cultivation starting from the root, spoke thus—“Faith is the seed”—planting for that brahmin the preliminary factor of his own cultivation, which is analogous to the seed as the preliminary factor of cultivation. Thus it is here.
The similarity of the preceding state (*pubbadhammasabhāga*) should be understood.

If it is asked: "Why was that which was not asked not mentioned later, after having stated only that which was asked?"—it is because of its being beneficial to him and because of its capacity to connect with the teaching (*dhamma*).
For this brahmin is wise, yet, due to being born into a family of wrong views, he is devoid of faith (*saddhā*). Being devoid of faith...
Furthermore, one who possesses wisdom but does not act within his own domain out of faith in others does not attain distinction.

Even his weak faith—characterized merely by a clarity resulting from the departure of the turbidity of the defilements—does not accomplish its purpose when it operates alongside powerful wisdom, like an ox yoked to the same pole as an elephant. Therefore, for him, faith is beneficial. Thus it is for that brahmin.
Because it possesses the quality of being helpful, one who establishes that brahmin in faith may later say this same point—

even though it was stated previously— as an expression of skill in teaching, just as elsewhere it is said: "Faith binds the provisions for the journey," and "Faith is a companion for a person," and "In this world,
faith is the best wealth for a person," and [beginning with] "By means of faith..."
As it is said: “He crosses the flood,” and “The Great Elephant has faith as his hand,” and “The noble disciple, bhikkhus, has faith as his guide.

Just as rain is beneficial to a seed and becomes effective when mentioned immediately after it, so too this meaning, because it is capable of connecting with the Dhamma, was stated previously even though it should have been stated later; it is not something else.

And such is the nature of faith (*saddhā*), beginning with "tranquillity" and so forth. Therein, faith has the characteristic of serene confidence, or the characteristic of conviction; its function is leaping forward;
it is manifested as resolution, or manifested as clarity; its proximate cause is the factors of stream-entry, or its proximate cause is the qualities that are to be believed in.
Or, like the clarity of the surface of a mirror or water, it is a state of clarity for the mind; like the water-clearing gem for water, it is that which clarifies the associated mental states.
As for "seed," it is fivefold: root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, crown-seed, and seed-seed as the fifth.
All of these are designated simply as "seed" in the sense of their capacity to grow.
It proceeds. As it is said: “And this is a seed in the sense of growing.

In that regard, just as for a brahmin the seed, which is the root of his farming, performs two functions—it establishes itself below by means of its root and causes a sprout to emerge above—so too, faith, which is the root of the Blessed One’s farming, [establishes itself] below...
It is established upon the root of virtue and causes the sprouts of serenity and insight to emerge above.
Just as that [stalk] grows by taking up the essence of the earth and the essence of water through its root for the purpose of attaining the ripening of grain via its stalk,

so too does this [mind] take up the essence of serenity and insight by means of the root of virtue, for the purpose of attaining the ripening of the grain of the noble fruit via the stalk of the noble path.

It increases. And just as that [tree], having been established on good ground, attains growth, development, and abundance through the production of roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and trunks, and having produced milk, brings forth a rice-head filled with many grains of rice;

even so, this [faith], having been established in the continuum of consciousness, [increases] by means of the purifications of virtue, mind, view, overcoming of doubt, knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, and knowledge and vision of the way.

Having attained growth, increase, and abundance, it produces the milk of purification of knowledge and vision, and brings forth the fruit of arahantship, which is filled with the various analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Faith is the seed.
Herein, one might ask: "When more than fifty wholesome states arise together, why is faith alone called the seed?"
"...is it so stated? It is said: because it performs the function of a seed.
For just as among those [faculties] consciousness alone performs the function of cognizing, so too does faith perform the function of a seed; and that [faith] is the root of all wholesome states.
As it is said: "One who has become endowed with faith approaches; approaching, he pays respect; paying respect, he lends an ear."
He listens to the Dhamma with attentive ears; having heard the Dhamma, he retains it; he examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained;
as he examines the meaning, the teachings become acceptable through reflection; when there is acceptance through reflection on the teachings, zeal arises;
being zealous, he exerts himself; having exerted himself, he weighs the matter; having weighed it, he strives; and being resolute, he applies himself.
"One realizes the supreme truth with the body itself, and one sees it through having penetrated it with wisdom.

*Tapo* means that which "burns up" unwholesome states and the body; it is a designation for the restraint of the sense faculties, energy, the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and the performance of difficult austerities.
Here, however, the restraint of the sense faculties is intended. *Vuṭṭhi* refers to rain-fall, wind-fall, and so forth.
It is of many kinds; here, however, the rain-fall is intended.

For just as the seed and the crop rooted in that seed, when sustained by a Brahmin’s rain-fall, sprout, do not wither, and reach fruition, so too the faith and the qualities such as virtue rooted in faith, when sustained by the Blessed One’s restraint of the faculties, sprout, do not wither, and reach fulfillment.
They reach fulfillment. Therefore he said: "Austerity is the rain. And here, the word "me" (mine) mentioned in the phrase "wisdom is mine" should also be applied to these other terms:
"Faith is my seed; austerity is my rain. What does this illustrate?
It shows, O Brahmin, that when a seed has been sown by you, it is well if there is rain; but if there is not, water must also be given.
Thus, when I have yoked the plow-pole of wisdom with the yoke-pin of moral shame, fastened it together with the rope of the mind,
and having hitched on the oxen of energy, pierced them with the goad of mindfulness, and sown the seeds of faith in the field of my own mental continuum,
there is no lack of rain. This constant and continuous austerity of mine is that very rain.

A person understands by means of this, or it itself understands; thus it is wisdom (*paññā*). That [wisdom] is of many kinds, distinguished as belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.
However, in this context, what is intended is the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*) together with insight (*vipassanā*). "Yoke and plough" (*yuganaṅgala*) refers to both the yoke and the plough.
For just as a Brahmin has a yoke and a plough, so too does the Blessed One have two kinds of wisdom. In that regard, just as the yoke...
The plowshare serves as a support, stands at the front, is bound to the pole, serves as a support for the yokes, and maintains the oxen’s movement together;
in the same way, wisdom serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for those qualities that have moral shame (*hiri*) as their foremost. As it is said:
“All wholesome states have wisdom as their leader,” and, “They say that wisdom is the best among wholesome things, like the king of the constellations.”
And [it is said]: "Of the stars... It stands at the forefront in the sense of being the precursor to wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). As it is said:

"Virtue, a sense of shame (*hirī*), and the Dhamma of the virtuous are the followers of one possessed of wisdom. Because it does not arise apart from a sense of shame (*hirī*), it is "yoked to the pole" (*īsābaddhā*);
because it serves as the supporting condition for the rope of concentration known as the mind, it is the support for the ropes.
It exists; by preventing the states of excessive tension and excessive laxity, it maintains the simultaneous movement of those bound by the power of energy (*vīriya*).

And just as a plough yoked with a ploughshare breaks through the density of the earth at the time of tilling and tears up the root-continua, so too wisdom (*paññā*) conjoined with mindfulness, at the time of insight (*vipassanā*), [breaks through] the density of the continuity, the collection, the function, and the object of phenomena.
It breaks and utterly shatters the continuities that are the roots of all defilements. And that is indeed supramundane; however, the other [type] may also be mundane.
Therefore he said: "Wisdom is my yoke and plough.
By this, a person is put to shame, or it itself puts one to shame, for it causes one to loathe the occurrence of unwholesome states; thus it is called *hirī*. By the inclusion of that—
Through its association with it, shame (*ottappa*) is indeed included. The *īsā* is a wooden pole that supports the yoke and plough.
For just as a brahmin’s *īsā* supports the yoke and plough, so too does the Blessed One’s sense of shame (*hirī*) support the yoke and plough known as mundane and supramundane wisdom (*paññā*);
for in the absence of shame, wisdom would not exist. And just as the yoke and plough are bound to the *īsā*, [so too is wisdom bound to shame].

Just as a well-made axle performs its function, being steady and not loose, so too wisdom bound by moral shame (hiri) performs its function, being steady, not loose, and uninterrupted by moral shamelessness (ahirika). Therefore it is said: "Shame is the pole.
It "thinks" (munāti), thus it is "mind" (mano); this is a designation for consciousness. But here, by the term "mind," the concentration associated with it is meant.

This is what is intended. "Yotta" means a rope-fastening. That is threefold: the fastening of the yoke together with the pole, the fastening of the oxen together with the yoke, and the fastening of the oxen together with the charioteer.
In this regard, just as the brahmin’s yotta, having bound the pole, the yoke, and the oxen into one, directs them toward their respective duties, so too [is it] for the Blessed One.

Concentration (samādhi) binds all those qualities—modesty (hiri), wisdom (paññā), energy (vīriya), and the [other] wholesome states—to a single object by way of non-distraction, and thus establishes them in their respective functions.
Therefore it is said: "The mind is the tether.
Memory (sati) is so called because by means of it a person remembers things done long ago and so forth, or because it itself remembers; its characteristic is non-forgetfulness.
It ploughs, thus it is a plough (*phāla*). One drives with this, thus it is a driver (*pājana*);
here it is called "the driver," which is a designation for a goad-stick. A plough and a driver are "plough-and-driver.

Just as a brahmin has a plough-and-driver, so too does the Blessed One have mindfulness associated with insight and associated with the path. In that regard, just as the plough protects the ploughshare, [so does mindfulness protect the mind].
And it goes before him; thus, when one is seeking the courses of wholesome states or establishing them upon the object, one guards the plow of wisdom.
For it is called "guard" in such passages as, "He dwells with a mind guarded by mindfulness.
And it stands before him by way of non-forgetfulness; for when the states have been cultivated by mindfulness, wisdom—

He understands it, not forgetting it. And just as a goad, while showing oxen the fear of being pierced, does not allow them to sink down, and restrains them from going off the path, so too mindfulness, while showing the oxen of energy the fear of the states of woe, does not allow them to sink into indolence;
and having restrained their wandering in the improper range known as the strands of sensual pleasure, it enjoins them to the meditation subject.
And he restrains one from going on a wrong path. Therefore he said: "Mindfulness is my ploughshare.
(78) "Guarded in body" means protected by the three kinds of good conduct of the body. "Guarded in speech" means protected by the four kinds of good conduct of speech.
Up to this point, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha has been explained. Regarding the phrase "restrained in food within the belly," here it is by way of food that...
Because all conditions are included therein, the meaning is: "one who is restrained and self-controlled regarding even the fourfold set of conditions, and thus free from defilement.

By this, the virtue of purity of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhisīla*) is stated. "Restrained in the belly" means one who is restrained and self-controlled in the belly, that is, one who eats moderately;
it is said that such a person knows the proper measure in food. By way of this moderation in eating, the virtue of using the requisites (*paccayapaṭisevanasīla*) is stated.

What does this illustrate? Just as you, brahmin, having sown seed, construct a fence of thorns, or a fence of trees, or a surrounding wall for the sake of protecting the crop, so that herds of cattle, buffalo, and deer, finding no entrance, do not ravage the harvest;
even so have I, having sown the seed of faith, [constructed a fence] for the sake of protecting the various kinds of wholesome crops.
I create a threefold enclosure consisting of the restraint of body, speech, and livelihood.
By means of this, the herds of unwholesome states such as lust—comparable to cattle, buffalo, and deer—being unable to gain entry, shall not destroy the various kinds of wholesome crops.
"I make truth my plowshare" (*saccaṃ karomi niddānaṃ*): here, truth is non-deception through the two doors [of body and speech]. "Plowshare" (*niddānaṃ*) means cutting.
The word *lūnānaṃ* means "uprooting"; here it should be understood as an accusative case used in the sense of the instrument. For this is the meaning here:

"I perform the weeding by means of truth. What is meant? Just as you, having ploughed the external field, perform the weeding of the weeds that damage the crops by hand or with a sickle; even so, I too, having ploughed the internal field...
"I make the mowing of the grasses of deception, which destroy what is wholesome, by means of truth.

Or, "truth" here should be understood as the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*), which is called "knowledge of things as they really are" (*yathābhūtañāṇa*). By that [truth], one makes the mowing of the grasses such as the perception of self;
thus it should be construed. Alternatively, "mowing" (*niddāna*) means that which cuts or reaps, that which uproots.
The meaning is as follows. This being so, it is appropriate to speak using the accusative case alone, saying:
"I make truth [the object] such that I make a servant or a laborer mow it—saying 'Mow the grass!'—making him one who cuts, reaps, and pulls out the grass.
Alternatively, *saccaṃ* means the truth of view (*diṭṭhisacca*). I make that [truth] something to be mowed down; it is to be cut away.
"It shall be plucked out; I shall do it"—even in this way, it is appropriate to speak using the accusative case.

Regarding the phrase "gentleness (soracca) is my liberation," that which is called "gentleness" here as "non-transgression of body and non-transgression of speech" refers specifically to virtue (sīla);
it is not what is intended here, for this has already been stated in the passage beginning with "one who guards the body."
According to this method, however, the fruit of arahantship is intended. For that too is called "gentleness" (*soracca*) because of its state of delighting in the beautiful Nibbāna.
"Release" (*pamocana*) means the relinquishing of what is yoked. What is meant?
Just as your release would not be a true release if you were to be yoked again this evening, or on the second day, or in a future year; [so it is with the other states].
It is not so for me. For there is no such thing as a "release from the middle" for me.

Indeed, from the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara onwards, having yoked the plow of wisdom with the oxen of energy, I did not cease plowing the great field until I had completed four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, and until I fully awakened to perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). And when it was [attained] by me...
Having spent all that time, while sitting on the invincible throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the fruit of Arhatship—accompanied by all its virtues—arose.
At that moment, I was liberated through the attainment of the subsiding of all exertion;
it shall not need to be applied again. It is with reference to this matter that the Blessed One said: "Gentleness is my liberation."
79. "Vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhaṃ" (Energy is my beast of burden for the yoke). Here, "vīriya" refers to the exertion described by such methods as "either physical or mental arousal of energy.
*Dhuradhorayhaṃ* means that which bears the yoke (*dhuraṃ dhorayhaṃ*); the sense is that it carries the burden.
For just as a ploughshare drawn by a beast of burden at the brahmin’s yoke breaks through the density of the earth and [severs] the root-creepers...
And it cleaves asunder; even so does the Blessed One’s ploughshare of wisdom, drawn by energy, break through the aforementioned mass and cleave asunder the continuities of the defilements.

Therefore he said: "Energy is my beast of burden. Alternatively, those that carry the initial load are "dhurā," while those that carry the fundamental load are "dhorayhā"; thus, "dhuradhorayhā" means both the dhurā and the dhorayhā. In this context—
Just as for a farmer, when each pair of oxen— distinguished by their fourfold strength— carries the yoke and burden,
they accomplish the destruction of both existing and non-existing weeds and the perfection of the grain crop; even so, when the Blessed One’s energy,
distinguished by the four right strivings, carries the yoke and burden, it accomplishes the destruction of both existing and non-existing unwholesome roots and the perfection of the wholesome.
Therefore he said: "Energy is my yoke-bearer.
Regarding the phrase "the bearer of security from bondage": here, Nibbāna is called "security from bondage" (yogakkhema) because it is secure from the bonds (yoga);
that which carries one toward it, or carries one facing toward it, is the "bearer" (adhivāhana). It is the bearer of security from bondage.

"Carrying security from bondage. What does this illustrate? Just as your draft-ox is yoked and driven toward the eastern direction, or the western, or any other direction, so too my draft-ox is yoked and driven toward Nibbāna.
And being thus driven, it goes without turning back. Just as your draft-ox carrying the plough...
Having reached the furrow’s edge, it turns back again; thus, from the time of Dīpaṅkara onwards, it goes on without turning back.

Or rather, because the defilements abandoned by each respective path do not need to be abandoned again and again—unlike the grass cut by your plow, which must be cut yet again at another time—for this reason also, this [path]...

It goes without turning back, abandoning the defilements associated with views by means of the first path, the gross defilements by means of the second, the residual defilements by means of the third, and all defilements by means of the fourth.
Alternatively, "it goes without turning back" (gacchati anivattanti) means it goes having become free from turning back. "It" (taṃ) refers to that draft-ox. Thus it is here.

The word-division should be understood thus: "And as this draft-ox of yours goes, it does not go to that place where, having gone, the farmer—becoming sorrowless, free from grief, and stainless—does not grieve;
rather, it goes to that place where, having gone, he does not grieve, where by the ripening of mindfulness this draft-ox of energy [is led]."
"Having gone forth while still admonishing [others], one such as I, having become a farmer free from sorrow, free from grief, and free from dust, does not grieve;
he goes to that state known as the deathless Nibbāna, which is the uprooting of all the arrows of sorrow.
Now, concluding [the discourse], the Blessed One spoke this verse:
“Thus this farming has been done; it bears the fruit of the Deathless.
Having performed this farming, one is released from all suffering.
This is its summary meaning: O Brahmin, this farming was performed by me with faith as the seed, supported by the rain of asceticism (tapas).
Having bound together the yoke and plough made of wisdom, the pole made of moral shame, and the yoke-tie made of mind;
having driven the ploughshare of mindfulness into the yoke of wisdom, having taken up the goad of mindfulness, having guarded it by the protection of body,
speech, and livelihood, having made truth the watering place, and gentleness the release— he proceeds with vigor as the draft-animal bearing the burden toward security from bondage.
By driving [the oxen] without turning back, he has brought to completion the fourfold fruit of recluseship, which is the culmination of the work of farming;
that fruit is the fruit of the deathless. This is that farming which has the deathless as its fruit. "The deathless" refers to Nibbāna; the meaning is that it has Nibbāna as its benefit.
Furthermore, this farming does not have the deathless as its fruit for me alone; rather, it is also...
"Whoever—whether a kshatriya, a brahmin, a vaisya, a sudra, a householder, or one gone forth—it is this plowing that they plow.

Having plowed this plowing, everyone is liberated from all suffering; they are liberated from the entire round of existence, from the suffering of pain, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change.
Thus the Blessed One concluded his teaching for the brahmin, bringing it to its conclusion with the attainment of arahantship as the goal and Nibbana as the ultimate end.
Then the brahmin, having heard the teaching of profound meaning, understood: "Having enjoyed the fruit of my own plowing, I become hungry again the very next day;
but his plowing has the deathless as its fruit, and by enjoying its fruit, one is liberated from all suffering.
Thus, being inspired with faith, he began to offer milk-rice in order to manifest that faith. Therefore it was said: "Then the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja..."

In that context, "mahatiyā" means "with a large [ladle]. "Kaṃsapātiyā" means in a golden bowl—specifically, in his own golden dish worth a hundred thousand [pieces]. "Vaḍḍhetvā" means having touched it;

what is meant is that he poured [the contents] into it. "Upanāmesi bhagavato" means that having made it variegated with ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, having covered it with a *dukūla* cloth canopy, and having lifted it up, he respectfully offered it to the Blessed One.
They brought it to the Tathāgata, saying: "May the venerable Gotama eat the milk-rice; the venerable one is a farmer.
Then he stated the reason that establishes his status as a farmer: "For... [he] plows," which means: because the venerable one... [he] plows.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said: "I do not accept a song in verse."
81. *Tattha gāthābhigītan* means "sung with verses"; it is said that [the food] was obtained after verses had been spoken.
*Me* means "by me. *Abhojaneyyan* means "not fit to be eaten. *Sampassatan* means "one who sees correctly," that is, one who perceives purity of livelihood;
or alternatively, "one who sees all around," which is what is meant by "sampassatan. *Buddhānan* means "of the Buddhas. *Nesa dhammo* means "this is not their practice."
"One should eat what is sung to with verses"—this is not the Dhamma, nor is it proper conduct;
therefore, the Buddhas reject, refuse, and do not eat what is sung to with verses. But was it for the sake of the milk-rice that the Blessed One sang the verses, such that he spoke thus?
They were not sung for that purpose; rather, from early morning onwards—
Standing near the field, having failed to receive even a spoonful of alms, he again proclaimed the entire range of the Buddha’s qualities;
what was thus obtained is like that which is gained by dancing and singing with actors and dancers. Therefore, it is called "accompanied by verses" (*gāthābhigīta*).
And because such a thing is not permitted for Buddhas, it is called "unfit for consumption" (*abhojaneyya*). This is in accordance with their fewness of desires (*appicchatā*).
It does not exist; therefore, it was also spoken thus out of compassion for future generations.

And when even those who reject gains arising from their own virtues proclaimed by others—such as the humble potter Ghaṭīkāra—refuse them, how much more so would the Blessed One, who possesses the perfection of fewness of wishes, do so by proclaiming his own virtues himself?
"He will accept the gain that has arisen; therefore, this is indeed appropriate conduct for the Blessed One.

To this extent, he frees himself from this worldly reproach: "The ascetic Gotama accepted food by making a Brahmin who was faithless and unwilling to give become willing to give through the singing of verses; his teaching is motivated by material gain."
Having elucidated purity of teaching, he now spoke to elucidate purity of livelihood: “O Brahmin, when this Dhamma exists, this is the mode of conduct.

The meaning of this is as follows: when the Dhamma of purity of livelihood, or the Dhamma of the tenfold good conduct, or the Dhamma of the Buddhas’ proper behavior exists—being present, unimpaired, and prevailing—this mode of conduct is exclusively pure, like the sky.
“Brahmins, the seeking and the quest for the livelihood of the Buddhas is limited to the stretching forth of the hand.
When this was said, the brahmin felt dejection, thinking, “He rejects my milk-rice; it seems this food is improper.
Alas, I am unfortunate; I do not get the chance to give a gift. He then thought, “Perhaps he might accept something else.”

And he thought thus. Knowing this, the Blessed One reflected: "I have come having delimited the time for my alms-round, thinking, 'In this much time I shall inspire confidence in this brahmin,' yet the brahmin has fallen into dejection.
Now, because of that dejection, his mind will be agitated toward me and he will not be able to penetrate the supreme Dhamma of the Deathless. [Thus he spoke] to the brahmin.
In order to inspire confidence and fulfill the aspiration he had made, he said: "And by another, the Kevalin.

Therein, "Kevalin" means one who is perfected in all virtues, or one who is dissociated from all bonds (*yoga*). He is a "Great Seer" (*mahesi*) because he seeks after the great qualities of the aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth.
He is "one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsava*) because all his taints have been utterly exhausted. [He is free] from the fidgeting of hands and feet, etc.
"Having calmed all remorse, it is 'one whose remorse is calmed' (kukkuccavūpasantaṃ). 'Serve' means provide food and show honor.
Even though this thought was thus aroused by the brahmin, he spoke only by way of indirect phrasing; he did not say, "Give," or "Bring it here.
The rest here is self-evident.
Then the brahmin, thinking, "This milk-rice has been brought for the Blessed One; I am not worthy to give it to anyone according to my own whim," said, "To whom then shall I give it?
Thereupon the Blessed One, knowing that apart from the Tathāgata and the Tathāgata’s disciples, no one else was capable of digesting that milk-rice, said, "I will not have it. In this context:

By the phrase "together with the devas" (sadevaka), the inclusion is of the devas belonging to the five sensual-sphere realms; by the phrase "together with Māra" (samāraka), the inclusion is of the devas of the sixth sensual-sphere realm;

by the phrase "together with Brahmā" (sabrahmaka), the inclusion is of the Brahmās of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). As for those of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), it is impossible that they would partake [of the merit].

By the phrase "together with recluses and brahmins" (sassamaṇabrāhmaṇi), there is the inclusion of those recluses and brahmins who are adversaries and enemies of the Teaching, as well as the inclusion of those recluses and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil.
By the word "generation" (pajā), the world of beings is included; by the phrase "together with devas and humans," conventional devas and the remainder of humanity are included.
Thus, it should be understood that here the world of space is included by three terms, while the world of beings is included by two terms through the word "generation.
This is the summary; however, we shall explain the detailed exposition in the Āḷavaka Sutta.
But why would it not undergo a complete transformation for anyone among those including the world of the devas? Because of the addition of subtle nutritive essence (*ojā*) to the coarse [food].

For in this milk-rice (*pāyāsa*), as soon as it was taken up for the sake of the Blessed One, the devas added nutritive essence—just as in the case of Sujātā’s milk-rice, while Cunda’s *sūkaramaddava* was being cooked, and with every morsel taken by the Blessed One at Verañjā.
And in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, regarding the sugar remaining in Kaccāna’s jar of sugar:
because he had added coarse [sugar] to fine, divine food, it did not digest for the gods. For the gods have subtle bodies; coarse human food does not properly digest for them.
Nor does it digest for humans. For humans have coarse bodies, while their [suitable food] is fine, divine food.
It does not digest properly. But for the Tathāgata, it is digested by his natural digestive fire alone and is properly assimilated.
