Some say this is due to the power of the body and the power of knowledge; for a disciple of the Tathāgata whose taints are destroyed, it is digested through the power of concentration and moderation in eating, whereas even for others who possess psychic powers, it is not so digested.
Or rather, the reason here is inconceivable; this is the domain of the Buddhas.
"Therefore, you indeed"—this means: because I see no other [who would do so], it is not permissible for me; and what is not permissible for me is also not permissible for my disciple.
Therefore, "you, O Brahmin," is what is meant. "In a place where there is little greenery" means:

where the green grass is sparse, or where the green grass has only recently sprouted, resembling a stone surface. "In a place free of living beings" means: devoid of living creatures, by reason of having strewn milk-rice (pāyāsa) over it.

Or [it is] in a great mass of water devoid of living beings that must be killed. This was said for the purpose of protecting the grass and the creatures dwelling in the grass along with those creatures themselves.
It makes a sound such as "cicciṭāyati" or "ciṭiciṭāyati.
"Saṃdhūpāyati" means it smokes all around; "sampadhūpāyati" means it likewise smokes intensely. Why did it become thus?
It was through the power of the Blessed One, and not through the power of the water, nor the milk-rice, nor the brahmin, nor any other gods, yakṣas, or the like.
For the Blessed One made such a resolution for the sake of inspiring a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in the brahmin. "Seyyathāpi nāma" is merely an illustration by way of a simile;
it means simply "just as," as much as was stated by the word "phālo. He was stirred in mind and his hair stood on end in his body.
It is said that on his body there were ninety-nine thousand hair-pores, which stood upright like jeweled pegs driven into a golden wall.
The rest is self-evident.
Having prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet and greatly rejoicing in the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! Here, this word *abhikkanta* is used in the sense of expressing great appreciation.
However, its detailed explanation of the meaning will be revealed in the commentary on the *Maṅgala Sutta*.
And because it is used in the sense of expressing great appreciation, it should be understood that what is meant is: “Well said, well said, Master Gotama!”
“A wise person should employ repetition in cases of fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, laughter, sorrow, and joy.

By this characteristic, it should be understood that here [the word] is stated twice by way of both joy and praise. Alternatively, *abhikkantaṃ* means *abhikantaṃ*, which is to say: exceedingly desired, exceedingly agreeable, exceedingly beautiful.
In this context, he praises the teaching with one instance of the word *abhikkanta*, and his own confidence with the other.
For this is the intended meaning here: "Excellent, Master Gotama, is this Dhamma-teaching of Master Gotama;
excellent is this Dhamma-teaching of Master Gotama by which my confidence has arisen. Or else, it is the Blessed One’s own speech.
He praises by way of two pairs of meanings: the word of Master Gotama is excellent because it destroys faults and because it leads to the attainment of virtues;
likewise, because it generates faith and because it generates wisdom; because it is meaningful and because it is well-phrased;
because its words are clear and its meaning is profound; because it is pleasant to the ear and heart-stirring; because it does not exalt oneself and does not disparage others.

It should be connected with such qualities as being cooled by compassion, purified by wisdom, delightful to the sight, capable of withstanding scrutiny, pleasant when heard, and beneficial when investigated.
Beyond that, he further praises the teaching itself by means of four similes. Therein, "upturned" (*nikkujjita*) means placed face downwards.
"Or with its opening facing downwards. "He should turn it upright" means he should make it face upwards. "Covered" means covered with grass, leaves, and so forth.

"He should uncover" means he should remove [the covering]. "Of one who is lost" means of one who has lost his sense of direction. "He should point out the way" means he should take him by the hand and say, "This is the way.
"In the dark" means [in darkness] caused by the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the middle of the night, dense forests, or masses of clouds.
"In the fourfold darkness. This, first, is the literal meaning of the words.

But this is the intended construction: "Just as one might set upright what had been overturned," so by raising me up from the unrighteousness into which I had fallen and from which I was turned away from the True Dhamma; "just as one might uncover what was concealed," so...
Since the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation, you have revealed the teaching that had been shrouded by the thicket of wrong views;
just as one might point out the path to one who is lost, so have you pointed out to me, who had entered upon a by-path and a wrong path, the way to heaven and liberation;
just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so have you done for me, who was submerged in the darkness of delusion.

Because the Blessed Gotama has taught to me through these various methods— by bearing the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which obscures my vision of the forms of the Jewels beginning with the Buddha—
the Dhamma has been elucidated by him in manifold ways.
Alternatively, it is because this Dhamma, through a certain measure [of practice], leads to the seeing of suffering and the abandoning of the perversion that perceives the "beautiful" in the "ugly."
It is like turning over what was overturned; it is like uncovering what was concealed by abandoning the perversion that perceives suffering as pleasure through the vision of its origin;
it is like pointing out the path to one who is lost by abandoning the perversion that perceives the impermanent as permanent through the vision of cessation;
and it is like [pointing out the path] by abandoning the perversion that perceives the non-self as self through the vision of the path.
And it is like a light in the darkness; therefore, just as one might set upright what had been overturned...
[and so on] ...or hold up a lamp, thinking, "Those with eyes may see forms," even so has this been made manifest.

Furthermore, herein the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) is manifested through faith, warmth, bodily restraint, and so forth; the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) is manifested through wisdom.
The aggregate of concentration is shown by means of moral shame (*hiri*) and so forth; cessation is shown by means of security from bondage (*yogakkhema*).

Thus, two Noble Truths—the Noble Path consisting of three aggregates and Cessation—are explained according to their specific nature. Therein, the Path is the antidote to the Origin, and Cessation is the antidote to Suffering;
thus, they are two [truths] by way of their respective antidotes. In this manner, the four Truths are explained.
Therefore, it should be understood that this has been explained by way of many methods.

Regarding the phrase "Esāham" and so forth: "Esāham" means "this I am. Although he had already gone for refuge by prostrating with his head at the feet through physical homage, he spoke now while formally undertaking [the precepts] through speech. Alternatively, it may mean that by means of prostration, he had already gone for refuge to the Buddha alone.
Now, beginning with that [ordination], he spoke in order to proceed to the rest of the Dhamma and Saṅgha. "From this day forward" (*ajjatagge*) means starting from today;
or the reading is *ajjadagge*, where the letter *da* is for the sake of euphonic junction (*padasandhi*), meaning "making today the limit.
"Endowed with life" (*pāṇupetaṃ*) means endowed as long as my life continues; it is "having no other teacher" through the three goings for refuge.
The meaning is: "May the venerable Gotama remember me as one who has gone for refuge; may he know [me as such].

Up to this point, the practice corresponding to what was heard has been shown by him. Alternatively, having shown the excellence of the Teacher through the "upside-down" bowl incident and others, the excellence of the disciple is shown by this passage beginning with "I am such a one.
Or, having shown the acquisition of wisdom by that [previous account], the acquisition of faith is shown by this [present account].
Now, desiring to perform that which must be done by one who possesses wisdom and has thus acquired faith, he requests the Blessed One, saying, "May I receive [it].

Therein, with a mind deeply inspired by the Blessed One’s supernormal powers and other qualities, thinking, "The Blessed One himself went forth, having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch;
how much more so should I?", he requests the going-forth out of faith.
In this context, one who aspires for the attainment of wisdom through its fulfillment [is described]. The rest is self-evident.
Regarding the passage beginning "one who is secluded," however: "one" means by physical seclusion; "secluded" means by mental seclusion;
"diligent" means by not abandoning mindfulness regarding the meditation subject; "ardent" means by ardor consisting of physical and mental energy; "resolute" means...
Dwelling with no regard for body or life, by means of a certain mode of deportment.
"Not long thereafter" refers to the time following his going forth. "Noble sons" (*kulaputta*) are of two kinds: noble sons by birth and noble sons by conduct;

this one, however, is a noble son in both respects. "From the home" means from the house. That which is beneficial to homes is "household life" (*agāriya*), consisting of the work of farming, cattle-herding, and so forth, for the sake of maintaining a family.
It is called "homeless" (*anagāriya*) because there is no household life (*agāriya*) here; this is a designation for the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
"They go forth" means they approach or draw near to it. "That unsurpassed" (*tadanuttaraṃ*) means that which is unsurpassed.

"The consummation of the holy life" (*brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ*) refers to the consummation of the holy life of the Path; what is meant is the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*). It is for the sake of that [fruit]...
Noble sons go forth into homelessness. "In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in that very same personal existence (*attabhāve*).

"Having realized for oneself through direct knowledge" (*sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā*) means having made it manifest to oneself by means of one's own wisdom; the meaning is that he knew it independently of others. "Having attained and dwelt" (*upasampajja vihāsi*) means that having reached and fulfilled [the goal], he dwelt.
And while dwelling thus, he understood: "Birth is exhausted... [etc. ...he directly knew. By this, his...
It shows the plane of reviewing.
But which birth of his has been destroyed, and how did he directly know it? It is said: First of all, his past birth has not been destroyed, because it was already destroyed previously;
nor has his future birth been destroyed, because there is no further effort to be made regarding the future; nor has his present birth been destroyed, because it still exists.

However, that birth— which, due to the non-cultivation of the path, would have arisen in one, four, or five-aggregate existences as the various divisions of one, four, or five aggregates— has been exhausted by the fact that,
through the cultivation of the path, it has reached the state of non-arising. Having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the cultivation of the path,
he sees that even though karma still exists in the absence of defilements, it will not lead to rebirth in the future.
"He knows" means he knows [that it] "has occurred.

"Lived" (*vusita*) means dwelt upon, fully lived through; the meaning is that it has been performed, practiced, and brought to completion. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the holy life of the Path.
"What was to be done has been done" means that, regarding the four truths, by way of the four paths, there has been full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development.

The meaning is that the sixteenfold duty has been brought to completion. "There is nothing further of this nature" means that now there is no further cultivation of the path for the sake of such a state of being—namely, for these sixteen duties or for the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*).
Alternatively, "of this nature" (*itthattāya*) means from this state of being;
from this very present continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*), there is no further continuum of aggregates [to arise].
There is none. However, he realized: "These five aggregates remain with their roots cut off, like a tree that has been felled.
"A certain one" means one person. "Among the Arahants" means among the Arahants who were great disciples;
the venerable Bhāradvāja was one of them—this, it is said, is the intended meaning here.
The commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Paramatthajotikā, is completed. 5.
Commentary on the Cunda Sutta.

83. *Cundasutta*: "I ask the Sage of abundant wisdom. What is its origin? Briefly stated, there are four types of origins—those arising from one's own inclination, from another's inclination, from a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), and from a question—and this sutta originates from a question.
In detail, however, at one time the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Mallas with a great community of monks, arrived at Pāvā.
There the Blessed One was staying at Pāvā in Cunda the smith’s mango grove. From this point until:

"Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and together with the community of monks, approached the residence of Cunda the smith; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat..."
"sat down"— this should be expanded upon according to the method already established in the Sutta.
When the Blessed One was thus seated with the community of monks, Cunda the smith, while serving the community of monks headed by the Buddha,
provided golden vessels for the monks to receive the side dishes, soups, and other foods.
He presented them. Since the training rule had not yet been laid down, some bhikkhus accepted the golden vessels while others did not.
However, the Blessed One had only one vessel, his own stone bowl;
Buddhas do not accept a second vessel. Therein, a certain wicked bhikkhu [offered] a golden vessel worth a thousand [pieces].
With a thieving mind, he placed [the food] into the key-case that had been brought for his own meal.
After Cunda had finished eating, washed his hands and feet, and was paying homage to the Blessed One while looking toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he saw that bhikkhu;
yet, having seen him, he acted as if he did not see him and said nothing to him, [focusing instead] on the Blessed One and the elders.
Furthermore, it was out of respect, thinking, "May the path of speech of those with wrong view not be heard.
Desiring to know, "Are ascetics only those who possess restraint, or are there also such as these whose restraint is broken?
he approached the Blessed One in the evening and said, "I ask you, O Sage."

In this context, "I ask" follows the method explained in the *Niddesa* by way of the passage beginning: "There are three kinds of questions: the question for the illumination of what has not been seen," and so forth.
As for "the sage" (*muni*), this also follows the method beginning: "'Sagehood' (*mona*) is said to be knowledge (*ñāṇa*). That which is wisdom, understanding...
right view—endowed with that knowledge one is a sage, one who has attained sagehood; there are three kinds of sagehood: bodily sagehood," and so forth.
It is exactly as stated there. This, however, is the summary here:

"I ask" (*pucchāmi*)—thus, seeking permission, he addresses the Sage (*muni*), the Blessed One who is the Sage of sages. "Of abundant wisdom" (*pahūtapañña*) and so forth are words of praise; with these, he praises that Sage.
Therein, "of abundant wisdom" means one of vast wisdom. Its vastness should be understood from its reaching the very limit of all that is knowable (*ñeyya*).
"Thus Cunda the smith's son"—these two [terms] follow the same method as stated in the Dhaniya Sutta.
From here on, however, without saying even this much and discarding the entire stated method, we shall explain only the unstated method.
"Buddha" refers to the third Buddha among the three Buddhas. "Lord of the Dhamma" is said because he is the progenitor of the Path-Dhamma, just as a father is to a son.
He is the father of the Dhamma, like a father to those who have produced the fields of craft and so forth;
he is the teacher, the Lord of the Dhamma, the King of the Dhamma, and one who wields mastery over the Dhamma—this is the meaning. And this has been said:
"For that Blessed One, brahmin, is the arouser of the path not yet arisen, the producer of the path not yet produced..."
“He is the proclaimer of the path not previously proclaimed; he knows the path, understands the path, and is skilled in the path.
Furthermore, his disciples now dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.
“Free from craving” means devoid of craving for sense-pleasures, existence, and non-existence. “Supreme among bipeds” means the highest among those with two feet. In this regard:
Furthermore, the Blessed One is not only the supreme among bipeds; rather, he is the supreme among all beings—whether they be footless, two-footed, or...
[as far as] those who are neither percipient nor non-percipient. However, he is specifically called "supreme among bipeds" by way of defining the highest limit.
For bipeds are the most exalted among all beings, such as the Wheel-turning Monarchs, the Great Disciples, and the Pacceka Buddhas.
In this context, when it is said that he is "the supreme among them" by virtue of his arising, it is effectively said that he is "the supreme among all beings.
Regarding the phrase "the most excellent of charioteers": one who guides is a *sārathi*; this is a designation for elephant trainers and the like.
And the Blessed One is the most excellent among them because of his capacity to tame those who are to be tamed by men through his unsurpassed method of taming. As it has been said:
“Monks, when an elephant tamer has trained an elephant, it runs only in one direction:
either east, west, north, or south. Monks, when a horse tamer has trained a horse… [as before] …when a bull tamer has trained a bull… [as before] …it runs only in one direction:
either east, west, north, or south. For, monks, by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—”
“The tamed person, when urged, runs in eight directions: possessing form, he sees forms—this is the first direction...
[and so on] ...having entered and dwelt in the cessation of perception and feeling—this is the eighth direction.

“How many? is a question regarding the classification of the meaning. “In the world” means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). “Ascetics” is an indication of the subject to be questioned. “Come now” (*iṅgha*) is a particle used in the sense of an entreaty. “Come now, tell me that” (*tadiṅgha brūhi*) means “come now, explain and speak of it.”
84. When this had been said, the Blessed One, seeing Cunda the smith asking not a question of a householder—beginning with "Venerable sir, what is wholesome?
What is unwholesome?"—but rather a question of a recluse, reflected and understood: "He asks this concerning that wicked bhikkhu.
Thereupon, demonstrating to him that the man was no recluse except in name alone, he spoke as follows:
He said, "There are four kinds of recluses. In this context, "four" is a numerical delimitation. Regarding "recluses" (*samaṇā*):
sometimes the Blessed One uses the term "recluse" for followers of other sects (*titthiya*), as he said: "Those various vows, ceremonies, and auspicious rites of the many recluses and brahmins.
Sometimes he uses it for worldlings (*puthujjana*), as he said: "Monks, people perceive them, saying, 'Recluses, recluses!'"
Sometimes it refers to those in training (*sekkha*), as it is said: "Right here, monks, is the ascetic; right here is the second ascetic.

Sometimes it refers to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), as it is said: "With the destruction of the taints, one becomes an ascetic. Sometimes it refers to the Tathāgata himself, as it is said:
"The term 'ascetic,' monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata. But here, by means of three terms...
He spoke of "four kinds of ascetics," including all those who are noble ones endowed with virtue, the worldling, and the fourth— the other who is not an ascetic at all,
a mere sham, with a saffron robe around his neck, who is an ascetic only by way of mere designation.
He said there is no fifth because in this Dhamma and Vinaya, there is no such thing as a fifth ascetic, whether by way of mere designation or even by way of mere profession.
"I reveal them to you" means I make those four ascetics manifest to you. "Questioned by witnesses" means questioned in their presence.
"Conqueror of the path" means one who has conquered all defilements by means of the path. "Teacher of the path" means one who teaches the path to others.
"Lives by the path" refers to any of the seven types of trainees (*sekha*) among those still in training, because they have not yet completed their dwelling in the supramundane path.

A virtuous worldling is said to "live in the path" in a worldly sense; however, it should be understood that a virtuous worldling also lives in the path by way of living for the sake of the supramundane path.
And as for the one who "defiles the path": this refers to one who is immoral and holds wrong view, meaning he is a defiler of the path through his practice which runs counter to the path.

85. When the Blessed One had thus briefly pointed out the four kinds of ascetics with the words, “These are the four ascetics,” Cunda, being unable to discern them by thinking, “This one here is the conqueror of the path, this one is the teacher of the path, this one lives by the path, and this one defiles the path,” asked again:
“Which is the conqueror of the path? In that context, [the one who thinks] “I live by the path” is...
"He lives according to the Path; tell me that when asked. The rest is self-evident.
Now, the Blessed One, pointing out the four kinds of ascetics with four verses, said: "He who has crossed over doubt and is free from the dart.
In this context, the phrase "crossed over doubt and free from the dart" follows the same method as explained in the *Uraga Sutta*. This...

However, there is a distinction. Since by this verse the "Buddha-monk who has conquered the path" is intended, he should be understood as "one who has crossed over doubt" (*tiṇṇakaṅkho*) because he has, through his knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), crossed over the ignorance regarding all phenomena that resembles doubt.
For, according to the method explained previously, those beginning with the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and ending with the pratyekabuddha have indeed crossed over doubt.

Because their power of knowledge was obstructed regarding the range of the once-returners and so forth, up to the range of the Buddhas, they were, in a figurative sense, still "not having crossed over doubt. The Blessed One, however, had in every respect "crossed over doubt.

"Delighting in Nibbāna" means being delighted in Nibbāna; the meaning is that his mind was always inclined toward Nibbāna by way of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). And such was the Blessed One. As it has been said:
“Thus, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very discourse, right there upon that same sign of concentration, I steadied my mind within myself, settled it, unified it, and concentrated it.

“Not greedily attached” (*anānugiddho*) means not being greedily attached to any phenomenon through the thirst of craving. “The leader of the world with its devas” means that by teaching the Dharma in accordance with the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions of beings, he led countless beings in numerous discourses such as the *Pārāyana* and the *Mahāsamaya*.

By means of accomplishing the penetration of truth for gods and humans, he is the leader, the guide, the deliverer, and the one who brings others to the further shore of the world including its devas—this is the meaning.
"Tādin" means "such a one," that is, one who is unshaken by the aforementioned worldly conditions (lokadhamma).
The rest here is self-evident.

87. Thus, having pointed out the Buddha-monk as the "Conqueror of the Path" with this verse, the Blessed One now spoke the words "The supreme, as supreme" while pointing out the monk whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

In that context, "the supreme" (*parama*) means Nibbāna; the sense is that it is the foremost and highest of all phenomena. Regarding the phrase "he who, having known here, [knows] the supreme as supreme": he who, in this world, [having known] that supreme [Nibbāna], [knows] it precisely as the supreme...
Having understood this within the Teaching by means of reflective knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), he "declares and analyzes the Dhamma right here.
He declares the Dhamma of Nibbāna; because he has realized it himself, he makes it manifest to others, saying, "This is Nibbāna.

He analyzes the Dhamma of the Path, saying, "These are the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on] ...the Noble Eightfold Path. Or alternatively, both of these are for those who understand through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
He declares by means of a concise teaching, and he analyzes by means of a detailed teaching for those who understand through elaboration.
Thus, both declaring and analyzing, he proclaims and analyzes while uttering the lion’s roar: "This Dhamma exists only within this dispensation, not outside of it.
Therefore it is said: "He declares and analyzes the Dhamma right here"; that [teaching] cuts through doubt.

They call such a person a second bhikkhu, a teacher of the path: a sage (*muni*) who is unmoving (*aneja*) through his own penetration of the Four Truths; a cutter of doubt (*kaṅkhacchida*) by cutting away the doubts of others through his teaching;
a sage (*muni*) by virtue of being endowed with sagely silence (*moneyya*); and unmoving (*aneja*) due to the absence of craving, which is designated as "movement" (*ejā*).

88. Thus, having himself realized the unsurpassed path through this verse, and being himself the unsurpassed teacher of the path through his teaching, he—just as one might designate a messenger or a letter-carrier who carries and conveys a king’s message as the "bearer of the message"—pointed out the monk whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) as the "teacher of the path.
Now, pointing out both the monk in training (sekkha) and the virtuous worldling-monk (puthujjana), he said:
He said: "In the *Dhammapada*. Herein, the word-by-word commentary is already evident. This, however, is the commentary on the meaning:

in the *Dhammapada*, because it is a "footstep" (*pada*) of the Dhamma that is Nibbāna; because it is well-taught by not approaching either extreme, or because it is taught in various ways such as the foundations of mindfulness according to the disposition [of the listeners];
and because even one possessing the Path has not yet completed the task of the Path—

He lives on the path, restrained by the restraint of virtue; he is mindful through mindfulness well-established regarding the body and so forth, or through mindfulness that has long been practiced and is a source of refuge;

and because they are blameless due to the absence of even the slightest fault, and because they are "steps" (pada) in the sense of being constituent parts, he—through the cultivation and frequent practice starting from the knowledge of dissolution—[attains] the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment known as the blameless steps.
"Practicing this, he is called by the monks the third type of monk who lives by the path.
(89) Thus, having indicated with this verse both the "path-liver"— the trainee ascetic (*sekkha-samaṇa*)—
and the virtuous worldling ascetic (*sīlavantaputhujjana-samaṇa*), the Blessed One now indicates the shaveling with the saffron robe around his neck, who is a mere ascetic in name only:
He said: "Having made a disguise. In this context, "having made a disguise" means having assumed a suitable appearance, having taken on a costume, or having adopted the outward marks [of another].
"Of those of good vows" refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples.
For their vows are beautiful; therefore, they are called "those of good vows. "One who leaps in" (pakkhandī) means one who leaps forward; the meaning is one who enters within.
For a person of immoral conduct, like one who covers filth with grass, leaves, and so forth,
creates a "canopy" of good vows to conceal his own immorality; he then thrusts himself into the midst of the monks, saying,
"I too am a monk," and when alms are being distributed according to seniority, saying, "I have been a monk for so many years," he seeks to receive them.
He leaps forward; therefore he is called "one who leaps forward after having covered over those of good conduct.
He is a defiler of families because he corrupts the faith that has arisen among the four classes of people, such as the Khattiyas, by means of improper conduct.
He is impudent through eight bases of bodily impudence, four bases of verbal impudence, and numerous bases of mental impudence.
The meaning is "endowed with. This is the summary here; however, we shall explain it in detail in the commentary on the *Mettasutta*.

He is called a "deceiver" (*māyāvī*) because he is endowed with deceit (*māyā*), which is characterized by the concealment of what has been done. He is "unrestrained" (*asaññata*) due to the absence of moral discipline and self-control.
He is "chaff" (*palāpa*) because he is like chaff. For just as chaff, though lacking the grain within, appears externally like rice because of its husk—

Just as that is seen, so too here someone who, though lacking the inner essence of virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), appears like a recluse on the outside through the guise of good conduct and the dress of a recluse, is called a "chaff" (*palāpa*) because he resembles chaff. However, in the *Ānāpānassati Sutta*, it is said:
"Monks, this assembly is not chaff; monks, this assembly is free from chaff; it is pure in its essence."

Thus, even an "excellent worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇa*) is called a "chaff" (*palāpa*). But here, in the *Kapila Sutta*, one who has been defeated—referring to those who are not true ascetics yet pride themselves on being ascetics—is called "chaff" in the passage: "Then drive out the chaff, those who are not ascetics but pride themselves on being ascetics.

"One who walks in a semblance [of virtue] while corrupting the community" means that, having created a facade of good conduct for those of pure vows, he behaves in such a way that [others might think]: "He is a forest-dweller..."
When people know him as "this one is a dweller at the foot of trees, a wearer of rag-robes, an alms-food eater, one of few desires,
and content," yet he conducts himself with such a semblance, a fitting outward appearance, and mere external decorum,
that person should be understood as a "corrupter of the path" because he defiles his own supramundane path and the path to a happy destination for others.

90. Having thus, by means of this verse, pointed out the immoral one—a mere sham ascetic—as a "corrupter of the path," he now said, "And these he penetrated," demonstrating their mutual non-confusion. Its meaning is as follows:
that householder, whether a khattiya or otherwise, who has penetrated, known, and realized these four types of ascetics according to the characteristics already described.
Whether he be a brahmin or anyone else, by merely hearing the characteristics of these four types of ascetics, he is "learned" (*sutavā*);
because he has heard those very characteristics in the presence of the Noble Ones, he is a "noble disciple" (*ariyasāvaka*);

and by the mere knowledge that "this and this ascetic possesses such-and-such a characteristic," he is "wise" (*sappañño*). Just as this one mentioned last is a "corrupter of the path," so too are the others.
"Knowing that 'all are not like this,' and seeing thus"—that is, having seen even this evil bhikkhu who is performing such evil deeds.

Herein, the construction is as follows: when a wise noble disciple, a learned householder, dwells having understood through his wisdom that "all are not like this," and having seen thus, his faith does not fail, even [when seeing] one who is performing such an evil deed.
"Even upon seeing a wicked bhikkhu, one's faith does not diminish, it does not decline, nor is it lost.
Having thus, by this verse, illustrated their state of being unmixed, he now spoke the verse beginning with "For how could one who is corrupt...
in order to praise the noble disciple who, even upon seeing such a person, knows that "all are not like this. Its connection is as follows: this very...
And it is not fitting for a learned noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) that, having seen someone committing a certain evil deed, he should know that "all [others] are not like this.
For what reason? How indeed could one who is corrupt make the uncorrupted equal to himself, or one who is pure make the impure equal to himself?
The meaning of this is: how indeed could a learned noble disciple, possessing wisdom, [regard] the failure of virtue...
One might equate—that is, recognize as identical—the other three types of recluses who are not corrupt with the corrupt one who defiles the path;
that is, one might regard the pure triad of recluses as being the same as the last type, the "recluse by mere designation," which is impure due to its lack of purity in bodily conduct and so forth.
At the conclusion of the sutta, neither the path nor the fruit was stated for the lay follower, for he had merely abandoned his doubts.
The commentary on the Cundasutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is completed. 6.
Commentary on the Parābhavasutta.
Thus have I heard: this is the Parābhava Sutta. What is its origin? It is said that after hearing the Maṅgala Sutta, the gods thought:
"In the Maṅgala Sutta, while the Blessed One was speaking of the growth and welfare of beings, he spoke exclusively of success (*bhava*) and not of failure (*parābhava*).
Come now, let us hear that by which beings decline and perish."

“Let us ask about failure as well. Then, on the day following the recitation of the Maṅgala Sutta, the deities from ten thousand world-systems, desiring to hear the Parābhava Sutta, assembled in this single world-system.
Occupying a space no larger than the tip of a single hair, they appeared in subtle forms numbering ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, and eighty.
Having manifested himself, he stood surrounding the Blessed One, who was seated upon a prepared, excellent Buddha-throne, outshining all the gods, Māras, and Brahmās with his glory and splendor.

Then, commanded by Sakka, lord of the devas, a certain son of the devas questioned the Blessed One regarding the discourse on decline (*parābhava*). Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke this sutta in response to that question.
In this regard, the passage beginning with “Thus have I heard” was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda.
The alternate verses, beginning with the method “A man who is perishing,” were spoken by a son of the gods.
The final verse, beginning with the method “One becomes easy to know,” was spoken by the Blessed One. Having combined all of these together, it is called the “Parābhava Sutta.”
It is said. Regarding that, whatever is to be said concerning the passage beginning with "Thus have I heard" will all be explained in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta.
91. As for the passage beginning with "The man who is perishing," "perishing" (*parābhavantaṃ*) means declining or being destroyed.
"Man" (*purisaṃ*) refers to any living being or person. "We ask you, O Gotama," [is said] after identifying oneself along with the other devas.
Seeking permission, that son of the gods addressed the Blessed One by his clan name.
"We have come to question your lordship" means that we have come from various world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) thinking, "We shall ask your lordship. By this, he shows his respect.
"Tell us, what is the cause of a man's downfall?"—this is what he asks of us who have thus arrived: "What is the opening through which a person falls away?"
"What is the door, what is the womb, what is the cause, by which we might know a man who is falling away?"—this is the meaning.
By this, he asks for the cause of the downfall of the person mentioned here as "a man who is falling away.
For when the cause of downfall is known, it is possible to recognize any man who is falling away through that commonality of cause.

92. Then the Blessed One, in order to make this clearly manifest, showed the opposite case and, by means of a teaching focused on the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā), spoke while illustrating the way of ruin: "Existence is easy to recognize. Its meaning is as follows:
that person who increases in existence and does not decline is easy to recognize; he can be known with ease, without difficulty, and without hardship.
To understand: that which is called "ruin" (*parābhava*) is that by which one is ruined, one declines, and perishes.
That person whose face you ask me about—whose ruin you inquire after—is also easy to recognize. How so? For this person is a lover of the Dhamma;
he desires, yearns for, and aspires to the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action; he listens to it and practices it. He, that [person]...
Because it is to be known by seeing and hearing the practice, it is easy to understand.

Likewise, the other—the ruin characterized by the teaching of the Dhamma—teaches that very same Dhamma, yet one does not desire it, does not yearn for it, does not long for it, does not hear it, and does not practice it;
because it is to be known by seeing and hearing that wrong practice, it is easy to understand. Thus, in this regard, the Blessed One...

It should be understood that, while showing the opposite side by way of the meaning, [the Blessed One] shows the door to the desire for the Dhamma (*dhammakāmatā*) as the cause of prosperity, and shows the door to the non-Dhamma (*adhamma*) as the cause of ruin. 93.
Then, rejoicing in the Blessed One’s speech, that deity said, "Thus indeed it is. The meaning of this is:
— "For indeed, just as it was spoken by the Blessed One, even so do we understand this, grasp it, and bear it in mind:
this is the first cause of ruin, characterized by the teaching of the Dhamma; this is the first cause of ruin.
Among those causes of ruin which we have come to understand, this is said to be one such cause of ruin. In this regard, the analysis is as follows:
"One is defeated by this, thus it is a cause of defeat (*parābhava*). And by what are they defeated? By that which is the door of defeat, the cause;

for here the difference is merely in the phrasing (*byañjana*), but in meaning there is no difference between 'defeat' and 'the door of defeat. Thus, having rejoiced, [he thought]: 'I understand one door of defeat.'"
Thereafter, out of a desire to know, he asked: "Lord, speak of the second; what is the cause of downfall?
Beyond this, the meaning in the cases of "the third," "the fourth," and so forth, should be understood by this same method.
Furthermore, even from the perspective of the explanation, it is because those various beings are possessed of those respective causes of downfall.
It should be understood that [the Buddha] did not teach all [causes of ruin] by means of a single [method], nor did he teach all [of them] by means of a single [person];

rather, in order to demonstrate those various causes of ruin for each respective case, he elucidated the diverse modes of ruin through a teaching based on individuals (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), beginning with the phrase "The unvirtuous have those dear to them," and so forth.
Herein, this is the brief explanation of the meaning: "The non-existent" refers to the six teachers, or whoever else is possessed of unpeaceful bodily, verbal, and mental actions;
they are "non-existent" because they are not dear to others, like Sunakkhatta and the rest, or the naked ascetics, the Korakhattiya, and so forth.
"The existent" refers to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, or whoever else is possessed of peaceful bodily, verbal, and mental actions.
"Those who are possessed [of such qualities], they do not make the good dear"—the meaning is that they do not make what is good, desired, wished for, and pleasing dear to themselves.
It should be understood that here the variation in expression is made according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Alternatively, "they do not make the good dear" means "they do not associate with the good"; for in the sense of "he serves the king," it is said "he makes the king dear."
Those who know the true meaning say this: "Piyanti" means being fond of, being pleased, and being delighted—the sense is "rejoicing.

"The doctrine of the wicked" (*asataṃ dhammo*) refers to the sixty-two types of views or the ten unwholesome courses of action. One takes pleasure in that doctrine of the wicked, desires it, longs for it, and cultivates it. Thus, by this verse, [three things are shown]: being fond of what is non-existent, being averse to what is existent, and taking delight in what is not the true Dhamma.
Three kinds of causes for downfall have been stated. For when a person is possessed of these, he falls away and declines;
he attains no growth either in this world or in the next. Therefore, they are called "the causes of downfall.
As for the detailed explanation here, we shall discuss it in the commentary on the verse beginning: "Not associating with fools, and associating with the wise."
96. One who is "habitually sleepy" is one who sleeps indeed while walking, sitting, standing, or lying down.
One who is "habitually social" is devoted to the pleasure of company and the pleasure of talk. One who is "not diligent" lacks the energy of effort and does not have the habit of exertion;
being exhorted by others, if he is a householder, he fails in his household duties, and if he is a renunciant...
Or one undertakes the work of a renunciant. An "idler" (*alasa*) is one who is idle by birth;

utterly overcome by sloth (*thina*), he remains exactly where he stands when standing, and remains exactly where he sits when sitting; through his own lack of effort, he does not adopt any other posture.
In this regard, the example is those who were too lazy to flee when a fire broke out in the forest in the past. This is the meaning here.
This is the superior limit; however, even by the inferior limit, one who is lazy is to be understood as simply "lazy.
Like a banner for a chariot, or smoke for a fire, anger is his distinguishing mark; thus he is "one whose mark is anger.

A person of a hateful temperament, quick to anger, and whose mind is like an open sore, is such a type. By this verse, [the characteristics of] a habit of sleeping, a habit of socializing, and a lack of exertion [are shown].
Laziness and being characterized by anger—these five modes of ruin have been stated.
For one who possesses these, neither a householder attains the excellence of a householder nor a renunciant attains the excellence of a renunciant;
rather, they only decline and indeed come to ruin. Therefore, they are called "the gates of ruin."
98. "Mother" should be understood as the one who gives birth; "father" likewise as the one who begets.
"Aged" refers to one whose body has become lax due to physical decay. "Past youth" means having transcended youth, being eighty or ninety years old, and thus incapable of performing tasks by oneself.
"Though capable and wealthy" means being competent and living in comfort. "Does not support" means does not nourish. By this verse, [the faults] of mother and father...
Failure to provide ornaments, failure to nourish, and failure to attend upon [one's parents] are stated as one single cause of ruin. For one who possesses these [failures], that which was said—
“By such service toward their mother and father, the wise praise him even here,
and after death he rejoices in heaven”— does not apply.
The benefits of supporting one's mother and father have been stated;

however, one who fails to do so, and instead incurs blame, censure, and rebirth in a miserable state—thinking, "He does not even support his own parents, so whom else will he support?"—is indeed ruined.
Therefore, this is called "a cause of ruin."
100. One is a *brāhmaṇa* because of having banished evil deeds; one is a *samaṇa* because of having stilled [the defilements].

Whether it be one born of a *brāhmaṇa* family who is a *brāhmaṇa*, or one who has gone forth as a *samaṇa*, or anyone else whatsoever who is a petitioner—if one deceives them with false speech, having invited them by saying, "Venerable sir, speak [your need]," or having been asked, having promised, and then subsequently failing to give to him—[this constitutes the offense].
One deceives that [person]. By this verse, the act of deceiving brahmins and others through false speech is stated as one single cause of ruin.

For one endowed with this, there is censure in this world, and in the future life, one encounters an unhappy destination; even if one reaches a happy destination, there is the failure of one’s purpose.
For it has been said:
“For one who is immoral, for one deficient in virtue, an evil reputation spreads abroad.
Likewise:
“Bhikkhus, one endowed with four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there. Which four? He is a speaker of falsehood,” and so forth.
Likewise:
"Here, Sāriputta, a certain person approaches a recluse or a brahmin and invites them, saying: 'Speak, venerable sir, for the sake of requisites.
Yet he does not give what he has invited. If, having passed away from there, he comes back to this state of being..."
Thus, whatever trade he engages in, it leads to his ruin. But here, Sāriputta...

[as before] ...whatever he offers in hospitality, he does not give according to his intention. If, having passed away from there, he comes back to this state of existence, whatever trade he engages in, it does not accord with his intention.”
Thus, one who encounters such things as blame and the like surely comes to ruin; therefore, it is said that these are "the causes of ruin. 102.

"Possessing abundant wealth" means possessing much gold, silver, gems, and jewels. "Together with silver" means having his own coins. "Provided with food" means being supplied with various soups and condiments.
"He eats alone the delicious [dishes]" means he eats the delicious foods even without his own sons.
"Eating in a concealed place without having given" means that one eats alone, [consuming] delicious foods.

By this verse, stinginess regarding food—due to greed for food—is stated as one very cause of ruin. For one who possesses this, encountering censure, things to be avoided, miserable rebirths, and so forth, one indeed comes to ruin; therefore, it is called "a cause of ruin."

Everything should be applied according to the method already stated, following the sequence of the Sutta; however, for fear of excessive prolixity, we shall now state only the essential meaning without showing the method of application. 104.
One "arrogant because of birth" is one who, having generated the conceit, "I am endowed with a noble birth," becomes stiffened by that [conceit], like a leather bag filled with air.
Having become bloated like a corpse, it does not bend for anyone. This same principle applies to those who are arrogant because of wealth or lineage.
"He despises his own kin" means that he despises even his own relatives on account of their birth, just as the Sakyans did toward Viṭaṭūbha.

Furthermore, on account of wealth, he despises others, thinking, "This person is poor and destitute," and he does not even show them the slightest courtesy; thus, those relatives of his lead only to his ruin.

They desire [this]. By this verse, four types of causes for ruin are stated from the perspective of their basis (*vatthu*), while only one cause of ruin is stated from the perspective of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).
106. A "woman-gambler" (*itthidhutta*) is one who is passionately attached to women; having given away whatever wealth he possesses, he pursues women again and again.
Likewise, a "liquor-gambler" (*surādhutta*) is one who, having staked all his own property, is intent on drinking liquor.
Having even set aside his lower garment, he is devoted to gambling with dice;
thus, because he squanders whatever he has acquired through these three means, it should be understood that "he destroys what he gains as soon as it is gained.
One of such a nature surely comes to ruin; therefore, by this verse, these three modes of ruin have been stated for him.

108. "With one's own wives" means with one's own wives. He who, being dissatisfied with his own wives, commits misconduct with courtesans, and likewise with the wives of others, is indeed ruined by the payment of wealth to courtesans and by the pursuit of others' wives through royal punishments and the like;
therefore, this twofold gateway to ruin is stated for him in this verse.
110. *Atītayobbano*: having passed beyond youth, being eighty or ninety years old, one brings [a woman] and takes her as a wife.
*Timbarutthaṇim*: a young girl with breasts resembling the fruit of the *timbaru* tree. *Tassā issā na supati*:
because of jealousy toward her, one does not sleep well, thinking, "Pleasure and cohabitation with an old man and a young woman are disagreeable; may she never desire a young man."
One who guards against envy does not sleep well. Since one who is consumed by both sensual lust and envy fails to apply oneself to external tasks and thus surely comes to ruin,
this verse mentions "not sleeping" due to envy as a single door to ruin.
112. *Soṇḍiṃ* means one who is greedy for fish, meat, and so forth, being by nature covetous.
*Vikiraṇiṃ* means one whose habit is to scatter wealth like dust for the sake of those [desires], and thus squander it. *Purisaṃ vāpi tādisaṃ* means even a man who is of such a kind;
whoever places such a person in a position of authority, or gives him seals, signets, and so forth, [in matters] of household life or labor...
Or he causes that very same person to be occupied with trade and other such dealings. Since he surely comes to ruin by losing his wealth through that person's fault,
this verse states that placing such a person in a position of authority is one single cause of downfall.
114. "Having little wealth" means having no source of income for the accumulation of riches.
"Possessing great craving" means being endowed with a great craving for wealth, being dissatisfied with whatever has been obtained.
"He is born into a family of kṣatriyas" means he is born into a clan of nobles. And "he aspires to sovereignty" means that because of this great craving...
If one, by improper means or in the wrong order, aspires to a kingdom that is either one’s own inheritance but unobtainable,
or the property of another, then by making such an aspiration, one indeed comes to ruin even when failing to attain the kingdom after giving away even a small amount of wealth to warriors and others;
therefore, this aspiration for a kingdom is stated in this verse as one single door to ruin.

115. Beyond this, if that deity were to ask, "O Blessed One, speak of the thirteenth... [and so on]... O Blessed One, speak of the hundred-thousandth," the Blessed One would have told him that as well. However, since that deity thought, "What is the use of asking these?
There is not even one among them that brings about growth," he ceased asking after having inquired only up to this point regarding those causes of downfall.
Having become remorseful, he remained silent; therefore, the Blessed One, knowing his disposition, spoke this verse—"These are the failures in the world"—concluding his teaching.
In that context, "the wise one" (paṇḍita) is one endowed with investigative discernment. "Having examined" (samavekkhiya) means having scrutinized with the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu).
"A Noble One" (*ariya*) does not mean one who possesses the path or the fruit; rather, he is called "Noble" because he does not conduct himself in this way that is termed ruinous or unwholesome.
Because he is endowed with that vision and that wisdom by which, having seen ruin, he avoids it, he is "endowed with vision.
Such a person "frequents the auspicious world," meaning he resorts to that which is auspicious, secure, supreme, and free from calamity.
It is said that he frequents, resorts to, and approaches the world of the gods.

At the conclusion of the teaching, having heard the causes of decline and having applied themselves with wise effort in accordance with the spiritual urgency that had arisen, countless deities attained the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning. As it has been said:
In the Mahāsamaya Sutta, as well as in the Maṅgala Sutta;
in the Samacitta, the Rāhulovāda, the Dhammacakka, and the Parābhava;
there, in the Devatāsaṃyutta, they are immeasurable and innumerable.
"And herein, the realization of the Dhamma is beyond counting.
The commentary on the Parābhava Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
7. Commentary on the Aggikabhāradvāja Sutta.
“Thus have I heard” refers to the Aggikabhāradvāja Sutta, which is also called the “Vasala Sutta. What is its origin?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. [The setting] is according to the method described in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.

At the conclusion of his post-meal duties, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, he saw that the brahmin Aggika-Bhāradvāja was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (upanissaya) for taking refuge and undertaking the training precepts. He thought: "When I go there, a conversation will arise;
then, having heard the teaching of the Dhamma at the end of that conversation, this brahmin will go for refuge and undertake the training precepts."
Having learned of this, he went there and, being requested by the brahmin for a teaching on the Dhamma based on the conversation taking place, he spoke this sutta.
Regarding that, we shall explain the portion beginning with "Thus have I heard" in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta;
the portion beginning with "Then the Blessed One, in the morning time" is to be understood according to the method already stated in the Kasībhāradvāja Sutta.
Now, at that time, regarding Aggikabhāradvāja—whatever has not been previously stated, we shall explain that here. That is to say:
because that brahmin offered oblations into and tended the sacrificial fire, he became well-known by the name "Aggika" (the Fire-worshipper), and by the clan-name "Bhāradvāja.
Therefore it is said, "of Aggikabhāradvāja. "In his dwelling" means in his house.
It is said that at the gate of that brahmin’s residence, there was a fire-chamber in the middle of the street.

Therefore, although one should have said "at the gate of the residence" (*nivesanadvāre*), it is stated as "in the residence" (*nivesane*) because that location is also included within the residence itself.
Alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity; the meaning is "near the residence. "The fire was kindled" means it was situated in the fire-vessel.
The fire, having performed its extraction of what was to be done and receiving the casting of fuel and the fresh breeze of air, blazes up, becoming turbulent with flames rising upward.

"Offerings have been prepared" means that after bathing including the head, they have been specially prepared with great honor as milk-rice, ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth; for whatever is to be offered into the fire, all that is called "an offering."

It is said: "In regular order" means from house to house. For the Blessed One wanders for alms without bypassing high or low families, both for the sake of benefiting all people and out of contentment with food. Therefore it is said: "Wandering for alms in regular order.
Now, for what reason did the brahmin, upon seeing the Blessed One—who was endowed with every excellence and was serene on all sides—[act as he did]?
Why does his mind not find confidence? And why does he address the Blessed One with such harsh words?
It is said: This brahmin, it seems, held the view that "seeing an ascetic during auspicious rites is inauspicious";
therefore, [he thought], "At the time when Mahābrahmā is about to eat, this ill-omened shaven-headed ascetic is approaching my residence."
Having reflected thus, he did not find faith in his heart; rather, he fell entirely under the sway of hatred.
Then, angry and displeased, he uttered words of displeasure, beginning with, "Right there, those shavelings!
And in that regard, because it was the view of the brahmins that "one who is shaven is impure," he thought, "This man is impure; therefore, he is not a worshiper of the gods and brahmins."
Feeling disgust, he said, "Shavelings" (*muṇḍaka*). Or, because of their shaven heads, he thought, "These people are defiled;

they do not deserve to come to this place," and thus, feeling disgust for their state as recluses (*samaṇa*)—thinking that even having become recluses, they do not praise such bodily affliction—he said, "Recluse-folk" (*samaṇaka*).
It was not only out of malice, but also because he had ordained *vasalas* and [was living] together with them.

Thinking, "This man has fallen away even from the status of a *vassala* by his practice of enjoying [impure] things; he is more wicked than a *vassala*," and feeling revulsion, the Blessed One said, "O *vassalas*.
He spoke thus either because he thought that "sin arises merely from seeing or hearing about those born of the *vassala* caste," or for some other reason.
Even when addressed in such a manner, the Blessed One, with a countenance serene as ever and in a sweet voice, [spoke] over the Brahmin.
With a mind cooled by compassion, demonstrating his state of *tādibhāva* (the state of being such) which is not shared with any of his own beings,
he said, "But do you know, O Brahmin? Then the Brahmin, having understood from the serenity of the Blessed One’s face that he possessed *tādibhāva*,
and having heard the sweet voice uttered with a mind cooled by compassion, felt his heart drenched as if by the Deathless (*amata*).
With a joyful mind and serene faculties, having subdued his pride and abandoned that mode of address and speech which was characteristic of his birth and like the vomiting of poison, he thought:
"Surely I am considered low-born and an outcast; yet in the ultimate sense, I am not an outcast, nor is low birth itself the factor that makes one an outcast.
Thinking thus, he said: "Indeed, Master Gotama, I am not [an outcast]."
This is the natural law (*dhammatā*): that one who is endowed with the cause, though harsh due to not obtaining the requisite conditions, becomes mild as soon as those conditions are obtained.
In this context, the word "sādhu" is seen in such senses as requesting, accepting, encouraging, excellence, and strengthening.
For instance, in "Venerable sir, it would be good (*sādhu*) if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief," it is used in the sense of a request. "Sādhu... [and so on].
In such passages as, "‘Venerable sir,’ that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words...," it refers to acceptance.
In such passages as, "Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!," it refers to encouragement. [And as in:
"Excellent is the king who delights in the Dhamma; excellent is the man possessed of wisdom."
In such passages as, "It is good not to deceive friends; the non-doing of evil is happiness," it means "beautiful.
In such passages as, "Listen to that, and pay close attention," it means "firm application. But here, it means "in the sense of a request.
The phrase *tena hi* (therefore) indicates his intention; it is equivalent to saying, "If you wish to know. Or, it is a statement of reason.
"Since you desire to know this, therefore, brahmin, listen and pay close attention;
I will speak to you in such a way that you will understand"—thus the connection with the subsequent words should be understood.
And therein, "listen" is a warding off of distraction of the sense-faculty of hearing, while "pay close attention" is by way of enjoining firmness in mental application (*manasikāra*).

It is the warding off of distraction of the mind-faculty. Herein, the former [verse] is for warding off the grasping of a distortion regarding the phrasing, while the latter is for warding off the grasping of a distortion regarding the meaning.
By the former, one is enjoined to listen to the Dhamma; by the latter, to the retention, examination, and so forth, of the teachings already heard.
And by the former, [one is led to think]: "This Dhamma possesses beautiful phrasing; therefore, it should be heard."
It illuminates [the meaning] by the latter [phrase], "it has a purpose; therefore, it should be attended to.

Alternatively, by joining the word "carefully" with both preceding phrases, it conveys this meaning: "Since this Dhamma is profound in its nature and profound in its teaching, therefore listen carefully.
Since it is profound in its meaning and profound in its penetration, therefore attend to it carefully."
Illuminating this, he said: "Listen well; attend closely.
Then, encouraging that brahmin who seemed to be despondent, thinking, "How shall I find a footing in such profound [teachings]?", he said:
"I shall speak. In that regard, [he spoke] so that you might understand, with perfectly rounded...
The intention should be understood as follows: "I shall speak by means of words and phrases in a manner that is clear and easy to follow.
Then, having become inspired with zeal, the brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja replied to the Blessed One, saying, "So be it, sir";
this means he accepted and took up [the teaching], or that he listened attentively, intent on practicing according to the instruction. Then, for him—
The phrase “the Blessed One said this” is stated with reference to what is now to be spoken, beginning with “hot-tempered and resentful.
116. In that context, *kodhana* means one whose nature is to be angry. *Upanāhī* means one who possesses resentment (*upanāha*) through the intensification of that very anger.
*Makkhī* means one who smears or wipes away the virtues of others; being both wicked and a smearer, he is called a “wicked smearer” (*pāpamakkhī*).
"One of failed view" (*vipannadiṭṭhi*) means one whose right view has perished, or one who is possessed of the ten-based wrong view that has become "failed," having gone to a distorted state.
"A deceiver" (*māyāvī*) means one who is possessed of deceit (*māyā*), which is characterized by the concealment of faults existing within oneself.
"One should know him as an outcaste" (*taṃ jaññā vasalo iti*) means that such a person is an outcaste because of the raining down—that is, the sprinkling—of these base qualities.
"One should know him as an outcaste (vasala) according to his conduct"—by all these [qualities], he is born at the very head of the brahmins. For in the ultimate sense, he is indeed an outcaste;

it is merely his own heart's satisfaction, not that of others. Thus, in this context, the Blessed One, having already suppressed the anger of that brahmin with the first word itself, [proceeds] by way of a person-centered teaching (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*) to show that "a person characterized by qualities such as anger is a lowly individual."
And while teaching on the phenomena such as anger, he first taught, by way of a single method, both who an outcaste is and the qualities that make one an outcaste. Teaching in this manner,
and without engaging in disparagement of others or self-exaltation— thinking "you" and "I"—
he established that brahmin in the state of an outcaste and himself in the state of a brahmin solely through the Dhamma, with impartiality, and according to the natural order.

117. Now, in order to refute the view of the brahmins—namely, "Even one who occasionally commits killing, taking what is not given, and so forth, is still a brahmin"—and [to show] those who, failing to see the danger, give rise to unwholesome states such as violence toward living beings while being possessed of them, [the Buddha says]:
"These states are base and make one a *vasala*."

Therein, while demonstrating the danger [of being an outcast], the Blessed One spoke these verses beginning with "Whether born once or born twice" in order to teach, by way of further methods, who is an outcast and the qualities that make one an outcast.
In this context, "born once" (ekaja) refers to those born from any remaining mode of birth except the egg-born; for such a one is born only once. "Born twice" (dvija) refers to the egg-born.
For he is born twice: once from the mother’s womb and once from the eggshell. Thus, he is "once-born" (*ekaja*) or "twice-born" (*dvija*).

"A living being here" (*pāṇam iha*) refers to a sentient being here. "He harms" (*vihiṃsati*) means that by means of an action arising from volition associated with the bodily door or volition associated with the vocal door, he deprives [the being] of life.
There is also a reading, "he harms living beings" (*pāṇāni hiṃsati*). In that context, "once-born" or "twice-born"...
The connection should be understood as follows: "Whosoever harms living beings that are thus divided.
By the phrase "for whom there is no compassion for living beings," he expresses the absence of mental sympathy (*anukampā*). The rest here is exactly according to the method already stated.

Regarding the subsequent verses, since we shall not say even this much more, from here on we will pass over the words whose meaning is obvious and provide only an explanation of those words that have not been commented upon.
118. *Hantīti* means he kills; *vināseti* means he destroys. *Parirundhatīti* means he stands surrounding [them] with an army.
Regarding the phrase "villages and towns," the word "and" (*ca*) implies that "cities" (*nagarāni*) should also be mentioned here.
By the expression "known as a suppressor" (*niggāhako samaññāto*), it is meant that through this killing and besieging, he is recognized in the world as a destroyer of villages, towns, and cities.
119. "In a village or in the forest": here, both a village, a town, and a city, together with their precincts, constitute what is meant by "village";

excluding that, the remainder is the "forest. In such a village or in the forest, whatever is cherished by others—that which is grasped and not relinquished by other beings, whether it be a living being or a conditioned formation—to take that ungiven thing by theft: this is [the offense].
With a thieving mind, one takes what has not been given and not authorized; by whatever means and by whatever method, one effects its appropriation for oneself. 120.
"Having taken a loan" means either by taking a deposit after setting aside something belonging to oneself as collateral, or by taking [something] without having set aside anything at all.

Having taken a loan either by entering into an agreement for interest, thinking, "I will give such an amount of increase after such a length of time," or by entering into various other types of contracts, thinking, "Whatever profit arises from this shall be my principal and yours alone," or "The profit shall be common to both of us.
Being pursued by the creditor, he flees, [thinking], "There is no debt for you. By that...
When a debtor is urged by a creditor, saying, "Give me my debt," he flees even while staying at home by saying, "You have no debt to me; who is your witness that I took it?
(121) "Desire for something trifling" means having a longing for even a very small thing. [The text refers to] people traveling on a road.
"Whatever woman or man he meets while traveling on the road"—having killed them, "he takes some trifle" means that having killed and beaten them, he seizes their property. 122.
"For his own sake" means for the sake of his own life; likewise for the sake of another. "For the sake of wealth" means for the sake of his own wealth or...
"Or for the sake of another's wealth. The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of an alternative (*vikappana*) in all instances.
"Questioned as a witness" means being asked, "Speak whatever you know. "He speaks falsely" means that either knowing [the truth], he says "I do not know," or not knowing, he says "I know";
thus he makes an owner non-owner, and a non-owner an owner.
123. "Of kinsmen" means of relatives. "Of friends" means of companions. "In wives" means in those who are the legally accepted partners of others.
"Is seen" means he is seen as something repulsive; the meaning is that he is seen transgressing. "By force" means against the will through physical compulsion.
"With affection" means being desired by them [the wives] and desiring them oneself; what is meant is that it occurs through the influence of mutual passion.
124. “To mother or father” refers to that which serves as the basis for loving-kindness (*mettā*).

“Decayed, past their youth” refers to that which serves as the basis for compassion (*karuṇā*). “Being able, he does not support them” means that although he is possessed of wealth and provided with necessities, he does not nourish them.

125. “Mother-in-law” (*sasū*) means the mother-in-law. “Strikes” means he strikes her with his hand, a clod of earth, or some other object. “Harasses” means he provokes anger in her by means of harsh speech.

126. "There is" (*atthi*) refers to anything among the benefits pertaining to the present life, the future life, or the ultimate goal (*paramattha*). "Being questioned" (*pucchito santo*) means being asked.
"He instructs in what is harmful" (*anattham anusāsati*) means he points out only that which is disadvantageous to him.

"He counsels with concealment" (*paṭicchannena manteti*) means that even while explaining what is beneficial, he does so with words and phrases that are obscure, such that the other person does not understand it.
He recites it "with omissions," meaning that either by keeping it as a "teacher's fist" (a secret) or by having him dwell with it for a long time, he recites it while leaving something remaining.
Regarding the phrase "having done so": here, I previously mentioned the state of being one who desires evil;
that which refers to "here someone, having practiced misconduct of body, having practiced misconduct of speech, and having practiced misconduct of mind, for the sake of concealing it..."
"He harbors an evil desire; he wishes, 'May they not know me'"—it is thus that [the term] comes to be used.

Because he acts in such a way that others do not know, and because he does not disclose his deeds once they have been done, his actions are concealed; thus, he is one "of concealed conduct" (*paṭicchannakammanta*). 128.

"Another's family" means either a family of relatives or a family of friends. "One who has come" refers to someone who has eaten at that family's home; the intention is that one does not honor such a person with food and drink when they have arrived at one's own house, or does not give to them, or gives what has already been consumed.
129. "Whoever [harms] a brahmin" is in the same manner as stated in the *Parābhava Sutta*.
130. "When mealtime has arrived" means when the time for eating has occurred. There is also a reading *upaṭṭhite*, meaning "arrived at mealtime.
"He offends with speech and does not give" means: "This person, though wishing me well, is making me perform a meritorious deed by force."
Without considering that [the person] has arrived, one provokes them with unseemly and harsh words;
one does not grant them even the mere presence of being face-to-face, let alone food—this is the intended meaning.
131. "He who here speaks of the non-existent": whoever here, according to how signs are seen—"on such-and-such a day, this and that..."
“They will become yours”—thus he speaks these words of the wicked.
There is also a reading “asantaṃ,” meaning “what has not come to be. He speaks thus: “In such-and-such a village I have a household fortune like this;
come, let us go there, you shall be my wife, and I will give you this and that”—[addressing] another's wife or another's daughter-in-law.
Or like a rogue deceiving [others]. "Desiring to win" (*nijigīsāno*) means desiring to win, seeking; the intention is that, having deceived them, he wishes to take anything at all and flee. 132.
"He who [praises] himself" (*yo cattānaṃ*) means he who praises himself. He exalts himself by means of birth and so forth, placing himself in a high position.

"He sets [himself] aside. And "he despises others" means that by those very [qualities], he despises others; he treats them as inferior. The letter *ma* is used for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).

"Degraded" (*nihīna*) means fallen away from the increase of virtues, or having entered into a state of non-dhamma. "By that conceit" means by his own conceit, which consists of exalting himself and despising others.
"Provocative" (*rosaka*) means one who generates provocation in others through body and speech. "Miserly" (*kadariya*) means one who is stubbornly stingy, who—toward others...

This is a designation for one who prevents others from giving or performing other meritorious deeds. "One of evil desires" (*pāpiccho*) means one who possesses the desire to gain credit for qualities not actually possessed.

"Miserly" (*maccharī*) means one who is bound by the miserliness of dwelling-places and so forth. "Deceitful" (*saṭho*) means one who possesses guile characterized by the manifestation of non-existent qualities;
or, one who speaks falsely, saying things such as "I am doing it," even though he does not wish to do it. He lacks the characteristic of revulsion toward evil.
Shame (*hirī*) has the characteristic of agitation due to its quality of causing fear; thus, one who lacks shame and lacks moral dread (*ahirika-anottappī*) is so called.

134. "The Buddha" refers to the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). "Reviles" means he slanders him with such terms as "not omniscient," and [he reviles] a disciple with such terms as "one of wrong practice.
"Whether a wanderer or a householder" is a qualification of the disciple, referring specifically to one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*).

Or his disciple, meaning a layperson who provides the requisites; or an external wanderer, or any layperson whatsoever—thus the ancients intend the meaning here when they say "he reviles with a false fault.
135. "Being one who is not an Arahant" means being one whose taints (*āsava*) are not exhausted. "He claims to be an Arahant" means he claims, "I am an Arahant."
He utters speech, exerts himself with the body, desires with the mind, and endures [the consequences] in such a way that people know him as "this one is an arahant.
"A thief" means a robber. He says "in the world with its Brahmās" by way of the highest limit; what is meant is "in the entire world.
For in the world, [he is known] through such acts as breaking into houses, plundering wealth, committing burglary, standing as an ambush, and so forth.

Those who plunder the wealth of others are called thieves. But in the Dispensation, those who plunder requisites and so forth by means of the excellence of their retinue and other such stratagems [are also called thieves]. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these five great thieves existing in the world. Which five? Here, bhikkhus..."

It occurs to a certain great thief: "When indeed shall I wander through villages, towns, and royal capitals surrounded by a hundred or a thousand [men], killing, having killed, cutting, having cut, cooking, and having cooked?
And at a later time, he wanders through villages, towns, and royal capitals surrounded by a hundred or a thousand [men].
He wanders about, killing... [and so on] ...cooking. In the same way, monks, it occurs to a certain evil monk:

"When indeed shall I wander on tour through the royal capitals with a hundred [monks], honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites from both householders and those who have gone forth?"
Then, at a later time, surrounded by a hundred or a thousand followers, he wanders on tour through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, honored...
[and so on] ...with the requisites for a monk. This, monks, is the first great thief existing in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here some evil monk, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, conceals it within himself. This, monks, is the second... [and so on] ...in the world.

“Furthermore, monks, here a certain wicked monk groundlessly accuses another pure monk who is living the perfectly pure holy life of unchaste conduct. This, monks, is the third [peril] in the world...
Furthermore, monks, here a certain wicked monk [misappropriates] those things which are the heavy property and heavy requisites of the Saṅgha, such as:
a monastery, a site for a monastery, a dwelling, a site for a dwelling, a couch...”

A seat, a mattress, a pillow, an iron pot, an iron pan, an iron bowl, an iron cauldron, a hatchet, a small axe, a large axe, a spade, a chisel, creepers, bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, grass, clay, wooden vessels, and earthenware vessels—with these he favors and gratifies householders. This, monks, is the fourth... in the world.
“Bhikkhus, in this world with its devas... including gods and humans, this is the foremost great thief: he who claims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state.

In this context, worldly thieves steal only worldly wealth, grain, and so forth. Among the types of thieves mentioned in the Dispensation, the first steals only the requisites such as robes and the like;
the second, the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma); and the third, the holy life (brahmacariya) of another.

The fourth is the heavy property belonging to the Saṅgha; the fifth is the wealth of mundane and supramundane qualities, distinguished as the attainments of the jhānas, samādhi, the paths, and the fruits, as well as the mundane requisites such as robes and so forth. As it is said: "Monks, you have eaten the alms of the realm by theft.
With reference to this fifth great thief, the Blessed One said: "A thief in the world including the Brahmās."
For it was said that he is the foremost great thief because of his theft of both mundane and supramundane wealth: "Bhikkhus, in this world with its devas...
including devas and humans, this is the foremost great thief, who proclaims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state.
