Therefore, even here, he has been declared by means of this superior delimitation as being "in the world with its Brahmās."
"This indeed is the lowest of outcasts. Here, the word "indeed" (*kho*) has the sense of emphasis; thus, it emphasizes that this person alone is the lowest of outcasts.
It emphasizes that he is the most inferior and the very last among outcasts. Why?

Because he pours forth the nature of theft upon a distinguished object, and because, as long as he does not relinquish that admission, he possesses the quality of being an outcast that has not yet departed.

"These indeed are outcasts. Now, those five beginning with the wrathful, who were mentioned in the first verse by way of failure of disposition (*āsaya-vipatti*), or six if "evil envy" is divided into two;
and the one who harms living beings by way of failure of application (*payoga-vipatti*) in the second verse;
and the one who oppresses villages and towns by way of failure of application in the third verse; and [the one] by way of theft and seizure in the fourth verse...
One [is included] by way of deceiving with a dice-game for the fifth; one, by way of seizing by force for the sixth, as a highwayman;
one, by way of false testimony for the seventh; one, by way of treachery toward a friend for the eighth; one, by way of ingratitude for the ninth;
one, by way of causing distress through the destruction of what has been done for the tenth; and one, by way of deceiving the heart for the eleventh.
Two [offenses] on the twelfth [day] by way of concealing one's actions; one on the thirteenth by way of ingratitude;
one on the fourteenth by way of deception; one on the fifteenth by way of harassment; one on the sixteenth by way of deception;
two on the seventeenth by way of self-exaltation and disparagement of others; and [one] on the eighteenth by way of failure in application and intention.

The seven beginning with the *rosaka* (the reviler), two from the nineteenth [verse] by way of reproaching, and one from the twentieth by way of the "chief thief"—thus thirty-three or thirty-four outcastes (*vasala*) have been mentioned. Pointing them out, he said:
"These indeed are the outcastes mentioned, those whom I have declared. The meaning of this is: those whom I previously [stated], "Do you know them, O Brahmin... [and so forth].
"Outcastes"—thus, outcastes have been described in brief; they are now explained in detail.
Alternatively, those who were described by me according to the individual (puggala), they are also explained here according to their qualities (dhamma).

Or else, these outcastes have been described by the Noble Ones (ariya) on account of their actions (kamma), not by birth; those who were explained by me in such a manner as "the angry one, the resentful one," and so forth.

136. Thus, having shown what a *vasala* is, the Blessed One now spoke the words, "One is not a *vasala* by birth," in order to refute that view, for the brahmin is excessively attached to his own view.
Its meaning is this: from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), one is not a *vasala* by birth, nor is one a brahmin by birth;
rather, one is a *vasala* by action, and by action [one becomes a brahmin].
One is a brahmin; one becomes an outcaste (*vasala*) because of the impurity of one's actions, while one is a brahmin because of pure action despite the impurity of one's vehicle.

Or, since you considered the lowly outcaste to be superior and the brahmin to be exalted, it is for this reason that one becomes an outcaste through low action and a brahmin through exalted action—it was with the intention of making this meaning known that he spoke thus.
137–139. Now, in order to establish that very point by means of an illustration, he spoke the three verses beginning with “Know this also through this.
Among them, two have four lines and one has six lines; their meaning is as follows:
know also through this [illustration] what I have stated, beginning with “One is not an outcaste by birth,” just as this example demonstrates it.

"Know it by way"—that is to say, know it by whatever manner or by whatever commonality this illustration has been stated. If one asks, "What is the illustration? It is: "Sopāka, the son of a caṇḍāla...
[up to] ...rebirth in the Brahma-world. He is the son of a caṇḍāla, thus "the son of a caṇḍāla.

Because he would obtain dead dogs and cook them for his own consumption, he is "Sopāka. He is known as "Mātaṅga," meaning he is famous by that name. Thus he was well-known for his low birth, his livelihood, and his name.
Connecting with the first line: "He" refers to that Mātaṅga who attained supreme glory—glory, fame, and praise that is wonderful, unsurpassed, and most distinguished.

Regarding the phrase "which is very hard to obtain": it is difficult even for one born into a noble family, and very difficult indeed for one born into a lowly family. And as he had thus attained such glory, the Kṣatriyas came to wait upon him.

There were many Brahmins; for the sake of serving that Mātaṅga, Khattiyas, Brahmins, and many others such as Vessas and Suddas—most of the human inhabitants of Jambudīpa—came to attend upon him. This is the meaning.
Thus, being endowed with such attendance, that Mātaṅga was "dustless" (*viraja*) because he was free from the dust of the defilements (*kilesa*). By the great ones, such as the Buddhas...

Because he had entered upon the Great Path, and because he was capable of reaching the divine world known as the Brahma-world, he mounted the vehicle of the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti-yāna), which is designated as the "vehicle to the divine world.
By means of that practice, having dispelled sensual lust, at the breaking up of the body, he became one who has gone to the Brahma-world.
Thus, even though his birth was inferior, it did not prevent him from being reborn in the Brahma-world; what is meant is that he attained rebirth in the Brahma-world.

This matter, however, should be understood as follows: In the past, it is said, the Great Man, performing what was beneficial for beings through various means, was born into a family of outcasts who lived by the profession of Sopāka scavengers. By name he was Mātaṅga;
being ill-favored in appearance, he lived in a leather hut outside the city, sustaining his life by wandering for alms within the city. Then, one day...
When the festival of the Surā constellation had been proclaimed in that city, the gamblers played with their respective retinues.
There was also a daughter of a certain wealthy brahmin, about fifteen or sixteen years of age, beautiful and lovely to behold like a celestial maiden;
thinking, "I shall play in a manner befitting my own family lineage," she prepared an abundance of provisions for play, such as various kinds of food and drink.
Having had [the goods] loaded onto carts, she would mount a vehicle yoked with all-white mares and go to the park grounds with a great retinue;
she was known by the name Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. It is said that because she did not wish to see anything ill-formed as being inauspicious, she came to be designated by the very name Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.

Then that Mātaṅga, rising early in the morning, dressed himself in a rag of cloth, tied a bronze gong to his hand, and entered the city with a vessel in his other hand, striking the bronze gong from afar as soon as he saw people.
Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā [was approached] by men who were driving low-caste folk away from her, shouting, "Move out! Move out! from the front.
As they were being led through the middle of the city gate, she saw the Mātaṅga and asked, "Who is this? He replied, "I am the Caṇḍāla Mātaṅga.
She said, "How can there be prosperity for those who go after seeing such a person as this? and had the vehicle turned back.

The people became angry, saying, "We would have obtained food, drink, and other delicacies by going to the park; that Mātaṅga has created an obstacle for us! and they cried out, "Seize him! Seize him!"
Thinking, "He is a Caṇḍāla," they struck him with clods of earth; thinking, "He is dead," they seized him by the feet, cast him aside in a secluded spot, covered him with refuse, and departed.
When he regained consciousness and rose up, he asked the people:
"Sirs, is a door common to all, or was it made for Brāhmaṇas alone? The people replied: "It is for everyone."

“Common property! Thinking, “People have brought this ruin and disaster upon me because they saw me entering by the common door and subsisting on alms-food,” he wandered from street to street announcing this to the people,
and then lay down at the door of the brahmin’s house, saying, “I will not rise until I have recovered Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.”
The brahmin, hearing that "a Mātaṅga is lying at the door of the house," said, "Give him a kākaṇika; let him go after anointing his limbs with oil.
He did not accept that, saying, "I will not rise until I have obtained the auspicious sight of a *diṭṭhamaṅgalika*.
Then the brahmin said, "Give two kākaṇikas; let him eat a cake for one kākaṇika and [anoint himself] with oil for the other."
“Anoint your limbs and go,” he said. He did not wish for that; he spoke in the same manner. Having heard this, the brahmin commanded, “Give a māsaka!
A pāda! Half a kahāpaṇa! A kahāpaṇa! Two, three! and so on, until he ordered a hundred.
He still did not wish for it; he spoke in the same manner. Even as they were thus entreating him, the sun set. Then the brahmin’s wife—
Descending from the palace and having a curtain-wall erected around it, he approached him and entreated:
"Dear Mātaṅga, forgive the offense of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā; take a thousand, two thousand, three thousand," and so on, until he said, "take a hundred thousand.
He remained silent and simply lay down.
When four or five days had passed in this manner, the princes and others, having given many gifts yet failing to obtain a sight of the auspicious one, whispered into Mātaṅga’s ear:
"Men indeed attain their desired goal even after exerting effort for many years; do not be discouraged, for surely within two or three days—"
“You shall receive the blessing of sight. He remained silent and lay down right there.
Then, on the seventh day, the neighbors all rose up and said, “Either rouse Mātaṅga, or give us the girl; do not destroy us all!
For this was their view: “If a caṇḍāla lies thus at the door of one’s house...”
“...and when he dies, the Caṇḍālas living in seven houses on each side of his own home shall become [his heirs].

Then, having dressed Diṭṭhamaṅgalika in a tattered blue cloth and given him a water-pot, a bowl, and other such items, they led her weeping into his presence and said, “Take the girl; get up and go! Standing by his side, she said, “Get up!”
He said, "Take me by the hand and help me up. She helped him up.
Once he was seated, he said, "We are not permitted to live within the city; come, lead me to my leather hut outside the city.
Taking him by the hand, she led him there. "Having lifted him onto her back," say the reciters of the Jātaka. Having led him there, she [anointed] his body with oil...
Having rubbed her with oil and bathed her with warm water, he cooked rice-gruel and gave it to her. Thinking, "This is a brahmin girl;
let her not perish," and without causing any confusion regarding their caste, he took strength for about half a month. Then, saying, "I am going to the forest;
do not be distressed thinking that I am staying too long," he departed from his home after instructing the household members, "Do not neglect her."
Having gone forth into the ascetic life of a forest-dweller and performed the preliminary exercises for the meditation kasinas,
he attained the eight meditative absorptions and the five supernormal powers within just a few days. Thinking, "Now I shall become pleasing to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā," he traveled through the air,
descended at the city gate, and sent a messenger to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.
Having heard this, she thought, "I suppose some kinsman of mine, having gone forth, has come to see me while knowing I am suffering.
She went there, and upon recognizing him, she fell at his feet and said, "Why have you left me, helpless as I am?
The Great Man replied, "Do not be distressed, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā; by all those dwelling throughout Jambudīpa..."
Having said, "I shall pay him honor," she spoke thus: "Go and make this proclamation:
'The Great Brahmā is my husband, not Mātaṅga; he will shatter the moon-palace and come into my presence on the seventh day.
She replied: "Venerable sir, though I am the daughter of a wealthy brahmin family, by my own evil karma I have reached this state of a caṇḍāla."

“I have reached [this state], yet I am unable to speak thus. The Great Being said, “You do not know the power of Mātaṅga,” and having displayed many miracles so that she would believe, he instructed her accordingly and returned to his own dwelling.
She did exactly as he had commanded.
People complained and laughed, saying, "How can this woman, having herself attained the state of a caṇḍāla through her own evil karma, now claim she will become a Great Brahmā again?
Full of overweening pride, she wandered through the city day after day, proclaiming, "He will come on the sixth day! The fifth! The fourth! The third! Tomorrow! Today!"

When the people heard her confident words, thinking, "It might even be so," they had pavilions constructed at the doors of their respective houses, prepared screens of cloth, and adorned their grown-up daughters.
Then, looking up at the sky, they sat waiting, thinking, "When the Great Brahmā arrives, we shall give our daughters in marriage. Then, on the full-moon day, the Great Being—
When the moon had ascended to the vault of the sky, he emerged in the form of Mahābrahmā, having split open the moon’s chariot while the great multitude was looking on.
The people thought, “Two moons have appeared,” and despised him. Then, seeing him approaching in due course, they realized, “What Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā said is true;
this is indeed Mahābrahmā himself, who previously came in the guise of Mātaṅga to subdue Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.”
He reached his goal. Thus, while being watched by the great multitude, he descended right into Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s dwelling place.
At that time, she was in her fertile period. He touched her navel with his thumb. By that touch, a conception was established.
Then he said to her, "A fetus has settled in you; when your son is born, you shall live supported by him."
Having spoken thus, he re-entered the Moon Palace while the great multitude looked on.
The brahmins, saying, "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, the consort of Mahābrahmā, has been born as our mother," came from here and there.
Due to the crowding of people desiring to pay her honors, the city gates were without space.
They placed Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā upon a heap of gold, bathed her, adorned her, and mounted her upon a chariot. With great honor,
they caused her to circumambulate the city, and having erected a pavilion in the center of the city,
they established her there in the place where she had been seen by Mahābrahmā as his "Pajāpatī," and they made her dwell there until a suitable husband was found for her.
“Let us prepare a place for her to dwell; let her stay right here for now. She gave birth to her son in that very pavilion.
On a day of purification, they bathed her and her son, including their heads, and because the boy was born in a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), they gave him the name “Maṇḍabyakumāra.
From that time on, the brahmins surrounded him and followed him about, saying, “He is the son of Mahābrahmā.”
Then, hundreds of thousands of kinds of gifts arrived; the brahmins established guards over the prince so that those who came did not obtain a quick sight of him.
As the prince gradually grew up, he began to give alms. In the hall, to the poor and the destitute who had assembled—
Without giving to the brahmins, he gave only to them. The Great Man, reflecting, "What is my son giving as alms?
and seeing him giving only to the brahmins, thought, "I shall act so that he will give to everyone.
He put on his robe, took his bowl, came through the air, and stood at the door of his son's house. When the prince saw him, [he asked], "From where..."
“Here has come this outcaste in such a hideous guise,” he said, and being enraged, he spoke this verse:
“From where have you come, you ill-clad one? You look like a ragged wretch, a dust-demon.
You wear a rag from the rubbish heap around your neck; who are you, you who are unworthy of offerings?”
The brahmins, crying out, "Seize him! Seize him!", took hold of him, beat him, and brought him to ruin and destruction.
He went through the air and alighted outside the city. The deities, becoming enraged, seized the prince by the neck and placed him with his feet upward and his head downward.
With his eyes bulging out and saliva trickling from his mouth, he gasped with a rattling sound, suffering intense pain.
He felt it. Having heard this, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā asked, "Has someone arrived? "Yes, a renunciant has come.
"Where has he gone? "He went in such a manner. She went there and, entreating him, saying, "Forgive your own servant, venerable sir," she prostrated herself on the ground at his feet.
At that time, the Great Being, having wandered for alms, [emerged].

Having received the rice gruel, he sat there drinking it; then he gave the small amount of gruel remaining to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, saying, "Go, stir this gruel in a water-jar and pour it into the eyes, mouths, ears, and nostrils of those who have undergone a change due to the spirits, and sprinkle it over their bodies;
in this way, they will become free from the affliction. She did exactly as she was told. Then...
When the boy was born with a body of natural form, [the father] said, "Come, dear Maṇḍabya, we shall ask him for forgiveness.
Having made both his son and all the brahmins prostrate at his feet and lie down, he asked for forgiveness.
He then instructed them, saying, "Alms must be given to everyone," and after delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, he returned to his own dwelling place.
Having gone there, he thought: “Among women, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā has been tamed; among men, Maṇḍabya Kumāra has been tamed. Now, who is to be tamed?
Then he saw the ascetic Jātimanta dwelling on the bank of the Kumbhavatī River near the city of Bandhumatī.
[The ascetic] thought: “I am distinguished by birth; I do not drink water that has been used by others,” and so he lived upstream from the river.
He lived there. The Great Man, having made his dwelling above him, chewed a tooth-stick at the time when the ascetic was using water and threw it into the water.
Seeing it being carried away by the current, the ascetic went against the stream asking, "By whom was this thrown?
Upon seeing the Great Man, he asked, "Who is here? "I am Mātaṅga the Caṇḍāla, teacher," he replied.
“Get away, outcaste! Do not live upstream from the river. The Great Man replied, “Very well, teacher,” and lived downstream from the river;
yet even against the current, his tooth-stick came back to the ascetic’s side. The ascetic went again and said, “Get away, outcaste!
Do not live downstream from the river; live only upstream. The Great Man replied, “Very well...”
The teacher did exactly as he was told, yet it happened just the same again.
The ascetic, becoming resentful that the Great Man was doing it once more, said, "May your head split into seven pieces at the time of the sun's rising!
The Great Man replied, "Very well, teacher; however, I shall not allow the sun to rise," and he thus prevented the sun from rising.
Then the night did not break; instead, darkness arose.
Terrified, the inhabitants of Bandhumatī went to the ascetic and asked, "Teacher, will there be safety for us? For they believed him to be an Arahant.
He explained everything to them. They then approached the Great Man and said, "Venerable sir, the sun..."
"Release him! they pleaded. The Great Being said, "If an Arahant comes to you and asks for my forgiveness, then I shall release him.
The people went and said to the ascetic, "Come, venerable sir, ask the wise Mātaṅga for forgiveness;
let us not be ruined because of this quarrel between you. He replied, "I will not ask a Caṇḍāla for forgiveness. The people said, "We..."
"You shall not escape! they said, and seizing him by his hands and feet, they led him into the presence of the Great Man.
The Great Man said, "I forgive him as he lies on his belly at my feet and asks for forgiveness. The people said, "Do so.
The ascetic replied, "I do not pay homage to a Caṇḍāla. The people said, "You shall not pay homage against your will."
Having seized him by his hands, feet, beard, neck, and so forth, they laid him at the Great Being’s feet.
He said, “I forgive this man; nevertheless, out of compassion for him, I do not release the sun.
For as soon as the sun has fully risen, his head will split into seven pieces. The people asked, “Venerable sir, what should be done now?”
The Great Man said, "In that case, place him in water reaching up to his neck and cover his head with a lump of clay;
when struck by the rays of the sun, the lump of clay will shatter into seven pieces. Once it has shattered, let him go elsewhere.
They seized the ascetic by his hands, feet, and so forth, and did exactly as he had said. As soon as the sun released its rays—
The lump of clay split into seven pieces and fell; the ascetic, terrified, fled. Seeing this, the people exclaimed, “Behold, sirs, the supernatural power of the recluse!
Starting with the throwing of the tooth-stick, they recounted everything in detail and, saying, “There is no other recluse like him,” they placed their faith in him.
From that time forth, the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others throughout the whole of Jambudvīpa...
Householders and renunciants went to attend upon the wise Mātaṅga. Having remained there for as long as his lifespan lasted, at the breaking up of the body, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “By this you may also know... [as far as] ...rebirth in the Brahma-world.

In order to establish that "one becomes a brahmin by birth" and "one becomes a brahmin by action," he said: "Born in a family of Vedic scholars...
[omission] ...or through misfortune or reproach. In this context, "born in a family of Vedic scholars" means born in a brahmin family that studies the mantras.
There is also the reading "born in a family of Vedic scholars" (*ajjhāyakākuḷe jātā*). It means born in a brahmin family that studies the mantras and is not held in contempt.
Meaning: "Those whose kinsmen are the mantras" means those for whom the mantras are their relatives. What is meant is that they have the Vedas as their kin and the Vedas as their refuge.

And if they are frequently seen engaging in evil deeds: even though they are born into such families and possess the mantras as their kinsmen, if they are repeatedly observed committing evil deeds such as the taking of life and so forth, then in this very life—
Being thus rebuked, they are censurable both in this life and in the future state of misery. Even in this very existence, their parents say:
"These are not our sons; they are ill-born, like embers to the family. Drive them away! And the brahmins also say:
"These are householders, not brahmins. Do not grant them admission to the offerings for the faithful, the sacrifices, the *thālipāka* oblations, and so forth."
"Do not converse with them. Other people also disparage them, saying, "These are doers of evil deeds; these are not brahmins.
Furthermore, in the future life, there is for them an unhappy destination consisting of hell and so forth; the meaning is that an unhappy destination awaits them in the world beyond.
Alternatively, *samparāye* is also read as *paraloke*; in the world beyond, their "going to suffering" is an unhappy destination, which is simply the attainment of suffering.
The meaning is "it happens. Birth does not prevent them from [falling into] a miserable state or from censure;

for even though that birth is so exalted, it is what you hold to be essential. Birth exposes these brahmins to evil deeds, either to the miserable state described here as "a miserable state in the future life," or to the censure described here as "censurable in this very life."
Or he does not restrain them from censure.
Thus the Blessed One, demonstrating that even those born into families of Vedic scholars fall into ruin in this very life through censurable deeds and the like,
and showing that there will be no further existence in the brahmin caste in the future due to their rebirth in miserable states, [spoke as follows].
Having established this point— that “one is not a brahmin by birth, one is a brahmin by action”— he now spoke thus, concluding both points: “O Brahmin,
one does not become an outcaste by birth, nor does one become a brahmin by birth.”
“By action one becomes an outcaste; by action one becomes a brahmin.

The rest is exactly as stated in the *Kasibhāradvāja Sutta*. Specifically, here the application of the phrases beginning with “one who would turn what is overturned” (*nikkujjitaṃ vā*) should be understood as follows:
just as someone might turn upright what has been overturned, so too [the Buddha] turned me, who was turned away from my actions...
By raising up from the false view that has fallen into the doctrine of birth—that "one becomes a *brāhmaṇa-vasala* by birth"—just as one would uncover what is concealed;
by revealing the doctrine of action which was concealed by the doctrine of birth, just as one would point out the path to one who is lost;
and by pointing out the unmixed, straight path for escaping the state of being a *brāhmaṇa-vasala*.
"Just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so too,
because my Lord Gotama has revealed the Dhamma through these various methods by means of such illustrations as Mātaṅga and others, the Dhamma has been revealed in many ways."—
From the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the Aggikabhāradvājasutta of the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
8. Commentary on the Mettasutta:
"What should be done by one skilled in the goal" is the Mettasutta. What is its origin? It is said that from the slopes of the Himalayas, by means of deities...
Harassed by these beings, the bhikkhus came to Sāvatthī into the presence of the Blessed One.
For their protection and for the sake of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), the Blessed One spoke this discourse. This, then, is the brief summary.
This, however, is the detailed account: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī when the commencement of the rains was approaching.

Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus from various kingdoms, having received a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Blessed One and desiring to enter the rains retreat in various places, approached the Blessed One. There,
the Blessed One [taught] to those of lustful temperament the elevenfold meditation subject on the foul (asubha), categorized by way of the animate and the inanimate.

For those of a temperament dominated by hatred, there are the fourfold meditation subjects beginning with loving-kindness; for those of a deluded temperament, the meditation subjects beginning with mindfulness of death;

for those of a discursive temperament, mindfulness of breathing, the earth-kasiṇa, and so forth; for those of a faithful temperament, the meditation subjects beginning with the recollection of the Buddha;
and for those of an intellectual temperament, the analysis of the four elements and so forth—in this manner, [the teachings] correspond to the eighty-four thousand different temperaments.
He taught the meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Then, about five hundred bhikkhus, having received the meditation subjects from the Blessed One,
traveled by stages in search of suitable dwellings and alms-resorts, eventually reaching a border region contiguous with the Himalayas.
They saw a mountain whose rocky surface resembled blue glass gems, adorned with cool, dense shade and groves of dark-blue forest, its ground strewn with sand like mother-of-pearl or silver plates,
and surrounded by pure, pleasant, and cool reservoirs of water. Then those bhikkhus,
having stayed there for one night and performed their bodily preparations at the break of dawn, entered a certain village nearby for alms.
They entered. The village was composed of a thousand families settled in dense dwellings, and the people there were faithful and devout.
Because it was rare for those in the border regions to see renunciants, they were filled with joy and gladness upon seeing the monks;
having fed them, they requested, "Venerable sirs, please stay right here for the three-month rains retreat," and they constructed five hundred meditation huts.
Having had it built, they prepared all the necessary requisites there, such as beds, chairs, water-jars, and vessels for drinking water.
On the following day, the bhikkhus entered another village for alms. There too, people attended to them in the same manner and requested that they spend the rains retreat.
The bhikkhus consented, saying, "Provided there are no obstacles," and having entered that forest grove, they settled there.
Exerting themselves with vigor throughout the entire night and day, striking the watch-sticks and dwelling frequently with wise attention, they approached the roots of trees and sat down.

By the spiritual power of those virtuous bhikkhus, the tree deities, their own power overcome, descended from their respective celestial mansions, took their children, and wandered here and there. Just as...
Just as when kings or royal ministers have gone to a village residence and occupied space in the houses of the villagers,
the householders emerge from their homes and, dwelling elsewhere, look out from afar wondering,
"When will they depart?"; even so do the deities, having abandoned their respective celestial mansions, wander here and there.
They watched from afar, thinking, "When will the venerable ones depart? Then they reflected thus:
"The monks who have entered their first year of residence will certainly stay for the three months of the rains. However, we shall not be able to go down and live there for so long with our children.
Come now, let us show the monks a terrifying object. So they did.
At night, during the time when the monks were performing their ascetic duties, [Māra] manifested terrifying forms of *yakkhas* and stood directly before them, making a dreadful noise.
As the monks saw those forms and heard that sound, their hearts trembled; they became discolored and turned pale. Because of this, they...
They were unable to make their minds one-pointed. Because of their distracted minds and because they were repeatedly agitated by fear, their mindfulness lapsed.
Then, while they were thus forgetful, [the devas] presented them with foul-smelling objects.
By that foul odor, their brain matter was as if crushed, and intense headaches arose.
And they did not report that occurrence to one another.
Then one day, at the time of waiting upon the senior elder of the Saṅgha, when they had all assembled together, the senior elder asked:
"Friends, for you who have entered this forest grove for these few days, why is the color of your skin so exceedingly pure?"
“[Previously] it was pure and the faculties were serene; but now you are thin, discolored, and jaundiced.

What is unwholesome for you here? Then one bhikkhu said: “Venerable sir, at night I see and hear such and such terrifying objects, and I smell such a scent; because of that, my mind does not [become settled].”
“He attains concentration. By this very means, they all reported that occurrence to him. The senior elder of the Saṅgha said:
“Friends, two periods for entering the rains-residence have been prescribed by the Blessed One. And this lodging of ours is unsuitable;
come, friends, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One and ask about another suitable lodging. “Very well, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied.
Having assented to the elder, they all put their lodgings in order, took up their bowls and robes, and—
being unstained by worldly things— they set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī without even taking leave of anyone among the families. Gradually reaching Sāvatthī,
they went into the presence of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, seeing those bhikkhus, said this: “Bhikkhus, I have laid down a training rule that one should not go on tour during the rainy season;
why then are you going on tour? They reported everything to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, reflecting, saw that throughout the whole of Jambudīpa there was not even a place the size of a four-legged stool that was suitable for them.
He did not see any lodging. Then he said to those bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, there is no other suitable lodging for you;
dwelling right there, you will reach the destruction of the taints. Go, bhikkhus, and dwell depending on that very same lodging. But if you desire safety from the deities, [use] this..."
“Learn this protective chant (*paritta*); for this shall be both a protection for you and a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*),” he said, and spoke this sutta.
Others, however, say that after saying, “Go, monks, and dwell depending on that very same lodging,” the Blessed One said:
“Furthermore, the forest-dweller must know how to maintain [the practice]. That is to say: in the evening and in the morning...”

By way of function, there are two kinds of loving-kindness (*mettā*), two kinds of protective meditation (*paritta*), two kinds of foulness (*asubha*), two kinds of mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*), and the adverting of the mind toward the eight great objects of spiritual urgency (*mahāsaṃvegavatthu*).
The eight great objects of spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, death, and the four sufferings of the woeful states (*apāya*).
Alternatively, birth, aging, sickness, and death are four, with the suffering of the woeful states as the fifth; these relate to the root of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭamūla*) in the past.
"Suffering in the past rooted in the round of existence, suffering in the future rooted in the round of existence, and suffering in the present rooted in the search for nutriment.
Thus, having explained the means of protection, the Blessed One spoke this discourse for the sake of loving-kindness toward those bhikkhus,
for their protection, and as a basis for jhāna leading to insight.
143. Regarding the first verse, "Therein, what ought to be done by one skilled in the goal," this is the word-by-word commentary:
"What ought to be done" (*karaṇīya*) means that which is to be performed, or that which is worthy of being performed. "Goal" (*attha*) refers to the path of practice;
or, whatever is beneficial to oneself, all that is called a "goal" because it is to be sought after (*araṇīya*), meaning because it is to be approached. In the context of the goal...
"By one who is skilled, skilled in welfare"—that is, one who is expert in what is beneficial (*atthakusala*). "That which" (*yaṃ*) is the indefinite nominative;
"this" (*taṃ*) is the definite accusative. Alternatively, both *yaṃ* and *taṃ* are nominative forms, while *santaṃ* and *padaṃ* are accusative forms.

In this context, "existent" (*santa*) is defined by its characteristic, and "state" (*pada*) is defined by that which is to be attained; this is a designation for Nibbāna. "Having realized" (*abhisamecca*)—
"Having fully understood. "Sakka" means one who is able; it is said to mean capable or competent. "Uju" means endowed with uprightness. "Sujū" means perfectly upright.
"Suvaco" means one for whom speech is easy; that is, one who is easy to speak to. "Assa" means he would be. "Mudu" means endowed with gentleness. "Anatimānī" means not conceited.
Now, here is the commentary on the meaning: "What is to be done by one skilled in the goal, having realized the state that is peaceful.
In this context, there is what is to be done and there is what is not to be done. Therein, in brief, the three trainings are what is to be done;
failure in virtue, failure in view, failure in conduct, failure in livelihood, and so forth, are what is not to be done. Likewise—

There is one skilled in what is beneficial, and there is one skilled in what is harmful. In this regard, he who has gone forth in this teaching does not apply himself rightly; he is deficient in virtue and maintains his livelihood by resorting to twenty-one kinds of wrong search. Namely: the gift of bamboo, the gift of leaves, the gift of flowers, [the gift of fruit, the gift of water, the gift of tooth-sticks, the gift of eye-salve, the gift of medicine, the gift of a bowl, the gift of a robe, the gift of a needle, the gift of a girdle, the gift of a razor, the gift of a water-strainer, the gift of a sitting mat, the gift of a walking staff, the gift of a shoulder-pole, the gift of a shoulder-strap, the gift of a sandal, the gift of a fan, the gift of a mirror, the gift of a comb, the gift of a collyrium-box]. He who lives thus is skilled in what is harmful. On the other hand, he who has gone forth in this teaching applies himself rightly; he is perfect in virtue and does not maintain his livelihood by resorting to those twenty-one kinds of wrong search. He is skilled in what is beneficial. Therefore, one should train oneself: "I shall be skilled in what is beneficial. This is how one should train oneself. Giving fruit, giving tooth-sticks, giving water for rinsing the mouth, giving baths, giving bath-powder,
giving clay, flattery, bean-soupery, servitude, running messages on foot, practicing medicine,
acting as a messenger, going on errands, giving alms-food or further gifts of alms-food, geomancy, astrology, and palmistry.
And he frequents six kinds of improper resort (*agocara*). Namely: the resort of prostitutes, widows, young girls, eunuchs, and nunneries.

And he dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and followers of other sects—through unbecoming intimacy with householders—or with those families that are faithless, lacking confidence, providing no refuge, and prone to reviling and abuse.

He frequents, associates with, and attends upon families that desire what is unbeneficial for monks... [and] for female lay disciples—families that desire what is harmful, unpleasant, and lacking in security from bondage. This is one who is skilled in what is unbeneficial.
But he who, having gone forth in this Teaching, rightly exerts himself, abandoning wrong search and abiding in the fourfold purification of virtue...

One who desires to be established fulfills the restraint of the Pātimokkha by means of the head of faith, the restraint of the sense faculties by means of the head of mindfulness, purity of livelihood by means of the head of energy, and the use of requisites by means of the head of wisdom; such a person is skilled in the goal.
Or else, one fulfills the restraint of the Pātimokkha by means of purifying the seven classes of offenses, and [the restraint of the sense faculties] regarding objects that strike the six doors...
He purifies the restraint of the sense faculties by way of the non-arising of covetousness and so forth;

livelihood purification by way of avoiding improper search and by using requisites praised by the wise and described by the Buddhas and their disciples; the use of requisites by way of the aforementioned reflection;
and clear comprehension in the turning of the four postures by way of reflecting on what is purposeful and so forth—he too is skilled in the meaning.
Just as a cloth is cleansed by depending on alkaline water,
a mirror by depending on ashes, and gold by depending on the mouth of a furnace, so too, knowing that virtue is purified by depending on knowledge,
one purifies virtue while washing it with the water of knowledge. And just as the quail bird [guards] its egg, or the yak [guards] its tail, or a woman with an only child [guards her child]...
Just as a woman protects her only beloved son, or as a one-eyed man protects his only eye, so too does he protect his own aggregate of virtue with extreme heedfulness;
reviewing it morning and evening, he sees not even the slightest fault. He is also skilled in the goal.
Or again, having established himself in virtue that produces freedom from remorse, he exerts himself in the practice for the suppression of the defilements.
Having exerted that [mind], he performs the preliminary work for the kasiṇa; having performed the preliminary work for the kasiṇa, he brings forth the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

He too is skilled in the goal (*atthakusala*). Or again, one who, having emerged from attainment, contemplates conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and reaches Arahantship—he is the foremost among those skilled in the goal.

In this context, those who are skilled in the meaning—whether by being established in virtue that brings about non-regret, or by exertion in the path that suppresses the defilements, and who are thus praised for the path and its fruit—are intended here as "skilled in the meaning.
Such are those bhikkhus. Therefore, with reference to those bhikkhus, the Blessed One [spoke] by way of a designation based on a single individual.
In the teaching, he said, "What should be done by one skilled in the goal.
Then, to those who had developed doubt as to what that which should be done was, he said, "Having realized that state which is peaceful.
This is the intended meaning here: [it refers to] that peaceful state of Nibbāna, praised by those awakened after the Buddha, through the mode of penetration.
"By one who desires to dwell having fully realized that which is to be done.

Here, in this verse-line, "that which is to be done" (*karaṇīya*) refers back to what was stated at the beginning of the preceding line: "having fully realized that peaceful state" (*taṃ santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca*).
However, since this reading is incomplete in its phrasing, it should be understood that the words "by one who desires to dwell" (*viharitukāmena*) are supplied.
Alternatively, "having realized the state that is peace" means that by means of mundane wisdom—through hearsay and so forth—one knows the state of Nibbāna to be peace;

then, by way of the context, it follows that "that which ought to be done" is what must be performed by one desiring to attain it. Thus, the intended meaning here should be understood as: "that which ought to be done by one skilled in the goal.
Alternatively, when it is said, "that which ought to be done by one skilled in the goal," [the question arises: "What?"
To those who were reflecting, he said: "Having realized that state which is peaceful. Its intended meaning should be understood as follows:
"Whatever is to be done after having realized with mundane wisdom that state which is peaceful—that is what is to be done. What ought to be performed is "that which is to be done" (*karaṇīya*);
thus it is said to be precisely that which is worthy of being done.

But what is that? What else could it be other than the means for attaining it? Granted, this was already stated by the first phrase itself, which illustrates the three trainings in the sense of "that which is to be done.
For we said in the commentary on its meaning: "There is that which is to be done, and there is that which is not to be done.
Therein, in brief, the three trainings are that which is to be done. Because it was taught in such extreme brevity...
However, among those monks, some had understood and some had not.

Therefore, for the sake of making it understood by those who had not, he spoke this half-stanza—“He is capable, upright, and very upright; he is easy to speak to, gentle, and free from pride”—expanding upon what must specifically be practiced by a forest-dwelling monk.

What is meant? A forest-dwelling bhikkhu who desires to dwell having realized the state of peace, or who, having approached it through mundane wisdom, is practicing for its attainment, would be able to practice for the penetration of truth by being endowed with the second and fourth factors of striving and being indifferent toward both body and life; likewise...

In undertaking the preliminary practices for the *kasiṇa* meditations and so forth, and in the mending of one’s own bowl and robes, he should be capable, skillful, diligent, and competent in those various high and low duties to be performed for his fellow celibates, as well as in other such matters.
And while being capable, he should be upright by way of possessing the third factor of striving. Upright—
And even if one is upright, one should not rest content with that state once, but should become more thoroughly upright by practicing without slackening again and again for as long as life lasts.

Or, one is upright through honesty and thoroughly upright through the absence of deceit. Or, one is upright through the abandonment of crookedness of body and speech, and thoroughly upright through the abandonment of crookedness of mind.
Or, one is upright through not manifesting non-existent qualities, and [thoroughly upright] through [the absence of non-existent qualities].

By not acquiescing in arisen gain, he is straight and upright. Thus, through the contemplation of the characteristics of objects and through the first two and the third trainings, as well as through purity of application and intention, he is both straight and upright.
Not only is he straight and upright, but moreover, he is easy to speak to. For that person who [thinks], "This..."
When told, "This should be done," if he says, "What have you seen? What have you heard? Who are you to speak to me? Is your preceptor or teacher personally known and trusted by me?

or if he harasses him with silence, or having accepted the instruction, does not act accordingly, he remains far from the attainment of distinction. But he who, when being exhorted, says, "Excellent, Venerable Sir..."
He says, "Well said! One's own faults are indeed difficult to see;
out of compassion, please speak to me again when you see me in such a state, for it has been a long time since I received instruction from you," and he practices according to the instructions given.
He is then not far from the attainment of distinction. Therefore, having thus accepted the words of another...

And he should be easy to speak to. Just as he is easy to speak to, so too should he be gentle. "Gentle" means that when being appointed by householders to tasks such as going on errands or sending messages, instead of acting with gentleness in those matters, he remains stubborn;
rather, he is gentle in his performance of duties and in the entire holy life (*brahmacariya*).
He should be like well-refined gold, capable of being employed for various purposes here and there.
Alternatively, "gentle" means he should be free from frowning, with an open face, easy to speak with, and disposed toward hospitality; he should be like a good ford, easy to enter.
Moreover, he should not only be gentle, but also free from excessive pride (*anatimānī*); he should not look down upon others on account of grounds for pride such as birth, clan, and so forth.
"And one should dwell with a mind like that of the young Caṇḍāla boy, just as the Elder Sāriputta did. (144) Thus,

having stated a certain duty specifically for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who desires to dwell having realized the state of peace, or who is practicing for its attainment, the Blessed One, wishing to speak further beyond that, said:
And he spoke the second verse: “*Santussako cā*.
Therein, one who is satisfied by the twelvefold contentment—divided as described under the phrase “*santuṭṭhī ca kataññutā*” (*contentment and gratitude*)—is called *santussako*.
Alternatively, one who is pleased (*tussati*) is a *tussako*; one who is pleased with what is one’s own (*sakena*), or one who is pleased with what is sufficient (*santena*).

One who is content with what is equal is a "santussaka. In this context, "one's own" (*saka*) refers to the fourfold requisites that were indicated during the ordination ceremony in the *upasampadā-māḷaka* by the words "depending on alms-food," and which have been accepted by oneself.
Whether they are excellent or not excellent, whether they are given respectfully or disrespectfully—at the time of receiving them and at the time of using them—[one remains content].

One who maintains himself without displaying any change [in his demeanor] is called "content with what is one's own" (*sakena tussako*). That which is obtained and exists for oneself is called "what is present" (*santa*);
being content with that very presence, not aspiring for more than that, and abandoning excessive desire, one is called "content with what is present" (*santena tussako*).
"Equanimity" (*sama*) refers to the abandonment of attraction and aversion toward the desirable and the undesirable. By means of that...
One who is satisfied with all objects of experience through equanimity is called "one who is satisfied by equanimity" (*samena tussako*).
One who is nourished by ease is "easy to support" (*subharo*); what is meant is that he is well-nourished.

For a bhikkhu who, even when given rice, meat, boiled rice, and so forth, filling his bowl to the brim, displays a sour face and a state of dissatisfaction, or [behaves similarly] in the presence of those donors—
If, upon receiving alms-food, he shows displeasure by asking, "What have you given? and gives it instead to novices, householders, and the like, he is difficult to support.
Seeing this, people avoid him from afar, thinking, "This monk is difficult to support; he cannot be maintained.
However, he who, having received anything—whether coarse or refined, little or much—is pleased and has a serene face...
Having sacrificed [the offering], he maintains himself; such a one is easy to support. Seeing this, people become exceedingly confident, thinking:
"Our venerable sir is easy to support; he is satisfied even with very little," and having given their word, they maintain him.
It is such a person as is intended here by the term "easy to support."
"One who has few duties" (*appakicco*) means one who is not preoccupied with various tasks such as delighting in work, delighting in talk, and delighting in socializing.
Alternatively, it means being free from duties such as overseeing new construction projects in the entire monastery, managing the community’s property, or supervising novices and temple attendants;

rather, having performed his own tasks such as shaving his hair and nails and preparing his bowl and robes, he is devoted solely to the duties of the ascetic’s dharma (*samaṇadhamma*). This is what is meant.

"Light in livelihood" means one whose mode of living is light. This refers to one who, unlike a certain monk with many possessions who, when departing for another region, causes a great crowd to carry away much—such as bowls, robes, rugs, oil, and molasses—on their heads or around their waists before departing;
instead, such a person possesses few requisites, having only the eight basic requisites of a recluse, beginning with the bowl and robes.
He avoids [unwholesome things]; at the time of departing for another region, he departs taking [only what is necessary] like a winged bird;
such a person is intended here by the term "one of light livelihood" (*sallahukavutti*). One who possesses peaceful faculties is "one of peaceful faculties" (*santindriyo*);

this means one whose faculties are not agitated by passion and so forth toward desirable objects and the like. "Clever" (*nipako*) means wise, discerning, and possessed of wisdom, specifically the wisdom that guards virtue (*sīla*).

The intended meaning is that he is endowed with the wisdom that discriminates between robes and other requisites, as well as the wisdom that thoroughly understands the seven types of suitability regarding dwellings and so forth.
"Not impudent" means "free from impudence"; the sense is that he is devoid of the eight grounds for bodily impudence, the four grounds for verbal impudence, and the many grounds for mental impudence.

The eight grounds for bodily impudence consist of [behaving improperly] when entering the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, a dining hall, a sauna, a bathing place, the path to almsround, or a private house.
Improper conduct by way of the body. For example: here someone sits with legs crossed in the midst of the Saṅgha, or with one foot placed over the other, and so forth;
likewise in the midst of a group. "In the midst of a group" means in an assembly of the fourfold congregation, as well as in the presence of more senior individuals.
Furthermore, in the dining hall, he does not give a seat to the elders, nor does he give a seat to the novices.
He obstructs [others] in the same way in the sauna. Furthermore, if he performs acts such as lighting the fire without asking permission from those who are senior, it is a fault.
Regarding the bathing ford, it has been stated: "One should bathe according to the order of arrival, without making the distinction of 'junior' or 'senior'.
Disregarding this, if he arrives later and enters the water, he causes distress to both the seniors and the juniors. On the path for alms-round...
Furthermore, it includes such acts as walking ahead of one's seniors while striking arm against arm for the sake of the best seat, the best water, or the best alms-food;
entering a house before one's seniors when they are about to enter; and engaging in physical play with juniors, and so forth.
What is called verbal immodesty in four instances is the utterance of improper speech within the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a house.
For example: here someone speaks on the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha without having asked for permission;
likewise in a group of the kind previously described, or toward elder individuals. Therein, when questioned by people, he answers without asking permission from an elder.
But within a house, [he asks]: "Lady so-and-so, what is there? Is there rice porridge, or solid food, or soft food?"
"What will you give me? What shall I eat today? What shall I consume? What shall I drink?"—he speaks such things as these.

"Mental immodesty in various matters" (*anekaṭṭhāna-manopāgabbhiya*) means that even without committing transgressions through body or speech in those various places, one engages in manifold improper thoughts in the mind alone, such as sensual thoughts and so forth.

"Not greedy for families" (*kulesvananugiddho*) means that regarding whichever families he visits, he does not [behave] either out of craving for requisites or by way of inappropriate intimacy with householders.
Or, it means one who is not greedy, not sorrowful with others' sorrow, not joyful with others' joy, not happy when others are happy, not miserable when others are miserable,
and not personally engaging in the various duties that have arisen. And regarding this verse,
the word "of her" (*assā*) which was stated in the phrase "she should be easy to speak to," is to be connected with all the preceding words as "one who is easily satisfied."
"And he would be easy to support"—thus it should be construed.

145. Thus the Blessed One, having explained what must further be done specifically for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who desires to dwell having personally realized the state of peace, or who wishes to practice for its attainment, now [explains] also what must not be done.
Desiring to explain this, he spoke this half-verse: “One should not perform even the slightest thing by which the wise might censure others.
Its meaning is as follows: while performing what ought to be done in this way, one should not perform that which is called “the slight” or “the base,” namely, misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
And by not performing it, one avoids not only the gross, but furthermore—
"One should not perform anything" means one should not perform even the slightest thing, however minute.
Thereafter, he shows the disadvantage of such conduct as being visible in this very life: "by which the wise would censure others.
And here, those who are unwise are not the standard, for they may perform what is blameless or what is blameworthy, or what is slightly blameworthy.
Or it may be a great offense. However, the wise alone are the authority.
For they, having investigated and scrutinized thoroughly, speak dispraise of that which deserves dispraise and praise of that which deserves praise; therefore, it is said, "the wise others.
Thus, with these two and a half verses, the Blessed One [has spoken] for one who desires to abide having fully realized the state of peace.

Having explained the approach to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)— distinguishing between what is to be done and what is not to be done— for one who wishes to practice for the sake of attaining that [state], specifically for a forest-dweller (*āraññaka*),

and for all those who wish to dwell having taken up a meditation subject under the heading of "forest-dwelling," [the author now speaks] regarding the purpose of the protective chant (*paritta*) for the warding off of fear of deities for those monks, by way of the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*).
And for the purpose of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he began to discourse on loving-kindness (*mettā*) in the manner beginning with, "May they be happy and secure.
Therein, "happy" (*sukhino*) means possessed of happiness. "Secure" (*kheminō*) means possessing security; it is said that they are fearless and free from calamity.
"All" (*sabbe*) means without exception. "Beings" (*sattā*) means living creatures. "With happy hearts" (*sukhitattā*) means with happy minds. And here, by bodily...

They should be understood as "happy" because they possess happiness, "glad at heart" because their minds are glad, or "secure" because both of these have occurred, or because all fear and calamity have vanished.
Why, then, was it stated in this way? It is for the purpose of showing the mode of developing loving-kindness (*mettā*).
For loving-kindness should be developed in this manner: either by thinking, "May all beings be happy," or "May they be secure," or "May they be glad at heart."

146. Having thus shown the development of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) in brief, from the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) up to the limit of absorption (*appanā-koṭi*), he now spoke the two verses beginning with "Whosoever... (*ye keci*) in order to show it in detail as well.
Alternatively, because a mind that is habituated to diverse objects does not settle in one-pointedness all at once, but rather follows the distinctions of the objects in sequence—

It becomes established; therefore, having followed after and followed after the object—which is divided into various categories such as the pairs and triads of moving and stationary beings—he spoke the two verses beginning with "Whatever... for the purpose of establishing it.
Alternatively, because the mind of one rests easily upon whichever object is clear to them, he [spoke] this for those bhikkhus regarding whatever was clear to each.

Desiring to establish the mind upon that object, he spoke these two verses beginning with "Whosoever" (*ye keci*), which illustrate the various classifications of objects such as the dyads and triads of the moving and the stationary (*tasa-thāvara*).
For herein are found the dyads of the moving and the stationary, the seen and the unseen, the distant and the near, and the beings and those seeking birth.

There are four pairs (*duka*). Because of the possibility of the meaning [of "living being"] occurring in three of the middle terms and two of the subsequent terms among the six terms beginning with "long" (*dīgha*), he illustrates three triads (*tika*):
the long-short-medium triad, the large-small-medium triad, and the thick-small-medium triad. In that context, "whosoever" (*ye keci*) is an expression denoting without remainder.
Living beings (*pāṇa*) themselves are the creatures (*bhūta*); thus, they are "living-creatures" (*pāṇabhūta*). Now...
Or, they breathe, thus they are "breathing beings" (*pāṇā*). By this, one includes five-aggregate beings who are bound to inhalation and exhalation.
They come to be, thus they are "beings" (*bhūtā*). By this, one includes one-aggregate and four-aggregate beings. They exist, thus they are "existent" (*atthī*); they are found.
Thus, by this expression "whatever breathing beings, beings, or existents there may be," all beings that are to be included within the three categories of suffering are [encompassed].
Having shown them together as one, he now shows them all—whether moving or stationary—as being without exception by means of this dyad.
In this context, "moving" (*tasa*) refers to those who tremble; it is a designation for those possessed of craving and fear. "Stationary" (*thāvara*) refers to those who stand firm;
it is a designation for the Arahants who have abandoned craving and fear. "Without exception" (*anavasesa*) means that there are no remnants of them remaining.
"Even all" is what is meant. And that which is stated at the end of the second verse is to be connected with every pair and triad:
"Whatever beings there are—whether trembling or stationary, without exception—all these beings may be happy-minded.
Thus it continues up to: "Whether already come to be or seeking birth, all these beings may be happy-minded."

Now, regarding the six phrases beginning with "long" (*dīghā*) in the triads illustrating long, short, and medium [stature], "long" refers to those with a long physical existence (*attabhāva*), such as nāgas, fish, and crocodiles.

For in the great ocean, the physical existences of nāgas may measure many hundreds of fathoms, and the physical existences of fish, crocodiles, and so forth, may measure many yojanas. "Large" refers to those with a large physical existence.
In the water there are fish, turtles, and so forth; on land there are elephants, nagas, and so forth; among non-human beings there are dānavas and so forth. And it is said: "The body of Rāhu.
For his body is four thousand eight hundred yojanas in height;
his two arms are twelve hundred yojanas in measure; the distance between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas, and likewise the distance between his fingers.
"Two hundred yojanas [in height] like the palms of the hands. "Medium-sized" refers to the individual existences (attabhāva) of horses, oxen, buffaloes, pigs, and so forth.
"Small-sized" refers to beings such as dwarfs and others within their respective species, whose dimensions are inferior to those that are long or medium-sized.
"Minute" refers to beings with subtle individual existences produced within water and other elements, who are beyond the range of the fleshly eye and are objects of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).

Or alternatively, they are "minute" (*aṇuka*) and so forth. Furthermore, those beings among various species who are inferior in size to the large and medium—both in stature and girth—are to be understood as "minute.
"Large" refers to beings such as fish, turtles, crabs, and shells, whose physical forms are massive.
Having thus shown all beings without exception by means of three triads, he now shows them again by grouping them under three dyads, beginning with "seen or unseen."
In this context, "seen" refers to those who have previously come within the range of one's own eye.
"Unseen" refers to those situated beyond the great ocean, beyond other mountains, in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), and so forth.

By the pair of verses beginning with "Whether they dwell far away or not far," he shows sentient beings dwelling far from and near to one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*). These [beings] are considered by way of their respective bases of clinging (*upādāna*).
They should be understood as follows: beings dwelling within one’s own body are near; those dwelling outside the body are distant. Likewise, those dwelling within the precincts are near;
those dwelling outside the precincts are distant. Those dwelling in one’s own monastery, village, district, island, or world-system are said to be near;
those dwelling in another world-system are said to be distant.
"Bhūta" means born or produced. This is a designation for those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), who have become such and will not again be reckoned as "those who have come to be.

"Sambhavesī" means those seeking rebirth. This is a designation for trainees (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana) who, because they have not abandoned the fetters of existence, seek rebirth even in the future. Alternatively, in the four...
Among the various wombs, those beings born from eggs and from a womb are called *sambhavesī* as long as they have not broken the eggshell or the amniotic sac;
once they have broken the eggshell or the amniotic sac and emerged outside, they are called *bhūta*.

Those born of moisture and those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) are called *sambhavesī* during the first moment of consciousness; from the second moment of consciousness onward, they are called *bhūta*. By which...
Or they are born by way of a posture; as long as they have not yet reached another state, they are called "seeking existence" (*sambhavesī*); beyond that, they are "beings" (*bhūta*).

148. Thus, having shown the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward beings by means of two and a half verses beginning with "May they be happy," in various ways through the aspiration for the attainment of welfare and happiness for those monks, the Blessed One now [proceeds] by means of the aspiration for the non-attainment of harm and suffering.
Showing this, he said: “One should not deceive another. This is the ancient reading; however, they now read it as “paraṃ hi,” which is not elegant.
In that context, “paro” means another person; “paraṃ” means another person. “Na nikubbetha” means one should not deceive. “Nātimaññetha” means...

One should not conceive [of oneself] as having transcended. "In any place" (*katthaci*) means in some location, such as in a village, a town, a field, in the midst of kinsmen, or in the midst of a guild, and so forth.

"This" (*naṃ*) refers to this [self]. "Any person whatsoever" (*kañci*) means any one at all—whether a kshatriya, a brahmin, a householder, a renunciant, one of high birth, or one of low birth, and so forth.
"Malice and perception of resistance" (*byārosanā paṭighasaññā*) [refers to these] through bodily and verbal manifestations.
“[It is] through resentment and through the mental alteration of the perception of aversion.

For where it should have been said “through resentment and the perception of aversion,” it is instead said “resentment and the perception of aversion,” just as where it should have been said “liberated through right knowledge,” it is said “liberated through right knowledge,” and just as [it is said] “through gradual training, gradual performance, and gradual practice.”
It should be stated: "gradual training, gradual practice, gradual path.
"One should not wish suffering for another" means one should not desire suffering for others. What is meant?
One should not cultivate loving-kindness (*mettā*) merely through the mental application of "May they be happy or secure," and so forth. Rather, [one should think]: "O, may some other person..."
One should develop this while attending to it thus: "One should not deceive any other person through frauds such as cheating;
one should not despise any other person anywhere on account of the nine grounds for conceit, such as birth;
and one should not wish suffering for another through mutual resentment or perceptions of aversion. Thus one should cultivate [the meditation].

149. Having thus shown the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) in its actual meaning by way of the aspiration for the non-arrival of harm and suffering, he now says, "As a mother [protects her own son]," illustrating that very point through a simile. Its meaning is as follows: just as a mother would protect her own son—her biological child born from her own body—and especially that only son, protecting him with her very life, even sacrificing her own life for the sake of warding off the arrival of suffering upon him; so too should one cultivate a boundless mind toward all living beings. This is the meaning. Thus it has been said: "Just as a mother protects her own son, her biological child born from her own body, and especially that only son, protecting him with her very life—even sacrificing her own life for the sake of warding off the arrival of suffering upon him—so too should one cultivate a boundless mind toward all living beings. This is the meaning. Thus it has been said. Furthermore, this is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*: "Just as a mother, having seen her only son fallen into a pit of filth, would not feel revulsion, but would rather take him out of that pit of filth and wash him with scented water, so too should one cultivate a boundless mind toward all living beings. This is the meaning. Thus it has been said. Furthermore, this is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*: "Just as a mother, having seen her only son fallen into a pit of filth, would not feel revulsion, but would rather take him out of that pit of filth and wash him with scented water, so too should one cultivate a boundless mind toward all living beings. This is the meaning. Thus it has been said. In this way, one should cultivate this mind of loving-kindness toward all beings; one should generate it again and again and increase it.
And that [loving-kindness] should be cultivated as immeasurable by way of having immeasurable beings as its object, or else by way of pervading even a single being without exception.
Having thus shown the cultivation of loving-kindness in every aspect, he now says, "And loving-kindness toward the whole world," in order to demonstrate its further expansion.

In this context, one who "measures" (mijjati) and "protects" (tāyati) is a *mitto* (friend); the meaning is that he is affectionate due to his inclination toward welfare and protects one from the arrival of harm.

The state of a friend is *mettā*. "In all" means without exception. "In the world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). It is called "mental" (*mānasa*) because it exists in the mind;
for it is so described because it is associated with consciousness (*citta*). "Cultivate" means increase. Of this... [text fragment ends].

“Immeasurable” (*aparimāṇa*) means “without measure”; it is so called because its object consists of immeasurable beings. “Above” (*uddhaṃ*) means upward; by this, the formless existence (*arūpabhava*) is included.
“Below” (*adho*) means downward; by this, the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) is included.

“Across” (*tiriyaṃ*) means the middle; by this, the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) is included. “Unconfined” (*asambādha*) means free from confinement; what is meant is that its boundaries are broken.
"Enmity" (sīmā) is said to mean an adversary; thus, they "proceed even against that" is the meaning. "Free from enmity" (avera) means devoid of enmity;
what is meant is that even from time to time there is an absence of the manifestation of an envious intention. "Free from hostility" (asapatta) means one whose adversaries have departed.
For a person who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings, and has no adversary whatsoever.
Because it has become free from its adversary, that mind of his is called "without enemies. For this is a figurative expression:
namely, that an adversary is an enemy (*sapatta*). This is the word-by-word commentary on the meaning.
Now, here is the commentary on the intended meaning: regarding that which was said, "In this way, one should cultivate the mind toward all beings..."
"It is immeasurable," it is said. And one should cultivate and increase this immeasurable mind of loving-kindness toward the entire world;
one should cause it to reach growth, expansion, and abundance. How?

Above, below, and across—above as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), below as far as the Avīci hell, and across as far as the remaining directions. Or, above, the formless realm (*ārūpya*); below, the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Pervading the entire horizontal dimension of the form realm without exception.

And while developing it in this way, one should develop it so that it becomes unconfined, free from enmity, and free from hostility, thereby effecting the absence of confinement, enmity, and hostility.
Or rather, for one who has attained perfection in that development, it is "unconfined" by virtue of obtaining space everywhere; [it is developed] by removing resentment toward oneself and others.
“Free from enmity”—by removing ill will toward oneself and others, it becomes free from enemies.

One should develop and increase that boundless mind of loving-kindness—free from confinement, free from enmity, and free from enemies—toward the entire world, defined by the threefold division of above, below, and across.

(151) Having thus shown the development of the cultivation of loving-kindness, he now says, “Standing, walking... [and so on]... one should resolve,” showing the absence of restriction regarding postures for one who dwells devoted to that cultivation.
The meaning of this is as follows: while developing this mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), he—

without imposing a restriction on his posture as in the passages beginning with “he sits, having folded his legs crosswise, setting the body erect”— but rather dispelling any discomfort from whichever posture he happens to be in as suits him,

He desires to resolve upon this mindfulness of loving-kindness jhāna. Or else, whether standing or walking, his standing and so forth do not act as obstacles;

“Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, as long as he is free from drowsiness, he should maintain this mindfulness.

This is its intended meaning: one should cultivate that mental state of loving-kindness toward the whole world, as it was said, in such a way that it persists through whatever posture one is in—standing and so forth—or even without regard for those postures, for as long as one remains awake.
If one wishes to resolve upon this mindfulness of loving-kindness meditation (*mettā-jhāna-sati*), one should, having first become free from sloth and torpor, resolve upon that mindfulness.

Thus, demonstrating mastery over the cultivation of loving-kindness, [the Blessed One] directed him toward that abiding in loving-kindness by saying, "One should resolve upon this mindfulness. Now, praising that very abiding, he said: "This is called the sublime abiding here.
Its meaning is as follows: beginning with "May they be happy and secure," and so on, up until "one should resolve upon this mindfulness."

From which [state] one dwells constantly, continuously, and uninterruptedly—whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—as long as one is free from sloth.

Through this delimitation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-pariccheda*), one does not fall into the view that "this is merely a heap of formations; no sentient being (*satta*) is found here.
Thus, gradually becoming possessed of supramundane virtue (*lokuttara-sīla*), and by means of that very virtue associated with the supramundane, [one proceeds].
He is endowed with the vision known as the right view of the path of stream-entry.

"Furthermore, he will not enter a womb again; having been reborn in the Suddhāvāsa heavens, he will attain Arahantship right there and pass away into Parinibbāna.
Having thus concluded his teaching, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus: "Go, bhikkhus, and dwell in that very grove.
And on the eight days each month when the Dhamma is heard, strike the gong and [recite] this discourse."
"Exhort one another, give Dhamma talks, converse together, and express appreciation; cultivate, develop, and frequently practice this very meditation subject.
Then those non-human beings will no longer show you that terrifying object;
instead, they will become desirous of your welfare and well-being. Having replied "Very well" to the Blessed One, they rose from their seats.

they themselves swept the lodgings, prepared hot water, performed massages for the backs and feet, and provided protection.

and all of them, within that very same month, attained the supreme fruit of Arahantship and, at the Great Pavāraṇā ceremony, performed the Pavāraṇā of purity.

9. Commentary on the Hemavatasutta.
"Today is the fifteenth" refers to the Hemavatasutta. What is its origin? Its origin is occasioned by a question. For by Hemavata...
When questioned, the Blessed One spoke such words as, "The world has arisen in six ways. Therein, the passage beginning with "Today is the fifteenth" was spoken by Sātāgira;
that beginning with "Thus said Sātāgira" was added by the compilers of the collection; that beginning with "Is your mind [at peace]? was spoken by Hemavata;
and that beginning with "In six ways the world... was spoken by the Blessed One. Having combined all of these together, it is called the "Hemavata Sutta."
Some call it the “Sātāgiri Sutta.
Regarding that, as for the verse beginning with “Today is the fifteenth day,” its origin is as follows:
in this very Bhaddakappa, after [the Buddha] had appeared when the lifespan of men was twenty thousand years and remained until the lifespan was sixteen thousand years, he attained final nibbāna.
They performed the funeral rites for the body of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with a great honor.
His relics remained there as a single solid mass, like a block of gold, without being scattered. For this is the natural law regarding Buddhas of long life.
However, because Buddhas of short life pass away into *parinibbāna* without having been seen by the majority of people, [their relics are not thus preserved].
Therefore, out of compassion, thinking, "By making offerings to the relics, people here and there will generate merit," they resolve, "Let the relics be scattered.
Consequently, their relics scatter like golden dust, just as those of our Blessed One did.
People built a single relic-shrine for that Blessed One and established a cetiya one *yojana* in extent.
In height and in circumference, it was thus. It had four gates, each separated from the next by one *gāvuta*.
One gate was taken by King Kikī; one by his son named Pathavindharo; one by the ministers headed by the general;
and one by the country folk headed by the guild-leader. It was made of solid red gold, a single mass, resembling the essence of gold itself.
And the bricks were made of various kinds of gems, each worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Having performed the function of mortar with yellow orpiment and realgar, and the function of water with fragrant oil, they consecrated that cetiya.
When the cetiya had been thus established, two young men who were friends went forth and [approached] the elders who were face-to-face disciples.
They went forth in his presence. For only in the presence of long-lived Buddhas do disciples go forth, receive full ordination, and receive formal dependence (*nissaya*);
others do not obtain these things. Then those sons of good family asked, "Venerable sir, how many duties (*dhura*) are there in the Dispensation?
The elders replied, "There are two duties: the duty of residence (*vāsadhura*) and the duty of study (*pariyattidhura*). Regarding this:
A son of good family who has gone forth, having lived for five years in the presence of his teachers and preceptors, having fulfilled the duties and counter-duties,
