having made the Pātimokkha and two or three recitation sections of the Suttantas thoroughly mastered, and having received a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna),
should enter the forest without attachment to family or groups, and strive for the realization of Arahatship.
One must exert effort; this is the duty of dwelling (*vāsadhura*).

However, according to one’s own capacity, having mastered either one *nikāya* or two to five *nikāyas*, one should devote oneself to the Teaching so that it is perfectly clear both in its textual form and in its meaning;
this is the duty of study (*pariyattidhura*). Then those sons of good family [considered]: "Of the two duties, the duty of dwelling alone is the best."
Having said, "We are indeed young; we shall fulfill the duty of providing lodging when we are old, but for now let us fulfill the duty of study," they began their studies.
Being naturally wise, before long they became masters of the entire word of the Buddha and were exceedingly skilled in the analysis of the Vinaya. Their study—
Relying on [him], a retinue arose; relying on the retinue, gain arose.
Each one had a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus. They dwelt proclaiming the Teacher’s dispensation, and it was as if the time of the Buddha were once again present.
At that time, two bhikkhus were dwelling in a village monastery: one who spoke according to the Dhamma and one who spoke contrary to the Dhamma. The one who spoke contrary to the Dhamma was fierce.
He is harsh and talkative; his transgression becomes evident to the other.
Then he reproves him, saying, "Friend, this action of yours is unbecoming of the Teaching. He evades the matter, asking, "What have you seen? What have you heard?
The other replies, "The masters of the Vinaya will know. Then the one who speaks what is not the Dhamma says, "If the masters of the Vinaya [investigate] this matter..."
Realizing, "They will decide [otherwise], and certainly I shall not be established in my Teacher’s dispensation," and desiring to form his own faction,
he immediately took his requisites, approached those two elders, gave them his monastic requisites,
and began to live under their sponsorship. He attended upon them all with great care, performing his duties and services with diligence.
He acted as if he wished to fill [the bowl]. Then, one day, having gone to wait upon him and paid his respects, he remained standing even though he was being dismissed by them.
The elders asked him, "Is there something that needs to be said? He replied, "Yes, venerable sirs;
I have a dispute with a certain bhikkhu concerning an act of misconduct. If he were to come here..."

He declared, "The case should not be decided according to the formal legal procedure. The elders said, "It is not permissible to decide a matter that has been brought forward without following the formal legal procedure.
He replied, "Venerable sirs, if it is done in this way, I shall have no standing in the Teaching;
let this evil be mine alone, do not you decide it. Being thus pressured by him, they consented.
Having thus obtained their consent, he returned to that residence and,

thinking even more contemptuously of that proponent of the Dhamma, saying, "Everything has been settled in the presence of the experts in the Vinaya," he addressed him with harsh words. The proponent of the Dhamma, realizing,
"He has become fearless," immediately departed and approached the thousand monks who were the retinue of the Elders.
He said: "But, friends, when a matter has been brought forward, it must be adjudicated according to the Dhamma;
or else, without having it adjudicated, harmony should be restored by making one another confess their transgressions. Yet these elders have neither adjudicated the matter nor restored harmony.
What does this mean? Having heard this, they too became silent, thinking: "Surely something [must have happened] to the teachers."
“[It is] known. Then the proponent of what is contrary to the Dhamma, having found an opportunity, pressured the proponent of the Dhamma, saying:
“Previously you said, ‘The holders of the Vinaya will know. Now report that matter to those holders of the Vinaya!
Having said, “From this day forward you are defeated; do not come to this residence,” he departed. Thereupon, the proponent of the Dhamma approached the elders.
“Disregarding the Teaching, you looked only to the person, thinking, ‘He served us and gladdened us.
Having failed to protect the Teaching, you protected the person. From this day forward, it is no longer permissible for you to pass judgment.
Today the Blessed One Kassapa has attained Parinibbāna! they cried out with a great sound, lamenting, “The Teacher is lost!”
Lamenting, "The Dispensation! he departed.
Then those monks, with hearts filled with agitation, felt remorse, thinking, "By protecting this individual, we have cast the jewel of the Dispensation into a pit.
Because their aspirations were shattered by that very remorse, they passed away.
Being unable to be reborn in the heavenly realms, one teacher was reborn on Mount Hemavata in the Himavat region by the name of the Yakkha Hemavata;
the second teacher was reborn in the Middle Country on Mount Sāta by the name of Sātāgira.
Their retinues of monks, following after them and likewise being unable to be reborn in the heavenly realms, became their attendants.
They were reborn as *yakkhas*. Their lay supporters, however, were reborn in the world of the gods.
Hemavata and Sātāgira became powerful *yakkha* kings among the twenty-eight *yakkha* generals. And this is the custom of the *yakkha* generals:
every month, for eight days, they sit in judgment on matters of Dhamma.
In the Himalayas, on a surface of ruby, in a pavilion of sapphires, there was an assembly of deities; it was there that they were to gather.
Then, at that gathering, Sātāgira and Hemavata, upon seeing one another, recognized each other and asked, "Friend, where were you born?
And where were you born? Having thus inquired about their respective places of birth, they felt remorse.
[They replied: “We are ruined, friend! Having practiced the ascetic life for twenty thousand years, we have been reborn in the womb of a *yakkha* because of one evil companion;
meanwhile, those who provided us with requisites have been reborn among the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*”).
Then Sātāgira said: “Noble sir, there is a place called Himavā, renowned as wonderful and marvelous; [something]—”
“Having seen or heard something wonderful, you should report it to me as well. Hemavata also said, “Friend, the Middle Country is renowned for its wonders;
having seen or heard anything wonderful there, you should report it to me as well.
Thus, after those two friends had made this agreement with one another, they continued to live there without ever leaving that very place of birth.
One interval between Buddhas had passed, during which the great earth rose only one *yojana* and three *gāvutas* in height.
Then our Bodhisatta, having made his aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha and fulfilled the perfections (*pāramīs*) from that time until the Vessantara Jātaka, was reborn in the Tusita heaven;
having remained there for the full duration of his lifespan, [he appeared] in the introduction to the Dhammapada.

Requested by the deities in the manner described, he performed the five great observations (*pañca mahāvilokanāni*), informed the deities, and while the thirty-two omens were occurring, he took rebirth here after causing the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*) to tremble.
Even though they saw those signs, these royal *yakkhas* did not know, "It is for this reason that these have arisen. "Because of being addicted to play..."
"Nor did they see [the Buddha]," say some. This same method applies to his birth, his Great Renunciation, and his attainment of Enlightenment.

However, regarding the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, when the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects, there was a great earthquake as a precursor and various miracles; yet among these, Sātāgira alone was the first to see him.
He saw them. Having understood the cause of their rebirth, he approached the Blessed One together with his retinue and listened to the teaching of the Dhamma;
yet he did not attain any distinction. Why was this? For while listening to the Dhamma, he recalled Hemavata and wondered, "Has my companion come?
Looking around at the assembly and not seeing him, he thought, "My companion has been deceived."
He whose mind was thus distracted thought, "I have not heard such a varied and inspired teaching of the Dhamma from the Blessed One.
And the Blessed One did not conclude his teaching even when the sun had set.
Then Sātāgira, thinking, "I will take my companion and go with him to hear the teaching of the Dhamma," [prepared] elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, and so forth.
Having had it built, surrounded by five hundred *yakkhas*, he set out toward the Himālaya;

at that time, [the signs] appeared from the Hemavata [region] as well. Since the thirty-two omens appear and then vanish immediately upon the moments of rebirth-linking, birth, the Great Departure, the Enlightenment, and the Parinibbāna, and do not remain for long, yet at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, those [signs...]
Having become especially magnificent and remaining for a very long time, they then cease; therefore, having seen that wondrous manifestation in the Himavat, [he thought]:
"Since I was born, this mountain has never before been so beautiful.
Come now, taking my companion with me, let us come here and enjoy this splendor of flowers together. Thus he set out toward the Middle Country.
He was coming. Both of them met above Rājagaha and asked one another the reason for their arrival.
Hemavata said: "Friend, ever since I was born, this mountain has never before been so beautiful with trees in untimely bloom;
therefore, I have come so that we may enjoy this splendor of flowers together with you."
Sātāgira said: “But do you know, dear sir, the reason why this miracle of out-of-season flowers has occurred?
“I do not know, dear sir. “This miracle, dear sir, has arisen not only in the Himālaya, but indeed throughout the ten-thousandfold world system;
for today a Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared in the world.”

"He set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma; for that reason," Sātāgira said this after having thus related the appearance of the Buddha to Hemavata, wishing to bring him into the presence of the Blessed One.
However, some say that while the Blessed One was staying at the Gotamaka Shrine, he spoke thus: "Today is the fifteenth."

153. In this context, *ajja* (today) refers to the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight according to the calculation of nights and days. It is called *uposatha* because it is to be observed as a fast-day.
Alternatively, among the three types of *uposatha*, today is the fifteenth-day *uposatha*, not the fourteenth-day *uposatha*, nor the *sāmaggī-uposatha* (concordance *uposatha*).
Or else, the term *uposatha* is used for many purposes, such as the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*, the eight factors of the fast, and the day of its formal proclamation.
It is applicable. For in such passages as, “Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha,” the word *uposatha* refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
In such passages as, “Thus, Visākhā, the Uposatha endowed with these eight factors is observed,” it refers to the eight factors beginning with abstention from taking life.
In such passages as, “For one who is pure, there is always Phagguna; for one who is pure, there is always the Uposatha,” it refers to the observance (*upavāsa*). “The Uposatha...”
In such passages as “the Naga king named...,” it refers to a designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as “on the fifteenth day of the Uposatha, having bathed his head...,” it refers to a day.
Therefore, having set aside other meanings and specifying the full-moon day of Āsāḷhī itself, he said:
“Today is the fifteenth Uposatha. When counted as the first, second, and so on, the meaning is that today is the fifteenth day.
"Divine" means existing in heaven; it is called "divine" because divine things exist therein. What are those things? They are forms (*rūpa*).

For that night, the entire Jambudīpa was adorned by the radiance of the bodies, garments, ornaments, and celestial mansions of the ten thousand deities who had assembled from the ten-thousandfold world-system, as well as by the moonlight which was free from the impurities of clouds and the like. And it was especially adorned for the Supreme Pure Deva.
By the radiance of the Blessed One’s body. Therefore he said, “A divine night has arisen.
Having thus spoken of the appearance of a Buddha—inspiring confidence in his companion even by way of describing the excellence of the night—he said:
“Come, let us see the Teacher named Aṇoma, Gotama. In that context, “Aṇoma” means those who are faultless and complete in every respect.
"One who has a name by virtue of qualities" means one whose name is "Incomparable. For instance, in such ways as "He is the Awakened One (Buddha) because he has awakened to the Truths;
he is the Awakened One because he awakens the world," his name "Buddha" is derived from incomparable qualities. And in such ways as "He is the Blessed One (Bhagavā) because he has destroyed lust;

he is the Blessed One because he has destroyed hatred," his name is derived from incomparable qualities. This same method applies to such titles as "The Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct."
He is the Teacher (Satthā) because he instructs gods and humans in matters such as those pertaining to the present life, saying, "Abandon this; proceed by undertaking that.

Furthermore, he is the Teacher according to the method explained in the Niddesa: "The Blessed One is the Teacher, the Caravan-Leader (Satthavāha); just as a caravan-leader leads beings across the wilderness," and so forth.
[He is] that Teacher of unsurpassed name. The particle *handā* is used in the sense of determination.
"Let us see," he said, including himself in that statement as a present-tense expression. "Gotama" refers to one of the Gotama clan.
What is meant? Do not entertain doubt as to whether it is the Teacher or not the Teacher;
rather, being resolutely determined, come and let us see, O Gotama.
154. When this was said, Hemavata [thought]: "This Sātāgira, by speaking of 'the Teacher of Uncommon Name,' proclaims his omniscience;
and omniscient ones are rare in the world, for the world is afflicted by those who claim omniscience while being like Pūraṇa and others.
But if he is indeed omniscient, he must certainly have attained the characteristics of a Tādi (One Thus-Gone). Therefore, him... [he spoke thus].
Thinking, "I shall examine him," and inquiring about his characteristic of suchness (*tādilakkhaṇa*), he said:
"Is the mind...? Therein, *kacci* is a question. *Mano* is the mind (*citta*). *Supaṇihito* means well-placed, immovable, and unshakable.
*Sabbesu bhūtesu* means among all beings. *Tādi* refers to one who has attained the characteristic of suchness. Or, it may simply be a question.
"This teacher of yours—is he one who is equanimous toward all beings, or not? Regarding "in the desirable and the undesirable," this refers to such objects.
"Intentions" means thoughts (*vitakka*). "Brought under control" means brought into subjection. What is meant?
Is the mind of that teacher whom you call your teacher well-directed toward all beings, he being one who has attained the characteristic of equanimity?

Or rather, as long as it does not encounter a condition for movement, it appears as if well-placed. Was that Teacher of yours one who was "such-like" (tādī), possessing an even mind toward all beings, or was he not?

And as for those intentions (saṅkappa) that might arise through the influence of lust and hatred toward desirable or undesirable objects—were they brought under his control, or did he sometimes act under their influence?
155. Then Sātāgira, having resolved upon the Blessed One’s omniscience and acknowledging all the qualities of an omniscient one, said:
“And his mind is well-directed,” and so forth. In this context, “well-directed” (*supaṇihita*) means properly established:

like the earth in the sense of being unobstructed; like Mount Sineru in the sense of being firmly rooted and immovable; and like a city gatepost (*indakhīla*) in the face of the fourfold hosts of Māra and the ranks of opponents.

In the sense of being unshakable. And this is not surprising, for now that the Blessed One is established in omniscience, possessing all perfections, his mind would naturally be well-directed and immovable.

Even when he was a mere animal, born in the Chaddanta elephant clan at a time when he still possessed lust and other defilements, he remained unshakable even when pierced by a poisoned arrow, despite that assailant.
He did not feel resentment; on the contrary, he cut off his own teeth and gave them [to the yakkha].
Likewise, even when he was struck on the head with a great rock by the one who had become the Great Monkey, he nevertheless showed the way for that very same person.
Similarly, even when he was seized by the feet and cast down a sixty-yojana precipice at Mount Kāla by the one who had become the Wise Vidhura, he acted solely for the sake of that yakkha.
He taught the Dhamma. Therefore, Sātāgira spoke correctly when he said, "And his mind is well-directed.

"Toward all beings" means that only for one who has attained the characteristic of equanimity (*tādilakkhaṇa*) toward all living beings is the mind well-directed; the meaning is not that it remains so as long as one does not encounter an adverse condition. In this regard, the Blessed One’s characteristic of equanimity should be understood in five ways, as it is said:

“The Blessed One is ‘such’ (tādī) in five ways: he is such toward the desirable and the undesirable; he is such because he has abandoned [defilements]; he is such because he is liberated; he is such because he has crossed over; he is such because of his designation. How is the Blessed One such toward the desirable and the undesirable?

The Blessed One is such even in gain,” and so forth—all this should be understood according to the method stated in the *Niddesa*. Gain and the rest should be understood according to the method detailed in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Or rather, this is simply a question: “He is your Teacher, such toward all beings.”
Or, in this alternative interpretation as well, the meaning is: “The Tathāgata is our Teacher because of his equanimity toward all beings.
For this Blessed One is even-minded toward all sentient beings through his desire to bestow happiness and his desire to remove suffering;
he is the same toward others as he is toward himself, and the same toward Ciñcā Māṇavikā as he was toward his mother Mahāmāyā. Just as he was [toward her]...
He was such toward his father Suddhodana as he was toward Suppabuddha; as he was toward his son Rāhula, so he was toward his executioners Devadatta, Dhanapālaka, Aṅgulimāla, and others.
Such he was even in the world with its gods. Therefore, Sātāgira spoke rightly: "toward all beings he is the same.
Furthermore, regarding "the desirable and the undesirable": here the meaning should be understood thus—whatever is desirable or undesirable...

Or, regarding any object whatsoever, whatever intentions might arise therein through the influence of lust and hatred—these have been brought under control by him because lust and the other defilements have been abandoned by means of the unsurpassed Path; he never acts under their sway.
For that Blessed One is one whose intentions are undisturbed, whose mind is well-liberated, and whose wisdom is well-liberated. And herein, by virtue of his well-directed mind...

The absence of improper mental attention (*ayoni-manasikāra*) has been stated. Regarding all beings, that which might exist as desirable or undesirable is stated to be the twofold object, distinguished by way of sentient beings and formations.

Through mastery over intention, the abandonment of defilements is stated because of the absence of mental attention toward that object. And through the state of having a well-directed mind, there is purity of mental conduct.
Purity of bodily conduct arises from being harmless toward all beings; purity of verbal conduct arises through mastery over intention, since speech is rooted in thought.
Likewise, through the state of having a well-directed mind, there is an absence of all faults such as greed;

through harmlessness toward all beings, there is the presence of virtues such as loving-kindness; and through mastery over intention, there is the absence of perceptions such as "non-repulsive" regarding what is repulsive.
It should be understood that noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*) is mentioned here, and by means of it, his state of omniscience (*sabbaññubhāva*) is declared.

156. Thus, after Hemavata had previously asked about the state of suchness (*tādibhāva*) solely by way of the mind-door, and having heard him acknowledge it, [the Blessed One] now asks by way of all three doors for the purpose of strengthening that conviction;
or rather, [this refers to] the purification of the body, speech, and mind-doors which was previously stated in brief.

Having questioned him and having heard his admission, the Blessed One asked, "Is it not so that you have abstained from taking what is not given?"—asking this in detail for the purpose of strengthening his resolve.
Therein, for the sake of the meter of the verses, he first asks regarding the abstention from taking what is not given.
With the words "far from negligence," he asks regarding the abstention from unchastity by virtue of being distant from the mental relaxation associated with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
He asks: "Far from negligence" (*ārā pamādā*)—some also read it as "far from women" (*ārā mātugāmā*).
By the phrase "he does not abandon jhāna," he asks about the strength of that very threefold abstinence from bodily misconduct;
for when one is possessed of jhāna, abstinence becomes powerful.

157. Then Sātāgira [thought]: "Since the Blessed One was not only now, but also in the past for a long time, abstained from taking what is not given and other such acts, and by the power of each such abstinence he acquired each of those marks of a Great Man, and the world together with its devas addressed him in such a manner as:
'The ascetic Gotama is abstinent from taking what is not given,' and so forth..."
He speaks in praise. Therefore, uttering a lion’s roar with confident speech, he said:
"He does not take what is not given. The meaning of this is self-evident. In the third line of this verse, there is a twofold reading: "pamādamhā pamadamhā.
And in the fourth line, regarding "jhānaṃ na riñcati," it means he does not make the jhāna empty or void; he does not abandon it.
The meaning should be understood as "he relinquishes.
158. Having thus heard of purity regarding the door of the body, he now asks about purity regarding the door of speech, saying:
"Does he not speak falsely? Here, "khīṇa" means that which perishes; it means he harms or kills. It is the path of speech.
*Byappatha* means speech; one whose speech is exhausted is *khīṇabyappatha*. By negating that with the particle *na*, he asks, "Is he not one whose speech is exhausted?
which means "one who does not speak harshly. There is also the reading *nākhīṇabyappatha*, meaning "not one whose speech is unexhausted.
For harsh speech remains, not being exhausted, within the hearts of others. One who speaks such words—
"Is it not heard?"—this is what is meant. "Vibhūti" means destruction; that which causes (*kāsati*) or effects (*karoti*) destruction is "vibhūtika.
"Vebhūtika" is simply another form of "vibhūtika," and it is also called "vebhūtiya"; this is a designation for slander (*pesuñña*).
For it brings about the destruction of beings by causing dissension among them. The rest is self-evident.

159. Then Sātāgira [thought]: "Since it is not only now, but even in the past, for a long time, that the Blessed One has abstained from false speech and so forth, and by the power of each such abstinence he acquired each of those marks of a Great Man, and the world with its devas praises him, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama abstains from false speech.'"
Therefore, uttering a lion’s roar with confident speech, he said: “And he does not speak falsely.
Herein, “falsely” (*musā*) refers to speech that deceives others by misrepresenting what has been seen and so forth; he does not speak such words.

Regarding the second line, according to the first sense, the reading is “he is not one whose speech is exhausted,” while according to the second sense, it is “he is not one whose speech is unexhausted.”

In the fourth line, "wise" (*mantā*) refers to wisdom (*paññā*). Because the Blessed One speaks only the meaning after having discerned it through that wisdom—speaking words that do not deviate from the meaning and are not frivolous—and because there is no meaningless speech among the Buddhas that prioritizes ignorance, he said:
"The wise man speaks for the sake of the meaning. The rest here is self-evident.
160. Having thus heard about the purity of the door of speech, he now asks about the purity of the door of mind, saying:

"Is it not that you take delight in sensual pleasures? Herein, "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) refers to sense-objects. By asking whether one does not take delight in them through the defilement of sensual desire, he asks about non-covetousness (*anabhijjhālutā*).
By asking whether one is "untroubled," he asks about non-ill-will (*abyāpādatā*), having in mind the state of being troubled by ill-will (*byāpāda*).
He asks: "One who has transcended delusion. By asking this, he inquires about the state of right view through the transcendence of that delusion by which one is deluded and grasps at wrong view.

"One with vision regarding phenomena": by asking this, he inquires about omniscience by way of the unobstructed eye of knowledge regarding all phenomena, or by way of the five eyes regarding the phenomena within the spheres of the five eyes.
He asked this, thinking: "Is it even through the purity of the three doors that one does not become omniscient? Then Sātāgira [considered]:

Since the Blessed One, even before reaching Arahantship, had abandoned sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*byāpāda*) by means of the path of the Non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*), he was neither stained by sensual desires nor turbid in mind due to ill-will; and by the path of Stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) alone, he had [abandoned] the condition for wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).
Because he has abandoned the delusion that conceals the truths, he has transcended delusion;
and having himself fully awakened to the truths, he attained the name "Buddha" which belongs to liberation, as well as the aforementioned eyes.
Therefore, proclaiming both his purity of the mind-door and his omniscience, he said: "He does not lust after sensual pleasures."
162. Having thus heard of the Blessed One Hemavata’s purity in the three doors and his omniscience, the king was joyful and elated.
With a wisdom clarified by great learning regarding his past lives, and his path of speech being unhindered, he—desiring to hear of the wondrous and marvelous qualities of the Omniscient One—said:
"Is he endowed with true knowledge (*vijjā*)? In this context, "endowed with true knowledge" means:
By the phrase "perfection of vision" (*dassanasampatti*), he asks about [the attainment]; by "one of pure conduct" (*saṃsuddhacāraṇo*), he indicates the perfection of progress.
Here, the vowel *ā* is pronounced long due to metrical exigency (*chandavasena*); the meaning is "one of perfectly purified conduct" (*saṃsuddhacaraṇo*).

By the phrase "the taints are exhausted" (*āsavā khīṇā*), he indicates the attainment of the first element of Nibbāna, known as the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*), which is to be reached through this perfection of vision and progress.

By the words "he asks, 'there is no further becoming,'" he demonstrates the capacity for attaining the second element of Nibbāna, or, through the knowledge of reviewing, his state of being established after attaining supreme consolation. 163.
Then, as for that [knowledge] which is threefold among the fears and terrors and so forth, according to the method beginning with "he recollects his manifold past abodes":

“In this way, with his mind thus concentrated... [as it is said] ...having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward knowledge and vision”—in such a manner, the eightfold clear knowledge (*vijjā*) was taught in the *Ambaṭṭha-sutta* and other discourses.

Since the Blessed One is endowed with all of that, in every aspect and in its entirety; and as for this: “Here, Mahānāma, the noble disciple is accomplished in virtue, [accomplished] in the faculties... [and so forth].

“...he is one who guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, is endowed with the seven true qualities, and is one who obtains at will the four jhānas—those higher mental states that provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
Having thus indicated [the path], he then explains: “And how, Mahānāma, is a noble disciple accomplished in virtue? and so forth.

The conduct (*caraṇa*) consisting of fifteen divisions, as demonstrated in the *Sekha-sutta* according to the method [of that text], is exceedingly pure in the Blessed One due to his abandonment of all defilements (*upakkilesa*).

Furthermore, those four taints (*āsava*)—beginning with the taint of sensual desire—which are accompanied by their retinues and latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), have all been exhausted in the Blessed One.
And because one who has exhausted the taints through this perfection of true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampadā*)...
Then, having made the offering, the Blessed One stood reflecting, “Now there is no further becoming.
Therefore, Sātāgira, his heart uplifted by his conviction in the Blessed One’s omniscience, spoke thus, acknowledging all his qualities:
“He is indeed endowed with true knowledge.”

164. Then Hemavata, having become free from doubt regarding the Blessed One, thinking, "The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One," while still standing in the air, spoke in praise of the Blessed One and to please Sātāgira: "The mind of the Sage is perfected. The meaning of this is:
"The mind of the Sage is perfected"—it is full because it possesses the qualities described in the passage beginning with, "And his mind is well-directed."

It is "complete" (*sampuṇṇaṃ*); it is "full" (*puṇṇaṃ*) because it is complete through the bodily action described as "he does not take what is not given," and through the mental action described as "he does not lust after sensual pleasures.

It is implied that it is also complete through the verbal action of speech described as "he does not speak falsehood. Thus, his mind is perfected with the unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampadā*).
Because he is perfected in these qualities, such as being endowed with true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*),

you praise him according to the Dhamma through the method beginning with "his mind is well-directed"; you praise him according to his very nature, as it truly and actually is, and not merely by way of faith alone— this is what is shown.
165–166. Then Sātāgira, with the intention, “It is so, dear sir;
this has been well understood and well rejoiced in by you,” spoke to him in order to please him: “The perfection of the Sage... [you] rejoice according to the Dhamma.
Having spoken thus, and further praising him upon seeing the Blessed One, he said: “The perfection... come, let us see Gotama.”
167. Then Hemavata, praising the Blessed One with qualities that were dear to him and by virtue of his great learning from previous births, addressed Sātāgira:
“... [with] shanks like those of an antelope... Come, let us see Gotama. The meaning of this is:
he whose shanks are like those of an antelope is *eṇijaṅgho*. For the shanks of Buddhas are rounded and tapering, just like those of the antelope.
They do not have fleshless backs that are bloated like the belly of a crocodile;
rather, the Buddhas are lean, possessing such perfection of limbs and members in places where they should be long, short, or symmetrical, and are not as stout as coarse men.
Or, they are lean because their defilements have been scraped away by wisdom, due to the destruction of both internal and external fetters.
The heroes. They were moderate in food by virtue of eating from a single sitting and eating in moderation, not by restricting themselves to only two or three mouthfuls. As it was said:
“Indeed, Udāyin, sometimes I eat from this bowl even until it is full, and sometimes I eat even more.
If, Udāyin, my disciples were to honor me with the thought: ‘The ascetic Gotama eats little and speaks in praise of eating little,’ [they would be honoring me for the wrong reason].”
“They would honor him, revere him, worship him, and having honored and revered him, they would dwell in dependence upon him.

But those disciples of mine, Udāyin, who eat only a single kosaka fruit, or half a kosaka, or a single beluva fruit, or half a beluva—those would not honor me on account of this quality... nor would they dwell in dependence upon me.”
Because they are free from desire and lust for food, they are not greedy; as sages endowed with the perfection of wisdom, they consume food possessed of the eight factors.
Due to their state of homelessness and because their minds are inclined toward seclusion, they meditate in the forest. Therefore, the Yakkha of Hemavat said:
"O Eṇijaṅgha... come, let us see Gotama."
168. Having spoken thus, and desiring again to hear the Dhamma in the presence of that Blessed One, he recited this verse:
"Like a lion walking alone. Its meaning is as follows: "Like a lion" means resembling a maned lion in terms of being difficult to approach, in terms of forbearance, and in terms of fearlessness.
By the absence of that craving through which a person is said to be "accompanied by craving," [he is like the lion].
He is a "solitary wanderer" because he wanders alone; he is also a solitary wanderer because two Buddhas do not arise simultaneously in a single world-system.
Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Khaggavisāṇa Sutta*. "Nāga" means one who neither goes to nor comes from renewed existence (*punabbhava*).

Alternatively, a "nāga" is so called because he commits no offense (*āguṃ na karoti*); or, a "nāga" is one who is powerful. That [Buddha] is the "Nāga. "He is without regard for sense pleasures": this refers to one who has no longing for the objects of sensual desire.

"Having approached, we ask about the release from the snare of Death"— that is, having approached such a Great Sage who is indifferent due to the absence of desire and lust for both kinds of sensual pleasures, we ask about *nibbāna*,
the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) which releases one from the snare of Death consisting of the round of existence in the three realms.
Or rather, we ask about that means by which one is released from the snare of Death known as the origin of suffering.
"I ask about the release from the snare of death. He spoke this verse with reference to Hemavata, Sātāgira, the assembly of Sātāgira, and his own assembly.
At that time, the Āsāḷhī festival had been proclaimed; then, from all sides, [the people] were adorned and prepared.
In Rājagaha, a female lay follower named Kāḷī Kuraragharikā— resembling one experiencing glory in Devanagara—
ascended her palace, opened the lion-window, and stood in a breezy spot to enjoy the weather, dispelling the fatigue of her pregnancy;
there she heard from beginning to middle to end that discourse concerning the Buddha’s qualities related to those generals of the *yakkhas*.
She heard it. Having heard it, and thinking, "Thus are the Buddhas endowed with manifold qualities," she gave rise to rapture (pīti) directed toward the Buddha.
By means of that rapture, she suppressed the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and, remaining right there, was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, among my female lay disciples who have gained confidence through hearsay, this is the foremost: namely..."
The laywoman Kālī Kuraragharikā was established as foremost among them.
Then those three generals of the yakṣas, with a retinue of a thousand yakṣas, arrived at Isipatana during the middle watch of the night;
having approached the Blessed One—who was seated on the very seat where he had set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion—and having paid homage to him, they [spoke] with this...
Having praised the Blessed One with a verse, they requested the opportunity [to hear the teaching], saying: “The one who declares and sets it forth. The meaning of this is:

setting aside craving, he is the one who, by way of the discourse defining the truths according to the method beginning with “But this, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering,” has declared the phenomena belonging to the three planes; and [he is the one who has declared]: “Now, this Noble Truth of Suffering...”

He is the one who, by means of the method beginning with “Bhikkhus, ‘it is to be fully understood’...,” sets in motion the knowledge of what is to be done and the knowledge of what has been done regarding those things;

or, he is the one who explains by describing those phenomena exactly as they should be designated; he is the one who causes those very same phenomena to proceed in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings;
or, he is the one who proclaims through his teaching for those who understand through a brief indication and those who understand through detailed exposition.

He is the one who causes [the Dhamma] to proceed by leading those who are to be led; or he is the one who declares it through a summary (uddesa) and causes it to proceed by speaking of it in various ways through an analytical exposition (vibhaṅga).

Alternatively, he is the one who declares the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya) by describing their specific characteristics, and he is the one who causes them to proceed by making them manifest within the mental continuum of sentient beings.
Or, in brief, he is the one who declares the Truths (sacca) by means of the three turnings.
The Proclaimer: the one who sets it forth in detail. "The faculty of faith is the Dhamma;

because he sets that Dhamma in motion, it is the Wheel of the Dhamma"—it is the Proclaimer because he sets in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma detailed according to the method of the *Paṭisambhidā* (analytical knowledges) in such passages.
Of all phenomena: of the phenomena belonging to the four planes. One who has gone to the further shore: one who has reached the further shore in six ways through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

Through full understanding, through abandoning, through development, through realization, and through attainment. For that Blessed One is one who has gone to the further shore of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), having directly known all phenomena;
he is one who has gone to the further shore of full understanding (*pariññā*), having fully understood the five aggregates of clinging;

he is one who has gone to the further shore of abandoning (*pahāna*), having abandoned all defilements; he is one who has gone to the further shore of development (*bhāvanā*), having developed the four paths.
One who has gone to the realization of cessation is "one who has reached the further shore of realization" (*sacchikiriyā-pāragū*);

one who enters all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) is "one who has reached the further shore of attainment. Thus, he is "one who has reached the further shore of all phenomena. Regarding "the Buddha who has transcended enmity and fear":

he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened from the bed of ignorance, or because he is "awakened" in the sense explained in the entire commentary on the refuges; [he is free] from the five fears of enmity.
Because he has transcended [the past], he has passed beyond enmity and fear. Thus, not being followers of other sects, they requested permission from the Blessed One, saying, "We ask you, Gotama.
Then Hemavata—the foremost among those *yakkhas* in both spiritual power and wisdom—asking the question he had intended to ask, recited this verse:
"In what does the world [rest]? Regarding the first word of that verse, *kismiṃ*, it is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe*).

The locative case (*bhummavacana*)—the intended meaning here being "when what has arisen does the world arise?"—is used with reference to the world of beings (*sattaloka*) and the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*).
"In what does one form intimacy? means in what does one form intimacy through craving and views, thinking "I" or "mine"?
Here, the locative case is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇatthe bhummavacana*). "Of what world? is the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) used in the sense of the object (*upayogatthe*).

On what basis does it receive the designation "the world"? This is the intended meaning here. In the phrase "in what [is there] a world," the locative case is used in the sense of the locus (*bhāve*), the characteristic (*bhāva-lakkhaṇa*), or the cause (*kāraṇa*).
The intended meaning here is: when what exists, and for what reason, is the world afflicted, oppressed, and tormented?
171. Then, because the Blessed One [saw that] the world of beings and... in the six internal and external sense-bases (*āyatana*) which have arisen—
And the world of formations arises by way of wealth, grain, and so forth;
for it is within these very things that the world of beings forms two kinds of intimacy. For one grasps the eye-base as "I" or "mine," or one of the remaining bases.
As it is said: "If one were to say 'the eye is the self,' that is not tenable," and so forth. Because...
And depending on these very six, the world is reckoned as being twofold;
for when those same six exist, the world of beings is distressed by the manifestation of suffering. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, when there are hands, there is the taking up and laying down of things; when there are feet, there is advancing and retreating."
"When there is a limb, there is its bending and stretching; when there is a stomach, there is hunger and thirst.
Even so, monks, when there is the eye, conditioned by eye-contact, pleasure and pain arise within. And so forth.
Thus, the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka) is frustrated when it encounters those [faculties] which serve as its bases. As it is said:
“It is struck against the invisible and impinging eye,” and:
“The eye, monks, is struck against agreeable and disagreeable forms,” and so forth.
In the same way, the world—comprising both types—is afflicted by those very things that serve as its causes. As it is said:
“The eye is afflicted by agreeable and disagreeable forms,” and:
“Bhikkhus, the eye is aflame; forms are aflame. By what are they aflame? By the fire of lust,” and so forth.
Therefore, answering that question by way of the six internal and external sense bases, he said: "In the six, the world has arisen.

Then that *yakkha*, not having properly grasped the answer given by the Blessed One—which condensed the question asked regarding the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) into the twelve sense bases—and desiring to know both that meaning and its opposite, [asked again].
Asking about the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) in brief, he said: "Which one is that?
In this context, "clinging" (*upādāna*) is so called in the sense of being something to be grasped; it is a designation for the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
Regarding the phrase "wherein the world is tormented," the Blessed One stated that the world is tormented within the sixfold clinging; therefore, what is that clinging?

Thus, by this very half-verse, he asked about the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) in its own form. As for the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*), it is already implicitly included as the cause of that [suffering].
By this next half-verse, "He asks about the escape" (*niyyāna*), he asked about the truth of the path (*maggasacca*).
For by means of the truth of the path, the noble disciple fully understands suffering, abandons its origin, and realizes cessation.
One who cultivates the path goes forth from the world; therefore, it is called "leading out" (*niyyāna*). How? In what manner?
"He is liberated from suffering": he attains liberation from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*), which was referred to by the term "clinging" (*upādāna*).
Thus, herein the truth of the path is asked about in its own specific form, while the truth of cessation is already implicitly included as its objective domain.

173. Thus, having been questioned by the Yakkha both through manifesting his form and through not manifesting it, regarding the Four Noble Truths, the Blessed One, answering in that very same manner, said: "The five strands of sensual pleasure.

Therein, by the inclusion of the objective sphere consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure, the five sense bases which have those as their objects are indeed included. "With the mind as the sixth" means those [five] for which the mind is the sixth. "Proclaimed" means...

It has been explained. Here, by the inclusion of the sixth internal base, the mind-base (*manāyatana*), its objective sphere—the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*)—is necessarily included as well.
Thus, in answering the question, "What is that clinging?", he again revealed the truth of suffering by way of the twelve bases alone. Or, by the inclusion of the mind, [he includes] the seven...

Because the elements of consciousness (*viññāṇadhātu*) have been included, by including the first five elements of consciousness among them, their bases—the five sense-fields (*āyatana*) beginning with the eye—are included; and by including the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), the sense-field of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*), which is the distinction between their bases and their objects, is likewise included.

Thus, in this way as well, he proclaimed the truth of suffering by way of the twelve sense-fields. [This includes] a portion of the supramundane sense-field of the mind and the sense-field of mental objects.
In this context, because it is taught with reference to that which causes the world to be distressed, it is not included [in the list].

Regarding the phrase "having dispassion for desire here": having analyzed those very bases (āyatana) among the twelvefold division of the Truth of Suffering according to their respective aggregates, elements, and mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa);
and having applied the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), one who practices insight meditation—
The meaning is: having completely dispassioned toward, led away from, and destroyed the desire known as craving (*taṇhā*) by means of insight (*vipassanā*) culminating in the path of arahantship.
"Thus one is released from suffering" means that in this manner one is released from this suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
Thus, with this half-verse—“Being asked about the way out, speak: how is one released from suffering?”—this [is explained].

The question has been answered, and the truth of the path (maggasacca) has been revealed. Furthermore, it should be understood that the truths of origin (samudayasacca) and cessation (nirodhasacca) are also effectively revealed here, as they are included by the same method as before.
Alternatively, within this half-verse: the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) is indicated; the truth of origin is indicated by the word "desire" (chanda);
the truth of cessation is indicated by the term "having become dispassionate" (virājetvā), because of the statement "one is liberated through dispassion" (virāgā vimuccati).
Or it is the truth of the path. By the indication of the means with the word “thus,” it is the truth of the path; or by the statement “the cessation of suffering,” it is the truth of cessation.
By the phrase “is released from suffering,” it is the truth of cessation through liberation from suffering.
Thus, it should be understood that the four truths are revealed here.

174. Having thus revealed the way out (*niyyāna*) by way of the characteristics of this verse containing the four truths, he spoke again, concluding that very same point with its own specific terminology:
"This is the way out of the world. Here, "this" (*etam*) is a demonstrative reference to what was previously stated;
"of the world" (*lokassa*) refers to the world of the three realms (*tedhātukaloka*). "As it truly is" (*yathātatham*) means unerringly. "I declare this to you" (*etaṃ vo ahamakkhāmi*).
"Even if you were to ask me a thousand times, I would tell you this and nothing else. Why?
Because it is by this alone that one is liberated from suffering, and not otherwise—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, the sense is:

'I tell you this even for those who have already emerged [from saṃsāra] once, twice, or thrice by means of this path of deliverance; I tell you this very same thing for the sake of attaining further distinction.'"
Why? Because he is thus liberated from suffering without remainder; thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, both generals of the *yakkhas*, together with a thousand *yakkhas*, were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then Hemavata, who was already by nature reverent toward the Dhamma, now being firmly established on the ground of the Noble Ones, [spoke] even more...

Unsatisfied with the Blessed One’s teaching of such diverse eloquence, he asked the Blessed One about the stages of those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*), and uttered the verse beginning, "Who here crosses over?
Therein, by the words "Who here crosses over the flood," he asks, without distinction, who it is that crosses the four floods;
for [the word] *aṇṇava* does not refer merely to something wide, nor...
Furthermore, that which is both more extensive and more profound is what is being referred to here.
Such is the ocean of saṃsāra. For this is extensive in its lack of boundaries on all sides;
it is profound because it has no foundation below and no support above. Therefore: "Who here crosses the ocean, which is without a footing?"
"Who would not sink in the deep ocean that has no support?"—with this, he asks about the stage of one beyond training (*asekkhabhūmi*).
Then the Blessed One [described] the monk who, even for the sake of his life, does not commit a transgression and is always perfected in virtue (*sīla*);

who is possessed of wisdom through both mundane and supramundane insight (*paññā*); and who, by means of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*), the postures (*iriyāpatha*), and the lower paths and fruits (*maggaphala*)...

Being well-composed, having applied the three characteristics, he is one whose nature is to contemplate his own internal states through insight, and he is endowed with the mindfulness of heedfulness that brings about constant practice.

Because he crosses over this flood, so difficult to cross, entirely without remainder by means of the fourth path, he abandons the stage of the trainee (*sekha*) and [utters] this core of the three trainings: "Always perfected in virtue."

He spoke this verse. For herein, the three trainings—with their requisites and their fruits—are stated: the training in higher virtue through the perfection of virtue; the training in higher mind through mindfulness and concentration; and the training in higher wisdom through internal reflection and wisdom.
Indeed, mundane wisdom and mindfulness are the requisites for the trainings, while the fruits of recluseship are their fruit.
177. Having thus shown the stage of the trainee (*sekkhabhūmi*) with the first verse, he now speaks the second verse to show the stage of the adept (*asekkhabhūmi*).

Its meaning is as follows: "Detached from perceptions of sensual desire" means that one is detached from all whatever perceptions of sensual desire whatsoever by means of the detachment through eradication (*samucchedavirati*) associated with the fourth path.
There is also a reading, "viratto" (dispassionate); in that case, "kāmasaññāya" is a locative expression.

In the Sagāthāvagga, however, there is also the reading "in perceptions of sensual desire" (*kāmasaññāsu*). Because the ten fetters have been transcended by means of all four paths, he has transcended all fetters;
or alternatively, by the fourth path alone, he has transcended all the higher fetters.

Because delight—consisting of craving characterized as "rejoicing here and there"—and the three realms of existence have been completely exhausted, such a one is an arahant whose taints are destroyed, with delight and existence utterly consumed.

The bhikkhu does not sink in the deep ocean of saṃsāra; through the exhaustion of delight, he reaches the state of Nibbāna with residue remaining (*saupādisesa*), and through the exhaustion of existence, he reaches the state of Nibbāna without residue remaining (*anupādisesa*), thereby attaining supreme consolation.
Then Hemavata, looking at his companion and the assembly of yakkhas, being filled with joy and gladness, [addressed them as] "one of profound wisdom."
Having praised the Blessed One with these and other verses, and having paid homage together with his entire retinue and his companion, he circumambulated him and departed for his own dwelling place.
Now, this is the commentary on the meaning of those verses: "Of profound wisdom" means endowed with profound wisdom.
In this context, profound wisdom (gambhīrapaññā) should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*. For it is said there:
"Knowledge that proceeds regarding the profound aggregates is profound wisdom," and so forth.

"One who sees the subtle meaning" means one who sees the meaning of questions formulated by subtle experts such as Kṣatriyas and scholars, or one who sees those subtle reasons for meanings which are difficult to penetrate.
He who sees the subtle meaning through the vision of others; who is "possessing nothing" (akiñcana) due to the absence of the burdens of lust and other defilements;
who is "unattached" (asatta) to sense-desires and the three realms of existence because of his lack of clinging to them;

who is "completely liberated" (vippamutta) from all objects—whether they be the aggregates or anything else—due to the absence of the bonds of desire and lust; and who is "treading the divine path" (dibbe pathe kamamāna), that is, the path consisting of the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti).

Walking by way of entering upon the divine path. Although at that time the Blessed One was not actually walking on the divine path, nevertheless, it is said thus because of his prior practice of walking, because of the presence of the power to walk, and because of his mastery attained therein.
Alternatively, it refers to the path of those pure devas who are Arahants.
It is said that he is "free from desire" because he dwells in peace. He is a "great seer" (*mahesi*) because of his seeking after great qualities.
179. Considering that praise has been commenced by another method in the second verse, [the author] again demonstrates the inclusion of the term "one who sees the subtle meaning.
Alternatively, the meaning is "one who shows the subtle meaning. [He is called] a "giver of wisdom" because [his teaching] conduces to the attainment of wisdom.
By speaking of the practice, he is the giver of wisdom. "Unattached to the abode of sensual pleasures" means unattached to that twofold abiding in sensual pleasures by way of craving and views.
"All-knower" means the knower of all phenomena; it is said, "the omniscient one.
"Sumedha" [refers to him] because of his intelligence (medhā), which consists of the perfections (pāramīs) that constitute the path to that state of omniscience.
Endowed with [this]. "In the noble path" means in the eightfold path, or in the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).
"Treading upon" means plunging into it with wisdom by knowing the characteristics of the path and teaching it; or entering it by repeatedly attaining the fruition-attainment moment by moment;
or having previously trodden upon it by the power of treading, which consists of the fourfold development of the path (*maggabhāvanā*).
180. "Truly, we have seen well today. Today we have seen what is beautiful;
or, today something beautiful has been seen by us—the meaning is "a sight. "It was a fine dawn, it was a good rising":
today our dawn was truly bright or beautiful; and today our rising from bed was beautiful, without obstruction.

It has arisen. For what reason? Because they have seen the Fully Enlightened One; thus, referring to their own attainment of gain, they proclaim their joy, thinking, "Since we have seen the Fully Enlightened One.
(181) *Iddhimanto* means those endowed with supernormal power born of the maturation of kamma. *Yasassino* means those possessed of the excellence of gain and the excellence of retinue.

“They go for refuge” (*saraṇaṃ yanti*): although they have indeed already gone by means of the Path, nevertheless, he breaks the silence [of the verse] in order to illustrate their state as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and to demonstrate their serene confidence (*pasāda*).

“From village to village” (*gāmā gāmaṃ*): from one divine village (*devagāma*) to another divine village. “From mountain to mountain” (*nagā nagaṃ*): from one divine mountain (*devapabbata*) to another divine mountain.
“Honoring the Fully Enlightened One and the excellent nature of the Dhamma”: “The Blessed One is truly a Perfectly Enlightened One; his Teaching is truly well-expounded... [and so forth].
By means of such passages as "The Dhamma of the Blessed One," one should proclaim the Blessed One’s excellent awakening and the excellence of his Dhamma.

By repeatedly praising the Sangha’s excellent practice with such passages as "The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well," it is meant that we shall wander about as proclaimers of the Dhamma, paying homage [to these qualities]. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the Hemavata Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is completed. 10.
Commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta.
"Thus have I heard" is the *Āḷavaka Sutta*. What is its origin? Its origin will be made clear by means of the method of commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*).
And in the commentary, the phrase "Thus have I heard; at one time the Blessed One" has already had its meaning explained.
Regarding the passage, "He was dwelling at Āḷavī, in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka," what is Āḷavī, and for what reason did the Blessed One [go there]?
"He dwells in the abode of a yakkha"? It is said: *Āḷavī* refers both to a kingdom and to a city;
both are applicable here. For even one dwelling in the vicinity of the city of Āḷavī is said to "dwell in Āḷavī.
That abode is located near that city, at a distance of only a *gāvuta*; thus, even while dwelling in the kingdom of Āḷavī...
“It dwells at Āḷavī” is what is said; this monastery is in the kingdom of Āḷavī.

However, because King Āḷavaka, having abandoned his various theatrical entertainments and luxuries, went out for a hunt every seventh day—for the purpose of warding off thieves, repelling rival kings, and exercising his strength—one day, together with his army...
He made an agreement with him, saying: "On whichever side the deer flees, that shall be the responsibility of that person.
Then, on the king's very side, the deer fled; the king, endowed with great speed, took up his bow and pursued that deer on foot for three *yojanas*.
Deer of the *eṇi* species possess a speed of exactly three *yojanas*. Then, when that deer’s speed was exhausted, [he reached] the water—

Having entered, he killed the deer that was standing there, cut it in two, and—though having no need for the meat—took it on a carrying-pole and came along to clear himself of the reproach, "He could not catch the deer.
Not far from the city, seeing a great banyan tree with thick foliage and leaves, he approached its base to dispel his fatigue. And in that banyan tree dwelt the yakkha Āḷavaka.
Having received a boon from the great king, he remained there eating living beings that entered the area shaded by that tree at midday. Seeing him, the king approached to eat.
Then the king made an agreement with him: "Release me; I shall give you a person and a *thālipāka* every day."
“I shall send it. But the yakkha would not release him, saying, “You will forget it while distracted by royal pleasures;
however, I am not permitted to eat that which has not entered my abode or been authorized for me, so I might even devour you yourself.
The king, consenting, said, “On whichever day I do not send it, on that day take me and eat me,” and he was released by him.
Having been released, he went toward the city.
The army, having established its camp on the road, stood waiting; seeing the king, they said, "Why, Great King, are you so distressed out of fear of a mere disgrace?
and they went out to meet him and received him. The king, however, did not inform them of what had occurred.
Having gone to the city and taken his morning meal, he summoned the city guardian and informed him of this matter.
The city guardian said, "Why, sire, has a time limit been set? The king replied, "No, my man. "It was poorly done, sire;
for if a limit is set, non-human beings receive only that which is within the limit, but if no limit is set, there will be affliction for the entire district."
"It will come to pass. Let it be, Your Majesty; although he has acted thus, you should remain unconcerned and enjoy the pleasures of kingship, while I shall do what must be done here.
Rising early in the morning, he went to the prison and, addressing those who were condemned to death, said: "Whoever wishes to live, let him go forth! Whosoever...
First, she sends out a woman; having led her to the house, bathed her, and fed her, she instructs her, "Give this *thālipāka* to the *yakkha*.
As soon as she has entered the foot of the tree, the *yakkha* manifests a terrifying form and devours her like a root or a tuber.
It is said that by the power of the *yakkha*, [the food] reaches the entire body of humans, including even their hair and so forth.
It was like a lump of fresh butter. When the men who had gone to fetch food for the *yakkha* saw it, they were terrified and reported it to their friends as best they could.
From that time on, people refrained from the work of theft, thinking, "The king captures thieves and gives them to the *yakkha*.
Then, after some time, due to the absence of new thieves and the exhaustion of the old ones, [the practice ceased].
The prisons became empty.

Then the city guard informed the king. The king had his own wealth cast away in the city streets, thinking, "Perhaps someone might take it out of greed. Yet no one even touched it with their foot. Not finding any thieves, he—
He informed his ministers. The ministers said, “We shall send one aged person at a time according to family seniority;
he will already be standing in the jaws of death by nature. The king said, “People will cause a disturbance, saying, ‘They are sending our father, they are sending our grandfather!
Do not let this please you,” and he forbade it. “In that case, Your Majesty, let us send a child.”
“We shall call him Uttaṇaseyyaka (‘One Who Lies on His Back’), for such a one has no affection [thinking], ‘He is my mother, he is my father,’” they said.
The king gave his permission; they did accordingly. In the city, the mothers of young children took their infants, and pregnant women fled to other districts;
there they raised the children and brought them back. In this way, all twelve years passed.
Then one day, having searched the entire city and not finding even a single boy, they reported to the king:
"Your Majesty, there is no boy in the city except for your son, Prince Āḷavaka, in the inner palace. The king said:
"Just as my son is dear to me, so he is to the whole world; yet there is nothing dearer than myself. Go!"

"Even by giving that, protect my life," he said. At that time, Āḷavaka Kumāra’s mother had bathed her son, adorned him, placed him on a pillow of fine linen, and was sitting with him resting in her lap.
By the king's command, the royal officers went there and, while she was lamenting along with sixteen thousand women, [seized her].
Taking him with her, the nurse departed, thinking, "Tomorrow he will become food for a *yakkha*. On that very day, the Blessed One,
having risen at dawn and entered the Great Compassion absorption within the Gandhakuṭī in the Jetavana Mahāvihāra,
again surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and saw that the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) was destined to arise for the youth Āḷavaka.
[He established] the decisive support for the Yakkha’s attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, and at the conclusion of the teaching,
eighty-four thousand beings obtained the eye of Dhamma. Therefore, when the night had dawned,
having performed his morning duties but before completing his post-meal duties on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, as the sun was setting—
Alone and without a companion, taking his bowl and robes, he traveled thirty yojanas on foot from Sāvatthī and entered the abode of that yakkha.
Therefore it is said: "In the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka.
But did the Blessed One dwell at the foot of the banyan tree where the abode of Āḷavaka was located, or rather within the abode itself?
It is said: in his own abode itself. For just as the *yakkhas* see their own abode, so too did the Blessed One.
Having gone there, he stood at the gate of the abode. At that time, Āḷavaka had gone to a gathering of *yakkhas* in the Himālayas.
Then a *yakkha* named Gadrabha, the gatekeeper of Āḷavaka, approached the Blessed One and paid homage to him.
“Why, venerable sir, has the Blessed One come at an improper time? he asked. “Yes, Gadrabha, I have come.
If it is not troublesome to you, would you let me stay for one night in Āḷavaka’s abode? “It is not troublesome to me, venerable sir;
however, that yakkha is harsh and cruel, and he does not even perform such acts as salutation toward his own parents. May it not please the Blessed One to stay here.”
“...clothing. “I know, jackal, his harshness; no obstacle shall come to me.
If it is not troublesome to you, may we dwell together for one night?
A second time the jackal-yakkha said this to the Blessed One: “He is like a bowl heated by fire, venerable sir.”
“Āḷavaka does not recognize ‘mother and father,’ nor ‘ascetics and brahmins,’ nor even ‘the Dhamma’;
he causes those who come here to lose their minds, rends their hearts, and even seizing them by the feet, hurls them across the great ocean or beyond the world-system.
A second time, the Blessed One said: “I know, you donkey; if it is not troublesome to you, let us dwell together for one night.”
For a third time, the yakkha Gadrabha said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, Āḷavaka is like a pot heated by fire;
he knows nothing of 'mother' or 'father,' nor of 'recluses and brahmins,' nor of 'the Dhamma.
He causes those who come here to lose their minds, he rends their hearts, and seizing them by the feet, he hurls them across the great ocean or beyond the world-system."
“Or he will hurl [me] away. A third time the Blessed One said: “I know, camel; if it is not troublesome for you, we might stay together for one night.
“It is not troublesome for me, Bhante, but that yakkha might deprive me of life even while I am granting permission without having informed him.
I shall inform him, Bhante. “Inform him as you please, camel. “In that case, Bhante...”
“Venerable sir, you alone know,” he said, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he set out toward the Himālaya mountains.

Even the door to his palace opened of its own accord for the Blessed One. Having entered the palace, the Blessed One sat upon that very celestial jeweled couch where Āḷavaka used to enjoy his glory on specially distinguished days such as auspicious festivals.
Having sat down, he emitted a golden radiance. Seeing this, the female yakkhas approached, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat surrounding him.
The Blessed One said: "In the past, you attained this prosperity by giving gifts, undertaking moral discipline, and honoring those worthy of honor;
now, do likewise, and do not be overcome by mutual envy and stinginess."
With these and other such methods, he delivered a miscellaneous discourse on the Dhamma to them.
Having heard the Blessed One’s sweet voice, they gave thousands of shouts of approval and sat surrounding the Blessed One.
The donkey, too, went to the Himālayas and informed Āḷavaka: "Truly, dear sir, you should know that the Blessed One is in your celestial mansion."
“...seated. He made a sign to the donkey, saying, “Be silent; having gone there, we shall do what needs to be done.
It was said that he was ashamed because of his human pride, and therefore he silenced him so that no one in the midst of the assembly might hear.
At that time, Sātāgira and Hemavata, having paid homage to the Blessed One at Jetavana itself, [said], “We shall go to the assembly of yakkhas.”
Accompanied by their retinues, they travel through the air by means of various vehicles. However, there is not a path for the *yakkhas* everywhere in the sky;
rather, avoiding the celestial palaces (*vimānas*) situated in the air, the path exists only where the way is clear.
But the palace of Āḷavaka was built upon the earth, well-guarded, surrounded by a wall, with its gates, watchtowers, and gatehouses well-arranged, and covered above by a network of bronze.
It was three yojanas in height, resembling Mañjūsa. Above it was a path. Having reached that place, they were unable to proceed.
For no one is able to go above the seat where the Buddhas sit, reaching even unto the peak of existence (bhavagga).
Reflecting, "What is this?", and seeing the Blessed One, [they were like] a clod of earth thrown into the air.
Having descended as if from the sky, paid homage, listened to the Dhamma, and performed a circumambulation, they went to the assembly of yakkhas, praising the Blessed One for three qualities.
When Āḷavaka saw them, he stepped back and gave them space, saying, "Sit here. They informed Āḷavaka: "It is a gain for you, Āḷavaka!"
“Friend, go and pay homage to the Blessed One, who is dwelling in your abode.
Thus the Blessed One dwelt in the very abode itself, not at the foot of the banyan tree where Āḷavaka’s abode was located.
Therefore it is said: “On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka.”
Then Āḷavaka... [as before] ...said this to the Blessed One: "Come out, ascetic! Why did he say this? It is said:
because of his desire to provoke him. In this regard, the connection from the beginning should be understood as follows:
since a talk on faith is ill-timed for one who lacks faith—just as a talk on virtue and so forth is for those who lack virtue and so forth—he therefore [addressed the Blessed One].
Having heard the praise of the Blessed One from the yakkhas, his heart began to throb with inner rage like salt-grit thrown into a fire,
and he said, "Who is this so-called Blessed One who has entered my abode?
They replied, "Friend, you do not know our Teacher, the Blessed One."

“Friend Āḷavaka, you did not see these wonders either,” they challenged him, recounting the thirty-two portents beginning with the rebirth-linking, following the method starting from: “He who, staying in the Tusita heaven, having performed the five great surveys,” and so on, up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
Although he had seen them, out of anger he said, “I did not see. “Friend Āḷavaka, you would have seen them! they said.
Whether you see it or not, what is the use of that to us?
What will you do for our Teacher—you who, in comparison to him, are like a calf born that very day near a great bull with trembling humps;
like a young bee near a rutting elephant whose temples are split in three ways; [or] like one near a trunk adorned with radiant, hanging manes?

"You are like an old jackal in the presence of a lion-king, or like a young crow with clipped wings in the presence of the king of the Supaṇṇas, whose body extends for one hundred and fifty yojanas; go and do whatever you must do.
When this was said, the enraged Āḷavaka rose up, stood upon the surface of the ruby floor on his left foot, and said, "Now behold you all..."
Thinking, "Either the Teacher is of great power, or I am," he stepped with his right foot upon the peak of Mount Kelāsa, which was sixty yojanas in extent;
struck by that iron foot, it shed splinters like a mass of glowing embers struck by an iron hammer.
Standing there, he proclaimed, "I am Āḷavaka! and the sound filled the entire Jambudīpa.
It is said that four sounds were heard throughout the whole of Jambudīpa:
first, when the yakkha general Puṇṇaka, having defeated King Dhanañjaya Koravya at dice, slapped his arms and proclaimed, "I have won!";

second, when Sakka, lord of the devas, seeing the teaching of the Blessed Kassapa declining, caused the deva-son Vissakamma to take the form of a dog and [proclaimed], "I shall [drive out] the wicked bhikkhus..."
He caused it to be proclaimed: "I devour all those who speak unrighteousness—whether they be wicked bhikkhunīs, laymen, or laywomen.

And regarding the Kusajātaka, when the city was besieged by seven kings on account of Pabhāvati, the Great Man himself mounted Pabhāvati upon the neck of his elephant, departed from the city, and declared: "I am the great king Sīhassara Kusā."
He proclaimed this, as did Āḷavaka standing upon the Kelāsa ocean, crying out, "I am Āḷavaka!

At that time, it was as if he had stood and proclaimed it at every door throughout the entire Jambudīpa; and by the power of the yakkha, even the Himālaya mountains, extending for three thousand leagues, trembled.
Thus he raised up a whirlwind, thinking, "By this very means I shall drive away the ascetic.
Those winds, distinguished as eastern and so forth, having arisen, shattered mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas;
they uprooted forests, thickets, trees, and the like, and entered the city of Āḷavī, pulverizing dilapidated elephant stables and other structures.
The winds blew fiercely in the sky. The Blessed One resolved, "Let there be no obstruction for anyone.
When those winds reached the One of Ten Powers, they were unable to move even the hem of his robe.

Then he raised a great rain, thinking, "I shall kill the ascetic by drowning him under water. Through his supernatural power, [the rain] manifested in layers upon layers, such as hundreds and thousands of strata.
Clouds arose and rained; by the force of the downpour, the earth was pierced.
A great flood came over the forest trees and other things, yet it was unable to moisten even a single drop of dew upon the Tathāgata’s robe.
Then he caused a rain of stones to arise—immense mountain peaks, smoking and blazing.
Having come through the air and reached the One of Ten Powers, they turned into divine clusters of garlands. Then he raised a rain of weapons;
single-edged and double-edged swords, spears, arrows, and so forth—smoking and blazing—came through the air and, upon reaching the One of Ten Powers, became divine flowers.
Then he raised a rain of embers; embers the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers came through the air and...
Having become divine flowers, they scattered at the feet of the One Possessing Ten Powers. Then he raised a rain of glowing embers;
the intensely hot embers came through the air and fell at the feet of the One Possessing Ten Powers as sandalwood powder.
Then he raised a rain of sand; the exceedingly fine sand, smoking and blazing, came through the air.
They fell at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers after becoming celestial flowers. Then he produced a slushy mire;
that slushy mire came through the air smoking and blazing, and fell at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers after becoming a divine fragrance.
Then he produced darkness, thinking, "I will terrify the ascetic and cause him to flee. That—
Having become like darkness endowed with four factors, it vanished upon reaching the One Possessed of Ten Powers,
just as darkness is dispelled by the radiance of the sun. Thus, the yakkha,

being unable to drive away the Blessed One with these nine showers of wind, rain, stones, blows, glowing embers, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness, [approached] with various weapons in hand, surrounded by a multitude of beings of many forms.

He himself approached the Blessed One with a fourfold army. Those hosts of spirits, having performed various kinds of transformations, seemed as if they were coming upon the Blessed One crying out, "Seize him! Strike him!
Nevertheless, like flies upon a red-hot iron ball, they became utterly unable to cling to the Blessed One. Even so, just as at the Seat of Enlightenment...
Māra turned back at the very moment he arrived; yet, instead of turning back, they caused a disturbance for about half the night.
Thus, being unable to move the Blessed One even by displaying many kinds of terrifying sights for about half the night, Āḷavaka thought:
"What if I were to discharge a weapon of cloth that cannot be defeated by anyone?"
It is said that there are four weapons supreme in the world: Sakka’s weapon of the thunderbolt, Vessavaṇa’s weapon of the mace, Yama’s weapon of the eye, and Āḷavaka’s weapon of the cloth.
For if Sakka, being enraged, were to strike Sineru’s summit with his thunderbolt weapon, it would pierce through Sineru, which measures one hundred thousand and sixty-eight thousand leagues.

It would go downward. Having struck down the heads of many thousands of *yakkhas* with the club (*gadā*) released during his time as an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*), it returns to Vessavaṇa’s handspan and stands there.
At the mere glance of Yama’s wrathful eye-weapon, many thousands of *kumbhaṇḍas* perish, scattering like sesame seeds in a heated pan. Āḷavaka...
If, in his anger, he were to discharge a cloth-weapon into the sky, the rain would not fall for twelve years.
If he were to discharge it upon the earth, all trees, grasses, and the like would wither, and for an interval of twelve years they would not grow again.
If he were to discharge it into the ocean, all the water would dry up like a drop of water on a heated pan. Even if [the target] were as large as Mount Sineru...
It would shatter the mountain and scatter it into pieces. He released that most powerful cloth-weapon, which he had been wearing as an upper garment, and seized it.
For the most part, the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system gathered together with speed, thinking:
