"Today the Blessed One will subdue Āḷavaka; we shall hear the Dhamma there. Those who desired to witness the battle also [gathered].
The deities assembled; thus the entire sky became completely filled with deities.
Then Āḷavaka, moving higher and higher near the Blessed One, released his garment and weapon.
Like a thunderbolt, it made a terrifying sound in the sky, smoking and blazing, but upon reaching the Blessed One, it returned to the yakkha.
In order to crush his pride, he became a foot-wiping cloth and fell at the Master’s feet.
Seeing him, Āḷavaka—like a bull with its horns broken, like a snake with its fangs pulled out, devoid of luster, devoid of pride, and with the banner of his conceit cast down—thought:
“Even though this ascetic has no weapons, you cannot overcome him; what then must be the reason? This was the reason: he was established in the dwelling of loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*).
“Let me provoke this ascetic and then deprive him of his loving-kindness. With this connection in mind, it was said:
“Then the yakkha Āḷavaka approached the Blessed One... ‘Come out, ascetic! Herein, this is the intention:
“Why have you entered my abode without my permission and sat down like a master of the house in the midst of my women’s quarters?”
"Is it not improper for a recluse to enjoy what is not given and to have contact with women?
Therefore, if you are established in the duty of a recluse, depart, O recluse!
Some, however, say that he spoke thus after having uttered these and other harsh words.
Then the Blessed One, knowing that one who is stubborn cannot be led by means of stubbornness— for if one were to apply stubbornness to him,
it would be as if one were to pierce the nose of a fierce dog with a lancet,
whereby it becomes even more fierce and thus even more stubborn, whereas he can be led by gentleness— said, "Very well, friend."
Having accepted his words with pleasant speech, he departed. Thus it is said: “‘Very well, friend,’ the Blessed One said, and he departed.
Then Āḷavaka, thinking, “How easy to speak with is this ascetic! He has departed at a single word. It was truly easy to make this ascetic depart;
for no reason at all, I have been engaged in battle with him throughout the entire night,” became soft-hearted.
Again he thought: “Even now it is not possible to know; has he gone out because of his being easy to speak with, or rather out of anger?

Come, let me test him. Then he said, “Enter, ascetic! Thereupon, speaking kind words once more for the purpose of determining whether his mind had become softened—that he was indeed "easy to speak with"—the Blessed One entered, saying, “Very well, friend.
Āḷavaka [repeated] that very same thing over and over again.
Examining his disposition for being easy to speak with, he said, "Come out! Enter! a second and even a third time. The Blessed One did likewise.
Had he not done so, the mind of one who was by nature stubborn and haughty would have become even more rigid, and he would not have become a fit vessel for the discourse on the Dhamma.
Therefore, just as a mother gives her crying child whatever it desires—

Just as one might pacify someone by giving or by doing something for them, so too the Blessed One did what the yakkha said in order to pacify that yakkha who was weeping with the "weeping" of the defilements.
And just as a nurse gives something to a child who will not drink milk,
coaxes him, and then feeds him, so too the Blessed One, in order to feed the yakkha the milk of the supramundane Dhamma, acted by fulfilling the words he had requested.
Consoling him in this way, he acted thus. Just as a man wishing to fill a gourd with the four sweet nectars first cleanses its interior,
so the Blessed One, wishing to fill the mind of the yakkha with the supramundane four sweet nectars,
went in and out of his presence up to three times in order to cleanse the impurity of anger from within him.
Then Āḷavaka, having conceived an evil thought—“This ascetic is easy to deal with; when told ‘Come out,’ he comes out, and when told ‘Enter,’ he enters.
What if I were to exhaust this ascetic in this very way throughout the entire night, seize him by the feet, and throw him across the Ganges?”—spoke for the fourth time: “Come out, ascetic!”

Knowing this, the Blessed One said, "Indeed, it is not so for me. He said this because he knew that when this was said, [the interlocutor], seeking something further to be done, would think he ought to ask a question; that would serve as the opening for a discourse on the Dhamma.
In this context, *na* is a particle of negation (*paṭikkhepa*), *kho* is a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), and *aham* is a designation of oneself (*attanidassana*).

This is the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "Friend, because you have thought thus, therefore I shall not go out; do whatever you must do.
Then, Āḷavaka, since even previously at the time of his arrival through the air he had thought, "What indeed is this golden palace?"...
"Or perhaps it is one of the silver-jewel palaces; come, let us see it.
Having thus questioned the powerful ascetics and wanderers who had come to his own palace, and finding them unable to answer, he torments them with mental derangement and other such means.
How so? For non-human beings [afflict them] either by showing terrifying forms or by crushing the physical heart-base.

They cause distraction of the mind in two ways. However, because [the deities] know that "those possessing psychic power do not tremble at the sight of terrifying forms," they manifest a subtle body through their own psychic power, enter within them, and crush the heart-base;
consequently, the continuity of consciousness does not stabilize, and as it fails to stabilize—

They become insane and deranged. To those who are thus deranged, he even splits their chests or seizes them by the feet and hurls them across the Ganges, thinking, "Lest they should ever come to my dwelling again.
Therefore, having remembered the questions, he thought, "What if I were now to harass this ascetic? and said, "That question, ascetic," and so forth.
"But from where did he get those questions? It is said that his parents, having attended upon the Blessed One Kassapa, learned eight questions along with their answers.
They had Āḷavaka memorize them while he was still young. With the passage of time, he forgot the answers.
Thereupon, thinking, "Let these questions not perish," he [wrote them] in vermilion on a golden plate.
Having had it written down, he deposited it in a celestial mansion (vimāna). Thus, these questions of the Buddha pertain exclusively to the domain of the Buddhas.

When the Blessed One heard this, since no one is able to create an obstacle to the acquisitions already relinquished by the Buddhas, nor an obstacle to their life-span, nor a hindrance to their omniscience or their fathom-wide radiance, he therefore demonstrated that unique majesty of the Buddhas which is not shared with the world.
He said: “Indeed, friend, I do not see such a person in the world with its devas.

Herein, a brief explanation has been given by showing the mere meaning of these words according to the method beginning with “By the term ‘with its devas,’ the inclusion of the gods of the five sense-sphere realms is intended,” and so forth;
it is not a detailed exposition following the sequence of the connection of the discourse. That [detailed exposition] is now stated:
For even though all the devas were included by way of the highest limit through the expression "together with the devas," there were those among the assembled host of devas who had doubts, thinking:
"Māra is of great power, the lord of the six sense-sphere devas, one who wields mastery, one who delights in opposition, one who shows the Dhamma, and one whose deeds are cruel;
could it be that he too would not cause such things as the derangement of the mind? To them...
He said, "together with Māra," for the purpose of dispelling doubt. Then, for those who thought, "Brahmā is of great power;

with one finger he creates light in a thousand world-systems, with two... [and so on]... with ten fingers in ten thousand world-systems, and he experiences the unsurpassed bliss of meditative absorption—could he not do this? it was for the purpose of dispelling their doubt.
He said, “together with Brahmā. Then, for those who thought, “There are various recluses and brahmins who are adversaries and enemies of the teaching, endowed with the power of mantras and so forth;

might they not do something [against it]?”—in order to dispel their doubt, he said, “of the generation together with its recluses and brahmins. Thus, having shown the absence of anyone in the most exalted positions, [he spoke].

Now, by the words "together with gods and humans," he shows that even in the rest of the world of beings, there is no one who surpasses him, taking as the upper limit the conventional gods (*sammutideva*) and the remaining humans;
thus should the sequence of the connection between the sections be understood here.
Having thus restrained his intention to cause harm, the Blessed One spoke as follows, generating enthusiasm for the asking of questions: "Moreover..."
“Friend, ask whatever you wish. The meaning of this is: “Ask, if you so desire; there is no burden for me in answering questions.

Or alternatively, he offered an invitation of omniscience, saying, “Ask whatever you wish, and I shall answer it all,” an invitation not shared even by Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, or Great Disciples. For they [would say], “Friend, having heard [the question], ask...”
They say, "We shall know. But the Buddhas say, "Ask, friend, whenever you desire," or, "Ask me, Vāsava, whatever question you wish in your mind. [As it is said:
"The doubts of Bāvari and of you, and the doubts of all—[let them be resolved]."
"Having been granted leave, ask whatever you desire"—in such a manner do gods and humans extend the invitation for the Omniscient One to speak.

And it is not surprising that the Blessed One, having reached the stage of a Buddha, should extend such an invitation; for even when he was still on the stage of a Bodhisatta, while abiding in partial knowledge, [he did so].
“Koṇḍañña, answer the questions; these sages of noble form are entreating you.
Koṇḍañña, this is the duty among men: that when one has grown old, this burden must be borne.
Thus was he entreated by the sages.
“Let the worthy ones ask whatever question they desire in their minds, having been granted leave;
for I shall answer each one of you, having known this world and the world beyond by myself.
Thus, during his time as Sarabhaṅga, and also in the Sambhava Jātaka, he traveled three times throughout the whole of Jambudīpa to [resolve] questions.
Without having seen the end of birth, while playing in the dust on the street at seven years of age, he was asked by a very aged brahmin:
"Truly, I shall tell you, just as one who is skilled [would];
though the king may not know it, whether he will do so or not."
Thus he invited the All-Knowing One to speak. When the Blessed One had thus invited Āḷavaka to speak on omniscience, the yakkha Āḷavaka addressed the Blessed One with this verse:
“What is wealth here? (183) In this context, *kiṃ* is the interrogative word. *Sū* is a particle used merely for the completion of the meter. *Idha* means in this world.
*Vittaṃ*—it is called *vitta* because it is found (*vidati*) or because it produces joy (*pītiṃ karoti*); it is a designation for wealth. *Suciṇṇaṃ* means well-performed.
*Sukhaṃ* means bodily and mental agreeableness (*sāta*). *Āvahāti* means it brings, leads, gives, or causes to enter; thus it is said.
*Haveti* is a particle used in the sense of firmness (*daḷhatthe*). *Sādutaraṃ* means exceedingly sweet. There is also a reading as *sādhutaraṃ*.
*Rasānaṃ* refers to those phenomena designated as "flavors" (*rasa*). *Kathaṃ* means in what manner or by what mode. *Kathaṃjīvino jīvitaṃ* means the life of one who lives in such a way.
However, it is pronounced with a nasalization (*sānunāsika*) for the sake of the ease of metrical composition. Alternatively, the reading is “*kathaṃjīviṃ jīvatan*.
Its meaning is: “How do those who live live? The rest here is self-evident. Thus, by means of this verse, [the following questions are posed]:
“What indeed is the best wealth for a man in this world? What indeed, when well-practiced, brings happiness? Of tastes...”
"What is sweeter? How does one live so that their life is called the best?"—thus he asked these four questions.
Then the Blessed One, answering him according to the very method explained by the Dasa-balas Kassapa, spoke this verse:
"Faith is the wealth here. In this regard, just as wealth such as gold and bullion provides the pleasure of enjoyment and use, [so too is faith].
It brings [prosperity], wards off the suffering of hunger, thirst, and so forth, pacifies poverty, serves as a cause for the acquisition of treasures such as pearls,
and brings about worldly renown; likewise, mundane and supramundane faith also brings, as the case may be, the happiness of mundane and supramundane results, wards off the suffering of birth, aging,
and so forth for those who have set out with faith as their primary burden, and pacifies the poverty of spiritual qualities.
It is the cause for obtaining the jewels beginning with the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.
As it is said: “The person endowed with faith and perfected in virtue, possessed of fame and wealth—whatever region he frequents, there indeed he is honored.”
It is called "wealth" (*vitta*) because it brings about worldly renown through one's speech.

Furthermore, this wealth of faith (*saddhāvitta*) is something that follows one [into future lives], is not shared by others, and is the cause of all success; it is also the source of mundane wealth such as gold and bullion.
For it is only by practicing meritorious deeds such as giving that one who possesses faith attains wealth, whereas one who lacks faith does not.
Wealth leads only to disadvantage; therefore, it is said to be "inferior. Regarding the phrase "of a person": this is a teaching defining the highest limit;
thus, it should be understood that not only for a man, but for women and others as well, the wealth of faith alone is superior.
"Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action, or the Dhamma of generosity, virtue, and mental development. "Well-practiced" means well-performed and well-conducted.
It brings happiness (*sukham āvahāti*): it brings human happiness, like that of Soṇa the merchant’s son, Raṭṭhapāla, and others;
it brings divine happiness, like that of Sakka and others; and finally, it brings the happiness of Nibbāna, like that of Mahāpaduma and others.
Regarding the word "truth" (*sacca*): this term *sacca* is seen in many senses. For example: "One should speak the truth... [and so forth].

In such passages as “one might become angry,” it refers to truthfulness in speech (*vācāsacca*). In such passages as “Samaṇas and brāhmaṇas are established in truth,” it refers to the truth of abstinence (*viratisacca*).
In such passages as “Why do they speak various truths, these who are skilled in proclaiming their own doctrines? it refers to the truth of views (*diṭṭhisacca*).

In such passages as “Bhikkhus, there are these four brahmin truths,” it refers to the truths of the brāhmaṇas (*brāhmaṇasacca*). And in such passages as “For there is but one truth, there is no second,” it refers to... [the ultimate truth].
Regarding ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*): in such passages as "Of the four truths, how many are wholesome?", it refers to the Noble Truths (*ariyasacca*).

Here, however, what is intended is either Nibbāna as ultimate truth, or the truth of speech (*vācasacca*)—the latter being internalized as the truth of abstinence (*viratisacca*)—by the power of which one brings water and other things under control and crosses to the further shore of birth, aging, and death. As it has been said:
“By truth even water flows; by truth the wise destroy poison;
by truth the rain-god pours down his showers; those established in truth aspire for Nibbāna.
Whatever tastes there are on this earth, truth is the sweetest of all tastes.”
“Established in truth, the recluses and brahmins cross to the further shore of birth and death.

“Sādutaraṃ” means sweeter, more refined. “Rasānaṃ” refers to those things that are to be tasted according to the method beginning with “the taste of roots, the taste of trunks,” etc., as well as these [fruits] which [the Buddha said]:
“Monks, I allow all fruit-juices for one who has no appetite.”
“Master Gotama, those flavors of form, flavors of sound, and flavors of smell—O Brahmin, these are not flavors in the true sense of the word;
this Dhamma-Vinaya has but one flavor, the flavor of liberation. Or rather, the Blessed One partakes of the flavor of the goal and the flavor of the Dhamma.
Following such a method, the remaining factors such as tastes and so forth, which are easily censured by verbal expression, are called “flavors. Of those flavors, truth is indeed the most sweet.
Truth alone is more sweet, more excellent, more sublime, and most supreme.

For while the juices of roots and other such things merely nourish the body and bring about defiled pleasure, the taste of truth—namely, the taste of truth as abstinence and the taste of truth as truthful speech—nourishes the mind through serenity, insight, and so forth, and brings about undefiled happiness.
Furthermore, the taste of liberation is [supreme] because it is permeated by the taste of the ultimate truth.

It is excellent; for it proceeds by relying upon both the meaning (*attha*) and the Dhamma, which possess the flavor of the goal and the flavor of the Dhamma, and which serve as the means for attaining them.

Regarding the term "living by wisdom" (*paññājīvin*): here, among those who are blind, one-eyed, or two-eyed, the person with two eyes—whether a householder or a renunciant—follows the practice of a householder, such as the performance of work, taking refuge, giving and sharing, undertaking moral discipline (*sīla*), and performing the Uposatha observances.

Or, having attained through wisdom the way of life of one gone forth—consisting either of the morality that causes freedom from remorse or the further divisions such as the purification of mind—one lives;
the life of such a person who lives by wisdom is "wisdom-life," or the life of that one living by wisdom is called the best.
Thus the meaning should be understood.
185–6. When the Blessed One had thus replied, the Yakkha, having heard all four questions, was delighted;
wishing to ask the remaining four questions as well, he spoke this verse: "How indeed does one cross the flood? Then the Blessed One, replying to him in the same manner as before, spoke this verse:
"One crosses by means of faith. In this regard, although it is one who crosses the fourfold flood—
Thus, he crosses the ocean of saṃsāra, transcends the suffering of the cycle of existence, and is purified of the stains of the defilements.
Nevertheless, because one who lacks faith does not leap forward, lacking conviction in the crossing of the flood;

and because one who is negligent through the surrender of the mind to the five strands of sensual pleasure does not cross the ocean of saṃsāra due to being stuck and entangled right there; and because one who is lazy...
One dwells in suffering, mired in unwholesome states; lacking wisdom and not knowing the path of purification, one does not become pure.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke this verse to show its opposite.
And since, when this has been spoken, the faculty of faith is the proximate cause for the factors of stream-entry, [he said]: "By means of faith..."
By the phrase "crosses the flood," the path of stream-entry—which crosses the flood of views—and the stream-enterer are revealed.
For the stream-enterer, being endowed with heedfulness (appamāda)—consisting of constant practice in the cultivation of wholesome states—attains the second path;
having done so, with the exception of merely returning once more to this world, all that remains...
One crosses the ocean of saṃsāra—the basis for the flood of existence that has not yet been crossed by means of the stream-entry path (sotāpattimagga).

Therefore, by this phrase "the ocean through heedfulness" (appamādena aṇṇavaṃ), he reveals the once-returner path (sakadāgāmimagga) and the once-returner (sakadāgāmi) as the crossing of the flood of existence.
Because the once-returner, having attained the third path through energy, [crosses] the basis for the flood of sensual desire that had not yet been transcended by the once-returner path;

And because one transcends the suffering of sensual desire, which is designated as the "flood of sensual desire," the phrase "one transcends suffering through energy" thus reveals the path of non-returning and the non-returner, who crosses over the flood of sensual desire. Furthermore, because the non-returner,

by means of wisdom that is utterly pure due to being free from the mire of sensual desire, has attained the wisdom of the fourth path which is exclusively pure, [he proceeds] by way of the path of non-returning.
One abandons the supreme stain known as ignorance which has not yet been abandoned;
therefore, by this phrase "he is purified by wisdom," he reveals the path of arahantship and the arahant himself, which cross over the flood of ignorance.
And at the conclusion of this verse, spoken with the culmination of arahantship, the yakkha was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

187. Now, taking up the word "wisdom" (paññā) mentioned here in the phrase "it is purified by wisdom," and asking a question—mixed with both mundane and supramundane matters—by means of his own inspired intuition, he spoke this six-line verse beginning, "How indeed does one obtain wisdom?
In this context, "how indeed" (kathaṃ su) is a question regarding the meaning and the method in every respect. For this...
Having understood that wisdom and the rest are the goal, he asks about their application: "In what way, by what application of the body, and for what reason does one obtain wisdom?
This same method applies to wealth and the other [aims].
Then, showing the attainment of wisdom through four reasons, the Blessed One said, "One who has faith," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:

Having faith in that Dhamma by which the Arahants— the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples— attained Nibbāna, through its classification as virtuous conduct of body and so forth in the prior stage, and its classification as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the subsequent stage,
one acquires mundane and supramundane wisdom for the attainment of Nibbāna. And this is not attained by faith alone.
But because one who has conceived faith approaches [the teacher], and approaching, attends upon him; attending upon him, lends an ear;
and lending an ear, listens to the Dhamma—therefore, from the moment of approaching until the listening to the Dhamma, one obtains the desire to hear.
What is meant? Even after having faith in that Dhamma, at the proper time toward the teacher and preceptor...
Having approached and attended upon them by performing the proper duties, when they— having been won over by such attendance—
are desirous of saying something, then one who has attained the desire to hear, listening with an attentive ear, gains [the teaching]. Thus,
being well-disposed through non-negligence by not being separated from mindfulness, and being discerning through the knowledge of what is well-spoken and ill-spoken...
One attains it, not the other. Therefore he said, "Diligent and discerning.

Thus, because one practices the way that leads to the attainment of wisdom through faith, listens attentively to the means for acquiring wisdom through a desire to learn, does not forget what has been grasped through diligence, and—through discernment—is neither deficient nor excessive;
Having grasped it without error, he causes it to spread widely. Or, through a desire to hear, with attentive ears, he hears the Dhamma that is the cause for the attainment of wisdom;
through diligence, having heard the Dhamma, he retains it; through discernment, he examines the meaning of the teachings he has retained;
then, by means of gradual practice, he realizes the ultimate truth. Therefore, the Blessed One [bestows this upon him].
When asked, "How does one easily obtain wisdom?", he spoke this verse—beginning with "One who has faith... [and] is discerning"—showing these four causes.
Now, answering the three subsequent questions, he spoke this verse beginning with "One who acts appropriately. In that regard:

One is "one who acts appropriately" (patirūpakārī) because one employs a suitable means for acquiring wealth—whether mundane or supramundane—without neglecting the proper place, time, and other such factors.
One is "steadfast" (dhuravā) by virtue of mental energy (*cetasika-vīriya*), never laying down the burden.
One is "energetic" (*uṭṭhātā*) by virtue of physical energy (*kāyika-vīriya*), according to the method beginning with: "And he who regards cold and heat no more than blades of grass," and so forth.

"One endowed with initiative and unremitting effort finds wealth"—by this, as in the case of the junior pupil (*cūḷantevāsī*), one obtains worldly wealth numbering two hundred thousand in no long time;
and as in the case of the Elder Mahā-Tissa the Great (*mahallakamahātissatthera*), one obtains supramundane wealth.
For he, having undertaken the practice, "I shall dwell in three postures," at the time when sloth and torpor approached—
Having soaked a tuft of straw, placed it upon his head, and entered water up to his neck,
he attained *arahantship* after twelve years while warding off sloth and torpor. By means of truth— both by verbal truth, as in "one who speaks the truth,
one who speaks what is real," and by ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*), as in "the Buddha, the Paccekabuddha, and the noble disciple"— he thus acquired renown.
He attains [this]. One who gives whatever is desired or wished for "binds friends"; the meaning is that he secures and accomplishes them.
Or, by giving what is difficult to give, he binds them; or it should be understood that all four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*) are included under the heading of giving.
By means of these, he makes friends—this is what is meant.

190. Having thus answered four questions by way of a method common to both householders and renunciants, and consisting of a mixture of mundane and supramundane factors, he now spoke the words "For whom these...
while answering this fifth question—"How does one not grieve after passing away?"—by way of the householder.
Its meaning is as follows: for whom [the following apply]... [referring to] that which was stated in the passage beginning, "Having faith in the Arahants."
Because he is endowed with faith that gives rise to all wholesome qualities, for the faithful householder seeking a home—
who, as a layman enjoying sensual pleasures, seeks and searches for the five strands of sensual desire—

the "truth" mentioned here in the phrase "one attains fame through truth," and the "wisdom" referred to by the term *sussūsa* (desire to hear) in the phrase "he gains wisdom through desiring to hear," [are both fulfilled].

The four qualities mentioned are as follows: in the phrase "steadfast and industrious," there is the quality of steadfastness (*dhiti*) expressed by the terms "steadfast" (*dhura*) and "industrious" (*uṭṭhātā*);
and in the phrase "giving binds friends," there is the kind of generosity (*cāga*) mentioned therein. Thus, these four qualities exist.
"He indeed does not grieve when gone"—this means that having gone from this world to the next world, he indeed does not grieve.
191. Having thus answered the fifth question, the Blessed One spoke to that *yakkha* as a challenge: “Come now, ask others too.
In this context, *iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation. “Ask others too” means: ask other numerous phenomena [or doctrines] from various ascetics and brahmins;
or else, ask various ascetics and brahmins such as Pūraṇa and others who claim to be omniscient. If...
Or rather, it is a truth superior to the kind of truth mentioned here in the verse, "By truth one attains fame," which is the cause for attaining fame;

or it is self-control (*dama*), mentioned here by way of the term "wisdom through listening" (*sussūsa-paññā*) in the verse, "One gains wisdom through listening," which is the cause for acquiring mundane and supramundane wisdom;
or it is generosity (*cāga*), of the type mentioned here in the verse, "The giver binds friends," which is the cause for binding friends.
Or, in the phrase "one who is persistent and energetic," it refers to the cause for obtaining mundane and supramundane wealth—
namely, the patience characterized as energy— which, depending on various specific purposes, is described by the terms "duty" (*dhura*) and "exertion" (*uṭṭhāna*),
has reached the state of *ussoḷhi* (extraordinary effort) in the sense of bearing a great burden, and is expressed as "truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity."
"Is there anything here found that is even greater than these four qualities for preventing sorrow when one has passed from this world to the next world?"—
this is the explanation of the meaning here, together with a brief summary of the construction. However, in detail,
it should be understood by analyzing each individual word through the methods of extracting the meaning (*atthuddhāra*) and extracting the words (*paduddhāra*).
192. When this was said, because the doubt by which he might have questioned others had been abandoned, [the Blessed One thought: "How indeed could I question now?

Having said, "Many are the recluses and brahmins," he spoke thus—"I understand today that which is for the sake of the future life"—thereby making known even to those who did not know the reason why he did not question them. In that context, "today" (*ajja*) refers to the present day.
"Having made [this]" is the intended meaning. "I understand" means I know in the manner already described.
By the phrase "whatever benefit," he shows the benefit pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) as stated in the sequence beginning with "One who desires to hear gains wisdom.

By the word "hereafter" (*samparāyika*), he shows the benefit pertaining to future lives (*samparāyika*) which causes the absence of sorrow after death, as stated in the verse: "He for whom these four qualities... Furthermore, "benefit" (*attha*) is a term for a cause.
It is a synonym. For this word *attha* functions in the sense of "text" in such passages as “well-meaning and well-phrased” (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanan*);

in the sense of "purpose" or "task" in such passages as “I have need of gold and silver, householder” (*attho me, gahapati, hiraññasuvaṇṇena*); in the sense of "prosperity" in such passages as “there is prosperity for those of virtuous conduct” (*hoti sīlavataṃ attho*);

in the sense of "wealth" in such passages as “many people resort [to someone] for the sake of wealth” (*bahujano bhajate atthahetu*); and in such passages as “he acts for the benefit of both” (*ubhinnamatthaṃ carati*).
In such passages as “The wise man [is one] who knows the benefit and the welfare,” it refers to a cause. But here, it refers to a cause.

Therefore, that which is the cause for the attainment of wisdom and so forth pertaining to this present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), and that which is the cause for the absence of sorrow in the future life pertaining to the world beyond (*samparāyika*)—that very thing I myself now understand by my own means according to the method spoken by the Blessed One today; how then could I now ask others?
"Ascetic and brahmin"—thus, in brief, the meaning here should be understood.

(193) Having thus said, "I understand that which is for the sake of the future life," the yakkha, showing that this knowledge is rooted in the Blessed One, said, "Truly, it is for my benefit that the Buddha [exists].
In that context, "for the benefit" (*atthāya*) means for one's welfare (*hita*) or for one's growth (*vuḍḍhi*). Where...
Regarding the phrase "what is given bears great fruit," the meaning is:

"I recognize the Buddha as the supreme recipient of offerings—that one in whom what is given becomes of great fruit, by virtue of the generosity described in the verse beginning 'He for whom these four qualities... However, some say that he spoke thus with reference to the Saṅgha.

194. Having thus shown his own attainment of welfare by means of this verse, he now spoke the words, “I shall wander,” demonstrating his practice for the welfare of others. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the *Hemavata Sutta*.

Thus, the conclusion of this verse, the breaking of the night, the arising of the sound of applause, and the bringing of the youth Āḷavaka to the abode of the *yakkha* all occurred at one and the same moment. When the king’s men heard the sound of applause, they...
“Such a sound of acclaim does not arise for anyone other than the Buddhas; has the Blessed One perhaps arrived?

Reflecting thus, they saw the radiance from the Blessed One’s body. No longer standing outside as before, they entered without hesitation and beheld the Blessed One seated in the abode of the yakkha, while the yakkha stood with his hands joined in reverential salutation.
Seeing him standing there, they said to the yakkha, "Great yakkha, this prince has been brought here for you as an offering;
come, eat him, consume him, or do with him as you see fit.
Because he was a stream-enterer, he felt ashamed, especially since he was being addressed in this way right in front of the Blessed One. Then, taking the prince with both hands, he...
He presented him to the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable Sir, this boy was sent to me; I give him to the Blessed One.
Buddhas are compassionate for the welfare of others; Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept this child for his benefit and for his happiness.
And he spoke this verse:

“This prince, endowed with a hundred marks of merit, complete in all limbs and perfect in his characteristics—I give him to you with a joyful and glad heart. Accept him, O Seer, for the welfare of the world.
The Blessed One accepted the prince; and while accepting him, he performed an auspicious rite for both the spirit and the prince.
He recited the verse with three lines. As the yakkha was going for refuge to the prince, he completed it with the fourth line three times, as follows:
“May this prince be long-lived.”
"And may you, O Yakkha, be happy!
May you remain free from illness for the welfare of the world.
This prince goes for refuge to the Buddha... to the Dhamma... to the Saṅgha."
The Blessed One gave the boy to the king’s men, saying, "Raise him up and give him back to me again. Thus,
because that boy passed from the hands of the king’s men into the hands of the yakkha, from the hands of the yakkha into the hands of the Blessed One,
and from the hands of the Blessed One back again into the hands of the king’s men, he was named "Hatthaka Āḷavaka" (the Hand-given of Āḷavī).

He was born. When the royal messengers returned carrying him and were seen, the farmers, woodworkers, and others asked in fear, "Is it a *yakkha* who does not wish for the prince because he is too young?
The royal messengers replied, "Do not be afraid; safety has been established by the Blessed One," and they related everything.
Then, with cries of "Excellent! Excellent! the entire city of Āḷavī broke into a single tumultuous roar.
It was facing toward the yakkha. When the Blessed One arrived at the time for his alms-round, the yakkha took his bowl and robe, went halfway along the road, and turned back.
Then the Blessed One, having wandered for alms in the city and finished his meal, stood at a certain secluded spot near the city gate.

He sat down upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared at the foot of the tree. Then the king and the citizens, having gathered together with the great multitude of people, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat around him.
They asked, "Venerable sir, how did you subdue such a fierce yakkha? To them, the Blessed One began by recounting the battle.
“Thus he rained down in nine ways, thus he created terrors, thus he asked a question, and thus I answered it,” he said, and related that very Āḷavaka Sutta.
At the conclusion of the discourse, there was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings.
Then the king and the citizens [built a shrine] near the abode of the Great King Vessavaṇa.
Having established a residence for the yakkha, they constantly offered him oblations accompanied by honors such as flowers and perfumes.
When that youth reached the age of discretion, they dismissed him, saying, "You obtained this life by depending on the Blessed One;
go, attend upon the Blessed One himself and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. He [then attended upon] the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

While attending upon him, he soon established himself in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), mastered the entire word of the Buddha, and came to be surrounded by a retinue of five hundred lay followers (*upāsaka*). And the Blessed One designated him as foremost among his disciples:
"Foremost, monks, among my lay disciple followers who gather assemblies by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*) is Hatthaka."
“Āḷavaka” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.251).
The commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
11. Commentary on the Vijaya Sutta.
Whether walking or standing, this is the Nanda Sutta. It is also called the Vijaya Sutta and the Kāyavicchandanika Sutta.
What is its origin? This sutta, it is said, was spoken on two occasions; therefore, its origin is twofold.
Therein, the Blessed One, having gradually arrived at Kapilavatthu, having guided the Sakyans, and having ordained Nanda and others, permitted the going forth for women.
Consequently, three Nandas went forth: the Elder Ānanda’s sister Nandā, Abhirūpanandā—the daughter of the Sakyan king Khemaka—and Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā. And at that time...
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī. Abhirūpanandā was indeed beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring;
for that very reason, they gave her the name Abhirūpanandā. Nandā, the most beautiful woman in the land, likewise saw no one who could equal her in beauty.
Both of them, intoxicated by the pride of their physical form, [thought]: "The Blessed One disparages form; he censures it in many ways."
"Because they perceive the danger in form," they do not go to attend upon the Blessed One, nor do they wish even to see him.
If it is asked why those who were thus lacking in faith went forth [into homelessness], it was because of misfortune.
For on the very day of her marriage, the husband of Abhirūpanandā, a Sakyan prince, passed away. Then her parents made her go forth against her will. As for Janapadakalyāṇī—
When the Venerable Nanda had attained arahantship, Nandā became despondent and thought, "My husband, my mother Mahāpajāpatī, and other kinsmen have all gone forth;
life at home is suffering without one's kin. Finding no satisfaction in the household life, she went forth—not out of faith.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that their knowledge had reached maturity, commanded Mahāpajāpatī:
“Let all the bhikkhunīs come for exhortation in their proper order. When their turn arrived, they sent someone else in their stead. Thereupon the Blessed One said:
“When one’s own turn arrives, one must come personally; another should not be sent. Then one day, Abhirūpanandā—
He arrived. The Blessed One, having caused him to be stirred by means of a manifested form, addressed him with this verse from the *Dhammapada*:
“Behold, Nanda, this body—a city made of bones, sick, impure, and putrid;
oozing and trickling, it is craved by fools.”
“Meditate on the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit;
then, through the full comprehension of conceit, you will wander at peace.
With these verses from the Therīgāthā, she gradually established her in Arahatship. Then one day, the inhabitants of Sāvatthī...

Having given their alms-food before the meal and having undertaken the Uposatha vows, they dress themselves well in lower and upper garments, take perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and go to Jeta’s Grove to hear the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the Dhamma discourse, they pay homage to the Blessed One and enter the city.
The community of bhikkhunīs likewise, having heard the Dhamma talk, returns to the bhikkhunī residence.

There, both men and bhikkhunīs spoke in praise of the Blessed One. Indeed, in this world inhabited by four types of beings, there is no one who, upon seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One, does not feel inspired confidence.

For those individuals who take form as their standard [of beauty] see the Blessed One—adorned with the primary marks, variegated with the secondary characteristics, draped in the radiant garlands of his halo and rays of light—as if he were a living ornament.
They have faith upon seeing the physical form (rūpa) that has arisen in the world;

they have faith upon hearing the report of their fame—measured by sound—which throughout hundreds of various births was endowed with eight qualities and possessed the sweet resonance of a karavīka bird and the voice of Brahmā;

they have faith upon seeing the austerity measured by material things, such as the coarseness of their bowl and robes or the austerity of their ascetic practices; and they have faith in the Dhamma measured by the aggregates of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth.
Having investigated any category of the Dhamma, they therefore speak in praise of the Blessed One in all places.
Even after arriving at the nuns' quarters, Nandā, the most beautiful woman in the land, heard them speaking in praise of the Blessed One in many ways;
desiring to approach the Blessed One, she informed the nuns. The nuns...
Taking it, they approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, having already known of her arrival, like a man wishing to extract a thorn with a thorn or a wedge with a wedge, desired to subdue the pride of form by means of form itself;
thus, through his power of psychic potency (*iddhi*), he [manifested] one appearing fifteen or sixteen years of age.
He manifested a woman of exceeding beauty standing to the side of the Blessed One and fanning him.
The nun Nandā approached together with the bhikkhunīs, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down within the community of bhikkhunīs.
Having beheld the Blessed One’s perfection of form from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair, she again [beheld] that [woman] standing to the side of the Blessed One.
Seeing her formless appearance, she thought, "Oh, this woman was once beautiful," and having abandoned her pride in her own beauty, she became enamored of her [the woman's] beauty.
Then the Blessed One made that woman appear as if she were twenty years of age;
for a woman is most radiant when she is about sixteen years old, and not beyond that. Then [he showed] the decline of her beauty.
Having seen this, Nandā’s desire and lust for that form became attenuated. Then the Blessed One, having displayed the appearance of a woman who has not yet given birth,
one who has given birth once, a middle-aged woman, and a mature woman— extending thus up to a hundred-year-old woman,
bent over, leaning on a staff, her limbs covered in spots— and while Nandā was still looking on, he showed her death in its various stages, beginning with the bloated corpse.
He showed her how it was being devoured by crows and other scavengers, its foul stench, and its loathsome, repulsive state.
When Nandā saw that corpse, she reflected, "In this very same way, this body is common to myself and to all others," and thus the perception of impermanence became firmly established.
Following from that, the perceptions of suffering and non-self also arose; the three realms of existence appeared to her like a house on fire, offering no refuge.
Having offered the sacrifice, they waited upon him. Then the Blessed One, knowing that Nandā’s mind had entered into the meditation subject, spoke these verses according to what was suitable for her:
“Behold, Nandā, this body: afflicted, impure, and putrid.”
Flowing out, trickling away—this is what fools long for.
"As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this. See it as empty according to its elements; do not return again to the world."
“Having dispelled desire for existence, you shall live in peace.

At the conclusion of this verse, Nandā was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Then, the Blessed One, speaking for the sake of her attainment of the higher paths, delivered this discourse while explaining the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) of insight (*vipassanā*) accompanied by emptiness (*suññatā*). This, first of all, is its origin story.
Furthermore, while the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, there occurred that incident which was related in detail in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*...
The daughter of the courtesan Sālavatī, named Sirimā, who was the younger sister of Jīvaka, obtained that position after her mother’s passing.
Having disregarded the daughter of the merchant Puṇṇaka on account of the verse, “One should conquer anger with non-anger,” she later sought forgiveness from the Blessed One.
Upon hearing his Dhamma teaching, she became a stream-enterer and established eight permanent alms-offerings.
He set it in motion. Regarding that, a certain monk who was a recipient of a regular meal (niccabhattika) gave rise to lust.
It is stated in the commentary on the Dhammapada verses that, being unable even to perform the function of eating, he lay down without food.
While he was lying there in that state, Sirimā died and became a queen of Suyāma in the Yāma heaven. Then, regarding the performance of the cremation rites for her body—

Having had [the body] removed from the raw charnel ground, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, went to see the body that had been deposited there by the king, taking that monk with him, as did the citizens and the king. There, people said:

"In the past, even for eight thousand and one hundred [people] possessing glory, a sight of her was difficult to obtain; yet today, even one who desires to see her for the sake of a mere kākaniṭṭha coin [can do so]."
“...there is none. Then the celestial maiden Sirimā also arrived there, surrounded by five hundred chariots.
There too, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the assembled multitude and as an exhortation to that bhikkhu, the Blessed One spoke this Sutta and this verse from the *Dhammapada*:
“Behold the painted image! This was its second origin.
195. "Whether walking there" means either going with the entire physical body directed toward the destination to be reached;
or "whether standing," meaning standing by virtue of that very same body being held up;
or "whether sitting or lying down," meaning sitting by virtue of the contraction of the lower part and the raising of the upper part of that same body, or [lying] horizontally.
Or sleeping in a state of extension. "He bends and extends" means he bends and extends those various joints.
This is the movement of the body: all this is the movement, the shifting, and the quivering of this very conscious body;
there is no other here who walks or extends [the limbs]. Nevertheless, when the thought "I am walking" arises...
The air element originating from that [volition] pervades the body;
by means of this, there is an extension of the body toward the direction in which one must go, meaning that a different form appears in another location. Therefore, it is called "moving.
Likewise, when the thought "I stand" arises, the air element originating from that pervades the body; by means of this, there is an uplifting of the body.
The meaning is: "the manifestation of form by standing successively higher. By that, one is said to be "standing.
Likewise, when the thought "I am sitting" arises, the wind element originating from that [thought] pervades the body;
thereby there occurs the contraction of its lower part and the raising of its upper part. The meaning is: "the manifestation of form through such a state. By that, one is said to be "sitting."
It is said thus. Likewise, when the thought "I lie down" arises, the air element originating from that mind pervades the body;
by means of this, there is the stretching out [of the limbs] across, and the meaning is that there is the manifestation of form through such a state. Therefore, one is said to "lie down.
And so, this venerable one—whosoever he may be, of such-and-such a name—whether walking, or standing, or sitting, or lying down...
That which is called "bending and stretching" refers to the bending and stretching of various limbs in their respective postures by means of contracting and extending them.

Since that too occurs in the same manner as previously described when the consciousnesses of bending and stretching arise, it is merely the movement of the body; there is no other agent here at all, for this is empty of any mover.
or by a being, or by a person. However, it is said:
“Depending on the diversity of the mind, there is diversity of wind;
from the diversity of wind, there is the movement of the body.”—thus it is.
This is the ultimate meaning here.

Thus, by means of this verse, the Blessed One [taught] that because physical strain arises from prolonged application to a single posture (*iriyāpatha*), one changes one's posture for the sake of dispelling that [strain];
therefore, [he spoke] "whether walking" and so forth, which conceal the postures.

It illuminates the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*). Likewise, by stating that at the time of walking there is an absence of standing and so forth, and thus saying "all this variety of walking and so on is the movement of the body," it reveals the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*) as concealed by continuity (*santati*).

And by stating "this is the movement of the body" while negating a self (*atta*) for each respective coordination that occurs, it [reveals] that which is concealed by the density of the perception of a self (*attasaññāghanapaṭicchanna*).
It illuminates the characteristic of non-self.

Having thus explained the meditation subject of emptiness by way of illustrating the three characteristics, he then began with the words, "Bound together by bones and sinews," for the purpose of showing the foulness of both the conscious and the unconscious body.
Its meaning is as follows: that movement which belongs to this body—this very body...

It is "bound together by bones and sinews" because it is joined by more than three hundred and sixty bones and nine hundred sinews, as described in the *Visuddhimagga* in the commentary on the Thirty-two Aspects (*Dvattiṃsākāra-vaṇṇanā*) through their distinctions of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation,

and by way of their lack of activity. It is [also bound] by the skin, such as that of the toes of the feet, as described in that same work, and by the flesh, which is divided into nine hundred pieces.
Because it is smeared with skin and flesh, it should be understood as supremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive.

What need is there to say more here? If this [skin] were the size of a jujube stone when gathered from the entire body of a man of medium stature, then even with that—[a surface] as delicate as a fly’s wing—colored with blue and other pigments, it would be like a house wall.
If it were not covered by such skin, this body—though covered by even such delicate skin as this—would not be seen for what it truly is by foolish worldlings who lack the eye of wisdom.

For, being colored by the hue of the skin, even the inner skin (chamman), which consists of things most loathsome and repulsive, is concealed by that outer skin; and as for that [inner flesh], its detailed classification is as follows:
“Nine hundred kinds of flesh are smeared upon the body;
it is a place of filth, like a cesspool, swarming with various families of worms.
Thus was the ninth hundredfold [section] spoken, concerning those who are smeared with flesh.
“There are nine hundred sinews in this body, a fathom in length;
they bind together the collection of bones as creepers bind a house.
These, too, arising from the sinews, are arranged in succession, putrid, and foul-smelling—three hundred and sixty-six in total.
Even the hundreds of bones are not seen as they truly are, because one has not yet grasped that skin which is as delicate as a fly’s wing.
However, those various kinds of internal filth— which, because they are enveloped by the skin colored by the hue of the flesh, are unknown to the whole world, and which are supremely impure,
foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive— these too [are seen] with the eye of wisdom.
Having penetrated [this], it should be seen thus: "full of entrails, full of stomach... and of bile and fat. 197.
Therein, "full of entrails" (*antapūro*) means filled with entrails. "Full of stomach" (*udarapūro*) means filled with the stomach.

And "stomach" (*udara*) is a designation for the *udariya* (the physical organ of digestion); for that is called "stomach" by way of its location. "Of the liver-bowl" (*yakana-peḷassa*) means of the mass of liver.
“Vatthi” means of urine; however, it is called “vatthi” here by way of its vicinity to its location.
“Full” (pūra) is the governing term; therefore, it should be construed thus: “the fullness of the liver-encasement, the fullness of the bladder. This same method applies to the heart and so forth.

And all these internal organs, etc., have been described in the *Visuddhimagga* according to their color, shape, direction, location, delimitation, and classification, by way of the method of non-agency.
They are to be understood in the same manner already described. 199–200.
Thus the Blessed One, having shown the internal filth by saying, "There is not even a single thing here fit to be grasped that is like a pearl or a gem;
rather, this body is filled with impurities," now [shows] that very same internal filth.
Having made it manifest by showing the corpse that had gone outside, and including what was stated previously, he spoke the two verses beginning with, “Then from his nine streams.
Therein, “then” (atha) indicates another method; it means: “See also the state of impurity by another method.”
"Of this body": of this physical frame. "From nine openings": from both eye sockets, the two ear canals, the two nostrils, the mouth, the passage for excrement, and the passage for urine.
"Impurity flows out": only all manner of world-renowned, extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and impure substances flow out, stream forth, and drip;
it is not any other kind of substance, such as fragrant scents like agallochum or sandalwood, nor precious gems like jewels or pearls.
"Always" means at all times—whether by night or by day, in the morning or in the evening, whether standing or walking. If it is asked, "What is that impurity? [the answer is]:
"From the eye comes the eye-excrement," and so forth. For from the two openings of the eyes there is eye-excrement, which resembles the skin and flesh removed [from them];
from the openings of the ears there is ear-excrement, which resembles dust and dirt.
From the nostrils, snot flows like before, and from the mouth one vomits. If it is asked what is vomited:
sometimes bile; the intention is that when unbound bile becomes provoked, then one vomits that.
And "phlegm" means not only bile, but also that phlegm which remains on the surface of the stomach in a quantity measuring a full *pattha*.
At times he vomits. This [vomiting] should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Visuddhimagga* regarding its color and other qualities.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "phlegm and" (*semhañca*), it is shown that he vomits not only phlegm but also other such impurities, such as the contents of the stomach, blood, and so forth.
Having thus demonstrated the vomiting of impurities through the seven openings, the Blessed One—knowing the time, knowing the individual, and knowing the assembly—furthermore...
Without specifically naming the two doors, he said, “From the body sweat and filth flow,” showing by another method that there is an outflow of impurity from the entire body.
Therein, “sweat and filth” (*sedajallikā*) refers to both sweat (*sedo*) and the filth (*jallikā*) consisting of layers of salt and impurities;
this is connected with the phrase “it flows at all times.”
201. Thus, just as when rice is being cooked, the dregs of the rice and the dregs of the water rise up together with the froth, smear the mouth of the cauldron, and overflow outside;

so too, when food consisting of various kinds such as what is eaten and drunk is being cooked by the fire born of karma, whatever dregs of what is eaten, drunk, and so forth arise—such as "the eye-excrement from the eye," and so on—[they overflow].
As it issues forth through the various openings, it smears the eyes and other parts and drips outside; by way of this too, having shown the impurity of this body,
one now shows the impurity even of the head— which, because of its extreme excellence, is regarded as the most superior limb in the world,
such that even those worthy of veneration do not perform salutations toward it— and which, due to its lack of essence and its filthiness, is likewise impure.
Showing this, he spoke this verse: “Then his hollow head.
In this context, *susiraṃ* means a cavity. “Filled with brain matter” means it is filled with brain matter like a gourd filled with curd.
Furthermore, that brain matter should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. He conceives of it as beautiful.
"The fool": thus, this fool, thinking evil thoughts, conceives that body—which is filled with such various kinds of corpses—as beautiful;
he conceives it as "beautiful, clean, desirable, lovely, and pleasing" by means of all three: craving, views, and conceit.
Why? Because he is preceded by ignorance—that is, preceded by delusion which obscures the Four Noble Truths—and is impelled by it.
The intention is that it was grasped [by the Blessed One] by being set forth thus: “Grasp in this way, adhere in this way, conceive in this way.
See how far-reaching this ignorance is in producing harm. 202.
Thus the Blessed One, having shown the foulness by way of the animate, now shows it by way of the inanimate.

Since even the body of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti-rāja) is filled with the aforementioned putridity, he has thus shown the foulness (*asubha*) in every respect within the state of prosperity;
now, in order to show it within the state of misfortune, he spoke the verse beginning, "And when he lies dead.
Its meaning is as follows: when this very body, being of such a nature, has died through the departure of life-force, heat, and consciousness, like a leather bag filled with wind...
Like one bloated by the disintegration of color, or like a livid corpse in a cemetery, he lies cast away and discarded like a useless log;
then, thinking, "There will be no rising up for him again," his kinsmen become utterly indifferent and devoid of regard.
In this context, "dead" demonstrates impermanence, and "lies" demonstrates lack of agency. And by both of these—
He enjoins [the practitioner] to abandon the pride of vitality. "Swollen" indicates the deterioration of shape; "bluish-black" indicates the deterioration of skin color.
By means of both these, he enjoins him to abandon the pride of physical form by relying on the loss of complexion and beauty, and to abandon conceit.
"Cast away" indicates the absence of anyone to take it up; "in the charnel ground" indicates that which is unfit to be endured within.
[He shows] the state of being loathsome. By both of these, he directs [the practitioner] toward the abandoning of the grasping at "mine" and the perception of beauty.
With the words "relatives are indifferent," he demonstrates the state of being rejected; by that, he directs [the practitioner] toward the abandoning of pride in one's retinue.
203. Having thus shown the foulness by way of an undecomposed corpse with consciousness remaining, he now [shows it] by way of a decomposed corpse.

To show this, he spoke the verse beginning with “They eat it. Therein, “and whatever others” means that whatever other creatures there are who feed on carrion, such as crows, kites, and so forth, they too eat it;
this is the meaning. The rest is self-evident. 204.

Thus, by way of the meditation subject on emptiness (*suññatā-kammaṭṭhāna*) according to the method beginning with “Whether walking,” and [the method] beginning with “Connected with bones and sinews,”...

Having shown the body by way of its impurity when possessed of consciousness through the passage beginning, "And when he lies dead," and by way of its impurity when devoid of consciousness, [the text] explains the conduct of the fool regarding this body—which is empty of a permanent, pleasant self and is utterly impure—with the verse:
"The fool, led by ignorance, perceives it as beautiful. And by way of ignorance, it shows the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

Having thus shown this, he now began with the words "having heard the Buddha’s word" (*sutvāna buddhavacanaṃ*) in order to demonstrate the conduct of a wise person therein by way of full understanding (*pariññā*) and the turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*).
Therein, "having heard" means having reflected thoroughly (*yoniso nisāmetvā*). "The Buddha’s word" refers to the word of the Buddha that brings about the dispassion of the body.

"A bhikkhu" means one who is either a trainee (*sekkha*) or an ordinary person (*puthujjana*). "Possessed of wisdom" (*paññāṇavā*): "wisdom" (*paññāṇa*) refers to insight (*vipassanā*), because it occurs in relation to the various aspects such as impermanence;
the meaning is that he is endowed with that. "Here" (*idha*) means in the Dispensation. "He thoroughly understands it" (*so kho naṃ parijānāti*):
he thoroughly understands this body by means of the three kinds of full understanding. How? Just as a skilled merchant [examines] goods, saying, "This is this," and "That is that."
Having observed it and weighed it, thinking, "If this much is taken, such an amount of profit will arise," he acts accordingly;
then, while taking the principal back along with the profit, he discards that merchandise.

In exactly the same way, observing with the eye of knowledge, "These are the bones, sinews, and so forth, as well as the head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth," one fully understands them through the full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*), [realizing]: "These phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self."

By weighing [them] with the full understanding through investigation, one fully understands them; having thus investigated, upon reaching the Noble Path, one fully understands them there through the full understanding of abandonment by means of the abandoning of desire and lust.

Or, seeing them as impure—both with and without consciousness—one fully understands them through the full understanding of the known; seeing them as impermanent and so forth, one does so through the full understanding of investigation; and by means of the path of Arahantship...
Then, having drawn out desire and lust and abandoning them, he fully understands them through the full understanding of abandonment (*pahānapariññā*).
If it is asked why he understands them in this way, it is because he sees things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*); the meaning is that he sees according to reality.
And since this meaning is already established by the phrase "possessing wisdom" (*paññāṇavā*) and so forth, [it is said] because, having heard the Buddha’s word, his...

It is a matter for wisdom; and because the body is a means evident to all people, such that it cannot be fully understood without hearing the Buddha’s word, he said, "Having heard the Buddha’s word," in order to show that this is the cause for its knowledge and to demonstrate the inability of those outside [the Teaching] to see it thus.
[He spoke of] the nun Nandā and that monk whose mind was perverted.
He said "bhikkhus" because the teaching was delivered with reference to them, and because it shows that among the foremost assembly there are those who have attained the practice thereof. 205.
Now, regarding the phrase "for he sees it as it really is," in order to show how one who sees sees it as it really is, he said: "As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this. Its meaning is: as...
This beautiful body possessed of consciousness moves, stands, sits, and lies down because life, heat, and consciousness have not departed from it.
Likewise, although this [body] now lies in the charnel ground devoid of consciousness, it was previously the same because those factors had not departed.
And just as this dead body does not move, stand, sit, or lie down now because those factors have departed, so too...
It does not sit down, nor does it lie down; likewise, through the departure of those factors, this conscious body will also become so.

And just as this conscious body does not now lie dead in a charnel ground, nor has it yet reached the state of being bloated and so forth, so too this dead body was previously [conscious] in the same way.
Furthermore, just as this [body] is currently an unattractive thing devoid of consciousness...
One thinks: "That which lies in the charnel ground has reached the state of being bloated and so forth; likewise, this [body] of mine, though still possessing consciousness, will become thus.
In this regard, by establishing the identity between one's own dead body and that [corpse], thinking "As this is, so is that," one abandons aversion toward external objects.
By establishing the identity of oneself with the dead body, thinking "As that is, so is this," [one abandons attachment].
He abandons lust for internal things. By understanding the manner in which he makes both equal, he abandons delusion regarding both.

Thus, having accomplished the abandoning of the unwholesome roots even at the preliminary stage through such vision of reality as it is, because a bhikkhu practicing in this way gradually reaches the path of Arahatship and is able to fade away all desire and lust—
He is capable; therefore he says, "One should cause passion for the body, both internally and externally, to fade away.
The phrase "a bhikkhu practicing in this way by stages" is the remainder of the text.
Having thus shown the stage of the trainee (*sekha*), he now says, "one who is detached from passion and desire," showing the stage of the adept (*asekha*).
"Thus. Its meaning is as follows: that bhikkhu, being wise through the knowledge of the path to arahantship, attains the fruit immediately following the path;
then, because desire and lust have been entirely abandoned, he is "dispassionate toward desire and lust";

and because there is no more death, or in the sense of being sublime, it is "the Deathless"; and because all conditioned phenomena are stilled, it is "peace," due to the absence of the craving known as "wandering-on."
It is said that he has attained the state praised as "the deathless" (*accuta*) because of the absence of passing away (*cavana*).

Alternatively, it should be understood that by means of the knowledge of the path to *arahantship*, that bhikkhu becomes one possessed of wisdom, established in the fruit immediately following the path, and is called "dispassionate through the fading away of desire and lust";
and it should be known that he has attained the aforementioned state. By this, it is demonstrated: "This has been abandoned by him, and this has been gained by him."

207–208. Having thus explained the meditation subject on the foul (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) together with its accomplishment by way of both the animate and the inanimate, he again spoke these two verses beginning with "The body of two feet" (*dvipādako yaṃ*) in order to censure the state of negligence, which acts as an obstacle to such great benefit, by means of a concise teaching.
Therein, although the bodies of those without feet and so forth are indeed impure, [the focus here is] by virtue of the specific context.
Alternatively, it is said "two-legged" in order to establish the upper limit, or because other bodies, though impure, are prepared with salt,
sour gruel, and so forth, and even offered as food for human beings, whereas the human body is not; thus,
even when demonstrating its state of extreme impurity, he says "two-legged."
It shows how they enter into human form. "The foul odor is concealed" means that, being foul-smelling, it is concealed by being mixed with the fragrance of flowers and the like.
"Filled with various kinds of filth" means it is packed full of many types of filth, such as hair and so forth.
"Oozing here and there" means that even when people strive to conceal it with flower perfumes and the like, their efforts are rendered fruitless.
Having produced saliva, nasal mucus, and so forth through the nine openings, and sweat and grime through the pores of the body, they simply flow out.

In this regard, now look: whatever foolish person—be it a man or a woman—who, by means of such a body, would think to exalt themselves through craving, views, conceit, and false notions, in the manner of "I," "mine," "permanent," and so on; whoever thus seeks to exalt themselves—
Or he might think himself superior, or despise another on account of birth and so forth, while placing himself in a high position;
what else could be the cause for such pride and contempt, except for a lack of vision—specifically, the absence of seeing the Noble Truths by means of the Noble Path?
At the conclusion of the teaching, the bhikkhunī Nandā was moved to a sense of spiritual urgency: "Alas! How foolish I am, who..."
“Thus, she did not come to attend upon the Blessed One, who was thus engaged in delivering various teachings on the Dhamma.
Being thus moved by spiritual urgency, she focused her mind on that very teaching and, within a few days, realized Arhatship by means of that very meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
It is said that at the conclusion of the teaching in the second instance as well, eighty-four thousand living beings [attained realization].

There was a realization of the Dhamma; the glorious celestial maiden attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).
Thus ends the commentary on the Vijaya Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, within the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.
12. Commentary on the *Muni Sutta* 209.
The *Muni Sutta* begins: "From intimacy arises fear. What is its origin? Not every sutta has a single origin;
however, first of all, this is the origin of the initial four verses. It is said that while the Blessed One was at Sāvatthī...
While they were living in a village monastery, a certain destitute woman whose husband had died ordained her son among the monks and she herself ordained as a nun among the nuns.
Both of them entered the rains retreat at Sāvatthī and became desirous of seeing one another frequently.
Whenever the mother obtained anything, she brought it to her son, and the son likewise did for his mother. Thus she too—

The nuns, too, having come together with one another, sharing whatever they had obtained, greeting each other with joy, and inquiring after one another’s welfare and suffering, became free from apprehension.
Through this frequent seeing, intimacy arose among them; from intimacy came trust;
from trust came an opening for passion; and for those whose minds were overcome by passion, both the perception of being ordained and the perception of being mother and daughter vanished.
It disappeared. Then, having transgressed the boundary, they practiced unrighteous conduct;
having incurred infamy, they left the order and lived among householders. The monks reported this to the Blessed One.
Having rebuked him, saying, "Monks, what does that foolish man think? Does a mother not feel passion for her son, or a son for his mother? he said, "I do not..."
“Monks, I do not see even a single other form [that is so dangerous],” and so on.
Having thus stirred the monks with this and other remaining suttas, he said:
“Therefore, monks—‘Just as the halāhala poison, just as boiling oil;’”

Having said, "One should avoid a woman like molten copper," he then spoke these four stanzas, beginning with "Fear arises from intimacy" (*santhavāto bhayaṃ jātaṃ*), as a personal application for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the bhikkhus.
Therein, "intimacy" (*santhava*) was previously stated to be threefold—by way of craving, views, and friends. Here, it refers to intimacy through craving and views.
This is what is intended. With reference to this, the Blessed One said: "Behold, monks, how this fear has arisen for that foolish man from intimacy.
For indeed, a powerful fear born of defilements—arising from his craving for the desire to see her constantly and so forth—had taken hold of him;
being unable to remain steadfast because of it, he acted improperly toward his mother. Or rather, it was the great fear consisting of self-reproach and the like.
By which he abandoned the Dispensation and became a wanderer. "Homes" (*niketa*) refers to the various kinds of objects of perception described in such passages as:
"Householder, one who is bound by the spreading out and confinement of the home that is the sign of form is called 'one who wanders among homes'.
"Dust arises" means the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion arises. What is meant? Not only did fear arise for him from intimacy (*santhava*), but...

Furthermore, that which is called a "home" (niketa) in the sense of being an abode for the defilements—that is, an object of consciousness associated with the taints (sāsavārammaṇa)—now, because his restraint has been broken and he has transgressed the bounds of propriety, dust arises from that home even more thoroughly;
by means of this, with a defiled mind, he will meet with ruin and disaster. Or else, monks, see how it is:
"This fear has arisen for that foolish person from intimacy;
and just as for all worldlings (*puthujjana*) 'dust' arises from their home, so too should these two phrases be construed.
In every way, however, by this first half-verse, the Blessed One, having censured the view of the worldling, [established] his own view.
Praising [this state], he spoke the second half-verse beginning with "aniketa" (homeless).

Therein, it should be understood that "aniketa" is by way of the negation of the aforementioned home (*niketa*), and "asanthava" (without intimacy) is by way of the negation of intimacy (*santhava*). Both of these are synonyms for Nibbāna.
"This indeed is the vision of the Sage": the meaning is that this state of being homeless and without intimacy has been seen by the Buddha-Muni. In that regard:
The particle *vā* should be understood here as having the sense of wonder (*vimhaya*). By this, the intended meaning is established as follows: "Aha!

How marvelous it is that the Sage has seen that very state which consists of being without a home and without social ties, when one's mother and son are acting perversely toward each other due to their attachment to a household and social intimacy.
Alternatively, the "vision of the Sage" (*munidassana*) may also mean the vision belonging to the Sage; for "vision" (*dassana*) refers to patience (*khanti*) and inclination (*ruci*).
The meaning is: "it is both approved and pleasing.

210. Regarding the second verse: "He who cuts off what has arisen"—this refers to one who, exerting effort so that the defilement (kilesa) arisen, come to be, and produced in regard to some particular matter is abandoned just as unwholesome states (akusala) are abandoned when they have arisen, [strives] in that matter not to let it arise again...
Having cut off [the defilement] by way of its non-arising, one would not plant even that future defilement which— because it is about to arise when the appropriate conditions converge—
is said to be "being born" (jāyanto) by means of the characteristic of the present as it stands near the present;
and while striving so that there may be the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, one would not allow it to be produced.

The meaning [of the term]. And how would it not be produced? If one were not to provide the requisite conditions by which it might be produced—that is, if one were not to introduce or assemble those conditions—then, by way of making the necessary components deficient, one would not cause it to be planted as it arises.
Alternatively, because even past defilements are cut off through the cultivation of the Path, there will be no future result.

Even those [defilements] currently arising are not planted because of their absence; even those yet to come do not enter the continuum of consciousness because their capacity to arise has been obstructed.

Therefore, he who, through the cultivation of the Noble Path, would cut off what has arisen and prevent it from being planted, and would not allow what is arising in the future to enter—him they call a sage wandering alone, and he has seen the state of peace.
"Mahesī" (the Great Queen) should be understood here as being construed in this way:
"one" (*eka*) because of her absolute freedom from defilements, or in the sense of being supreme (*seṭṭha*). "Munim" means the Sage (*muni*), or "one among the Sages.

"Carantam" means moving about with world-benefiting conduct that is complete in every aspect, as well as with other forms of conduct. "Addakkhi" means she saw. "Sā" refers to her who, having cut off birth, does not enter into rebirth.

And because of his capability, the Buddha-Muni said: "One should not plant [the seed], nor should one fail to provide what is growing. Regarding the phrase "the state of peace" (*santipada*): it refers to a portion of peace.

Among the three types of peace—conventional peace (*sammuti-santi*), peace by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-santi*), and ultimate peace (*accanta-santi*)—which are distinguished as the sixty-two views, insight (*vipassanā*), and Nibbāna respectively—the Great Seer saw that which is supreme, namely ultimate peace, in a world that is otherwise unpeaceful; such is the meaning to be understood.
In the third verse, *saṅkhāya* means having counted, delimited, investigated, and understood according to reality;

the meaning is "having fully understood through the full comprehension of suffering. *Vatthūni* refers to those bases—classified as aggregates (*khandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—which are the locations of defilements where this world becomes attached. *Pamāya bījaṃ* refers to the seed of those very bases.
The meaning is: having abandoned the formative consciousness by letting it go, harming it, afflicting it, and relinquishing it through its total eradication.
