One does not provide it with moisture—that moisture of craving and views by which that seed, being moistened, would grow in the future as rebirth-linking within the aforementioned soil of the physical basis; one does not provide that moisture for it.
The meaning is: "By means of the cultivation of the path which is the antidote to that [speculation], one should not allow it to enter. "That sage indeed is a seer of the end of birth":
such a Buddha-sage, because he has realized Nibbāna—which is the end of both birth and death—by the actualization of Nibbāna, is a "seer of the end of birth" (*jātikkhayantadassī*);
having abandoned reasoning (*takka*), he does not fall into reckoning. By means of this cultivation of the Four Noble Truths...

Having abandoned the ninefold unwholesome thought and attained the element of nibbāna with residue remaining, while performing deeds for the welfare of the world, he eventually, through the exhaustion of the final consciousness, attains the element of nibbāna without residue; thus, he no longer falls within the reckoning of "god" or "human.
Or, even while not yet fully extinguished, because thoughts such as sensual desire have not been abandoned, [he remains subject to rebirth].
One comes to be designated as "this person is lustful" or "hateful"; having abandoned such reasoning, one does not come to be so designated—thus should the meaning here be understood.
In the fourth verse, "having known" means having understood by way of impermanence and so forth. "All" means without exception; "abodes" (nivesanāni) means...
In existence such as the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*) and others, beings indeed dwell; therefore, they are called "abodes" (*nivesanāni*).
Not desiring even one of those—thus, because he has seen their disadvantage—he does not long for even a single one of those abodes.
Such a Buddha-sage, through the power of cultivating the Path, is free from greed because craving has departed; and precisely because he is free from greed...
And he is not greedy; he does not, like some who are actually not free from greed yet claim "we are free from greed," make such a profession.
He does not strive means that he does not perform either wholesome or unwholesome deeds that would produce this or that state of existence.
For what reason? Because he has gone beyond; the meaning is that such a person has gone to the further shore of all states of existence, which is Nibbāna.
Thus, having censured the view of the worldling (*puthujjana*) in the first verse, he praises his own view in the second verse. Then, in the third verse,
praising his own attainment of the state of peace through the absence of those defilements by which the worldling remains unpeaceful,
[he describes] how the worldling, not having abandoned conjecture regarding various objects, applies such and such designations...
Having attained these [states] and abandoned reasoning through the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths, he praises his own conformity with the conditioned nature of things in the fourth verse.
Then, praising his own lack of accumulation through craving for those very "abodes" that an ordinary person— desiring them— accumulates by means of the craving for existence even in the future,
he concludes with four verses at the pinnacle of Arahantship.
He brought this teaching, which arose from a single occasion, to its conclusion. 213.

What is the origin of the discourse on "The Conqueror of All"? After the Great Being had made the Great Renunciation and gradually attained omniscience, he was traveling toward Bārāṇasī for the purpose of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, between the Seat of Enlightenment and Gayā.

On the way, he encountered the Ajīvaka Upaka. When Upaka questioned him in the manner beginning with, "Friend, your faculties are serene," he replied with the verses beginning with, "I am the Conqueror of All.
Upaka said, "May it be so, friend," shook his head, took a by-path, and departed. By degrees, he reached a certain hunters' village in the district of Vaṅkaha.
He arrived there. When the head of the hunters saw him, he thought, "Oh, what a man of few desires this ascetic is!
He does not even wear a cloth; he must be an Arahant in this world. He led him home, served him with meat broth, and once he had finished eating, he and his wife and children paid homage to him.
Then, having invited him, saying, "Venerable sir, please stay right here; I shall provide for your requisites," he prepared a dwelling place.
Having prepared it, he gave it [to the monk]. He lived there.

During the summer season, when the deer had gone far away to roam in cool, water-abundant places, the hunter went there and, instructing his daughter named Chāva, said: "Serve our Arahant with due respect."
He arrived together with his sons and brothers. His daughter was beautiful to behold and possessed of perfect limbs.
On the second day, when Upaka returned home, he saw that girl having performed all the customary services and approaching to serve him food;
overcome by passion and unable even to eat, he took the rice from the bowl and went to his dwelling place.
Having set aside his meal to one side, he lay down without food, thinking: "If I obtain a doe, I shall live;
if not, I shall die. On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter about Upaka’s condition.
She said, "He came for only a single day and has not come back since. The hunter thought, "I will approach him in the guise of a visitor and ask him."
He went at that very moment and, touching [Upaka’s] foot, asked, “What is it, Bhante?
Are you unwell? Upaka merely turned over while groaning. He said, “Speak, Bhante; whatever I am able to do, I shall do it all.
Upaka replied, “If I obtain some broth, I shall live; if not, death right here would be better. “Do you know,” he asked,
“But, venerable sir, do you know any craft? “I do not know any. “Venerable sir, it is not possible for one who does not know any craft to maintain a household life. He said: “I do not know any craft;
however, I shall be a meat-provisioner for you, and I will sell meat. The hunter also said: “This is exactly what we desire.”
Having given him an upper robe, he brought him home and gave him his daughter. Following their union, a son was born;
they named him Subhadda. Because of his fondness for singing songs about his son, the wife mocked Upaka.
Unable to endure this, he said, "My dear, I am going into the presence of Anantajina," and set out toward the Middle Country.
And at that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Great Monastery of Jeta’s Grove.
Then the Blessed One gave instructions beforehand to the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, whoever comes asking for ‘Anantajina,’ you should show him to me.
And Upaka, traveling by stages, arrived at Sāvatthī and [stood] in the middle of the monastery.
Having stood there, he asked, "In this monastery, there is a companion of mine named Anantajina; where does he dwell?
The monks led him into the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma in a manner suited to him.
At the conclusion of that teaching, he was established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala). Having heard his previous history, the monks initiated a discussion.
“The Blessed One taught the Dhamma first to the naked ascetic Nissirika.

When the Blessed One understood that this was the origin of their conversation, he emerged from the Gabled Hall and, performing a miracle appropriate for that moment, sat upon the Buddha’s seat and addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now? They [told him] everything.
They spoke thus. Then the Blessed One said: “Monks, the Tathāgata does not teach the Dhamma without cause or condition;
the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma is stainless, and it is impossible to find fault with it.

Monks, it is by virtue of that very support for the teaching of the Dhamma that Upaka has now become a non-returner. Having said this, he spoke this verse, which illustrates the absence of any stain in his own teaching:

The meaning of this is as follows: He is "All-Conqueror" (*sabbābhibhū*) because, through the abandonment of desire and lust for all the aggregates, bases, and elements that are subject to the taints (*āsava*), he is not overcome by them, and because he himself proceeds having conquered all those phenomena.
He is "All-Knowing" (*sabbavidū*) because he has known all those and other phenomena in every aspect. He is endowed with beautiful wisdom capable of teaching all phenomena.

The Wise One (*sumedha*). Because of the absence of those stains of craving and views by which one is smeared among all phenomena—such as the aggregates subject to taints (*sāsavakhandha*) and so forth—he is unsmeared (*anupalitta*) by all those phenomena.
And because he stands having abandoned all those phenomena through the absence of desire and lust (*chandarāga*) for them, he is the "Renouncer of All" (*sabbañjaha*).
With a mind inclined toward seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*), in the destruction of craving...
Because it is specifically liberated in Nibbāna through the destruction of craving, it is said to be "liberated" (*vimutta*); that is to say, it is "resolutely intent" (*adhimutta*).
"The wise sages perceive that too"—the wise beings perceive and know that [Nibbāna] as the sage (*muni*).
Behold how exceedingly distinguished this sage is; from where could there be even the scent of teaching for him? Thus he reveals himself. This is the sense of "revealing" (*vibhāvana*).

For here the word *vā* means "or. However, some explain it thus: "Even though Upaka saw the Tathāgata at that time, he did not believe that 'this is the Buddha-Muni,'" and so the monks raised this question;
thereupon the Blessed One spoke this verse, showing: "Whether he believes or not, the wise nevertheless perceive that Muni."
214. Regarding the "Power of Wisdom" (*paññābala*): what is its origin? This verse was spoken concerning the Elder Revata.

Therein, according to the method stated in this verse beginning with "Whether in the village or in the forest," [it describes] the Elder Revata’s initial going-forth from the very beginning, his dwelling in the Khadira Forest after having gone forth, the attainment of distinction while dwelling there, and [the Blessed One’s presence] there.

The going forth and the returning back must be understood. Now, when the Blessed One had returned, that elderly bhikkhu, having forgotten his sandals and turned back, saw them caught on a khadira tree;
having arrived at Sāvatthī, he asked the bhikkhus of the laywoman Visākhā, "Venerable sirs, is the dwelling place of the elder Revata pleasant?"
When he was asked by those monks who had praised [the place], he spoke disparagingly, saying: "Lay follower, these people are speaking empty words;
this location is not good; it is nothing but a forest of acacia trees, exceedingly coarse and harsh.
Having eaten Visākhā’s guest-meal, after the meal, when the monks had assembled in the pavilion, he spoke with reproach: "What, friends?"

“You have seen the delightful dwelling place of the Elder Revata. The Blessed One, knowing this, emerged from his fragrant chamber and, performing a miracle appropriate for that moment, arrived in the midst of the assembly.
Sitting upon the Buddha’s seat, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now? They replied:
—“Venerable sir, a conversation has arisen concerning Revata: ‘When will this novice monk perform the duties of a recluse?

“Revata is not a novice monk, bhikkhus; Revata is an arahant whose taints are destroyed,” he said, and then, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those bhikkhus concerning him, he spoke this verse.

The meaning of this is as follows: it is "the power of wisdom" (*paññābala*) because it is endowed with the power of wisdom, which is distinguished by the transformation and resolution that accomplish the abandoning of the defilements that cause weakness;
it is "endowed with virtue and vows" (*sīlavatūpapanna*) because it is produced through the fourfold purification of virtue and the practice of the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*);

it is "concentrated" (*samāhita*) by means of the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruit, and the concentration of the postures; [and it is so] by way of the distinction between access and absorption.
Because he delights in meditation through meditation, he is "one who delights in meditation" (*jhānarata*); because he has attained the fullness of mindfulness, he is "mindful" (*satima*);

because he is liberated from attachment such as lust, he is "liberated from attachments" (*saṅgā pamutta*); and because of the absence of the five mental barrennesses and the four taints, he is "barrenless" (*akhila*) and "taintless" (*anāsava*).
The wise know that sage to be such; the learned know him to be thus endowed with qualities such as wisdom and dissociated from the faults of attachment and the like.
Beings perceive the sage [in this way]. Behold how exceptionally distinguished is this sage whose taints are destroyed;

how could he be spoken of as a "laborer" or asked, "When will he perform the duties of a recluse"? For he brought that monastery to completion through the power of his wisdom, not by means of manual labor;
his task is already accomplished, and he will not now perform the duties of a recluse.
This clarifies the Elder Revata. For here, the word *vā* has the sense of clarification (*vibhāvana*).

215. As for the phrase "wandering alone," what is its origin? When the Blessed One had arrived in Kapilavatthu from the Seat of Enlightenment and was engaged in the meeting of father and son in due order, the Blessed One [was addressed] by King Suddhodana, who was greeting him with joy: "You..."
“Venerable sir, when you were a householder, you wore fine garments such as those from Kāsī perfumed in scented caskets; how is it that you now wear these torn rag-robes?
When addressed in this way and others like it, the King, seeking to conciliate him, said:
“O dear one, as for what you say to me regarding my fine woolens, silks, and Kāsī cloth;”
"Rags from a dust heap are better than that; this is what I desire.
Having spoken these words, and demonstrating his own unshakability by the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), he recited these seven-line verses for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the king.

Their meaning is as follows: [He is] one who wanders through various modes of conduct such as the postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, characterized by the state of renunciation (*pabbajjā*); and by being endowed with the qualities of the "moneyya" (the state of a sage).
The Sage. Because of the absence of negligence in all circumstances, he is "heedful" (*appamatta*).

He is "unshaken" by these things—censure consisting of abuse, reproach, and so forth, and praise consisting of eulogy, flattery, and so forth—due to the absence of repulsion or attachment toward such censure and praise.
It should be understood that by way of this censure and praise, the eight worldly conditions (*aṭṭha lokadhammā*) are also implied here. Like a lion amidst the sounds of drums and the like...

Not being agitated or non-agitated by the eight worldly conditions (*loka-dhamma*) because it does not undergo natural change or transformation; or, by the absence of agitation even in secluded lodgings.
Like the wind, it is unattached to the net of craving and views through the four paths, just as [the wind] is unattached to a net made of thread and so forth;
or, it is unattached to the eight worldly conditions by way of aversion or attachment. Like a lotus, though born in the world, it is not defiled by the water.
Because those stains of craving and views by which beings are smeared in the world have been abandoned, they are unsmeared by the world;
having generated the path leading to Nibbāna, they lead others—gods and humans—by that path.
But because they cannot be led by any other path shown by anyone else, the wise call them "not to be led by another."
"Those who make known the Sage" means they make known the Buddha-Sage; thus he reveals himself. The rest here is exactly as previously stated.

216. As for "He who [crosses] the deep abyss," what is its origin? It refers to the Blessed One, having first attained full enlightenment, having fulfilled over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons the perfections of aspiration and the perfections of virtue, which are distinguished as the ten pāramīs, the ten upapāramīs, and the ten paramatthapāramīs.
Having fulfilled [these], [he possesses] the quality of rebirth in the Tusita heaven, the quality of dwelling there, the quality of the Great Survey,

the descent into the womb, the stay in the womb, the emergence from the womb, the treading of steps, the surveying of the quarters, the proclamation to Brahmā, the Great Renunciation, the Great Exertion,
the Perfect Enlightenment, the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the fourfold knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of the fruits.

The knowledge of imperturbability regarding the eight assemblies; the knowledge of the ten powers; the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth; the knowledge that delimits the five destinations; the sixfold uncommon knowledge;
the eightfold Buddha-knowledge shared with disciples; the fourteenfold Buddha-knowledge;
the knowledge that delimits the eighteen qualities of a Buddha; and the nineteenfold knowledge of retrospection.

On account of this, when the Blessed One’s reputation had been damaged in the midst of the four assemblies by Ciñcā Māṇavikā—whom certain sectarians had incited because they could not endure the great gain and honor arising from his reliance on one hundred thousand qualities such as the seventy-seven bases of knowledge—the incident occurred according to the manner described in the verse beginning, "Of one who has transgressed a single Dhamma... and so forth. Because of that, [the Saṅgha was convened].
The monks raised this discussion: "Even when such infamy has arisen, there is no change in the Blessed One’s mind.
Knowing this, the Blessed One emerged from his fragrant chamber and, performing a miracle appropriate for that moment, arrived in the midst of the assembly.
Sitting upon the Buddha’s seat, he addressed the monks: "Monks, what is it that you..."
“Why have you sat down here now for this discussion? They related everything to him.
Then the Blessed One, saying, “Monks, Buddhas remain equanimous (*tādino*) toward the eight worldly conditions,” spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.
Its meaning is as follows: just as, for example, at a bathing ford in a river where people bathe, there is a square stone slab for the purpose of scrubbing the limbs—
Or, when a pillar is driven into the ground—whether it be of a high-born or low-born family—their limbs may rub against it, yet there is no rising up or sinking down of that pillar.
In the same way, he who is born like a pillar in the midst of a conflict, even when others speak against him with limitless words.
What is meant by this? That upon whatever matter others—whether they be members of other sects (titthiyā)—[may speak]...
Or others may speak a limit of speech by way of praise for what is above or by way of blame for what is below;

one who, regarding that matter, does not fall into either attachment or aversion, but remains like a pillar in the midst of immersion due to his state of equanimity (tādibhāva)—him they call "one free from lust, with well-composed faculties.
He is "free from lust" because of the absence of lust toward desirable objects.
And because of the absence of hatred and delusion regarding an unattractive object, his faculties are well-composed;

that is to say, his faculties are properly gathered and established, guarded, and protected. "The wise sages perceive him"—that is, they perceive him as the Buddha-sage—[thinking], "How could there be any alteration in his mind?
Thus he makes himself known. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

217. As for the origin of the verse beginning, "He who is indeed steadfast" (*yo ve ṭhitatto*): It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain daughter of a wealthy merchant descended from her palace and went to a weavers’ workshop on the ground floor.
Seeing the weavers spinning their shuttles, she took them as a sign corresponding to their straightness, thinking:
"O, may all beings, having abandoned crookedness of body, speech, and mind, become straight in heart like these shuttles!"
"May they come to be. Having ascended the palace, she sat there repeatedly reflecting upon that very same sign.

As she practiced in this way, before long the characteristic of impermanence became manifest to her; and by following from that, the characteristics of suffering and non-self likewise became manifest.
Then, the three realms of existence appeared to her as if they were ablaze. Thus...
Knowing that she was practicing insight meditation, the Blessed One, while remaining seated in his fragrant chamber, emitted a radiance. Seeing it, she reflected, "What is this?
and perceiving the Blessed One as if sitting right before her, she rose and stood with palms joined in reverence.
Then, the Blessed One, understanding what was appropriate for her, spoke this verse by way of teaching the Dhamma.
The meaning of this is as follows: He whose mind is one-pointed and who, through unshakable liberation, is established in himself because there is no longer any waxing or waning;

because the cycle of birth has been exhausted and there is no further passage into another existence; who is straight like a shuttle because he has abandoned the crookedness of body, speech, and mind, or because he does not go on wrong paths;
and who, being endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, feels disgust for evil deeds—[such a one] performs no evil actions.

He feels disgust as if toward excrement and urine; what is meant is that he is ashamed. For according to the grammatical analysis (*yogavibhāga*), the instrumental case can be used in the sense of the accusative in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). Examining both the uneven and the even:

by means of accomplishing the tasks of abandoning and cultivating through the wisdom of the Path (*maggapaññā*), he examines the unevenness of the body, such as bodily irregularity, and the evenness of the body, such as bodily regularity.
"Examining him. "The wise perceive him as a sage whose taints are destroyed. What is meant by this?
Examining with the wisdom of the path according to the method already described, he who is established in himself—whether in the uneven or the even—becomes straight like a shuttle;
not committing any transgression, he feels disgust for evil deeds. The wise perceive him as such a sage.
They experience [the results]. Since he is such as this, the Teacher, pointing out the Sage whose taints are destroyed, taught the verse culminating in the state of Arahantship.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the merchant’s daughter was established in the fruit of stream-entry. And here, the word *vā* should be understood as meaning either "optionally" (*vikappe*) or "and" (*samuccaye*).

218. As for the origin of the verse beginning with "He who is self-restrained": it is said that while the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī, a certain weaver in the city of Āḷavī commanded his seven-year-old daughter: "Daughter, there is not much thread left over from yesterday;
having wound the shuttle, come quickly to the weaving hall; do not delay. She replied, "Very well."

He accepted it. Having gone to the hall, he stood weaving the cloth. On that day, the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) and surveying the world, saw that the girl possessed the necessary support for attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and that at the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand living beings would attain realization of the Dhamma.
Thus, having already attended to his physical needs early in the morning, he set out.
Taking his bowl and robe, he entered the city. When the people saw the Blessed One, they thought, "Surely there is someone to be favored today;
for the Blessed One has entered even earlier than usual," and they approached him.
The Blessed One stood on the very path by which that girl was going to her father's house. The city-dwellers swept that spot clean.
Having sprinkled [the ground], offered flowers, and tied up a canopy, they prepared a seat.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat, and a great multitude of people stood surrounding him.
When that girl reached that place and saw the Blessed One surrounded by the great multitude, she paid homage to him with the fivefold prostration. The Blessed One addressed her.
“‘Maiden, from where have you come? he asked. ‘I do not know, Blessed One,’ she replied. ‘Where will you go?
‘I do not know, Blessed One. ‘Do you not know? ‘I do know, Blessed One. ‘Do you know? ‘I do not know, Blessed One.
Hearing this, the people complained: ‘Look, sirs! This maiden, though she has come from her own home, [is questioned] by the Blessed One...”
“When questioned, she said, ‘I do not know. Even when questioned while going to the weavers’ hall, she said, ‘I do not know.
When told, ‘You do not know,’ she said, ‘I know. When told, ‘You know,’ she said, ‘I do not know.
She acts entirely in opposition. The Blessed One, wishing to make this matter clear to the people, questioned her.
“What was asked by me, and what was said by you? She replied: “Venerable sir, no one does not know me;
it is well known that I have come from my home and am going to the weavers’ hall. Moreover, when you ask me, ‘From where have you come?
regarding the moment of rebirth (*paṭisandhi*), or ‘Where will you go? regarding the moment of death (*cuti*), I do not know. From where... [text fragment ends]”
“I do not know whether I have come from hell or from the world of the devas,” I said, for I did not know, “Where shall I go—whether to hell or to the world of the devas?
That is why I said, “I do not know. Then the Blessed One asked me about death:
“Do you not know? and I replied, “I know that for all beings death is certain. That is why I said, “I know.”
Then the Blessed One, referring to the time of my death, asked me, "Do you know? Since I did not know—"When shall I die?
Is it today, or perhaps tomorrow?"—I said, "I do not know. The Blessed One expressed his approval of my answer, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
And the great multitude of people, thinking, "How wise this girl is," raised thousands of shouts of "Well done!"
She gave it. Then the Blessed One, knowing what was suitable for the girl, taught the Dhamma:
"This world is blind; here, few possess insight.
Like a bird escaped from a net, few go to heaven."

He spoke this verse. At the conclusion of that verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and there was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings.

She paid homage to the Blessed One and went into the presence of her father. When her father saw her, he said, "You have come after a long time," and in his anger, he violently threw a shuttle at her.
It struck her and pierced her belly. There, right then and there—
She passed away. Seeing this, he thought, “I did not strike my daughter;
rather, this arrow, having come out with great force, pierced her womb. Is she alive or not? While investigating, he saw that she was dead and reflected:
“If people were to find out that I killed my daughter, they would revile me, and because of that, even the king would impose a heavy penalty.”

“I might be punished; come now, I shall flee beforehand. Fleeing out of fear of punishment, he approached the Blessed One, received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and reached the dwelling place of monks living in the forest.
He went to those monks and requested the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). They ordained him and gave him the meditation subject of the five aggregates of clinging (*tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna*).
They gave it to him. Having mastered it and exerting himself, he attained Arahantship before long, with those very men as his teachers and preceptors.
Then, at the Great Invitation ceremony (Mahāpavāraṇā), they all went into the presence of the Blessed One, thinking, "We shall perform the invitation for the sake of purification.
After the Blessed One had performed the invitation and completed the rains retreat, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he was wandering on tour through villages, market towns, and other places.
Gradually he arrived at Āḷavī. There, people invited the Blessed One and were performing acts of giving and other meritorious deeds;
seeing that monk, they mocked him, saying, "Having killed your daughter, who will you kill now? and so forth.
When the monks heard this, they approached the Blessed One at the time of his attendance and reported the matter to him. The Blessed One...
—"No, monks, this monk did not kill his daughter; she died by her own karma," he said.
Then, declaring that monk’s state as a sage whose taints were exhausted—a state difficult for ordinary people to discern—he spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the monks.
Its meaning is as follows: he who has restrained his self through the restraint of virtue at all three doors of action—whether by body, speech, or mind—

He does not commit evil such as violence; moreover, whether he is young, standing in the prime of youth, or middle-aged, standing in middle age, and by this same principle, even when old, standing in the final stage of life, he never commits it at any time.
For what reason? Because he is self-restrained (*yatatto*); that is to say, because his mind has desisted from all evils through unsurpassed abstinence.
Now, regarding these words, "The Sage is not one to be provoked to anger;
he does not provoke anyone," this is the construction and the intended meaning: that Sage whose taints are destroyed is not one to be provoked to anger;
it is not possible to provoke, irritate, or distress him by way of body or speech through such means as calling him "a child-murderer" or "a weaver. For he himself does not provoke [others].
Having said such things as, “I do not kill my daughter; you are killing her, or someone like you is killing her,” he does not provoke, irritate, or harm anyone;
therefore, he too is not one to be provoked.
Furthermore, he is simply to be honored in the manner described by the words, “Let alone the Naga; do not provoke the Naga; pay homage to the Naga.”
"Even that, the wise sages perceive. Here, however, the analysis of the words should be understood as:
"Only the wise sages perceive even that. The intended meaning here is this: those foolish people, not knowing that "this one is not to be provoked," provoke him.
But those who are wise—only those wise ones perceive even that sage; they know, "This is a sage whose taints are destroyed."
219. As for "the foremost" (yadagga), what is its origin? It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a brahmin named Pañcaggadāyaka.

When his crops were ripening, he would give five kinds of "first-fruits": the first from the field, the first from the heap, the first from the granary, the first from the cooking pot, and the first portion of food.
Therein, having had the very first harvested heads of rice, barley, and wheat brought to him...

Having prepared rice gruel, porridge, fresh grain, and so forth, one gives a gift to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha while holding the view: "The wise man who gives the best obtains the best.
This is his gift of the choice field (*khettagga-dāna*). Furthermore, when the crops have been harvested, threshed, and winnowed, one takes the finest grains and gives a gift in that same manner.

He gives this; this is his "gift of the best of the heap. Furthermore, having filled the storehouses with those grains, when the first storehouse is opened, he takes the grains that were first drawn out and gives a gift in the same manner; this is his "gift of the best of the granary.
Moreover, whatever is cooked in his house, from that he does not give the best portion to those who have gone forth until at least to the children.

He gave nothing at all; this was his "pot-top offering. Furthermore, at the time of his own meal, he would not eat the first portion of food brought to him unless he had first given it to the Saṅgha before the meal, or to beggars who arrived after the meal, or, in their absence, even to dogs;
this was his "food-top offering. Thus, he became renowned as one who gave five kinds of "top" offerings.
Then one day, in the early morning, the Blessed One, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, saw that the favorable conditions for the path of stream-entry existed for that brahmin and his wife.

Having attended to his bodily needs, he entered the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) very early. When the bhikkhus saw the door of the fragrant chamber closed, they thought: "Today the Blessed One is alone."
Knowing that [the Blessed One] desired to enter the village, they circumambulated the Fragrant Chamber at the time for the alms-round and entered for alms.
At the time for the brahmin’s meal, the Blessed One also went out and entered Sāvatthī.
When people saw the Blessed One, they thought: "Surely there must be some being to be assisted today, for thus does the Blessed One..."
Knowing that he had entered all alone, they did not approach the Blessed One to invite him.
The Blessed One, having reached the door of the brahmin’s house in due course, stood there.
At that time, the brahmin was seated with his food, while his wife stood nearby holding a fan. Seeing the Blessed One, she...
"If this brahmin were to see me, he would take his bowl and give me all the food; then I would have to cook it again," he thought.

Having conceived a lack of faith and stinginess, he shielded [the Buddha] with a palm-leaf fan so that the brahmin would not see the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing this, emitted a radiance from his body.
He released it. Seeing that golden radiance, the brahmin looked up, wondering, "What is this?
and saw the Blessed One standing at the door. The brahmin woman also thought, "The Blessed One has been seen by him," and immediately set aside her palm-leaf fan.
She approached the Blessed One and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. As she was rising after having paid homage, the Blessed One, perceiving what would be beneficial for her—
“Completely regarding name-and-form, for whom there is nothing cherished;
who does not grieve over what is non-existent—he indeed is called a bhikkhu.
Having spoken this verse, at the very conclusion of that verse, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The brahmin [also] addressed the Blessed One...
Having led him into his inner house, seated him on a noble seat, and offered him water for the feet, he presented the food brought for himself, saying:
"Venerable sir, you are the foremost among those worthy of offerings in the world with its devas; please, out of compassion for me, place this food into your own bowl.
Out of favor toward him, the Blessed One accepted it and partook of it.
Having finished his meal and perceiving what was suitable for the brahmin, he spoke this verse.
Its meaning is as follows: that which was taken from the very top of the pot because it was first taken;
that which was taken from the middle of the pot after coming from a pot that had only half its contents remaining; and that which was taken from a pot that had only one or two ladlefuls remaining.
Or he may receive almsfood by means of his knowledge. One who lives depending on what is given by others is a renunciant;
for, having set aside water and tooth-sticks, he lives depending on everything else that is given by another, and therefore he is called "one who lives depending on what is given by others.
He is neither fit to praise nor to speak with excessive humility; because he has abandoned all attachment, he is not even capable of praising himself or the donor when receiving from them.

Having learned [the truth], because he has abandoned aversion (*paṭigha*), he does not even utter unpleasant words by disparaging the donor through such means as asking, "What was given by this man? The wise sages recognize him as such;
thus, the Buddha taught this verse to the brahmin from the pinnacle of *arahantship*, which is the abandonment of both attachment (*anunaya*) and aversion. At the conclusion of the verse—
"The brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry. 220.

As for "The Sage wandering": what is its origin? It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain son of a wealthy merchant, while enjoying all the luxuries in three palaces according to the seasons, became desirous of going forth even while still young; he [approached] his mother and father...

Having made his request, according to the method described in the *Khaggavisāṇa Sutta* in the introduction to the verse beginning “For sensual pleasures are manifold,” he went forth three times and returned from the life of a monk three times; on the fourth occasion, he attained Arahantship.

Because of his previous familiarity with the practice, the monks said to him, “It is time, friend, to return from the life of a monk. He replied, “Friend, I am no longer capable of returning [to the world].”
He said this. Having heard it, the bhikkhus reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, saying, "It is even so, bhikkhus;
he is now incapable of renouncing the order," spoke this verse while revealing that the state of that sage was one whose taints were exhausted.
Its meaning is as follows: [he is] a sage by virtue of being endowed with the qualities of a sage (*moneyya-dhamma*), through dwelling alone, and regarding the types previously described...

Or, while practicing any of the various modes of conduct, he does not set his mind on sexual intercourse as he did before, but remains abstinent from sexual misconduct through supreme abstinence. As for the connection with the second quarter:

if it is asked, "What kind of sage is he who practices and is abstinent from sexual misconduct?"—it is one who, even while in the prime of youth, is not bound to anything. Even while remaining in auspicious youth...
In some cases, as before, he does not become attached through the lust for sexual intercourse even toward a female form.
Alternatively, the meaning here is that he does not become attached through lust even toward the youthfulness of himself or another, thinking, "I am still young, or this person is young;
let me enjoy sensual pleasures for now. Furthermore, he is not only abstinent from sexual intercourse, but moreover—
Furthermore, it is detached from the forms of intoxication such as pride in birth, and from the negligences consisting in the loss of mindfulness regarding the strands of sensual pleasure;
thus, because it is detached from intoxication and negligence, it is liberated from all bonds of the defilements.

Or rather, it is not merely detached in the way one might be detached through a mundane form of abstinence; instead, it is "detached" in the sense of being "completely liberated" from all bonds of the defilements.
The meaning is also that it is "abstinence" because of its being transcendentally liberated (*vippamuttattā*).
"The wise sages perceive that as well"—this shows that only the wise perceive that [abstinence] as the sage, whereas you do not perceive it; therefore, you speak of him in this way. 221.
Regarding the phrase "having understood the world," what is the origin [of this discourse]? The Blessed One was dwelling at Kapilavatthu. At that time...
They performed three auspicious ceremonies for Nanda: the auspicious ceremony of ornaments, the auspicious ceremony of consecration, and the auspicious ceremony of marriage.
The Blessed One, having been invited there, went with five hundred bhikkhus, and after eating, as he was departing, he placed his bowl into Nanda’s hand. Seeing him departing, Janapadakalyāṇī...
“You should come quickly, noble son,” he said. Out of reverence for the Blessed One, he was unable to say, “Come, Blessed One, take the bowl,” and so he went straight back to the monastery.
The Blessed One, standing in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber, said, “Nanda, bring the bowl.
Having taken it, [the Blessed One] asked, “Will you go forth? Out of reverence for the Blessed One, he was unable to refuse.
Unable [to remain], he said, "I go forth, Blessed One. The Blessed One ordained him.
However, as he repeatedly recalled the words of Janapadakalyāṇī, he became discontented. The monks reported this to the Blessed One.
Desiring to dispel Nanda’s dissatisfaction, the Blessed One said, "Nanda, have you not been to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven before? Nanda replied, "No, I have not."
“Venerable sir, have you been here before? he asked.
Then the Blessed One, by his own supernormal power, led him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and stood at the gate of the Vejayanta Palace.
Knowing that the Blessed One had arrived, Sakka descended from the palace, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs. All of them [approached] Kassapa...
Having given oil for massaging the feet of the Blessed One’s disciples, they came to have the feet of a cock. Then the Blessed One addressed Nanda:
"Do you see, Nanda, these five hundred celestial nymphs with the feet of cocks?
All of this should be related in detail. [The Buddha said: "One must not take up the physical marks and secondary characteristics of a woman. This applies throughout the entire Word of the Buddha.

This was not the case. Nevertheless, here the Blessed One—out of his skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), like a physician wishing to make a sick man vomit up and expel his humors by means of wholesome food—permitted Nanda to grasp at signs and secondary characteristics (*nimittānubyañjanaggahaṇa*) in order to make him vomit up and expel his passion (*rāga*).
Thus did the Blessed One, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, act for the sake of Nanda. Then, for the sake of a celestial nymph (*accharā*), the Blessed One...
Seeing his delight in the holy life, the Blessed One commanded the bhikkhus: "Exhort Nanda by calling him a 'hireling'.
Being thus exhorted by them, he felt ashamed; applying himself with wise attention and practicing accordingly, he soon realized arhatship.
At the end of his walking path, a deity dwelling in a tree [reported] this matter to the Blessed One.
He reported this. Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One. Since the monks did not know [the truth], they continued to reprove the Venerable one in that same manner.

The Blessed One, saying, "Monks, Nanda should not be reproved in this way now," spoke this verse for the sake of teaching the Dhamma to those monks, illustrating his state as a sage whose taints were exhausted.
The meaning of this is as follows: having understood, known, and defined the world of the aggregates and so forth by means of the determination of the truth of suffering;
having seen the ultimate reality for the sake of realizing the truth of cessation;

and, through the abandoning of the origin [of suffering], having crossed over the fourfold flood and the ocean of the sense bases such as the eye—having overcome it by enduring the impulse of pride regarding form and the rest because the origin has been abandoned.
Having transcended by means of the cultivation of the path, he is "Tādi" (the Such-like One) because of having attained the characteristic of suchness described as "one who is such-like.
Or else, he is one who has now crossed over the flood and the ocean— wherein the very mass of defilements such as sensual lust is called a "flood" in the sense of sweeping away,
and an "ocean" in the sense of a place for going to what is base— and having thus crossed over that flood and ocean through the very abandonment of their origination.
Even when you speak thus, because there is no alteration of mind, the meaning and the intention here should be understood in this way:
"He who has cut the bonds, is unattached, and is free from taints" (Taṃ chinnaganthaṃ asitaṃ anāsavaṃ) is merely a word of praise for him.
Because the four bonds have been severed by this cultivation of the Four Noble Truths, he is "one who has cut the bonds"; [this refers to] views or craving.
"Because it is not dependent on anything anywhere, it is 'unsupported' (asita); because of the absence of the four taints (āsava), it is 'taintless' (anāsava)—this is what is meant.
'The wise sages experience that too' means that only the wise sages who have destroyed the taints experience that;
he shows that you, however, speak thus while being entirely unaware of it."
222. How did the pair of incomparable ones come to be? A certain bhikkhu was dwelling in a forest near a frontier village in the kingdom of Kosala.
In that village, a deer-trapper would go to the place where the bhikkhu resided and set snares for deer.
As he entered the forest, he saw the elder entering the village for alms, and [later] from the forest...
He saw him even as he was leaving the village after arriving. Through this frequent seeing, he developed an affection for the Elder.
Whenever he obtained much meat, he would give a flavorful alms-offering to the Elder as well. People complained:
"This bhikkhu says, 'In such-and-such a place deer are standing, walking about, and drinking water.'"
“He informs the hunter. Then the hunter kills the deer; thus, the two of them live together by that means.
Now, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, the Blessed One arrived at that district.

As the monks were entering the village for alms, they heard this account and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One [then spoke] regarding the fact of sharing a common livelihood with a hunter:
Proclaiming that monk’s state as a sage whose taints were exhausted, he spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.
Its meaning is as follows: “O monks, that monk and that hunter—these two are not alike.
What people say, ‘They lead similar lives,’ is false. Why? Because they dwell far apart; their dwelling is distant.”
And they both live far apart. "Abode" (*vihāra*) means a place of residence; for the monk, it is the forest, and for the hunter, it is the village.

"Livelihood" (*vutti*) means a means of subsistence; for the monk, it is the practice of alms-gathering from house to house in the village, and for the hunter, it is the killing of deer and birds in the forest.
Furthermore, the householder supports his wife; through that occupation, the hunter supports his children and wife.

He supports [others]. And he is virtuous (*subbata*); free from craving, views, and the conceit of "mine" regarding children and wife, that bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted is virtuous because of his pure conduct and beautiful conduct.
Furthermore, a householder is unrestrained in obstructing the lives of other beings;
that hunter, the householder, is unrestrained in body, speech, and mind for the purpose of obstructing other beings—that is, for the purpose of cutting off their life-faculty.

The sage who is restrained always protects living beings; moreover, the other—the sage whose taints are exhausted—always protects living beings by being restrained and self-controlled in body, speech, and mind. This being so, how will they be of equal livelihood?
223. Regarding the verse "Just as the crested one": what is its origin? While the Blessed One was dwelling at Kapilavatthu, there arose a discussion among the Sākiyas.
The thought arose: "One who has first attained stream-entry is, by Dhamma, senior to one who later attains stream-entry;
therefore, a monk who has later attained stream-entry should perform acts such as bowing to a householder who first attained stream-entry.
A certain alms-collecting monk heard this discussion and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "It is otherwise..."
Indeed, having in mind that "this birth is a ground for veneration and a mark [of status]," and having stated, "Bhikkhus, even if a non-returner is a householder,

he must still perform such acts as salutation toward a novice who has gone forth on that very day," he later further demonstrated a very great distinction between a stream-enterer monk and a householder who is a first-time stream-enterer.
For the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the bhikkhus, he spoke this verse.

Its meaning is as follows: That bird called the peacock is known as "Sikhī" (the Crested One) by virtue of the crest born upon his head, and as "Nīlagīva" (the Blue-necked One) because of his neck which resembles a jeweled rod. Just as among the green swans, copper swans, milk swans, black swans, wild swans, and golden swans—
This golden swan does not equal even a sixteenth part of that [other] swan’s speed.
For the golden swan travels a thousand yojanas in a mere moment, whereas the other is incapable of traveling even a single yojana.
Yet, in terms of beauty, both are beautiful to behold; likewise, although a lay follower who is a stream-enterer, by virtue of seeing the Path—
He becomes worthy of being seen. Yet, he cannot match the speed of even a monk who has subsequently entered the stream and possesses a vision equal to his own.
In what respect does he lack that speed? In the speed of the knowledge of insight into the higher paths.
For that knowledge is sluggish for a householder because he is entangled in the tangle of children, wife, and so forth; but for a monk, it is sharp.
This is because of the unravelling of that matted hair. This very meaning was illuminated by the Blessed One with this line: "Of the sage dwelling secluded in the forest, meditating.

For this bhikkhu, a sage-in-training (*sekkhamuni*), is secluded through both physical and mental seclusion, and he constantly meditates in the forest by means of contemplation upon the characteristics of phenomena as objects. From where could such seclusion come for a householder?
And "jhāna" is [the meaning]— this is the intended sense here.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Muni-sutta* in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, within the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*).
The first chapter, by way of an explanation of the meaning, is finished; it is known by the name the Uraga Chapter.
2. The Minor Chapter (Cūḷavagga).
1. Commentary on the Ratana Sutta:
"Whatever beings there are here... This is the Ratana Sutta. What is its origin? It is said that in the past, calamities such as famine arose in Vesālī.
To pacify them, the Licchavis went to Rājagaha and, having made a request, [brought] the Blessed One [back].
They brought him to Vesālī. Once brought there, the Blessed One spoke this discourse for the purpose of pacifying those calamities.
This is the summary here. However, the ancients describe its origin starting from the time it occurred in Vesālī;
that should be understood as follows: it is said that a fetus was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. She, [perceiving] that...
Having learned of this, she informed the king. The king granted her the necessary care for her pregnancy.
While her pregnancy was being properly maintained, she entered the birth chamber at the time when the fetus reached maturity. For those possessed of merit, the delivery of a child occurs at dawn;
as she was one such person, she gave birth at dawn to a lump of flesh resembling a coating of lac or a bandhujīvaka flower.
Then, thinking, "Other queens give birth to sons resembling golden images, while the chief queen gives birth to a mere strip of flesh; thus,
ill-repute regarding me might arise before the king," and fearing such disrepute, she placed that strip of flesh in a vessel,
covered it with another, sealed it with the royal seal, and had it cast into the current of the Ganges.
As soon as it was abandoned by the people, the deities established a protective guard over it. There, they fastened a golden plate upon which was inscribed with vermilion:
"The offspring of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Then that vessel, unharmed by the dangers of waves and the like, proceeded along the current of the Gaṅgā.
At that time, a certain ascetic was living on the bank of the Ganges, supported by a cowherd’s family.
Having gone down to the Ganges at dawn, he saw that vessel coming toward him and, perceiving it to be a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), he seized it.
Then, seeing the strip of cloth with the letters and the royal seal-mark upon it, he released it and saw that piece of meat. Upon seeing it, his...
The thought occurred to him: "There may be a fetus, for there is no foul odor or putrefaction in it. Having led it to the hermitage, he placed it in a clean spot.
Then, after the lapse of half a month, two pieces of flesh had formed. Seeing this, the ascetic placed them with even greater care.
Then, after another half-month, from each piece of flesh, there appeared [limbs] for the sake of hands, feet, and a head.
Five boils appeared on each of his five limbs. Then, after the lapse of half a month, from one [boil] there was a boy resembling a golden image, and from the other a girl.
Affection for children arose in the ascetic toward them, and milk issued from his thumb;
from that time forth, he obtained milk-rice. Having eaten his meal, he gave the milk to the children.
He poured [the liquid] into their mouths. Whatever entered their stomachs appeared as if it were contained within a vessel of precious gems.
Thus they became "skinless" (nicchavī). Others, however, say: "Their skin became adhered to one another, as if sewn together.
Thus, because they were either skinless or had adhered skin, they became known as Licchavis.
While the ascetic was raising the two boys, he would enter the village for alms only after the sun had risen and would return only when it was well past midday.
Knowing of this activity, the cowherds said to him, "Venerable sir, the raising of children is an impediment for those who have gone forth.
Give the boys to us; we will raise them, while you attend to your own duties. The ascetic consented, saying, "Very well."
On the second day, the cowherds leveled the road, scattered flowers over it, raised flags and banners, and arrived at the hermitage while musical instruments were being played.
The ascetic said, "These children possess great merit; raise them with diligence.
Once they have grown up, arrange marriages between them. After pleasing the king with the five products of the cow, [secure] a plot of land..."
"Take them and build a city; there, consecrate the prince," he said, and gave the boys to them.
They replied, "Very well," and taking the boys away, they raised them.
As the boys grew up, while playing, at points of contention they [struck] other cowherd boys with their hands and feet.
They struck them, and they wept. When asked by their parents, "Why do you weep? they replied, "These people, who have no parents and are raised by ascetics, strike us excessively.
Thereupon their parents said, "These children harass and cause suffering to other children;
these should not be favored, but should be shunned. From that time on, it is said, he...
That region was called “Vajjī,” measuring one hundred yojanas in extent. Then, having satisfied the king, the cowherds took possession of that region.
Having established a city right there, they consecrated the prince, who was sixteen years of age, and made him king.
And having held a wedding for him together with that maiden, they made an agreement: “From outside [the city]...”
"A girl must be brought; no girl is to be given from here to anyone.
By their first union, two children were born—a daughter and a son—and in this manner, sixteen times they had two children each.
Then, as those children grew up in succession, that city became unable to accommodate the abundance of their gardens, parks, residences, and retinues.
They surrounded it with a wall at intervals of one gavuta each, three times over.
Because it was repeatedly expanded (*visālīkata*), the name "Vesālī" arose for it.
This is the account of Vesālī. Furthermore, at the time of the Blessed One’s appearance, this Vesālī was prosperous and had reached a state of great abundance; for there, among the kings alone—
There were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings; likewise for the crown princes, generals, treasurers, and so forth. As it is said:
"At that time, Vesālī was prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food;
there were seven thousand palaces, seven hundred palaces, and seven palaces, as well as seven thousand gabled chambers."
“Seven hundred gabled houses, seven gabled houses, seven thousand parks, seven hundred parks, seven parks, seven thousand lotus ponds, seven hundred lotus ponds, and seven lotus ponds.
Later on, at another time, there was a famine, a failure of rain, and a crop failure. First, the destitute people...
They died, and people cast them outside. Due to the stench of the corpses of the dead humans, non-human spirits entered the city.
Consequently, even more people died, and because of that repulsiveness, a plague broke out among the beings.
Thus, the inhabitants of the city of Vesālī, being afflicted by these three fears—famine, non-humans, and disease—approached the king and said:

“Great King, a threefold danger has arisen in this city; such a thing has never occurred before, even throughout seven successive royal dynasties. It seems to me that it has arisen now because of your unrighteousness.
The king had everyone assembled in the assembly hall and said, “Investigate my state of unrighteousness. They [began] everything...
Searching through their lineage, they saw nothing.
Then, seeing no fault in the king, they thought, "How might this danger be pacified for us?
Thereupon, some pointed to six teachers, saying, "Upon his merely approaching these, it will be pacified. Others said:
“It is said that a Buddha has appeared in the world; that Blessed One, possessed of great psychic power and great majesty, teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of all beings.
By his mere arrival, all fears would be stilled. Thereupon, they became joyful and asked, “Where does that Blessed One dwell at present? Would he come if we were to send for him? Then others said:
They said, “The Buddhas are indeed compassionate; why would they not come? However, that Blessed One is currently staying at Rājagaha, and King Bimbisāra attends upon him;
perhaps he might not allow him to come. [Vaiśravaṇa replied,] “In that case, let us persuade the king and bring him here.
Then the two Licchavi kings, with a great military force and many gifts, set out.
Having given [the gifts], they sent word to the king: “Convince Bimbisāra and bring the Blessed One here.
They went, presented the king with the gift, informed him of the situation, and said, “Great King, please send the Blessed One to our city.
The king did not accept, saying, “You yourselves must know. They [then approached] the Blessed One...
Having approached and paid homage, they said this: "Venerable sir, three fears have arisen in our city.

If the Blessed One would come, there would be safety for us. The Blessed One, having reflected, [considered that] when the Ratana Sutta was recited in Vesālī, that protection would pervade hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems; and at the conclusion of the sutta, for eighty-four...
“...there will be a realization of the Dhamma by thousands of beings,” he consented.
Then King Bimbisāra, having heard the Blessed One’s consent and learning that “the Blessed One has accepted the journey to Vesālī,” had a proclamation made throughout the city.
He then approached the Blessed One and asked, “Venerable sir, what did you accept regarding the journey to Vesālī? “Yes.”
“Great King. “In that case, venerable sir, please wait until I have prepared the road.

Then King Bimbisāra, having leveled the ground for five leagues between Rājagaha and the Ganges, and having established a monastery every league, informed the Blessed One that it was time for his departure. The Blessed One [set out] with the five hundred monks...
Surrounded by hundreds of bhikkhus, he set forth. The king had the road for five *yojanas* strewn knee-deep with flowers of five colors;

having raised up banners, flags, full water-jars, plantain trees, and other ornaments, and having caused two white parasols to be held over the Blessed One and one for each bhikkhu, he went along with his own retinue, offering flowers, perfumes, and other gifts.
While performing worship, he had the Blessed One reside in each monastery in turn, gave great alms-offerings, and in five days brought him to the banks of the Ganges.
There, decorating a boat with all kinds of ornaments, he sent a message to the people of Vesālī:
“The Blessed One has arrived; prepare the road and all of you go out to meet the Blessed One. They—
Thinking, "We shall perform a twofold honor," they leveled the ground for three leagues between Vesālī and the Ganges;
having prepared four white parasols for the Blessed One and two for each monk,
they performed the worship and stood on the bank of the Ganges.
King Bimbisāra, having joined two boats together, constructed a pavilion, and adorned it with flower garlands and other ornaments, arranged there a Buddha-seat made entirely of precious gems.
The Blessed One sat upon it. Five hundred bhikkhus also boarded the boat and sat down according to their rank.
As the King followed after the Blessed One, he reached up to his neck [in depth].
Having descended into the water, he said, "Venerable sir, until the Blessed One arrives, I shall remain right here on the bank of the Ganges," and then turned back.
Above, the deities as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm made offerings; below, the Nāgas dwelling in the Ganges, such as Kambala and Assatara, made offerings.
Thus, amidst such a great offering, the Blessed One traveled a distance of one *yojana*.
Having gone to the Ganges, he entered the boundary of the Vesālī territory.
Then the Licchavi kings, doubling the honor previously shown by King Bimbisāra, went out to meet the Blessed One in water reaching up to their necks.
At that very moment, at that very instant, the darkness was pierced by the radiance of lightning, like a mass of spreading peaks.
A great cloud, thundering and rumbling, rained down in the four directions. Then, as soon as the Blessed One had set his first foot upon the bank of the Ganges, a rain of lotuses fell.
Those who wished to be drenched were drenched, while those who did not wish to be drenched were not drenched.
Everywhere, water flowed up to the knees, the thighs, the hips, and even to the neck; all corpses [were swept away].
The ground was sprinkled with water from the Ganges and became completely purified.
The Licchavi kings, having had the Blessed One stay at intervals of one *yojana* each, gave great alms-offerings and, performing double the usual honor for three days, escorted him to Vesālī.
When the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī, Sakka, the lord of the devas, [approached].
Honored by the assembly of devas, he arrived; because of the gathering of the highly powerful devas, the non-human beings for the most part fled.
The Blessed One, standing at the city gate, addressed the Elder Ānanda:
“Ānanda, having learned this Ratana Sutta and taking the requisites for the offering, go with the Licchavi youths to the three inner walls of Vesālī.”
"Wandering about, perform the protection rite (*paritta*). Thus he spoke the Ratana Sutta.
In this way, the answers to these questions—"By whom was this sutta spoken? When? Where? And for what reason?"—are described in detail by the ancients, beginning from the occasion at Vesālī.
Thus, on the very day the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī, for the purpose of warding off those calamities at the gates of the city of Vesālī...
Having mastered this Ratana Sutta, the Venerable Ānanda, reciting it for the sake of protection,
took water in the Blessed One’s bowl and walked through the entire city, sprinkling it everywhere. As soon as the Elder had uttered the words,
"Whatever [beings there may be]," those non-human beings who had previously not fled— residing in rubbish heaps, walls, and other such places— [were overcome] by the four...
They fled through the gates, but the gates were found to be blocked. Then some, unable to find an opening at the gates, escaped by breaking through the wall.
As soon as the non-human beings had departed, the disease in the bodies of the people subsided;
they emerged and honored the Elder with all kinds of perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. A great multitude gathered at the assembly hall in the center of the city.
Having anointed [the hall] with all kinds of perfumes, having spread a canopy, and having adorned it with every ornament, he prepared a Buddha-seat there and brought the Blessed One.
The Blessed One entered the assembly hall and sat down on the seat prepared for him. The community of monks and the kings and people likewise...
And they sat down in a suitable place. Sakka, the lord of the gods, sat down together with the assembly of gods from two celestial realms, as did other gods.

The Elder Ānanda, having patrolled the entire Vesālī and provided protection, arrived together with the inhabitants of the city of Vesālī and sat down to one side. There, the Blessed One [spoke] that very same thing to all of them.
"He spoke the Ratana Sutta.
Regarding that, in the first verse, "whatever beings here" (*yānīdha bhūtāni*): *yāni* means "of whatever kind," whether they be of little power or great power.
*Idha* means "in this place," referring to the location where they had assembled at that moment. *Bhūtāni* means...
Furthermore, although the word *bhūta* occurs in such contexts as "an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for [killing] a living being (*bhūta*)," where it refers to a sentient being;
in such contexts as "Behold, monks, this as it has come to be (*bhūtam idam*)," where it refers to the five aggregates;

in such contexts as "Monk, there are four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as causes," where it refers to the fourfold material form beginning with the earth element; and in such contexts as "And he who has become a consumer of time (*kālaghasa-bhūta*)," where it refers to one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
In such passages as “All beings in the world shall lay down their composite frame,” it refers to all sentient beings;

in such passages as “for the destruction of the forest of living beings,” it refers to trees and the like; and in such passages as “one perceives a being as a being,” it applies to the category of beings below the realm of the Four Great Kings.
However, in the present context, it should be understood specifically as referring to non-human spirits.
“Gathered together” means assembled. “Terrestrial” means those produced on the earth.

“Vā” (or) is used in the sense of an alternative. Thus, having made this first alternative—namely, “whatever beings here that are terrestrial have gathered together”—he said “or whatever [beings] in the sky” in order to state a second alternative. Whatever beings are produced in the sky, all of them...

The meaning is: "assembled here. Furthermore, in this context, those beings produced from the Yāma realm up to the Akaniṭṭha realm should be understood as "beings in the sky," because they are produced within celestial mansions manifested in space.
From below that, starting from Sineru down to the earth, those residing in trees, creepers, and so forth, as well as those produced in the earth itself, [are included].

As for the spirits (*bhūtāni*), all of them should be understood as "earth-dwelling spirits" (*bhummāni bhūtāni*) because they are produced upon the earth and on things connected to the earth, such as trees, creepers, and mountains.
Thus, the Blessed One [includes] all non-human spirits with the two phrases: "those that are earth-dwelling or those that are in the sky."
Having assigned [the merit] and again encompassed it with a single phrase, he said:

"May all beings indeed be well-disposed. "All" means without exception. "Indeed" (*eva*) is used for emphasis; the intention is that not even one should be excluded. "Beings" (*bhūtā*) refers to non-human spirits (*amanussā*).

"May they be well-disposed" (*sumanā bhavantu*) means may their minds be happy; the sense is that they may become filled with joy and gladness. "And also" (*athopi*) is for the purpose of enjoining another duty.
The two particles [in the phrase] *sakkacca suṇantu bhāsitaṃ* serve to introduce the statement. [It means:

"Having made it their core purpose, having applied their minds, and having directed their whole heart toward it, let them listen to my teaching, which brings about divine success and supramundane happiness.
Thus, in this context, the Blessed One, by using the unrestricted expression "whatever beings have gathered here," encompasses all beings.

Furthermore, having first divided [the beings] into two categories with the words “those on earth or those in the sky,” and then having unified them again with the words “all beings indeed,” he enjoins them toward the perfection of intention (*āsayasampatti*) with the phrase “may they be well-disposed,” and toward the perfection of application (*payogasampatti*)—
as well as the perfection of wise attention (*yonisomanasikārasampatti*)— with the words “let them listen attentively to what is spoken.”

And by directing [the listener] toward the excellence of hearing from others, as well as toward the excellence of one’s own right aspiration and reliance upon noble friends, and toward the excellence of the causes for concentration and wisdom, he concluded the verse. 225.
Therefore, "For this reason, O beings" is the second verse. Therein, "therefore" (tasmā) is a word expressing a reason; "O beings" (bhūtā) is a word of address.

*Nisāmetha* means "listen. *Sabbē* means "without exception. What is being said? Since you have come here for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, having abandoned celestial abodes and the excellence of enjoyments therein—not for the purpose of seeing actors, dancers, and the like—therefore, "all you beings, listen attentively. Alternatively, by the words "let them be well-disposed and listen respectfully," it is implied: *Sumanaso hontu sakkacca suṇantu.* Let them be well-disposed; let them listen respectfully. *Suṇantu Seeing their state of gladness and their earnest desire to hear, he said:

"Since you are endowed with a state of gladness through the purity of intent consisting in self-righteous resolve and systematic attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), and with a purity of application through reliance on true persons (*sappurisa*), the voice of others, and the foundation of the words [of the Dhamma], as well as through the earnest desire to hear—therefore, all of you listen to what is real.
Alternatively, that which was [stated] in the previous verse...
Previously it was stated, "spoken"; pointing to that as the reason, he said:

"Because my spoken word is exceedingly rare—since the opportune moment is difficult to find, being free from the eight inopportune moments—and because it possesses manifold benefits by proceeding through the qualities of wisdom and compassion;
and desiring to speak it, I said, 'Listen to my spoken word. Therefore..."
"Indeed, all you beings, listen!"—this is what is expressed by this line of verse.
Having thus presented this reason and directed them toward listening to his own speech, he began to state what should be listened to:
"Practice loving-kindness toward the human race. Its meaning is as follows: toward those humans who are afflicted by the three calamities...
"Establish a state of friendship and a disposition toward the welfare of this human race.
Some, however, read "mānusiyaṃ pajaṃ," but that is not tenable because the locative sense is impossible here. Furthermore, the interpretation offered by others is also not tenable.
The intended meaning here, however, is: "I am not a Buddha [merely] by virtue of my sovereign power..."
I say this, and furthermore, I say it for the benefit of you and this human race:
"Practice loving-kindness toward the human race.
And in this regard: "The royal seers who, having conquered the earth with its seven divisions, went about performing sacrifices;..."
The horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the *sammāpāsa*, the *vājapeyya*, and the *niraggaḷa*—
these do not equal even a sixteenth part of a well-developed mind of loving-kindness.
If one with an uncorrupted mind feels loving-kindness toward even a single living being, one becomes skilled thereby.
"Compassionate toward all living beings with his mind, the noble one performs abundant merit"—
by means of such suttas and the eleven benefits, it should be understood that loving-kindness is beneficial for those who practice it.
"A person who is compassionate toward the deities always beholds auspicious things."—
By means of these and other such [examples], it should be understood that [loving-kindness] is for the benefit of those toward whom it is directed.
Thus, showing the state of being beneficial for both [parties], he said, "Practice loving-kindness toward the human race," and now, showing the benefit [it brings], he said:
"Since they carry offerings by day and by night, therefore protect them."

"Be heedful. This is its meaning: those people who, having fashioned deities even from paintings or woodwork, approach shrines, sacred trees, and the like, and offer a daily oblation (bali) dedicated to those deities;
or who offer an oblation at night during the dark fortnight and so forth;

or who, by giving "ticket-meals" (salākabhatta) and the like, extend the offering of merit (pattidāna) starting from the guardian deities up to the deities of the Brahma world—[all these are included].

They offer oblations by day; and having caused the raising of parasols, the lighting of lamp garlands, and the hearing of the Dhamma throughout the entire night, they offer oblations at night through the dedication of the merit.

How then could these not be protected? Since they thus perform oblations both by day and by night for your sake, therefore you must protect them. For this reason, even on account of the performance of the oblation—
"Protect those people, guard them; remove what is harmful for them and bring them what is beneficial, being heedful and keeping that gratitude in your hearts, constantly mindful of it.
(226) Having thus shown how humans are of service to the deities, [the text continues] for the purpose of pacifying their misfortunes...

And by way of proclaiming the qualities of the Buddha and others, he began to employ a declaration of truth (*saccavacana*)—in the manner beginning with "whatever wealth"—for the sake of the gods and humans hearing the Dhamma.
Therein, "whatever" (*yaṃkiñci*) includes everything without exception by way of an unrestricted sense;
it refers to whatever is conventionally designated therein. "Wealth" (*vitta*) means riches; for that indeed produces prosperity (*vitti*).
“Vittaṃ. Here, “hither” (idha) indicates the human world; “thence” (huraṃ) indicates the remaining worlds beyond that.

Since, by this, it would follow that all worlds except for humans are included, and because it is stated later, “or in the heavens” (saggesu vā), one should understand that this refers to the inclusion of all others—nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth—excluding both humans and the heavens. Thus, by these two...
By these words, there is indicated that gold, silver, pearls, gems, beryl, coral, rubies, emeralds, and so forth— which are used by humans for trade,

ornamentation, and enjoyment— as well as the wealth of the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others who dwell in jewel-encrusted palaces and residences extending for many hundreds of yojanas on ground strewn with sand of pearls and gems.

"In the heavens" (*saggesu*) means in the celestial worlds of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). For they are called "heavens" (*sagga*) because beings are born and go there due to beautiful (*sobhana*) karma;
or alternatively, they are "heavens" because they are exceedingly excellent (*suṭṭhu agga*). "Which" (*yaṃ*) refers to whatever [object], whether it has an owner or is ownerless.
"Jewel" (*ratana*) means that which leads to, carries, produces, or increases delight (*rati*); it is anything that is esteemed and of great value.
This is a designation for that which is incomparable, difficult to behold, and enjoyed by extraordinary beings.
As it has been said: "That which is honored, of great value, incomparable, difficult to behold, and enjoyed by extraordinary beings—therefore it is called a 'jewel' (ratana)."

"Exquisite" (*paṇīta*) means supreme, best, and unsurpassed. Thus, by this line of verse, [he refers to] that which has an owner in the heavens—within celestial mansions made of every kind of jewel, measuring many hundreds of yojanas, such as the Sudhamma and Vejayanta halls;
and that which is ownerless, connected to empty mansions, while beings fill only the states of misery due to the absence of a Buddha's appearance;
or whatever else is situated upon the earth, in the great ocean, on Mount Himavat, and so forth.
That jewel is shown to be without an owner.
In the phrase "There is nothing equal to the Tathāgata," *na* is a negation and *no* is a particle of emphasis.
*Samam* means equal; *atthi* means exists; *tathāgatena* means by the Buddha. What is meant? That which is this wealth and treasure...
It has been declared that there is not even a single jewel here comparable to the Jewel of the Buddha. For even that which is called a "jewel" in the sense of being highly esteemed—
such as the Wheel-jewel and the Gem-jewel of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*),
at whose appearance the great multitude does not direct their esteem elsewhere, nor anyone takes flowers, perfumes, and so forth to the abodes of *yakkhas*— [is not equal to it].
Whether he goes to a place of assembly or to a royal court, all people honor and worship only the Wheel-treasure and the Jewel-treasure;
they pray for various boons, and some of those things prayed for are fulfilled.
Yet even that treasure is not equal to the Buddha-treasure. For if a "treasure" is so called in the sense of being highly esteemed, it is the Tathāgata alone who is such.
The Jewel. For when a Tathāgata has appeared, whatever gods or humans possess great influence do not direct their veneration elsewhere, nor do they worship anyone else.

Thus, for instance, Brahmā Sahampati honored the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland as large as Mount Sineru, while other gods, humans, King Bimbisāra, King Pasenadi of Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others did so according to their respective means.

Even after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, King Asoka, having disbursed ninety-six crores of wealth for his sake, established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the entire Jambudīpa; what need is there to mention other acts of veneration?
Furthermore, who else—even after their final Nibbāna—possesses such places as those of birth, enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and final Nibbāna?
Or, with respect to images, shrines, and so forth, such honor and reverence are practiced as toward the Blessed One.
In the sense of being thus honored, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Likewise, that which is a jewel in the sense of being of great value—such as Kāsī cloth—as it is said:
