“Bhikkhus, even a worn-out cloth from Kāsī is both beautiful in color, pleasant to the touch, and of great value”—yet even that is not equal to the Jewel of the Buddha.
For if a jewel is defined by its great value, then the Tathāgata alone is the jewel.
Indeed, whatever even a mere scrap of rag the Tathāgata accepts becomes of great fruit and great benefit for those who offer it.
It is just like that of King Asoka. This is its great value. Thus, regarding the statement of its great value, this Sutta passage should first be understood as establishing the absence of fault:
"But for those from whom he accepts robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick..."
For them, that becomes of great fruit and great benefit. This, I say, is because of its high value.
Just as, monks, a cloth from Kāsī is of high value, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
Thus, in the sense of being of high value, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Likewise, that which is a treasure in the sense of being incomparable is as follows:
for a wheel-turning monarch, the Wheel-treasure appears, with a hub made of sapphire, a thousand spokes made of the seven precious gems, a rim made of coral, and joints made of red gold;
above every ten spokes there is a single hollow spoke, intended to produce sound by catching the wind.
The sound produced by it is like the sound of a five-piece musical ensemble played with great skill.
There is no maker or one who causes it to be made for that [drum], whose two sides at the navel have two lion-faces and whose interior is hollow like a chariot wheel;
it arises from temperature conditioned by karma. This tenfold duty of a Wheel-turning Monarch which the King...

Having completed [the preparations], on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, the full moon day, he—having bathed his head, observing the Uposatha, and having gone to the top of the excellent palace—sat purifying his precepts.
There he saw [the Buddha] rising like the full moon and like the sun;
whose voice could be heard from twelve yojanas away and whose form could be seen from one yojana away, whom the great multitude thought was "a second [Buddha]," as it were.
Thinking, "Has the moon or the sun risen?", the [light], appearing amidst great wonder, came over the city and remained above the king’s inner palace—
neither too high nor too low— at a place suitable for the great multitude to worship with perfumes,
flowers, and other offerings, as if it were fixed there by an axle-pin.

Following that, the Elephant-Treasure appears: entirely white, with red feet, standing on seven points, possessed of supernormal power, able to travel through the air, and coming from either the Uposatha lineage or the Chaddanta lineage.
For when it comes from the Uposatha lineage, it is the eldest; when from the Chaddanta lineage, it is the youngest, well-trained, and endowed with self-mastery.
Thus, taking a retinue twelve *yojanas* in extent and having traveled throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he returns to his own royal capital at the very break of dawn.

Following after him, the horse-treasure appears; entirely white with red hooves, a crow-black head, and a mane like *muñja* grass, it comes from the royal lineage of Valāhaka. The rest here is exactly the same as for the elephant-treasure.
Following after that, the jewel-treasure appears. It is a beryl gem, beautiful, of pure birth, eight-faceted, well-polished, and in length like the hub of a wheel; it comes from Mount Vepulla.
Even in darkness possessing four factors, it illuminates for a league the tip of the king’s banner. By its radiance, people, thinking "it is day," [proceed about their business].
They employ in their work, down to even the smallest ant;
and following after that [work], the Woman-Treasure (itthiratana) appears. She is either the natural chief queen, or she comes from Uttarakuru, or from the Madda royal family.
She is free from defects such as being too tall, and she surpasses human beauty.

She had not yet attained celestial beauty; however, for that king, his limbs were warm in the cold season and cool in the hot season, and his touch was like that of cotton wool beaten a hundred times.
Sandalwood fragrance issued from his body and the scent of blue lotuses from his mouth, and he was endowed with many virtues such as rising before others.
Following after that [Wheel-treasure], the Householder-treasure arises as a merchant who serves as the king’s natural minister.
As soon as the Wheel-treasure has appeared, divine vision becomes manifest to him, by which he sees treasures for a league all around—both those with owners and those without.
He approaches the king and invites him, saying: "Be at ease, sire..."
“Sire, be at ease; I shall perform for you whatever must be done with wealth.
Then, following that, the Counsellor-treasure appears as the king’s eldest natural-born son.
As soon as the Wheel-treasure has appeared, he becomes endowed with an exceptional clarity of wisdom for a retinue extending twelve leagues.
Having fully understood the mind with his own mind, he becomes capable of restraining and exerting it. He approaches the king and offers his services, saying:
"Your Majesty, be free from anxiety; I shall govern your kingdom for you.
Or whatever else is such a jewel in the sense of being incomparable, whose value cannot be determined by weighing or measuring—[such as] a hundred...
"Does it cost a hundred, a thousand, or even ten million? In this regard, not even a single jewel is equal to the Jewel of the Buddha.

For if a "jewel" (ratana) is defined by its incomparability, then only the Tathāgata is a true jewel. Indeed, it is impossible for anyone to weigh or determine the Tathāgata in terms of virtue, concentration, wisdom, or any other quality, saying, "He possesses only so many virtues," or "By this..."
or equal, or even comparable,” one cannot so delimit it. Thus, in the sense of being incomparable, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.

Likewise, that which is a jewel in the sense of being difficult to behold—namely, the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) who is difficult to encounter, and his jewels such as the wheel—is also not equal to the Jewel of the Buddha. For if...
It is a treasure in the sense that it is difficult to see; the Tathāgata alone is the treasure.
How could there be the status of a treasure for wheel-turning monarchs and the like, since many such beings arise within a single eon?
However, because the world remains empty of a Tathāgata even for incalculable eons, the Tathāgata alone is difficult to see, arising only once in a great while. Thus it has been said:
This was said by the Blessed One at the time of his final Nibbāna:
“Ānanda, the deities are complaining: ‘Alas, we have come from afar to see the Tathāgata!
Rarely indeed do Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, arise in the world; yet this very night, in the last watch...”
"In the very watch of the night when the Tathāgata will attain final nibbāna, this highly esteemed bhikkhu stands before the Blessed One shielding him;
we shall not have the opportunity to see the Tathāgata at his final hour.
Thus, in the sense that he is so difficult to behold, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Likewise, that which is a "jewel" (ratana) in the sense of being enjoyed by extraordinary beings— for example, the wheel-jewel and so forth of a universal monarch (cakkavatti)—
is such that even for those of low birth and inferior status, such as caṇḍālas, venas, nesādas, chariot-makers, and pukkusas,
it would not serve for enjoyment even in their dreams, despite their possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of coins or dwelling on the floors of magnificent seven-storied palaces.

It does not arise [from ordinary causes]. However, because it arises for the enjoyment of a well-born Khattiya king who has fulfilled the tenfold duty of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakravartin*), it is exclusively the enjoyment of an extraordinary being;

even that is not equal to the Jewel of the Buddha. For if a "jewel" is so called in the sense of being the enjoyment of an extraordinary being, then the Tathāgata alone is the jewel. Thus, the Tathāgata...
For in this world, even those esteemed as extraordinary beings— such as the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa,
who possessed perverted views and lacked the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya)— are not to be relied upon even in a dream; whereas for those endowed with the supporting conditions,
it is possible to attain even Arhatship at the conclusion of a single four-line verse, provided they possess penetrative knowledge and vision.
It was the possession of Bāhiya Dārucīriya and other great disciples born of noble families.
For they made use of it in various ways while accomplishing the unsurpassed vision, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed service, and so forth.
Thus, in the sense of being possessed by extraordinary beings, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
That which is a treasure (*ratana*) in the sense of generating delight without distinction is as follows: the wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*) of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*).
Upon seeing it, the universal monarch becomes joyful; thus, too, it generates delight for the king.
Furthermore, the universal monarch, having taken the golden water-vessel with his left hand, [presents] the wheel-treasure with his right hand.
He sprinkles [water] and says, "May your Wheel-treasure roll forth; may your Wheel-treasure conquer!

Then the Wheel-treasure, emitting a sweet sound like a fivefold musical ensemble, proceeds through the air toward the eastern direction, while the Cakkavatti king follows right behind it by the power of the wheel across a distance twelve yojanas wide.
With a fourfold army, neither too high nor too low— by the lower part of tall trees and the upper part of short trees—
he received the tribute of flowers, fruits, sprouts, and leaves from the hands of rival kings who had come with the utmost humility,
saying, "Come, Great King," and so forth, while they approached [saying], "Living beings..."
He proceeds instructing [the people] in such a manner as, "One must not be killed," and so forth.

However, wherever the king desires to eat or wishes to take his midday rest, there the Wheel-Treasure descends from the sky and stands upon a level stretch of ground—capable of withstanding all tasks such as washing—that remains as if fixed in place like a wheel struck by an axle-pin.
Then, when the king's intention to depart arises, it proceeds again in the same manner as before.
It proceeds making a sound, hearing which even an assembly extending twelve *yojanas* travels through the air.
The Wheel-Treasure gradually plunges into the eastern ocean; as it plunges in, the water recedes for a distance of one *yojana* and stands as if forming a wall.
The great multitude takes the seven treasures according to their desire.
Again, the king takes the golden pitcher, sprinkles water with the words, "From this point on, let my sovereignty begin," and turns back.
The army is in front, the Wheel-Treasure is behind, and the king is in the middle. At every place where the Wheel-Treasure halts, the water fills it completely.
By this very means, he proceeds to the southern, western, and northern oceans as well.
Having thus traveled in the four directions, the Wheel-Treasure ascends into the sky to a height of three yojanas.
Standing there, by the power of the Wheel-Treasure, the King conquers Pubbavideha, which is seven thousand yojanas in circumference and adorned with five hundred minor islands;
likewise, he conquers Uttarakuru, which is eight thousand yojanas in circumference, and likewise [Jambudīpa], which is seven thousand yojanas in circumference.

"Aparagoyāna, and Jambudīpa measuring ten thousand yojanas in circumference"—thus he gazes upon a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), adorned with four great continents and two thousand minor islands, like a forest of full-blown white lotuses. As he gazes thus, an immeasurable joy arises within him.
In this way, that Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*) produces delight for the king; it too is equal to the Jewel of the Buddha.
It does not exist. For if it were a "jewel" (ratana) in the sense of producing delight, then only the Tathāgata is a jewel.

What would this Wheel-Jewel (cakkaratana) accomplish? For even the delight of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti), which is produced by all [the seven jewels] beginning with the Wheel-Jewel, does not approach even a fraction, a part, or a portion of that divine delight belonging to the Tathāgata; indeed, the Tathāgata possesses a delight far superior even to that.
And even more excellent than that is the joy of the first jhāna, the joy of the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas,
the joy of the base of infinite space, the joy of the bases of infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception,

as well as the joy of the path of stream-entry, the joy of the fruit of stream-entry, and the joy of the paths and fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship— experienced by countless gods and humans who follow his instruction.
It generates [delight]. Thus, in the sense of generating delight, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this so-called "jewel" is of two kinds: sentient and insentient.
Among these, the insentient consists of the wheel-jewel and the gem-jewel, or whatever else is not bound to the sense-faculties, such as gold, silver, and so forth. The sentient [jewels]...
This includes the elephant-treasure and so forth, ending with the counselor-treasure, or whatever else of a similar kind is bound to sense faculties.

Of these two kinds, the sentient treasure is declared to be the foremost here. Why? Because the insentient treasures—such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls—are brought forward for the purpose of adorning the sentient treasures, such as the elephant-treasure and the rest.
The jewel possessing consciousness is also twofold: the animal jewel and the human jewel.
Among these, the human jewel is declared to be the foremost. Why? Because the animal jewel serves as a vehicle for the human jewel.
The human jewel is also twofold: the woman-jewel and the man-jewel. Among these, the man-jewel is declared to be the foremost.
Why? Because the woman-treasure enters into the service of the man-treasure. The man-treasure is also twofold:
the householder-treasure and the homeless-treasure. Among these, the homeless-treasure is declared to be supreme. Why?
Because even a wheel-turning monarch, the foremost among householders, cannot equal the homeless-treasure who is endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*).
Having paid homage with the fivefold prostration, having attended upon and served [the Teacher], and having attained celestial and human prosperities, one finally attains the prosperity of Nibbāna.
Thus, the jewel of the homeless life is also twofold, according to the distinction between the Noble Ones (ariya) and worldlings (puthujjana). The jewel of the Noble Ones is also twofold.

By way of those in training (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha). The jewel of those beyond training is twofold: by way of the dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) and the one who takes serenity as their vehicle (samatha-yānika).
The jewel of the one who takes serenity as their vehicle is also twofold: having attained the perfection of a disciple (sāvaka-pāramippatta) and not having attained it.

Among these, that which has attained the perfection of a disciple is declared supreme. Why? Because of the greatness of its qualities. Even compared to the jewel of the disciple who has attained perfection, the jewel of the Paccekabuddha...
It is declared to be supreme. Why? Because of the greatness of its qualities.
For even hundreds of disciples like Sāriputta and Moggallāna do not equal even a hundredth part of the qualities of a single paccekabuddha.

Even compared to the jewel of the paccekabuddhas, the jewel of the perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha) is declared to be supreme. Why? Because of the greatness of its qualities. For [the qualities of] the entire Jambudīpa...

Even when seated cross-legged upon another cross-legged seat, the Paccekabuddhas, having filled it, do not equal even a fraction, a part, or a minute portion of the virtues of a single Sammasambuddha.
And this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings—whether footless... [and so forth]...
the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them," and so on. Thus, by no one whatsoever...
In a figurative sense, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata. Therefore the Blessed One said: “There is nothing equal to us, [namely] the Tathāgata.

Thus the Blessed One, having spoken of the incomparability of the Buddha-jewel with other jewels, now—without regard for birth, clan, lineage, or physical beauty and so forth—[speaks] for the sake of pacifying the calamities that have arisen for those beings.

Furthermore, relying on the incomparable nature of the Buddha Jewel—by virtue of qualities such as the aggregates of virtue and concentration throughout the world from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence—he employs a word of truth: "This too is the sublime Jewel in the Buddha;
by this truth, may there be well-being."

The meaning of this is as follows: Whatever wealth or treasure there may be here, or in the world beyond, or in the heavenly realms, the Jewel of the Buddha is superior to all of them because it is not equaled by those various qualities.
If this is true, by this truth may there be safety for these living beings; may there be the presence of beauty, health, and freedom from calamity.
And here, just as in such passages as, "The eye, Ānanda, is empty of self or of what belongs to self," the meaning is "by way of a self-nature or by way of a nature belonging to a self"—
for otherwise, it would not have been stated that "the eye is self or belongs to self"— so too,
in the phrase "the jewel is excellent," the meaning should be understood as "the state of being a jewel is excellent" or "the quality of being a jewel is excellent."
Otherwise, it would not be established that the Buddha is a "jewel" (*ratana*). For where a jewel exists, it is not established as a "jewel" merely by its presence;

rather, it is because there exists a state of being a jewel (*ratanatta*)—characterized by qualities such as being honored—and which, through some method or other, enters into a relationship [with the subject], and because, depending upon that state of being a jewel, it is designated as a "jewel," therefore, for him...
Because of the existence of that which is precious, it is established as a "jewel" (*ratana*).
Alternatively, by the phrase "this too is a jewel in the Buddha," for this reason also, the Buddha alone is the jewel; thus should the meaning here be understood.

As soon as this verse was spoken by the Blessed One, well-being arose for the royal family, and fear was stilled. The authority of this verse extends throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Accepted by non-human beings.
Having thus spoken the truth by means of the Buddha’s qualities, he now begins to speak by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna: "The destruction, the fading away.
Therein, because through the realization of Nibbāna, lust and the other defilements are exhausted and utterly destroyed; because—
Or rather, it is merely their non-arising, cessation, and destruction;

and because it is dissociated from lust and the other defilements both by way of association and by way of object, or because when it is realized, lust and the rest become utterly detached, departed, and shattered, it is therefore called "destruction" (*khaya*) and "dispassion" (*virāga*).
Furthermore, because its arising is not perceived, [it is called "cessation"].
There is no aging, nor any alteration of what stands; therefore, because it is not born, does not age, and does not die, it is called "the Deathless" (amata).
Furthermore, in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being insatiable, it is called "sublime" (paṇīta).
"Yadajjhagā" means that which he attained, found, acquired, and realized for himself through the power of his own knowledge. "Sakyamuni" refers to one who is born of the Sakya clan.
He is a Sakyan because he is endowed with the qualities of a sage (*moneyya-dhamma*); thus, a Sakyan who is a sage is the Sakyan Sage (*Sakyamuni*).
"Concentrated" means one whose mind is concentrated by means of the concentration of the Noble Path (*ariya-magga-samādhi*).

"There is nothing equal to that state" means there is no other class of phenomena equal to that Dhamma attained by the Sakyan Sage, which is named after its destruction [of defilements] and so forth. Therefore, it is also said in another Sutta: "To whatever extent..."

“Monks, whether phenomena are conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them,” and so forth. Thus, having stated that the phenomenon of Nibbāna is unequalled by other phenomena,
the Blessed One now [praises] the jewel of the Nibbāna-phenomenon by way of its qualities of destruction (*khaya*),
dispassion (*virāga*), peace (*santa*), and excellence (*paṇīta*), for the purpose of pacifying the calamities that have arisen for those beings.
Relying on his peerless nature, he utters a word of truth: “This too is the sublime Jewel of the Dhamma;
by this truth, may there be well-being. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as stated for the previous verse.
The command of this verse, too, was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.

228. Having thus spoken the truth by way of the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna, he now begins to speak by way of the qualities of the Dhamma of the Path, starting with "The Best Buddha" (*yaṃ buddhaseṭṭho*).
In this context, one is a "Buddha" (*buddho*) in the sense of having awakened to the Truths (*saccāni*), and so forth;

one is "Best" (*seṭṭho*) because one is supreme and praiseworthy. Thus, being both a Buddha and the best, he is the "Best Buddha. [He is distinguished] from those known as the *Anubuddhas* (Followers) and the *Paccekabuddhas* (Solitary Buddhas).
Or, he is the best among Buddhas, thus "Buddha-best" (*buddhaseṭṭho*).

That Buddha-best one praised it—saying, "The eightfold path is the foremost among paths for the attainment of the secure *nibbāna*," and, "Monks, I will teach you noble right concentration together with its proximate cause and its requisites"—and so forth;
in such ways, he extolled and made it manifest here and there. It is "pure" (*sucim*).
It is "absolute purity" because it effects the total eradication of the stains of the defilements. Regarding the statement, "They call samādhi 'uninterrupted'":
because it invariably yields its fruit immediately following its own occurrence, they call it "uninterrupted samādhi.
For when the path-samādhi has arisen, there is no obstacle whatsoever that can prevent the arising of its fruit. As it is said:
“Suppose this person were practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and it were the time for the world-age to be incinerated;
the world-age would not be incinerated until this person has realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Such a person is called one who ‘stays for an eon. Indeed, all persons possessing the path are those who stay for an eon.”

"There is nothing equal to that concentration" means that there exists no concentration—whether of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*)—equal to this pure "uninterrupted concentration" (*ānantarikasamādhi*) praised by the Best of Buddhas. Why?

Because while those [other concentrations] may lead to rebirth in various Brahma-worlds through their cultivation, there remains the possibility of falling back again into the hells and other lower realms; whereas for this [concentration], such is not the case.
Because of the cultivation of the concentration of arahantship, there arises for the noble person the total eradication of all arising [of defilements].
Therefore, it is said in another sutta: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost among them," and so forth.

Having thus stated that the *ānantarika-samādhi* (the concentration of immediate succession) is unequalled by other concentrations, the Blessed One now employs a declaration of truth (*saccavacana*) based on the peerless nature of the Jewel of the Dhamma of the Path, according to the same method as before: “May this too [be established] in the Dhamma….
The meaning of this should be understood in the manner already explained. In this verse as well, the command extends throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Accepted by non-human beings.
(229) Having thus spoken the truth by way of the qualities of the Path and the Dhamma, he now began to speak by way of the qualities of the Saṅgha as well, starting with "those individuals.
Therein, "those" (*ye*) is an indefinite enumeration; "individuals" (*puggalā*) refers to sentient beings; "eight" (*aṭṭha*) is the numerical limit of them.
For these consist of eight individuals: the four who are practicing the path and the four who are established in the fruit.
They are "praised by the good" because they are lauded by true persons—namely, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples—as well as by other gods and humans. Why?

Because of their possession of innate qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. For just as the colors and fragrances of flowers like the *campaka* and *vakula* are innate to them, [so too are these qualities innate to them].

Just as flowers endowed with color, fragrance, and so forth possess co-nascent qualities such as virtue and concentration, by that [analogy], they become dear, pleasing, and praiseworthy to hundreds of gods and humans. Therefore it was said: “Those persons who are praised as eight hundred.
Alternatively, *ye* (those who) is an indefinite enumeration; *puggalā* (persons) refers to sentient beings; and *aṭṭhasataṃ* (eight hundred) is the numerical limit of them.
For these consist of three types of stream-enterers—the single-seed, the family-to-family, and the one who will be reborn seven times at most;
three types of once-returners who have attained the fruit in the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms; and all of them, by way of the four modes of progress, amount to twenty-four:
those who attain nibbāna in the interval, those who attain nibbāna upon landing, those who attain nibbāna with exertion, and those who attain nibbāna without exertion.
"An upstreamer bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm": there are five in the Aviha [heaven], and likewise five each in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī heavens.
In the Akaniṭṭha heaven, however, there are four, excluding the upstreamer; thus, there are twenty-four non-returners.

There are two types of Arahants—the dry-insight practitioner and the one whose vehicle is serenity—and four who are established on the path; these make fifty-four. All of them belong to those whose burden is faith or whose burden is wisdom.
By doubling [the four], they become one hundred and eight. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding the statement "these constitute four pairs," all these individuals—whether eight or one hundred and eight—are those enumerated by way of detail.

By way of summary, however, there is one pair consisting of the one standing on the path of stream-entry and the one established in its fruit; and so on, up to the one standing on the path of arahantship and the one established in its fruit.
"Those at the stage of fruition" (*phalaṭṭha*) means one pair; thus there are four pairs. "They are worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*):

here, the word "they" (*te*) is a specification that determines those previously mentioned without specific designation. Those individuals who were stated to be eight or one hundred and eight in detail, or four pairs in brief—all of them are worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇa*).

Worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). An "offering" (*dakkhiṇā*) refers to a gift given while having faith in both the action and its result, without regard for such things as thinking, "This will perform medical work for me," or "He will carry out errands on foot," and so forth.
Those individuals endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) are said to be "worthy of it. And since these [monks] are of such a nature, they are called "worthy of offerings."

“Disciples of the Sugata,” said the Blessed One: he is the *Sugata* because he is endowed with a beautiful gait, because he has gone to a beautiful state, because he has gone well, and because he has spoken well; [they belong] to that Sugata.
They are called *sāvakā* (disciples) because they all hear his word. Granted that others also hear it, yet having heard it, they do not perform the duty that ought to be done. These [do].
However, having heard [the Dhamma], they have practiced the way of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma and attained the paths and fruits; therefore, they are called "disciples" (sāvakā).

Regarding the phrase "gifts given to them yield great fruit": gifts, even small ones, given to these disciples of the Sugata yield great fruit because, by virtue of the recipient, the offering attains the state of purity of the sacrificial gift (dakkhiṇā-visuddhi). Therefore, it is also said in another sutta:

“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are assemblies or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost among them—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples...
[as before] ...has the highest fruit.”

Thus the Blessed One, having described the qualities of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of all those established in the paths and the fruits, now employs a word of truth based on those very qualities, saying, "This too is in the Saṅgha.
Its meaning should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The command of this verse was received by non-human beings throughout a hundred thousand million world-systems.

230. Having thus spoken the truth by way of the qualities of the Saṅgha—referring to those established in the paths and fruits—he now begins to speak by way of the qualities of those very individuals whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), who experience the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), starting with the words, “Those who are well-yoked.
Therein, “those who” (ye) is an indefinite pronoun. “Well-yoked” (suppayuttā) means thoroughly yoked; [to the many kinds of...]
The meaning is that, having abandoned seeking, they began to apply themselves to insight (vipassanā) by relying on a pure livelihood.
Alternatively, "well-applied" means endowed with perfectly pure bodily and verbal exertion; by this, he shows their aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
"With a firm mind" means with a firm mind, that is, with a consciousness joined to stable concentration (samādhi); by this...

He shows them the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*). "Having gone forth" (*nikkāmī*) means having become indifferent toward both body and life, and having gone forth from all defilements by means of energy dominated by wisdom (*paññādhura*).
By this, he shows them the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) endowed with energy.

"In the teaching of Gotama" (*gotamasāsanamhi*) means in the teaching of the Tathāgata Gotama himself by virtue of his lineage (*gotta*). By this, [he excludes] even the various kinds [of teachings] outside of this [teaching].
It illustrates the absence of emergence from the defilements due to the lack of qualities such as skillful application in those performing the austerity of immortality.
*Tesaṃ* is a term of explanation referring back to those previously mentioned. Regarding *pattipattā*: here, *patti* means that which is to be attained (*pattabbā*);
"to be attained" means worthy of being attained—that which, having been reached, one becomes one who has attained ultimate security from bondage; this is a designation for the fruit of arahantship.
"Foot-soldiers for foot-soldiers" means those who are foot-soldiers among foot-soldiers. "The Deathless" refers to Nibbāna. "Having plunged in" means having entered [it] by way of the object.
"Having obtained" means having acquired it. "Worthily" means without spending even as much as a single *kākaṇika* coin, that is, without waste.

"The state of peace" refers to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), wherein the distress of the defilements has been stilled. "Enjoying" means experiencing it. What is meant? Those who, in this teaching of Gotama—
Because they are endowed with virtue, they are well-directed; because they are endowed with concentration, they possess a firm mind; because they are endowed with wisdom, they are free from desire.
Through this right practice, having plunged into the Deathless and attained by chance the extinction known as the attainment of fruition, they are said to have "reached what was to be reached."

Thus, having described the quality of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of those individuals whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) as they experience the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), the Blessed One now employs a declaration of truth (saccavacana) based on that very quality, saying: "This too is in the Saṅgha.
Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The command of this verse also extends throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (cakkavāḷa).
"Accepted by non-human beings.

(231) Having thus spoken the truth based on the Saṅgha through the qualities of individuals whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), he now begins to speak through the qualities of even a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) as witnessed by many people, starting with "Just as a gatepost...
(*yathindakhīlo*). Therein, "just as" (*yathā*) is a word of comparison.

*Indakhīla* is a designation for a pillar made of solid wood that has been driven into the ground after digging eight or ten cubits into the earth within the threshold (*ummāra*) for the purpose of securing the city gate. *Pathaviṃ* means the earth.
*Sito* means having entered and settled within. *Siyā* means it might be. *Catubbhi vātehī* means by winds coming from the four directions.
"Unshakable" (*asampakampiya*) means one who cannot be shaken or moved. "Of such a kind" (*tathūpama*) means of that sort.

"A true person" (*sappurisa*) means a supreme person. "I say" (*vadāmi*) means I speak. "Who sees the noble truths through penetration" (*yo ariyasaccāni avecca passati*) means one who sees the four noble truths by plunging into them with wisdom.
In this regard, the noble truths are to be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

This, however, is the summary of the meaning here: Just as a city-gate pillar, being fixed in the earth with a deep socket, would be unshakable by the four winds, even so, I say, is this true person who sees the Noble Truths through direct penetration. Why?
Because he, like that gate-pillar, remains unshaken by the four winds of the doctrines of all other sectarians.
He is unshakable; it is impossible for anyone to shake or move him from that vision.
Therefore, it is said in another sutta:
"Just as, bhikkhus, an iron pillar or a city-gate post, deeply rooted and firmly planted, is immovable and unshakable..."
If a violent wind and rain were to come from the eastern direction, it would not cause it to tremble, nor shake, nor make it wobble.
[The same applies if they were to come] from the western direction... from the southern direction... or from the northern direction... it would not make it wobble. Why is that?
Because of its depth, monks, and because the city-gate pillar is firmly planted. Even so, monks, [is this body].
“Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’...

[and so on] ...‘This is the way leading to its cessation,’ they do not look to the face of any other ascetic or brahmin, thinking, ‘Surely this worthy one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen. Why is that? Because, monks, the Four Noble Truths have been well-seen.”

Thus the Blessed One, having described the quality of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of one who has attained stream-entry (sotāpanna) before the eyes of many people, now employs a declaration of truth (saccavacana) based on that very quality, saying: "This too is in the Saṅgha.

Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The command of this verse was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (cakkavāḷa).

232. Having thus stated the truth based on the Saṅgha by way of the qualities of a stream-enterer in general, [the text now addresses] those three types of stream-enterers: the one-seeded (ekabījī), the family-to-family (kolaṃkolo), and the one who returns seven times at most (sattakkhattuparamo).
As it is said: "In this case, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer...
having been reborn only once more, he makes an end of suffering; this is the one-seeded. Likewise, [having passed through] two or three families..."
"Having run and wandered through [births], one makes an end of suffering; this is the kolaṅkola.
Likewise, having run and wandered seven times among gods and humans, one makes an end of suffering; this is the sattakkhattuparama.
He then began to speak of the qualities of the latter, the most junior of them all, the sattakkhattuparama, with the words: "Those which are the Noble Truths..."
In this context, "the Noble Truths" is exactly as previously explained.
"They manifest" means that by the light of wisdom, they dispel the darkness of the defilements that obscures the truths, making them luminous and evident to themselves.

"By one of profound wisdom" means by one whose wisdom is immeasurable, whose wisdom finds no foothold even for the world with its devas through its knowledge—by which it is meant he is the All-Knowing One (Sabbaññū).
"Well-taught" means they have been excellently taught through various methods such as concise and detailed expositions,

complete and partial presentations, and so forth. "Even though they may be greatly negligent" means that even if those individuals who have discerned the Noble Truths become greatly negligent by resorting to grounds for negligence such as divine sovereignty or the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch,
nevertheless, by means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, [they ensure] the cessation of volitional consciousness...

Excluding those [beings] who have attained cessation, because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that would otherwise arise in the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra) throughout the seven existences have ceased and passed away,
they do not take up an eighth existence; rather, having begun insight (vipassanā) within the seventh existence itself,
they reach Arahantship.

Thus the Blessed One, having described the quality of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of its being "at most seven times reborn," now employs a word of truth (saccavacana) based on that very quality, saying:
"This too [belongs] to the Saṅgha. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
The command of this verse was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.

233. Having thus spoken the Truth based on the Saṅgha by virtue of not taking up an eighth existence for one who is limited to seven more births, he now begins to speak of that very person’s excellence, which is distinguished from other individuals who have not abandoned the grasping of existence, even regarding those seven births, with the words:
“Sahāvassā. Therein, *sahāva* means "together with. *Assā*... [text fragment] ...means "of him."

Regarding the statement, “They do not take up an eighth existence,” this refers to one among those mentioned. “Perfection of vision” (*dassanasampadā*) means the attainment of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).
For the path of stream-entry is called “vision” because it is the very first vision of *nibbāna* by way of the perfection of the task to be done after having seen *nibbāna*.
The manifestation of that [path] within oneself is the perfection of vision; by means of that perfection of vision—
“Together indeed. Regarding the phrase *tayo su dhammā jahitā bhavanti*, here *su* is a particle used merely to fill out the meter, as in such expressions as:
“This, Sāriputta, was my [thought] regarding the great repulsive food,” and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning here is precisely this: that together with the perfection of his vision, three things are abandoned—that is, they become relinquished.
Now, in order to show the phenomena that have been abandoned, he said: “The view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt, and whatever rules and observances there may be.

Therein, while the body exists—that is, while the body consisting of the five aggregates of clinging exists—the view based on twenty bases is the view of a personal body; or alternatively, it is the view regarding that body, and thus it is called the view of a personal body.
The meaning is: views existing within the body of the kind already described. Or alternatively, "personality-view" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) means that view itself is the personality;
the meaning is: the view that occurs as "there is a self consisting of form, etc.," while the body of the aforementioned type exists.
And because that [view] has been abandoned, all modes of view are indeed abandoned, for it is their root. This is because it brings about the subsiding of all the diseases of the defilements.
Wisdom (*paññā*) is called "the cure" (*cikicchita*); that which has departed from this wisdom-cure, or from which the wisdom-cure has departed, is "wavering" (*vicikicchita*).
This is a designation for the eightfold doubt described by the method beginning with "he is uncertain regarding the Teacher.
Because that [doubt] has been abandoned, all forms of wavering are abandoned. For that—

This is their root. In such passages as, "Outside of this [teaching], for recluses and brahmins, purification comes through virtue (sīla) and purification comes through observance (vata)," the virtue consisting of the cow-virtue, dog-virtue, and so forth, and the observance consisting of the cow-observance, dog-observance, and so forth, are called "virtue-and-observance" (sīlabbata).
Because that has been abandoned, all forms of "immortality-penance" (amaratapa), such as nakedness, shaving the head, and so on, are also abandoned. For that [penance]...
That is its root. Therefore, at the very end, it is said: "Whatever there is.

It should be understood that here, personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is abandoned through the perfection of the vision of suffering; doubt (*vicikicchita*) through the perfection of the vision of the origin [of suffering];
and rules-and-observances (*sīlabbata*) through the perfection of the vision of the path and the vision of Nibbāna.

234. Having thus shown the abandoning of the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), he now says, "And liberated from the four states of misery," demonstrating that when this cycle of defilements exists, there must be a corresponding cycle of results (*vipākavaṭṭa*); and by abandoning the former, the latter is also abandoned.

Therein, the "four states of misery" (*apāya*) are hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), and the host of asuras; from these, this [Buddha] has been liberated throughout the seven existences.
The meaning is: "even while grasping, he is utterly liberated.

Having thus shown his abandonment of the cycle of result (vipākavaṭṭa), he now says, "he is incapable of performing the six acts of transgression," showing the abandonment of the cycle of kamma (kammavaṭṭa) which is the root of this cycle of result. Therein:
"Abhiṭhānāni" (the bases) refers to gross offenses; he is incapable of committing these six.

And these are stated in the Ekakanipāta according to the method beginning: "It is impossible, monks, it cannot happen, that a person endowed with right view should deprive his mother of life," and so forth—namely, the acts of matricide, patricide, killing an arahant, shedding the blood of a Buddha, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and setting oneself up as another teacher.

These [offenses] are to be understood. For although a noble disciple endowed with right view does not deprive even an ant or a termite of life, nevertheless, these [offenses] were stated for the purpose of censuring the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Indeed, because he is not endowed with right view, the ordinary person commits such highly blameworthy transgressions; however, one who is perfected in vision...
"He is incapable of doing those things. Here, the inclusion of the term "incapable" (abhabba) is for the purpose of showing that he will not do them even in another existence.

For even in another existence, although he does not know his own status as a noble disciple, by the very nature of things (dhammatā), he does not commit these six points—either these six or the five natural enmities such as the taking of life—along with the teaching of another teacher; it is with reference to these that some [say]:
They recite: “The six abodes. Here, the dead fish-catchers and others serve as examples for the noble disciple village boys.

Thus, having described the quality of the Saṅgha-ratana by way of the superior qualities of the noble disciple—who, even when taking up seven existences, is distinguished from other persons who have not abandoned the grasping for existence—the Blessed One now, relying on that very same quality, [utters] a word of truth.
He applies [the formula], saying, "This too is in the Saṅgha. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
The command of this verse was also received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems. 235.
Thus, by way of taking up the seven existences (*bhava*), he is distinguished by his superior qualities from those individuals who have not abandoned the grasping for existence.
Having spoken the truth based on the resolve of the Saṅgha, he now began to speak regarding the quality of one who possesses right view (*dassanasampanna*), even if they dwell in negligence:

"Not only is one endowed with right view incapable of performing the six transgressions, but having committed even a slight evil deed, they are also incapable of concealing it. Thus he said: "Even though..."
“He thus performs an evil deed.

Its meaning is as follows: although that person endowed with vision has, through a lapse of mindfulness, come to abide in negligence, regarding that which was spoken by the Blessed One concerning the intentional transgression of what is forbidden in the world—namely, the training rule for his disciples: [he might think,] “I shall not transgress this training rule...”

"Whatever has been prescribed by me, my disciples do not transgress even for the sake of their lives"—setting that aside, if one performs with the body an evil deed censured by the Buddha, such as building a hut or sleeping in a group of more than two; or with speech, such as teaching the Dhamma by footstep, or by more than five or six sentences, or idle chatter, harsh words, and so forth;
or even with the mind, such as the acceptance of gold, silver, and the like, or in the enjoyment of robes and other requisites—[these constitute offenses].
Or he commits an evil deed without reflecting upon it. He is incapable of concealing it;
knowing that "this is improper and not to be done," he does not conceal it for even a moment.
Rather, at that very instant, he reveals it to the Teacher or to wise fellow-celibates and makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, [vowing]: "Never again..."
"Shall I do it"—thinking thus, he either restrains himself or has already restrained himself. Why? Because "incapacity" is said of one who has seen the state;
the meaning is that for a person who has seen the state of Nibbāna and is endowed with vision, incapacity is said regarding the performance of such evil deeds and their concealment.
How so? "Just as, monks, a young child, weak and lying on its back, having stepped on a coal with a hand or a foot,
quickly withdraws [it], even so, monks, this is the natural law for one who is endowed with right view."
Even if a person commits such an offense for which a means of rehabilitation is prescribed,
they nevertheless quickly confess it, disclose it, and lay it bare before the Teacher or wise fellow-celibates;
having confessed, disclosed, and laid it bare, they undertake restraint for the future.”

Thus the Blessed One, having described the quality of the Jewel of the Saṅgha through the virtue of one who dwells in negligence yet is possessed of vision and lacks the habit of concealing [faults], now employs a declaration of truth based on that very same quality, saying: "This too is in the Saṅgha.
The meaning of this should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The authority of this verse extends throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Accepted by non-human beings.

236. Having thus spoken the truth based on the Saṅgha, by way of the various kinds of qualities belonging to those individuals included within the Saṅgha, [the author] now, while the Blessed One was illuminating the qualities of the Three Jewels, speaks here in brief—rather than elsewhere—[as follows]:
And the Dhamma of the scriptures was taught in detail; relying on that as well, he began again to speak the Truth with reference to the Buddha:
"As in a forest thicket, when its top is in bloom," and so forth. Therein, a *vana* (forest) is a collection of trees situated in close proximity;
a *gumbo* (thicket) is that which has grown up with roots, heartwood, sapwood, bark, branches, and foliage; in the forest...
The *pagumba* and *vanappagumba*; this [latter] is called “*vanappagumbe*” (in the *vanappagumba*).

For it is also possible to speak in this way, as in such expressions as “there is [that which is] with initial application and sustained application (*savitakka-savicāra*), there is [that which is] without initial application but with sustained application (*avitakka-vicāramatta*), in pleasure, in pain, in the soul (*jīva*),” and so forth.
“Yathā” is a word used for comparison. “Phussitagga” means that its tips are covered in blossoms; it is one upon whose branches and twigs flowers have appeared.
This is the meaning. It was previously stated by the same method as “at the peak of blossoming. Regarding the phrase “in the first month of summer”:
of the four months of summer, it refers to one of those four summer months.
If you ask which month it is, it is the first of summer; the meaning is “the month of Citta. For that is called both “the first summer” and “the beginning of the rains.”
Thus it is said. Beyond that, the meaning of the words is already evident.

Here, however, is the summarized meaning: just as in the early spring known as the first summer, in a forest thick with various kinds of trees, a *pagumba*—a term synonymous with a young grove of trees whose branches and tips are in full bloom—is exceedingly beautiful.

In the same way, because it is exceedingly magnificent with the various kinds of flowers that are the analytical meanings—the aggregates, bases, and so forth; the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, and so forth; or the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and so forth—it is like that [tree].

Since it illuminates the path leading to Nibbāna, it is the excellent Dhamma of the scriptures leading to Nibbāna. It was not for the sake of gain, nor for the sake of honor and the like, but solely out of great compassion.

“With a heart uplifted, he taught for the supreme welfare of beings. Regarding the phrase “for the supreme welfare” (*paramahitāya*): here, the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is used for the sake of metrical ease in the verse composition;
however, the meaning is “he taught for the supreme welfare, that is, for *nibbāna*.
Thus, having spoken this Dhamma of the scriptures—which is like a forest thicket with trees in full bloom—the Blessed One now [proceeds] with that very same...
Relying upon the Buddha’s resolve, he utters a declaration of truth: “This too is in the Buddha.
Its meaning should be understood according to the method already explained; however, it should simply be applied thus:

“This jewel of the Dhamma, consisting of the scriptural teachings (pariyatti) of the aforementioned kind, is sublime in the Buddha. The command of this verse [resounds] throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
"Accepted by non-human beings.

(237) Thus, having spoken the truth regarding the Buddha's resolve through the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*), the Blessed One now began to speak through the supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttara-dhamma*) with the words, "The Excellent One, who knows the excellent.
In that context, "the excellent" (*vara*) refers to what is desired by those whose inclinations are toward the sublime: "O, may..."
"May we too become such as this. Or, he is "vara" because of his possession of excellent qualities; the meaning is that he is supreme and most excellent. "Varaññū" means one who knows Nibbāna.
For Nibbāna is the "vara" (excellent) among all phenomena in the sense of being the highest; and he himself realized it at the foot of the Bodhi tree and thus came to know it.
"Varada" means [the giver] of [the gift] to the group of five, the auspicious group, the matted-hair ascetics, and other gods and humans.
The meaning is: "the giver of the supreme Dhamma, which partakes of penetration and partakes of purification. He is called *Varāhara* because he has brought forth the excellent path (*vara-āhara*).

For that Blessed One, fulfilling the thirty perfections from the time of Dīpaṅkara onwards, brought forth the ancient, excellent path followed by previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones; therefore, he is called *Varāhara*.

Furthermore, he is *vara* (excellent) because of his attainment of omniscient knowledge; *varaññū* (knower of the excellent) because of his realization of Nibbāna; *varado* (giver of the excellent) because of his bestowing the bliss of liberation upon sentient beings;
*varāharo* (bringer of the excellent) because of his bringing forth the supreme path. He is *anuttara* (unexcelled) because there is no one superior to him by virtue of these supramundane qualities.
According to another method: he is *vara* through the fulfillment of the foundation of tranquility (*samatha*); *varaññū* through the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom (*paññā*).

He is the Giver of Boons through the fulfillment of the resolve for generosity; the Remover of Boons through the fulfillment of the resolve for truth; and he brought forth the sublime Truth of the Path. Likewise, he is "Excellent" (*vara*) due to his abundance of merit;
"Knower of the Excellent" (*varaññū*) due to his abundance of wisdom; the "Giver of Boons" (*varada*) to those desiring Buddhahood by bestowing the means thereto;
the "Remover of Boons" (*varāhara*) to those desiring the state of a Paccekabuddha by bringing them the means thereto; and "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because of his peerlessness in various respects.
Or, having himself become one who has no teacher, he taught the excellent Dhamma to others by acting as their teacher;
for the sake of those seeking the state of disciples, he taught the excellent Dhamma endowed with qualities such as being well-expounded. The rest is according to the method already stated.
Thus, having described his own quality by means of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, the Blessed One now [describes] that very same quality...
Relying upon the Buddha’s resolve, he employs the word of truth: “This too is in the Buddha. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

However, it should be applied thus: “The noble jewel in the Buddha is this—that which he has known, that which he has given, that which he has brought forth, and that which he has taught—the nine supramundane states.”
The command of this verse was also received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
Thus, having spoken the Truth based on the Buddha through two verses concerning both the Dhamma of the scriptures and the supramundane Dhamma,
the Blessed One now [addresses] those who heard that Dhamma of the scriptures and, practicing according to what they had heard, [attained] even the ninefold [Tipiṭaka].
They attained the supramundane Dhamma; relying on their quality of having reached Nibbāna without residue, he again began to speak the Truth with reference to the Saṅgha, saying:
"The old is destroyed. Therein, "destroyed" (khīṇa) means cut off.

"The old" (purāṇa) means that which is ancient. "The new" (nava) means that which is currently occurring. "Non-arising" (natthisambhava) means the non-manifestation of what was not present. "With minds detached" (virattacittā).
Their minds are free from passion. "In future existence" means in a renewed state of being during the course of the future.
"They" refers to those for whom the old is exhausted and there is no production of the new, and whose minds are dispassionate toward future existence;
these are the bhikkhus whose taints are destroyed. "With seeds destroyed" means with the seed cut off. "Without desire for growth" means devoid of the desire for growth. "They go out" means...
They go out. "The wise" means those endowed with wisdom (*dhiti*). "Just as this lamp" means like this very lamp.

What is meant? That past karma of beings which, though having arisen and ceased, is ancient and belongs to a bygone time, remains indeed unexhausted because the moisture of craving has not been abandoned and it is still capable of bringing about rebirth-linking; that ancient [karma]...

The karma of those [Arahants] has been exhausted by the path of Arahantship because the moisture of craving has been dried up; like a seed burnt by fire, it is incapable of yielding fruition in the future.

Furthermore, the karma that is currently occurring for them through such acts as worshiping the Buddha is called "new," yet even that is incapable of yielding fruit in the future because its root has been severed by the abandonment of craving, like the flower of a tree whose roots have been cut.
Those for whom there is no further arising, and whose minds are dispassionate toward future existence through the very abandonment of craving—
those bhikkhus whose taints are destroyed are "destroyed in seed," because the rebirth-linking consciousness mentioned here as "kamma is the field,
consciousness is the seed" has been destroyed by the destruction of kamma. Furthermore, whatever desire they previously had for the growth known as renewed existence, that too...
Because they have abandoned [the defilements] precisely through the abandoning of their origination, they do not arise at the time of death as they did before;

because they lack the desire for growth and are endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*), these wise ones (*dhīra*)—through the cessation of the final consciousness—extinguish like this lamp that has gone out.
They transcend the path of designation (*paññatti-patha*) such as "possessing form" or "formless," and so forth. At that moment, it is said, the city deities...
When the lamps lit for the purpose of worship were extinguished, one lamp remained burning; pointing this out, he said: "Just as this lamp.

Thus, the Blessed One [described] the quality of those who heard the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) expressed in the two preceding verses, and by practicing in accordance with what they had heard, attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma) and reached the state of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna).
Having spoken thus, he now concluded the teaching with the words, "And this too is in the Saṅgha," while employing a declaration of truth (saccavacana) based on that very same quality.
Its meaning should be understood in the manner already explained; however, it is simply this:
in the Saṅgha there is the jewel consisting of the extinction (nibbāna) of those bhikkhus whose taints are exhausted, in the manner previously described.

It should be construed thus: "excellent. Furthermore, at the conclusion of this verse, the command was received by non-human beings throughout a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
At the end of the teaching, there was safety for the royal family, all calamities were pacified, and eighty-four thousand living beings attained realization of the Dhamma.
Then Sakka, lord of the gods, [thought]: "The Blessed One, relying on the virtues of the Triple Gem, has uttered a word of truth..."
Thinking, "The welfare of the city has been secured by him while he was engaged [in his task];
for the sake of the city's welfare, I too shall say something based on the qualities of the Triple Gem," he recited at the conclusion three verses beginning with, "Whatever beings there are here.
In this context, because the Buddha has come just as one should come when those who have exerted themselves for the benefit of the world arrive, [he speaks thus].
He is called "Tathāgata" because he has gone in the way that those [noble ones] must go; because he has understood in the way that they must understand;

because he knows in the way that it must be known; and because he has proclaimed that which is exactly so. Furthermore, because he is honored by gods and humans with external requisites such as flowers, perfumes, and the like, and through the practice of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammappaṭipatti), and so forth...
And because he was exceedingly honored by [the deity] born within himself, Sakka, the lord of the gods, gathered the entire assembly of deities together with himself and said:
"Let there be well-being as we pay homage to the Tathāgata, the Buddha, who is worshipped by gods and humans.

Furthermore, regarding the Dhamma, it is the path-dhamma which—just like the pair of oxen (*yuganandha*)—must proceed by the power of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) against the side of the defilements.

Because he has gone thus by completely cutting them off, he is called the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Dhamma of Nibbāna is also called the Tathāgata because it has been "gone to" (penetrated) by wisdom in such a way that it becomes effective for the destruction of all suffering; it was understood in this very manner by the Buddhas and others, and therefore it is called the "Tathāgata.
And because the Saṅgha also goes by those various paths in the same way as those practicing for their own welfare must go, [he is called the Tathāgata].
Because he has gone [thus], he is therefore called the "Tathāgata. Therefore, in the remaining two verses as well, it is said: "We pay homage to the Tathāgata and the Dhamma;
may there be well-being! We pay homage to the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha; may there be well-being! The rest is exactly according to the method already stated.
Thus, having spoken these three verses, Sakka, lord of the gods, circumambulated the Blessed One and returned to the city of the gods.

He departed together with the assembly of devas. The Blessed One, however, taught that very Ratana Sutta on the second day as well, and once again there was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings. In this manner, the Blessed One taught until the seventh day;
day after day, there was likewise a realization of the Dhamma. The Blessed One [taught] for exactly half a month.
Having stayed at Vesālī, [the Blessed One] informed the kings, saying, “Let us go.
Then the kings, with double the honor, led the Blessed One back to the banks of the Ganges in three days.
The Nāga kings born in the Ganges thought, “The humans are paying honor to the Tathāgata; why should we not do so? [And they prepared] vessels made of gold, silver, and jewels.

Having had boats constructed made of gold, silver, and jewels, and having prepared couches within them, they filled the water with lotuses of five colors and approached the Blessed One, saying, "Please show us your favor. The Blessed One consented;
he boarded a jeweled boat, as did the five hundred bhikkhus, each boarding their own boat. The nāga kings [honored] the Blessed One...
Together with the community of monks, they entered the abode of the nāgas. There, the Blessed One indeed taught the Dhamma to the assembly of nāgas throughout the entire night.
On the following day, they offered a great almsgiving of divine hard foods and soft foods.
After the Blessed One had expressed his appreciation, he departed from the nāga abode.
The earth-dwelling deities thought, "Humans and nāgas are paying honor to the Tathāgata; why should we not do so?
and they raised parasols and over-parasols upon the forest thickets, trees, mountains, and other places.
By this very means, an extraordinary display of great honor was established as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world. Bimbisāra, along with the Licchavis—
When he arrived, [the king] performed double the honors he had previously shown; and in the same manner as described before, he led the Blessed One to Rājagaha in five days.
When the Blessed One had arrived at Rājagaha, after the meal, while the monks were assembled in the Maṇḍalamāḷa, this discussion arose among them:
"Oh, how great is the power of the Buddha, the Blessed One, that for his sake the Ganges..."
“An area of eight yojanas from this side to that side—both the lowlands and the highlands—has been made level and strewn with sand and covered with flowers;
the water of the Ganges for a distance of one yojana is covered with lotuses of various colors;
and as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, parasols and double-parasols have been raised. Having learned of this occurrence, the Blessed One [emerged] from the fragrant chamber.
Having emerged and proceeded by means of a miracle appropriate for that moment, he sat down upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the pavilion.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, with what discussion are you sitting gathered here at present?
The bhikkhus reported everything to him. The Blessed One said this: "Bhikkhus, this is not..."
“This extraordinary honor for me has arisen through the power of the Buddha, not through the power of the nāgas, devas, or brahmās;

rather, it has arisen through the power of a small gift given in the past. The bhikkhus said, “We do not know, venerable sir, what that small gift was. It would be well if the Blessed One would tell us so that we might know it.”
The Blessed One said: "In the past, monks, there was a brahmin named Saṅkha in Takkasilā.
He had a son, a young brahmin student named Susīma, sixteen years of age.
One day, he approached his father, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. His father said to him: 'What is it, dear Susīma? He replied: 'I wish, father...'"
“Father, go to Bārāṇasī and learn a craft. “In that case, dear Susīma, there is a brahmin named so-and-so who is my friend;
go to him and learn it,” he said, and gave him a thousand kahāpaṇas.
Taking that money and paying homage to his parents, he gradually traveled to Bārāṇasī and, according to the prescribed etiquette, approached the teacher.
Having approached the teacher and paid homage, he introduced himself.
The teacher, recognizing him as "the son of my friend," accepted the young man and treated him with all the hospitality due to a guest.
Once he had dispelled the fatigue of his journey, he placed those one thousand kahāpaṇas at the teacher’s feet and requested permission to learn the craft. The teacher—
Having granted him the opportunity,
he had him learn. Learning both quickly and extensively, and retaining everything he learned without loss—
like lion’s oil poured into a golden vessel— he completed his twelve-year craft in just a few months.
While reciting it, he saw only the beginning and the middle, but not the end. Then, having approached his teacher, he said:
"In this craft, I see only the beginning and the middle; I do not see the end. The teacher said:
"I too, my dear, see exactly the same. "Then who, teacher, knows the end of this craft?"
“There are seers, dear one, at Isipatana; they will know. Having approached them, he said, “I ask you, teachers. “Ask, dear one, as you please.
He went to Isipatana, approached the Paccekabuddhas, and asked, “Do you know the beginning, the middle, and the end? “Yes, friend, we know. “Then teach that to me as well.”
“Therefore, friend, go forth; it is not possible to train without having gone forth. “Very well, venerable sir, let me go forth, or do whatever you wish and let me know when it is finished.

Having ordained him, they were unable to assign him a meditation subject, so they instructed him in the higher conduct by way of such rules as: “It should be worn thus; it should be put on thus,” and so forth.
They instructed him. While training there, because he was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), he soon after awakened to the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha.
Throughout all of Benares, he became renowned as "Susīma the Paccekabuddha," attaining the highest gain and honor, and surrounded by a complete retinue.
Because he had performed an action conducive to a short lifespan, he passed away into final Nibbāna before long.
The Paccekabuddhas and the great multitude of people, having performed the funeral rites for his body and taken the relics,
established a stupa at the city gate.
Then the brahmin Saṅkha, thinking, "My son has been gone for a long time, and I do not know his fate," desired to see his son.
Having departed from Takkasilā, he eventually reached Bārāṇasī.
Seeing a great multitude of people gathered there, he thought, "Surely among these many people, someone will know news of my son. Approaching them, he asked:
"Is there a young brahmin named Susīma who has come here? Do you perhaps know his whereabouts? They replied, "Yes."

“Brāhmaṇa, we know,” they said, “that in this city there was one who, having become a master of the three Vedas in the presence of a brāhmaṇa, went forth in the presence of paccekabuddhas, became a paccekabuddha, and attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue;
this stupa has been erected for him. Having struck the ground with his hand, he wept and lamented.
Having gone to that cetiya courtyard, he cleared away the grass, brought sand in his upper robe, and scattered it over the precincts of the Paccekabuddha’s cetiya.
He sprinkled water from his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) all over the ground, made an offering with wild forest flowers, and hoisted a banner with his upper robe.
Then, having tied his own sunshade to the top of the stupa, he departed.
Having thus shown the past, he connected that Jātaka with the present and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, it may be that you think, 'Perhaps at that time Saṅkha the brahmin was someone else.
But it should not be viewed in this way; at that time I myself was Saṅkha the brahmin."
I cleared away the grass on the terrace of the shrine of the Paccekabuddha Susīma;
as the result of that deed, they made the road eight yojanas long level and pure, removing all stumps and thorns.
I scattered sand there, and as the result of that, they scattered sand over the road for eight yojanas. There, with forest flowers by me...
Worship was performed; through the result of that, they spread a carpet of various flowers on both land and water for nine yojanas along the road.
There, I sprinkled the ground with water from my water-pot; through the result of that, a rain of lotuses fell in Vesālī.
There, I hoisted a banner upon that shrine and fixed a parasol; through the result of that—
"By the result of this [act], banners were raised as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, and parasols and super-parasols were hoisted.
Thus, monks, this particular distinction of my honor was produced neither by the power of the Buddhas, nor by the power of the Nāgas, Devas, or Brahmas;
rather, it was produced by the power of a small sacrifice. At the conclusion of this discourse on the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“By relinquishing limited pleasure, one may see abundant pleasure;
seeing that abundant pleasure, the wise person should renounce limited pleasure.
—From the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the Ratana Sutta in the Suttanipāta-ṭṭhakathā is finished.
2. Commentary on the Āmagandha Sutta:
“Sāmāka, ciṅgūlaka, and cīnaka”—this is the Āmagandha Sutta. What is its origin? Before the Blessed One had appeared, there was a foul odor (āmagandha).
A certain brahmin, having gone forth into the ascetic life together with five hundred young students, entered the Himālaya mountains.

Having caused a hermitage to be built in a mountain cleft, he dwelt there subsisting on forest roots and fruits, never eating fish or meat. Now, as those ascetics were not consuming salt, sour liquids, and the like—
Jaundice arose among them. Thereupon, thinking, "Let us go to a human settlement to partake of salt, sour gruel, and other provisions," they arrived at a frontier village.
There, the people gained confidence in them, invited them, and fed them.
After they had finished their meal, the people brought them beds, stools, utensils for use, foot-unguents, and so forth, saying, "Venerable sirs, dwell here; do not be disheartened."

Having shown them their dwelling place, they departed. On the second day as well, having given them alms, they continued to give alms to each of them in turn, one day at a time, following the order of their households.

After the ascetics had stayed there for four months, their bodies having attained firmness through the practice of salt and sour gruel and other such foods, they informed the people, saying, "Friends, we are going. The people [prepared] oil, rice, and other provisions for them.
They gave them. Taking those [fruits], they went back to their own hermitage. And they came to that village in this very same way year after year.
The people, knowing the time of their arrival, would remain having prepared rice and other provisions for the sake of giving;
and when they arrived, they honored them in that same manner.
Then the Blessed One, having arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, eventually arrived at Sāvatthī.
While residing there, he perceived the spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) of those ascetics;
consequently, departing from that place and wandering on tour surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he gradually reached that village. When the people saw the Blessed One, they offered great alms.
They gave [it]. The Blessed One taught them the Dhamma.
Through that teaching of the Dhamma, some among them became stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners; others went forth and attained arahantship.
The Blessed One returned again to Sāvatthī. Then those ascetics came to that village. The people—
Seeing that the ascetics were not as they had been before, the people were filled with curiosity. The ascetics asked them:

"Friends, why are these people not as they were before? Has this village been oppressed by royal punishment, or perhaps by famine, or has some renunciant endowed with superior qualities such as virtue arrived in this village? They...
They said, “Venerable sir, this village has not been afflicted by royal punishment nor by famine;
rather, a Buddha has arisen in the world, and that Blessed One, teaching the Dhamma for the welfare of many, has come here.
Having heard this, the ascetic Āmagandha asked, “Householders, do you say ‘Buddha’? “We say ‘Buddha,’ venerable sir.”
Having spoken thus three times, thinking, "Even this sound, 'the Buddha,' is rare in the world," he, being delighted, uttered words of delight and asked:
"Does that Buddha eat raw stench-food, or does he not?
"Venerable sir, what is 'raw stench-food'? "Householders, 'raw stench-food' means fish and meat. "Venerable sir, the Blessed One..."
“...and he eats fish and meat. Upon hearing this, the ascetic was filled with remorse, thinking, “May it not be that he is indeed a Buddha!
Then he thought, “The appearance of Buddhas is rare;
I shall go, see the Buddha, and ask him so that I may know. Thereupon, he asked people for the path leading to where the Blessed One was staying.
Like a cow greedy for her calf, he arrived at Sāvatthī with his entire retinue in great haste, staying only one night everywhere along the way, and entered the Jeta Grove itself.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated on his seat precisely for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
The ascetics approached the Blessed One and remained silent, without even offering a salutation.
They sat down to one side. The Blessed One exchanged greetings with them in the usual manner, asking, "I hope it is well with you, sages?
and so forth. They replied, "It is well, Master Gotama," and so forth. Then Āmagandha asked the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, do you eat 'raw stench,' or do you not? "What is this 'raw stench,' brahmin?"
“What is it, Master Gotama? “Fish-meat, Brahmin,” he replied. The Blessed One said, “Brahmin, fish-meat is not ‘raw stench.
Rather, ‘raw stench’ refers to all defilements, all evil and unwholesome states.
Having said this, he continued, “Brahmin, it is not only now that you asked about raw stench; in the past as well, a Brahmin named Tissa asked the Blessed One Kassapa about it.”
He asked. And thus he asked, and thus the Blessed One answered him.
Having brought forward these very verses spoken by the Blessed One to the brahmin Tissa and to Kassapa, and thereby persuading the brahmin with those verses, [the Blessed One] said:
“Sāmāka, ciṅgūlaka, and cīnaka... This, then, is the origin of this sutta here.
In the past, it is said, the Bodhisatta Kassapa, having fulfilled the perfections for eight incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons,
took rebirth in the womb of a Brahmin lady named Dhanavatī, the wife of the Brahmin Brahmadatta in Bārāṇasī.
On that very same day, his chief disciple also descended from the world of the gods and [took rebirth] in the womb of the Brahmin Anupurohita.
He was conceived in the womb of Pajāpatī. Thus, for them both, the taking of rebirth and the emergence from the womb occurred on the very same day;
on that same day, they were given names: one was named Kassapa and the other Tissa.
Playing together in the dust, those two companions grew up in due course. Tissa’s father commanded his son: “This, dear son—”
“Kassapa will go forth and become a Buddha; you too, having gone forth in his presence, should achieve liberation from existence.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he went into the presence of the Bodhisatta and said, “Friend, let us both go forth.
The Bodhisatta agreed, saying “Very well. Then, even when they had not yet reached maturity...
Tissa said to the Bodhisatta, “Come, friend, let us go forth,” but the Bodhisatta did not leave.
