Thinking, “His knowledge has not yet reached full maturity,” Tissa himself went forth, took up the ascetic life of an *isi*, and dwelt in a forest hermitage at the foot of a mountain.
Meanwhile, after some time, while the Bodhisatta was still remaining at home—
Having mastered mindfulness of breathing and having aroused the four jhānas and the higher knowledges (abhiññā), he went to the vicinity of the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) with his palace.
He then made this resolution: "May the palace be established once again in its very original place. It was established in its own place.
It is said that one who has not gone forth into homelessness is unable to approach the seat of enlightenment. Having gone forth and reached the seat of enlightenment, he—
Having sat down and applied himself to strenuous effort for seven days, he realized perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*) within those seven days.
At that time, twenty thousand renunciants were residing at Isipatana.
Then the Blessed One Kassapa addressed them and set the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*) in motion. At the conclusion of the discourse, they all became arahants. Indeed, that Blessed One...
Surrounded by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus, he dwelt right there at Isipatana. King Kikī of Kāsī served him with the four requisites.

Then one day, a certain man living in Bārāṇasī, while searching for the heartwood of sandalwood and other such materials on the mountain, arrived at the hermitage of the ascetic Tissa; having paid homage to him, he stood to one side. The ascetic—
Seeing him, he asked, "Where have you come from? "From Bārāṇasī, venerable sir," he replied.
"What is the news there? "Venerable sir, a Perfectly Enlightened One named Kassapa has appeared there.
Hearing these rare words, the ascetic was filled with joy and gladness and asked, "Does he eat raw meat, or does he not? "Who, venerable sir, would eat raw meat?"
“Is it raw meat? “It is fish and meat, friend. “Does the Blessed One, Bhante, eat fish and meat?
Having heard this, the ascetic became remorseful and thought again: “I shall go and ask him;
if he says, ‘I consume what is raw meat,’ then I will say to him: ‘Venerable sir, according to your birth, your clan, and your lineage...”
Thinking, “This is improper,” he restrained himself, went forth in the presence of that man, and resolved, “I shall effect my escape from existence.
Taking only light requisites and staying only one night everywhere on his journey, he arrived at Bārāṇasī in the evening and entered Isipatana.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated on his seat for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
The ascetic approached the Blessed One, but instead of paying homage, he stood silently to one side.
Seeing him, the Blessed One greeted him with a friendly inquiry in the same manner as previously described. He too, having said, "Is it bearable, Master Kassapa?
and so forth, sat down to one side and asked the Blessed One: "Do you eat 'raw-smell' food, Master Kassapa?"
“Do you not eat [it]? “I do not eat the raw stench, brahmin. “Excellent, excellent, Master Kassapa!
By not eating the carrion of others, you have done well; this is worthy of Master Kassapa’s birth, family, and lineage.
Then the Blessed One, referring to the defilements, said: “I do not eat the raw stench.”
“I say that the brahmin accepts fish and meat; what if I were to go tomorrow for alms not into the village, but instead consume the alms-food brought from the house of King Kikī?
In this way, a discussion concerning raw flesh will arise, and then I shall convince the brahmin through a teaching on the Dhamma.
On the following day, at an early hour, he performed his bodily preparations.

Having prepared it, he entered the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi). When the bhikkhus saw that the door of the Fragrant Chamber was closed, they realized, "The Blessed One does not wish to enter today with the bhikkhus," and so, keeping the Fragrant Chamber to their right, they entered for alms.
The Blessed One also emerged from the Fragrant Chamber and sat down on the seat prepared for him. The ascetic, too, having cooked the leaf-vegetables...
Having eaten, he sat down in the presence of the Blessed One. King Kikī of Kāsi, seeing the bhikkhus wandering for alms, asked, "Where is the Blessed One, venerable sirs?
Upon hearing, "In the monastery, Great King," he sent food to the Blessed One, consisting of various sauces and flavors and many kinds of meat preparations.
The ministers brought it to the monastery, informed the Blessed One, and [offered] the water of donation.
While serving him, they first gave rice gruel prepared with various kinds of meat. Seeing this, the ascetic stood there thinking, "Is he eating it?
Even as the ascetic watched, the Blessed One took a piece of meat into his mouth while drinking the gruel.
Upon seeing this, the ascetic became angry. Then, after he had finished the gruel, they served him a meal consisting of various flavorful side dishes.
Seeing him take even that and eat it, he became exceedingly angry and said, "While eating fish and meat, you say, 'I do not eat [meat]'!
Then, approaching the Blessed One after he had finished his meal, washed his hands and feet, and sat down, he said, "Master Kassapa, you speak falsely;
this is not the conduct of a wise man. For false speech is censured by the Buddhas."
"Even those seers who dwell at the foot of the mountains, subsisting on forest roots, fruits, and the like, do not speak falsehood," he said;
and then, praising the virtues of the seers with a verse, he spoke: "Sāmāka, ciṅgūlaka, and cīnaka...
(242). Therein, *sāmāka* refers to a species of grass-grain that is gathered by either shaking it or picking off the heads. Likewise...

By the mention of “the fruit of trees and creepers,” one should understand fruits such as *siṅghātaka* and *kaseruka* that grow in water.
“Obtained in accordance with the Dhamma” means obtained through the practice of gleaning in the forest, having abandoned wrong livelihoods such as acting as a messenger or going on errands.

“The virtuous ones” (*satā*) refers to the noble ones (*ariyā*). “While eating” (*asnamānā*) means while consuming food. “Not speaking falsehood out of desire for sensual pleasures”—thus they [spoke].

Free from "mine-ness" and without possessions, these seers, while consuming such things as wild rice (*sāmāka*), do not speak falsely when they say, "O Brahmin, I do not consume 'raw stench' (*āmagandha*)," whereas you, longing for sensual pleasures such as sweet flavors and the like, are indeed consuming raw stench.
Thus, those who desire pleasure do not speak falsely; those who long for sensual pleasures do not utter lies—so it was said of the seers.
By means of praise for the Blessed One, he reveals censure.

(243) Having thus censured the Blessed One under the pretext of praising the seers (*isī*), he now speaks—censuring the Blessed One directly by showing the object of his own intended censure—with the words "yad asnamāno. In this context, the letter *da-* [is used].

This is the construction of the words. The meaning is as follows: whatever meat—whether it be the flesh of a quail or the flesh of a partridge—that has been well-prepared by prior preparation such as washing and cutting, and well-finished by subsequent preparation such as cooking and seasoning;
and which was not given by a mother or a father, but rather was given by others who, out of desire for the Dhamma, thought, "This person is worthy of offerings"; [that is what is meant].
Eating and consuming food that is prepared with honor, refined, and adorned— exquisite because of its superior flavor,
its nutritional essence, and its capacity to sustain strength and power— and not merely meat, but indeed even this very rice-food,
white rice-gruel from which the black grains have been winnowed: it is such as this that you eat, Kassapa.
“Foul smell! You, who eat whatever meat you find while consuming this fine rice—Kassapa, you eat ‘foul smell’!
Thus he addressed the Blessed One by his clan name.
Having thus reviled the Blessed One regarding his food, he now spoke, reviling him by charging him with falsehood: “No...”
“Raw stench... [etc. ...by those well-prepared. The meaning of this is: Previously, when questioned by me, you spoke thus, “Raw stench is not allowable for me”;
in this way you speak with absolute certainty. He speaks thus while reproaching him, saying, “O *brahmabandhu*—a mere Brahmin by birth who lacks the qualities of a true Brahmin.
“Rice-gruel of fine rice” means boiled rice made from fine rice grains. “While enjoying” means while eating.
"By means of well-prepared bird meat"—saying this, he was pointing out the bird meat that had been brought to the Blessed One at that time.

And while speaking thus, looking up at the Blessed One’s body from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair, he saw the perfection of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, as well as the fathom-wide aura; and seeing such a one, [he thought: "One of such a form..."
One whose body is adorned with the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) and so forth is not fit to speak falsehood.
For even in other existences, it was solely through the result of truthful speech that a single white, soft hair, like cotton-wool, grew between his eyebrows;
and from each and every pore, hairs grew individually. How then could he now speak falsely? Surely there must be some other "stench" in him.
Thinking, "There must be something he has in mind for which he said, 'Brahmin, I do not eat raw stench';
what if I were to ask him about this? he felt great respect arise and, addressing him by his clan name, spoke this remainder of the verse:
"I ask you this matter, Kassapa: of what kind is your 'raw stench'?"
245. Then the Blessed One, in order to dispel that "raw stench," spoke these words beginning with "killing living beings" (*pāṇātipāta*).
Therein, "killing living beings" means the slaughter of living beings. Regarding "killing, cutting, and binding": here, "killing" is the beating of sentient beings with sticks and the like;
"cutting" is the severing of hands, feet, and so forth; "binding" is the fettering with ropes and the like. "Theft and false speech" refers to both theft and lying.
*Ca*. "Deception" (*nikati*) means causing disappointment after having generated hope by such means as saying, "I will give," or "I will do.
"Frauds" (*vañcanāni*) refers to making one accept what is not gold as being gold, and so forth. "Quackery" (*ajjhenakutta*) is the useless mastery of many books.

"Adultery" (*paradārasevanā*) is engaging in sexual conduct with women who are under the protection of another. "This is a foul-smelling thing, for it is not the eating of meat"—[this is the meaning].
This practice of unwholesome states such as the destruction of life is a raw stench, a putrid stench, a corpse-like stench. For what reason?
Because it is unpleasant, because it is mixed with the impurities of the defilements (*kilesa*), because it is loathsome to the virtuous, and because it brings about an extremely foul state of odor.
Indeed, those beings whose defilements are excessive become exceedingly foul-smelling because of them; even the dead body of one free from defilements [is not so].

It does not have a foul odor; therefore, it is called "raw-flesh-smell" (*āmagandha*). However, meat-eating that is unseen, unheard of, and unsuspected is blameless; therefore, meat-eating is not indeed "raw-flesh-smell.
Having thus answered the question regarding "raw-flesh-smell" by means of a single method through this teaching based on the Dhamma, [the Blessed One] now—since...
Those various beings were possessed of those various "raw stench" (āmagandha) qualities; it was not that every single one possessed them all, nor that all possessed the same one.

Therefore, in order to reveal those various raw stench qualities of theirs, he spoke two verses by way of addressing individuals in the teaching, beginning with the words, "Those people here who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures," thus setting forth the raw stench.
In this context, "those who are unrestrained here in sensual pleasures" refers to those ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) in this world who,

lacking restraint and having broken their moral vows, are unrestrained even toward their mothers, maternal aunts, and others— toward those things known as sensual pleasures consisting in the pursuit of sense-objects.
"Greedily attached to flavors" means they are greedy, infatuated, maddened, and clinging to flavors cognizable by the tongue, failing to see the danger therein.

They enjoy flavors with wisdom that lacks deliverance. "Mingled with impurity" means that, due to that greed for flavors, they are mingled with the impurity known as various kinds of wrong livelihood for the sake of obtaining those flavors.
"Possessing the view of nihilism" means being endowed with the ten-based wrong view, such as "there is no gift," and so forth.

"Uneven" means being endowed with uneven bodily action and so forth. "Hard to lead" means difficult to instruct, being endowed with the stubborn adherence to one's own views, holding firmly to them, and being difficult to relinquish.
"Raw stench" (*āmagandha*) is that which has been demonstrated by means of this verse with reference to a person:

"lack of restraint in sensual pleasures, greed for flavors, failure in livelihood, the view of nihilism, bodily misconduct, and other forms of unevenness, as well as the state of being difficult to follow.
Furthermore, by the same meaning already stated previously, the raw stench should be understood as sixfold. "Not indeed meat-eating"—[this refers to] meat-eating.
However, by the very meaning already stated, it is not a "raw stench" (āmagandha).
Regarding the second verse as well: "those who are coarse" (lūkhasā) means those who are harsh and tasteless; the sense is that they are devoted to self-mortification.
"Cruel" (dāruṇā) means hard-hearted and prone to difficult speech. "Backbiters" (piṭṭhimaṃsikā) refers to those who speak sweetly in one's presence but [act otherwise] behind one's back.
Those who speak dispraise. For these, being unable to look one in the face, are like those who eat the flesh on the back of those with their backs turned;
therefore they are called "back-biters" (*piṭṭhimaṃsikā*). "Deceivers of friends" (*mittadduno*) means deceivers of friends;
it is said that they act wrongly toward those friends who have placed trust in them regarding their wives, wealth, and lives. "Merciless" (*nikkaruṇā*).
Devoid of compassion, they desire the harm of sentient beings. "Arrogant" means: "In this case, someone, on account of birth...
[or] on account of some other basis, treats others with contempt; such pride, a state of mind desiring to display it"—those who possess such arrogance as described here.
"Having a nature of non-giving" means those whose disposition is not to give, who are intent on not giving, and who delight in not sharing. Not...
"And they give nothing to anyone" means that because of their habit of not giving, even when asked, they do not give anything to anyone;
though appearing like humans, they belong to the class of *nijjhāmataṇhika* petas who were formerly from families that gave nothing.
Some, however, read it as "ādānasīlā," meaning they are merely of a habit of taking, but they do not give anything to anyone. This is the stench of raw flesh, for it is not the eating of meat.
This has been explained by way of reference to individuals through this verse: "Austerity, harshness, backbiting, treachery toward friends,
mercilessness, arrogance, lack of generosity, and lack of giving"— thus, by the same meaning already stated previously,
the eightfold "stench" (*āmagandha*) should be understood, and not merely as the eating of meat.

248. Having thus spoken two verses by way of a teaching based on persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), [the Buddha] again, having understood the underlying disposition (*āsaya*) of that ascetic, spoke one verse by way of a teaching based on phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*).
Therein, anger (*kodha*) is to be understood according to the method explained in the *Uragasutta*.
Pride (*mada*) is [to be understood] according to the method in the *Vibhaṅga* beginning with "pride of birth, pride of clan, pride of health," and so forth.

The state of being agitated in the mind is what has been described as its classification. "Stiffness" (*thambho*) is the state of being rigid. "Obstruction" (*paccupaṭṭhāpanā*) means the act of setting up opposition;
it is standing in contradiction to that which has been stated according to the Dhamma and the proper method.

"Deceit" (*māyā*) is the concealment of evil deeds performed, as analyzed in the *Vibhaṅga* by way of the passage beginning, "Here someone, having practiced misconduct with the body... "Envy" (*usūyā*) [is the resentment] toward the gains, honor, and so forth of others.
Envy (*issā*). A "pile-up of talk" (*bhassasamussayo*) means talk that has been piled up;
what is meant is self-exaltation. "Pride and overweening pride" (*mānātimāno*): "In this case, someone—on account of birth...

or on account of some other basis—regards himself as equal to others at an earlier time, but later regards himself as superior and others as inferior; such pride... [and so on] ...the desire for a flag."
This is analyzed in the *Vibhaṅga* [as] "of the mind. "Familiarity with the unrighteous" means intimacy with unworthy persons.
"This is a raw stench, not the eating of meat": this ninefold mass of unwholesome states, beginning with anger, should be understood as a "raw stench" in the sense already stated previously;
it is "not the eating of meat."

249. Having thus shown the ninefold "stench of raw flesh" (*āmagandha*) through a teaching based on the Dhamma, he spoke three verses to explain those same stenches through a teaching based on individuals (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), following the same method as previously stated.

Therein, "those of evil conduct" (*pāpasīla*) refers to those who are well-known in the world as "of evil conduct" due to their wicked behavior. "Debt-killers and informers" (*iṇaghātasūcaka*)... [text continues]
According to the method stated in the *Vasala-sutta*, those who take a loan and fail to repay it are "debt-killers"; those who use slander are "informers.
Here, "cheats in business" refers to those who stand in the place of the upholders of the Dhamma (*dhammaṭṭha*) and, having taken bribes, defeat the rightful owners;

they are called "cheats in business" because they possess fraudulent dealings, and they are called "counterfeits" (*pāṭirūpika*) because they are mere imitations of the upholders of the Dhamma. Then...

"Or here" means in this Teaching (*sāsana*). "Counterfeiters" (*pāṭirūpikā*) refers to those of immoral conduct (*dussīla*); for because they possess a semblance (*paṭirūpa*) of the virtuous through their excellence of deportment and so forth, they are "counterfeit" (*paṭirūpa*), and being counterfeit, they are "counterfeiters" (*pāṭirūpika*).

"Those who are the lowest of men and commit evil here" refers to those who, being the lowest of men in this world, commit toward their parents, the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and others, that which is termed wrong practice (*micchāpaṭipatti*).
They commit evil deeds. This "raw stench" (*āmagandha*) is not indeed the eating of meat; this has been demonstrated by means of this verse with reference to specific persons:
"bad character, debt-burdening, betrayal, fraudulent business, forgery, and the committing of evil deeds.
Furthermore, by the same meaning already stated previously, this "raw stench" should be understood as sixfold: "it is not indeed the eating of meat."

250. Those people who here are unrestrained toward living beings—those individuals in this world who, by acting according to their own whims, kill even a hundred or a thousand creatures, being unrestrained because they do not practice even the slightest compassion;
and those who, having seized the property of others—whether wealth or life—engage in harming them, or [seize it] from those who entreat them, saying, "Do not do this."
They are intent on harassing others with their hands, clods of earth, sticks, and so forth;
or they have taken other beings captive and, having vowed, "Today ten, today twenty," are intent on harassing them with killing, binding, and the like.

They are unvirtuous and cruel because of their lack of moral discipline and their wicked conduct; they are fierce because of their cruel deeds and their blood-stained hands—namely, fishermen, hunters, fowlers, and the like.
"Here" refers to what is intended in this context. "Harsh" means harsh speech. "Disrespectful" means devoid of respect, thinking, "We will not do it now;

we will refrain from such things. This "stench of raw flesh," namely "meat-eating," is indicated here by way of a specific person, and it includes both what was previously stated—by way of the method beginning with "killing living beings, slaughter, cutting, and binding"—and what was not previously stated.
“Lack of restraint toward living beings, harming others, immorality, greed, harshness, and lack of respect”—this sixfold ‘stench of raw flesh’ (āmagandha) is to be understood;

it is not merely the eating of meat. For even though it was stated previously, it is stated again for such reasons as to arouse the listeners' desire to hear, to ensure their comprehension, and to provide reinforcement. And for that very reason, later on...
He will say: “The Blessed One, who has reached the further shore of the mantras, has declared this matter again and again; he has made it known.
(251) “Those who are greedy for these, hostile toward them, and destroyers of life”: through greed they are greedy for these living beings; through hatred they are hostile toward them;
and through delusion, failing to see the danger, they are destroyers of life by repeatedly committing transgressions against them—or [it refers to] “the taking of life” regarding these.

Regarding the evil kamma described by such methods as "killing, cutting, and binding," those who are greedy, hostile, and murderous—meaning those possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion—corresponding to these acts, are "constantly engaged" (*niccuyyutā*): they are perpetually intent upon performing unwholesome deeds, never abstaining from them even when reflecting upon them.
"Having passed away" (*pecca*) means having gone from this world to the next; they go to darkness.
Those beings who fall headlong into hell, or those who go into the darkness known as the intermediate space between worlds, or into the darkness consisting of low birth and the like;
and those beings who fall headlong—meaning with their heads turned downward—into hells such as Avīci:
for these beings, this foul odor is the cause of being born in darkness and falling into hell, namely, this division of greed, hostility, and violence.
In the sense already explained, the threefold "raw stench" (*āmagandha*) is the root of all foul odors.
For while there is indeed the eating of meat, the eating of meat itself is not the "raw stench.
Thus, having rejected the "raw stench" in its ultimate sense and having revealed its nature as the path to miserable rebirths, the Blessed One—

Now, demonstrating that he was incapable of purifying himself—and others like him—regarding the consumption of fish and meat, [the Blessed One] spoke this six-line verse beginning with "Not fish or meat. In this regard:
[The ascetic], while eating fish and meat, perceived it as a raw stench and as the path to a miserable rebirth; desiring purity by abstaining from it, he did not eat it.
[The verse is spoken] to show his inability to purify himself and others of such a kind. Therein:

All the phrases should be construed with the final phrase: "Neither fish and meat purify a person who has not crossed over doubt, nor does the offering of oblations and seasonal sacrifices purify a person who has not crossed over doubt"—thus it is said.
And here, the ancient teachers explain that "neither fish and meat" means that fish and meat, when not being eaten, do not purify; likewise for fasting.
But it might be even more appropriate [to say]: "The fasting from fish and meat does not purify one from the non-fasting of fish and meat;
the fasting from fish and meat does not cleanse one, O King. If that were so, would it not follow that fasting is abandoned?
That is not so, because it is included within the austerity of immortality. As it is said: "And those many ascetics in the world who are immortal... [in this context].

For indeed, everything remaining that has been mentioned is included within self-mortification. "Nakedness" means the state of being unclothed (*acelakatva*). "Shaven-headedness" means the condition of having a shaved head.
"Matted locks and dust" means both matted hair and the dust and dirt [that covers it]. "Rough antelope skins" means coarse skins of the black antelope.
"Attendance upon the fire-sacrifice" means the practice of tending the sacrificial fire. "Immortals" refers to the bodily afflictions practiced for the sake of aspiring to the state of immortality.
"Many" means numerous, categorized by such practices as the exertion of squatting. "Austerities" (*tapas*) refers to the mortification of the body. "Mantras" are the Vedas.

"Offerings" (*āhuti*) are the rites of fire-sacrifice (*aggihoma*). "Sacrifices and seasonal observances" (*yañña-utu-pasevana*) refers both to sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (*assamedha*) and to seasonal observances.
Seasonal observances consist of: staying in the heat of the sun during the summer, staying at the foot of a tree during the rainy season, and entering the water during the winter.

"They do not purify a person who has not crossed over doubt" means they do not purify a person who has not crossed over uncertainty regarding either purification from defilements (*kilesa*) or purification from existence (*bhava*).
For as long as the stain of doubt exists, one is not purified; and you, indeed, still possess doubt.

And here, regarding the phrase "one who has not crossed over doubt," having heard [the prohibitions] such as "not fish meat" and so forth, [one might wonder]: "What, then, is the nature of fish and meat?"...
When the ascetic’s doubt arose as to whether "the path to purification might be through fasting and such," it was said by the Blessed One that it "might be so"—
this is our intended meaning. Furthermore, it should be understood that this was said with reference to the doubt that arose in him toward the Buddha upon hearing that "he eats fish and meat."

253. Having thus demonstrated that abstaining from fish, meat, fasting, and so forth, are incapable of purifying [one], he now speaks this verse beginning with "Guarded in the sense-faculties" (sotesu gutto) to show those qualities capable of purifying.
In this context, "in the sense-faculties" (sotesu) refers to the six sense-faculties. "Guarded" (gutto) means endowed with the protection of restraint over the faculties.
By this much, he demonstrates the virtue consisting of the retinue of restraint over the faculties (indriyasaṃvara-parivāra-sīla).

"One who has understood the faculties" (*viditindriyo*) means that having understood the six faculties through full comprehension by knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), one should conduct oneself, making them manifest;
"one should dwell," is what is meant. By this much, he shows the discernment of name-and-form for one whose virtue is purified.

"Established in the Dhamma" means established in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths to be realized by means of the Noble Path. By this, he shows the stage of stream-entry (*sotāpattibhūmi*). "In straightforwardness and gentleness" (*ajjavamaddave*)...
"Delighting in" means delighting in uprightness (*ujjubhāva*) and in gentleness (*mudubhāva*). By this, he shows the stage of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*);
for a once-returner, due to the attenuation of greed and hatred—which cause crookedness of body and so forth, as well as stiffness of mind—delights in uprightness and gentleness.
"Transcending attachment" means transcending the attachment of greed and hatred; by this, he shows the stage of the non-returner (*anāgāmī*). "One who has abandoned all suffering" means...
By abandoning the cause of all the suffering of saṃsāra, he has abandoned all suffering. By this, he shows the stage of Arahatship.

"The wise one is not smeared by what is seen or heard": having thus attained Arahatship through successive stages, the wise one—endowed with steadfastness—is not smeared by any defilement regarding things seen or heard. And it is not only regarding things seen and heard...
And he does not cling to things cognized by the mind; rather, having attained supreme purity, he concludes the teaching with the summit of Arahantship.
Following this, two verses beginning with "Thus this meaning" were spoken by the compilers of the collection.
Their meaning is as follows: Thus the Blessed One Kassapa, again and again, through many verses, [taught] by way of the Dhamma and by way of the person.
And he explained, spoke, and detailed it through his teaching until the ascetic understood.

"He who has mastered the mantras perceived that"—meaning that the brahmin Tissa, a master of the mantras (*mantapāragū*) and a master of the Vedas (*vedapāragū*), perceived and understood both that meaning and [the teaching]. For what reason?
Because the Sage (*muni*) had revealed it through various verses, according to its meaning, its words, and its method of exposition. Of what sort was it?

"Free from the stench of raw flesh (nirāmagandha), unattached (asita), and difficult to lead (durannaya)": he is "free from the stench of raw flesh" due to the absence of the defilements of the stench of raw flesh;

he is "unattached" due to the absence of reliance on craving and views; and he is "difficult to lead" because it is impossible for anyone, by means of external views, to lead him [astray] with the thought, "This is better," or "This is superior.
Having heard these well-spoken words and the well-delivered Dhamma teaching of the Buddha who has thus proclaimed them...

Having heard that which is free from the stench of raw flesh, joined with the absence of defilements, the dispeller of all suffering, and the dispeller of the suffering of the entire cycle of existence, the brahmin Tissa—with humbled mind and humbled heart—paid homage to the Tathāgata; he prostrated himself before the feet of the Tathāgata with his five limbs touching the ground.
And right there, while Kassapa was seated on his seat, he expressed his desire for the going forth.
The ascetic Tissa expressed his desire for the Blessed One’s going-forth; that is to say, he requested it. The Blessed One said to him, "Come, monk.
At that very moment, equipped with the eight requisites, he arrived through the air and, like a monk of a hundred years' standing, paid homage to the Blessed One.
Within just a few days, having penetrated the knowledge of the disciple's perfections, he was named Tissa.
The first chief disciple was [Tissa], and the second was named Bhāradvāja. Thus, that Blessed One had a pair of disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja.
As for our own Blessed One, there were the three verses first spoken by the brahmin Tissa and those spoken by Kassapa.
The Blessed One recited nine verses in the middle, and the compilers of the collection then brought forward the two verses at the end;
having thus introduced all fourteen verses and made it complete, he explained the "Stain of Raw Meat" (*āmagandha-sutta*) to the five hundred ascetics headed by their teacher.
Having heard that, the brahmin likewise became humble in mind and paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
He requested the going-forth together with his retinue. “Come, monks,” the Blessed One said.

Having attained the status of "come, monk" in that very manner, they came through the air, paid homage to the Blessed One, and within a few days, all of them were established in the fruit of the highest attainment, Arhatship.
(From the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.)
The commentary on the Āmagandha Sutta in the Suttanipāta-ṭīkā is finished.
3. Commentary on the Hirī Sutta:
"Crossing over with shame" is the Hirī Sutta. What is its origin? Before the Blessed One had arisen, in Sāvatthī, a certain...
There was a wealthy brahmin mahāsāla whose fortune consisted of eight hundred million pieces of wealth. He had an only son who was dear and beloved to him.

Raising him with various kinds of pleasant comforts like a young god, he passed away together with his brahmin wife, without having handed over that inheritance to him. Then, for that young man’s mother and father...
After a short while, the treasurer opened the inner chamber and, presenting the property, said:
"Master, this belongs to your mother and father; this belongs to your grandfather and grandmother;
this has come down through seven generations. When the young man saw the wealth, he thought: "Only the wealth itself is seen, but by whom was this..."
Though they were accumulated, they are not seen [now]; all have fallen under the power of death. And as they departed, they did not go taking anything from here;
indeed, one must depart for the next world leaving behind such wealth. It is not possible to take anything with one, except for the wealth of good conduct.
What if I were to renounce this wealth and take up the wealth of good conduct, which is possible?
"and depart. Day after day, while distributing a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he thought again:
"This wealth is abundant; what is the use of such a small sacrifice? Suppose I were to give a great gift. He informed the king:
"Great King, there is this much wealth in my house; I wish to give a great gift with it."
“Give it away. It would be well, Great King, if you were to have a proclamation made throughout the city. The king had this done.
He filled the vessels of those who came one after another and gave away all his wealth within seven days. Having given it away, he thought:
“Having made such a great renunciation, it is not fitting for me to live at home; what if I were to go forth? Then he told this matter to his attendants.
He informed them. They said, "Master, do not think that your wealth is exhausted;
we shall accumulate a store of riches by various means in a short time," and they entreated him in many ways.
But he, disregarding their entreaties, went forth into the ascetic life.

In this regard, there are eight kinds of ascetics: those with wives and children, those who live by gleaning, those who eat only what they have obtained at the proper time, those who do not cook over fire, those who use their fingernails as a mortar, those who use their teeth as a mortar, those who eat only fallen fruit, and those who eat only fruit detached from the stalk.

Among these, "those with wives and children" refers to those such as Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic and others, who went forth together with their sons and wives and made their living through agriculture, trade, and so forth.
"Those who live by gleaning" (*uñchācārika*) are those who have a hermitage built at the city gate, where they teach crafts and other skills to the sons of kshatriyas, brahmins, and others;
having rejected gold and silver, they accept allowable goods such as sesame and rice. They are superior even to householders with their wives and children.
"Those who take what is timely" (*sampattakālika*) are those who take food that has arrived at the time for eating.
Those who subsist by this means are superior to those who live on gleanings. "Not cooking with fire" means those who subsist by eating fruits from trees that have not been ripened by fire;

they are superior to those who eat what is obtained at the proper time. "Eaters of stone-powder" means those who wander about carrying a handful of stones or some other tool such as an axe or a knife, and when they become hungry, [they take fruit] from a tree that has come into their reach.
Having taken and eaten the bark, they resolve upon the factors of the Uposatha and develop the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*);
these are superior to those who do not cook with fire. "Those who live on tooth-sticks" refers to those who wander about without even taking stone mortars and the like;
at times of hunger, having torn off the bark from a tree they encounter with their teeth, they eat it and resolve upon the factors of the Uposatha and [develop] the divine abodes.
Those who cultivate [these virtues] are superior even to those who live on their own excrement. As for the "those who eat what falls":

dwelling near a natural lake or a forest grove, they eat whatever lotus roots, stalks, and so forth are found there in the lake, or whatever flowers there are in the grove during the flowering season and fruit during the fruiting season;
when flowers and fruit are absent, they eat even the bark of the trees there.
They eat and dwell there, but they do not go elsewhere for the sake of food. They observe the precepts of the Uposatha and cultivate the divine abodes (brahmavihāra);

they are superior even to the tooth-pickers. Those called "stalk-pearl" (vaṇṭamuttika) eat only the fallen leaves of the stalk-pearl trees; the rest is the same as before, and they are the very best of all.
But this son of a brahmin family, thinking, "I shall go forth in the foremost of the ascetic renunciations," went forth specifically in the Vaṇṭamuttika renunciation.
Having crossed over two or three mountains in the Himalayas, he built a hermitage and dwelt there.
Then the Blessed One, having arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, eventually arrived at Sāvatthī and stayed in Sāvatthī.

He was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time, a certain man from Sāvatthī, while searching for the heartwood of sandalwood on the mountain, arrived at his hermitage; having paid homage, he stood to one side.
Seeing him, [the ascetic] asked, “Where have you come from? “From Sāvatthī, venerable sir. “What is there?”
“Is there progress? “In that place, venerable sir, people are diligent in performing meritorious deeds such as giving.

“Having heard whose instruction? “The Buddha, the Blessed One. At the sound of the word “Buddha,” the ascetic was struck with wonder and asked three times, in the same manner as when he had spoken of the “stench of raw flesh”: “Do you say ‘Buddha,’ good man? “Even the sound—”
Thinking, "This one is indeed rare," he was delighted and, desiring to go into the presence of the Blessed One, reflected:
"It is not fitting to go into the presence of a Buddha empty-handed; what, then, should I take with me? He thought again:
"Buddhas do not value material things; well then, I shall go taking the gift of the Dhamma."
He formulated four questions:
"What kind of friend should not be cultivated? What kind of friend should be cultivated?
What kind of practice should be undertaken? And what is the foremost of tastes?"
Taking those questions with him, he set out toward the Middle Country and, traveling by stages, arrived at Sāvatthī and entered the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated on his seat for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, he did not pay homage but stood to one side. The Blessed One addressed him in this manner: "O seer, I hope you are faring well," and so forth.

He exchanged greetings with him. The brahmin, having likewise exchanged greetings in the manner beginning with "Is it bearable, Master Gotama?", thought, "If he is a Buddha, he will answer the questions asked mentally by means of speech," and so he asked the Blessed One those questions mentally.
When the Blessed One was questioned by the brahmin, in order to answer the first question, he spoke the verse beginning with *hiriṃ tarantaṃ*.
Having begun, he spoke two and a half verses.

256. Their meaning is as follows: *Hiriṃ tarantaṃ* means crossing over or transcending shame—that is, the shameless one who lacks modesty. *Vijigucchamānaṃ* means looking upon [shame] as if it were impurity.
For the shameless person loathes shame and looks upon it as if it were filth; therefore, by that...
He does not associate with nor does he adhere to [them]. Therefore it is said, "feeling disgust. "Speaking thus:
'I am yours'" means speaking in such a manner as, "Friend, I am your companion; I desire your welfare and your happiness; even my life has been surrendered for your sake.
And "not undertaking tasks that are possible" means that even after speaking in this way, [he does not perform] those tasks that are possible...
One who does not undertake or take up even those tasks that can be done for him;

or rather, one who does not show even the slightest regard for them with his mind, but instead shows only distress when duties arise—“He is not mine,” thus one should recognize such a person: “This is a counterfeit friend; he is not my true friend.”
Thus should a wise person understand.
257. "Incoherent" means that which does not follow upon the purpose one declares, saying, "I shall give," or "I shall do.
"He who utters pleasant speech toward friends" refers to one who greets with words concerning the past and future, yet [speaks] without substance.
While seeking to win them over, he utters pleasant words to his friends merely through the mere shadow of the literal expression.
Regarding such a person who speaks without acting—whom the wise understand as one who does not act but speaks—the wise discern him, defining him thus:
"This is a 'speech-obsessed' enemy, a counterfeit friend. It is in this way that the wise recognize him.
258. He is not a friend who, though always heedful, suspects division and looks only for faults.
This refers to one who, fearing only a rift, dwells constantly heedful through artificial and formal conduct;
whatever is done out of forgetfulness or lack of attention, or left undone out of ignorance, he does so thinking, "When he reproaches me, then I shall counter-accuse him with this."
Thus, one perceives only a flaw; such a friend is not to be cultivated.
Having thus answered this first question—"What kind of friend is not to be cultivated?"—the Blessed One spoke this half-verse, "In whom he lies," in order to answer the second.
Its meaning is: in whichever friend that [other] friend enters, having penetrated his heart...
Just as a son lying on his father’s breast lies there free from apprehension, without suspecting that "if I lie here on his breast,
there might be pain or displeasure for him," so too, placing his trust in wife, wealth, life, and so forth,
he lies free from apprehension through the state of friendship. And he who [is trusted] by others— even for a hundred or a thousand reasons—
"Having spoken thus, he is unshakable; he indeed is a friend who should be cultivated.
(259) Having thus answered the second question—"What kind of friend should be cultivated?"—the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "causing joy" in order to answer the third.
Its meaning is as follows: it causes joy (*pāmujja*), therefore it is "joy-causing" (*pāmujjakaraṇa*).
"Ground" (*ṭhāna*) means a cause. But what is that? It is energy (*vīriya*).

For that, being associated with the Dhamma, is called "the producer of gladness" because it generates the happiness of rapture and joy. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, in a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, he who has aroused energy dwells happily.
It brings praise, thus it is "praise-bringing. From the beginning, it brings the happinesses of the divine and human realms.
It is "bliss" (*sukha*) by way of figurative designation for the fruit, because it brings about the bliss of Nibbāna at its conclusion.

It is the "advantage of the fruit" (*phalānisaṃsa*) because one expects the fruit from it. "He develops" means he increases. "Bearing the human yoke" means dwelling while having taken up a burden appropriate for a man;
such a person develops this state known as the energy of right striving (*sammappadhāna-vīriya*), thinking, "Such an application should be practiced."

260. Thus, having answered the third question—“What kind of practice (payoga) should be employed?”—the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with “The flavor of seclusion” (pavivekarasa) in order to answer the fourth.
Therein, “seclusion” (paviveka) refers to the supreme fruit (aggaphala), because it arises from seclusion from the defilements (kilesa).
Its “flavor” (rasa) is the pleasure associated with that fruit, in the sense of its being a source of gratification. “Tranquility” (upasama) also...
Because it has arisen through the subsiding of the defilements, or because its object is the subsiding known as Nibbāna, that very [joy] is such;
and the flavor of the joy of the Dhamma is also that very [joy], because it is the flavor of the rapture arising from the Dhamma known as Nibbāna, which is not apart from the Noble Dhamma.
Having drunk that flavor of seclusion and the flavor of subsiding, and drinking that very flavor of the joy of the Dhamma, one becomes free from distress.
"Free from evil": even after drinking, he is "without fever" because of the absence of the fever of the defilements; even while drinking, he is "free from evil" because evil has been abandoned.

Therefore, this is called the foremost of tastes. However, some connect these three qualities—the taste of seclusion and so forth—with the reviewing of jhāna and Nibbāna, and with the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites; yet the former [explanation] alone is superior. Thus...
The Blessed One, answering the fourth question, brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the brahmin went forth in the presence of the Blessed One and, within just a few days, attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and became an Arahant.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Hirī-sutta of the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
The first volume is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Sutta Nipāta in the Khuddaka Nikāya (Second Part)
2. Cūḷavagga 4.
Commentary on the Maṅgalasutta.
"Thus have I heard" is the Maṅgalasutta. What is its origin? It is said that in Jambudvīpa, here and there—in city gates, assembly halls, meeting halls, and so forth—
A great multitude of people gathered together and, giving gold and bullion, engaged in various kinds of external talk concerning the abduction of Sītā and other such matters;
each individual discourse was concluded only after the lapse of four months. On one occasion, a discussion on auspiciousness arose among them:
"What indeed is auspicious? Is it that which is seen as auspicious, heard as auspicious, or touched as auspicious?"
“Who knows what is auspicious?
Then a certain man named Diṭṭhamangalika said: “I know what is auspicious. What is seen is auspicious in the world;
‘what is seen’ means a form that is considered highly auspicious. For example, here someone, having risen early in the morning...”
Or he sees a cātaka bird, or a beluva staff, or a pregnant woman, or young children, or a full water-jar adorned and prepared,
or a raw red fish, or a thoroughbred horse, or a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds, or a bull, or a cow, or a tawny animal;
or whatever other such form he sees that is regarded as auspicious— this...
"It is called 'the seen as an auspicious sign. Some accepted his words, while others did not.
Those who did not accept them argued with him.
Then a certain man named Sutamaṅgalika said: "Sir, this so-called eye sees both the pure and the impure."
Likewise, both the beautiful and the ugly, the pleasant and the unpleasant—if what was seen by him were auspicious, then everything would be auspicious;
therefore, what is seen is not auspicious. Rather, what is heard is auspicious.
"What is heard" refers to a sound regarded as highly auspicious, such as: here someone, having risen early, recites [the Veda].
"Or 'increasing,' or 'full,' or 'prosperous,' or 'joyful,' or 'glory,' or 'increase of glory'—or whatever sound he hears that is generally regarded as auspicious, such as:
'Today is a favorable constellation, a favorable moment, a favorable day, a favorable omen'—this is called the 'auspiciousness of what is heard. Some accepted his words, while others did not.
They did not accept it. Those who did not accept it argued with him about that matter.
Then a certain man named Mutamaṅgalika said: "For indeed, sirs, this ear hears both the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant.
If everything heard by it were auspicious, then everything would be auspicious."
Therefore, what is heard is not an auspicious factor; rather, what is sensed is an auspicious factor. By "sensed" is meant that which is regarded as highly auspicious:

odors, tastes, and tangibles. For example—here someone, having risen early, smells the fragrance of flowers such as the lotus, chews a tooth-stick of *puṣpa* wood, touches the earth, or touches green crops or fresh cow dung.
or a tortoise, or a sesame carrier, or a flower, or a fruit; or he touches it, or he smears himself well with yellow clay, or he puts on a yellow robe, or he wears a yellow turban;
or whatever else of this kind is considered an auspicious omen, whether he smells a fragrance, tastes a flavor, or touches a tangible object.
or touches—this is called the blessing of what is heard. Some accepted his words, while others did not.
Among them, Diṭṭhamangalika was unable to convince either Sutamangalika or Mutamangalika, nor could either of those two convince the other two.
And among those people, those who had accepted the words of Diṭṭhamangalika [said]: “Only what is seen...
They concluded, "It is *maṅgala*. Those who took up the words of Suta, Mutta, and Maṅgalikā concluded, "Only what is heard is *maṅgala*, only what is sensed is *maṅgala*.
Thus, this discourse on *maṅgala* became well-known throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
Then, people throughout the whole of Jambudīpa gathered in groups and pondered over *maṅgala*, asking, "What indeed is *maṅgala*?"
When the guardian deities of those people heard that talk, they likewise reflected upon auspicious signs.
The earth-dwelling deities were friends to those deities; having heard it from them, the earth-dwelling deities also likewise reflected upon auspicious signs.
The space-dwelling deities were friends to those deities as well, and the deities of the Realm of the Four Great Kings were friends to the space-dwelling deities.
By this same means, as far as the Sudassī deities and even the Akaniṭṭha deities became friends, they too, having heard from them, gathered in clusters and likewise reflected upon auspicious signs.
Thus, throughout all the ten thousand world-systems, the reflection on auspicious signs arose.
And once arisen, although it was being determined as "this is an auspicious sign, this is an auspicious sign," it continued to spread.

Without reaching a decision, twelve years passed. All humans, devas, and Brahmas—except for the noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*)—were divided into three groups according to what they had seen, heard, or inferred.
Not even one person reached a conclusion as to the true nature of the matter, thinking, "This alone is the auspicious sign" (*maṅgala*);
instead, a clamor regarding auspicious signs arose in the world.

There are five kinds of tumultuous cries: the tumult of the world-age (*kappa-kolāhala*), the tumult of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-kolāhala*), the tumult of a Buddha (*buddha-kolāhala*), the tumult of auspiciousness (*maṅgala-kolāhala*), and the tumult of nobility (*moneyya-kolāhala*).
In that regard, the gods of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara-deva*) have their turbans fallen off and their hair disheveled;
with tearful faces, they wipe away their tears with their hands, dressed in red garments and wearing exceedingly hideous attire.
Having offered the sacrifice, he said: "At the end of one hundred thousand years, the dissolution of the aeon will occur. This world will be destroyed;

the great ocean will dry up; and this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be consumed by fire and perish, until the destruction of the world reaches as far as the Brahma-world. Friends, cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, and gladness."
“Venerable sirs, cultivate equanimity; attend upon your mothers; attend upon your fathers; be respectful toward the elders of the family; be vigilant; do not be negligent.
Having wandered along the human paths, they proclaim this. This is called the "clamor concerning the eon" (*kappa-kolāhala*).

Only the deities of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara-deva*), having wandered along the human paths, proclaim: “At the passing of a hundred years, a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) will arise in the world. This is called the "clamor concerning the wheel-turning monarch" (*cakkavatti-kolāhala*).

The Suddhāvāsa deities, having adorned themselves with Brahma-ornaments and placed the Brahma-diadem upon their heads, filled with joy and gladness, proclaim while praising the virtues of the Buddha as they wander through the human realm:
"At the end of a thousand years, a Buddha will arise in the world.
This is called the "Buddha-proclamation" (buddhakolāhala).

The deities of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), having known the minds of human beings, wander along the paths frequented by humans and proclaim: "After twelve years have passed, the Perfectly Enlightened One will discourse on the blessings. This is called the "clamor of blessings" (maṅgalakolāhala).

The deities of the Pure Abodes alone, [knowing] that "after seven years have passed, a certain bhikkhu will approach the Blessed One and inquire about the practice of the state of a sage (moneyya)," wander along the paths frequented by humans and proclaim it. This is the "clamor of the state of a sage" (moneyyakolāhala).
Thus it is called. When these five kinds of clamor— divided into three types such as "seeing what is auspicious" and so forth—
had arisen among gods and humans in the world, and when gods and humans, having searched and searched among themselves, were unable to find any [true] auspicious signs, [they looked to] the twelve...
At the end of the rains, the deities belonging to the Tāvatiṃsa host gathered together and deliberated thus:
"Just as, dear sirs, a master of a house is foremost among those within the house, a lord of a village among the village dwellers,
and a king among all men, even so this Sakka, lord of the gods, is our chief and our best, that is to say, by virtue of his merit and his splendor."
"By virtue of his sovereignty and wisdom, Sakka is the lord of two divine worlds. What if we were to ask Sakka, the lord of the devas, about this matter?

Having said this, they went into the presence of Sakka. There they found Sakka, the lord of the devas, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, seated upon a magnificent throne of yellow silk, his body resplendent with garments and ornaments suited to the occasion, surrounded by a retinue of two hundred and fifty million nymphs.
Having paid homage and stood to one side, they said this: "Please, dear sir, you should know that at present questions regarding auspiciousness have arisen.
Some say that what is seen is auspicious; some say that what is heard is auspicious; some say that what is sensed is auspicious.
In this matter, both we and others have reached a deadlock. It would be well if you were to explain it to us as it truly is."
“Please explain it. The King of the Gods, who was naturally wise, asked, “Where did this discourse on auspiciousness first arise?
They replied, “We heard it from the gods of the Four Great Kings, O King. Then the gods of the Four Great Kings [recounted it] to the space-dwelling deities;
the space-dwelling deities to the earth-dwelling deities; the earth-dwelling deities to the deities who protect humans; and the deities who protect humans...
“They have arisen in the world of humans,” they said.
Then the Lord of the Devas asked, “Where does the Perfectly Enlightened One dwell? “In the world of humans, O Devas,” they replied.
“Has anyone questioned that Blessed One? they asked. “No one at all, O Devas,” they replied. “What indeed is it, dear sirs? he asked.

"Abandoning the fire, light the glowworm! You who think that you should question me, passing over that Blessed One who is the teacher of every auspicious thing—come, sirs, let us question that Blessed One;
we shall surely receive a beautiful answer to our questions. Thus he commanded one son of the gods: "You, [go to] the Blessed One..."

“Ask,” [said the Blessed One]. That son of the gods, having adorned himself with ornaments appropriate for that moment, shining like lightning and surrounded by a host of deities, arrived at the Great Monastery of Jeta’s Grove.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side, he addressed him with a verse while asking a question on auspiciousness. The Blessed One [answered] that question of his.
While answering, he spoke this sutta.
Therein, the meaning of "Thus have I heard" and so forth has been stated in brief in the commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta;
however, those who desire a detailed account should take it according to the method explained in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
In the *Kasibhāradvāja Sutta*, it is said: "He was dwelling among the Magadhans at Dakkhiṇāgiri, in the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa";
here, however, it says: "He was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Therefore, beginning with this word "Sāvatthī," we shall now provide an explanation of the words not previously discussed.
“Seyyathidaṃ, Sāvatthiyaṃ” means in the city named Sāvatthī. It is said that this was the dwelling place of the seer Savattha;
therefore, just as Kusamba’s dwelling place is called Kosambī and Kākaṇḍa’s dwelling place is called Kākaṇḍī, so too, by way of the feminine gender, it is called “Sāvatthī.
However, the ancients explain it thus: because at that place, when there was a gathering of weapons...
When asked, "What goods are there? they replied, "Everything is there.
Taking that statement as its basis, it is called "Sāvatthī" (All-Exists). In that Sāvatthī—by this, its village of resort is indicated. A prince named Jeta;
because it was planted and nurtured by him, it is the "Jeta’s Grove" (Jetavana); in that Jetavana. For those who are without a protector...
"Anāthapiṇḍika" means one who has "a ball of alms-food" (*piṇḍa*) for those who are without a protector (*anātha*); thus it refers to that Anāthapiṇḍika. The meaning is:
"in the monastery completed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika through the relinquishment of forty-five crores. By this, his dwelling place suitable for renunciants is indicated.
The word *atha* is used in the sense of non-interruption, while *kho* is a particle used to indicate a change of subject. By that, [it is shown] that it was indeed uninterrupted...
Therein, he shows that "this other incident arose" while the Blessed One was dwelling [there]. What is it? "A certain deity," and so forth.
Therein, "a certain" (*aññatarā*) is an indefinite designation; for she was not well-known by name or clan, and therefore she is called "a certain.
A *deva* itself is a *devatā*; this term is common to both male and female, but here it refers to a man.
He was indeed a son of the gods, but he is called "deity" by way of a common designation.
Regarding the phrase "when the night had advanced," the word *abhikkanta* is seen in the senses of passing away, beautiful, handsome, and expressing approval, among others.
In that context: "The night has advanced, venerable sir; the first watch has passed; the community of monks has been seated for a long time."
In such passages as "Let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus," it is seen in the sense of *destruction*.
In such passages as "This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons," it is seen in the sense of *beautiful*.
"Who is worshipping my feet, shining with the glory of psychic power?"...
“In the phrases ‘With surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions,’ it refers to one who is handsome.

In phrases such as ‘Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! it refers to rejoicing. But here it refers to the passing away [of time]. Thus, by the phrase ‘at the passing of the night,’ what is meant is ‘when the night has completely worn away.

In the expression ‘abhikkantavaṇṇā’ (of surpassing beauty), the word *abhikkanta* refers to being handsome, while the word *vaṇṇa*, however, refers to complexion, praise, lineage, class, cause, shape, measure, the sense-base of form, and so forth.”
It is seen. In this context, in such passages as “The Blessed One is golden-hued,” it refers to the skin.
In such passages as “But when, householder, were these praises of the ascetic Gotama uttered by you? it refers to praise.

In such passages as “There are these four castes, Master Gotama,” it refers to the social class. And in the passage “Now, by what quality is one called a ‘seeker of fragrance’? it refers to [fragrance].
In such cases as these, it refers to the cause. In such cases as “having manifested the form of a great king of elephants,” it refers to shape.

In such cases as “there are three colors of the bowl,” it refers to measure. In such cases as “color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence,” it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
Here, however, it should be understood as the skin; by this, it is meant that she possesses a most excellent complexion and a beautiful skin.
Regarding the term *kevalakappa*: here the word *kevala* has many meanings, such as "without remainder," "for the most part," "unmixed," "not exceeding," "firm," "disjoined," and so forth.
For instance, in such passages as “the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that is complete (*kevala*), perfect, and pure,” its meaning is "without remainder.
Likewise, in the passage, “And the people of Aṅga and Magadha, having taken abundant hard food and soft food, will approach [the Blessed One],” it means "for the most part" or "entirely."
In such cases as these, it is "preponderance. In such cases as "There is the origin of this entire mass of suffering," it is "unmixedness.
In such cases as "Surely this venerable one has only mere faith," it is "non-excess.
In such cases as "Venerable sir, the venerable Anuruddha’s co-resident named Bāhika has stood for the schism of the entire Saṅgha," it is... [as above].
“Firmness of purpose. In such passages as “He is called a solitary one, one who has lived the life, a supreme person,” it means dissociation.
But here its meaning is intended in the sense of “without remainder.
Furthermore, this word *kappa* has many meanings, including: conviction, conventional usage, time, designation, cutting off, alternative, a small portion, and all-inclusiveness.
For instance, in such passages as, "This is indeed to be settled by the venerable Gotama, since he is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened one," its meaning is *abhisaddahana* (firm conviction).
In such passages as, "I allow you, monks, to consume fruit according to the five monastic conventions (*samaṇakappa*)," its meaning is *vohāra* (convention or usage).
And in such passages as, "By which, indeed, I always abide according to the convention (*niccakappa*)," [its meaning is usage].
Time. In such passages as “Thus the venerable Kappa,” it means designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as “adorned, with hair and beard trimmed,” it means cutting (*chedana*).

In such passages as “the two-finger-breadth allowance is permitted (*kappati*)”, it means modification (*vikappa*). In such passages as “there is the opportunity (*kappo*) to lie down,” it means a slight amount (*leso*).
In such passages as “having illuminated the entire (*kevalakappa*) Veḷuvana grove,” it means all-aroundness (*samantabhāvo*). Here [in this context]...

The meaning intended here is its state of being all-around (*samanta-bhāva*). Therefore, regarding the phrase "the entire Jeta’s Grove" (*kevalakappaṃ Jetavanaṃ*), the sense should be understood as "the Jeta’s Grove in its entirety, on every side.
"Having illuminated" (*obhāsetvā*) means having pervaded with radiance; the sense is that he made it a single expanse of light and a single blaze, like the moon or the sun.
"Approached the place where the Blessed One was": here the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative;

the meaning should be understood as "he approached that place where the Blessed One was. Or alternatively, the meaning should be understood as: "by whatever reason the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans, by that very same reason he approached him. And for what reason is the Blessed One [to be approached]?

Is he to be approached? He is like a great tree that bears fruit constantly, which flocks of birds approach with the intention of attaining various distinguished qualities and with the intention of enjoying sweet fruit. "He approached" (*upasaṅkami*) means "he went. "Having approached" (*upasaṅkamitvā*) indicates the completion of the act of approaching.
Alternatively, having gone in this manner, he reached a place even closer to the Blessed One.
It is also said that she went as far as what is reckoned as "nearby. "Having paid homage to the Blessed One" means having bowed to the Blessed One, having prostrated, having reverenced.

"To one side" is a neuter locative designation; it means to a single place or to a single spot. Alternatively, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. "She stood" is a negation of sitting and so forth; the meaning is that she took her standing position, that she remained standing.
But how did she stand, standing to one side?
“Neither behind nor in front, neither too near nor too far;
not in the armpit, nor in the lee, nor even where it was sloping down or up.”
"Having avoided these faults, they stood to one side.
But why did she stand and not sit down? It was because of her desire to depart quickly.
For devas come to the human world for some purpose, like a pure person coming to a place of excrement. By nature...
From five hundred yojanas onwards, the human world becomes repulsive due to its foul odor, and they do not take delight there.
Therefore, having performed her duty upon arrival, she did not sit down because of her desire to return quickly.
Furthermore, the exhaustion resulting from postures such as walking—which is what they seek to dispel by sitting—does not exist for the devas.
Therefore he did not sit down. And as for those great disciples who stood surrounding the Blessed One, he dismissed them;
therefore they too did not sit down. Moreover, it was out of reverence for the Blessed One that he did not sit down.
For when devas desire to sit, a seat manifests for them; yet, not desiring it and not even directing their minds toward sitting, he stood to one side.
"Standing to one side, that deity"— thus, for these reasons, she stood to one side.
"She addressed the Blessed One with a verse" means she spoke to the Blessed One with speech composed of syllables,
words, and fixed metrical structure.
261. In that context, "many" (*bahū*) is a designation for an indefinite number. By this, it is meant that there are many hundreds, many thousands, and many hundreds of thousands.
They "shine" (*dibbanti*), thus they are "gods" (*devā*); the meaning is that they sport with the five strands of sensual pleasure, or they shine by means of their own glory.
Furthermore, gods are of three kinds, according to convention (*sammuti*), rebirth (*upapatti*), and purity (*visuddhi*). As it has been said:
“There are three kinds of deities: conventional deities, deities by birth, and deities by purification.
Among these, ‘conventional deities’ refers to kings, queens, and princes. ‘Deities by birth’ refers to the deities beginning with those of the Four Great Kings and those above them.
‘Deities by purification’ refers to those called Arahants.”
Among those, the gods of rebirth (*upapatti-deva*) are intended here. They are called "human beings" (*manussa*) because they are the offspring of Manu.
However, the ancients say: "They are human beings because of the abundance of mind (*manas*). They are fourfold: those of Jambudīpa, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and Pubbavideha.
Here, those of Jambudīpa are intended. "Auspicious" (*maṅgala*) means that these seven are auspicious; [they are so called] because of their success (*iddhi*).
The meaning is: "and they attain growth. *Acintayuṃ* means they thought. *Ākaṅkhamānā* means wishing, longing for, and yearning for.

*Sotthānaṃ* means the state of well-being; what is meant is the existence of all beautiful, excellent, and auspicious qualities pertaining both to this present life and to future lives. *Brūhi* means teach, explain, and declare.
"Explain it clearly; make it manifest. "Auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*) means the cause of success, the cause of growth, and the cause of all prosperity.
"Supreme" (*uttama*) means distinguished, excellent, and bringing welfare and happiness to the entire world. This is the word-by-word commentary on the verse.
As for the summarized meaning: that son of the gods, desiring to hear the discourse on auspiciousness from the deities throughout the ten thousand world-systems...
Having assembled in this single world-system, even within the space of a single hair-tip, they manifested ten,
twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, and eighty subtle bodies; then, having surpassed all devas, Māras, and Brahmas in glory and splendor,
they beheld the Blessed One seated upon the excellently prepared Buddha-throne, shining with majesty.

Seeing them standing there surrounding him, and at that time, having known with his own mind the mental reflections of all the people throughout Jambudīpa who had not yet arrived, and for the purpose of extracting the arrow of doubt from all gods and humans,
he said: "Many gods and humans have reflected upon auspicious signs, desiring their own well-being and their state of safety."
“Desiring it, speak the supreme blessing! Being questioned by me with the consent of those gods and out of favor toward human beings,
O Blessed One, out of compassion for us, please speak that which is the supreme blessing, since it brings about absolute welfare and happiness for all of us.”
262. Having heard these words of the deva-son, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with “Non-association with fools.

In this context, *asevanā* means not associating with, not attending upon, or not honoring. Regarding the term *bālānaṃ*: they are called “fools” (*bālā*) because they merely breathe; the intention is that they live by the mere act of inhaling and exhaling, and not by the life of wisdom (*paññājīvita*).
As for the phrase “of those fools, [the opposite] of the wise” (*paṇḍitānaṃ*): they are called “wise” (*paṇḍitā*) because they possess discernment (*paṇḍanti*).
The intention is that they proceed by way of knowledge regarding matters pertaining to the present life and the future life. Of those wise ones:
"service" means attending upon, revering, waiting upon, being their companions, and being devoted to them; "worship" means honoring, respecting, esteeming, and saluting;
"of those worthy of worship" means of those deserving of worship; "this is the supreme blessing" refers to both the non-service of fools and the service of the wise.
Service and the honoring of those worthy of honor—all this taken together, he says, "This is the supreme blessing.
Regarding what you asked—"Tell me the supreme blessing"—it is meant here that you should take it as: "This is the supreme blessing.
This is the word-by-word commentary on that verse.
The commentary on this [verse] should be understood as follows: Having heard these words of the devaputta, the Blessed One spoke this verse.
In that regard, discourse is fourfold: discourse asked, discourse unasked, discourse with a sequence, and discourse without a sequence.
Therein, [the Blessed One said]: "I ask you, Gotama of vast wisdom: how acting is a disciple..."
In such instances as, "It is well," and "How indeed, dear sir, did you cross the flood?"—when one who has been questioned speaks—this is "discourse when questioned" (*pucchitakathā*).

In such instances as, "What others call happiness, that the Noble Ones call suffering"—when one speaks by one's own inclination even without being asked—this is "discourse not [previously] questioned" (*apucchitakathā*). All the discourse of the Buddhas is of this nature.
“Monks, I teach the Dhamma with its cause,” because of these words, it is a discourse with a logical sequence (*sānusandhikathā*).

In this dispensation, there is no discourse without a logical sequence. Thus, among these types of discourses, this is a "discourse on what was asked" (*pucchitakathā*), since it was spoken by the Blessed One when questioned by the son of a deva.
And in a discourse on what was asked, just as a clever man is skilled in the path and skilled in what is not the path, [so too is the speaker].
Having first explained what must be abandoned when asked about the path, he subsequently explains what should be taken:
"At such-and-such a place there is a forked road; there, leaving the left and taking the right.

In this way, regarding those things to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated, having explained that which is not to be cultivated, he explains that which is to be cultivated. And the Blessed One is like a man skilled in the path. As it has been said:
“‘A man skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

For he is skilled in this world, skilled in the other world, skilled in the realm of death, skilled in the realm beyond death, skilled in the realm of Māra, and skilled in the realm beyond Māra. Therefore, first, one should not associate with him.
Explaining what should be cultivated, he said: “Not associating with fools, and associating with the wise.
For just as one first avoids a path that must be abandoned, so too fools should not be associated with nor attended upon;
thereafter, just as one takes a path that must be followed, so too the wise should be associated with and attended upon.
But why, when the Blessed One was teaching on auspiciousness, did he first speak of not associating with fools and associating with the wise?
It is said: because, through associating with fools, gods and humans grasped at this view of auspiciousness regarding the seen and so forth;
and since that is actually inauspicious, [the Blessed One spoke thus] to show them that such association with unwholesome friends destroys their welfare in this world and the next.

By censuring [the former] and by praising association with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta), which accomplishes the welfare of both worlds, the Blessed One first spoke of not associating with fools and associating with the wise.
In this context, "fools" refers to any beings who are possessed of the unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapatha), such as the taking of life; they are [described] in three ways:
They are to be known as such. As it is said in the Sutta: "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool.
Furthermore, the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa; Devadatta, Kokālika, Kaṭamodaka, Tissa Khaṇḍadeviyāputta, Samuddadatta, and Ciñcamāṇavikā;
and in the past, Dīghavidassa’s brother—these and other such beings are to be understood as fools.
Like embers set ablaze by fire, they destroy themselves and those who follow their words through their own misapprehension—
just as the brother of Dīghavidas was cast face down into the Great Niraya hell with a body sixty *yojanas* in height to roast for the interval between four Buddhas,
and just as the five hundred families who delighted in his view suffered the same fate.
Having been reborn in companionship with them, they are cooked in hell. For it has been said:

"Just as, monks, a fire released from a reed-thicket or a grass-thicket burns even gabled houses—those plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with doors bolted and windows closed—even so, monks, whatever fears there may be..."
Whatever misfortunes arise, all of them arise from the fool, not from the wise person. Whatever calamities arise... [and so on] ...whatever afflictions arise...
[and so on] ...they arise from the fool, not from the wise person. Thus, monks, the fool is full of peril, while the wise person is free from peril;
the fool is beset by misfortune, while the wise person is free from misfortune; the fool is beset by affliction, while the wise person is free from affliction.”
Furthermore, the fool is like rotten fish, and one who associates with him is like a leaf-basket containing rotten fish; he incurs the state of being discarded and loathed by the wise.
And this has been said: “Just as a man who carries rotten fish on a blade of kusa grass finds that even the kusa grass becomes foul-smelling, so it is from associating with fools.”
And when Sakka, the lord of the devas, was offering a boon, the wise Akitti said:
“May I neither see nor hear a fool, nor dwell with a fool;
may I neither engage in conversation or discourse with a fool, nor take pleasure in him.”
“What has this fool done to you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa.
For what reason, Kassapa, do you not wish to see this fool?
“The witless man leads one into ruin; he yokes one to what is not his burden.”
"One of poor judgment is better than one who, when rightly spoken to, becomes agitated;
he does not understand discipline, and it is better not to see him.
Thus the Blessed One, censuring in every way the companying of fools, declared that not associating with fools is "an auspicious sign" (*maṅgala*).
Now, praising the service of the wise, he said: "The service of the wise is an auspicious sign.
In this context, those called "wise" are any beings endowed with the ten courses of wholesome action, beginning with abstention from taking life;
they are to be known by three characteristics. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a wise person."

Furthermore, it should be understood that the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the eighty great disciples, and other disciples of the Tathāgata— such as Sunetta, Mahāgovinda, Vidhura, Sarabhaṅga, Mahosadha, Sutasoma, King Nimi, Ayoghara-kumāra,
Akitti the Wise, and others— are truly wise. To them,
[the Dhamma] is like protection in the face of danger, like a lamp in the darkness, and like the acquisition of food and drink when one is overcome by the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and so forth.
They are capable of destroying all fears, calamities, and misfortunes for those who act according to their word.

For it is by coming to the Tathāgata that incalculable and immeasurable gods and humans have attained the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*), established themselves in the Brahma-world, established themselves in the world of the gods, and been reborn in the world of happy destinies. Having inspired confidence in the Elder Sāriputta—
Having attended upon the Elder with these four conditions, eighty thousand families were reborn in heaven.
