Likewise, among all the great disciples beginning with Mahāmoggallāna and Mahākassapa, some of the Teacher Sunetta’s disciples arose in the Brahma-world, while others attained companionship with the Paranimmitavasavatti devas... [and so on].
Some were reborn into companionship with great householder clans. And this has been said:
“Bhikkhus, there is no fear from the wise, no calamity from the wise, and no misfortune from the wise.

Furthermore, the wise person is like fragrant goods such as tagara and garlands; one who associates with them is like the leaf that wraps those fragrant goods, and thus attains refinement and agreeableness in the eyes of the discerning. And this has been said:
“The man who wraps tagara with leaves—
though it is only the petals that waft the fragrance— so too is the service of the wise.
And when Sakka, the lord of the devas, was offering a boon, the wise Akitti spoke thus:
“Behold the wise one, listen to the wise one, dwell together with the wise one;
engage in conversation and discussion with the wise one, and take delight in that.
“What has the wise one done for you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa.”
“By what means, Kassapa, do you desire the vision of the wise one?
“The wise man leads by the right method; he does not yoke himself to what is not his burden.
The right method is superior; when spoken to rightly, he does not become angry.”
“He understands the Vinaya; it is good to associate with him.

Thus, while the Blessed One praised associating with the wise in every respect and declared that such association with the wise is a “blessing,” he now [describes] how, through that very non-association with fools and association with the wise, one gradually attains the state of being worthy of honor.
Praising the worship of those who have arrived, he said: "Worship of those worthy of worship—this is the supreme blessing.
In this context, those "worthy of worship" are the Blessed Buddhas, because they are free from all faults and endowed with all virtues;
following them are the Paccekabuddhas and the noble disciples (ariyasāvakas). For even a small amount of worship offered to them leads to welfare for a long time.
It leads to happiness; here, the jasmine garland-maker Sumana and others serve as examples.

We shall cite one example from among them. It is said that one day, during the morning, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then, the jasmine garland-maker [Sumana] of King Māgadha...

While going along after taking flowers for Seniya Bimbisāra, he saw the Blessed One who had arrived at the city gate—gracious, inspiring confidence, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, and blazing with the glory of a Buddha.
Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him: "The king has taken flowers worth a hundred or a thousand..."
"Or if one were to give it, that would result in happiness pertaining only to this world;
however, an offering to the Blessed One yields immeasurable and incalculable fruit, bringing benefit and happiness for a long time. Come now, let me honor the Blessed One with these flowers.
With a mind full of faith, he took a handful of flowers and threw them toward the Blessed One; the flowers went through the air and reached the Blessed One.
Having become a canopy of garlands above, they remained there. Seeing that supernatural power, the garland-maker’s heart became even more serene, and he threw another handful of flowers;

these went and remained as a floral cloak. In this manner, he threw eight handfuls of flowers, which went and remained as a pavilion of flowers. The Blessed One appeared as if he were inside that pavilion.
A great multitude of people gathered together. Seeing the garland-maker, the Blessed One manifested a smile.
The Elder Ānanda, thinking, "Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition," asked the reason for the smile. The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, by the power of this offering, this garland-maker will [dwell] among devas and humans for a hundred thousand eons."
"And having wandered through the cycle of existence, at its conclusion, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Sumanissara.
At the conclusion of these words, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"That deed is well done which, having been done, one does not regret."
“Whose [deed] one, thrilled and joyful, experiences as its result.
At the conclusion of this verse, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma.
Thus, it should be understood that even a small act of worship toward them leads to welfare and happiness for a long time. And that is merely material worship; what then—?

This is the discourse on the worship of practice. Since those sons of noble family worship the Blessed One with their own virtues—namely, by going for refuge, by undertaking the training precepts, by observing the factors of the Uposatha, and by the fourfold pure morality and so forth—who could describe the fruit of their worship?
For it is said that they worship the Tathāgata with the supreme form of worship. As it has been said:
“Ānanda, whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, lay follower male or female,
dwells practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing correctly, and living in conformity with the Dhamma, they honor, revere, esteem, worship,
and pay homage to the Tathāgata with the highest form of worship.”
Following this same principle, it should be understood that making offerings to Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples (ariyasāvakas) also brings about welfare and happiness.
Furthermore, among householders, one’s elder brother or sister is worthy of honor by a younger sibling;
likewise, parents are worthy of honor by a son, and for daughters-in-law, the husband, mother-in-law, and father-in-law are worthy of honor. Indeed, making offerings to these as well—

Because they are comprised of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) and because they are the cause for the increase of longevity and so forth, they are indeed auspicious (*maṅgala*). For this has been said:
"They will be filial toward their mothers, filial toward their fathers, respectful toward recluses, respectful toward brahmins, and honoring those who are senior in the family;
having undertaken this wholesome state (*kusala dhamma*), they will conduct themselves accordingly. By reason of undertaking those wholesome states, they will increase in longevity..."
"...and they will increase in beauty," and so forth.
Thus, in this verse, three blessings are stated: not associating with fools, associating with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor.

Among these, "not associating with fools" is a blessing because it is a cause for welfare in both worlds, by providing protection from the fear and other dangers that arise from associating with fools.
Service to the wise and honoring those worthy of honor should be understood as "auspicious" because they are causes for Nibbāna and happy rebirths,
according to the method already stated in the commentary on the manifestation of their fruits. Hereafter, however, without displaying the full list of headings,
we shall define whatever is auspicious in each case and clarify its nature as an auspicious factor.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, "And the non-association with fools," is concluded.

263. Thus, although requested with only one phrase—"Speak of the supreme blessing"—the Blessed One, like a noble person who gives much even when asked for little, spoke of three blessings in a single verse;
thereafter, [he continued] because of the deities' desire to hear more.

And because of the existence of auspicious factors, and with the desire to enjoin various beings here and there to those specific auspicious things that are suitable for them, he began to speak again on many auspicious factors through such verses as "Dwelling in a suitable locality" (*patirūpadesavāso*).
Therein, in the first verse, "suitable" (*patirūpa*) means appropriate. "Locality" (*deso*) refers to a village, a town, or a city.
“Country” (*janapada*) refers to any place where beings dwell. “Dwelling” (*vāsa*) means residing there. “Formerly” (*pubbe*) means in past, bygone births.
“Having performed merit” (*katapuññatā*) means having accumulated wholesome deeds (*kusala*). “Self” (*atta*) refers to the mind, or the entire personal existence (*attabhāva*).
“Right aspiration” (*sammāpaṇidhi*) means the right directing, engaging, or placing of that self; this is what is meant.
"The rest is exactly as previously stated"—this is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*) here.
The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows:

A "suitable place" (*patirūpadesa*) is where the four assemblies dwell, where the bases for performing meritorious deeds such as giving are practiced, and where the ninefold teaching of the Teacher shines forth. Dwelling there—

It is called a "mangala" (auspiciousness) because it serves as a condition for beings to perform meritorious deeds. In this regard, the fishermen who entered the island of Siṃhala and others are examples.
According to another method: a "suitable place" refers to the site of the Blessed One’s seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); the site where the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion;
and the site at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree where, in the midst of an assembly twelve leagues wide, he shattered the doctrines of all other sectarians and displayed the Twin Miracle.
The place of the descent of the gods, or any other place where Buddhas and others have resided, such as Sāvatthī and Rājagaha;
dwelling there is called a "mangala" (auspicious) because it is a condition for sentient beings to obtain the six unsurpassed attainments.
Another method: in the eastern direction there is a market town named Kajaṅgala, and to its west is Mahāsālā.
Beyond that are the bordering districts; on this side of it is the Middle Country.
In the southeast direction is the river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side of it is the Middle Country.
In the south direction is the market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side of it is the Middle Country. In the west direction is Thūṇa...
There is a brahmin village named [Name], beyond which lie the bordering districts; on this side lies the Middle Country.
To the north is the mountain named Usiraddhaja, beyond which lie the bordering districts; on this side lies the Middle Country.
This Middle Country is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference.
This is what is called a "suitable place.
Here, among the four great continents and two thousand minor islands, universal monarchs (*cakkavatti*) arise who exercise sovereign power and lordship;
and having fulfilled the perfections (*pāramitā*) for one incalculable eon and a hundred thousand aeons, [beings such as] Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, and others [arise].
Great disciples arise; Paccekabuddhas arise after fulfilling the perfections for two incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons;
and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas arise after fulfilling the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons.
Therein, beings, having received the instruction of a Wheel-turning Monarch, become established in the five precepts.
They become destined for heaven by establishing themselves in the instruction of the Paccekabuddhas.
However, by establishing themselves in the instruction of the disciples of the Fully Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha), they become destined for both heaven and Nibbāna.
Therefore, dwelling there is called a "mangala" (an auspicious blessing) because it is the condition for these attainments.
"Having performed merit in the past" means having accumulated wholesome kamma directed toward the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed in a previous birth;

that too is an auspicious sign. Why? Because it is held that by having been shown the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas face-to-face, or having heard even a four-line stanza in the presence of the Buddhas or their disciples, one attains Arahantship at its conclusion. Whoever...
Furthermore, a person may have performed meritorious deeds in the past and possess abundant roots of wholesome merit;
by means of those very roots of wholesome merit, they give rise to insight and attain the destruction of the taints (*āsava*), just as King Mahākappina and his chief queen did. Therefore it is said:
"The performance of merit in the past is an auspicious sign."
“Right aspiration for oneself” means that here someone establishes himself, who is immoral, in virtue; establishes one lacking faith in the perfection of faith;
and establishes one who is miserly in the perfection of generosity. This is called “right aspiration for oneself.
And this is an auspicious sign. Why? Because it is the cause for the abandoning of enmity pertaining to both the present life and the future life, and for the attainment of various benefits.

Thus, for this verse as well, only three blessings are stated: dwelling in a suitable locality, having performed merit in the past, and right aspiration for oneself; and their status as blessings has been explained in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of the verse beginning with "dwelling in a suitable locality" is concluded.
264. Now, regarding the phrase "and erudition": here, "erudition" (*bāhusacca*) means the state of being well-learned. "Craft" (*sippa*) refers to any manual skill.
*Vinaya* means the disciplining of body, speech, and mind. *Susikkhita* means well-trained. *Subhāsita* means well-spoken.
*Yā* is an indefinite demonstrative. *Vācā* means speech or utterance. The remainder is exactly as previously stated. This is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*) here.

The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood thus: "Great learning" (*bāhusacca*) is that which is described as "being a bearer of what has been heard, an accumulator of what has been heard."
And when it is praised—in such a manner as, “In this case, monks, a certain person has heard much:

discourses, songs, and expositions”—that state of being a bearer of the Teacher’s instruction is called a “blessing” because it is the cause for abandoning the unwholesome and attaining the wholesome, and because it is the cause for the gradual realization of the ultimate truth. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Moreover, monks, the learned noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity.
Furthermore, it is said:
“He examines the meaning of the teachings he has mastered; as he examines their meaning, those teachings become acceptable to him through reflection.”
“When there is acceptance through contemplation of the Dhamma, zeal arises; when zeal has arisen, one exerts effort;
exerting effort, one weighs [the matter]; weighing it, one strives; striving, one realizes the ultimate truth with the body and, having pierced through it with wisdom, sees it.”

Furthermore, even the secular learning (*bāhusacca*) of a householder, if it is blameless, should be understood as a "good omen" (*maṅgala*) because it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds.
"Craft" (*sippa*) refers both to the craft of a householder and the craft of one who has gone forth.

Among these, the craft of a householder—such as the work of a jeweler or a goldsmith, provided it is free from harming others and devoid of unwholesome states—is a good omen because it brings about benefit in this world.
The "craft of the homeless" (anagārika-sippa) refers to the preparation of the requisites of a recluse,

such as the sorting and sewing of robes; that which has been praised here and there in various passages beginning with, "In this case, monks, a monk is skillful in those various high and low duties for his fellow celibates," and which is called "the Dhamma that makes one a protector."
And it has been said that this should be understood as a "maṅgala" (auspicious) because it brings about welfare and happiness for both oneself and others in both worlds.

"Vinaya" (discipline) refers to both the discipline of the householder and the discipline of the homeless one. Therein, the discipline of the householder consists in abstaining from the ten courses of unwholesome action;
when well-trained therein by not falling into defilement and by establishing oneself in the qualities of right conduct, it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds.
Auspiciousness. The "discipline of the homeless" (*anagārikavinaya*) consists in not committing any of the seven classes of offenses; that too is well-trained by the method already described.
Alternatively, the "discipline of the homeless" is the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).

Just as one attains Arahantship by being established therein, it should be understood as "auspicious" because, through training in that way, it is the cause for the attainment of mundane and supramundane happiness.

"Well-spoken speech" (*subhāsitā vācā*) refers to speech that is free from faults such as false speech (*musāvāda*). As it is said: "Bhikkhus, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken. Alternatively, speech that is devoid of idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is itself well-spoken.
As it is said: "The virtuous say that what is well-spoken is supreme;
one should speak the Dhamma, not non-Dhamma—that is the second [supreme]."
“One should speak what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant—this is the third;
one should speak the truth, not what is false—this is the fourth.
This too should be understood as a “maṅgala” (auspicious factor) because it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds. And since this [verse] is included within the Vinaya...
Thus, therefore, by the inclusion of the Vinaya, this [wrong speech] should not be included; rather, the Vinaya itself is to be included. Alternatively, what is the use of this exertion?
Here, the voice of teaching the Dhamma to others should be understood as "well-spoken speech.

For that, just like dwelling in a suitable locality, is called a "mangala" (auspicious factor) because it is a condition for the attainment of Nibbāna and for the welfare and happiness of beings in both worlds. And so it is said:
“The word that the Buddha speaks for the attainment of Nibbāna, for the making of an end to suffering—that indeed is the supreme among words.
Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: great learning, craft, well-trained discipline, and well-spoken speech; and their status as blessings has been clarified in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, "And proficiency," is concluded.
265. Now, regarding the phrase "service to mother and father": here, "mother and father" (*mātāpitu*) refers to both the mother and the father.

"Service" (*upaṭṭhāna*) means attending upon them. "Sons and wives" refers to *puttadāra*. "Gathering" (*saṅgaṇhana*) means inclusion or support. "Not distracted" (*anākulā*) means undisturbed. [This concerns] activities.
Such are the duties. The remainder is exactly as previously stated; this is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).
The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows: "Mother" refers to one who gives birth, and likewise "father.
"Attendance" (*upaṭṭhāna*) means performing service by washing the feet, massaging, anointing, bathing, and providing the four requisites.
In this regard, because parents are of great service to their children, desiring their welfare and compassionate toward them—
seeing their little children return from playing outside with bodies smeared with dust, they wipe away the dust, smell their heads, and kiss them,
thereby generating affection; and even for a hundred years, children carry their parents upon their heads.

They are unable to repay them. And because these progenitors and nurturers are the revealers of this world, honored as Brahmas and honored as the ancient teachers, therefore attending upon them brings praise in this life and the happiness of heaven hereafter;
for that reason, it is called a "mangala" (an auspicious blessing). For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Parents are called ‘Brahmā,’ and they are called ‘the first teachers’;
they are worthy of offerings from their children and are compassionate toward their offspring.
Therefore, a wise person should indeed honor and revere them.”
With food and drink, with clothing and bedding,
with anointing and bathing, and with the washing of the feet—
by such service toward one’s mother and father, the wise [attain merit].
“Right here they praise him, and after death he rejoices in heaven.

Another method: “Attendance” (upatthāna) consists of five kinds, such as providing maintenance, performing one’s duties, and establishing the family lineage. It should be understood as a “mangala” because it is a cause for welfare in the present life through five ways, beginning with the warding off of evil. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“In five ways, householder’s son, should a son attend upon his mother and father as the eastern quarter.”
‘I will support those who have supported me; I will perform their duties; I will maintain the family lineage;
I will hand over the inheritance; or else, I will offer funeral oblations for the deceased ancestors.
It is in these five ways, householder’s son, that parents are attended upon by a son as the eastern quarter in five ways.
“They show compassion for their son; they restrain him from evil; they establish him in what is wholesome; they train him in a craft; they unite him with a suitable wife;
and at the proper time, they hand over the inheritance.
Furthermore, one who inspires confidence in his mother and father in three respects—by undertaking moral discipline, by going forth into homelessness, or [by other virtuous deeds]—[is truly a son].”
He attends upon them; this is the foremost among those who attend upon their mother and father.

That service rendered to one's parents is called a "mangala" (auspicious blessing) because it serves as the basis for many benefits pertaining both to the present life and to future lives, being itself a reciprocal repayment for the assistance provided by the parents.
"Of children and wife": here, both sons and daughters begotten by oneself are reckoned simply as "children.
"Wife" refers to any one among the twenty wives. "Children and wife" is a compound; [the phrase means] "of that child and wife.

"Support" (saṅgaha) is the act of providing assistance through honoring and so forth. That [support] arises from the cause of welfare in the present life, such as the state of having well-ordered undertakings.
It should be understood as a "source of blessing. For this was said by the Blessed One: "The western direction should be understood as one's children and wife.
Here, having included "children and wife" under the term *bhariyā* (wife), it is stated:
"In five ways, householder’s son, should a wife be attended to by her husband as the western direction."
By honoring her, by not disparaging her, by not being unfaithful, by relinquishing authority to her, and by providing ornaments.
In these five ways, householder’s son, is the wife established as the western quarter by the husband;
and in turn, she shows compassion toward the husband in five ways: she manages the household duties well, and she keeps the servants under control.
“Furthermore, she is not unfaithful, she protects what has been gathered together, and she is skillful and untiring in all her duties.
This is another way: “Inclusion” means winning over others through righteous acts of giving, kind speech, and beneficial conduct.
For example: providing travel expenses on Uposatha days, and arranging for the viewing of auspicious constellations on festival nights.
It is the performance of auspicious rites on auspicious days, and the instruction and admonition regarding matters pertaining to the present life and the future life.

That should be understood as "auspicious" (maṅgala) precisely because it is a cause for welfare in the present life, a cause for welfare in the future life, and a cause for being worthy of homage even by the deities.
As Sakka, Lord of the Devas, said:
“Those householders who perform meritorious deeds, those virtuous lay followers who support their wives in accordance with the Dhamma— to them I pay homage, Mātali.
Unconfused occupations mean acting appropriately through knowledge of the right time, through lack of laziness, and through the perfection of initiative and energy.

And occupations such as plowing, cattle-rearing, and trade— which, because they are not subject to ruin, are free from the disturbances of neglecting the proper time, improper performance, non-performance, or laxity—
are called "auspicious" (*maṅgala*) when carried out by oneself or by one's wife, children, slaves, or laborers with proficiency,
since they are the cause for obtaining an increase in wealth and grain in this very life.
It has been said. And this was said by the Blessed One:
“One who acts appropriately, who is steadfast, and who exerts effort, finds wealth”; and:
“Not one whose habit is to sleep by day, nor one who looks toward waking at night...”
A house can be maintained by one who is constantly intoxicated and heedless.
“It is too cold,” “It is too hot,” “It is too late”— with such thoughts,
while their work is neglected, the goals of the young man pass him by.
“He who regards cold and heat as no more than grass, performing his duties as a man, does not depart from happiness. And:
“As he gathers wealth, moving about like a bee...”
“Enjoyments lead to accumulation, just as an anthill is built up”—
and so forth. Thus, in this verse as well, there is the service of mother, the service of father, the support of wife and children, and freedom from distress.
And "occupations" refers to the four blessings (*maṅgala*) mentioned; or, by dividing the support of wife and children into two, there are five;
or, by treating the service of mother and father as one, there are three. Furthermore, their status as blessings has been clearly explained in various places.
Thus concludes the commentary on the meaning of this verse beginning with "service of mother and father."
266. Now, regarding the phrase "and giving" (*dānañca*): it is called "giving" (*dāna*) because one gives by means of it; what is meant is that one's own property is bestowed upon another.
"Practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammacariyā*) means the practice of the Dhamma, or a practice that does not deviate from the Dhamma.
"Relatives" (*ñātaka*) are those who are known as "these are ours. "Blameless" (*anavajja*) means not blameworthy; what is meant is that they are irreproachable and beyond censure. The rest...
"This is the word-commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*) according to the method already stated.

The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows: Giving (*dāna*) is the volition of relinquishing objects for the ten bases of giving, such as food and so forth, preceded by a wise intention, directed toward another;
or it is non-greed (*alobha*) associated with that [volition]. For it is through non-greed that one hands over that object to another. Therefore it was said:"

“Giving is so called because one gives by means of this. It is called a “blessing” (maṅgala) because it is the cause for attaining specific fruits pertaining to both the present life and future lives, such as being dear and agreeable to many people.
In this regard, discourses such as, “O Sīha, the donor, the master of giving, becomes dear and agreeable to many people,” should be recollected.

Another method: Giving is twofold—namely, the gift of material goods (*āmisa-dāna*) and the gift of the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāna*). Among these, the gift of material goods is of the kind already described.

However, the gift of the Dhamma is the teaching to others, out of a desire for their welfare, of the Dhamma proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One, which brings about the happiness that consists in the destruction of suffering in this world and the next.
Of these two kinds of giving, this alone is the foremost. As it has been said:
“The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts;
the taste of Dhamma excels all tastes;
the delight in Dhamma excels all delights.”
“The destruction of craving conquers all suffering.

In this context, the auspiciousness of the gift of material goods (*āmisa-dāna*) has already been stated. However, the gift of the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāna*) is called “auspicious” because it is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for qualities such as experiencing the benefit (*atthapaṭisaṃveditā*). For this was said by the Blessed One:
“In whatever way, monks, a monk explains in detail to others the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has mastered it...”
"...teaches; in such and such a way, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that Dhamma," and so forth.

"Dhamma-conduct" (dhammacariyā) refers to the practice of the ten courses of wholesome action. As it is said: "Householders, there are three kinds of bodily conduct that constitute dhamma-conduct and conduct in accordance with the Dhamma," and so forth.
Furthermore, this dhamma-conduct is [the cause] for rebirth in the heavenly world.
It should be understood as a "blessing. For this was said by the Blessed One:

"Householders, it is for the sake of practicing the Dhamma and practicing equanimity that some beings here, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
Those called "relatives" are those connected on the mother’s side or the father’s side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors. Through the loss of their wealth...

Or, for those who have been struck down by disease or loss, the act of gathering them into one's own presence and providing them with food, clothing, wealth, grain, and so forth according to one's ability—
because it is the cause of worldly distinctions such as praise and the like, as well as of future attainments such as rebirth in a happy destination—
it is called "an auspicious sign" (*maṅgala*).

“Blemishless deeds” refers to actions consisting of good conduct of body, speech, and mind, such as undertaking the factors of the Uposatha, performing services, planting groves and forests, building bridges, and so forth.
Indeed, because they are the cause for attaining various kinds of welfare and happiness, they are called “auspicious.
“It is possible, Visākhā, that here some woman or man who possesses the eight factors...”
In this regard, such suttas as "Having observed the Uposatha, with the breakup of the body, after death, one may be reborn in the company of the Cātumahārājika devas" should be recollected.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: giving, righteous conduct, the supporting of relatives, and blameless deeds; and their status as blessings has been explained in detail in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, “And giving,” is finished.
267. Now, regarding the terms *āratī* and *viratī*: here, *āratī* means cessation (*āramaṇa*). *Viratī* means abstaining (*viramaṇa*), or it is called *virati* because beings abstain by means of it.
“Evil” refers to unwholesome states. In the sense of intoxicating, it is *majja*; the drinking of that intoxicant is *majjapāna*.

Next, regarding "from the drinking of intoxicants": restraint (*saṃyama*) is the act of restraining; heedfulness (*appamāda*) is the state of not being negligent. "In regard to phenomena" means in regard to wholesome states.
The remainder is exactly as explained by the method already stated; such is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).
However, the commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*) should be understood as follows: "Aversion" (*ārati*) refers to the mental disinclination of one who sees the danger in evil.
Abstention (*virati*) means desisting from bodily and verbal actions by way of the doors of karma.
This abstention is threefold: abstention by attainment, abstention by undertaking, and abstention by eradication.
Among these, that which belongs to a clansman based on his own birth, family, or lineage—thinking, "It is not fitting for me to kill this living being"—is abstention by attainment.
Abstention from the objects of attainment by way of the method beginning with “one would take what is not given,” this is called abstention by way of attainment (*sampattavirati*).

However, that which proceeds by way of undertaking the training precepts (*sikkhāpada*) is called abstention by way of undertaking (*samādānavirati*), from the moment it is undertaken after which a clansman no longer practices such acts as the taking of life.
That which is associated with the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is called eradication-abstention (*samucchedavirati*).
From the moment it was set in motion, the five fears and enmities of the noble disciple were stilled.

As for what is called "evil," it has been explained in detail thus: "Householder’s son, the destruction of life is indeed a defilement of action; taking what is not given... sexual misconduct... false speech... and so forth.
“Killing living beings, taking what is not given, false speech,
and likewise going to another’s wife— the wise do not praise these. Thus,
the fourfold unwholesome action known as defilement of action, which is summarized by this verse, is more evil than all these [other evils].
Both non-attachment and detachment are called "auspicious" (*maṅgala*) because they are the causes for attaining various specific distinctions,

such as the abandonment of fear and enmity pertaining to both the present life and the future life. In this regard, discourses such as, "Householder’s son, a noble disciple abstains from the destruction of life," should be recollected.
"Restraint from the drinking of intoxicants" is a designation for the abstinence from the occasion of negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants as previously stated.
For one who drinks intoxicants does not know the goal, does not know the Dhamma, and creates obstacles even for his mother;
he creates obstacles for his father, for Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata, even in this very life.
Through intoxicants, one incurs blame, rebirth in a state of misery in the future life, and madness in successive existences.
However, one who is restrained from drinking intoxicants attains the pacification of those faults and the excellence of qualities that are their opposite.
Therefore, this restraint from drinking intoxicants should be understood as a "blessing."
Regarding wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*), what is called "heedlessness" (*appamāda*) is:

lack of careful performance, lack of constant performance, lack of steadfast performance, sluggish conduct, abandonment of desire, abandonment of the burden, non-cultivation, non-development, non-repetition, lack of resolve, lack of application, and heedlessness. Such is the nature of heedlessness.

Regarding the statement, "Negligence (pamajjanā) and a negligent state of mind—this is called negligence (pamāda)," one should understand that its opposite, in terms of meaning, is the non-departure of mindfulness from wholesome states (kusala-dhamma).

Because it is the cause for attaining various kinds of wholesome qualities and the cause for attaining the Deathless (amata), it is called a "blessing" (maṅgala). In this context, [the phrases] "for one who is heedful and ardent" and "heedfulness... [are used].
One should recollect the Teacher’s instruction beginning with “the state of the Deathless” and so forth.

Thus, in this verse, three blessings are stated: abstaining from evil, restraint regarding the drinking of intoxicants, and heedfulness in wholesome states. Furthermore, their nature as blessings has been clarified in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, “Relinquishing and abstaining,” is concluded.

268. Now, regarding the phrase "and reverence" (*gāravo ca*): here, "reverence" (*gārava*) means the state of being respected. "Living in seclusion" (*nivāta*) means a lowly or humble mode of life. "Contentment" (*santuṭṭhi*) means satisfaction.
"Knowing what has been done" (*katajānanatā*) is gratitude (*kataññutā*). "At the proper time" (*kālena*) means at the right moment or occasion.
"Hearing the Dhamma" (*dhammassavana*) is listening to the Dhamma. The remainder is exactly as previously explained; such is the word-commentary.

The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*) should be understood as follows: "Reverence" (*gārava*) means the act of honoring, the state of honoring, and the quality of being reverential toward those worthy of honor—namely, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Tathāgata-disciples, teachers, preceptors, mothers, fathers, elder brothers, sisters, and so forth—according to their respective worthiness. This reverence is the cause for rebirth in happy realms and other such benefits. As it is said:
"One honors what is worthy of honor, respects what is worthy of respect, and worships what is worthy of worship. By that kamma..."
When practiced in this way and undertaken in this way, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
But if, with the breakup of the body... [as before] ...one is not so reborn, and if one comes back to the human state, wherever one is reborn, one is born into a high family.
And as it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these seven qualities that prevent decline. Which seven? Reverence for the Teacher," and so forth. Therefore, it is called a "blessing."
“Humility” (nivāta) means a lowly state of mind and a humble way of living. A person endowed with this quality has subdued pride and subdued arrogance;
like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with its horns cut off, and like a snake with its fangs extracted, he becomes gentle, amiable, and pleasant to converse with—this is humility.
And because it is the cause for obtaining qualities such as renown and so forth, it is called a “good omen” (maṅgala).
It is said: "One who is humble in conduct and free from arrogance—such a person gains renown," and so forth.

Contentment means satisfaction with whatever requisites are obtained; it is of twelve kinds. Namely: regarding robes, there is threefold contentment—contentment with what is obtained, contentment with what is suitable to one's strength, and contentment with what is appropriate.
It is the same for alms-food and the other requisites. This is the explanation of its divisions: here, a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether beautiful or ugly.
He maintains himself with that alone, he does not long for anything else, and even if he obtains more, he does not take it; this is his contentment with whatever robe-material is obtained.

Furthermore, if he becomes afflicted by illness and, when wearing a heavy robe, he leans forward or becomes exhausted, he exchanges it with a robe of similar quality belonging to another monk and maintains himself with a light one; even so, he remains truly contented. This is his...
Contentment with robes according to one’s ability. Another monk might be one who obtains superior requisites;

having received a costly robe such as a cloth made of fine silk (*paṭṭacīvara*), he thinks, "This is suitable for the elders who have long been gone forth and are of great learning," and gives it to them.
He then collects rags from a rubbish heap or from somewhere else, and...
Even when wearing his outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) after having made it [from rags], he remains content; this is his contentment with robes as they are appropriate.

Furthermore, here a monk receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined; he sustains himself with that alone, does not long for another, and even if he receives more, he does not take it; this is his contentment with almsfood according to what is obtained. Then, however—
He becomes afflicted; having eaten coarse almsfood, he falls into severe illness.
Yet, by giving that food to a fellow monk of similar standing and eating ghee, honey, milk, and so forth from his hand, he remains content even while practicing the duty of a recluse.
This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another monk [receives] excellent almsfood...

He receives [almsfood] and, thinking, "This almsfood is suitable for the elder bhikkhus who have long been gone forth and for my fellow celibates who do not obtain choice almsfood," he gives it to them;
then, even though he himself wanders for alms and eats mixed food, he remains contented.
This is his contentment with almsfood as is appropriate.
Furthermore, when a bhikkhu obtains a lodging and is content with that alone, not taking another even if a more beautiful one becomes available,
this is his contentment regarding lodgings according to what is obtained. Moreover, if he becomes ill and, while staying in a sheltered lodging,
suffers excessively from bile diseases and the like, he [should give] that to a fellow bhikkhu of similar status...
Having given [the lodging] away, even while dwelling in a wind-cool lodging that has come to him and practicing the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), he remains content;
this is his contentment with regard to lodging according to his strength. Another monk does not accept even when he obtains a beautiful lodging, thinking:
"A beautiful lodging is a ground for negligence; for one sitting there, sloth and torpor descend."
"And when one who has been overcome by sleep wakes up again, sensual thoughts assail him";
having rejected that, he remains content even while dwelling anywhere at all—in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in leaf-huts.
This is his contentment with a dwelling as is appropriate for him.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives medicinal requisites such as *harītaka* or *āmalaka* and sustains himself with those alone;

he does not long for ghee, honey, molasses, or other items received by others, and even if he receives them, he does not take them. This is his contentment with what is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine.
Moreover, if one who is ill and in need of oil receives molasses, he gives it to a fellow practitioner.
Having given it to a bhikkhu and prepared a medicinal oil from his hand, even while performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), he remains content;

this is his contentment according to his strength regarding the requisite of medicine. Another bhikkhu, having placed fermented urine and myrobalan (*harītaka*) in one vessel and the four sweets (*catumadhura*) in another, is told, "Venerable sir, take whichever you wish"; if he—
If the illness of either of those two is pacified, then one should reflect: "The so-called *pūtimuttaharītaka* (rotten-urine myrobalan) was praised by the Buddha and others;
this going-forth is dependent upon medicine made of rotten urine; therefore, you must apply yourself to that for as long as life lasts.
Thinking thus, one should reject the four sweet medicines and [use] *muttaharītaka*.
Even while preparing medicine, he remains perfectly content; this is his appropriate contentment with the requisite of medicine for the sick.

Thus, this entire classification of contentment is called "santuṭṭhi" (contentment). It is so called because it is the cause for abandoning and attaining evil states such as excessive desire, wicked desire, and great desire;
because it is the cause for a happy rebirth; because it serves as a provision for the Noble Path; and because it is the cause for being one who belongs to all four quarters [of the Saṅgha].
And it should be understood as "an auspicious sign. For it has been said:
"He is impartial and free from aversion, being content with whatever comes his way," and so forth.
Gratitude (*kataññutā*) is the state of knowing—by means of repeatedly recollecting—a benefit rendered by anyone, whether small or great.

Furthermore, since it is meritorious deeds alone that provide great assistance to living beings by protecting them from the sufferings of hell and other realms, the recollection of those benefits should be understood as "gratitude. It is a cause for attaining various distinguished qualities, such as being praised by the virtuous.
It is called a "blessing. And it has been said: "Bhikkhus, these two persons are rare in the world.
Which two? He who is a doer of good first, and he who is grateful and mindful of benefits.
Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time means that at whatever time the mind is accompanied by restlessness, such as when thoughts of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth arise...
Or, when someone is overcome by some affliction, at that time, listening to the Dhamma for the purpose of dispelling it is called "listening to the Dhamma. Others say:
"Listening to the Dhamma every fifth day is what is meant by 'listening to the Dhamma at the proper time. As the Venerable Anuruddha said:
"But, venerable sir, we sit together every five days throughout the night engaged in talk on the Dhamma."

Furthermore, at whatever time one is able to approach a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) and hear the Dhamma that dispels one’s own doubts, even at that time, listening to the Dhamma should be understood as "listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.
As it is said: "From time to time they approach [the teacher] and inquire and question," and so forth. This is that...

Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time should be understood as a "blessing" (maṅgala) because it is the cause for attaining various specific distinctions, such as the abandonment of the hindrances, the four benefits, and the destruction of the taints (āsava).
For this has been said:

"Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma with earnestness, with attention, with his whole heart, and with an attentive ear, on that occasion the five hindrances do not exist in him."
“Monks, for those teachings that have been heard, ... [and] well-penetrated, four benefits are to be expected. And:

“Monks, these four things, when properly developed and properly cultivated from time to time, lead gradually to the destruction of the taints. What are the four? Hearing the Dhamma at the proper time,” and so forth.

Thus, in this verse, five blessings are stated: reverence (*gārava*), humility (*nivāta*), contentment (*santuṭṭhi*), gratitude (*kataññutā*), and listening to the Dhamma at the proper time. Furthermore, their status as blessings has already been clarified in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of the verse "Reverence and Humility" is concluded.
269. Now, regarding the phrase "and forbearance" (*khantī ca*): forbearing is "forbearance" (*khanti*). Because one grasps [the teaching] in a favorable way, there is ease in speech within me.

"Easy to speak to" (*suvaco*) means one who is compliant; "the act of being easy to speak to" is *sovacassaṃ*; the state of being easy to speak to is *sovacassatā*. Because they have stilled (*samita*) the defilements (*kilesa*), they are "ascetics" (*samaṇā*).

"Seeing" (*dassana*) means beholding. "Discussion of the Dhamma" (*dhammasākacchā*) is a discussion concerning the Dhamma. The rest is exactly as previously explained; such is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).
The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood thus: "Patience" (*khanti*) refers to patience as endurance (*adhivāsanakkhanti*), endowed with which—

When a bhikkhu is reviled with the ten grounds for abuse, or when individuals inflict harm such as beating or binding upon him, he remains unperturbed, as if not hearing and as if not seeing them, like one who preaches patience. As it is said:
"In the past, there was a recluse who manifested patience."
"Even while he remained established in patience alone, the King of Kāsi cut him down.
Or else, one attends to Bhaddakata; beyond that, by virtue of the absence of further transgression, as in the case of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa. As it was said:
"If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta should abuse and revile me, there [I shall remain patient]."
Thus it will be: “These people of Sunāparanta are indeed fortunate, these people of Sunāparanta are truly blessed, in that they do not strike me with their hands,” and so forth.
And endowed with which [quality] one becomes praiseworthy even among the seers (isī), as the seer Sarabhaṅga said:
“Having slain anger, one never grieves;
the seers praise the abandonment of hypocrisy.
One should endure all harsh speech uttered [by others].”
“The virtuous call this patience supreme.
One becomes worthy of praise even by the deities, as Sakka, Lord of the Devas, said:
“He who, though himself powerful, endures one who is weak;”
Of him they say this is the supreme patience: that the weak man is always patient.
He is also worthy of praise even by the Buddhas. As the Blessed One said:
“He who, being free from malice, endures abuse, violence, and imprisonment;”
“The army of strength that is the power of patience—him I call a brahmin.
Now, this patience should be understood as a “good omen” (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for the attainment of these and other qualities described here.

What is called “being easy to speak with” (*sovacassatā*) means that when one is being addressed according to the Dhamma, one avoids distraction or silence, and instead reflects upon the merits and faults [of the advice].
Alternatively, it is the state of acting upon the words "well" (sādhū) by placing extreme care, reverence, and humble deference before oneself without transgressing;

this is called a "mangala" because it is the cause for receiving exhortation and instruction from one's fellow celibates, and because it is the cause for the abandoning of faults and the attainment of virtues.

"Visiting ascetics" (samaṇānaṃ dassanaṃ) means approaching, attending upon, recollecting, hearing, and seeing those who have gone forth—those whose defilements have been stilled, who have developed their body, speech, mind, and wisdom, and who are endowed with the highest self-control and tranquility. All of this is termed "seeing" according to the teaching on the inferior [level].
This should be understood as a "blessing" (maṅgala). Why? Because it is of great benefit. And it has been said:
“Bhikkhus, I say that even the mere sight of those bhikkhus is of great benefit,” and so forth.
Therefore, a son of good family who desires his own welfare, upon seeing virtuous bhikkhus arrive at his door, should—if he has anything to give—honor them with a gift according to his means;
if he has nothing, he should pay homage to them by performing the five-prostration salutation.
If that is not possible, one should pay homage with hands joined in *añjali*;
if even that is not possible, one should look upon them with a clear mind and loving eyes.

For by merit rooted even in such a vision, for many thousands of births, there will be no disease, burning, swellings, or boils in the eye; rather, it will be radiant and beautiful with the five clear colors.
The eyes become like the opened jeweled windows in a celestial palace, and for the duration of a hundred thousand eons,
one obtains all forms of excellence among both devas and humans. And this is not surprising, that one born as a human being, endowed with wisdom,
should attain such a perfection of karmic result through merit consisting in the proper act of visiting a recluse.
One would experience [the result], where they describe such excellence of karmic fruition even for animals who merely see a recluse out of simple faith—
such as the owl Maṇḍalakkhika.
Having resided for a very long time at Vediyaka,
this Kosika is indeed happy that he beholds the Supreme Buddha who has arisen at the proper time.
“Having placed confidence in me and in the unsurpassed Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
for a hundred thousand eons he will not go to an evil destination.
Having passed away from the world of the devas, impelled by his wholesome karma...”
"He will possess infinite knowledge and be renowned as Somanassa.
Regarding "discourse on the Dhamma at the proper time": in the evening or at dawn, two monks who are experts in the Suttas discuss the Suttas with one another;
those who are masters of the Vinaya discuss the Vinaya; those who are experts in the Abhidhamma discuss the Abhidhamma; and those who are reciters of the Jātakas [discuss the Jātakas].

The Jātaka and the Aṭṭhakathā; or, for the purpose of purifying a mind that is sluggish, agitated, or overcome by doubt, they engage in discussion on those various occasions—this is timely discussion of the Dhamma.
Because it is the cause of qualities such as proficiency in the Āgamas, it is called a "mangala" (an auspicious blessing).

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: patience (*khanti*), amenability to advice (*sovacassatā*), visiting ascetics (*samaṇadassana*), and timely discussion of the Dhamma (*kālena dhammasākacchā*). And their status as blessings has already been clarified in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, "Patience," is concluded.
270. Now, regarding the phrase "Austerity" (*tapo*): it is called austerity because it burns away (*tapati*) evil, unwholesome states; it is the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

"Brahma-conduct" means the practice of the holy life (*brahmacariya*); it is said to be the "supreme conduct. "Vision of the noble truths" (*ariyasaccānaṃ dassanaṃ*) refers to the seeing of the noble truths.
Some say that the noble truths are themselves the vision, but that is not correct. "Nirvana" (*nibbāna*) is so called because one has departed from craving (*vāna*).
"Realization" (*sacchikiriyā*) means making manifest; thus, "realization of nirvana" is the manifestation of nirvana.
"The rest is exactly as stated" refers to this word-commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).
The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows: "Austerity" (*tapo*) is called such because it scorches (*tapanato*) covetousness, dejection, and so forth;
it is either the restraint of the sense faculties or energy (*vīriya*) because it scorches laziness. A person endowed with that is called "ardent" (*ātāpī*). This [person]...

It should be understood as a "mangala" (auspicious) because it is the cause for the abandonment of covetousness and the like, and for the attainment of the jhānas and the like. "Brahmacariya" is a designation for celibacy, the duty of a recluse, the teaching, and the Path.
For instance, in such passages as "Having abandoned unchastity, he becomes one who lives in chastity," celibacy is referred to as *brahmacariya*.
It is called [the holy life]. In such passages as, “Friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One,” it refers to the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).

In such passages as, “Evil One, I shall not attain final Nibbāna until this holy life has become successful, prosperous, widespread, and well-known,” it refers to the Dispensation (*sāsana*). “This, monk, is indeed the Noble... [and so forth].
In such passages as, "The noble eightfold path is the holy life; that is to say, right view," and so forth, it refers to the path.
However, in this context, since the path is already grasped subsequently through the vision of the Noble Truths, everything else is also appropriate.
And this should be understood as a "mangala" (auspicious factor) because it is the cause for the successive attainment of various specific distinctions.

The "vision of the Noble Truths" refers to the vision of the Path by way of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four Noble Truths whose meanings were explained in the *Kumārapañha*. It is called a "good omen" (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for transcending the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
The "realization of Nibbāna" here intends the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*), which is designated as "Nibbāna.

For that too is called "Nibbāna" because it has "departed" (*nikkhanta*) from craving, which is known as "departure" (*vāna*) due to its leading to wandering through the five destinies. Its attainment or its reviewing is [the subject].
Or it is called "realization" (sacchikiriyā). However, since the realization of the other Nibbāna is accomplished through the very vision of the Noble Truths, it is not what is intended here.
Thus, this realization of Nibbāna should be understood as a "mangala" (auspicious) because it is the cause for dwelling in happiness in this very life and so forth.

Thus, in this verse as well, four blessings are stated: asceticism (*tapo*), the holy life (*brahmacariya*), the vision of the Noble Truths, and the realization of Nibbāna; and their status as blessings has already been elucidated in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, "Asceticism... (tapo ca), is concluded. 271.
Now, regarding the phrase "by one touched by worldly conditions" (*phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi*): here, "touched" (*phuṭṭha*) means struck, contacted, or encountered.
“Worldly conditions” (lokadhammā) means the phenomena of the world; what is meant is that they do not turn back as long as the world continues to evolve.

“Mind” (citta) means the intellect (mano), the mental faculty (mānasa). “Of whom” (yassa) refers to one who is either young, middle-aged, or old. “Does not waver” (na kampati) means it does not shake or tremble.
“Sorrowless” (asoka) means free from sorrow, having pulled out the arrow of grief. “Dustless” (viraja) means devoid of passion-dust (raja).
"Shattered of dust. "Secure" means fearless and free from calamity. The remainder is exactly as previously explained; this, then, is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).
The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows:

"Whose mind does not waver when touched by the worldly conditions"—that is, whose mind does not waver or tremble even when touched and overwhelmed by the eight worldly conditions, beginning with gain and loss.
It does not waver, it does not tremble; that mind should be understood as a "blessing" because it brings about a supramundane state that cannot be shaken by anything.
Whose mind does not tremble when touched by these? That of the Arahant whose taints are destroyed, and no one else's. For this has been said:
"Just as a solid mass of rock is not moved by the wind,"
“Thus forms, tastes, sounds, smells, and tangibles in their entirety—
whether desirable or undesirable phenomena— do not cause one who is such (a Tādin) to tremble.
His mind is steady and liberated, and he contemplates its passing away.”

"Free from sorrow" (*asoka*) refers to the mind of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). For it is "sorrow"—which is described by such terms as "sorrowing, the state of sorrowing, inward sorrow, inward burning, and the brooding of the mind"—that is absent;
thus it is "free from sorrow. Some say this refers to Nibbāna, but that does not connect with the preceding term. And just as it is free from sorrow, so too is it "dustless" (*viraja*).
"Secure" (*khema*) is also the mind of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). For it is "dustless" (*viraja*) because of the departure of the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion;

and it is "secure" (*khema*) because of its security from the four bonds (*yoga*). Since this [mind], having been apprehended in various ways at each respective moment of its occurrence, brings about the supramundane state—such as the non-occurrence of the aggregates and so forth—and brings about the status of being worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*) and so on, it is described in these three ways according to those respective modes.
And it should be understood that this is a "blessing.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: a mind unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, a sorrowless mind, a stainless mind, and a secure mind; and their status as blessings has already been clarified in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, beginning with "phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi," is concluded.
272. Thus, having expounded the thirty-eight blessings with the ten verses beginning with "And not associating with fools," the Blessed One now uttered this final verse,
"Having performed such [deeds]," while praising these very blessings he himself had spoken.
This is the commentary on its meaning: "Such as these" means these aforementioned types of things, such as the non-association with fools and so forth.
"Having done" means having performed. For "having done," "having performed," and "having made" are not different in meaning.

"Unconquered in every respect" means [unconquered] by even one among the four adversaries, namely the Māras consisting of the aggregates (*khandha*), the defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the son of a deva (*devaputta*).
"Having become invincible, they themselves shall conquer those four Māras"—this is what is meant.
And here, the letter *m* should be understood as serving merely for the euphonic junction of words (*padasandhi*).
"They go everywhere in safety": having performed such auspicious rites, they remain unconquered by the four Māras.
In all places—both in this world and the next, and whether standing or walking—they go in safety.
Because of the absence of those taints (*āsava*), afflictions, and fevers that might arise from associating with fools and the like, they go in safety;

it is said that they go untroubled, unhindered, secure, and fearless. Furthermore, it should be understood that the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) is used here for the sake of metrical ease in the verse composition.
With this line of verse, "That is their supreme blessing," the Blessed One brought his teaching to a conclusion.

How so? O son of the gods, because those who perform such things as these go everywhere in safety, therefore that thirty-eightfold practice—beginning with the non-association with fools—is the supreme blessing for those who perform such deeds.
"Take the best and most excellent.
And when the Blessed One had thus concluded his teaching, at its very end, one hundred thousand times ten million deities attained Arahatship;
those who reached the fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, and Non-returning were beyond counting. Then...
On the second day, the Blessed One addressed the Elder Ānanda:
“Ānanda, last night a certain deity approached me and asked a question concerning auspiciousness. I then explained to her the thirty-eight auspicious signs.
Learn this discourse on auspiciousness, Ānanda; having learned it, teach it to the bhikkhus. Having learned it, the Elder—
He taught it to the bhikkhus. This [teaching], handed down through a succession of teachers, continues even to this day;

thus it should be understood that this holy life (*brahmacariya*) has become successful, prosperous, widespread, well-known, and extensive, and is well-proclaimed as far as the world of gods and humans.
Now, for the sake of proficiency in the cultivation of knowledge regarding these very auspicious verses, here is the construction starting from the beginning: "Thus these..."
Beings who desire the happiness of this world, the next world, and the supramundane, having abandoned the company of foolish people and relying on the wise, honoring those worthy of honor,
urged toward the practice of wholesome deeds by their residence in a suitable locality and by their past accumulation of merit,
and having rightly directed themselves, their persons adorned with great learning, craft, and discipline, [should speak] well-spoken words in accordance with that discipline.
While they are living as householders and have not yet abandoned that state, they purify the root of their ancient debt by attending upon their mother and father;
they produce the root of new debt through the maintenance of wives and children; they attain abundance in wealth, grain, and so forth through orderly management of their affairs;
and they secure the essence of enjoyment through generosity and the essence of life through righteous conduct.
Having taken them up, while benefiting their own kin through the support of relatives and benefiting others by means of blameless conduct,

and having avoided harming others through abstention from evil and self-harm through restraint from intoxicants, and having increased the side of wholesome qualities through heedfulness regarding the teachings,
they cast off the marks of a householder and, in the state of one gone forth due to that increased wholesomeness—
Remaining steadfast through reverence for the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, preceptors, teachers, and others, and by fulfilling one’s duties with composure;
through contentment, abandoning greed for requisites; through gratitude, standing upon the ground of the virtuous; through listening to the Dhamma, abandoning mental sluggishness;
through patience, overcoming all perils; and through being easy to admonish, making oneself possessed of a protector—
Having done so, perceiving the application of practice through the sight of the ascetic,
dispelling doubt regarding those things that give rise to doubt through discussion of the Dhamma, and accomplishing purification of virtue by the austerity of restraint of the faculties,
purification of mind by the holy life of the ascetic’s duty, and the four subsequent purifications, they [proceed] by this path toward the method of seeing the Noble Truths.
Having attained purification of knowledge and vision, they realize Nibbāna, which is designated as the fruit of Arahantship.
Having realized this, their minds remain unshaken by the eight worldly conditions—just as Mount Sineru is unshaken by winds and rains—and they become sorrowless, stainless, and secure.
Those who are secure are undefeated everywhere by even a single opponent, and in all respects...
They go in safety. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having performed such deeds as these, undefeated everywhere, they go in safety everywhere; that is their supreme blessing.”
Thus ends the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, which is part of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā. 5.
Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta.
Thus have I heard: this is the Sūciloma Sutta. What is its origin? Its origin will be made clear by means of the method of commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*).
And in the commentary on the meaning, the phrase "Thus have I heard" and so forth has already been explained.

Regarding the passage, "He was dwelling at Gayā, at the Ṭaṅkitamañca, in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma": what is Gayā here, what is the Ṭaṅkitamañca, and for what reason did the Blessed One [dwell there]?
"Does he dwell in the abode of that *yakkha*? It is said: "Gayā" refers both to a village and to a bathing place (*tittha*);
both are applicable here. For even one dwelling in a region not far from the village of Gayā is said to "dwell at Gayā.
And near that village, not far away, close to the gate, was that bedstead with spikes. Even one dwelling at the Gayā bathing place [is likewise described].
“He dwells at Gayā,” it is said; and at the ford of Gayā is the stone couch (*ṭaṅkitamañca*).
A stone couch is a stone bed constructed by placing a broad stone upon four other stones.
Near it was the abode of a *yakkha*, like the abode of Āḷavaka. Or rather, because on that day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One—

Emerging from the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*), he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and saw that both the yakkhas Sūciloma and Kharaloma possessed the necessary conditions for attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Therefore, taking up his bowl and robes,
even before sunrise, he went to a spot where the ground was drenched by the outflow of various kinds of impurities such as saliva and mucus from the crowds of people gathered from all directions.
Having come to that bathing-place, he sat down on the Ṭaṅkitamañca in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma.
Therefore it is said: "On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Gayā, on the Ṭaṅkitamañca, in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma.
And at that time means: at the time when the Blessed One was dwelling there. Kharo...
And the yakkha Sūciloma and the yakkha [Sūta] were passing by not far from the Blessed One. Who were those yakkhas, and why were they passing by?
It is said: Among them, one had previously taken oil belonging to the Saṅgha without asking permission and smeared it on his own body.
Because of that deed, having been boiled in hell, he was reborn in the womb of a yakkha on the banks of the Gayāpokkharaṇī.
He was reborn. Due to the remaining result of that very same karma, his limbs and members were deformed, and his skin had a rough touch like a roof of bricks.
It is said that whenever he wished to terrify another, he would lift up plates of skin resembling roof-bricks and thereby cause terror.
Thus, because of his rough touch, he received the name "Kharayakkha" (the Rough Yakkha).
In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, this man was a lay follower who would go to the monastery on eight days of each month to listen to the Dhamma.
One day, while the proclamation for the Dhamma assembly had been made, he heard the announcement at the gate of the Saṅghārāma that his own field was being plowed.
Thinking, "If I bathe, it will take too long," he went to the Uposatha hall with his body still soiled.
Having entered, he lay down with indifference upon a costly floor-covering and fell asleep. "This is merely a bhikkhu, not a lay follower," said the Saṃyutta-bhāṇakas.
Having been boiled in hell because of that deed and other deeds, he was reborn in the womb of a yakkha on the bank of the Gayā-pokkharaṇī.
Due to the remaining ripening of that karma, he became difficult to see; his body...
His body hairs were like needles. For he terrified beings who ought to be terrified as if piercing them with needles;
thus, because his body hairs resembled needles, he received the name "Sūciloma" (Needle-hair) Yakkha.
Having departed from their dwelling for the sake of their own range, and having gone for a short while, they turned back by the very path they had come and [encountered] the other...
As they were traveling toward their destination, they passed by the Blessed One at no great distance.
Now, why did Kharo speak to them in this way? It was because he saw the ascetic’s appearance and spoke thus.
Sūciloma, however, held the view that "he who is afraid is not an ascetic; rather, he is a 'pseudo-ascetic' (samaṇaka) because he merely resembles an ascetic."
Therefore, thinking such a one was the Blessed One, even though he had hastily said, "This is no ascetic;
this is a mere pseudo-ascetic," wishing to investigate further, he said, "Wait until I know. Having spoken thus, [the phrase] "Then" (*atha kho*) refers to what followed from that point.
From here on, up until the words "but contact with you is indeed evil," the meaning is entirely straightforward; however, in this section, there is only... [the rest of the passage continues].
The connection should be understood as follows: "He offered his own body to the Blessed One's body.
Then, seeing that the Blessed One was not afraid, he said, "Ask him a question, O ascetics," and so forth.
For what reason? He thought: "Even though this man is a human being, he is not [frightened] by such a harsh touch from a non-human being as this..."
“He is afraid; well then, I shall ask him this question regarding the domain of the Buddha.
Surely he will not be able to manage it there, and then I will trouble him thus. When the Blessed One heard this, he said, “Indeed, I am not that, friend,” and so forth.
All of this is to be understood in every detail according to the method already stated in the Āḷavaka Sutta.
273. Then the yakkha Sūciloma addressed the Blessed One with a verse: “Lust and hatred... Herein, lust and hatred are exactly as previously described.
*Kutonidāna* means “having what as its source,” “having what as its cause. It should be understood that the substitution of *to* for the genitive case-ending (*paccattavacana*) has occurred;
furthermore, there is no elision of the case-ending within the compound. Alternatively, *nidāna* means “born from” or “arisen from.”
Therefore, it is asked: from what cause, from what birth, from what origin [do they arise]? As for the phrase "from what is born aversion, delight, and horripilation":

that "aversion" which has been analyzed as "dislike, state of dislike, lack of delight, lack of enjoyment, longing, and agitation regarding secluded lodgings or various other higher wholesome states"; and that [which occurs] regarding the five...
Delight in the strands of sensual pleasure; and mental terror, which, because it causes the hair to stand on end, is reckoned as "horripilation.
He asks: "From where are these three states born? From what are they born? "From what do they arise? means from what do they originate? "Mind" refers to wholesome consciousness;
"thoughts" refers to the nine types of thoughts beginning with sensual desire, as stated in the *Uraga Sutta*. "Like boys releasing a hawk" means...
Just as village boys, while playing, bind a crow by its foot with a string and let it go or throw it away, [the speaker] asks:
"From where do unwholesome thoughts arise and let go of wholesome mental states?
(274) Then the Blessed One, answering those questions, spoke the second verse beginning with "Lust (*rāga*)... In that regard:
The word "from this" (*ito*) is said with reference to the personal existence (*attabhāva*). For lust and hatred have their source in personal existence;

likewise, discontent, delight, and horripilation are born from personal existence; and unwholesome thoughts such as sensual thought arise from personal existence itself and cause the wholesome mind to be abandoned.
Therefore, rejecting any other primary cause such as primordial nature (*pakati*), he says: "From this as source, from this as birth, from this as origin."
The grammatical derivation (*saddasiddhi*) here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the preceding verse.

Having thus answered those questions, he now speaks—proving the meaning that was stated in the passages beginning with "from this source" (*itonidāna*), namely, "having the individual existence (*attabhāva*) as its source, born from individual existence, arisen from individual existence"—with the words: "born of moisture" (*snehaja*).
“Born from oneself. For all these states, beginning with lust and ending with applied thought, are born from the moisture of craving;

and being so born, they are produced within the self, according to the conventional designation of the self as the five aggregates of clinging. Therefore he said: “Born from moisture, born from oneself.
Now he provides a simile to illuminate this meaning: “Like the branches of a banyan tree.”
In this context, "born from the trunk" (*khandhajā*) refers to those things produced from the trunk; this is a designation for offshoots (*pāroha*).

What is meant? Just as the so-called trunk-born offshoots of a banyan tree arise when there is the moisture of sap and resin, and while arising, they take root in that very banyan tree upon various branches, even so these [defilements] such as lust arise through the internal moisture of craving.
When they arise, they come into being within that very selfhood (*attabhāva*) in those various bases of doors and objects, such as the eye and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood: "These have selfhood as their cause, are born from selfhood, and originate from selfhood.
Now, for the remaining one and a half stanzas, this is the comprehensive commentary on the meaning: thus, arisen from selfhood...
And these are variously attached to sense pleasures. For lust is [attached] by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth;
hatred by way of the bases for resentment and so forth; and discontent and the rest by way of their respective subdivisions.

Thus, in every respect, all these defilements, being manifold and of many kinds, become attached and cling in various ways to those various objective sense pleasures by way of the bases, doors, and objects.
It is stuck, having become entangled and remaining so. Like what? "Like a *māluvā* creeper spread in the forest":

just as a *māluvā* creeper spread in the forest becomes attached, clings to, and remains entangled among the various branches, twigs, and parts of trees, even so, those who understand from what source this mass of defilements (*kilesagaṇa*)—which is attached to the manifold objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*)—arises.
They dispel it; listen, O Yakkha.
In this context, "yatonidānaṃ" is a neuter demonstrative pronoun. What does it indicate?

It indicates that those beings who understand that mass of defilements as "arising from a source" [know] that it arises within a personal existence (attabhāva) moistened by the moisture of craving (taṇhāsneha).

"Having recognized that craving and affection, O Yakkha, listen to this well-spoken word of mine: drying them up with the fire of the knowledge of meditation such as the contemplation of danger, they dispel, abandon, and bring them to an end.

In this way, he illustrates here the full understanding of suffering through the knowledge of one's own personal existence (attabhāva), and the abandonment of its origin through the dispelling of the mass of defilements such as craving, affection, and lust.
And those who dispel it cross this flood so difficult to cross, which was never crossed before, for the sake of non-renewal of existence.
By this, he illuminates the cultivation of the path and the realization of cessation. For those who dispel that mass of defilements necessarily cultivate the path;
indeed, there is no dispelling of defilements without the cultivation of the path. And those who [cultivate] the path...

Those who develop [this path] cross over this fourfold flood—the flood of sensual desire and the rest—which is difficult to cross by means of ordinary knowledge. For the development of the Path is indeed the crossing of the floods.
"Never crossed before" means never previously transcended, even in a dream, throughout this long period of time.
"For the sake of non-becoming" means for the sake of Nibbāna. Thus, those hearing this verse which illuminates the Four Noble Truths, having heard the Dhamma...
As they proceeded through this discourse— beginning with “They retain them, and they examine the meaning of the teachings they have retained”—
those two yakṣa friends, by means of their well-cultivated wisdom, were established in the fruit of stream-entry at the very conclusion of the verses;
and they became beautiful, golden-hued, and adorned with celestial ornaments.
The commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, part of the *Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*, is completed. 6.
Commentary on the Kapila Sutta (also known as the Dhammacariya Sutta).

*Dhammacariya* refers to the *Kapila Sutta*. What is its origin? According to the method stated in the *Hemavata Sutta*, after the Blessed One Kassapa had attained final Nibbāna, two sons of noble family who were brothers went forth as disciples under the followers of the Buddha.
The elder was named Sodhana, and the younger was named Kapila. Their mother was named Sādhanī, and their younger sister was...
As for those called the Tāpanas: they too went forth among the bhikkhunīs.
