Then, both of them, having asked and heard according to the method described in the Hemavata Sutta—"How many duties (*dhura*) are there in the Dispensation?"—the elder said, "I shall fulfill the duty of residence (*vāsadhura*)," and having lived in the presence of his teachers and preceptors for five years, and being thus five years ordained, he [practiced] until he attained Arahantship.
Having heard the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he entered the forest and, through his exertion, attained *arahantship*.
Kapila, thinking, "I am still young; I shall fulfill my duty as a resident when I am old," began his studies of the scriptures and became a master of the Three Piṭakas (*tepiṭaka*).
Relying on his mastery of the texts, a following arose for him, and from that following, gain (*lābha*) followed.
Thus, intoxicated by the pride of his great learning and imagining himself a wise man, he—though lacking true knowledge—imagined himself to possess it;
and when others spoke of what was permissible as impermissible, or the impermissible as permissible, or the blameworthy as blameless, or the blameless as blameworthy, he would say the same.
When he was being exhorted by the virtuous monks in this manner, saying, "Friend Kapila, do not speak thus," he [replied], "You..."
Mocking and reviling him with such words as, "What do you know? You are like an empty fist," he continued his conduct in this manner.
The monks reported this matter even to his brother, the Elder Sodhana. He too approached him and said:
"Friend Kapila, the life of the Dispensation depends upon the right practice of those such as yourself. Do not, friend Kapila..."
“Speak thus: ‘What is allowable is not allowable, what is not allowable is allowable, what is blameworthy is blameless, and what is blameless is blameworthy.
But he did not heed those words either. Then, after Elder Sodhana had spoken thus two or three times, he said:
“A compassionate one might speak once or twice;”
“One should not speak beyond that in the presence of a fellow slave.
Having avoided him, saying, “Friend, you yourself shall be known by your own deeds,” he departed. From that time on, the well-behaved monks shunned him.
Living as one of misconduct surrounded by those of misconduct, one day he thought, “I shall recite the Uposatha.”
Having ascended the lion throne and taken up a variegated fan, he sat down and said three times, "Friends, does the Pātimokkha proceed here for the bhikkhus?
Not even a single bhikkhu said, "It proceeds for me. Yet neither his nor theirs did the Pātimokkha proceed.
Then he thought: "Whether the Pātimokkha has been heard or not, there is indeed what is called the Vinaya."
"There is none," he said, and rose from his seat. Thus he caused the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa to decline and perish.
Then, on that very day, the Elder Sodhana attained final Nibbāna. That Kapila, having likewise caused the teaching to decline, passed away and was reborn in the great Avīci hell;
his mother and sister also followed in his footsteps.
Having committed [these offenses], they reviled and insulted the virtuous monks and, having passed away, were reborn in hell.
At that very time, five hundred men who had lived by robbery, committing acts such as plundering villages, were pursued by the people of the countryside;
while fleeing, they entered a forest, but finding no thicket or place of refuge there, they remained.
Seeing a certain forest-dwelling bhikkhu living on a rock not far away, they paid homage to him and said, "Venerable sir, please be our refuge.
The Elder said, "There is no refuge for you equal to virtue;
all of you, undertake the five precepts. Having accepted with the words, "Very well," they undertook the precepts.
The Elder said, “You are virtuous; even now, though you are destroying your own lives, do not let your minds become corrupted.
They accepted this, saying, “Very well. Then those countryfolk arrived, searching here and there, and seeing those thieves, they deprived them all of their lives.
Having passed away, they were reborn in the world of the gods of the sense-sphere.
Among them, the eldest thief was the eldest son of a deva, and the others were his attendants.
Wandering through the cycle of existence in forward and reverse order, they spent an entire interval between Buddhas in the world of the devas;
then, in the time of our Blessed One, having passed away from the world of the devas, the eldest son of the deva [was reborn] in a fisherman’s village located at the gate of Sāvatthī. There...
He took rebirth in the womb of the wife of the chief fisherman, who was the head of five hundred families;
the others were conceived in the wombs of the remaining wives of the fishermen. Thus, on that very same day, their conception and their emergence from the womb occurred simultaneously.
Then the chief fisherman, searching about, thought, "Are there any other children born today in this village?"
Seeing those boys, he thought, "These shall be companions for my son," and gave them all the means for their upbringing.
All of them, playing together in the dust as companions, gradually reached maturity; among them, Yasa was the eldest.
At that time, Kappa, due to the remainder of his karma from being roasted in hell, became a golden-colored fish with a foul-smelling mouth in the Aciravatī River.

Having offered the sacrifice, he was reborn. Then one day, all the fishermen’s children took their nets and went to the river, thinking, "We shall catch fish," and they cast the nets. That fish entered their net.
Seeing this, the entire village of fishermen raised a great clamor and noise, crying out, "Our sons, while catching fish for the first time, have caught a golden fish!"
“They have been bound; these boys are growing up, and now the King will give us abundant wealth.
Then those five hundred companions of the boys placed the fish in a boat, hoisted the boat, and went into the presence of the King.
Upon seeing it, the King asked, “What is this, my men? “It is a fish, Your Majesty. The King [beheld] the golden-colored...
Seeing the fish, [the king thought], “The Blessed One will know the reason for its golden color,” so he had the fish caught and went into the presence of the Blessed One.
At the moment the fish’s mouth was opened, the Jeta Grove became exceedingly foul-smelling.
The king asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, why has the fish become golden-colored, and why does its mouth [emit this odor]?”
“...or a foul odor blows? “Great King, this was a monk named Kapila in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa;
he was learned and had mastered the tradition. He was one who reviled and abused those monks who did not accept his words.
Because he destroyed that Blessed One’s dispensation, by that [kamma]...”
By that kamma he was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell; and by the remainder of the result of that kamma, he has now been born as a fish.
Because he recited the Buddha’s word for a long time and spoke in praise of the Buddha, through the influence of that, he has obtained such a beautiful color.
Because he was one who reviled and insulted the bhikkhus, a foul odor issues from his mouth. “I shall make him speak.”
“Is that so, Great King? “Yes, Blessed One. Then the Blessed One addressed the fish:
“Are you Kapila? “Yes, Blessed One, I am Kapila. “From where have you come? “From the great Avīci hell, Blessed One. “Where has Sodhana gone?
“He has attained final Nibbāna, Blessed One. “Where has Sādhanī gone? “She has been reborn in the great hell.”
“Blessed One,” he said. “Where has Tāpanā gone? “She has been reborn in the Great Hell, Blessed One.
“And where will you go now? “To the Great Hell, Blessed One. Immediately overcome by remorse, he struck his head against the boat and died, being reborn in the Great Hell.
The great multitude was moved with awe, their hair standing on end. Then—
The Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma appropriate to that moment to the assembly of householders and renunciants who had gathered there, spoke this Sutta.

In this context, "practice of the Dhamma" (*dhammacariyā*) refers to the practice of virtue consisting of good conduct of body and so forth. "Holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya*).

"This they call the supreme wealth" (*etadāhu vasuttamaṃ*): both of these—worldly and supramundane good conduct—are called the supreme wealth because they lead to the attainment of the happiness of heaven and liberation.

"The Noble Ones say it is the supreme treasure (vasuttama). The meaning is that the 'supreme treasure' is a most excellent jewel that follows one, is dependent upon oneself, and is not shared with kings and others.
Having thus far shown that "for both the householder and the renunciant, right practice alone is the refuge," [the text continues:]
Now, seeing the worthlessness of the renunciation that is devoid of practice, he censures Kapila and others of like nature, saying: "Even if one has gone forth," and so forth.
Herein, this is the commentary on the meaning: whoever, having removed the marks of a householder, merely takes up the shaven head, the saffron robes, and so on—
Even if one has gone forth by approaching [the Saṅgha] for the sake of the meaning previously explained— namely, from the home to the homeless life—
if he is of a talkative nature, harsh in speech, delighting in various forms of harassment due to his fondness for harming others,
and like a deer due to the absence of shame and fear of wrongdoing, then his life is worse; the life of such a person as this is extremely evil and exceedingly base.
Why? Because by means of this wrong practice, he increases within himself the manifold defilements such as lust and so forth.

Not only for this reason is his life made worse, but furthermore, because this monk—being talkative by nature and delighting in quarrels—is possessed by the quality of delusion through his confusion regarding the understanding of the meaning of well-spoken words.
Even when the well-behaved monks explain to him in this manner, saying, "Friend Kapila, do not speak thus;
grasp it by this method as well," he does not understand the Dhamma taught by the Buddha.
Whatever Dhamma has been taught by the Buddha, he does not understand it even when it is being told to him in various ways. Thus his life becomes even more wretched.

280. Likewise, because he delighted in causing harm and had cultivated such harmfulness, he harassed those bhikkhus whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava), such as the Elder Sodhana and others, in the manner beginning with:
"You do not know the Vinaya, nor the Sutta, nor the Abhidhamma; you are merely old men who went forth [into the order].
For this genitive case-ending is used here in the sense of an object. Alternatively, it may be understood according to the very method already stated.

The phrase "causing harm to one who has cultivated the self" (*vihesaṃ bhāvitattānaṃ karonto*) should be understood as a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*). In this way, the genitive case is established in its direct sense (*nippariyāya*).

"Preceded by ignorance" (*avijjāya purakkhato*) means being preceded, impelled, and incited by ignorance—which conceals the vision of the danger in harming one who has cultivated the self—and thus proceeding with the state of harming other renunciants who have cultivated the self.
In this very life, through the affliction of the mind, he does not know the defilement; and for the future, he does not know the path leading to hell, which brings about rebirth in hell.
Not knowing this, he has fallen into the ruinous states of woe, consisting of the fourfold division of the lower realms.
And in that ruinous state, from womb to womb, from darkness to darkness, within each single class of beings, he has been born from a mother’s womb even hundreds and thousands of times.
He has entered a darkness even more profound than that which cannot be pierced by the moon and sun within the mother’s womb.
Such a monk, having passed away from here to the world beyond, undergoes manifold kinds of suffering, just like this Kapila fish.
For what reason? Because he is like a cesspool full for eighty years, like a latrine or a pit of excrement.
Suppose there were a cesspit many years old, many years established, and for many years filled and overflowing with excrement from the mouths [of people];
even if it were washed with hundreds or thousands of water-jars, it would be difficult to cleanse because its foul odor and unsightliness would not depart.
In the same way, such a person would be like a cesspit whose deeds have been defiled for a long time.
Because he is filled with evil, like a person filled with excrement, that individual is difficult to cleanse;
for even while experiencing the ripening of that blemish over a long period of time, he is not purified.
Therefore, even after an immeasurable length of time counted by years, such a bhikkhu indeed encounters suffering after death. Alternatively, this [is the meaning] of this verse:
Regarding the connection—concerning what was said, “Such a bhikkhu indeed, having passed away, undergoes suffering”—there might occur to you the thought:
“But is it possible to act in such a way that one does not undergo suffering after passing away?
It is not possible. Why? Because [the body] is like a cesspool... [and so on]... full of filth.
283–4. Therefore, monks, you should know beforehand that such a person is dependent on the household life; you should know that such a person is dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure;
that he possesses evil desires because he is possessed of an evil longing that proceeds in the form of a pursuit for unreal qualities;
that he possesses evil intentions because he is possessed of thoughts of sensual desire and so forth; and [that he possesses evil conduct] by means of bodily transgressions and the like.
Because he is possessed of evil conduct through various forms such as the giving of bamboo, he is one of "evil conduct" (*pāpācāra*);
because his resort is to prostitutes and other such evil haunts, he is one of "evil resort" (*pāpagocara*). "All of you, being in harmony, should avoid him.
In this context, "avoid him" means you should shun him and not associate with him; yet, do not fall into a state of indolence merely by avoiding him. Furthermore—
Furthermore, you must expel the *kāraṇḍava* weed; you must cast out the dregs. Expel that person who has become like refuse, disregarding him as if he were mere trash.

And cast out that one who has become like dregs when he enters among the Kṣatriyas and others—like a Caṇḍāla with leprosy broken out and oozing—seizing him by the hand or by the head, you must drive him away.

Just as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna would seize that person of evil character by the arm, cast him out beyond the gateway, and hand him over to the needle-makers, saying, "Get away like this," so too does he show [the way]. For what reason?
Because the Saṅghārāma was established for those possessed of virtue, not for those who are immoral.
285–6. Therefore, you should winnow away these very ones who are mere chaff, those who are not ascetics yet pride themselves on being ascetics.

For just as chaff, though devoid of grain within, appears like rice externally due to its husks, so too do evil monks, though lacking virtue and other qualities within, appear like true monks externally due to their yellow robes and other requisites. Therefore, they are called "chaff. These chaff—
"Drive them out, clear them away, dispel those who are not true recluses but merely pride themselves on being recluses by outward appearance. Having thus expelled them...
[as before] ...be mindful. In this context, "make it fit" (*kappayavho*) means "you should make it fit," that is, "you should act.
"Mindful" (*patissatā*) means having mutual respect and deference toward one another. Then, being united and prudent, you will make an end to suffering.
"In this way, you who are pure, dwelling in communion with the pure, being in harmony through the commonality of view and virtue,
and being prudent through wisdom that has reached full maturity— you will bring an end to all this suffering of the round of existence and so forth.
Thus he concluded the teaching by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred sons of fishermen were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Aspiring to bring an end to suffering, they went forth in the presence of the Blessed One.

Before long, having brought an end to suffering, they came to share in the same enjoyment as the Blessed One through the attainment of the imperturbable dwelling (*āneñjavihāra*) and the enjoyment of the Dhamma. And this was their [experience]:
The practice of sharing a single meal with the Blessed One is to be understood according to the Udāna,
specifically by way of the Udayasīva Sutta. Thus ends the commentary on the Kapila Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
7. Commentary on the *Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta*.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the *Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta*. What is its origin?

It is that very account which was related in the introduction by way of the passage beginning, "Then, a great number... and so forth. In that context, "a great number" means many, numerous. "Kosalakas" means inhabitants of the kingdom of Kosala.
“Brāhmaṇamahāsālā” means those who are brahmins by birth and are “great sāl trees” (mahāsālā) due to their great worth.
It is said that those who possess eighty koṭis of wealth deposited and kept in store are called “brāhmaṇamahāsālā. These [brahmins] were of such a kind; therefore, it is said, “brāhmaṇamahāsālā.
“Jiṇṇā” means they have become decrepit, having been brought to a state of brokenness and so forth by old age.
*Vuḍḍhā* means having reached the limit of growth in their limbs and members. *Mahallakā* means endowed with the state of being advanced in years;
it is said they have been lying in bed for a long time. *Addhagatā* means gone along the path; the intention is that two or three royal successions have passed.
*Vayo anuppattā* means having reached the final stage of life. Furthermore, *jiṇṇā* means ancient.
"Of long-standing family lineage" is what is meant. "Venerable" means endowed with the growth of qualities such as virtue and conduct.
"Elderly" means possessed of great wealth and vast possessions due to the greatness of their prosperity.

"Advanced in years" refers to those who have entered the path, walking without transgressing the boundaries of the Brahmins' ascetic practices and so forth. "Reached the final stage of life" refers to having attained the state of being aged by birth, even reaching the ultimate stage of life.
"Anuppattā" (arrived) should be understood here as being construed in this way. The rest here is self-evident.
"They exchanged greetings with the Blessed One" means that, by inquiring after his well-being and so forth, they became mutually engaged in the exchange of joyful conversation.
And by [the inquiry]: "I hope it is bearable for Master Gotama, I hope it is sustainable, with little affliction, little discomfort... [and so on].
They exchanged greetings with such talk as, “Strength! Agility! Comfortable living!

This [talk] is "conducive to greetings" (*sammodanīya*) because it generates the kind of greeting known as joy and gladness, and it is "conducive to recollection" (*sāraṇīya*) because, owing to the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, it is worthy of being remembered and continuously maintained even for a very long time;
and furthermore, it is so called because it is pleasant while being heard.
"Sammodanīyaṃ" means "to be remembered with pleasure," because it brings happiness when recollected;
likewise, it is "sammodanīya" due to the purity of its phrasing and "sāraṇīya" due to the purity of its meaning.

Having thus exchanged such pleasantries and memorable words in many ways—concluding, completing, and finishing them—those who had come for a certain purpose, wishing to ask about that matter, sat down to one side. This is what [the text] refers to.
“Neither behind nor in front, nor near nor far;
neither in the windward direction nor in the leeward, nor even on a slope”—
this has been stated in the manner of the commentary on the *Maṅgala Sutta*.
Thus, as they were seated to one side, those wealthy brahmins said this to the Blessed One: “What is it?

[The reply begins with] “Are they seen, indeed? and so forth. All of that is of plain meaning. However, here, setting aside the *brāhmaṇa-dhamma* of the brahmins—that is, the phenomena pertaining to place, time, and so on—it refers specifically to that which is the true *brāhmaṇa-dhamma*. Therefore, [the address] “O brahmins” is used because...
"You have entreated me; therefore, O brahmins, listen, lend an ear, attend well, and attend thoroughly.
Listen with purity of application, attend well with purity of intention.
Listen without distraction, attend well with exertion"—in such a manner [the Buddha spoke] to them.
The intended meaning of these words, though not previously stated, should be understood.
Then, accepting those words spoken by the Blessed One, those wealthy brahmins replied to the Blessed One, "So be it, sir," and they listened with their faces turned toward the Blessed One's words;
or rather, they gave their assent. [This refers to] the matter already stated: "Listen and pay close attention."
It is said that they promised out of a desire to act. Then, to those who had thus made their promise, the Blessed One said this:
"What is it? "The seers of old," and so forth. 287.
Therein, regarding the first verse: *saññatattā* means having minds restrained by the restraint of virtue (*sīla*). *Tapassino* means...

"Engaged in the austerity of restraint of the sense faculties. They accomplished their own welfare through the mastery of mantras, the meditative abodes of the Brahmās, the cultivation of mental states, and so forth.
The rest is self-evident. 288.
This is the brief commentary on the second verse and those that follow: "Cattle are not [the property] of the Brāhmaṇas"—this refers to the ancient Brāhmaṇas.
There were no cattle, nor did they practice the keeping of cattle. There was no gold or grain;

among the brahmins, there was not even a cowrie-shell made of lac, and likewise, there was no grain for them consisting of the various kinds of early and late crops such as rice, paddy, barley, and wheat.
For they, having laid aside gold and silver, being those who do not store up possessions, possessed only the wealth of their recitation and their grain.
They were endowed with wealth and grain consisting precisely of their own mastery of the mantras;

and they constantly guarded that "Brahma-treasure"— which, because it is supreme and because it follows one wherever one goes, is called the Brahma-treasure— by means of constant application to its cultivation.
289. For those who dwell thus, that which was prepared for them—that which had been prepared by these [laypeople] specifically for these brahmins—was food set out at their doors.

"Food set out at the door" means food prepared by various donors with the thought, "We shall give this to the brahmins," and placed at the door of each person's own house. "Prepared with faith" means prepared out of faith.
“Saddhādeyyaṃ” means what has been given out of faith. “Esānaṃ”: those who seek are “esā”;
for them, “of those seeking,” which is to say, “of those searching. “Dātavā” means it should be given. “Tadamaññiṃsu”: they thought that;
they thought that the food prepared and set at the gate was to be given to these brahmins who were seeking what had been given out of faith.
The donors [gave] up to that point, and no further. For they had no desire for anything else; the intention is that they were content with nothing more than food and clothing.
(290) "With various-colored cloths" means with garments dyed with various kinds of colors, spread over beds with variegated coverlets.
With excellent palaces of one, two, or more stories; with such dwellings and furnishings as these;

and with flourishing districts—both those that were individual provinces and those that were entire kingdoms—they paid homage to the brahmins morning and evening, saying, "Homage to the brahmins," just as if they were worshipping deities.
291. Thus being honored by the world, the brahmins were unslayable;
and not only were they unslayable, they were also invincible, being unconquerable because they could not be overcome. For what reason?

Because they were protected by the Dhamma, for they were protected by the Dhamma. Indeed, they guarded the five excellent precepts of the Dhamma, according to the saying: "The Dhamma truly protects those who live by the Dhamma."
The intention is that, having become protectors of the Dhamma, they became inviolable and unconquerable.
"No one could restrain them" means that those brahmins were at the doors of the families—both at the outermost and inner gates—and at all entrances;
for people placed their absolute trust in them, as they were beloved and esteemed, and endowed with excellent virtue, just like mothers and fathers.
Therefore, no one forbade them, saying, "You must not enter this place.

Thus, Dhammarakkhitā and the others, moving about unobstructed at the doors of the families, practiced the celibate life of a youth (komāra-brahmacariya) for forty-eight years from the time they were youths, by virtue of their conduct. This applied even to those who were brahmins and caṇḍālas.
This is how the intended meaning here should be understood: "How much more so, then, in the case of those like Brahmā?
For it was precisely while practicing the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that the brahmins of old pursued knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇapariyeṭṭhi*), not by being non-practitioners of the holy life.
In this context, "pursuit of knowledge" refers to the mastery of the mantras. And this has been said: "For forty-eight years he [practiced] the youth..."

“He practices the holy life while studying the mantras. “Seeking conduct” (*caraṇapariyeṭṭhi*) means the guarding of virtue. There is also a reading, “seeking knowledge and conduct” (*vijjācaraṇapariyeṭṭhu*);
the meaning is that they practiced in order to seek knowledge and conduct.
And having practiced the holy life for the aforementioned period, even those who thereafter establish a household life do not...
The Brahmins went to others—whether they were Kshatriyas or some among the Vessas and so forth—who were either equal to gods or of the same standing;
this is the intended meaning. Likewise, even after giving a hundred or a thousand [pieces of gold], they did not buy a wife, as some do nowadays.
For they sought a spouse in accordance with the Dhamma. How? Forty-eight...
Having practiced the holy life for years, the brahmins wander about begging for maidens, saying: “I have practiced the holy life for forty-eight years;
if there is a girl of marriageable age, give her to me.
Then, whoever has a girl of marriageable age adorns her, brings her out, and presents her to the brahmin standing right at the door.
Pouring water into his hand, he says, "Brahmin, I give this wife of yours for the purpose of raising offspring," and thus gives her.
But why, even after practicing the holy life (brahmacariya) for so long, do they seek a wife and not remain celibate for as long as life lasts?
It is because of wrong view. For they hold such a view as this: "He who does not [beget] a son..."
"He who causes [a lineage] to arise [in such a way] becomes one who cuts off his family line, and because of that, he is tormented in hell.

It is said that four things fear what should not be feared: the gadfly, the hen, the female quail, and the brahmin. It is said that the gadfly eats only its fill out of fear of the exhaustion of the great earth;
it does not eat much clay. The hen-bird [fears] the danger of flying into the sky.
She lies flat on her back upon the egg. The female quail, out of fear of the earth’s trembling, does not step firmly upon the ground with her feet.
The brahmins, out of fear that their family lineage might be cut off, seek a wife. And regarding this, it is said:
“The frog, the woodpecker, the quail, and the brahmin who follows his duty;”
“These four types of people, being deluded, fear that which is fearless.
Thus, even after seeking a wife in accordance with the Dhamma, they joined together in cohabitation out of mutual affection;
indeed, out of mutual affection and love for one another, they became blended, united, and intimately associated in both body and mind.
"Having performed the sacrifice, they consented to cohabitation; it is said that this was neither through what was unpleasant nor by means of compulsion.

(294) Furthermore, even while living together with mutual affection, "except at that time"—that is, setting aside that specific season when the brahmin woman ought to be approached by the brahmin—apart from that time.
To her husband who has abstained from sexual intercourse and is observing the vow of celibacy, [she goes] until that time returns;
she does not stop in the interval. "Sexual intercourse" (*methunaṃ dhammaṃ*) means for the purpose of sexual intercourse.
This accusative case is used as a recipient case (*sampadāna*) out of respect. "They do not go" means they do not go at all. "Brahmins" refers to those who are equal to the gods.
And the intended meaning is "a boundary. 295.

But generally speaking, all [of them] disparaged both the holy life (*brahmacariya*)... [and so forth]... the lack of praise. In that context, "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means abstention from sexual intercourse.
"Virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the remaining four precepts. "Uprightness" (*ajjava*) is the state of being straight; in terms of its essential meaning, it is honesty.

And freedom from deceit (*amāyāvitā*). Gentleness (*maddava*) is softness of disposition; in meaning, it is the absence of rigidity and the absence of pride. Austerity (*tapo*) is the restraint of the sense faculties.

Kindness (*soracca*) is the state of being well-disposed, having a pleasant character, and conduct that is not disagreeable. Non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) is the nature of not harming with hands and so forth, and the state of possessing compassion.
Patience (*khantī*) is patience as endurance. Thus they praised these virtues. And those who were unable [to do so]...
In order to fully accomplish their practice, they too, regarding those [teachings] as essential,
praised and extolled them with words. And while they were thus praising, he who was their supreme Brahmā—
the highest Brahmin named Brahmasama— on account of his being endowed with firm exertion, did not come.
“Of firm exertion”: the word *vā* is used here in the sense of clarification; by it, he clarifies that such is the nature of this brahmin.

“Sexual intercourse” (*methunaṃ dhammaṃ*): this refers to the act of sexual union. “Even in a dream he did not go”: even in his dreams, he did not engage in it. 297. Then, regarding his conduct... [they] censured him.
By means of this verse, [the author] summarizes, from beginning to end, the very virtues already described in the ninth verse.
By describing them, he reveals those brahmins who are equal to the gods. For they are of a wise nature and are learned;
they train themselves in the conduct of that brahmin who is equal to Brahmā, both in the life of renunciation and in the cultivation of meditative absorption (jhāna).

And these qualities, such as the holy life (brahmacariya), they praise only through actual practice. All those brahmins are to be understood in the same manner as described in the *Doṇa Sutta* of the *Pañcaka Nipāta*.
298. Now, showing the brahmins who observe the boundary (mariyāda), he says: "Rice and bedding. Its meaning is as follows:

among those [brahmins], those who are observers of the boundary, if they desire to perform a sacrifice, then—because they abstain from accepting raw grain—they [offer] various kinds of rice, bedding consisting of couches, stools, and so forth, and [garments] consisting of linen cloth and so forth.
Having requested cloth, and ghee, oil, and so forth—such as varieties of ghee and oil—in accordance with the Dhamma;
that is, having requested according to the principle known as "the designated place" (uddissaṭṭhāna), as it is said: "The Noble Ones stand designated; this is the designation of the Noble Ones";
then, whatever one wishes to give, such as rice and so forth, having gathered and collected it together from those [donors]. It is also called "having procured" (samudānetvā).
The reading is the same; the meaning is identical. "Then they prepared a sacrifice" means that, taking [the aforementioned items] from there, they gave them as a gift.
And while performing it—while this sacrifice, known as giving, was thus being carried out—they did not slaughter cows;
they did not kill those cattle. Here, by the mention of "cows," it should be understood that all living beings are implied. For what reason?
"Did they not kill [them]? Because they were endowed with virtues such as the holy life (*brahmacariya*). Furthermore, specifically, just as a mother... [and so on] ...they did not kill those cows.
In that context, "in which the medicinal herbs are born" means in which the five products of the cow, which serve as remedies for bile and other ailments, are produced.
Regarding the passage beginning with "givers of food," etc., it is because for those who consume the five products of the cow, hunger is pacified and strength increases.
The complexion of the skin becomes serene, and physical and mental happiness arises;
therefore, it should be understood that the gift of food is a giver of strength, a giver of beauty, and a giver of happiness. The rest here is of plain meaning. 301.
Thus, those who did not slaughter cows at sacrifices, their bodies sustained by the power of merit, being delicate... [and so on] ...thrived in happiness.
"Those people": therein, they are delicate because their hands, feet, and so forth are soft and smooth; they are large-bodied because of the perfection of their height and girth;
they are beautiful because of their golden complexion and well-proportioned form; and they are renowned because of their success in gain and retinue.
"By their own qualities" means by their own modes of conduct. "Zealous in what should and should not be done" means regarding duties, [thinking] "this must be done."
The meaning is: having become diligent regarding what should not be done, thinking, "This must not be performed.

Thus, those ancient brahmins, being such as they were—beautiful to behold, inspiring confidence, and supremely worthy of offerings—through this practice, for as long as they remained in the world, they flourished and attained manifold kinds of happiness, being free from illness, fear, and calamity.
"He thrived in happiness" means he attained growth in happiness. This verse indicates the world of beings (*sattaloka*).
But in the course of time, for those who desired to reach a state where the boundaries were broken down, there arose a perversion... [etc] ... "divided into portions.
Therein, "perversion" (*vipallāsa*) means distorted perception (*viparīta-saññā*). "From atom to atom" (*aṇuto aṇuṃ*) means in the sense of being base or limited (*paritta*).
"Seeing sensual pleasure as slight"—that is, seeing it as minute because it has become so due to its lack of gratification;

or, by comparison with the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of the state of a recluse, and the bliss of Nibbāna, it does not even admit of being reckoned [as a fraction of them]; or, by comparison with supramundane bliss, it has become minute;
or, even though it is itself meager, it is seen as "slight" because it is minute compared to the mundane bliss of attainment (samāpatti) obtained by oneself.
The intention (*adhippāyo*). "And of the king" (*rājino ca*) means "and of the monarch. "They proclaimed" (*viyākāraṃti*) means [they proclaimed] prosperity.

"In connection with thoroughbred horses" (*ājaññasaṃyutte*) means in connection with noble steeds. "Well-finished" (*sukateti*) means well-completed by means of woodwork and metalwork. "In variegated stitching" (*cittasibbane*) means in variegated stitching by way of decorating with lion skins and so forth.
"Dwellings" (*nivesane*) refers to house-sites. "Houses" (*nivese*) refers to the houses established thereon. "Distributed" (*vibhatte*)...

They are divided according to length and breadth. "Measured by parts" means they were measured by being divided into portions, such as courtyards, gates, palaces, gabled chambers, and so forth. What is meant?

For those brahmins, the sensual pleasure known as the subtle (aṇu), the king’s reply, the adorned women, and the aforementioned chariots and dwellings were [all] contained within the dwelling (nivese).

And having seen these very objects as suffering, because they proceeded [in their minds] as "pleasure," there previously existed a perverted perception (viparītasaññā) consisting of a perversion of the perception of renunciation (nekkhammasaññā). 304.

Having thus possessed such perverted perceptions, [they saw] that which was surrounded by a herd of cows... [etc. ...by the brahmins. In this context, "surrounded by a herd of cows" means encircled by herds of cattle.
"Joined with a multitude of excellent women" means associated with a group of choice women. "Exalted" means vast.
"Human enjoyment" means the objects of enjoyment for humans, such as dwellings and so forth.
"They were covetous" means that they meditated while increasing their craving and longing, thinking, "O, may this be ours!
And while thus coveting, [they saw] these humans well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beards trimmed, adorned with necklaces and ornaments.

They enjoy themselves with the five strands of sensual pleasure, yet we, though being thus honored by them, dwell having reached a state of supreme misery—our bodies defiled by sweat and grime, our armpits, nails, and body hair grown long, and destitute of wealth. They travel on the backs of elephants, on horseback, in palanquins, and in golden chariots, while we travel on foot.
They dwell on the floors of two-storied mansions and the like, while we dwell in the wilderness, at the roots of trees, and so forth.
“While these people sleep on excellent beds covered with woolen rugs and the like, we sleep on the ground after spreading out mats, pieces of hide, and so forth.
While these people eat foods of various flavors, we subsist by gleaning grains.
How might we too become their equals? Having thought this, [he realized] that wealth must be sought; it is not...
Having determined that "this prosperity can be attained even by those devoid of wealth," they split the Vedas;
having destroyed the ancient mantras consistent with the Dhamma, they composed fraudulent mantras inconsistent with the Dhamma.
Then, those seeking wealth approached King Okkāka, uttered words of blessing and the like, and said: "O Great King, there is an ancient mantra-verse that has come down through our brahmin lineage."
“There is such a thing, but because we were held in the grip of our teacher’s secrecy, we did not tell anyone;
it is worthy for the Great King to hear it,” they said, and then they extolled the horse-sacrifice and other offerings. Having praised them, they urged the king on: “Sacrifice, O Great King!
You possess such abundance of wealth and grain that there is no lack of materials for the sacrifice. For by sacrificing in this way, seven generations of your family...”
“They will be reborn in heaven,” they said. To show them this occurrence, the Blessed One said:
“There they [recite] the mantras... there is much wealth for them.
In that context, “there” means for the sake of that very object of wealth which they coveted; it is stated thus in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
For this is a word denoting the present tense (*bhummavacana*). "Tadupāgamun" means "they approached at that time. "Pahūtadhanadhaññosī" means "you will possess abundant wealth and grain";
the intended meaning is "in the future life" (*abhisamparāya*). For those skilled in grammar accept the present tense even for the future when expressing a hope.
"Yajassu" means "perform sacrifices. "Vittaṃ dhanaṃ" means gold and other such jewels, because they are the cause of prosperity.

*Vitta* is said to mean "wealth" (*dhana*) because it is a cause for prosperity. Alternatively, *vitta* refers to requisites such as ornaments that serve as the cause for prosperity—those which appear in passages such as "possessing abundant wealth and requisites. *Dhana*, however, refers to gold, bullion, and so forth. What is meant [by this]?
Those brahmins, having composed the mantras, then approached Okkāka. How so? "O Great King," [they said].
“You have much wealth and property; perform sacrifice! Even in the future, you will possess abundant wealth and grain.
(306) Having thus stated the reason, the king—being thus exhorted by those who were persuading him—gave away his wealth.

In this context, *saññatto* means “informed” or “persuaded. *Rathesabho* means one who is like a bull (*usabha*) among the great chariot-warrior kṣatriyas in the sense of being unshakable. Regarding the terms “horse-sacrifice” (*assamedha*) and so forth:

*Assamedha* means "the sacrifice where horses are immolated"; this is a designation for that sacrifice which is to be performed with two *pariyañña* rites, has twenty-one sacrificial stakes (*yūpa*), and consists of all remaining wealth as the offering fee (*dakṣiṇā*), with the exception of the earth and men.
*Purisamedha* means "the sacrifice where men are immolated"; this refers to the sacrifice which is to be performed with four *pariyañña* rites, including the earth...
This is a designation for the sacrifice in which the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of the wealth previously mentioned in the *Assamedha*. "Sammāpāsa" means "those who look on correctly here";

it refers to that which is to be sacrificed by one who, having thrown the *samma* stake day after day, has constructed an altar (*vedi*) at the spot where it fell, and then proceeds upstream from the place where the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and other items were collected, starting from the point where they submerged in the river Sarassatī.
This is a designation for a sacrificial session (*sattra-yāga*). Because they drink the *vāja* (grain-offering) therein, it is called the *vājapeyya*.
This is a designation for a sacrifice consisting of a single enclosure with seventeen animals, an oblation of *veluva* wood, and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of seventeen items.
It is called *niraggaḷa* because there are no bolts (*aggaḷa*) here; it is a sacrifice to be performed with nine enclosures together with the ground.

And this is a designation for the variant of the horse sacrifice (assamedha-vikappa), which is called by all the names of the "all-sacrifice" (sabbamedha) and for which the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is as described in the case of the horse sacrifice, along with men. The rest here is self-evident.
307–8. Now, showing what was stated in the phrase "He gave wealth to the brahmins," [the text says]: "Cows and a bed..."

He spoke these two verses. For that king, thinking, "Let them who have long been exhausted by coarse food now enjoy the five products of the cow," gave them entire herds of cows together with their bulls;

likewise, [thinking], "Let those who have long been exhausted by sleeping on the bare ground, wearing coarse hempen garments, sleeping alone, traveling on foot, and dwelling at the roots of trees and so forth, now rest upon excellent beds spread with woolen blankets and the like."
Thinking, "May they experience happiness," he gave them costly beds and other such items. In this way, he gave these various things as well as other wealth, such as gold and bullion.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Cows, beds, and clothing...
[and so forth] ...he gave wealth to the brahmins."
309–10. Thus, having received [wealth] from that king at those sacrifices... they returned once again. What is meant by this?

Having obtained wealth from that king at those sacrifices, those brahmins sought food and clothing in this very manner day after day for a long time, and they accumulated various kinds of material objects of desire.

Then, as their minds were overwhelmed by craving for flavors—due to their indulgence in the five products of the cow, such as milk and the rest—their craving increased even further with respect to meat, [thinking]:
"If even the milk and so forth of cows are so delicious, surely the flesh of these [beings] must be even more delicious.
Thereupon, they thought: "If we kill them and eat [the flesh],"...
“We shall become objects of reproach; what if we were now to compose mantras?
Then, having once again split the Veda and composed mantras there that corresponded to it, those brahmins, having composed fraudulent mantras for that purpose, approached King Okkāka once more.
Speaking this matter, they said: “Just as water and... [pe] ...much wealth is yours.”

What is meant by this? Great King, it is stated in our mantras that just as water is utilized by living beings for all tasks such as washing the hands and so forth, there is no evil for them arising from that cause.
Why? Because it is an accessory (*parikkhāra*) for living beings;
the intention is that it has arisen for the purpose of being a requisite. And just as this great earth [is used] for all tasks such as walking and standing...
Gold known as *kahāpaṇas*, wealth consisting of gold, silver, and so forth, and grain consisting of varieties such as barley and wheat, are put to use in all activities such as commerce;
in the same way, cattle have arisen for the purpose of being employed in all the affairs of human beings.
Therefore, having slaughtered these, perform various kinds of sacrifices; you possess much wealth, perform many sacrifices—you have abundant riches.

311–12. Thus, in the same manner as before, the king from that point on... [omitted] ...did not have any living being killed, nor did he cause anyone to be killed by his feet... [omitted] ...as he had done previously.
At that time, it is said, the brahmins filled the sacrificial enclosure with cows, bound a bull for the auspicious ceremony, and led them before the king, saying:
"Great King, perform the Gomedha sacrifice; in this way, [you shall attain] the Brahma-world."
"The path will become purified," they said. Having performed the auspicious rites, the king took up his sword and, together with Puṅgava, slaughtered many hundreds of thousands of cows.
In the sacrificial enclosure, the brahmins cut the meat and ate it;
they slaughtered them while wearing yellow, white, and red blankets. It is said that from that time on, when cows see someone wearing such blankets, they become terrified.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Neither with his feet... [etc. ...

did he cause them to be slain. (313) Then, “the gods”: when that queen had thus begun to have the cows slaughtered, immediately thereafter, having seen that cow-killer, these gods—beginning with those of the Realm of the Four Great Kings—and the *pitaraḥ* (fathers), who are a designation used among the brahmins...
Brahmā and Sakka, lord of the devas, as well as the asuras and rakkhasas known as dānavas and yakkhas who dwell at the foot of the mountains, let out cries of "Injustice!
Injustice! and wailed, saying, "Shame on humans! Shame on humans!
Thus, from the earth upwards, that sound reached the Brahma-world in an instant, filled with a single cry of reproach.
The world was afflicted. For what reason? Because the weapon fell upon the cow; for it is said that the weapon fell upon the cow.
314. And not only did the gods and others cry out, but this other misfortune also arose in the world:
those three diseases which existed before—desire, hunger, and old age—and whatever slight craving for objects there might be, as well as physical hunger.
And it is said that there is also decay born of ripening. "From the commencement of those animal sacrifices, they reached ninety-eight":
the meaning is that they attained the state of being ninety-eight through the division beginning with eye diseases.
Now, the Blessed One, censuring that undertaking of animal sacrifice, said: "This is unrighteousness" (*adhamma*). The meaning of this is as follows:

That which is designated as the slaughter of animals—being one of the three types of violence (daṇḍa) such as bodily violence and so forth—was an "unrighteousness" (adhamma) because it had departed from the Dhamma;
it had descended, meaning it had come into being. And because it has been in existence since that time, it is "ancient.
From the moment it descended, cows—which were previously harmless because they were not harmed by anyone with their feet or other means—were killed. Those who kill them...
"Phenomena crumble, pass away, and decline; so know, O sacrificers who perform sacrifices.
(316) "In this way, this is a minor phenomenon (*aṇudhamma*)," meaning that this is a base phenomenon, a low phenomenon—in other words, it is called "non-phenomenon" (*adhamma*).
Alternatively, because there is even a small amount of the phenomenon of giving here, he said "a minor phenomenon" with reference to that. "Ancient" (*porāṇa*)...
It is called "ancient" because it has been in practice for such a long time.

It should be understood as "condemned by the wise" because it is censured by those who possess discernment. And because it is condemned by the wise, people therefore censure the sacrificer wherever they see such a thing.
How so? With such words as: "This is a source of corruption produced by the brahmins; having slaughtered cows, they eat their meat," and so forth.
"Having spoken"—this is the oral tradition here.
317. "When the Dhamma had thus fallen away": when the ancient Dhamma of the brahmins had perished.
There is also the reading "viyāvatta," meaning having turned back or become otherwise. "The Suddas and Vessikas were divided": those who formerly lived in harmony.
The *suddas* and the *vessas* are divided; the *khattiyas* are widely divided—many *khattiyas* are split from one another.

"A wife despised her husband" means that wives, having been established in authority and power for the sake of household life and being endowed with the strength of their sons and so forth, despised their husbands;
they treated them with contempt, slighted them, and did not serve them with due respect.
318. Thus, though they are mutually divided—both the kṣatriyas and those who are mere nominal brahmins (brahmabandhu)—... [they all] fall under the sway of sensual desires.

Whether they be kṣatriyas, brahmins, or others such as vaiśyas and śūdras, they are "protected by lineage" because they are guarded by their respective lineages so that they do not fall into intermixture. All of them, having set aside that doctrine of birth, [say]: "I..."

Having utterly destroyed all such [distinctions] as "I am a khattiya" or "I am a brahmin," they fell under the sway of and became attached to the sensual pleasures known as the five strands of sense-pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). It is said that for the sake of sensual pleasure, there was nothing they would not do that should not be done.
Thus, in this context, the Blessed One [described] the praise of the ancient brahmins with these nine verses beginning with "The seers of old."
Having spoken thus, he [described] one equal to Brahmā with the verse beginning “He who is their supreme”; one equal to a deva with the verse beginning “Training in accordance with his conduct”;
the boundary with the four verses beginning “Rice and a bed”; the transgression of that boundary with the seventeen verses beginning “There was a perversion among them”;
and for the purpose of illustrating the fleeing and other reactions of the devas and others due to his misconduct.
Having thus shown this, he brought his teaching to a conclusion. As for the "outcaste Brahmin," however, he is not mentioned here.

Why? Because he is not a cause for failure. For it is the fulfillment of the qualities of a Brahmin that is the cause for being equal to a Brahmā, equal to the gods, and possessing noble boundaries; whereas one who has breached those boundaries is the cause for failure.
Yet this "outcaste Brahmin" of the type described in the Doṇa Sutta [is not such a case], even regarding the failure of the qualities of a Brahmin.
It is not the reason. Why? Because it arises when the Dhamma has already perished. Therefore, he concluded his teaching without even showing that [reason].
Nowadays, even such a "brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍāla" is rare. Thus, this Dhamma of the brāhmaṇas has been ruined.
For this very reason, the brāhmaṇa Doṇa said: "This being so, Master Gotama, we do not even fulfill the status of a 'brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍāla'."
The rest here is exactly according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā,
within the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Dhamma-sutta* (also called the *Nāvā-sutta*). 319.
It is called the *Dhamma-sutta* because it begins with the words "The Dhamma," and it is also referred to as the "*Nāvā-sutta*" (Ship Sutta). What is its origin?
This sutta was spoken concerning the Venerable Elder Sāriputta. This is the summary; for the detailed account, however—
This should be understood from the time of the appearance of the two Chief Disciples. That is to say:
it is said that before the Blessed One had arisen, the two Chief Disciples fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable age and a hundred thousand aeons and were reborn in the world of the gods.
Of them, the first, having passed away, was born in a brahmin village called Upatissa-gāma, not far from Rājagaha, which was a wealthy settlement of brahmins.
There, in the womb of a brahmin woman named Rūpasārī—the wife of a village headman who possessed a wealth of five hundred and sixty million coins—he took rebirth.
Not far from that place, there was another wealthy brahmin village called Kolitagāma. There, in the womb of the wife of a village headman of similar means...
A brahmin woman named Moggallānī conceived that very same day; thus, their conception and birth from the womb occurred on one and the same day. On that very same day, they were given names:
because one was born in the village of Upatissa, he was named Upatisso, and because the other was born in the village of Kolita, he was named Kolito.
Playing together in the dust, those companions gradually reached adulthood, and each came to have a retinue of five hundred young men.
Whenever they went to a park or to a river crossing, they went only with their respective retinues;
one went with five hundred golden palanquins, and the second with five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses. And at that time, in Rājagaha...
From time to time, there was a festival known as the "Mountain-top Festival.

At evening time, in the center of the city, where all the renowned young nobles and others dwelling in Aṅga and Magadha would assemble and sit upon well-prepared couches and seats, they would behold the splendor of the festival.
Then those companions, together with that retinue, went there and sat down on the prepared seats.
Then Upatissa, observing the splendor of the assembly and seeing the great multitude gathered together, thought:
"This entire mass of people will die before even a hundred years have passed. Death, as it were, came upon him and settled upon his forehead;
it was the same for Kolita. Even while they watched the many kinds of dancers performing their dances, [death remained present].
His mind did not incline toward it; rather, only a sense of spiritual urgency arose.
Then, when the festival had ended and the crowd had departed, and those companions had left with their own retinues, Kolita asked Upatissa:
"Friend, did you not experience even a mere glimmer of joy from seeing the dancers and other performances?"
Thus, having reported his own situation to him, he questioned the other in the same manner.
The latter also reported his own situation to him and said, "Come, friend, let us go forth and seek the Deathless. "Very well, friend," Upatissa agreed.
Then both men, casting aside their prosperity, returned once more to Rājagaha.
At that time, there lived in Rājagaha a wanderer named Sañcaya.
Having gone forth in his presence together with five hundred young brahmins, they mastered the three Vedas and the entire system of the wanderers in just a few days.
As they examined the beginning, middle, and end of those teachers' doctrines, they failed to see any conclusion.

They asked their teacher: "The beginning and middle of these teachings are seen, but the end is not seen—that is, where these teachings would reach such that there would be nothing further to be reached.
He replied: "I too do not see such an end for them. They said: "In that case, we..."
“Let us search for the end of these [questions]. The teacher said to them, “Search as you please.
Thus, having been permitted by him, they wandered about Jambudīpa searching for the Deathless (amata) and became well-known.

When the wise among the Kṣatriyas and others were questioned by them with a question, they could not provide a superior answer. But when it was said, “Upatissa and Kolita,” they asked, “Who are these?”

"We do not know," they said, and thus they became so renowned. While they were thus wandering in search of the Deathless, our Blessed One arose in the world; having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, he eventually arrived at Rājagaha. And those wanderers, having wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa—let alone [the rest]— [The text continues: ...they heard that the ascetic Gotama had arrived at Rājagaha and was staying on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain. Hearing this, they thought: "We have heard that the ascetic Gotama is a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. It is good for us to go and see him. Then those wanderers went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma. Having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, those wanderers rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on their right, departed. Then, after some time, those wanderers approached the Blessed One again and said to him: "Master Gotama, we wish to enter the holy life under Master Gotama. The Blessed One replied: "Come, monks! Thus did they become monks. Then, after some time, those monks approached the Blessed One and said to him: "Venerable sir, we wish to go forth into homelessness in the various directions. The Blessed One replied: "Monks, it is difficult to find a teacher such as I am. Monks, it is difficult to find a Dhamma such as mine. Monks, it is difficult to find a Sangha such as mine. Monks, you should dwell here; it is not fitting for you to depart. But those monks, being insistent and persistent, said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, we wish to go forth into homelessness in the various directions. The Blessed One replied: "Monks, if you cannot live without seeing me, then let each of you take a single robe and a bowl and go out through the gateway. When you have gone out, turn back and come back to me. "Very well, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. Taking a single robe and a bowl, they went out through the gateway. Having gone out, they turned back and came to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, when you have gone out through the gateway, turn back and come back to me. "Venerable sir, we have done exactly as the Blessed One commanded. The Blessed One said: "Monks, when you have gone out through the gateway, turn back and come back to me. But when you have gone out, do not turn back; instead, go straight on until you reach the edge of the ocean. There, having reached the edge of the ocean, build a hut of leaves and grass and dwell there. Do not speak to anyone who approaches you, whether they ask you questions or not. If anyone asks you, 'Who are you? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where are you going? you should answer, 'We do not know. "Monks, when you have gone out through the gateway, turn back and come back to me. But when you have gone out, do not turn back; instead, go straight on until you reach the edge of the ocean. There, having reached the edge of the ocean, build a hut of leaves and grass and dwell there. Do not speak to anyone who approaches you, whether they ask you questions or not. If anyone asks you, 'Who are you? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where are you going? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where do you come from? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where do you stay? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'What is your name? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Whose disciples are you? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where is your Teacher? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where is your Teacher dwelling?

you should answer, 'We do not know. "Monks, when you have gone out through the gateway, turn back and come back to me. But when you have gone out, do not turn back; instead, go straight on until you reach the edge of the ocean. There, having reached the edge of the ocean, build a hut of leaves and grass and dwell there. Do not speak to anyone who approaches you, whether they ask you questions or not. If anyone asks you, 'Who are you? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where are you going? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where do you come from? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where do you stay? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'What is your name? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Whose disciples are you? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where is your Teacher? you should answer, 'We do not know. If anyone asks you, 'Where is your Teacher dwelling? you should answer, 'We do not know. While those monks were thus wandering in search of the Deathless, our Blessed One, having arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, eventually arrived at Rājagaha. And those wanderers, having wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa—let alone [the rest]—stood [there].
Failing to obtain even the final answer to their question regarding the Deathless, they returned once more to Rājagaha.
Then, from the venerable Assaji’s dressing of his robes in the morning until their full admission into the order,
everything should be understood in detail according to the method already set forth in the Pabbajjā-kkhandhaka.
When those two companions had thus gone forth, the Venerable Sāriputta realized the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*) within half a month.

Whenever he lived in the same monastery as the Elder Assaji, he would first go to attend upon the Blessed One and immediately thereafter go to attend upon the Elder, thinking: “This venerable one is my former teacher; it is to him that I [should go].”
"Out of reverence, he attained final knowledge by relying on the Blessed One’s teaching.

However, when he did not reside in the same monastery as the Elder Assaji, he would look toward the direction in which the elder was staying, prostrate himself with the five limbs touching the ground, raise his joined palms, and pay homage. Seeing this, some monks raised a discussion.
“Sāriputta, having been the chief disciple, pays homage to the direction; even today, it seems, he has not abandoned his brahminical views.
Then the Blessed One, having heard that conversation with his divine ear-element, while remaining seated right there on the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, about what discussion are you gathered here now?”
They reported that occurrence to him. Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, Sāriputta is not worshipping the directions;
rather, he is paying homage, worshipping, and honoring his own teacher, by whom he came to understand the Dispensation. Monks, Sāriputta is one who honors his teachers.
Having said this, he spoke this discourse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those assembled there.

In this context, because of the phrase "for a person should understand the Dhamma," it means that a person—having heard the *pariyatti*-Dhamma, which is the scriptural teaching divided into the Three Piṭakas, or having heard the *pariyatti*—should understand, know, and realize the *paṭivedha*-Dhamma, which is the realization of the ninefold supramundane states (*navalokuttara*).
There is also a reading, "yassā" (of whom), which has the same meaning. "The deities would worship him as they do Indra."

Just as the deities in two celestial worlds worship Sakka, the lord of the gods, even so that person, rising at the proper time, should worship, honor, and revere that person by performing all the duties and services, such as removing his sandals.
For what reason? When he is thus honored... [he] reveals the Dhamma; that teacher, being honored in this way...
With a mind full of confidence toward that pupil, being himself well-versed through both mastery of the scriptures and penetration of their meaning,
he manifests and teaches the Dhamma of the scriptures by way of exposition, and the Dhamma of penetration which is to be realized through practice as instructed after hearing the exposition;
or else, by means of the exposition, he manifests the Dhamma of the scriptures, and by means of similes, he manifests the Dhamma of penetration attained by himself.

"Having taken it to heart and reflected upon it, the wise one": thus, having taken to heart and heard the Dhamma manifested by the teacher who is so confident, the person is "wise" (*dhīra*) because of his capacity for retention.

"Practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma" means cultivating insight (*vipassanā*), which is the "Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhamma*) because it conforms to the supramundane Dhamma. "He becomes discerning, perceptive, and subtle."
He is "wise" (*viññū*) through the attainment of wisdom known as discernment; he is "discerning" (*vibhāvī*) because of his capacity to make things clear and manifest even to others;
and he is "subtle" (*nipuṇo*) due to his penetration of the most refined meanings.
"One who associates with such a person heedfully" means that one who is heedful should associate with such a learned person as previously described, being intent on winning his confidence.
321. Having thus praised the service of wise teachers, he now spoke this verse beginning with “The fool, small...,” censuring the service of foolish teachers.
In that context, “small” (*khudda*) means one who is possessed of inferior bodily actions and so forth; “fool” (*bāla*) means one lacking wisdom.

“One whose aim is not attained” (*anāgatattha*) means one who has not achieved the goal of mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and penetration (*paṭivedha*). “Envious” (*usūyaka*) refers to one characterized by jealousy.
[This refers to] a teacher who cannot endure the prosperity of his pupil. The rest here is clear from the words themselves. But in terms of the underlying intention (*adhippāya*):

it is when a teacher who receives many robes and other requisites is unable to give robes and so forth to his pupils, yet is also unable to give even a single word concerning impermanence, suffering, and non-self within the gift of the Dhamma.
This is because he is possessed of qualities such as meanness (*khuddatā*) and the like.
By attending upon such a teacher— one who is petty, foolish, ignorant of the future goal, and envious— one becomes foolish oneself,
according to the method described in the passage beginning, “Like a piece of rotten fish on the tip of a blade of kusa grass. Therefore, in this Dispensation,

one who has not clarified or understood even a small portion of either the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) or the Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedha*), and who has not crossed over the doubt regarding those teachings—
"He approaches death"—thus is its meaning to be understood.
Now, in order to make that very meaning clear, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Just as a man. Therein, *āpagaṃ* means a river.
*Mahodakaṃ* means having much water. *Salilaṃ* means that which has gone hither and thither; *vitthiṇṇaṃ* means broad.
It has been said. There is also the reading “saritaṃ,” which has the same meaning. “Sīghasotaṃ” means carrying away; it is said to be “possessing velocity.
Regarding the phrase “kiṃ so,” since that man is indicated here by the expression “so vuyhamāno” (being carried away), the syllable “so” is merely a particle.
It is meant as “kiṃ su” (what indeed?), just as in the expression “na bhavissāmi nāma so, vinassissāmi” (I shall not exist, indeed, I shall perish).
"Named thus. "Dhamma" refers precisely to the two kinds previously mentioned. "Without having examined the meaning" means without having investigated the meaning.
The rest here is clear from the words themselves.
As for the underlying intention (*adhippāya*), it is as follows: suppose some man were to descend into a river of the kind described and [enter] that river...
Being carried away, going with the current, and following that very current—how can he lead others to the further shore?

(The reading *sakkati* is also found. In the same way, one who has not clarified the twofold Dhamma through his own wisdom, and has not investigated its meaning in the presence of those who are well-versed, does not know because he has not clarified it himself, and is not free from doubt because he has not investigated it.
"How can others make one understand or see [the truth]?"—this is how the meaning here should be understood.
Furthermore, the Sutta passage beginning with "How indeed, Cunda, could he who is himself mired in the mire... should be recalled here.
(324–5) Thus, for the purpose of making manifest the fact that through associating with fools, a fool is unable to make another understand [the truth].

Having provided the simile, he now recited the two verses beginning with “Just as with a boat” (*yathāpi nāvaṃ*) in order to make manifest the wise person’s capacity to convince others, as described in the verse: “He who, being heedful, associates with such a one. Therein, *phiyena* means with a paddle;
*rittena* means with a bamboo pole. *Tattha* means on that boat. *Tatrūpayaññū* means one who knows the proper means for that [situation].
He is "one who knows the means" (upāyaññū) because he knows the methods for bringing that boat, warding it off, and so forth, and because he has set out upon the path.
He is "skilled" (kusala) because he has trained in the precepts and possesses great dexterity of hand. He is "wise" (mutīmā) because of his capacity to counteract arisen calamities.

He is a "knower of the Vedas" (vedagū), meaning he has gone by means of the four kinds of path-knowledge known as the Vedas. He is "one whose self is cultivated" (bhāvitatta) because his mind has been developed by that very cultivation of the path.

"Bahussuto" (learned) is according to the method already explained above. "Avedhadhammo" (one whose nature is unshakable) means one whose essential nature is unshakeable by the eight worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
"Sotāvadhānūpanisūpapanno" (endowed with the basis for lending an ear) means endowed both with the application of the ear and with the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits.
The rest has its meaning plain on the surface. Since the construction of the intended meaning can also be understood through the previous method, it has not been elaborated upon here.

326. Having thus spoken a simile to reveal the wise person’s capacity to inspire others, the Buddha spoke this final verse, beginning with "Therefore indeed," in order to direct one toward such service to the wise. Herein is the summary of the meaning:
because those endowed with the necessary supporting conditions attain distinction through service to the wise, therefore indeed one should serve a true person (*sappurisa*).
One should associate with such a person. With what kind of true person (sappurisa) should one associate?
With one who is both wise and learned—that is, wise by virtue of the perfection of wisdom, and learned by virtue of the two kinds of learning already mentioned.

For by associating with such a person, one comes to understand the meaning of the Dhamma spoken by him; and having understood it thus, by practicing according to the instructions, through that very practice—
"By means of penetration, one who has understood the Dhamma would obtain, attain, and reach supramundane happiness,
which is distinguished by the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna"— thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
From the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Dhamma-sutta of the Suttanipāta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Kiṃsīla-sutta (What-kind-of-conduct-sutta) 327.
"Kiṃsīlo" refers to the Kiṃsīla-sutta. What is its origin? A certain lay friend of the Venerable Sāriputta...
The son of a brahmin who was a friend of that very same elder’s father, the brahmin Vaṅganta—
having renounced wealth exceeding five hundred and sixty crores— went forth in the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera and mastered the entire word of the Buddha.
After the Elder had exhorted him many times, he gave him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and by means of that...
He did not attain any distinction. Then the Elder, knowing that "this one is to be led by the Buddha," took him and went into the presence of the Blessed One.
Regarding that monk, without specifying the individual, he asked, "Of what character is he?

Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke further concerning him. In this context, "of what character" means endowed with what kind of morality of restraint (*vāritta-sīla*), and of what kind of natural disposition (*pakati*).
"Of what conduct? means endowed with what kind of behavior. "What actions do they cultivate? means increasing which bodily actions and so forth.
"A person who is well-established" means that a person who delights [in the teaching] would be properly established in the dispensation.
"And he attains the supreme goal" means that he would attain the state of Arhatship, the highest of all states; this is what is meant.
Then the Blessed One, reflecting—“Sāriputta has been ordained for only half a month and has attained perfection as a disciple;

why does he ask a question concerning a beginner who is still an ordinary person?”—and knowing that it was "concerning his co-resident," he taught the Dhamma according to what was suitable for him, without yet analyzing the conduct and virtue mentioned in the question, saying: "One who honors those senior," and so forth.
In this context, there are four types of elders: one advanced in wisdom, one advanced in virtue, one advanced by birth, and one advanced by age.

For even a young bhikkhu who is well-versed in the scriptures is "advanced in wisdom" because of his seniority in learned knowledge (*bāhusacca-paññā*) when compared to elder bhikkhus of little learning;
indeed, even elder bhikkhus learn the Buddha’s word from him, as do his instructions, deliberations, and answers to questions.
And they look back [to him] for support. Likewise, even a young bhikkhu who is endowed with realization is called "grown old in virtue.
For by establishing themselves in his instruction, even those who are elderly take up the embryo of insight and attain the fruit of arahantship.
Likewise, even a young king—an anointed khattiya—or a brahmin is "grown old by birth" in relation to other people who ought to pay him homage.
...by name. However, everyone who has reached their first birth is called "grown old.

In this regard, because there is no one equal to the Elder Sāriputta in wisdom—except for the Blessed One—and likewise because he had penetrated the knowledge of the perfections of all disciples within half a month;
and because by birth he was born into a great brahmin family, therefore, by virtue of that monk's age...
Although he is equal to these [other elders] in terms of these three causes, he is "grown old" (vuddha) specifically with respect to the qualities of wisdom.
With this meaning in mind, the Blessed One said, "one who honors the aged" (vuddhāpacāyī). Therefore, the meaning of the first line is:

by performing acts of veneration toward such elders, one is "one who honors the aged," and by being free from envy regarding the gains and other benefits of those very elders, one is "one who is not envious."
"And he knows the right time": here, even when passion has arisen, one who goes to see the teachers for the sake of its removal is "one who knows the right time";
likewise, when hatred... or delusion... or laziness has arisen, one who goes to see the teachers for the sake of its removal is "one who knows the right time.
Thus, he is "one who knows the right time" for seeing the teachers. "A discourse on the Dhamma" means one connected with serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Erāyitaṃ" (uttered) is what was said. "Khaṇaññū" means one who knows the proper occasion for that discourse, or one who recognizes that this is a rare opportunity to hear such a talk.
"Suṇeyya sakkaccaṃ" means one should listen to that discourse attentively.

The meaning is that one should not only listen to that [discourse] with care, but also to other well-spoken words connected with the qualities of the Buddha and so forth, listening with full attention.

329. Regarding the phrase, “He should know the proper time for visiting his teachers,” the method explained here is as follows: even when one knows the time has come to dispel the lust and other defilements that have arisen within oneself, one should visit the presence of the teachers at the appropriate time.

One should not go to the teachers’ presence at such times as when paying homage to a cetiya, while on the grounds of a Bodhi tree, while on the alms-round, or during the middle of the day, thinking, “I am a practitioner of meditation subjects and a bearer of the ascetic virtues (dhutaṅgas).”
The meaning is that one should approach the teacher wherever he may be staying for the purpose of inquiry;

however, having observed him seated on his own seat in his own lodging, his agitation calmed, one should approach for the purpose of asking about the method of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
And even when approaching in this way, one should cast aside arrogance and behave with humility, [avoiding] whatever causes rigidity.
Having destroyed pride, one should approach with humble conduct, like a foot-wiping cloth, a broken horn, or a snake whose fangs have been removed.
Then, one should practice the meaning and the Dhamma spoken by that teacher... [and so on] ...and act accordingly. "Meaning" (attha) refers to the sense of what was spoken.
