"Dhamma" refers to the canonical Dhamma (pāḷidhamma). "Restraint" (saṃyama) refers to moral virtue (sīla). "The holy life" (brahmacariya) refers to the remaining aspects of the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsana).

"Both by recollecting and by practicing": in the context where the meaning has been explained, one should recollect [the virtues]; in the context where the Dhamma, restraint, and the holy life have been explained, one should recollect them.

And not being satisfied with mere recollection, one should practice all of that—meaning, one should undertake it and conduct oneself accordingly; one should exert effort toward the manifestation of those teachings within oneself. Thus...
For by doing so, one becomes a doer of what ought to be done.
Beyond that, one should become one who delights in the Dhamma, rejoices in the Dhamma, is established in the Dhamma, and is a knower of the discernment of the Dhamma.
And in all these instances, "Dhamma" refers to serenity and insight; "delight" and "rejoicing" have the same meaning; one’s delight is in the Dhamma.

He is one who delights in the Dhamma (*dhammārāmo*). He is one who rejoices in the Dhamma (*dhammarato*) because, delighting in the Dhamma, he does not long for anything else. He is established in the Dhamma because he conducts himself according to the Dhamma.

He is a knower of the determination of the Dhamma (*dhammavinicchayaññū*) because he knows the discernment of the Dhamma, thinking, "This is the knowledge of arising; this is the knowledge of passing away. Such a person he should be.
Now, as for these worldly talks on kings and so forth, or the "jackal-talk" regarding external forms and the like, for a young practitioner of insight...
By generating approval, one defiles that Dhamma of serenity and insight; therefore, it is called the "doctrine of the corruption of the Dhamma.

One should not practice that doctrine of the corruption of the Dhamma, but rather, while resorting to what is suitable—such as one's residence and sphere of activity—one should be led by words that are truly well-spoken.
In this context, "truly" refers exclusively to those things associated with serenity and insight; by such [words]...
"One should be led by well-spoken words; one should lead [others] [by them]; one should spend one's time"—this is the meaning.

Now, regarding the phrase "the doctrine of the corruption of the Dhamma," in order to make manifest the defilement of a bhikkhu engaged in serenity and insight meditation—which was previously stated very briefly—the author explains it along with other defilements as "laughter and muttering."
He spoke this verse. (The reading *hāsanti pi* is also found. For a monk who practices insight (*vipassaka*), when there is a cause for laughter, he should merely smile;
he should not engage in useless chatter. When facing the loss of relatives and such, he should not lament.
Toward stumps, thorns, and the like, he should not give rise to mental malice. *Māyākata* refers to what is called "deceit" (*māyā*).
These faults— namely, the threefold hypocrisy, greed for requisites, pride based on birth and so forth, agitation characterized by constant opposition,
harshness marked by rough speech, the dregs of passion and the like, and infatuation characterized by excessive craving—
should be avoided by one desiring happiness as if they were a pit of glowing coals, by one desiring purity as if it were a place of excrement, and by one desiring life as if it were a murderer.

And like venomous snakes and the like, they are to be abandoned. Having abandoned them, one should live with a mind established through the absence of mental distraction and the lack of intoxication resulting from the disappearance of the pride of health and so forth.

For one who practices in this way, through a meditation purified of all defilements, one attains Arahatship before long. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Laughing, prattling... [and so on] ...one whose self is established."
332. Now, because a bhikkhu who possesses that defilement—which was described by way of the method beginning with "laughing and prattling"—is impulsive and acts without reflection;
because he proceeds with lust through the power of passion and with hatred through the power of malice;
and because he is negligent, lacking persistence in the cultivation of wholesome states—for such a person [one] might hear:
Advice spoken in such a manner as "with due respect for well-spoken words" would be useless;

therefore, demonstrating that this teaching—which is based on the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhāna)—is the opposite of what causes the decline of learning and so forth, he spoke this verse beginning with "those whose essence has been understood.
Its meaning is as follows: regarding those well-spoken words connected with serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), their comprehension...
The essence is this: if what has been cognized is good, then even if only the mere sound is grasped, nothing is accomplished;

for that by which these things are cognized through knowledge consisting in what is heard is "the heard" (*suta*), and this knowledge consisting in what is heard has concentration on what is cognized as its essence—that concentration upon those cognized phenomena which is the non-distraction of the mind and the practice toward suchness is its [essence].

This is the essence. For no purpose whatsoever is accomplished by mere understanding alone. However, that person who is reckless because he conducts himself under the influence of lust and other defilements, and who is negligent due to a lack of persistence in the cultivation of wholesome states—he is merely a grasper of sounds.

Because he lacks the discernment of the meaning through that [mere grasping], he possesses neither the wisdom that discerns well-spoken words nor the practice for the sake of becoming such [a wise person].
"Because of non-existence, what has been heard does not increase.
(333) Having thus shown the decline of wisdom and the decline of learning for heedless beings, he now spoke—"Those who...
have attained the essence"—showing how those who are heedful achieve the realization of both of these essences. Therein, that which is proclaimed by the Noble Ones...
"Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). For there is no Buddha who has attained final *parinibbāna* without having taught the Dhamma of serenity and insight.
Therefore, those who delight in and are devoted to this Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones—being heedful, persistent, and devoted to practice—are unsurpassed in word, mind, and deed;
they are [unsurpassed] through the fourfold good conduct of speech.
Because they are endowed with the threefold good conduct of mind and the threefold good conduct of body, they are unsurpassed in speech, thought, and action;
they are peerless, supreme, and distinguished among all other beings. By this much, he shows the virtue associated with the Noble Path together with the preliminary virtue.
Thus, being of such pure virtue, they are established in peace, gentleness, and concentration.
Those who have found the essence of what has been heard and of wisdom, and who delight in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones—they are not merely unsurpassed in words and such;

rather, having become established in tranquility and concentration, they should be understood as having "found" and attained the essence of what has been heard and of wisdom. This is a statement of fact regarding that which is expected. In this regard:
“Peace” (*santi*) refers to Nibbāna; “gentleness” (*soracca*) is the wisdom that penetrates reality as it is by virtue of delighting in what is beautiful;
“peace and gentleness” (*santisoracca*) is a designation for the path-wisdom that has Nibbāna as its object. “Concentration” (*samādhi*) is the path-concentration associated with that [wisdom].
“Established” (*saṇṭhitā*) means established in both of those. This is the essence of learning and wisdom.
This is indeed the liberation that is the fruit of arahantship. For this holy life has liberation as its essence.

Thus, here the Blessed One [taught] the preliminary practice by way of the Dhamma; and by means of the phrases beginning with "unsurpassed in speech," he taught the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha);
and by means of peace, gentleness, and concentration, he taught the aggregates of wisdom and concentration. In this way, through these three aggregates, he also taught the subsequent practice.
Having thus shown [the path], he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship, demonstrating unshakable liberation through the essence of learning and wisdom.
At the conclusion of the discourse, that bhikkhu attained the fruit of stream-entry and, not long thereafter,
established himself in the supreme fruit of Arahantship.
The commentary on the *Kiṃsīla-sutta* in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, within the *Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā* known as the *Paramatthajotikā*, is completed. 10.
The commentary on the *Uṭṭhāna-sutta*.
334. "Arise" refers to the *Uṭṭhāna Sutta*. What is its origin? At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
Having stayed at the Jetavana Monastery during the night, in the morning he went for alms in Sāvatthī surrounded by the community of monks.
Having walked for alms and departed from the city through the eastern gate, he went to the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother for his midday rest.

It is said that it was the custom of the Blessed One to spend the night dwelling in the Jeta Grove Monastery and go for his daytime rest to the Palace of Migāra’s Mother, and to spend the night dwelling in the Palace of Migāra’s Mother and go for his daytime rest to the Jeta Grove. Why?
For the sake of favoring two families and for the purpose of demonstrating the quality of his great renunciation. And below the Palace of Migāra’s Mother...
There were five hundred gabled-chamber apartments in which five hundred bhikkhus resided.
On those occasions when the Blessed One dwelt in the lower palace, the bhikkhus, out of reverence for the Blessed One, did not ascend to the upper palace.
But on that day, the Blessed One entered a gabled-chamber apartment in the upper palace; consequently, [the bhikkhus remained] even in the five [apartments] of the lower palace.
Five hundred monks entered the Gabbhasata Hall. They were all novices who had recently joined this Dhamma and Vinaya;
they were restless, arrogant, and of unrestrained senses.
Having entered, they slept during the day, and rising in the evening, they gathered on the great terrace and said, "Today at the meal hall, what did you have? Where did you go?"
"Friends, I went to the house of the King of Kosala; I went to that of Anāthapiṇḍika; there such and such a variety of food was served.
Thus they spoke various kinds of talk about material things, making a loud noise and a great clamor.
Hearing that sound, the Blessed One thought: "Even while living with me, these men are so negligent; alas, they are acting improperly!"

He thought of the arrival of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. At that very moment, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having known the Blessed One’s mind, arrived by means of his psychic power and was right there, prostrating at the Blessed One’s feet. Then the Blessed One addressed him:
“Moggallāna, these fellow-celibates of yours are negligent; it would be well if you were to stir them with a sense of urgency. “So be it, Blessed One,” he replied.
Having given his assent to the Blessed One, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna immediately entered the water-kasiṇa attainment and,
standing upon the dung-pasture, shook with his big toe the great palace situated there— along with the patch of earth on which it stood—
just as a great wind shakes a ship. Then those bhikkhus, terrified, cried out and [clutched] their respective robes.
Having abandoned [the palace], they went out through the four doors. The Blessed One, showing himself to them, appeared as if entering the Gandhakuṭī through another door;
seeing the Blessed One, they paid homage and stood aside. The Blessed One asked, "What is it, monks?
Are you terrified? They replied, "Venerable sir, this Palace of Migāra’s Mother has shaken."
They said, "Do you know, monks, by whom [this was done]? "We do not know, Bhante.

Then the Blessed One, having said, "Monks, this was shaken by Moggallāna for the purpose of producing a sense of spiritual urgency in those like you—those who are muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, and dwelling in negligence," spoke this discourse for the sake of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.
In this context, "arise" means arise from your seats; strive, exert yourselves, and do not be indolent.
"Sit down" means sit down with your legs crossed for the purpose of devoting yourself to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "What is the use of sleeping? means:
what use is there for sleep for you who have gone forth for the sake of final *nibbāna* through non-clinging? For it is not possible [to achieve that] while sleeping.
No purpose whatsoever can be attained [by sleep]. For what kind of sleep can there be for those who are afflicted?

They are tormented as if pierced by arrows. Indeed, when even a slight disease such as an eye ailment arises in a small part of the body, or when they are struck by any one of the following arrows—an iron arrow, a bone arrow, a tooth arrow, a horn arrow, a thorn arrow, or a wooden arrow—having entered even a mere inch or two into the body, those who are afflicted [find no rest].

For people who are being tormented there, there is no sleep; for what sleep can there be for those afflicted by the various diseases of the defilements (*kilesa*) that arise having shattered the entire continuum of your mind and body?
And for those pierced by arrows, as the five arrows—the dart of passion (*rāga-salla*) and the rest—have entered and pierced their inner hearts, they are tormented.
335. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One spoke again to further encourage and stir those bhikkhus, saying:
“Arise... [and] live under the control of the Dhamma. Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning with its underlying intention:
“For it is time for you, bhikkhus, who have been pierced by the thorn of the defilements, to awaken. Why is that? Bhikkhus, this holy life is like a medicinal broth.”

The Teacher is present before you; yet until now, for a long time, you have been asleep—slept among the mountains, slept among the rivers, slept on level ground, slept on uneven ground, and even slept at the tops of trees—because of not seeing the Noble Truths.
Therefore, arise and sit up for the sake of ending that sleep; train yourselves firmly in peace.
In this regard, the meaning of the first line is exactly as previously explained. As for the second line, "peace" (*santi*) refers to three kinds of peace:
absolute peace (*accanta-santi*), partial peace (*tadaṅga-santi*), and conventional peace (*sammuti-santi*). These are designations for Nibbāna, insight, and various speculative views, respectively.
Here, however, absolute peace—Nibbāna—is intended; therefore, train yourselves firmly for the sake of Nibbāna, with unremitting effort.
"Having offered [the sacrifice], train yourselves"—this is what is said. For what reason? "Lest King Death, knowing you to be negligent, should delude you while you are under his sway.
This means: lest Māra—who bears the name of King Death—should, perceiving that you are negligent, delude you while you are under his control;
lest he should act so as to bring you under his power, thus making you his followers. This is what is meant.
336. Since gods and humans do not come under its sway...

[as previously described] ...by which they are bound, and by which gods and humans—those who desire and those who seek forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—remain clinging, dependent, and attached to those forms and so forth;
cross over and transcend this, for it spreads out, expands, and becomes vast among the various kinds of sense objects.
"Attachment is craving for existence and enjoyments. Let not the opportune moment pass you by;

this is your moment for performing the duty of a recluse—let it not elapse. For those to whom such a moment passes away, and those who let this moment slip by, they grieve when the moment has passed, having been consigned to hell—in all its fourfold form, which is designated as 'hell' in the sense of being devoid of essence."
Established in a state of ruin, they grieve according to the method beginning with, "Alas, we have not done what was good.

(337) Thus, having encouraged and stirred those bhikkhus, the Blessed One now censured their dwelling in negligence and, directing them all toward heedfulness, spoke this verse: "Negligence is dust... In this regard:
“Negligence” (*pamāda*) is, in brief, the loss of mindfulness; it is “dust” in the sense that it is a defilement of the mind.
One who has fallen into such negligence is “one fallen into negligence. Because he has fallen into negligence, the negligence that arises repeatedly is itself dust;
for there is never such a thing as negligence that is not dust. What does this illustrate? It shows: “Do not think, ‘We are still young; we will know [the truth] later.’”

He attained confidence. For even in youth, negligence is dust; in middle age and even in old age, because one is beset by negligence, it becomes a great heap of dust, just as the dust in a house for one or two days is merely dust, but when it has increased over many years, it becomes a heap of refuse.
Even though this is so, during the first stage of life, the word of the Buddha...

Whether one practices the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) after having mastered [the teachings] in later life, or masters them in the first stage of life and practices the duty of a recluse after hearing them in middle age,
such a bhikkhu does not dwell in negligence, because he has entered upon the practice that conforms to diligence (*appamāda*).
However, he who dwells in negligence throughout all stages of life, being devoted to sleeping by day and to talk about worldly gain, [is negligent].
"Just as for you, that negligence in the first stage of life is but dust; whereas the negligence that has entered into the other stages of life is great negligence and great dust.
Having thus rebuked their dwelling in negligence, he spoke, directing them toward heedfulness: "By heedfulness and true knowledge..."

"Extract the dart from yourself"—the meaning of this is as follows: since negligence (*pamāda*) is thus always a defilement (*raja*), therefore, by means of heedfulness (*appamāda*)—defined as non-separation from mindfulness—and by means of true knowledge (*vijjā*)—defined as the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-khaya-ñāṇa*)—the wise son of good family should extract the fivefold dart of lust and so forth residing within his own heart.
Thus he concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching...
Having attained a sense of spiritual urgency and attending to that very teaching on the Dhamma,
those five hundred bhikkhus, while reflecting and undertaking insight (vipassanā), were established in Arahatship.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Anthologies (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the Uṭṭhāna Sutta in the Suttanipāta-ṭīkā is finished.
11. Commentary on the Rāhula Sutta: 338.
“Is it because of constant association? This is the Rāhula Sutta. What is its origin? After the Blessed One had awakened to perfect enlightenment...

Having proceeded gradually from the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to Kapilavatthu, he was there requested for his inheritance by Prince Rāhula, who said, "O ascetic, give me my inheritance. He then commanded the Elder Sāriputta, "Ordain Prince Rāhula.
All of this should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary on the Khandhaka. Once Prince Rāhula had thus been ordained—
The Elder Sāriputta alone conferred full ordination upon him who had reached maturity, while the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was his preceptor for the formal ritual (kammavācā).
From his youth until he attained the stage of an Arahant, the Blessed One [instructed him], saying: "This youth is endowed with excellence of birth and other qualities;
do not, on account of your birth, clan, family, beauty, or physical splendor, give way to pride or intoxication."
While instructing him repeatedly, he spoke this sutta. Therefore, at the conclusion of this sutta it is said:
"In this way, indeed, the Blessed One repeatedly instructed the Venerable Rāhula with these verses. Therein, the summary meaning of the first verse is as follows:
"O Rāhula, I hope that because of living together for a long time, you do not—due to birth or any other such factor—"
"You do not despise the wise because of their physical appearance; for you uphold the lamp of knowledge and the lamp of the teaching of the Dhamma.
O torch-bearer among men, are you honored by people? Are you constantly worshipped by them?"—this he says with reference to the Venerable Sāriputta.

When this was said, the Venerable Rāhula, demonstrating that "O Blessed One, I do not harbor pride or arrogance merely because of living together [with others] like a lowly person," spoke this verse in reply: "Not because of constant association... This has an obvious meaning.
340. Then the Blessed One, instructing him further, spoke the remaining verses beginning with "The five strands of sensual pleasure.

Therein, because the five strands of sensual pleasure are dear in form and dear by nature to beings, being exceedingly desired and longed for by beings, and because they delight their minds—and yet the Venerable Rāhula has gone forth from the home out of faith having abandoned them—[he spoke thus].

He had not been driven by a king, nor driven by thieves, nor oppressed by debt, nor oppressed by fear, nor compelled by the need for a livelihood; therefore, the Blessed One, having encouraged him with the words,
"Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are dear and delightful, having gone forth from home out of faith," spoke thus—
"become one who makes an end of suffering"— in order to direct him toward the practice appropriate to this renunciation.
In this regard, it might be asked: "Was not the Venerable One forcibly ordained while he was longing for his inheritance?
Then why did the Blessed One say, 'Having gone forth from home out of faith'? It is said because of his inclination toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
For long ago, this Venerable One had been inclined toward renunciation and was the son of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Padumuttara, named Uparevata.
Having seen the novice monk, the Nāga king named Saṅkha gave alms for seven days and made a resolution for that state;
from then on, perfected in his aspiration and perfected in his resolve, he fulfilled the perfections (*pāramitā*) for a hundred thousand aeons and was reborn in his final existence.
Thus the Blessed One knows his inclination toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*). For this is one of the powers of a Tathāgata.

This is knowledge. Therefore he said: “Having gone forth from the home out of faith. Alternatively, the intended meaning here is: “Having gone forth from the home out of faith for a long time, may you now become one who makes an end of suffering.
Now, in order to show his practice for making an end of the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*) starting from the beginning, [he says] “friends... [etc.]
He said, beginning with the words, "Associate with the virtuous. In this context, those who excel in virtue and the other perfections are called "virtuous friends" (*kalyāṇamitta*).
By associating with them, one grows in virtue and the rest—just as great sal trees grow from their roots and so forth by depending on the Himalayas. Therefore he said: "Associate with the virtuous.
And as for "a secluded lodging, a remote place, free from noise": that which is a lodging in a remote location...
Frequent a dwelling that is remote, secluded, uncrowded, and quiet—a place where the perception of the forest arises from the sounds of deer, wild boars, and the like.
Be moderate in eating; that is to say, know the proper measure. The meaning is: know the measure of receiving and the measure of consumption.
In this regard, for one who knows the measure of receiving, even if the gift to be given is small...

If the donor wishes to give little, one should accept only a little, even if the gift to be given is abundant. If the gift to be given is meager, however, one should accept only a little, even if the donor wishes to give much.
If the gift to be given is more abundant, one should accept only a little, even if the donor wishes to give little.
But if both the gift to be given and the donor’s intention to give much are present, one should accept according to one’s own capacity. Furthermore:

"The Blessed One has praised moderation itself"— thus, one who knows the measure of enjoyment should consume food with wise reflection (*yoniso manasikāra*), regarding it as if it were the flesh of one's own son or as oil for an axle. Having thus,
by means of this verse which serves as an aid to the holy life (*brahmacariya*), directed [the practitioner] toward the cultivation of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitta-sevanā*).

Having encouraged [them] to observe the virtue of purity in the use of requisites by way of lodgings and food, he now speaks this verse beginning with “In robes and almsfood,” in order to prohibit craving for robes and so forth—which constitutes wrong livelihood—and to encourage them in the virtue of purity in livelihood.
In that context, “requisites” refers to the requisite for the sick; “in these” refers to...

Regarding these four requisites, such as robes and so forth, which are the bases for the arising of craving in monks: "Do not produce craving" means that you should not generate craving while seeing the danger [of these things] in this manner:
"These four requisites are merely for the purpose of covering one's private parts and so on;

they are the remedy for men who are constantly afflicted by illness, and they serve as a support for this exceedingly frail body, like a prop for a dilapidated house. Thus, do not produce craving. By not producing it—
The meaning is: "Dwell without producing [them]. For what reason? "So that you do not return to this world.
For by creating craving for these things, being dragged along by craving, one returns again to this world. Therefore, do not create craving for these;
if this is so, you will not return to this world again.
When this was said, the Venerable Rāhula thought, "The Blessed One told me, 'Do not let there be craving for robes,'" and he undertook two ascetic practices related to robes:

the practice of wearing rag-robes and the practice of wearing only three robes. [He thought], "The Blessed One told me, 'Do not let there be craving for almsfood,'" and he undertook five ascetic practices related to almsfood: the practice of eating only almsfood...

The practice of going for alms from house to house, the practice of eating at a single sitting, the practice of eating only from the alms-bowl, and the practice of not accepting food after the proper time.
“Do not let there be craving for lodgings,” said the Blessed One to me; thus he undertook the six ascetic practices related to lodgings:

the practice of dwelling in the forest, the practice of dwelling in the open air, the practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree, the practice of accepting whatever seat is offered, and the practice of dwelling in a charnel ground.
Regarding the practice of always sitting: thinking, "The Blessed One told me,

'Do not harbor craving for the sake of illness,'" he was content with three kinds of contentment— according to what is obtained, according to one's strength, and according to what is suitable— with respect to all requisites,
just like a well-spoken son of good family who receives instruction with a sense of direction.

343. Thus, having exhorted the Venerable Rāhula to the virtue of purity of livelihood, the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with “restrained according to the Pātimokkha” in order to exhort him further to the remaining virtues and to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

Regarding that, in the phrase “restrained according to the Pātimokkha,” there is an ellipsis of the word “be. Alternatively, it should be understood as being connected with the final word [of the verse], “be.”
The same applies to the second phrase. Thus, by these two statements, he exhorted him to the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha and the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties.
Here, the five sense faculties are mentioned by way of their manifest form; however, it should be understood that by way of their characteristic, the sixth is also indeed included.
"May mindfulness be established in you regarding the body"—thus [he spoke] to one who is thus established in the fourfold purification of virtue.

"May mindfulness directed to the body—consisting of the analysis of the four elements, the fourfold clear comprehension, mindfulness of breathing, the perception of repulsiveness in food, and so forth—be yours; cultivate it," is the meaning. "Be full of disenchantment" means:
be one who is weary of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) and possesses the perception of non-delight in the entire world.

344. Having thus far shown the access stage (upacārabhūmi) pertaining to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), he now says, beginning with “Avoid the sign,” in order to show the absorption stage (appanābhūmi).
Therein, “the sign” (nimitta) refers to the sign of beauty (subhanimitta) which is a basis for lust.
For that very reason, distinguishing it further, he says: “beauty associated with lust. “Avoid” means by way of non-attention (amanasikāra).

"Relinquish [them]. Develop the mind with regard to the foul": develop the mind in such a way that the meditation on the foul succeeds, whether with respect to a body possessing consciousness or one devoid of consciousness.

"One-pointed and well-concentrated": one-pointed by means of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and well-concentrated by means of absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*). The meaning is: develop it so that your mind becomes like this.
345. Having thus shown him the plane of absorption (*appanā*), he spoke the words beginning with "the signless" (*animitta*) in order to show insight (*vipassanā*).
Therein, "cultivate the signless" means that one whose mind is concentrated by means of concentration conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya-samādhi*) should cultivate insight;
for insight is called "signless" because the knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence is liberated from the sign of permanence.
By the method beginning with the words "liberation," it receives the designation "signless" (*animitta*) through the non-apprehension of the signs of lust and so forth. As it is said:
"Friend, by not attending to any signs, I enter and dwell in the signless concentration of mind. While I was dwelling in this state, friend, my consciousness followed after signs.

By means of this development of the signless, one eradicates the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) after having acquired the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*). For one who possesses the perception of impermanence...

“Meghiya, the perception of non-self becomes established; one who perceives non-self attains the eradication of the conceit ‘I am’”—the meaning of such passages is that you should, in this gradual sequence, extract, abandon, and relinquish the underlying tendency to conceit. Then, “through the full realization of conceit, you will live in peace”;
thus, through the full realization, destruction, vanishing, abandoning, and relinquishment of conceit by means of the Noble Path.
"Being peaceful, extinguished, cooled, and free from all distress and fever, until you attain final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue,
you shall move about and dwell in one or another of the meditative attainments of fruition— emptiness, the signless, or the desireless.
Thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
Following that, the words beginning with "Thus indeed the Blessed One" are the speech of the compilers of the collection.
Therein, "itthaṃ sudaṃ" means "itthaṃ su idaṃ," which is to say, "exactly thus. The rest here is of plain meaning.
While the Venerable Rāhula was being exhorted in this way, when the factors conducive to the ripening of liberation had reached maturity at the conclusion of the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta—
Together with many thousands of deities, he was established in Arhatship.
Thus ends the commentary on the Rāhula Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Paramatthajotikā* commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*).
12. Commentary on the Nigrodhakappa Sutta (also called the Vaṅgīsa Sutta).
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Nigrodhakappa Sutta, which is also called the Vaṅgīsa Sutta. What is its origin?

It is the very same as that which was stated in its introduction. In this context, "Thus have I heard" and so forth have already had their meaning explained; for these and other similar expressions [have been dealt with].
Setting aside that which has already been explained, we shall describe it according to the method not yet stated. Regarding "at the Aggāḷava Cetiya":
this refers to the foremost shrine in Āḷavī. Before the Blessed One had appeared, there were many shrines such as Aggāḷava and Gotamaka, which were the abodes of *yakkhas*, *nāgas*, and others.
When the Blessed One had appeared, people destroyed those [shrines] and established monasteries (*vihāras*) there; they continued to refer to them by those very same names.
Thus it is said: "He dwelt in the monastery known as the Aggāḷava Cetiya. Regarding the phrase "of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa":
here, "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment, and "Vaṅgīsa" is the name of that Elder. He should be understood from his very birth as follows:
he was, it is said, the son of a wandering ascetic, born from the womb of a female wandering ascetic, and possessed a certain branch of knowledge (*vijjā*).
He knows [this], by the power of which he strikes a corpse’s head and discerns the destiny of beings.
Indeed, people would bring the heads of their deceased relatives from the charnel ground and ask him about their destiny.
He would say, “He was reborn in such-and-such a hell,” or “In such-and-such a world of humans. Amazed by this, they would give him much wealth. Thus...
Thus he became famous throughout the entire Jambudīpa.

Having fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand eons and being perfected in his resolve, he traveled through villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals surrounded by five thousand men, and eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. At that time, the Blessed One...

He was staying at Sāvatthī. After giving alms before the meal, the residents of Sāvatthī—well-robed and well-covered—would take flowers, perfumes, and other offerings and go to Jeta’s Grove to hear the Dhamma.
Seeing them, he asked, "Where is this great multitude going? Then they explained it to him: "The Buddha has appeared in the world..."
"He has arisen; he teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of many people. Let us go there.
He too, together with his retinue, went along with them, exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and sat down to one side.
Then the Blessed One addressed him: "Vaṅgīsa, do you know such a spell by which the skulls of beings can be struck?"
“...do you proclaim the destination? “Yes, Master Gotama, I know it. The Blessed One had the head of one reborn in hell brought and showed it to him;
he tapped it with his fingernail and said, “This, Master Gotama, is the head of one reborn in hell.
In this way, the Blessed One showed him the heads of those reborn in all the various destinations, and he likewise recognized each and reported accordingly. Then the Blessed One—
He showed him the foremost of those whose taints were destroyed, but though he struck it again and again, he did not recognize it.
Then the Blessed One said, "In this matter, Vaṅgīsa, it is beyond your scope; this is my domain alone, that of the foremost of those whose taints are destroyed," and he spoke this verse:
"The forest is the resort of deer, the sky is the resort of birds;
“Cessation is the destination of all phenomena; Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant.
Having heard this verse, Vaṅgīsa said, “Sir Gotama, give me this knowledge.
The Blessed One replied, “This knowledge does not come to those who have not gone forth. He then said, “Either ordain me, Sir Gotama, or give me whatever you desire.”
“Having done that, give me this knowledge,” he said. At that time, the Elder Nigrodhakappa was near the Blessed One;
the Blessed One commanded him, “In that case, Nigrodhakappa, ordain him.

Having ordained him, he instructed him in the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka*). By degrees, Vaṅgīsa attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and became an Arahant.
And he was designated by the Blessed One as foremost among them: "Monks, this is the foremost among my disciples, the monks, in eloquence, namely Vaṅgīsa.
For the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, who had thus attained such a state, his preceptor [acted] by contemplating what was proper and improper, and so forth. Thus...
The elder named Nigrodhakappa is one who has received that designation. "Kappa" is the name of that elder;
however, because he attained *arahantship* at the foot of a banyan tree (*nigrodha*), he was addressed by the Blessed One as "Nigrodhakappa," and for that reason the monks also address him thus.
He is called a "thera" (elder) because he has reached a state of stability in the Teaching. He had recently passed away at the Aggāḷava Cetiya.
"He had recently attained final Nibbāna" means that he had not long since passed away at that cetiya. "To one who had gone into seclusion and retired" means:
having withdrawn from the crowd, he was secluded in body; and being retired, his mind had turned back from various sense objects and was withdrawn.
"Thus a reflection arose in his mind" means that a thought arose in this manner. Why?
"But it arose" means: because [the Buddha] was not present and because of past association. For he was not present at the time of his (Sudinna’s) final Nibbāna;

moreover, he had previously seen his past association with such things as hand-washing and so forth. And such [remorse] occurs even for those whose taints are exhausted, due to former habituation, just as it does for those whose taints are not yet exhausted.
For instance, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja would go to King Udena’s park after his meal for his midday rest because of his former acquaintance there,

having enjoyed himself there when he was previously a king; and the Elder Gavampati would go to an empty celestial mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven because of his former acquaintance there, having enjoyed himself there as a son of the gods.
Pilindavaccha addressed the bhikkhus with the word "outcaste" because of his past habituation—having been a brahmin for five consecutive hundred births, he had spoken thus.
Therefore, because he was not in their presence and because of his association with them in the past, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Has my preceptor attained final Nibbāna, or has he not yet attained final Nibbāna?"
Beyond that, the meaning is self-evident. Regarding the phrase "having arranged the robe over one shoulder": this is stated because of readjusting it once again.
Furthermore, "over one shoulder" is a designation for one who stands having draped [the robe] over the left shoulder. Therefore, its meaning should be understood as:
"having arranged the robe in such a way that it remains draped over the left shoulder. The rest is plain.
346. "Of matchless wisdom" (*anomapañña*): *oma* means inferior, limited, or base; one who does not have such wisdom is "of matchless wisdom," meaning one of great wisdom.
"In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in direct experience, or in this very selfhood (*attabhāva*).

"Of doubts" (*vicikicchānaṃ*): of such kinds of discursive thoughts. "Renowned" (*ñāto*) means well-known. "Famous" (*yasassī*) means endowed with gain and retinue. "One whose heart is fully calmed" (*abhinibbutatto*)...

"With a virtuous mind, with a mind not burning. (347) "Made by you": because he was sitting at the foot of a *nigrodha* tree, the one speaking says "Nigrodhakappa" [the Nigrodha-like One] as if to characterize him according to how he himself perceives it;
thus he speaks. However, the Blessed One did not address him in that way merely because of his sitting position.
Moreover, it was because he had attained *arahantship* there. He says "of the brahmin" with reference to his birth;
for it is said that he went forth from a prominent brahmin family. "He wandered paying homage" means he lived while offering homage.
"Expecting liberation" means looking toward liberation known as *nibbāna*; it is said that he aspired to *nibbāna*. "One who sees the firm Dhamma."
He addresses the Blessed One. Nibbāna is indeed "firm in its nature" (daḷhadhamma) in the sense of being directly realized, and the Blessed One demonstrates this;
therefore, he calls him "the Seer of the Firm Nature" (daḷhadhammadassī).
[Verse 348] He addresses the Blessed One by his family name as well, saying "O Sakyan. "We too, all" refers to the entire assembly without exception.
He speaks while showing himself as one who has gathered [the assembly] together. With the words "Samantacakkhu," he addresses the Blessed One himself by means of his omniscient knowledge.
"Samavaṭṭhitā" means correctly established, remaining there having applied attention. "No" means "to us.
"Savanāya" means for the purpose of hearing the explanation of this question. "Sota" refers to the sense-faculties of hearing. "You are our teacher; you are unsurpassed."
This is merely a word of praise. "Let us cut off our doubt"—he is free from unwholesome doubt;
however, he spoke thus with reference to that kind of deliberation which resembles doubt. "Tell me this"—tell me that which you were asked by me.
“O Sakyan, we too all wish to know that disciple. Speaking thus, O Brahmin of vast wisdom, declare him who has attained final Nibbāna right here in our midst!

Having known that the one of great wisdom has attained final Nibbāna, O Blessed One, speak right here in our midst so that we all may know it—just as Sakka, the thousand-eyed lord of the gods, does among the deities.
This, however, is merely a word of praise. Furthermore, its underlying intention is this:
"Just as Sakka, the thousand-eyed one, speaks in the midst of the gods when his words are respectfully received by them, so may you speak in our midst when your words are received by us.
(350) Reciting this verse as well while praising the Blessed One, he speaks in order to generate a desire [to hear] what is about to be said.

The meaning of this is as follows: because there is no abandoning of delusion (*moha*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*) when those fetters (*gantha*) such as covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and the rest are not abandoned, they are called "paths of delusion," "sides of ignorance," and "stations of doubt.
All of these, upon encountering the Tathāgata, are shattered by the power of the Tathāgata’s teaching; they do not persist, but perish. Why is that? Because it is the eye (*cakkhu*).
"This is the supreme among men," because the Tathāgata, by generating the eye of wisdom that dispels all fetters, is said to be the supreme eye for humanity. 351.
Even while reciting this verse, "No ce hi jātū" (Never indeed...), he speaks with the intention of arousing a desire to speak. In that regard:

*Jātu* is a term used in the sense of "once. *Puriso* (the man) refers to the Blessed One. *Jotimanto* (possessing light) refers to Sāriputta and others who are endowed with the light of wisdom (*paññā*).

This is what is meant: if the Blessed One, like the wind from the east and other directions that disperses clouds and mist, did not likewise dispel the defilements (*kilesa*) by the force of his teaching; and if, as when the sky is shrouded by clouds...
The world would become as if shrouded in darkness, a single mass of gloom; likewise, one who is veiled by ignorance would be dark.
Even those such as Sāriputta and others who now appear radiant would not shine among men.
(352) He recites this verse, "And the wise," in the same manner as the previous one. Its meaning is: "And the wise, the learned..."

Men are makers of light; they produce the light of wisdom. Therefore, O Hero, I consider you, the Blessed One who is endowed with the vigor of striving, to be truly a Hero and indeed a maker of light.
For we have approached you, the Blessed One, knowing you to be a Vipassin—one who sees all phenomena as they really are—and therefore [we have come] amidst the assemblies.
"Do not reveal the *kappa*; explain and proclaim the *nigrodhakappa*.
(353) He speaks this verse also in the same manner as before. Its meaning is: "Quickly utter your voice;
speak your words without delay, O Blessed One, beautiful and delightful, like a golden swan returning from its feeding ground."
Having seen a grove of *jātassara* reeds, he stretches out his neck and, with his red beak, slowly and without haste, utters and emits a sweet, warbling sound;
even so, you too should utter it slowly, with this other mark of a Great Man—a voice like a drop (*bindu*), well-modulated, perfectly modulated, and refined. We are all here, upright.
"Having become undistracted in mind, I shall hear your warbling.
(354) He speaks this verse, "Abandoned is birth and death," in the same manner as before. In that context, "without remainder" (*asesa*) means that which leaves nothing behind;

thus it is said, "birth and death have been abandoned without remainder," meaning that nothing whatsoever remains, as is the case with those who have attained the stage of stream-entry (*sotāpanna*) and beyond.
"Having restrained" means having entreated earnestly and bound [him]. "The Shaker" (dhona) means one who has shaken off all evil.
"'I shall speak' means I shall cause the Dhamma to be told. "For there is no doing according to one's own will among worldlings" means that indeed for worldlings alone there is no freedom of will;
whatever they desire to know or to say, they are unable to do so. "And there is the acting according to [one's] measure among the Tathāgatas" refers to the Tathāgatas.
However, for one who investigates, activity is preceded by wisdom. The intention is that they are able to know or speak whatever they desire to know or say.
Now, in order to explain that quality of being concise, he spoke the verse beginning with "accomplished in exposition" (*sampannaveyyākaraṇa*). Its meaning is as follows:
For indeed, in such cases as these— where the Blessed One, for you who possess upright wisdom, has grasped, spoken, and set forth a perfected explanation, saying:
"The minister Santati will pass away after rising to the height of seventy palm trees," or "Suppabuddha the Sakyan will enter the earth on the seventh day"— your vision is seen to be unerring.
Then, bowing his joined palms even more reverently, he said: "This final salutation with joined palms is well offered; this other salutation, too, is offered most reverently.
Do not delude us"—that is, do not delude us by remaining silent, you who know the course of the eon as one who knows all.
He addresses the Blessed One as "of peerless wisdom."
356. Furthermore, reciting this verse, he spoke while requesting non-delusion once more by way of another method.
Therein, "the near and the far" refers to the beautiful and the ugly, or the distant and the proximate, according to the mundane and supramundane levels.

"The noble Dhamma" is the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Having known" means having penetrated [it]. "Knowing" means knowing all phenomena that are to be known (*ñeyya*). "I desire speech" means...
"Just as a man, scorched by the heat of summer and exhausted and thirsty, longs for water, so do I long for your word.
'Rain down what is heard' (*sutaṃ pavassa*): rain down, pour forth, and release that sense-sphere of sound which is designated as 'heard'; let it flow.
There is also the reading *sutassa vassa*, which means: 'rain down the rain' (*vassa*) of the aforementioned sense-sphere of sound."
357. Now, demonstrating the kind of speech he desires:
"Whatever purpose for which Kappāyana practiced the holy life—has that not been in vain for him?"
“He has attained Nibbāna, or does he have a residue remaining?
Listen to how he was liberated”—this is the verse he spoke.
In that context, "Kappāyana" is said by way of honorific address. "How he was liberated" means: "In what manner..."

"Is it as the ones beyond training (asekha) in the element of nirvana without residue (anupādisesa), or rather as the ones still in training (sekha) in the element of nirvana with residue (sopādisesa)? Thus he asks.
The rest here is self-evident.
358. Being thus requested with these twelve verses, the Blessed One, answering him—
“He has cut off craving here for name-and-form,” said the Blessed One,
“the stream of Kaṇha that had lain dormant for a long time;
he has crossed over birth and death without remainder.”
"Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Best of the Five," he said, and recited this verse.

Regarding that, first the meaning of the initial phrase: even that craving—which, in this name-and-form, is classified as sensual craving and so forth, and which has lain dormant (*anusayita*) for a long time because it has not been abandoned—is called the "stream" (*sota*) of Māra, who is named "Black."
"Kappāyana cut through that craving for name-and-form here, which had been latent for a long time and served as the ear for Kaṇha.
Thus says the Blessed One—this, moreover, is the statement of the compilers of the collection.

"He has crossed over birth and death without remainder": having cut off that craving without remainder, he has crossed over birth and death and attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.
[The Buddha] shows this. Thus spoke the Blessed One; when asked by Vaṅgīsa, the Blessed One said this:
"The best of the five" means he is the most excellent among the first five disciples, the group of five (pañcavaggiya);

or he is the best because of the five faculties such as faith, or because of the five aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue which are preeminent, and because of his eyes—this is the statement of the compilers of the collection.
359. When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Vaṅgīsa, with a mind rejoicing in what the Blessed One had said, recited the verses beginning with “Having heard this.

Therein, in the first verse, he addressed the Blessed One as “the Seventh of the Sages” (*isisattama*). He is called the Seventh of the Sages because he has appeared as both a sage and the seventh in the sense of being supreme, making himself the seventh together with the six sages named Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa. Addressing him thus, he spoke. Not... [text continues]
"‘He does not deceive me’ means that because he has attained final Nibbāna (*parinibbuto*), he does not deceive or mislead me who desires his state of final Nibbāna;
this is the meaning. The rest here is self-evident.
Regarding the second verse: because he dwelt seeking liberation (*mutyapekkho*), it was said with reference to him: ‘As he spoke, so he acted.’"
“He was a disciple of the Buddha. The net of Death is spread wide throughout the cycle of existence in the three realms; it is the net of craving belonging to Māra.
“Deceitful ones”: those possessed of much deceit. Some read “tathā māyāvino,” for which the intended meaning is:
“those who, through various deceits, approached the Blessed One even many times.”
In the third verse, "the beginning" (*ādi*) refers to the cause. "Of clinging" (*upādānassa*) means of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

For here, the round of existence is called "clinging" in the sense of that which is to be clung to; it is appropriate to say that the Blessed One saw the beginning—that is, the cause consisting of the divisions of ignorance, craving, and so forth—of that very clinging.
He speaks with this intention. "He has indeed transcended" (*accagā vata*) means he has gone beyond.

"Vata. Regarding "the realm of death" (*maccudheyya*): it is called the realm of death because death is fixed (*dhiyati*) therein; this is a designation for the cycle of existence consisting of the three planes.
"He has indeed crossed over that realm of death so difficult to cross"—thus he speaks, having become filled with knowledge. The rest here is self-evident.
From the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Nigrodhakappa Sutta in the Suttanipāta-ṭṭhakathā is finished.
13. Commentary on the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta (also known as the Mahāsamaya Sutta). 362.
"I ask the Sage of abundant wisdom"—this is the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta, also called the "Mahāsamaya Sutta."
It is so called because it was spoken on the day of the Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya). What is its origin? Its origin is contingent upon a question.
For the Blessed One, having been questioned by a created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha), spoke this sutta; together with that question, it is called the "Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta.
This is the summary here; however, in detail, it is described by the ancients starting from the origins of the Sākiyas and Koliyas.
In this regard, here is the commentary on the summary of the lineage: It is said that among the first eon’s people, King Mahāsammata had a son named Roja.
Roja’s son was Vararoja; Vararoja’s was Kalyāṇa; Kalyāṇa’s was Varakalyāṇa; Varakalyāṇa’s was Mandhātā;
Mandhātā’s was Varamandhātā; Varamandhātā’s was Uposatha; Uposatha’s was Vara; and Vara’s...
Upavara’s son was Maghadeva; from Maghadeva onwards there were eighty-four thousand kings in direct succession.
After them, there were three Okkāka lineages. Among them, the third Okkāka had five chief queens—Hatthā, Cittā, Jantu, Jālinī, and Visākhā—and each of these had five hundred women.

[Her] retinue. To her eldest son were born four sons—Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍu, Hatthinika, and Sinipura—and five daughters—Piyā, Suppiyā, Ānandā, Vijitā, and Vijitasenā. Having thus obtained nine children, she passed away.
Then the king brought another young and beautiful royal maiden and established her in the position of chief queen. She too...
She gave birth to a son named Jantu. On the fifth day, having adorned the young Jantu, she presented him to the king.
The king, being pleased, granted a boon to his chief queen. She consulted with her kinsmen and requested the kingdom for her son.
The king said, "Begone, you outcaste! You seek to create an obstacle for my sons," and did not grant it. She [requested it] again and again.
Having gratified the king in private, he spoke such words as, "Great King, lying is not permissible," and so forth, and thus made his request.

Then the king addressed his sons: "Sons, when I saw your youngest brother, Prince Jantukumāra, I rashly granted a boon to his mother. She now wishes to divert the kingdom to her son. After my passing, you..."
"Having come back, you shall exercise sovereignty," he said, and dispatched them along with eight ministers.
Taking their sisters with them, they departed from the city with a fourfold army. Thinking, "The princes will return and exercise sovereignty upon the passing of their father;
let us go and attend upon them," many people followed after them. On the first day, they traveled for about a *yojana*.
The army became two yojanas long on the second day, and three yojanas long on the third day. The princes thought: "This army is vast;
if we were to attack some neighboring king and seize his territory, he would not be able to withstand us.
What is the use of a kingdom obtained by oppressing others? Jambudīpa is vast; let us dwell in the forest."
"Let us build a city," they said, and set out toward the Himalayas.
While searching for a site to establish a city there, they came upon a place where a severe ascetic named Kapila lived on the bank of a lotus pond amidst a great thicket of *sāka* trees;
they went to his dwelling. Upon seeing them, he questioned them and [learned] everything.

Having heard of their conduct, he felt compassion for them. It is said that he knew a spell called *Bhummajāla*, by which one perceives the virtues and faults [of beings] eighty cubits above in the sky and below on the earth.
Then, in a certain place, he caused pigs and deer to terrify and drive away lions, tigers, and other beasts; he caused frogs and mice to frighten the snakes.
Seeing this, he thought, "This spot of ground is the foremost of the earth," and he established a hermitage in that place.
Then he said to the princes, "If you build a city after my name, I will give you this site. They agreed to do so.
The ascetic said, "Standing upon this very spot, even the son of a *caṇḍāla* can, by his power, [conquer] a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*)."
Having said, "He passes [the time] too quickly," he granted them that space, saying, "Build a hermitage for the king and then build a city.
He himself then established a hermitage at the foot of a nearby mountain and lived there. Subsequently, the princes built a city there;
because it was constructed on the site where Kapila had dwelt, they gave it the name "Kapilavatthu" and made it their residence.
Then the ministers thought, "These princes have reached maturity; had their father been present, he would have arranged their marriages.
Now, however, this burden falls upon us. Having reflected thus, they consulted with the princes.

The princes said, "We do not see any daughters of kṣatriyas who are our equals, nor any kṣatriya princes who are the equals of our sisters, nor any [marriage] that would avoid the confusion of caste."
“We will not do so. Out of fear of the confusion of castes, they placed their eldest sister in the position of mother and entered into marriage with the remaining sisters.
When their father heard of this occurrence, he uttered this exclamation: “Truly Sakyan are these youths! Truly most Sakyan are these youths!
This, then, is the origin of the Sakyans. And this was also said by the Blessed One:
“Then, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka addressed his ministers and counselors: ‘Sirs, where do the princes dwell now?
‘Your Majesty, on the slopes of the Himalayas, by the bank of a lotus pond, there is a great thicket of sāla trees; it is there that the princes dwell now.
Out of fear of the confusion of castes, they cohabit with their own sisters.’”
“They are called Sakyas. Then, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka uttered this inspired exclamation: “Truly these princes are Sakyas!
Truly these princes are supreme Sakyas! It was from that time on, Ambaṭṭha, that they became known as Sakyas, and he was the ancestor of the Sakyas.
Then, leprosy broke out upon their eldest sister; her limbs became like the blossoms of the *koviḷāra* tree.

Thinking, "Even as we sit, stand, or eat together with her, this disease will spread over us," the princes placed her in a carriage as if they were going on a pleasure excursion to the park, and having entered the forest, they departed.
Having had a lotus pond dug, they placed various kinds of solid and soft foods within it,
covered it over with a stone slab, and after spreading earth over it, they departed. At that time, a king named Rāma,
afflicted with leprosy and loathed by his harem and dancers, out of a sense of spiritual urgency [renounced] the kingdom for his eldest son.
Having given [these things] away, he entered the forest and, subsisting there on leaves, roots, and fruits, soon became healthy and golden-hued.
Wandering here and there, he saw a large hollow tree;
having cleared out that interior to a height of sixteen cubits, and having made a door and a window, he constructed a ladder and took up residence there.
He established this practice. Having made a fire in a charcoal pit, he would sleep at night listening for cries and sounds;
observing that "in such-and-such a place a lion made a sound, in such-and-such a place a tiger," he would go there at dawn, take the meat of scavenged remains, cook it, and eat it.
Then one day, at the time of dawn, he sat down after having kindled a fire.
At that same time, a tiger, having smelled the scent of the king’s daughter, dug up that spot and made an opening in the floor-covering.
Seeing the tiger through that opening, she cried out in terror. Hearing that sound, he thought, "This is the voice of a woman."
Having observed this, he went there early in the morning and asked, "Who is here? "It is a woman, sir. "Come out! "I will not come out! "For what reason?
"Because I am a noble maiden. Thus, even though she was buried in a pit, she maintained her pride.
He questioned her about everything, declared his own birth, saying, "I too am a noble," and said, "Come now."
"It has become like ghee poured into milk," he said. She replied, "My lord, I am afflicted with leprosy;
it is not possible for me to go out. He said, "I have now performed the necessary rites; it is possible to cure you.
Having provided a ladder, he helped her up, led her to his own dwelling, and gave her only the medicines he himself had used. In no long time, he made her healthy and golden-hued.
Thus, he lived in cohabitation with her. By their very first cohabitation, she conceived and gave birth to two sons;
again two more, and so on, until she had given birth thirty-two times. Thus, they became his thirty-two brothers.
When they had gradually reached maturity, their father instructed them in all the arts and crafts.
Then one day, a certain inhabitant of King Rāma’s city, who had come to that region while searching for jewels on the mountain, recognized the king upon seeing him.
He said, “I know you, Sire. When asked by the king, “Where have you come from?
he replied, “From the city, Sire. Thereupon, the king questioned him about all the current events. While they were thus conversing—
Those boys arrived. Seeing them, he asked, "Who are these gods? "They are my sons, sir," they replied.
"Now that you are surrounded by these thirty-two princes, what will you do in the forest? Come, rule the kingdom! "Enough, sir; here alone is happiness.
Thinking, "I have now obtained a subject for conversation," he went to the city.

He informed the king’s son. The king’s son, thinking, “I shall bring my father back,” went there with a fourfold army and entreated his father in various ways. But he [the father] said, “Enough, dear prince;
it is well here indeed,” and did not wish to come. Then the prince thought, “The king no longer wishes to come; well then, I shall have a city built right here for him.”
Having reflected thus, he uprooted that *kola* tree, built a house, and established a city;

because he had removed the *kola* tree, it was given the name "Kola-nagara," and because it was established on a tiger's path (*vyaggha-pattha*), it was given the name "Vyagghapajja"—thus assigning these two names, he departed.
Later, when the prince had reached maturity, his mother commanded him: "Dear son, the Sakyas residing in Kapilavatthu are your maternal uncles."

“Let them take their daughters. On the day the kṣatriya maidens went to play in the river, they went there, blocked the river crossing, announced their names, and took whichever princesses they desired.
When the Śākya kings heard this, they said, “Very well, sirs; they are our own kinsmen,” and remained silent.
This is the origin of the Koliyas.
Thus, the lineage of the Sākyans and Koliyas, who intermarried with one another, should be understood in detail as it extends back to King Siha-hanu.
It is said that King Siha-hanu had five sons: Suddhodana, Amitodana, [Sukkodana, Dhotodana, and Amittodana].

Dhotodana, Sakkodana, and Suddhodana. While Suddhodana was reigning, the Great Being—who had fulfilled the perfections—passed away from the Tusita heaven and took rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā, the daughter of King Añjana, according to the method described in the Jātaka-nidāna; and having gradually performed the Great Renunciation...
Having awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma,
he eventually went to Kapilavatthu and established Suddhodana Mahārāja and others in the fruits of the Noble Path. Departing on a tour of the countryside,
he returned at a later time to Kapilavatthu together with fifteen hundred bhikkhus.
He was dwelling in the Nigrodha Park.
While the Blessed One was dwelling there, a dispute arose between the Sākiyas and the Koliyas concerning water.
How so? It is said that between their two cities—Kapilavatthu and Koliyapura—the river named Rohiṇī flowed.
Sometimes it had little water, and sometimes it had much water. When there was little water, the Sakyans and the Koliyans built a dam and brought water for their respective crops.
One day, while those men were building the dam, they quarreled with one another, saying:
"Hey! Your royal family practiced cohabitation with their own sisters; they are like poultry, dogs, jackals, and other such lower animals!"
"Your royal family is like a goblin dwelling in a hollow tree.
Having thus reviled them with insults regarding their birth, they each reported this to their respective kings. Enraged, they prepared for battle and arrived at the banks of the Rohiṇī River.
Thus, an army as vast as the ocean stood ready.
Then the Blessed One, thinking, "The kinsmen are quarreling; come now, I shall restrain them," came through the air and stood between the two armies.
According to some, he had come from Sāvatthī after having perceived that situation. Having thus stood there, he recited the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.
Upon hearing it, they all were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), cast away their weapons, and [approached] the Blessed One.

They stood paying homage and prepared a costly seat. The Blessed One descended and, having sat down on the prepared seat, recited the Phandanajātaka beginning with “A man with an axe in hand,” and the Laṭukikajātaka beginning with “I bow to you, O elephant. [He also recited:
“The birds go along in harmony, taking up their net;”
“When they begin to quarrel, then they will come under my power.
Having told this Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, he further related this Mahāvaṃsa, demonstrating to them their kinship that had persisted for a long time.
Then those Sakyans gained even greater confidence, thinking, “It seems we were indeed kinsmen in the past. Thereafter, the Sakyans...
Two hundred and fifty Koliyan youths and two hundred and fifty other youths gave five hundred youths to the Blessed One for the purpose of his retinue.
Seeing their past causes, the Blessed One said to them, "Come, monks. Through supernormal power, they all appeared equipped with the eight requisites;
rising into the air and returning, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood before him. Taking them with him, the Blessed One went to the Great Forest.
He arrived. Their wives sent messengers to them, and being tempted by them in various ways, they became discontented.
The Blessed One, knowing their state of discontent, showed them the Himālaya mountains;
desiring to dispel their lack of delight there by means of the Kuṇāla Jātaka, he said: "Bhikkhus, have you seen the Himālaya before? "No, Blessed One."
“Come, monks, look! Saying this, he led them through the air by means of his own psychic power, showing them various kinds of mountains, saying, “This is the Golden Mountain;
this is the Silver Mountain; this is the Jewel Mountain. Then he alighted upon the surface of emerald at Kuṇāla Lake.
Thereafter, [he showed] all the animals dwelling in the Himalayas, distinguished as quadrupeds, many-footed creatures, and so forth.

"Let them come, and let the Kuṇāla bird follow behind all of them," he resolved. As they were coming, describing them according to their species, names, and characteristics, he showed them to them, saying:
"Monks, these are swans; these are cranes; these are ruddy geese, cuckoos, elephant-trunk birds, and lotus-attendants."

With hearts filled with wonder, as they watched, they saw Kuṇāla the bird coming from behind them all, seated in the middle of a stick held by two young birds who were pecking at him with their beaks, and surrounded by a retinue of a thousand female birds;
and having conceived a sense of amazement and marvel, they said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, is it possible that even the Blessed One is King Kuṇāla here?"
“Was it not so in the past? “Yes, monks, this Kuṇāla bamboo grove was made by me. For in the past we four lived here:
the seers Nārada and Devila, Ānanda the king of vultures, Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo, and I, the bird Kuṇāla.
He related the entire Mahākuṇāla Jātaka. Having heard that, those monks—
The dissatisfaction that had arisen regarding their former wives was stilled. Then the Blessed One preached the discourse on the Truths to them;
at the conclusion of the discourse, the very last among them became a stream-enterer and the very first became a non-returner;
there was not even one who remained a worldling or an arahant. Then the Blessed One, taking them with him, descended once more into the Great Forest. As they were coming along...
And those bhikkhus arrived by means of their own psychic power (*iddhi*).
Then the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to them once more for the sake of the higher path.
Those five hundred, having begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*), were established in Arahatship. The one who had first attained it went first of all, thinking, "I shall inform the Blessed One."
Having arrived, he said, “I am delighted, Blessed One; I am not weary,” and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
In this manner, they all arrived in succession and sat surrounding the Blessed One on the evening of the Uposatha day of the month of Jeṭṭha.
Then, [he beheld] the Blessed One seated upon the excellent Buddha-throne, surrounded by five hundred whose taints were destroyed.
Excluding the non-percipient beings and the formless-brahmas,
all the remaining deities and others throughout the ten thousandfold world-system assumed subtle bodies in the manner described in the *Maṅgala-sutta-vaṇṇanā* and surrounded [the Buddha], thinking,
"We shall hear the Dhamma teaching with its manifold eloquence. Therein, four Brahmās whose taints were exhausted emerged from meditative attainment and [addressed] the host of Brahmās:
Not seeing him, they wondered, "Where has he gone? and having reflected, they understood the matter.
Later, arriving and finding no space [within the assembly], they stood upon the summit of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) and uttered individual verses. As it is said:
"Then, it occurred to four deities belonging to the company of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsakāyika*): 'This Blessed One...'"
The Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Great Forest together with a large Saṅgha of monks, numbering about five hundred, all of whom were arahants.
Deities from ten world-systems had for the most part assembled to see the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks. "What if we too were to approach the Blessed One?"
“Having approached, let us each recite a verse in the presence of the Blessed One.

All this is to be understood according to the method already stated in the Sagāthāvagga. Having gone there in this manner, one Brahmā, having found space above the eastern world-system (cakravāḷa), stood there and recited this verse:
“A great assembly is gathered in the forest... [and so on].”
“For the sake of alms, to the unconquered Saṅgha.
As he was reciting this verse, one who stood on the western world-system mountain heard his voice.
A second, having found space atop the western world-system mountain, stood there and, hearing that verse, recited this verse:
“Therein, monks, they concentrated themselves...
[as before] ...the wise guard their sense-faculties.
Having obtained space at the zenith of the southern world-system, he stood there and, hearing that verse, spoke this verse:
“Having cut the pillar, having cut the crossbar... [and so on] ...like a well-bred noble elephant.
Having obtained space above the fourth outer rim of the world-system (*uttaracakkavāḷa*) and standing there, he heard that verse and spoke this verse:
“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha... [and so on] ...”
“They will fill the body of a god.

Standing upon the summit of the southern world-system, he too heard that sound. Thus, at that time, these four Brahmās stood having praised the assembly; the Great Brahmās stood covering a single world-system.
Then the Blessed One, looking over the assembly of gods, addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, those who were... [they too...]”
In the past, for those Blessed Ones who were Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas,
it was only to this extent that the deities assembled. Just as it is for me now, so too, monks,
for those Blessed Ones who will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas in the future, it will be only to this extent that the deities assemble.
“They will become just as I am now. Then, he divided that assembly of deities into two groups according to their capacity and lack of capacity, saying, “So many are capable; so many are incapable.

Therein, knowing that “an assembly of the incapable does not understand even when a hundred Buddhas teach the Dhamma, whereas an assembly of the capable can be awakened,” he [addressed] the individuals who were capable.

He divided them into six types according to their temperament (*carita*): "So many are of lustful temperament (*rāga-carita*), so many are of those with temperaments of hatred, delusion, discursive thought, faith, or intelligence.
Having thus discerned them by way of temperament, he investigated what kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for that assembly.
Then he again brought that assembly to mind: "Would they understand through his own inclination, or through the inclination of another?"

“Either by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) or by way of a question. Then, understanding that [the answer] should be known by way of a question, he again surveyed the entire assembly to see whether there was anyone capable of asking the question. Finding that there was no one, he thought:
“If I myself were to ask the question and I myself were to provide the answer, this would not be suitable for this assembly. What if I were now—”
"Let him fashion a created Buddha. Having entered the foundational jhāna and emerged, he fashioned a created Buddha by means of mind-made supernormal power (*manomayiddhi*), resolving:
"Let him be complete in all limbs and members, endowed with the [thirty-two] marks, wearing the bowl and robes, and perfect in his manner of looking forward and looking around.
Simultaneously with this act of resolve (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*), he appeared. Having come from the eastern world-system, he [stood] before the Blessed One.
Seated on a seat of equal height, having thus arrived, [the Blessed One] spoke these six discourses according to their practice in this assembly.
Namely: the Purābheda Sutta, the Kalahavivāda Sutta, the Cūḷabyūha, the Mahābyūha, the Tuvaṭaka, and this very Sammāparibbājaniya.
Among these, [this discourse was spoken] for the sake of being suitable for the deities of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*).
In order to cause this sutta to be promulgated, he asked a question by reciting this verse:

“I ask the Sage of abundant wisdom. Therein, “of abundant wisdom” means one of great wisdom. “Crossed over” means one who has crossed over the four floods. “Gone to the further shore” means one who has attained Nibbāna.
“Parinibbūta” means one who has attained parinibbāna by way of Nibbāna with residue remaining. “Steadfast” means one whose mind cannot be shaken by worldly conditions (lokadhamma).
"Having gone forth from the home, having cast off sensual pleasures"—that is, having cast off sensual pleasures regarding material things and having gone forth from the household life.
"How should that bhikkhu wander rightly in the world?"—it is asked how that bhikkhu should wander and dwell rightly in the world, remaining unsullied by the world;
it is said, in other words, that he should transcend the world. The rest here is exactly as previously explained.

363. Now, because there is no such thing as one who rightly goes forth in the world without having attained the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya), the Blessed One—therefore, within that entire assembly of persons categorized according to their temperaments such as those dominated by passion (rāgacarita) and so forth—in order to cause various groups of deities who share similar faults to abandon those very faults, began with the verse "For whom [the blessings]... and proceeded by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship.
Explaining the practice of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), he spoke fifteen verses.
Regarding these, first, in the opening verse, the term "omens" (*maṅgala*) is a designation for the seen omens and so forth mentioned in the *Maṅgala Sutta*.

"Uprooted" (*samūhatā*) means thoroughly uprooted, severed by the sword of wisdom (*paññā*). "Portents" (*uppāta*) refers to such things as the falling of meteors and the burning of the quarters of the sky.
"Such are the results"—thus do these fixations on portents arise. As for dreams: "Having seen a dream in the morning, such-and-such happens;
at midday and so forth, such-and-such; when seen while lying on the left side, such-and-such happens; when on the right side and so forth, such-and-such;
seeing the moon at the end of a dream, such-and-such happens; seeing the sun and so forth, such-and-such."

Thus proceed the misapprehensions regarding dreams. As for "characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa*): having recited the texts on the characteristics of staffs, the characteristics of garments, and so forth, one proceeds with the misapprehension of characteristics, thinking, "By this, such-and-such a thing occurs.
All of these are to be understood according to the method stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
"He has abandoned the faults of auspicious signs" refers to the remaining faults of auspicious signs, setting aside the thirty-eight great auspicious signs.
[This is] the name. However, he for whom these [superstitious] omens and so forth have been eradicated is one who has abandoned the faults of omens.

Alternatively, because both omens and defects such as portents have been abandoned, he is one who has abandoned the faults of omens; having attained the Noble Path, he does not rely on purification through omens and the like.
Therefore, he would wander rightly in the world; he, whose taints are destroyed, [wanders] rightly in the world.
"One should go forth, unsullied by the world.
(364) In the second verse, "A bhikkhu should remove passion for human [pleasures] and even for divine pleasures":
he should remove passion by bringing about the state of non-arising through the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) with respect to both human and divine strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
"Having transcended existence and having fully understood the Dhamma"— having thus dispelled passion, and thereafter accomplishing through the path of Arahatship the full comprehension (*pariññā*),
