clear realization (*abhisamaya*), and so forth in every aspect, he has "fully understood the Dhamma," which is the analysis of the Four Noble Truths.
Having transcended the threefold existence by means of this practice, that monk too would wander rightly in the world.

In the third verse, “one who has abandoned both attraction and repulsion” means one whose lust and hatred have been relinquished in all circumstances. The remainder is exactly as previously explained.
In all the verses, the phrase “that bhikkhu too would wander rightly in the world” is to be applied.
Hereafter, however, we shall explain the unspoken method without even providing the application.
In the fourth verse, both the pleasant and the unpleasant are to be understood by way of the seven formations;
therein, one has abandoned them through the relinquishing of desire-lust and aversion. "Without clinging" means without grasping at any phenomenon by means of the four types of clinging.
"Not dependent on anything" refers to the hundred-and-eightfold basis of craving and the sixty-two-fold basis of views.

"And not dependent on anything anywhere, such as the phenomena of form and so forth, or on existence. "Completely liberated from the fetters" means that all phenomena of the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) are "fetters" (*saṃyojaniya*) because they are the objects of the ten kinds of fetters;
and he is "completely liberated" from them because they have been fully understood (*pariññāta*) through every aspect by the cultivation of the Path (*magga-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, in this context, the first quarter-verse states the abandoning of lust and hatred, while the second states the absence of clinging and dependence.

By the third [verse], there is liberation from the remaining unwholesome states and the bases of the unwholesome. Alternatively, it should be understood that by the first [verse] there is the abandoning of lust and hatred;
by the second, the means for that; and by the third, liberation from the fetters due to their having been abandoned.

In the fifth verse, "in the acquisitions" (*upadhīsu*) refers to the acquisitions consisting of the aggregates (*khandha*). They are called "acquisitions" (*ādāna*) in the sense of being things to be grasped.
"Anaññaneyyo" means that because he has clearly seen impermanence and the other [characteristics], he cannot be led by anyone else to think, "This is better. The rest is of plain meaning.

This is what is meant: having completely removed desire and lust for acquisitions (*ādāna*) by means of the fourth path, he—having thus removed desire and lust—does not find substance in those bases (*upadhi*);
he sees all bases as being entirely without substance. Therefore, in regard to them, by both kinds of...
A bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted— one who is independent of support and cannot be led by anyone else with the thought,
"This is better"— would wander rightly in the world.
In the sixth verse, "unopposed" (*aviruddho*) refers to being free from conflict due to the abandonment of these three types of misconduct, in conjunction with good conduct.
"Unopposed. "Having understood the Dhamma" means having known the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the Path.
"Aiming for the state of Nibbāna" means aspiring toward the state of parinibbāna in the aggregates where nothing remains (*anupādisesa*). The rest is self-evident. 369.
In the seventh verse, "reviled" means being assailed by the ten grounds of abuse. "One would not be reconciled" means...
One should not be elated, nor should one be angry. Having obtained food from others, one does not become intoxicated;
having received what was given in faith by others, one should not become intoxicated with the thought, "I am well-known, famous, and a recipient of gains.

The rest is of plain meaning. Regarding the eighth verse: *lobha* means improper greed; *bhava* refers to existence such as the realm of sensual desire (*kāmabhava*) and so forth. Thus, by these two...
By the [first] words, craving for existence and enjoyment is expressed; or else, by the former [words], all craving is meant, and by the latter, kamma-existence.
"Abstaining from the bonds of cutting" means that because these kamma and defilements have been abandoned, he is one who abstains from the bonds of cutting others.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.

371. "Having recognized what was appropriate for himself" means having recognized—by establishing himself therein—that which is suitable for his state as a bhikkhu, namely, purity of livelihood through right seeking and so forth, having abandoned wrong seeking and the like, as well as other forms of right practice.
For something does not become [a reality] by mere knowledge alone. "Yathātathiyaṃ" means according to that which is such, i.e., as it truly is. "Dhammaṃ" means...

Having understood, through knowledge of things as they truly are, the classification of the aggregates, bases, and so forth, or having understood the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the Path—*the rest is of plain meaning*.

372. Regarding the tenth verse, "he is without hope, not hoping for anything": because his underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have been destroyed by the Noble Path and his unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*) have been uprooted, he is "without hope," that is, free from craving. Consequently, due to the absence of hope, he [does not hope] for anyone...
He does not long for phenomena such as form (*rūpa*). Therefore, he said: "hopeless, longing for nothing. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
In the eleventh verse, *āsavakhīṇo* means one whose four taints (*āsava*) are exhausted. *Pahīnamāno* means one who has abandoned the ninefold conceit (*māna*).

*Rāgapathaṃ* refers to the mass of phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) that constitute the objective sphere of lust (*rāga*). *Upātivatto* means having transcended them by means of full understanding (*pariññā*) and abandonment (*pahāna*).
He has transcended. "Tamed" means that, having abandoned the indulgence of all sense-doors, he has reached the plane of taming through noble self-restraint.
"Parinibbūta" means he has become cooled through the subsiding of the fire of the defilements. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
In the twelfth verse, "faithful" (saddho) refers to one who, being free from dependence on others regarding the qualities of the Buddha and so forth, is endowed with faith in every respect.
“Endowed with verified confidence” means possessing confidence through one’s own realization of the practice, rather than by following another’s faith. As it is said:

“In this matter, venerable sir, I do not proceed by faith in the Blessed One. “Learned” means possessing the learning that pertains to the ultimate truth (*paramattha*), because the task of learning has been accomplished.
“A seer of the fixed course” means one who, in a world lost in the wilderness of *saṃsāra*, sees the path leading to the city of the Deathless.
He is a seer of the path that has become the certainty of rightness; thus, it is said, "one who has seen the path.
Regarding the phrase "not shifting among factions" (*na vaggasārī*): those who have gone to factions are called the sixty-two types of speculative views, because they are mutually contradictory.
Thus, among beings who have gone to such factional views, he does not shift among factions, thinking, "This will be annihilated," or "This will remain exactly as it is."

Thus, it is because of not proceeding by way of views. "Repulsion" (*paṭigha*) means that which repels; it is said to be the "affliction of the mind. This is merely a specific term for hatred (*dosa*).
"Having removed" (*vineyya*) means having led away [from]. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

In the thirteenth verse, "the perfectly pure Victor" (*saṃsuddhajina*) refers to one who has conquered the defilements by means of the perfectly pure path of Arahantship. "With the veil removed" (*vivaṭacchada*)— [The remainder of the commentary follows.]
"One who has removed the covering of lust, hatred, and delusion" means one who has attained mastery over the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths.
For it is not possible for anyone else to alter those phenomena as they have been known by him; therefore, the one whose taints are destroyed is called "one who has mastery over phenomena.
"One who has gone to the further shore": the further shore is called Nibbāna; he has gone there, having realized it by way of the state with residue remaining.
This is what is meant. "Unshakable" (*anejo*) means one from whom the movement of craving has departed. "Skilled in the knowledge of the cessation of formations" (*saṅkhāranirodhañāṇakusalo*):

the cessation of formations is called Nibbāna; the knowledge regarding that is the wisdom of the Noble Path. One who is skilled therein—meaning expert because it has been cultivated four times—is what is meant.

376. In the fourteenth verse, "in the past" (*atītesu*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*) that have reached their occurrence and have already passed away. "In the future" (*anāgatesu*) refers likewise to the five aggregates that have not yet reached their occurrence.

"One who has transcended conceptual construction" (*kappātīto*) means one who has transcended all conceptualization (*kappana*) such as "I" and "mine," or indeed all conceptual constructions of craving and views (*taṇhā-diṭṭhi-kappa*).
"One with exceedingly pure wisdom" (*aticca suddhipañño*) means one whose wisdom is extremely pure, or one who, having transcended...

"Purified wisdom. Having transcended what? The three periods of time. For the Arahant, having transcended all of this—the past period consisting of ignorance and volitional formations, the future period consisting of birth, aging, and death, and the present period beginning with consciousness and ending with existence—and having overcome doubt, he has attained wisdom that has reached supreme purity.
He stands firm. Therefore he is called “one whose pure wisdom has transcended. “From all sense-bases” means from the twelve sense-bases.
For the Arahat has thus transcended the world-age (kappa). Because he has transcended the world-age and because his pure wisdom has transcended, he does not enter into any sense-base in the future.
Therefore it was said: “Completely liberated from all sense-bases.”
377. Regarding the phrase "another quarter" in the fifteenth verse, those who have said "the four quarters of the truths" refer to each individual quarter;

having known these through the wisdom that defines the truths during the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), one then "having fully understood the Dhamma" means having fully understood the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the four noble paths. "Having seen the opening up, the abandoning of the taints" means then—
Having seen with the knowledge of review that Nibbāna— known as the destruction of the taints— is unveiled, manifest, and unobstructed;
because of the complete exhaustion of all acquisitions (*upadhi*)— namely, the aggregates, sense-pleasures, defilements,
and volitional formations— the bhikkhu, not clinging anywhere, would wander rightly in the world, dwelling therein without adhering to the world.
"May he go" thus he concluded the teaching.
Then that created being, praising the teaching of the Dhamma, spoke this verse beginning with "Surely, O Blessed One.
Therein, "he who dwells thus" refers to one who, having eradicated [unwholesome states] such as the notion of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), dwells having abandoned all faults regarding auspiciousness.

He spoke thus, pointing out the monk described by each respective verse as one who, having removed passion for divine and human sensual pleasures and having transcended existence, dwells in the realization of the Dhamma. The rest is self-evident. This, however, is the construction:
"Surely, Blessed One, it is exactly as you have said in the verses beginning with, 'For him whose auspicious signs are uprooted...'"
At the conclusion of each verse, he said, "He would wander rightly in the world. For what reason?
Because that bhikkhu who dwells in such a way is tamed by the supreme taming; he has transcended all ten fetters and the four bonds.
Therefore, he would wander rightly in the world; there is no [other] for me in this matter.
Having spoken even this summary verse of the teaching, "Doubt," he brought the discourse to its conclusion precisely at the peak of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the sutta, one hundred thousand million deities attained the supreme fruit (Arahantship), while those who attained the fruits of stream-entry,
once-returning, and non-returning were beyond counting.
The commentary on the *Sammāparibbājanīya-sutta* within the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*,
which is part of the *Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*,
is completed.
14. Commentary on the Dhammika Sutta.
"Thus have I heard" begins the Dhammika Sutta. What is its origin?

It is said that while the Blessed One, the Protector of the World, was still living, there was a lay follower named Dhammika, so called both by name and because of his practice. He was indeed endowed with the Refuges and endowed with virtue.
He was one who had heard much, a bearer of the Three Piṭakas, a non-returner, an attainer of the higher knowledges, and a traveler through the air.

His retinue consisted of five hundred lay followers, and they too were exactly like him. One day, while he was observing the Uposatha, having gone into seclusion and retired for meditation, at the conclusion of the middle watch of the night, this reflection arose in him:
"What if I were to [distinguish] between those in the household life and those who have left the household life..."
“...should ask about the way of practice. Surrounded by five hundred lay followers, he approached the Blessed One and asked about that matter;
the Blessed One answered him. In this regard, what has already been described should be understood according to the method previously stated;
we shall now describe what has not been mentioned before.
379. Regarding that, first of all, in the initial verse: *kathaṃ karoti* means "how does he act," "while acting how," or "while practicing how"?
*Sādhu hoti* means it becomes beautiful, blameless, and conducive to one's welfare. *Upāsakāse* is simply said as *upāsakā*.
The rest is clear in meaning. This, however, is the construction: "Whoever goes from home to homelessness" means one who goes forth.
"Among these two kinds of disciples—those who live at home and those who are lay followers (*upāsaka*)—what kind of disciple is excellent?

Now, demonstrating the Blessed One’s capacity to answer when thus questioned, he spoke the two verses beginning with "For you. Therein, "course" (*gati*) refers to the course of one's underlying disposition (*ajjhāsayagati*).
"Final goal" (*parāyana*) refers to the ultimate attainment. Alternatively, "course" refers to the fivefold division beginning with hell.
"Parāyaṇa" means the supreme destination beyond all states of existence, the liberation from rebirth, which is parinibbāna.

"There is no one equal to you" means there is no one like you. "Having fully understood all phenomena through knowledge, you proclaimed them out of compassion for beings" means that you, O Blessed One, having penetrated without exception everything that is to be known, proclaimed it out of compassion for beings.
He proclaimed all knowledge and all Dhamma. Whatever was beneficial for anyone, that alone he revealed and taught;
it is said that he had no "teacher’s fist" (no secrets withheld).
"You shine, stainless"—like the moon free from smoke, dust, and the like, you shine stainless due to the absence of the stains of passion and so forth. The rest here is of plain meaning.

382. Now, having praised those sons of the gods to whom the Blessed One taught the Dhamma at that time, and extolling the Blessed One, he spoke these two verses beginning with “He came into your presence.
Therein, regarding the phrase “the Nāga king named Erāvaṇa”:
it is said that this son of the gods named Erāvaṇa, who can assume any form at will, dwells in a celestial palace. Whenever Sakka goes for a pleasure excursion to the gardens, [he accompanies him].
Then, having manifested a body one hundred and fifty yojanas in height and fashioned thirty-three frontal lobes, he became the elephant named Erāvaṇa.
On each of his frontal lobes there were two tusks; on each tusk there were seven lotus ponds;
in each lotus pond there were seven lotus plants; and on each lotus plant there were seven...
There were seven lotuses; on each lotus were seven leaves;
and on each leaf danced seven celestial nymphs known as the *paduma-accharās*, the female dancers of Sakka who are mentioned even in the *Vimānavatthu* in the verse:
"The well-trained maidens wander among the lotuses. In the midst of those thirty-three *saṅkumbhas* was the *sudassana-kumbha*.
It is thirty *yojanas* in extent; there, a jeweled couch the size of a *yojana* is spread within a flower pavilion three *yojanas* high.
There, Sakka, the lord of the devas, surrounded by a host of nymphs, enjoys celestial splendor.
But when Sakka, the lord of the devas, returns from his pleasure excursion in the park, that form is withdrawn once more, and he becomes a young deva again.
It exists. With reference to this, he said: “The Nāga king named Erāvaṇa has come into your presence. “Having heard ‘Jina’” means:
having heard that “this Blessed One is one who has conquered evil states. “He too, having consulted with you” means: having consulted together with you;
the intention is that he asked a question. “Ajjhagama” means he went toward (adhi-agamā); it is said that he arrived.
“Having heard ‘Excellent! he was greatly pleased”: the meaning is that having heard that question, he rejoiced, saying, “Excellent, venerable sir,” and departed in a state of satisfaction.
383. Regarding the passage “The king... Vessavaṇa Kuvera”: here, that *yakkha* is called a “king” (*rājā*) in the sense of being one who causes others to rejoice;

he is called “Vessavaṇa” because he exercises sovereignty over the royal capital of Visāṇā; and he should be understood by his former name as “Kuvera. It is said that he was a wealthy brahmin named Kuvera.
Having performed meritorious deeds such as making offerings and giving, he was reborn as the sovereign of the royal capital named Visāṇā.
Therefore, he is called “Kuvero Vessavaṇo. And this has been stated in the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta:
“The royal capital of the Great King Kuvera, dear sir, is named Visāṇā; therefore the Great King Kuvera is called ‘Vessavaṇo.’”
The rest here is quite clear.
In this regard, it might be asked: why did Erāvaṇa, who dwells in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven which is much further away, arrive first;
why did Vessavaṇa arrive later; and how is it that this lay follower, though dwelling in the very same city, arrived last? And how was he [able to do so]?
How did he know of his arrival so as to speak thus? It is said:

At that time, it is reported, Vessavaṇa mounted a coral palanquin twelve *yojanas* long, drawn by women, and raising a coral banner, surrounded by ten thousand *koṭis* of *yakkhas*, thought, "I shall ask the Blessed One a question.
Then, bypassing the celestial mansions situated in the sky, he proceeded along the path.
While traveling along the road, he arrived at the upper story of the residence of the female lay follower Nandamātā in the city of Veḷukaṇḍaka.

This was the power of that female lay follower: she possessed pure virtue, was constantly abstinent from eating at improper times, was a bearer of the Three Piṭakas, and was established in the fruit of non-returning. At that time, she had opened the lion-window.
Standing in a place stirred by the wind for the purpose of testing the time, he recited the *Aṭṭhaka* and *Pārāyana* chapters with perfectly rounded words and syllables in a sweet voice.
Vessavaṇa, having parked the vehicles right there, remained until the laywoman reached the conclusion:
"Thus spoke the Blessed One while dwelling among the Magadhans at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine, concerning the sixteen brahmin attendants."

He spoke, and having heard it all, at the conclusion of the discourse, he raised his great neck—which resembled a golden drum—and gave his approval, saying, "Excellent, excellent, sister! She asked, "Who is here? "I am Vessavaṇa, sister," he replied.
It is said that the laywoman had first become a stream-enterer, and only later did Vessavaṇa do so; thus, by virtue of their Dhamma, he was her brother from the same womb.
Having made an intentional reference, he addressed the female lay follower with the word "sister. And when the female lay follower said to him, "It is the wrong time, brother, dear sir;
do now as you think fit," he replied, "Sister, I am devoted to you and am showing my devotion.
[She said,] "In that case, dear sir, the laborers are unable to bring the rice that has ripened in my field."
"Command that for your assembly," he said. "Very well, sister," he replied, and he commanded the *yakkhas*.
They filled one hundred and twenty-five storehouses. From that time on, there was no storehouse that was empty;
it became a proverb in the world, saying, "It is like the storehouse of Nanda’s mother. Having filled the storehouses, Vessavaṇa approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "You have arrived at an improper time. Then he reported everything to the Blessed One.
For this reason, although Vessavaṇa was dwelling in the abode of the Four Great Kings, which is much closer, he arrived later.
However, Erāvaṇa had no business to attend to in the interval; therefore, he arrived first.
Now, although this lay follower was already a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) and naturally ate but one meal a day, nevertheless, considering it to be the Uposatha day,
he resolved upon the Uposatha precepts. In the evening, well-robed and well-clad, surrounded by five hundred lay followers,

he went to Jetavana, listened to the teaching of the Dhamma, and upon returning to his own home, [he spoke] to those lay followers concerning the distinctions such as the benefits of the refuges, the precepts, and the Uposatha.
Having taught the duties of lay followers, he dismissed those laymen.
In their very own house, five hundred permissible couches with legs measuring a handful in height had been prepared in separate inner chambers.
Each of them entered his own chamber and sat down having attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*); the lay follower did exactly the same. At that time, in the city of Sāvatthī...
Seven hundred and fifty thousand families dwell there, which by human calculation amounts to eighteen koṭis of people.
Therefore, during the first watch of the night, Sāvatthī city resounds with a single great noise like the ocean, due to the sounds of elephants, horses, humans, drums, and so forth.
Immediately following the middle watch, that sound subsides. At that time, the lay follower [emerges] from meditative attainment.
Having risen and reflected upon his own virtues, he thought, "By depending on whom have I obtained this happiness by which I dwell happy in the bliss of the Path and the bliss of the Fruit?
Thinking, "It is by depending on the Blessed One," he clarified his mind toward the Blessed One;
then, reflecting with his divine eye as to "in what dwelling does the Blessed One currently abide? he [saw].

Having seen Erāvaṇa and Vessavaṇa, having heard their Dhamma teaching with his divine ear-element, and having known their state of serene mind through the knowledge of penetration of others' minds, he thought:
"What if I too were to ask the Blessed One about the practice that leads to the welfare of both worlds?
Therefore, although he was living in the same city, he arrived last of all, and in this way he knew of their arrival.
Therefore he said: “The Naga king came into your presence... and having heard [your words], he was filled with joy.

(384) Now, praising the Blessed One for his superior status over the ascetics and brahmins esteemed by the world outside [the Buddhist fold], he spoke the two verses beginning with “Whosoever these...
In that context, the term *titthiya* refers to Nanda, Vaccha, Saṅkicca, and others.
Those born in the sectarian systems (diṭṭhitittha) established by the three original persons who were founders of sects—
namely the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa, who had gone forth in their dispensations—
are all indicated by the phrase, “whatever these heretics (titthiyā) are, whose habit is disputation,” [thinking] “we are practicing rightly, others are practicing wrongly.”
Thus, those whose nature is to engage in such speech wander about piercing the world with the weapons of their mouths.

By the phrase "or the Ājīvakas," he shows them as being included together in a single group. "They do not overstep" means they do not transcend [the truth]. By saying "all," he includes others as well—any followers of other sects (tīrthikas) and so forth—taking them into account.
"As one standing [beholds] one who is running": just as someone standing still, being devoid of movement, looks upon one who is moving swiftly.
"One should not overtake a man who is walking"—thus, because you lack the range of wisdom (*paññāgati*), you remain unable to comprehend those various distinctions of meaning;
the sense is that you do not overtake the Blessed One, whose wisdom is exceedingly swift.
(385) "The brahmins, who are habituated to debate and are aged"—by this much [he refers to] Caṅkī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, Jāṇussoṇi, and others.
By the phrase "there are some who are brahmins," he indicates that there are indeed some—whether middle-aged or young—who are exclusively brahmins, meaning they exist and are found;
thus he points to Assalāyana, Vāseṭṭha, Ambaṭṭha, Uttara Māṇava, and others.
"Intent on the goal" means: "Would he perhaps explain this question? Would he cut through this doubt? and so forth.

"They have their interests bound up in you. And as for "others"—those others who wander about thinking, "We are the proponents," such as the immeasurable number of noble warriors (*khattiya*), wise brahmins, deities of Brahmā, *yakkhas*, and so forth—he shows that all of them likewise have their interests bound up in you.
Having thus praised the Blessed One in various ways, he now praises him by means of the Dhamma itself.
Requesting a discourse on the Dhamma, he spoke these two verses beginning with “For this is the Dhamma.
Therein, “for this is the Dhamma” refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. “Subtle” means delicate and difficult to penetrate.
“Blissful” means that once penetrated, it brings about supramundane bliss; therefore, because it brings bliss, it is called “blissful. “Well-proclaimed” means...
"Well-taught. "Desiring to hear" means "wishing to listen. "Tell us that" means "tell us that Dhamma.
There is also the reading "you to us," which means "you tell us.
"All these monks" refers to the five hundred monks who were seated at that moment; he makes his request while pointing them out. And "the lay followers as well" refers to his own retinue.
And he shows others as well. The rest here is self-evident.
388. Then the Blessed One, in order first to show the practice of the homeless life, addressed the bhikkhus and said, "Listen to me, bhikkhus," and so forth.
In that context, regarding the phrase "the Dhamma that shakes, practice that too in its entirety": it is called "shaking" because it shakes off the defilements (*kilesa*).
"I proclaim to you this ascetic practice (*dhuta*), such a Dhamma of the path that shakes off the defilements; having proclaimed it, all of you should practice and undertake it—do not be negligent.

This is what is meant. "Postures" (*iriyāpatha*) refers to the fourfold set beginning with walking. "Conducive to the life of one gone forth" means suitable for a recluse, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
By way of application to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) in the forest...
"Only while it is occurring," say others. "One should cultivate" means one should resort to that posture. "Seeing the benefit" means perceiving the welfare.
"The wise" means the intelligent. The rest of this verse is self-evident. 389. "Not at the wrong time":
thus, while cultivating a posture suitable for one who has gone forth, [one should avoid] the passing of the midday [hour].
A bhikkhu should not wander at an improper time; rather, he should wander for alms in the village only at the proper time.

For what reason? Because attachments cling to one who wanders at an improper time. To a person wandering at an improper time, many attachments—such as the attachment of passion—cling, embrace, envelop, and adhere.
Therefore, the Buddhas do not wander at an improper time; therefore...
"Those noble individuals who have awakened to the Four Noble Truths do not wander for alms at an improper time.
At that time, it is said, the training rule regarding eating at an improper time had not yet been laid down;

therefore, demonstrating the danger to worldlings by way of teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse. However, the noble ones, from the very moment they attain the Path, have already desisted from such conduct.
This is the natural law (*dhammatā*).
Having thus prohibited wandering at improper times, the Buddha said, "Forms and sounds," etc., showing that even when wandering at the proper time, one must conduct oneself in this manner.
Its meaning is as follows: those forms and so forth which produce various kinds of intoxication—

They cause beings to rejoice; having dispelled desire toward them in the manner described in the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta and other texts, one should enter for the morning meal at the proper time. And here, "morning meal" (pātarāsa) means that which is to be eaten in the morning;
this is a name for almsfood (piṇḍapāta). Furthermore, the place where it is obtained is also called "morning meal" by metaphorical extension. Therefore, [one enters] for almsfood...
"he obtains it"—thus the meaning here should be understood as "he might go to that place. 391.
Having entered thus:
"And when a bhikkhu has obtained almsfood at the proper time..."
Having withdrawn alone, let him sit in seclusion;
reflecting inwardly, with his mind not directed outward,
let him utter no speech, his being held in restraint.
In this context, "alms-food" (*piṇḍa*) refers to mixed alms; for it is called "alms" (*piṇḍa*) in the sense of being gathered together and collected from here and there.
"At the proper time" (*samayena*) means at the time before midday. "Having gone back alone" means having turned back without a companion, thereby achieving physical seclusion.
"Reflecting inwardly" means reflecting upon the continuity of the aggregates after having applied the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*).

“He does not let the mind go outward” means he does not lead the consciousness away toward external forms and so forth by way of lust. “With his person well-restrained” means one whose mind is thoroughly held in check.
And while dwelling thus:
“Even if he should converse with a disciple...”
Or by some other monk; he should proclaim that sublime Dhamma,
neither with malice nor with disparagement of others.
What is meant? If that practitioner of yoga should converse even with a disciple who has approached him out of a desire to hear something,
or with anyone else— whether a lay follower of another sect, or a monk who has gone forth right here—
and if [the subject] is connected with the paths and fruits, consisting of the ten bases of discourse, or is "excellent" in the sense of being unsurpassed;
The Dhamma. One might proclaim that sublime Dhamma, yet one would not utter even the slightest bit of malicious speech or slander against others.
Now, showing the fault in such slander, he said: "For some [utter] a dispute. Its meaning is as follows: here, some...
Foolish men respond with various kinds of contentious speech connected with the censure of others;
they oppose and conflict, acting like those who, desiring to fight, advance head-on against an army.
We do not praise them, O men of inferior wisdom. Why? Because from that very source they fall into strife, since they are such as they are.
From this or that path of speech, individuals arise and become entangled in disputes; they cling to them.
For what reason do they become entangled? Because they direct their minds toward those distant things;
for those opponents direct their minds toward those [objects] which, once reached, lie far from serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
394–5. Having thus shown the activity of those of limited wisdom, he now speaks—beginning with “The alms-food, the dwelling... the disciple”—to show the activity of those of great wisdom.
In that context, by the three terms *vihāra*, *patissaya*, and *sayanāsana*, it is the lodging itself that is expressed;
*āpa* means water; and *saṅghāṭirajūpavāhana* refers to [the removal of] dust, dirt, and so forth.

The washing away of the dust from the outer robe. Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Sugata—meaning, having heard the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a manner as, "Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe for protection against cold," and so forth, within the context of the restraint of all taints—one who is a disciple of supreme wisdom should practice after due reflection. This is what is meant here by the term "alms-food."

A disciple of supreme wisdom, having understood the fourfold requisite— almsfood, lodgings such as monasteries, medicinal requisites for the sick indicated by the word "and so forth," and robes consisting of the outer cloak—
and having reflected upon them according to the method beginning with, "Only for the maintenance of this body," should utilize them;
indeed, one who possesses supreme wisdom, like the Tathāgata, is capable of utilizing them in this way.
Whether he be a disciple who is still in training (*sekkha*), an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*), or, in the ultimate sense, an Arahant—he is indeed one who has the four supports (*caturāpassena*).
For it is said of him: "Having reflected, he pursues one thing; having reflected, he endures one thing; having reflected, he avoids one thing; having reflected, he dispels one thing.
And as for that reflection with which the disciple of supreme wisdom pursues [his practice], therefore, in the mass of food... [as in the verse] ...just as on a lotus leaf.
A drop of water; it should be understood that it is just so.

396. Having thus demonstrated the practice of one whose taints are exhausted and having brought the path of homelessness to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship, he now spoke the words beginning with "But as for the duty of a householder" in order to show the path of the householder. Therein, regarding the first verse:
“A disciple” here refers to a householder-disciple. The rest is self-evident. This is the construction [of the meaning]:

“That entire, unmixed, whole, and complete Dhamma of a bhikkhu which was taught by me previously cannot be touched—that is, it is not possible to attain it—by one who possesses acquisitions such as fields, lands, and so forth.”
397. Having thus rejected the way of the monk, he spoke the words "one should not kill a living being" in order to demonstrate the way of the householder.
Therein, by the first half-verse, abstention from taking life that is pure in three respects is stated; by the second half-verse, the practice of benevolence toward sentient beings is shown.
Furthermore, the third quarter-verse here corresponds to the fourth quarter-verse in the *Khaggavisāṇa Sutta*, which is distinguished by its state of being stationary and its state of being a bull.
This has been described in every detail in the commentary on the *Mettasutta*. The remainder is self-evident. However, the construction should be made by reversing the order:
"Having laid aside the rod toward all beings, whether weak or strong, one should not kill, nor cause others to kill, nor approve of killing.

Alternatively, after the phrase "having laid aside the rod," the word "should conduct oneself" (*vatteyya*) must be supplied from the preceding context; otherwise, [the meaning would remain incomplete].
For indeed, there is no connection between what precedes and what follows.
(398) Having thus shown the first training rule, now, in order to show the second training rule, he said: "Then, what is not given.
Therein, "anything" means whether little or much. "Anywhere" means either in a village or in the forest. "A disciple" means...
A householder disciple. "Awakening" means knowing, "This belongs to another.
"One should avoid all that is not given" means that by practicing in this way, one avoids all that is not given; it shows that there is no other way.
The rest here is according to the method already stated and is self-evident.
399. Having thus shown that the second training rule is pure in three respects, he says “unholy life” (*abrahmacariya*) while showing the third from the point of the highest limit.

Therein, “unable” (*asambhuṇanto*) means being incapable. 400. Now, showing the fourth training rule, he says “having gone to an assembly” (*sabhaggato vā*). Therein, “having gone to an assembly” (*sabhaggato*) means having gone to a council hall (*santhāgāra*) and so forth. “Having gone to a gathering” (*parisaggato*) means having gone to the midst of a multitude. The rest here is according to the method already stated and is self-evident.
401. Having thus shown that even the fourth training rule is pure in three respects, he spoke [the fifth] as "and drinking intoxicants" (*majjañca pānaṃ*).
Therein, it is stated thus for the sake of the ease of metrical composition. But the meaning is:
"one should not practice the drinking of intoxicants. "This Dhamma" (*dhammaṃ imaṃ*) refers to this Dhamma of abstaining from the drinking of intoxicants.
"Ending in madness" means having madness as its conclusion. For even the lightest result of drinking intoxicants leads to madness for one who has become human.
"Having understood this" means having known this drinking of intoxicants.
The rest here is according to the method already stated and is self-evident.

402. Having thus shown that even the fifth training rule is pure in three respects, he now speaks—having shown that among the previous training rules it is specifically the drinking of intoxicants that causes defilement and causes dissension—in order to more firmly enjoin abstention from them, saying:
"For through intoxication they commit evil deeds. In this context, *mada* means "on account of intoxication. The particle *hi* is used merely for the completion of the metrical line.
“Nipāto” (the prefix). “Committing evils” means committing all unwholesome deeds, such as the destruction of life and so forth.
“Delusion in the next world and infatuation in this world” means being deluded regarding the next world and being infatuated in this world. The rest is of plain meaning.
Having thus far shown the perpetual virtue of the householder disciple, [the author] now shows the factors of the Uposatha:
He spoke two verses beginning with “One should not kill a living being. Therein, “unholy conduct” (*abrahmacariya*) refers to conduct that is not noble.
“Sexual intercourse” (*methuna*) refers to the engagement in the act of sexual union. “One should not eat at night; it is eating at the wrong time”:

one should not eat even at night, nor should one eat during the day once the proper time has passed. “And no perfumes”: here, by the mention of “perfumes,” ointments, powders, and so forth are also included.
These should be understood as being already included. "On a couch" means on a permissible (kappiya) couch. "Spread with" means spread with permissible coverings such as mats and so forth.
However, on the bare ground, it is also permitted even if it is spread with a woolen rug (gonaka) and the like.

"Eightfold" refers to the [path], not like a musical instrument which lacks its constituent parts. "To the end of suffering" means by one who has reached the end of the suffering of saṃsāra. The rest here is as follows.
This is quite clear. However, they say that it was also spoken by the compilers of the Council regarding the latter half [of the fortnight]. 405.
Having thus shown the factors of the Uposatha, he now says, “And then, of the fortnight,” in order to show the time for the Uposatha.
In this context, *tato* is a particle used merely to fill out the meter. [The phrase] “the Uposatha of the waxing fortnight” is connected with the subsequent word.

It should be connected thus: “Having observed the Uposatha on these three days—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight—having approached and dwelt in this Eight-Factored Uposatha.

Regarding the phrase “and the fortnight of wonders,” here the month of Āsāḷha preceding the commencement of the rains, the three months of the rainy season itself, and the month of Kattika—these five months are called the “fortnight of wonders.”
[They] are so called. Others say there are only three months: Āsāḷha, Kattika, and Phagguṇa.
Still others say that, according to the first and last days of the fortnight and Uposatha days, there are four days in each fortnight—namely, the thirteenth, the first, the seventh, and the ninth.
One may accept whichever one prefers; or rather, all of this should be spoken of for those who desire merit. Thus is this [account of] the Fortunate Fortnight (*pāṭihāriya-pakkha*).
"With a serene mind, not omitting even a single day while observing the eightfold Uposatha with its well-perfected and perfectly complete form"—
this is how the connection should be understood. Having thus shown the time for the Uposatha, [the text now] explains what should be done during those times while observing this Uposatha.
Showing this, he said, "And then at dawn. Here too, *tato* is a particle used merely for the completion of the phrase, or it refers to the sense of immediate succession;
thus, "then" (*atha*) is what is meant. "At dawn" (*pāto*) means in the early part of the following day. "Having observed the Uposatha" (*upavutthuposatho*) means having kept the Uposatha fast.

"With food" (*annenā*) means with rice gruel, cooked rice, and so forth. "With drink" (*pānenā*) means with the eight kinds of beverages. "Rejoicing" (*anumodamāno*) means rejoicing after [having been invited].
"Rejoicing continuously" means having constant joy. "As is fitting" means according to one's own suitability; that is to say, according to one's power and according to one's strength.
"One should share" means one should divide and distribute. The rest is self-evident. 407.
Having thus explained the duty of one who has observed the Uposatha, [the text now] explains the lifelong service to teachers and the purity of livelihood.
Having thus spoken, he said, "By means of righteousness, [one should support] mother and father," showing the state to be attained by that practice.
Therein, "by means of righteousness" (*dhammena*) means by wealth acquired through righteous means. "Should support" (*bhareyya*) means should nourish.

"Righteous trade" (*dhammikaṃ vaṇijjaṃ*) refers to the five unrighteous trades: trading in living beings, trading in weapons, trading in poison, trading in meat, and trading in intoxicants. These are the five unrighteous trades.
Excluding those [prohibited trades], the remainder are righteous trades (*dhammikavaṇijjā*).
By way of "trade," other righteous occupations such as agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth are also included here. The rest is self-evident. This, however, is the construction:

that noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), endowed with the constant morality, the Uposatha morality, and the practice of giving, should engage in righteous trade; and from what is obtained therefrom, because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is "righteously" (*dhammena*).
He should support his mother and father with enjoyments. Then, that householder, being thus diligent and performing this aforementioned duty from the very beginning,

at the breaking up of the body, approaches and associates with those gods known as the *sayampabha*— the six classes of sense-sphere deities who, by dispelling darkness with their own radiance, have acquired the name "Self-Luminous" through their making light.
It clings; it is reborn in the place where those [beings] are reborn.
Thus ends the commentary on the Dhammika Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Paramatthajotikā* commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*).
The second chapter is concluded according to the method of explaining the meaning; by name, it is called the Cūḷavagga.
3. The Mahāvagga.
1. Commentary on the Pabbajjā Sutta 408.
Regarding the *Pabbajjā Sutta*: "I shall praise renunciation. What is its origin?
It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a reflection arose in the Venerable Ānanda: "Of the great disciples such as Sāriputta and others..."
"The going forth has been proclaimed, and that is known by the monks and the lay followers. But it has not yet been proclaimed for the Blessed One;
what if I were to proclaim it? Then, sitting on a seat in the Jetavana monastery and taking up a fan, he recited this sutta, proclaiming the Blessed One’s going forth to the monks.
In this context, since one praising the going-forth must praise how he went forth, and since one praising how he went forth must praise how,
while investigating, he found the going-forth pleasing, therefore, having said "I shall praise the going-forth," he spoke the words beginning with "how he went forth.
"Possessing eyes" means possessing eyes by way of the five kinds of eyes.
The meaning is "one endowed with vision. The rest of the first verse is self-evident. 409.
Now, explaining that same meaning with the words "just as one investigating," he said: "It is a confinement" (*sambādho*).
Therein, "confinement" (*sambādho*) means being devoid of opportunity for wholesome action due to the pressure of wife and children, etc., and the pressure of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"The realm of passion" (*rājassāyatana*) refers to a place where passion and the like arise, such as Kamboja and other lands for horses and the like.
"Open space" (*abbhokāsa*) means wide open, being the opposite of the confinement previously mentioned, like the sky. Having seen this, he went forth:

having thus examined the disadvantages and advantages of household life and the life of renunciation, with his heart strongly urged on by sickness, old age, and death, he undertook the Great Renunciation.
Having gone forth and cut his hair with a sword on the bank of the Anomā River, he immediately acquired the appearance of a recluse with hair and beard trimmed to the length of two finger-breadths;
then, taking the eight requisites presented by the Brahmā Ghaṭīkāra, and though uninstructed by anyone as to how they should be worn or put on,
he was trained solely by his own habituation to the life of renunciation practiced throughout many thousands of births.

He went forth. This means that having put on one saffron robe, having arranged the other as an upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*), having placed a third robe upon his shoulder, and having slung an earthen bowl over his shoulder, he resolved upon the appearance of one who has gone forth. The rest here is self-evident.
Having thus praised the Blessed One’s going forth, [the text] thereafter describes his practice after having gone forth at the bank of the Anomā River.
In order to announce his departure for the sake of striving after having renounced the world, he spoke all that beginning with the words, "Having gone forth in body," and so on.
Therein, "he avoided evil action with the body" means he shunned the threefold misconduct of the body. "Vocal misconduct" refers to the fourfold misconduct of speech.
"He purified his livelihood" means that, having abandoned wrong livelihood, he practiced only right livelihood.
411. Having thus purified his virtue according to the eightfold way of livelihood, the Buddha traveled from the banks of the Anoma River to Rājagaha in thirty *yojanas* over the course of seven days.
Although he was not yet a Buddha when he arrived at Rājagaha, it is nevertheless permissible to speak thus, considering it his conduct prior to becoming a Buddha: "Here the King was born; here..."
“...took hold of the kingdom,” and so forth, is like a common worldly expression. “Of Magadha” means the city of the Magadha country; this is what is stated. *Giribbaja* is also its name.
For it stands like a cow-pen (*vaja*) in the midst of five mountains named Paṇḍava, Gijjhakūṭa, Vebhāra, Isigili, and Vepulla; therefore, it is called “Giribbaja. [For] alms...
"Abhihāresi" means he wandered through that city for the purpose of begging. It is said that standing at the city gate, he thought:

"If I were to announce my arrival to King Bimbisāra, saying, 'The prince named Siddhattha, the son of Suddhodana, has come,' they would bring me many requisites. Yet, that would not be fitting for me."
“Having informed the one who has gone forth, I shall receive the requisites; come now, I will go for alms.
Having put on the rag-robe belonging to Devadatta and taking a clay bowl, he entered the city by the eastern gate and went from house to house for alms.
Therefore the Venerable Ānanda said: “You brought it for alms. Regarding the phrase “endowed with excellent marks,” this refers to the body.
He is one who possesses excellent marks as if they were strewn [over him], or rather, one who possesses vast and excellent marks.

For even that which is "vast" is called "strewed" (*ākiṇṇa*). As it is said: "The man who is strewed with greed is like a nurse’s cloth that has been smeared. The meaning is: one who is vastly greedy. 412. *Tam addasa* (He saw him):
It is said that for the seven days prior to that, a festival had been proclaimed in the city.
On that day, however, the drum was beaten with the proclamation: “The festival has passed;
the works must be set in motion. Then the great multitude gathered in the royal courtyard.
The king, thinking, “I shall inspect the works,” opened the lion-window and, while looking at the army, saw the Great Being approaching for alms. Thus spoke the Venerable Ānanda.
—“Bimbisāra saw him, while standing in his palace. He spoke this matter to his ministers. 413.
Now, showing the matter spoken by those ministers, he said: “Listen, sirs!
Therein, “this” refers to that Bodhisatta whom the king points out; “sirs” is an address to the ministers; “listen” means “behold.”
"Abhirūpa" means having limbs and members that are beautiful to behold. "Brahma" means endowed with perfect height and proportion. "Sucī" means having a complexion of perfectly pure skin.
"Caraṇena" means by his gait. 414–5.
"Nīcakulāmiva" means he is not one who has gone forth from a lowly family; the letter *m* is used for metrical conjunction (*padasandhi*).
"Where will this bhikkhu go?"—let royal messengers go quickly to find out where this bhikkhu will go and where he will stay today.
He spoke with this intention: "For we wish to see him. He is "one whose sense-doors are guarded" by virtue of having downcast eyes;
he is "well-restrained" by virtue of mindfulness. Or, he is "one whose sense-doors are guarded" by virtue of mindfulness, and he is "well-restrained" by virtue of being inspiring.
By wearing the saṅghāṭi robe.
"He quickly filled his bowl" means that because of his clear comprehension and mindfulness, he did not take more than was necessary;
rather, by fulfilling his intention with the thought, "This much is enough," he quickly filled his bowl. He is called a "muni" because he has practiced for the sake of silence (mona).
Even one who has not yet attained the state of a sage is called a "sage" (muni) according to worldly convention;
for worldly people call even a renunciant who has not achieved the perfection of a sage a "sage. He ascended that mountain, Paṇḍava.
It is said that he asked the people, "Where do the renunciants live in this city? Then they [pointed it out] to him: "On Paṇḍava..."
They informed him, "In a cave facing the east above. Therefore, thinking, "The dwelling shall be here," he directed his course toward that very Paṇḍava mountain. (Verses 419–23:
"Like a tiger or a bull, like a lion in a mountain cleft"—that is, in a mountain cave, like a tiger or like a bull.
And the meaning is "seated like a lion. For these three best [beings], free from fear and terror, sit within mountain caves;
therefore, he made this comparison. "By means of a noble vehicle" means by an excellent vehicle such as an elephant, horse, chariot, or palanquin.
"Having conveyed them to their place of rest" means having gone as far as the ground can be traversed by vehicles such as elephants and horses.
*Āsajja* means having reached or having gone near him; *upāvisi* means he sat down. *Yuvā* means endowed with youth. *Dahara* means young by birth.
*Paṭhamuppattiko susū* is merely a further qualification of both those terms. *Yuvā susū* means exceedingly youthful.
*Paṭhamuppattiko* means arisen in the very first stage of youth. *Daharo cāsī* means that he was young.
"And you eat like a very young child in your youth.
(424–5) "The vanguard of the army" means the front of the military force. "I give you wealth; enjoy it" means here:
"I give you as much wealth as you desire throughout Aṅga and Magadha. Adorning yourself with that, preceded by a multitude of elephants, [enter] the vanguard of the army."
The connection should be understood as: "Eat! When the Great Man was thus addressed by the King—"I give you wealth; eat!
Tell me your birth when asked"—he thought:
"If I were desirous of kingship, even the Cātumahārājika gods and others would invite me with their own respective kingdoms while I remained in my home."
“Indeed, I might exercise the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch. But this king, being ignorant, said: ‘Come now, let me make him know.
Raising his arm and pointing toward the direction from which he had come, he said, ‘The king of the Ujju country,’ and so forth.
In that context, by saying ‘from the side of the Himalayas,’ he shows the abundance or scarcity of crops. For the Himalayas...”
Even the great sāl trees growing in the stone clefts increase by way of the five kinds of growth; how much more so, then, the crops sown in the fields!

By saying "endowed with wealth and heroism," he demonstrates his lack of deficiency in the seven treasures and his state of being presided over by heroic men, such that he cannot be assailed by rival kings. "Having his dwelling among the Kosalans."
By saying this, he rejects the status of a new king (*navakarāja*). For a new king is not said to be "one whose home is [there]";
rather, one for whom that very territory has been his residence by way of lineage from the beginning of time is called "one whose home is [there].
King Suddhodana was of such a kind; it is with reference to him that it is said, "those whose home is among the Kosalans. By that, even what is inherited through lineage...
He illuminates his perfection of wealth.

Having thus far illuminated his own perfection of wealth, and having declared his perfection of birth with the words, "By lineage I am an Ādicca, by birth I am a Sākiya," he [responds to] what was said by the king: "I give you wealth; enjoy it."
Refusing [the offer], he said: "I have gone forth from that family; I do not long for sensual pleasures.

For if I were to long for sensual pleasures, I would not have abandoned such a family—endowed with wealth and heroism, and filled with eighty-two thousand heroic men—and gone forth; this, it is said, was his intention here.
427. Having thus rejected the king’s words, he spoke next, showing the cause for his own going forth:
“Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, and having seen renunciation as security. This should be connected with the phrase “I have gone forth.
In this context, *daṭṭhū* means “having seen. The rest here, as well as whatever was [stated] in the preceding verses, is as follows... [end of fragment].
It should be understood that all those points have already been examined and are not further analyzed here because their meaning is self-evident.
Having thus stated the reason for his own renunciation, the king, desiring to depart for the sake of striving (*padhāna*), addressed the king, saying: "I shall go for the sake of striving;
herein my mind finds delight. Its meaning is this: O Great King, because I have seen renunciation as security...

“Having gone forth, I shall therefore go for the sake of striving, aspiring toward that ultimate renunciation—the deathless state of Nibbāna—which is the foremost and preeminent among all phenomena; my mind delights in this striving, not in sensual pleasures.
When this was said, it is said that the king spoke to the Bodhisatta: “Venerable sir, I have heard this before regarding King Suddhodana...”
“It is said that Prince Siddhattha, having seen the four omens, will go forth and become a Buddha.
Therefore, venerable sir, seeing your resolute intention, I am confident that you will surely attain Buddhahood.
It would be well, venerable sir, if after attaining Buddhahood, you would be the first to enter my realm.”
The commentary on the Pabbajjā-sutta from the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā within the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā is completed. 2.
Commentary on the Padhāna-sutta.
428. This is the *Padhāna-sutta* (The Discourse on Exertion), beginning with the words, "I am one intent upon exertion. What is its origin?
After the Venerable Ānanda had concluded the *Pabbajjā-sutta* with the verse, "I shall go forth for the sake of exertion;
my mind delights therein," the Blessed One, while seated in the Gandhakuṭi, reflected: "For six years, desiring exertion, I performed ascetic practices. That..."
"Today I shall speak to the bhikkhus. Then, having emerged from the fragrant chamber and sat upon the Buddha-seat, he began with the words "Me, who am intent on striving," and delivered this sutta.
In that context, he refers to himself alone by both terms: "me" (*maṃ*) and "intent on striving" (*padhānapahitattaṃ*). "Intent on striving" means for the sake of Nibbāna.
"Whose mind was directed [toward it] or who had surrendered their own person. The phrase "toward the river Nerañjarā" indicates a defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).
For the river Nerañjarā is the defining characteristic because of its preeminent power to purify. For this very reason, the locative case is used here.
However, the meaning is "by the river Nerañjarā," which is to say, "on the bank of the Nerañjarā. "Viparakkamma" means "exceedingly."

"Having exerted effort": *jhāyantaṃ* means one who is devoted to breathless meditation (*appāṇakajjhāna*). "For the attainment of security from bondage" (*yogakkhemassa pattiyā*) means for the sake of reaching Nibbāna, which is secure from the four bonds (*yoga*).
(429) "Namuci" is Māra; for he does not release gods or humans who wish to depart from his domain, creating obstacles [on their way].
He causes them [to suffer], therefore he is called "Namuci. "Speaking words of compassion" means speaking words endowed with sympathy.
"Approached while speaking"—this is self-evident. But why did he approach? It is said that one day the Great Being thought:
"One who constantly seeks food remains dependent on life; and it is not possible for one dependent on life..."
“...in order to attain the Deathless. Thereupon, he applied himself to the cutting off of food, and because of that, he became emaciated and ill-favored.
Then Māra, thinking, “This man is performing such a terrible asceticism because he does not know whether this is the path to enlightenment or not;
perhaps he might transcend my domain,” became afraid and approached with the thought, “I shall stop him by saying this and that. For this very reason, it was said:
“You are thin and disfigured; death is near for you.
Having spoken thus, and further making known to him the proximity of his own death, he said: “Death is a thousandth part [of your life];
one part remains of your life. The meaning of this is: that which has a thousand parts is a “thousand-parted” (*sahassabhāga*). What is it? [It is your life.]

“*Maraṇassa paccayo*” (the condition for death) is the remainder of the text. “*Eko aṃso*” means one part. This is what is meant: this thousandth part of yours, consisting of breathless meditation and so forth, is the condition for your death;
from that, however, only one part remains for your life. Thus, death is close at hand for you.
Having thus made known the proximity of death, he then spoke to encourage him toward life: “Live...”
"O, life is better! If it is asked, "In what way is it better? [the answer is]: "While living, you will perform meritorious deeds.
Then, demonstrating the meritorious deeds approved by himself, he said: "And while you practice the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
In this context, "holy life" refers to the periodic abstinence from sexual intercourse, which is what ascetics (*tāpasa*) practice.
"Juhato" means "of one who is sacrificing. The rest here is self-evident. 432.
However, he spoke this half-stanza beginning with "A difficult path" (*duggo maggo*) in order to generate a sense of urgency for striving (*padhāna-vicchanda*).

In that context, it is "difficult" (*duggo*) because it must be traversed with difficulty due to the profundity of the breathless meditative absorption (*appāṇaka-jjhāna*) and so forth; it is "hard to do" (*dukkaro*) because it must be performed by one whose body and mind are afflicted; and [it is hard] because of death occurring in close proximity.
The meaning should be understood thus: it is "difficult to attain" because it cannot be reached even by such [a person].

From this point on, while Māra was reciting these verses, the half-verse beginning "He stood in the presence of the Buddha" was spoken by the compilers of the collection (*saṅgītikāra*). Some say that the entire verse was [spoken by them].
However, it was the Blessed One himself who spoke all of this here, presenting himself as if he were another.
"This is what was said regarding such a kind of matter"—this is our interpretation. In that context, *aṭṭhā* means "he stood. The rest is self-evident. 433.

Regarding the sixth verse, in the phrase "for the sake of which purpose," the intended meaning is: "O Evil One, you have come here for your own sake by creating obstacles for others. The rest is self-evident. 434.

Rejecting the statement, "While living, you shall perform meritorious deeds," he spoke this verse beginning with "not even a tiny bit. In that context, "by merit" refers to the merit spoken of by Māra, which leads one back into the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The rest is self-evident.
435. Now, referring to the words, "Your life is at one end," he spoke this verse beginning with "There is faith" in order to terrify Māra.
The intention here is as follows: "O Māra, were there anyone who lacked faith in the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace;
or even if possessing faith, were indolent; or even if possessing faith and being energetic, were lacking in wisdom;"
While you might look splendid if you were merely asking after my life, I possess unwavering faith (*okappana-saddhā*) in the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace;
likewise, I possess energy (*vīriya*) characterized by tireless physical and mental exertion, as well as wisdom (*paññā*) comparable to a thunderbolt.
Why, then, do you ask after the life of one such as me, who is thus self-resolute and possessed of the highest aspiration?
"Why do you ask about my life? "And wisdom is mine. Here, by the word "and," mindfulness and concentration are also included.
This being so, since they reach Nibbāna by means of these five faculties, why do you ask me—who am thus resolute—whether I still live, when I am not lacking even one of them?
Is it not said: "A single day of life for one who has aroused energy is better"?
"Strong. For the wise one who meditates, seeing the arising and passing away [of formations].
(436–8) Having thus intimidated Māra, he spoke the triad of verses beginning with "Even of rivers... to show the state of his own body and mind. This is evident in its meaning;
however, this is the explanation of its underlying intention: that which has arisen in my body through the force of the energy of breathless meditation (*appāṇaka-jhāna*).
The wind blows, drying up even the currents of rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the world;
why then would it not dry up my blood, which is no more than four nāḷis, as I am thus resolute?
Not only does my blood dry up, but along with that drying blood, the bile residing within the body—whether bound or unbound—is also dried up.
The phlegm that covers what has been eaten, drunk, and so forth is only about four finger-breadths thick;
furthermore, the urine and the nutritive essence (*ojā*) likewise dry up. As these dry up, even the muscles waste away.
As my flesh thus gradually wastes away, my mind becomes even more serene; it does not falter on account of that. You, therefore—
Not understanding such a state of mind, and seeing only the physical body, you say, "You are thin and ill-favored; death is near for you.
Not only does my mind find confidence, but moreover, mindfulness, wisdom, and concentration abide within me; there is not even the slightest negligence, delusion, or distraction of mind.
As I dwell thus, there is no instance of any ascetics or brahmins who, in the past, future, or present,
experience self-inflicted pains that can serve as a comparison for the supreme pain I have attained.
Just as others, when touched by suffering, find relief in pleasure— cold after heat, heat after cold, or food after hunger— [so too is my state].
The mind of those afflicted by thirst longs for water; but my mind does not long for even a single one of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"Oh, that I might eat fine food and lie down in comfort"—my mind has never arisen in such a manner. See, Māra, the purity of this being!

439–41. Having thus demonstrated his own purity, and in order to shatter the desire of Māra—who had arrived thinking, "I shall turn him back"—the Blessed One recited the six verses beginning with "Lust is your first army," after describing Māra’s host and showing that he was unconquered by it.

Therein, because from the very beginning, while beings are still householders, the defilements of lust (kilesakāmā) delude them regarding sensual objects (vatthukāmā), [the Blessed One] said this having overcome them.
In those who have gone forth into the homeless life, either in remote lodgings or in various other superior wholesome states, a lack of delight arises.
And this has been said: “For one who has gone forth, friend, it is difficult to find delight.
Then, because their livelihood is dependent on others, hunger and thirst afflict them; and being afflicted by that, the craving for seeking arises.
It fatigues the mind; then, for those whose minds are fatigued, sloth and torpor descend.
Consequently, for those who fail to attain distinction while dwelling in dwelling-places in remote forest and jungle retreats that are difficult to master, a fearful apprehension arises.
As they dwell there, filled with suspicion and dread, yet finding delight in the flavor of seclusion for a long time, [the following occurs].
“Could this not be the path?”—thus doubt arises regarding the practice;
having dispelled that, as they dwell [on], pride, disparagement, and rigidity arise due to the attainment of even a slight distinction.
Having dispelled those as well, as they dwell [on], gain, honor, and fame arise based on a further superior attainment. Being infatuated with gain and the rest...
Displaying counterfeit dharmas and having attained false fame, they stand therein and exalt themselves by means of birth and other such factors while disparaging others;
therefore, desire and the rest should be understood as being like the first army and so forth.
Having thus pointed out these ten kinds of armies, because they are possessed of dark qualities (kaṇhadhamma), they belong to the Dark One (kaṇha).
It conduces to the benefit of Namuci; therefore, identifying it as "your army," he said:
"This, O Namuci, is your army, the assailant of Kaṇha. In this context, "assailant" means that which slays and crushes ascetics and brahmins;
the meaning is that it creates obstacles. A coward does not conquer it, but having conquered it, one obtains happiness.
Thus, a man who is not a hero, being full of attachment for his body and life, does not conquer your army;

but a hero conquers it, and having conquered, he attains the happiness of the Path and the happiness of the Fruit. And because he obtains such happiness, therefore I too, desiring happiness, shall likewise carry this *muñja* grass.
These men who engage in battle do not retreat. Their own...
To signify their state of non-retreat, they bind muñja grass to their heads, banners, or weapons;
know that I carry this as well. "Fie on my life, defeated by your army!
Therefore, hold me thus: death in battle is better for me than a life lived in defeat—that life by which one is defeated."
"Let me live; therefore, rather than living while acting as an obstacle to those who have entered the right path, it is better for me to die in battle"—this is the meaning.

Why is death better? Because: "In this [battle], some recluses and brahmins... well-vowed ones," having plunged into, sunk into, and entered here—into your army which culminates in self-exaltation and the disparagement of others, beginning with sensual pleasures—they are no longer seen, on account of their virtue and other qualities.
They do not shine forth by means of their virtues; they are as if entered into darkness.

Being thus submerged, even if they occasionally emerge like a person who has been diving and then surfaces—thinking, for example, "Excellent is faith," and so forth—even then, because they are overwhelmed by that army, they do not know that path which leads to the security of Nibbāna; indeed, all of them...
"By which path the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others go, O you of good vows. Having heard this verse, Māra departed without saying anything further.
But when he had gone, the Great Being, not attaining any distinction whatsoever through that practice of austerities, [reflected:]...
In due course, having reflected on such thoughts as, "Could there perhaps be another path to enlightenment?", he partook of solid food and regained his strength.
On the full moon day of the month of Visākha, he consumed the milk-rice offered by Sujātā early in the morning.
Having sat for his midday rest in the Bhadravana grove and spent the day there developing the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), at the time of evening...
Having gone toward the Great Seat of Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa) and scattered the eight handfuls of grass given by Sotthiya at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he—
honored with great respect by the deities of the ten thousand world-systems— declared:
“Let there remain only skin, sinew, and bone;”
"Let the flesh and blood in my body dry up entirely"—
having thus resolved upon the fourfold energy and made the vow, "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained Buddhahood," he sat upon the invincible throne.
Knowing this, Māra the Evil One [thought], "Today Siddhattha has made his vow..."
“Having sat down, his promise must be repelled this very day!

Thus, having raised up Māra’s army—extending from the seat of enlightenment as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountains, twelve yojanas in width and nine yojanas high—he mounted the royal elephant Girimekhala, who was one hundred and fifty yojanas in size;
then, manifesting a thousand arms and seizing various weapons, he cried out, “Seize him! Seize him!”
Saying, "Strike! Hit! he conjured up showers of the kind described in the Āḷavaka Sutta;
when these reached the Great Man, they turned out exactly as described therein.
Then, having struck the elephant on the temple with his adamantine goad, he led it near the Great Man and said, "Arise, sir Siddhattha, from your cross-legged posture. The Great Man—
Having said, "I shall not rise, O Māra," he looked all around at that army and spoke these verses beginning with "Samantā dhajiniṃ.
Therein, "dhajini" means an army. "Yuttaṃ" means deployed. "Savāhanaṃ" means accompanied by the Nāga king Girimekhala.
"Paccuggacchāmi" means I shall go forward to meet it; however, this shall be by means of my spiritual power (tejo) alone, and not with my physical body. Why?
"Do not move me from my place" means: "O Māra, do not shake me from this place, the invincible throne.
"He does not prevail" means he is unable to endure it, or he does not overcome [the Buddha]. "A raw vessel" refers to an earthenware pot that has not yet been fired.
"With a stone" means with a rock. The rest here is self-evident.

447–8. Now, demonstrating: “Having shattered this army of Māra, thereafter, having won the battle and attained the consecration as a King of Dhamma, I shall do this,” he said, “having brought [thought] under control. Therein, “having brought thought under control” means:
by abandoning all wrong intention through the cultivation of the Path and causing only right intention to proceed, one has brought thought under control.

"And with mindfulness well-established": having established my own mindfulness well in the four places, such as the body and so forth, and thus having brought my intention under control, with mindfulness firmly established, I shall wander from country to country, training many disciples among the various classes of gods and humans.
Then, those being trained by me, being heedful... [as before] ...they shall not grieve; the intention is that they shall reach that very nectar of Nibbāna.
449–51. Then Māra, having heard these verses, said: “Seeing such a faction as this, do you not fear, O Bhikkhu?
“Yes, Māra, I do not fear. “Why do you not fear? “Because of the performance of the perfections of giving and the other merits.
“Who knows that you have performed the acts of giving and so forth? “What need is there for a witness here, O Evil One? Furthermore, in this very [place]...”
"By the power of the gift I gave when I was Vessantara, this very great earth—trembling in seven ways and six manners—is itself the witness.
When he had spoken thus, the great earth, bounded by the waters, shook and let out a terrifying sound;
hearing which, Māra, like one struck by a thunderbolt, became terrified and lowered his banner.

He fled together with his retinue. Then the Great Being, having realized the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) over the course of three watches of the night, at the break of dawn uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*):
“Through many a birth in saṃsāra... [I have wandered on]... now I have reached the destruction of craving. Māra, coming upon the sound of the utterance, thought:
“This one claims, ‘I am a Buddha. Come now, I shall follow him to observe his conduct.”
Thinking, "If he should commit any lapse with body or speech, I shall harass him," [Māra] followed the Bodhisatta for six years while he was on the stage of a bodhisatta;
then, when the Buddha had attained Buddhahood, he followed him for one year.
Seeing no lapse whatsoever in the Blessed One, he uttered these verses of reproach: "For seven years... and so forth.
In this context, *otāra* means a flaw or an opening. *Nādhigacchissanti* means they did not find [such a flaw].
*Medavaṇṇaṃ* means resembling a lump of fat. *Anupariyagā* means he went all around. *Muduṃ* means soft.
*Vindema* means we might find or attain. *Assādanā* means the state of being delicious. *Vāyasetto* means the crow from here. The rest here is self-evident.
This is the construction [of the meaning]: For seven years I followed the Blessed One, seeking an opening, never leaving him even for a single step.
Yet, despite following him in this way, I did not find an opening.
Just as a crow, perceiving a stone that has the color of fat to be fat, pecks at it with its beak on one side but finds no flavor; so too was it for me.
“Perhaps we might find something soft here; perhaps there might be some flavor from this,” thinking thus, he pierced it all around and went about it in every direction;
but finding no flavor anywhere, he became disillusioned, thinking, “This is just a stone,” and departed.
In the very same way, I went about piercing the Blessed One on all sides with the tip of my own small wisdom-mouth, beginning with his bodily actions and so forth.
“Perhaps we might find some degree of softness in someone whose bodily conduct and so forth are not entirely pure; perhaps there might be some gratification from such a source.
But now, finding no gratification, they—like a crow striking against a rock—have become disillusioned with Gotama;
having struck against Gotama, they have become disillusioned with him and have departed. It is said that for Māra, who spoke thus, seven years of effort were in vain.
Relying upon it, a powerful sorrow arose within him. As his limbs and members failed from despondency, his lute named Beluvapaṇḍu fell from his armpit.
That lute, when once played by skilled musicians, would emit a sweet sound for four months;
it was that very lute which Sakka had given to Pañcasikha. Even as it was falling, he did not perceive it. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“While he was overcome with grief, his lute slipped from his armpit;
then that dejected yakkha vanished right there.
Some say this was spoken by the compilers of the collection, but we do not accept this.
The commentary on the *Padhāna-sutta* in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, which is part of the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*), is completed. 3.
The commentary on the *Subhāsita-sutta*.
"Thus have I heard" refers to a well-spoken discourse (*subhāsita-sutta*). Its origin lies in the Master’s own inclination;

for the Blessed One is fond of what is well-spoken, and wishing to restrain beings from the practice of ill-spoken words by demonstrating his own practice of well-spoken words, he spoke this discourse.
In that context, "Thus have I heard," and so forth, are the words of the compilers. Therein, "In that place... [and so on].
"Bhagavā... pe... 'Bhadante'—those monks"—this much is new; the rest is exactly as previously stated. Therefore, for the purpose of explaining the new portion, this is said:

"Therein" (*tatra*) is an indication of place and time. For it indicates that at whatever time he dwells, it is "at that time," and in whichever monastery he dwells, it is "in that monastery. Or else, it indicates the place and time appropriate for what is to be spoken.
For the Blessed One does not preach the Dhamma at an improper place or time. In this regard, the passage beginning, “It is not the right time, Bāhiya,” serves as proof.
The particle *kho* is a mere filler (*padapūraṇa*) or a particle used for emphasis or to indicate a specific time. *Bhagavā* is an indication of one who is honored by the world.
*Bhikkhu* is an indication of a person fit to hear the discourse. *Āmantesi* means he addressed, spoke to, or called out to.
"Bhikkhave" is an expression indicating a form of address. It is spoken because [the Buddha] has achieved the qualities such as the habit of begging for alms.
By this, while illustrating their mode of livelihood—which is practiced by those who are neither inferior nor superior—he effects a restraint against both arrogance and dejection.
