And with this word "Bhikkhave," [he speaks] with speech preceded by the casting of a glance from eyes that are gentle and cool due to the expansion of compassion.
Placing them face-to-face with themselves, they generate in them a desire to hear by means of that very speech which indicates their own desire to speak;
and by that same speech in the sense of an address, they enjoin them toward careful hearing and attention.
For the success of the Dispensation depends upon careful hearing and attention. This is so even though other gods and humans are present.
If it is asked why he addressed the monks alone, it is because they were the eldest, the most excellent, and those who were constantly present and near.
For this teaching of the Dhamma is common to the entire assembly, not intended for individuals alone.

Among the assembly, the monks are the eldest because they were the first to arise [in the dispensation], and they are the most excellent because, from the time they first entered the homeless life, they followed the conduct of the Teacher and received the entirety of the Dispensation.
*Ca*: Because they were seated nearby, being in the presence of the Teacher; because they were always in attendance, being within the sphere of the Teacher’s proximity.
Therefore, while teaching the Dhamma common to the entire assembly, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus alone.
Furthermore, he addressed them alone because they were the proper vessels for this discourse, owing to their possession of the practice as it has been instructed. *Bhadante* (Venerable Sir).
This is a designation for respect. "Those monks" refers to those whom the Blessed One addressed; thus addressing the Blessed One, they replied to him.
"By four factors" means by four causes or constituent parts. For the four—abstaining from false speech and so forth—are [the factors] of well-spoken speech.
The causes. The four factors beginning with truthful speech (*saccavacana*) are the [causes]; and the word *aṅga* is used in the sense of a cause.
The term *catūhi* is in the ablative case, while in the sense of a factor it is in the instrumental case. *Samannāgatā* means fully possessed, occurring, and endowed.
*Vācā* refers to the speech of utterance; that which is described in such passages as "speech, voice, expression" and "gentle, pleasing to the ear," and so forth.
It comes as follows: first, there is the intimation expressed thus, "Whatever action is performed by speech";
second, there is the abstinence expressed thus, "That which is the refraining from and desisting from the four types of verbal misconduct... this is called right speech";
and third, there is the volition expressed thus, "O monks, harsh speech, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently repeated, leads to rebirth in hell. Thus it comes as "speech."
That [speech] is not intended here. Why? Because it would not have been spoken [in this context]. "Well-spoken" means it is properly spoken; by this, it indicates that it brings about benefit.
"Not ill-spoken" means it is not poorly spoken; by this, it indicates that it does not bring about harm.

"Blameless" means it is free from faults such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which are reckoned as blameworthy; by this, it indicates the purity of its cause and the absence of the aforementioned defects.
It illuminates. And "blameless" means free from reproach; by this, he illuminates her perfection in every respect.
"By the wise" means by the learned; by this, he shows that fools are no standard in matters of blame or praise.
"By which four? is a question arising from a desire to speak. "Here" means in this teaching. "O bhikkhus" refers to those...
"Desirous of speaking" refers to the act of addressing [the Buddha]. "Bhikkhu" is a designation pointing to a person who speaks with the aforementioned manner of speech.
"He speaks only what is well-spoken" is a statement indicating one of the four factors of speech within a teaching that is focused on the person.
"Not what is ill-spoken" is a prohibition against speaking the opposite of that very factor of speech. By this, [it is implied that] even false speech and so forth...
By saying "never should it be spoken," he negates wrong view. By the phrase "not ill-spoken," he indicates the abandoning of wrong speech;
by the phrase "well-spoken," he indicates the characteristic of speech that should be uttered by one who has abandoned wrong speech.
Likewise [he teaches] the non-doing of evil and the undertaking of what is wholesome. However, for the purpose of indicating the factors, that which should not be spoken was mentioned previously.
He says only what ought to be said without having descended [into unwholesome states]. This same method applies to the phrases "only the Dhamma," and so forth.
And here, by the phrase "he speaks only what is well-spoken, not what is ill-spoken," speech that creates harmony and is free from the fault of malicious talebearing (pisuṇa) is expressed;
by the phrase "he speaks only the Dhamma, not non-Dhamma," speech that is not devoid of the Dhamma and is free from the fault of harshness (pharusa) is expressed.
The word "wise" has been stated; by the other two [terms], pleasant and truthful speech—devoid of harshness and frivolity—is expressed.
Then, with the words "By these, indeed," etc., he concludes that speech while demonstrating those factors directly.
And here, specifically, by saying, "Monks, speech endowed with these four factors is well-spoken," he [concludes].

When others consider speech endowed with constituent parts such as propositions and so forth, with words such as nouns and so forth, and with excellences such as gender, number, case, tense, and grammatical relation to be "well-spoken," [the Buddha] refutes that from the standpoint of the Dhamma.
For even speech endowed with constituent parts and the like is indeed ill-spoken if it is possessed of slander and so forth, because it brings harm to oneself and others. By these...
However, if [a verse] possesses four qualities, even if it is included in a foreign language or included in the songs of a water-carrier girl,
it is nevertheless well-spoken because it brings about mundane and supramundane benefit and happiness. For example,
there is a song concerning birth, aging, and death composed in the Sinhalese language by a Sinhalese girl guarding a crop on the side of a path in the island of Sri Lanka.
The illustration here is that about sixty insight-practicing bhikkhus, while traveling along the road after hearing [the song] being sung, attained arahantship.
Likewise, a bhikkhu named Tissa, who had begun the practice of insight, was walking near a lotus pond;
as he went, he kept breaking off lotuses from the lotus pond—
“Like a red lotus that has blossomed at dawn and is withered by the light of the sun, so too are beings who have attained human birth crushed by the force of old age.

Upon hearing this song from the maidservant, he attained *arahantship*. Furthermore, during the interval between Buddhas, a certain man came from the forest with his seven sons and saw a woman pounding rice with a pestle.
“This is worn away by old age, dependent on withered skin and hide;
it is shattered by death, the bait for the devouring of Mortality.
This is an abode of worms, filled with various kinds of filth.”
"This is a vessel for impurity; it is like the trunk of a plantain tree.
Having heard this song, he attained *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) together with his sons. Others, too, reached the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*) through such means;
this is an illustration. It is not surprising that the Blessed One, being skilled in discerning the underlying tendencies (*āsayānusaya*), [said]: "All..."
Having heard the verses spoken in such a manner as "formations are impermanent," five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship;
and many other gods and humans did so upon hearing discourses connected with the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth.
Thus, speech endowed with these four factors, even if it falls within the language of barbarians or is contained within the songs of a water-carrier girl, [is still Dhamma].

Even so, it should be understood as "well-spoken. And precisely because it is well-spoken, it is blameless and irreproachable for wise sons of noble family who seek the meaning and rely on the meaning rather than relying on the letter.
"This the Blessed One said" means that the Blessed One spoke this definition of what constitutes well-spoken speech. Having said this, the Sugata [spoke] further.
"Having spoken this, the Teacher," it is said; having stated this characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), the Teacher then spoke this other [verse] as well.

Having shown the verse now to be recited, the compilers of the collection (*saṅgītikāraka*) said all of this. In that context, the word "furthermore" (*aparam*) is used with reference to the phrasing of the verse composition.
That [verse] is twofold: [it serves] for the assembly that has arrived later, for the sake of hearing, listening closely, retaining, strengthening [the memory], and so forth.

Or, it may be intended as that which illuminates the meaning of that [preceding statement]. Furthermore, there is that which illuminates a specific meaning by way of illustrating a point previously omitted for some reason, such as in the passage beginning, "For when a man is born, an axe is born in his mouth.
However, in this instance, it is only that which illuminates the meaning of that [preceding statement].
453. "Those who are peaceful" refers to the Buddhas and others, for they praise well-spoken words as "supreme" and "best.
The sequence "the second, the third, and the fourth," however, is stated in accordance with the order previously indicated.
At the conclusion of the verses, the Elder Vaṅgīsa gained confidence in the well-spoken words of the Blessed One.
Thus, in order to show both the manner in which [Sāriputta] expressed his confidence and the words the Blessed One spoke, the compilers of the collection said, "Then the Venerable... and so forth.
In that context, *paṭibhāti maṃ* means "it occurs to me" or "my portion is revealed. *Paṭibhātu taṃ* means "may it occur to you" or "may your portion be revealed.
*Sāruppāhi* means "with appropriate" or "suitable" [words]. *Abhitthavi* means "he praised."

454. "One should not cause distress" means one should not cause distress through remorse. "One should not harm" means one should not injure by causing mutual division. "That indeed is speech"—that speech is exclusively well-spoken. To this extent, he praises the Blessed One for his non-divisive speech (*apisuṇavācā*). 455.
"Welcomed with joy" means having gone toward them with a joyful heart, welcomed and delighted.
"Speaking that which, taking nothing evil, is dear to others"—speaking such words that are not dear, not unlovely, and not repulsive to others, while taking no evil [for oneself].
Not taking up harsh words, he speaks only speech that is pleasant, sweet in both meaning and phrasing;
the sense is that one should speak only such pleasant speech. With this verse, he praised the Blessed One with pleasant words.
456. "Amata" means like the deathless (ambrosia) because of its sweetness. And it has been said: "Truth, indeed, is the sweetest of tastes."
Or it is "deathless" because it has Nibbāna as its condition for immortality. "This Dhamma is ancient":
this which is called true speech is an ancient Dhamma, a practice, and a tradition; for this alone was the habit of the ancients, and they did not speak falsely.
Therefore it was said: "In truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma, the good have stood firm. Therein, because of being established in truth...

Thus, they should be understood as being established in both their own welfare and the welfare of others. And because they are established in welfare, it should be known that they are likewise established in the Dhamma.
Alternatively, these two [terms] should be understood as qualifiers of "truth" (sacca). They are established in truth—of what kind?
In welfare and in the Dhamma; for, since it does not depart from the welfare of others, it brings about welfare without obstruction.

This is what is meant. And although it does not cause obstruction, because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is called "Dhamma"; thus, it is said that it accomplishes only a purpose that is in accordance with the Dhamma.
With this verse, he praised the Blessed One by means of a declaration of truth.
457. "Secure" (khemam) means fearless and free from calamity. If one asks for what reason, it is because of the attainment of Nibbāna, which is the making an end of suffering.
Because it leads to the extinction of defilements (*kilesanibbāna*) and conduces to the making of an end to the suffering of the round of existence—this is the meaning.

Alternatively, because the Buddha speaks words that are secure (*khema*) for the sake of the two elements of Nibbāna—namely, for the attainment of Nibbāna and for the making of an end to suffering—by revealing the secure path, those words are indeed the supreme among all words. Thus, that speech is the best of all speeches.

"Best" (seṭṭha) is how the meaning should be understood here. By means of this verse, praising the Blessed One with words of counsel, he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship;
this is the commentary on the previously unexplained words. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
[From] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Subhāsita-sutta of the Suttanipāta-ṭīkā is finished.
4. Commentary on the Pūraḷāsa-sutta (the Sundarikabhāradvāja-sutta).
"Thus have I heard" begins the Pūraḷāsa-sutta. What is its origin? At the conclusion of his post-meal duties, the Blessed One, with the eye of a Buddha...
While surveying the world, he saw that the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja was endowed with the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship.

Knowing that "when I go there, a conversation will arise; then, having heard the teaching of the Dhamma at the conclusion of that talk, this brahmin will go forth and reach Arahatship," he went there, initiated the conversation, and spoke this Sutta.

In this regard, the passage beginning with "Thus have I heard" and so forth is the speech of the compilers of the collection. The passage beginning with "Of what caste was he? and so forth belongs to that brahmin;
the passage beginning with "I am not a brahmin" and so forth belongs to the Blessed One. Having combined all of these together, it is called the "Pūraḷāsa Sutta.

What is stated therein should be understood in the same manner as already explained; we shall, however, comment on what has not yet been stated, and that only where the meaning is not immediately obvious.
"Without uttering words. Regarding "among the Kosalans": the Kosalans were royal princes belonging to a particular province.
The single province where they resided is, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhisadda*), called "the Kosalans. [The phrase means] "in that province, among the Kosalans. However, some say:
"Because in the past, having heard that the royal prince Mahāpanāda did not even so much as smile upon seeing various theatrical performances and the like, the King..."
He commanded, "Whoever makes my son laugh, I shall adorn him with all manner of ornaments.
Then, discarding their ploughs, a great multitude of people gathered.
Although those men displayed various games and diversions for more than seven years, they were unable to make him laugh. Thereupon, Sakka sent a celestial dancer, who performed a divine dance.
Having shown them this, he made them laugh. Then those people departed toward their respective dwelling places.
On the way back, seeing friends, relatives, and others, they exchanged greetings, saying, "Is it well with you, sir? Is it well with you, sir?
Therefore, because of that sound "kusala," that region is called "Kosala."
They describe it thus: "On the bank of the Sundarikā" means on the bank of the river named Sundarikā.

"At that time" means at the time when the Blessed One, desiring to guide that brahmin, went and sat at the foot of a tree on the bank of that river, dwelling in the posture known as sitting with his head covered.
The brahmin named Sundarikabhāradvāja lived on the bank of that river and maintained a sacrificial fire;
since Bhāradvāja was his clan name (*gotra*), he is called by that name. "He maintains the fire" means he kindles it by casting oblations (*āhuti*) into it.
"He attends to the fire-sacrifice" (*aggihuttaṃ paricarati*) means he honors the fire-sanctuary by sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, making offerings, and so forth. Who indeed...?
"Let him eat this remnant of the offering. It is said that when the brahmin had offered the oblation into the fire and saw what remained of the milk-rice, he thought:
"The milk-rice that was placed in the fire has been eaten by Mahābrahmā; but this remnant still remains.
If I were to give it only to a brahmin born from the mouth of Brahmā, then my son would be eating together with his father."
"He would be satisfied, and the path leading to the Brahma-world would be well-cleansed; come now, I shall search for a brahmin.
Then, rising from his seat to see a brahmin, he looked toward the four quarters, thinking, "Who indeed might eat this choice offering?"
"At the foot of a certain tree" means at the foot of the best tree in that grove. "Covered up to his head" means with his body covered together with his head.

But why did the Blessed One do this? Was he unable to ward off the falling snow and the cold wind despite possessing the strength known as Nārāyaṇa? There is a reason for this; for the Buddhas are not entirely...
They were indeed attending to their bodies; however, the Blessed One did this for the purpose of initiating a conversation, thinking:
“When the brahmin arrives, I shall uncover my head; seeing me, how will the brahmin speak? Then, following the course of his speech, I shall teach him the Dhamma.
Having seen [him], with his left hand... he approached him. It is said that upon seeing the Blessed One, the brahmin...
Thinking, "This man has covered his head with his robe and has been devoted to striving all night;
having given him the water for the guest-offering, I shall give him the remains of the sacrificial food," he approached him while still perceiving him to be a brahmin.
As soon as the head was uncovered, seeing the hairline, he said, "This honorable man is shaven-headed; this one is a shaveling. Then, even more clearly...
Looking at him and not seeing even a small tuft of hair, he looked down upon him and said, "A shaveling. For such was the view of those brahmins.
"From there" means from that place where he stood and saw him; "shavelings" means they have their heads shaved for some reason.

Regarding the phrase "I am not a brahmin," here the particle *na* is used in the sense of negation, while the particle *no* is used in the sense of emphasis, as in "not equal to us" (*na no samam*) and so forth.
By this he shows: "I am not thus a brahmin. "I am not a prince" means I am not a khattiya by name.
"Nor am I a vessa" means I am not a vessa either. "Nor am I anyone else" means I am not even a *sudda* or a *caṇḍāla*.
In this way, he categorically rejects the conventional usage of talk regarding birth. Why? For those who have entered the homeless life are like rivers that have reached the great ocean.
Noble sons abandon their former names and clans. In this regard, the *Pahārādasutta* is the supporting proof.
Having thus rejected the doctrine of birth, revealing himself as he truly is, he said: "Having fully understood the clan of worldlings, I wander the world possessing nothing.
If it is asked, "How did he fully understand the clan?"—the Blessed One [did so] by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*).
He fully understood the five aggregates, and when those were fully understood, his lineage (*gotta*) was likewise fully understood.

Because of the absence of the encumbrances of lust and so forth, he is "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*); having known through wisdom (*mantā*), he conducts himself with bodily actions and the rest that follow after knowledge.
Therefore it is said: "His lineage... in the world. By *mantā* is meant wisdom (*paññā*); he conducts himself by means of that. For this very reason it is said: "Wisdom..."
“I wander in the world”—this was said by shortening the word through the influence of *chandasa* (poetic license).
Having thus revealed himself, he now spoke the words beginning with “wearing a patched robe...

[down to] ...the question of lineage,” in order to level a reproach against the brahmin, saying: “Even upon seeing such a coarse outward sign as this, you do not know what should or should not be asked.”
And here, in the sense of being composed of joined pieces, all three robes are intended by the term "saṅghāṭī"; he wears and puts on those, thus he is "one who wears the saṅghāṭī.

"Ageha" means without a house; the intention is that he is free from craving (nittaṇha). As for the dwelling places of the Blessed One, they were of many kinds in the Jeta Grove: the Great Fragrant Chamber (Mahāgandhakuṭi), the Karerimaṇḍalamāḷa, the Kosambakuṭi, the Candanamāla, and so forth.

With reference to him, [the statement] is not appropriate. "One whose hair has been removed" (*nivuttakeso*) means one from whom the hair has been taken away; it is said that his hair and beard have been shaved off.
"One who is fully extinguished" (*abhinibbutatto*) means one whose mind’s fever has become exceedingly calmed, or one whose mind is guarded.

"Unstained here by youths" (*alippamāno idha māṇavehi*) means, because of having abandoned attachment to requisites, he is unstained by humans, unassociated with them, and entirely secluded. "I am not fit... (*akallaṃ maṃ*)...
"O Brahmin, as for me who thus wear the outer robe...
[and so on] ...being unsullied here among these young brahmins—since I have abandoned my former name and clan upon going forth, it is unbecoming for you, O Brahmin, to ask me about my clan.
When this was said, the Brahmin, seeking to release himself from the reproach, said: "Indeed, sir, Brahmins ask questions of Brahmins."
“Are you a brahmin?”—in this context, “*brāhmaṇo nu*? means “*brāhmaṇo nu*? (Is it that you are a brahmin?). This is what is being said:

“Sir, I do not ask what is improper. For in our brahminical tradition, when brahmins meet with other brahmins, they inquire about birth and clan, asking such things as: ‘Are you a brahmin? Are you Bhāradvāja?’”
461-2. When this had been said, the Blessed One, in order to soften the brahmin’s mind and to demonstrate his own proficiency in the mantras, said:
“If you say, ‘I am a brahmin’... [etc. ...twenty-four syllables. The meaning of this is:
if you say, “I am a brahmin,” yet you call me a non-brahmin, therefore, sir, [the Sāvitrī]—
“I ask about that which consists of three words and twenty-four syllables; tell that to me.

And here, the Blessed One [spoke] the verse beginning with the Three Refuges—which is the foundation of the three Piṭakas of ultimate meaning, proclaimed by all Buddhas who are ultimate brahmins, and endowed with both meaning and phrasing:
“I go for refuge to the Buddha; I go for refuge to the Dhamma; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.”
He asks this with reference to the noble *Sāvitti* formula: "I go for refuge.

For even if the brahmin were to speak of something else, the Blessed One would certainly have shown its worthlessness by saying, "Brahmin, this is not called the *Sāvitti* in the discipline of the Noble Ones," and would have established him right here. But the brahmin [asks], "I ask about the *Sāvitti*..."

Upon hearing these words—“three feet, twenty-four syllables,” which were uttered with a Brahmā-like voice, expressing the characteristics and phonetic features of the Sāvitrī as established in his own tradition—he thought:
“Surely this ascetic has reached the ultimate conclusion in the Brāhmaṇa tradition;
out of ignorance, I insulted him, thinking, ‘This man is no Brāhmaṇa,’ yet he is a truly noble one who has mastered the mantras, a true Brāhmaṇa indeed.”
Having reached the conclusion, "This is it," he thought, "Well then, let me ask him about the procedure for sacrifice and the procedure for those worthy of offerings.
Asking about that matter, he spoke these three uneven verse-lines: "What is their support... in the world? The meaning of this is as follows:
what is their support, what is their intention, and what do they aspire to—sages, kshatriyas, brahmins, and other men—when [they offer] to the deities?
They performed the sacrifice for the sake of welfare. In the phrase “they performed the sacrifice” (*yaññaṃ akappayiṃsu*), the letter *m* is used as a sandhi-conjunction.
“They performed” (*akappayiṃsu*) means they arranged or carried out [the sacrifice]. “Many” (*puthū*) means numerous;

in various ways by means of gifts of food, drink, and so forth, or in many different forms, the many seers, men, kshatriyas, and brahmins—based on what did they perform the sacrifice? How was it for them?
He asks with the intention that "kamma succeeds.

Then, the Blessed One, explaining that matter to him, spoke these two remaining lines: "When he who has reached the end and is a knower of the Vedas [offers] at the time of sacrifice—of him whose oblation is received, I say that it succeeds.
Therein, "he who has reached the end" (*antagū*) means one who has reached the limit.
The letter *a* replaces the letter *o*, and the letter *da* functions as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*), just as the letter *m* does in such phrases as “*asādhāraṇamaññesan*” and so forth.

This, however, is the meaning: he who is an *antagu* because he has reached the end of the suffering of saṃsāra by means of the three thorough knowledges (*pariññā*), and an *vedagū* because he has gone after piercing through the defilements with the four kinds of knowledge of the paths—that [Buddha] of whom the seers, men, khattiyas, and brahmins...
I say that for a certain person at the time of a sacrifice, whenever any kind of food is presented— even if it be as little as forest leaves,
roots, or fruits— if they obtain an offering, or if they receive some gift to be given away, then that sacrificial act of theirs succeeds,
it prospers, and it becomes of great fruit.

464. Then the brahmin, having heard that teaching of the Blessed One—which was profound through its application to the ultimate truth (*paramattha*), possessed an exceedingly sweet voice, and was endowed with a flavor free from affectation—contemplated his perfection in all virtues as indicated by his physical excellence. Filled with rapture and joy, he spoke the verse beginning with "Addhā hi tassa.
Therein, "iti brāhmaṇo" (thus the brahmin) is the speech of the compilers; the rest [is the verse].
To the brahmin. Its meaning is this: "Surely my sacrifice will succeed today;
this gift to be given will be successful, it will be fulfilled, and it will be of great fruit, since we have seen such a master of knowledge (vedagu) as you.
For you alone are that master of knowledge, and no other. Previously to this...

"But because of the failure to see those like you—possessors of true knowledge (*vedagu*) and those who have reached the further shore—it is others like us who consume what has been prepared for the sacrifice:
the sacrificial cake (*pūraḷāsa*), the boiled rice (*caruka*), and the cakes (*pūva*).
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the brahmin was well-disposed toward him and ready to receive his words, [spoke] so that he...
They become very clear; thus, wishing to reveal the various kinds of those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*), he spoke the verse beginning with "Therefore, then, you.
Its meaning is as follows: "Since you have faith in me, therefore, O Brahmin, come here and ask," saying this while pointing to himself.
Now, the word expressing purpose (*atthena-atthika*) from before this must be connected with the subsequent word.

One who seeks the goal will, while remaining right here, or within this very teaching, find and attain that which is peaceful through the subsiding of the fire of defilements corresponding to that state of seeking the goal; smokeless through the disappearance of the smoke of anger;

“Sumedha, of excellent wisdom, whose taints are destroyed, worthy of offerings. Alternatively, because you have faith in me, therefore, O brahmin, since you are seeking a specific goal, approach and ask.
Thus he spoke, showing himself to be one who is peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, and desireless.
By asking in this way, “Perhaps here you might find Sumedha, whose taints are destroyed and who is worthy of offerings,” [he seeks to know].
In this case, the application [of the terms] should be understood in this way.
Then, practicing according to the instruction, the brahmin said to the Blessed One: "I am devoted to sacrifice...
[etc. ...tell me that. In this context, "sacrifice" (*yañña*), "offering" (*yāga*), and "giving" (*dāna*) are one in meaning. Therefore, "I am devoted to giving," by means of that—
Thus, desiring to give a gift out of a delight in giving, yet not knowing [how], he says: "May your lordship instruct me, who am thus ignorant.

And as for his saying, "While instructing me, please tell me in a straightforward manner where an offering becomes successful," this is how the construction of the meaning should be understood here. There is also a reading: "yathāhutaṃ" (as offered).
467. Then the Blessed One, wishing to speak, said: "In that case... I shall teach you.
And for the sake of instructing him who had lent an ear, he first spoke this verse: "Do not ask about birth. Therein, "do not ask about birth" means:

if you expect a great fruit from your gift by virtue of its being well-offered, do not ask about the birth [of the recipient]. For the investigation of those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇeyya*) is not dependent on birth.

"Birth and conduct": he asks about "conduct," which refers to the various qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth; for this is the basis for investigating those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
Now, explaining that meaning, he provides an illustration: "From wood, indeed, fire is born," and so on. Herein, the intention is this:
in this world, fire is born from wood, yet it does not perform the function of fire merely because it was born from wood such as that of a *sāla* tree.

It is not because it is produced from a source such as a vessel for impurity that fire performs its function; rather, it performs it precisely because it is endowed with its own qualities, such as heat and light.
In the same way, it is not only one born into a brahmin family or similar high castes who is worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), while one born into a *caṇḍāla* family or similar low castes is not;

rather, even one of low birth and one of high birth alike—the sage whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava-muni*), possessed of fortitude, restrained by moral shame (*hirī*), and of noble breeding—is worthy of offerings.
By means of this perfection of qualities, headed by fortitude and moral shame, one who is well-born becomes a supreme object of offerings.
For through fortitude one maintains virtuous qualities, and through moral shame one restrains faults. And it has been said: "For by means of moral shame, the virtuous do not commit evil.
Therefore, I say this to you:
“Do not ask about birth; ask about conduct.
For it is from wood that fire is born.
Even a sage of low birth, if he possesses steadfastness, [is truly noble].”
"He is a noble steed, restrained by a sense of shame.
This is the summary; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the Assalāyana Sutta.
468. Having thus instructed regarding the purification of the four castes, the Blessed One now [explains] where an offering succeeds and how it does so.

And so that this offering may succeed, he spoke the verse beginning with “Tamed by truth” (saccena danto) to demonstrate that meaning. Therein, “by truth” means by the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca).
For one who has attained that is truly tamed; hence he said, “tamed by truth. “Endowed with self-mastery” (damasā upeto) means possessed of the restraint of the sense faculties.
“One who has reached the end of knowledge” (vedantagū) means either one who has gone to the end of the defilements by means of knowledge (veda), or [one who has mastered] the Vedas.
He has reached the end, which is the knowledge of the fourth path. "One who has lived the holy life" (*vūsitabrahmacariyo*) means one who has completed the holy life of the path that was to be lived.

"At the proper time he should offer an oblation to him" means that, having observed both the time when his own property to be given is available and the time when the recipient is present, he should at that time offer, present, and bestow the gift upon such a person worthy of offerings.
469–71. *Kāma* refers to both sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) and defilements (*kilesakāma*). *Susamāhitindriyā* means those whose faculties are well-composed;
it is said that their faculties are undistracted. *Candova rāhuggahaṇā pamuttā*:
just as the moon is released from the grasp of Rāhu, so too are they released from the grasp of defilements—those who shine and blaze exceedingly. *Satā* means endowed with mindfulness.
"Things clung to as 'mine'" means things clung to by craving and views. "472.

Having abandoned sensual pleasures"—from this point onward, he speaks with reference to himself. Therein, "having abandoned sensual pleasures" means having abandoned the sensual pleasures that are defilements.
"Walking having overcome them" means, because they have been abandoned, walking while having overcome the sensual pleasures that are objects. Of birth and death...
The "end" (anta) is called Nibbāna; and he who knows it has realized it by the power of his own wisdom.

"Like a pool of water" refers to these seven great lakes in the Himālayas—namely, Anotatta-daha, Kaṇṇamuṇḍa-daha, Rathakāra-daha, Chaddanta-daha, Kuṇāla-daha, Mandākinī-daha, and Sīhapapāta-daha—which, because they are not touched by the heat of fire or the sun, are eternal.
"Cool" (*sītalā*): one among them is cool like a pool of water because the fever of the defilements has been extinguished.
(473) "Equal" (*sama*) means identical. "By the equals" (*samehi*) refers to Buddhas such as Vipassī and others.

For they are called "equal" due to their perfection of penetration (*paṭivedha*). There is no diversity among them regarding the qualities to be attained through penetration or the faults to be abandoned.
However, there is a difference among them regarding their life-span, lineage, renunciation, striving, and enlightenment.

For they fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) within a minimum limit of four incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya) and a hundred thousand kappas, and within a maximum limit of sixteen incalculable eons and a hundred thousand kappas. This is their distinction.
Difference in duration: they arise at the lower limit during a time when the lifespan is one hundred years, and at the upper limit during a time when the lifespan is one hundred thousand years.
This is their difference in lifespan. They arise either in a khattiya family or in a brāhmaṇa family.
This is their difference in clan. They are either tall, measuring eighty-eight cubits, or short, measuring fifteen or eighteen cubits.
This is the difference in the means of departure. They depart by means of elephants, horses, chariots, palanquins, and so forth, or by traveling through the air.
For instance, Vipassī and Koṇāgamana departed by horse-chariot; Sikhī and Koṇāgamana by the back of an elephant;
Vessabhū by palanquin; Kassapa by traveling through the air; and Sakyamuni on the back of a horse. This is the difference in renunciation. For seven days...
Or they apply themselves to striving for half a month, a month, two months, three months, four months, five months, six months, one year, or two, three, four, five, or six years.
This is the diversity of striving (*padhāna-vemattatā*). The Bodhi tree may be an *assattha* tree, or one of others such as the *nigrodha*.
This is the diversity of the Bodhi tree (*bodhi-vemattatā*). [The Buddha] was endowed with a fathom-wide radiance that was infinite.
They exist. In that regard, the fathom-wide radiance or the eighty-fold radiance is the same for all;
however, the infinite radiance reaches both far and near—whether one *gāvuta*, two *gāvutas*, a *yojana*, many *yojanas*, or even to the limits of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
The bodily radiance of the Buddha Maṅgala reached ten thousand world-systems. Even so, it is by means of the mind...
All Buddhas are dependent upon their own intention; whatever extent anyone desires, to that extent it proceeds for them.

This is the diversity of rays. Apart from these eight diversities, there is no distinction among them regarding the remaining qualities to be attained through penetration or the faults to be abandoned;
therefore, they are called "equal. Thus, he is equal with those who are equal by means of these [qualities].
The unequal are far from the equal; the unequal are not equal. These are the Paccekabuddhas and all other remaining beings.

They are "far" because of their dissimilarity to those [equals]. For even Paccekabuddhas, who might fill the entire Jambudīpa and sit touching one cross-legged posture to another, do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single Sammasambuddha in terms of qualities; how much less [others]?
The term *vāda* refers to [the teaching] among disciples and others. Therefore he said: "far from the uneven. The phrase "is a Tathāgata" should be construed with both words as "far.
"Of infinite wisdom" means of immeasurable wisdom. For, compared to the wisdom of worldly humans, the wisdom of the eighth-rank practitioner (*aṭṭhamaka*) is superior;
compared to his wisdom, that of the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) is superior; and so on, up to the wisdom of the arahant.

The wisdom of a paccekabuddha is superior; however, it cannot be said that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is superior when compared to the paccekabuddha’s wisdom—it must rather be said to be infinite. Therefore, he says: “of infinite wisdom.
“Unstained” means unstained by the smears of craving and views. “In this world or the next” means either in this world or in the world beyond.
The interpretation here is as follows: "The Tathāgata is the same toward the equal and the unequal, and likewise toward those far away. Why?
Because his wisdom is infinite and he is unsullied, whether in this world or in the world beyond; therefore, the Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake (pūraḷāsa).

As for the verse beginning "In whom there is no deceit," this and other such verses were intended to eliminate the perception of those brahmins—who are possessed of faults such as deceit—as being worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya).

These [terms] are to be understood as they have been stated. Therein, "without 'mine'" (*amama*) refers to the state of having abandoned the sense of "this is mine" regarding the seven formations of sentient beings.
"Abode" (*nivesana*) refers to the abiding of craving and views. For by means of these, the mind dwells within the three realms of existence; therefore, it is called the "abode of the mind.
Or rather, it is because the mind dwells right there, being unable to depart once it has left that [abode].
Even these are called "abodes" (*nivesana*). "Possessions" (*pariggaha*) refers specifically to craving and views, or to those phenomena grasped by them. "Some" (*keci*) means even a few.
"Not clinging" (*anupādiyāno*) means not grasping at any phenomenon due to the absence of those abodes and possessions.

(Verse 476) "Concentrated" (*samāhito*) means through the concentration of the Path. "He crossed over" (*udatārī*) means he has gone beyond. "He understood the Dhamma" (*dhammaṃ caññāsī*) means he knew all that is to be known. "By supreme vision" (*paramāya diṭṭhiyā*) means by the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
477. *Bhavāsava* means the lusts (*rāga*) accompanied by craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*), attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*), and the view of eternalism (*sassata-diṭṭhi*).

*Vācā* means speech. *Khara* means harsh and rough. *Vidhūpita* means burnt away. *Atthagata* means gone to destruction. They "do not exist" because they have been burnt away and because they have gone to destruction.
Furthermore, both [terms] should be applied to both; *sabbadhi* means in all cases, such as among the aggregates (*khandha*) and the sense-bases (*āyatana*).

478. "In mental attachments" (*mānasattesū*) means attached by conceit (*māna*). "Having fully understood suffering" (*dukkhaṃ pariññāya*) means having thoroughly known the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) through the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*). "Together with its field and site" (*sakhettavatthuṃ*) means together with its causes and conditions; it is said to be together with karma and the defilements (*kilesa*). 479.

"Not relying on hope" (*āsaṃ anissāya*) means not clinging to craving (*taṇhā*). "One who sees seclusion" (*vivekadassī*) means one who sees Nibbāna. "That which is to be experienced by others" (*paravediyaṃ*) means that which is to be made known by others.
"One who has transcended views" (*diṭṭhimupātivatto*) means one who has gone beyond even the sixty-two types of wrong views (*micchādiṭṭhi*).
"Objects" means conditions; it is said that they are the causes for renewed existence.
"High and low" means superior and inferior, beautiful and ugly; or alternatively, external and internal.
"Having fully understood" means having penetrated with wisdom. "Phenomena" refers to the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth. "Liberated through the destruction of clinging" means in Nibbāna.
"Released by means of Nibbāna as the object" means one who has attained release with Nibbāna as its object.
"One who sees the end of the destruction of fetters and birth" means one who sees the end of the destruction of fetters and one who sees the end of the destruction of birth.
Herein, by the end of the destruction of fetters, the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining is indicated; by the end of the destruction of birth, the [Nibbāna-element] without residue remaining.
It is said. "The state of exhaustion" (*khaya*) is a designation for absolute exhaustion, which is abandonment through eradication (*samuccheda*).

And here, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) has not been applied, as it is in cases such as "joy and happiness born of seclusion" (*vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ*). "He who dispelled" means he who removed.

"The path of lust" (*rāgapatha*) refers either to the object of lust or to lust itself. For lust is also called "the path of lust" because it is the path to miserable destinies, just as a course of action is called a "path of action."
"Pure" (*suddha*): It is pure because of its perfectly purified bodily conduct and so forth. "Faultless" (*niddosa*):
It is faultless because of the absence of those things by which it is said, "This generation has the fault of lust, the fault of hatred, and the fault of delusion.

"Stainless" (*vimala*): It is stainless due to the departure of the eight stains of a person. "Unblemished" (*akāca*): It is unblemished due to the absence of defilements (*upakkilesa*). For that which is defiled by a defilement is called "blemished" (*sakāca*).

Because it is pure (*suddha*), it is faultless (*niddosa*); because it is faultless, it is stainless (*vimala*); and because it is stainless due to the absence of external impurities, it is "without blemish" (*akāca*).

For that which possesses impurity is called "with blemish" (*sakāca*). Alternatively, because it is stainless, it does not commit an offense (*āga*); thus it is "without blemish. Indeed, the act of offending is called "blemish" (*kāca*) because it causes harm. 482.

"He does not perceive himself as self" means that while one is practicing insight (*vipassanā*) with a consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampayutta*), regarding one's own aggregates (*khandha*).
He does not see any self other than [the aggregates]; he sees only the mere aggregates.
And as for that view which arises in him "I perceive a self by means of a self," because of the absence of such [a view], he does not regard a self as a self;
rather, through wisdom, he sees the aggregates. Being concentrated by means of the concentration of the Path, [he abandons] bodily crookedness and so forth.
He is "without absence" (*abhāva*) because he has gone straight; he is "steadfast" because he is unshakable by worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*);
and he is "unwavering," "without barrenness," and "without doubt" because of the absence of wavering—which is to say craving—of the five mental barrennesses, and of the eightfold doubt.
(483) "The causes of delusion" (*mohantara*) means the causes of delusion, the conditions for delusion; this is a designation for all defilements (*kilesa*). In all [these]...
"One who has knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena" means one who has realized the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

For that is the knowledge regarding all phenomena, and the Blessed One saw it; having realized it, thinking "I have attained it," he dwelt [in that state]. Therefore, he is called "one who has knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena.
"Supreme enlightenment" refers to *arahantship*. "Unsurpassed" means not shared with *paccekabuddhas* or disciples.
"Peaceful" means secure, free from calamity, or glorious. "Of the *yakkha*" means of the person. "Purity" means the state of being cleansed.

For herein, through the absence of the obstruction of delusion, there is the absence of all defects; by that, there is the total eradication of the causes of saṃsāra, the maintenance of the final body, and the arising of all virtues through the possession of knowledge and vision.
By that, there is the attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment; beyond this, there is nothing further to be abandoned or to be realized.
Or rather, there is none. Therefore he said: “To this extent is there purification for a *yakkha*.
When this was said, the brahmin became even more deeply devoted to the Blessed One; manifesting his faith, he said:
“And my offering... The meaning of this is: that which I previously offered into the fire, directed toward Brahmā.
I do not know whether that offering of mine was true or false;
but today, as I pray, "May this offering of mine be true, may it indeed be an offering of truth," I have obtained such a master of knowledge (vedagu).
Because, while remaining right here, I have obtained a master of knowledge from another existence. For Brahmā is my witness, right before my eyes.

"Indeed, you are Brahmā; therefore, may the Blessed One accept from me, and having accepted it, may the Blessed One eat this sacrificial cake (*pūraḷāsa*), presenting him with that remnant of the oblation (*habya-sesa*)," he said.
Then the Blessed One recited two verses in the manner described in the *Kasibhāradvāja Sutta*. Thereupon, the Brahmin...

“‘This man does not desire it for himself; he speaks with reference to another, saying: “Serve the Perfect One, the Great Seer, whose taints are exhausted and whose remorse is stilled, with food and drink.
Not having grasped the meaning of the verse in this way, and desiring to know [the truth], he said:
“Very well, Blessed One. In that context, *sādhu* is a particle used in the sense of a request. *Tathā* means “in the manner that you have said.”

"In that manner. "I would know" (*vijaññaṃ*) means I would understand. "Whom" (*yaṃ*) refers to the one worthy of offerings whom, while searching at the time of sacrifice, one might attend upon—this is the ellipsis of the text.
"Having reached" (*pappuyya*) means having attained. "Your instruction" (*tava sāsananti*) means your exhortation. This is what is meant:
"It would be well, Blessed One, if by relying on your exhortation I might know in that way; please declare that to me, O All-Knowing One."

The intention was: "Show me such a person worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya) as one who might consume an offering from someone like me, and whom I, while seeking [such a one] at the time of sacrifice, might attend upon—if you do not eat [it yourself].
Then the Blessed One, showing him such a person worthy of offerings by way of a manifest method, said: "From hostilities... [and so forth].

He spoke these three verses beginning with “yassā. Therein, regarding the phrase “the guide of the boundaries” (*sīmantānaṃ vinetāraṃ*): “boundary” (*sīmā*) means a limit or the conduct of virtuous people;
taking the “ends” (*antā*) of that to mean its limits, its conclusions, or its subsequent stages, the term “boundaries” (*sīmantā*) refers to the defilements.

Thus, the meaning is “the guide of those [defilements]. Alternatively, some say that “boundaries” (*sīmantā*) refers to those who are to be guided by the Buddha—the trainees (*sekkhā*) and worldlings (*puthujjanā*)—and it means “the guide of them.”
“Skilled in birth and death” means skilled in this regard, [knowing] “birth is thus, death is thus.
“Endowed with modesty” means endowed with wisdom, or endowed with bodily modesty (*kāyamoneyya*) and so forth.
“Having removed frowns” means having removed that frown which some of dull intellect make upon seeing a beggar; the meaning is, having a serene face. “With palms joined” means...
Having joined his palms in reverent salutation, the brahmin then, praising the Blessed One, spoke this verse: “May you become a Buddha. In this context, *āyāga* means that which is to be offered;
or, it is so called because one comes from here and there to offer therein; thus, it is the locus for the things to be given.

This has been stated. As for the rest here, as well as that which was not commented upon in the preceding verses, it was not commented upon precisely because its meaning is obvious and can be understood even without such commentary.
From this point onward, however, the method is exactly as explained in the *Kasibhāradvāja Sutta*.
[End of] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the Pūraḷāsa Sutta of the Suttanipāta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Māgha Sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Māgha Sutta. What is its origin? It is the very same that was stated in its introduction. For this Māgha—
The young man was a donor, a master of giving. It occurred to him: "Is a gift given to those who have arrived, to the poor, to travelers, and so forth, of great fruit, or is it not?
I shall ask the ascetic Gotama about this matter;
for it is said that the ascetic Gotama knows the past, the future, and the present. He approached the Blessed One and asked him. The Blessed One—
He answered in accordance with his question. This [text] is called the "Māgha Sutta" because it combines the words of all three—the Brahmin, the Blessed One, and the compilers of the Council.
Therein, "at Rājagaha" means in the city of that name; for it was presided over by Mandhātu, Mahāgovinda, and others.
“It is called ‘Rājagaha. Other ways of describing it are also explained here; but what is the use of them? This is simply the name of that city.

During the time of a Buddha or the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti), this is a city; at other times, it is empty and presided over by *yakkhas*, remaining as their dwelling forest (*vasantavana*).
Having thus shown the alms-resort village, he states the place of residence: ‘On Vulture Peak...’”
"on the mountain. It should be understood that it is called "Vulture Peak" (Gijjhakūṭa) because vultures dwelt upon its peaks, or because its peaks resemble vultures. Then... [as before] ...he said;
here, "Māgha" is the name of that brahmin. "Young man" (māṇava) refers to his living as a resident pupil.
It is spoken of in terms of its non-past state, yet it is old by way of birth. "By way of former habit" means, according to some, like the young Brahmin Piṅgiya.
For even though he was one hundred and twenty years old, he came to be known simply as "the young Brahmin Piṅgiya" on account of his former habit.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
“Indeed, Master Gotama... [as before] ...I am one who gives,”—here, “a giver and a master of giving” means he is both a giver and a master of giving.
For one who gives what belongs to another without being commissioned by that person is indeed a giver, but because he lacks authority over that gift, he is not a master of giving.
This person, however, gives only what belongs to himself. Therefore he said: “Indeed, Master Gotama, I am a giver.”

"A donor" (*dānapati*). This indeed is the meaning here; however, elsewhere it is also appropriate to speak by way of such terms as "giver" (*dāyaka*) when one is occasionally overcome by stinginess, or "one not overcome" (*anabhibhūta*), and so forth. "Generous" (*vadaññū*):

he knows the speech of supplicants; as soon as it is uttered, by discerning the specific qualities of the person—thinking, "this one deserves this, that one deserves that"—and by perceiving their state of being highly helpful.
"Or: 'Fitted for begging' (yācayogo) means one who is fit to beg. For he who, upon seeing a beggar, frowns and speaks harsh words and the like, is not 'fitted for begging.

He [the Buddha] indicates, however, that he is not such a person. 'By the Dhamma' (dhammena) means by way of wandering for alms, avoiding taking what is not given, dishonesty, deception, and so forth;
this is the meaning of 'by begging' (yācanā). For begging is the means for Brahmins in the pursuit of wealth."
The Dhamma: when those who are begging receive wealth from others who desire to help them, it is called "rightly obtained" (*dhammaladdha*) and is "attained through the Dhamma" (*dhammādhigata*).
And he, having sought it in such a way, obtained it. Therefore he said: "I seek wealth righteously... attained righteously.
"I give even more" means I give even beyond that; there is no limit here.
He shows that he gives according to the measure of the wealth he has obtained.
*Taggha* is a particle used for an emphatic statement. For indeed, giving—even when given to those as low as animals—is praised in every way by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples.
And this has been said: "Giving is commended in all circumstances."
“Giving is never censured anywhere. Therefore, the Blessed One, praising it with absolute certainty, said: “Truly, young man...

[you] produce [merit]. The rest has its meaning already explained. Thus, although the Blessed One had said, “He produces much merit,” the brahmin, desiring to hear about the purification of the offering (*dakṣiṇā*) by way of the recipient (*dakṣiṇeyya*), addressed the Blessed One further.
He asked. Therefore, the compilers said: "Then the young brahmin Māgha addressed the Blessed One in verse.
This is explained in meaning exactly according to the method already stated.
Regarding the verses beginning with "We ask you," however, *vadaññū* means one who is skilled in speaking—that is, one who knows the intended meaning of the words spoken by beings in every way.
This has been said. It purifies; by way of those worthy of offerings, it becomes pure and of great fruit. The construction here, however, is as follows:

that householder who is devoted to sacrifice, a lord of giving, and desiring merit, performs a sacrifice while giving food and drink to others—not merely casting an oblation into the fire—and who does so solely out of a desire for merit, not out of a desire for reciprocal favors, fame, reputation, or the like.

How could the oblation of such a sacrificer be purified? (493) “One such as he should satisfy those worthy of offerings” means that one who is devoted to making requests—being such a person—should satisfy, accomplish, and purify [the offering] through those worthy of offerings;
he would make that oblation highly fruitful, and not otherwise. By this, his [question] “how the oblation... [is answered].
“...the sacrificer is purified”—thus has this been explained. 494.

Regarding the phrase “Tell me, Blessed One, about those worthy of offerings,” the construction should be understood thus: “He who, engaged in making requests, sacrifices for others while giving—tell me, Blessed One, about those worthy of his offerings.
495. Then the Blessed One, elucidating those worthy of offerings through various methods, spoke the verses beginning with “Those indeed who are unattached... and so forth.

He spoke these verses. In this context, "unattached" means unclinging by way of attachment such as lust and the like. "Perfect" means having completed their task. "Self-controlled" means having guarded their minds.

(Verses 496–497: "Tamed" by the unsurpassed taming; "liberated" by the liberation of wisdom and the liberation of mind; "free from affliction" due to the absence of the suffering of the cycle of existence in the future.
“Hopeless” means due to the absence of defilements at present. It should be understood that this second verse of the present stanza is stated by way of illustrating the power of meditation.
“Monks, when a monk dwells devoted to the practice of meditation, even if no such wish should arise in him as:
‘O, may my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging,’ yet...”
“His mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging”—this is the supporting sutta here.

(498–502) “And passion... [etc. ...in whom there is no deceit... [etc. ...they have not fallen into craving”: they are not intent upon craving for sense pleasures and so forth. “One would cross over”: having crossed over. “Craving”:
the sixfold craving, beginning with craving for form. “For existence and non-existence”: either for eternalism or...
Or for annihilation. Or else, "for the non-existence of existence" means for the non-becoming of existence, that is to say, for the non-production of renewed existence.
"In this world or in the next" is, however, an explanatory expansion of the phrase "anywhere in the world.

504. "Those who are free from lust... those who have attained peace": they are possessors of peace (*samitavant*); the meaning is "those who effect the subsiding of the defilements. Because they have attained peace... [the rest of the verse follows].
And they are free from passion and free from anger. "Having abandoned here" means having abandoned the aggregates existing in this world;

what is meant is that there is no further going for them beyond that. Following this, some recite this verse as well: "Those who, having left behind sensual desires, wander homeless, are straight like a shuttle because of their excellent self-restraint."
506–8. *Jahitvā* means having abandoned. There is also the reading *jahitvāna*, which has the same meaning.

*Attadīpā* refers to those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), who wander about making their own virtues their own island. *Ye hettha*: the syllable *ha* is a particle used merely to fill out the verse.
Its meaning, however, is this: those here, within the continuity of the aggregates, bases, and so forth, [regard] these aggregates, bases, and so forth as they truly are.
They know; they perceive that which has such a nature as having precisely that nature, knowing by way of impermanence and so forth.
"This is the last, there is no further becoming"—thus they know: "This is our last birth; now there is no further becoming. 509. "He who is a knower" (vedagu):
the Blessed One spoke this verse with reference to himself. In that context, "mindful" (satimā) refers to mindfulness regarding the six hundred and one abodes.

"Endowed [with these qualities]. Having attained full enlightenment" means having attained omniscience. "A refuge for many" means being a refuge for many gods and humans by protecting them from fear and harm. 510.
Having thus heard about those worthy of offerings, the brahmin, being delighted, said: "Truly, it is not in vain. In that regard, you here—
"You know this in this world, however it is"—this means that you know all this that is to be known (*ñeyya*) here in this world exactly as it is;
you know it according to its true nature (*yāthāvato*); what it is like, that you know it just so—that is what is meant.

"For thus has this Dhamma been understood by you" means that for you this element of Dhamma (*dhammadhātu*) has been well-penetrated, and through the state of its being well-penetrated, [that which...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.*
The intention is: "Whatever you desire, that you know.

(511) Having thus praised the Blessed One and understood the perfection of the sacrifice through the perfection of the recipient worthy of offerings, that brahmin—desiring to hear about the perfection of the sacrifice as being complete with its six factors even through the perfection of the donor—posed a further question: "He who is devoted to begging..."
He asked. Herein, this is the construction [of the verse]: "To him who, engaged in sacrifice, gives and offers to others—tell me, Blessed One, what constitutes the perfection of that sacrifice.

(512) Then the Blessed One explained it to him with two verses. Herein, this is the construction of the meaning: "Sacrifice, Māgha! And while sacrificing, be serene in mind in every respect; be serene in mind throughout the three times.
Thus for you: 'Before the gift, he is joyful; while giving, he clarifies his mind;'"
“Having given, he becomes glad; this is the perfection of sacrifice.
Thus the perfection of sacrifice has been stated; by means of that, the sacrifice will be perfected. Herein, one might ask: “How is the mind to be gladdened?
By the abandoning of hatred. How does the abandoning of hatred occur? Through taking the sacrifice as its object. For this [sacrifice] is the object for the one who is sacrificing.

The sacrifice stands here as a basis for abandoning hatred. For one who sacrifices with a mind preceded by loving-kindness toward sentient beings—a mind in which the darkness of delusion has been dispelled by the lamp of right view—the sacrifice, consisting of the object to be given, becomes the focal object.
Standing here in this sacrifice by way of its occurrence as an object, it abandons greed conditioned by the gift, anger conditioned by the recipient, and the delusion that is the source of both.
Thus, by abandoning even this threefold delusion, he abandons hatred.

Being thus free from passion for possessions and having removed hatred toward living beings, and with the five hindrances abandoned through that very removal, he gradually develops immeasurable loving-kindness—distinguished as access and absorption—by pervading either a single being or all beings without exception. Then, for the sake of further expanding that meditation:
Being constantly heedful throughout all postures day and night, one extends that very state known as the jhāna of loving-kindness toward all directions;
thus it is called an "immeasurable" (appamaññā).
Then, the brahmin, not knowing that this loving-kindness is "the path to the Brahma-world," [regards] only that which is beyond his own sphere.
Having heard the discourse on the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*), his conviction in the Omniscient One’s perfection was further strengthened.

Because he himself was intent upon the Brahma-world, and imagining that rebirth in the Brahma-world alone constituted purity and liberation, he asked about the path to the Brahma-world by reciting the verse beginning, “Who is purified?
In this context, he spoke with reference to one performing the merit that leads to the Brahma-world: “Who...”
“He is purified and liberated,” he said with reference to one who does not [commit the offense]; “and he is bound,” he said with reference to one who does. “By what means? means by what cause.
“Brahmā was seen as a witness today” means that Brahmā was seen as a witness this very day.
“Truly” means he makes a solemn oath concerning the Blessed One’s equality with Brahmā. “How is it established? he asks again with even greater earnestness.
Jutimātī addressed the Blessed One.

In this regard, because a bhikkhu who, having produced the third or fourth jhāna through loving-kindness (*mettā*), takes that very state as a basis and reaches Arahantship by means of insight (*vipassanā*), is purified and liberated; and such a person does not [re-enter] the Brahma-world.
He goes. However, he who, having produced the third or fourth jhāna of loving-kindness (*mettā*), relishes it by way of such passages as "This attainment is peaceful," becomes bound.
And one whose jhāna has not been lost goes to the Brahma-world by means of that very jhāna;
therefore, the Blessed One, without mentioning the going to the Brahma-world for one who is purified and liberated, [does not permit it].
He speaks this verse, "He who sacrifices," by way of what is suitable for the brahmin, demonstrating that such a person—who is bound [to the result]—goes to the Brahmā-world by means of that jhāna.
Therein, he says "threefold" with reference to faith in the three times; by that, he shows the three factors from the perspective of the donor.

"May he, such as he is, accomplish the threefold perfection of sacrifice through those worthy of offerings"—this means that such a person, one who accomplishes the threefold perfection, should accomplish and achieve the threefold perfection of sacrifice by means of those worthy of offerings, the *khīṇāsava* (those whose taints are destroyed). By this, he shows the three factors from the perspective of the recipient.
"Having sacrificed thus, may he be devoted to right entreaty"—thus, by way of having loving-kindness meditation (*mettā-jhāna*) as its proximate cause...

"Having performed a sacrifice endowed with six factors correctly, that practitioner of offerings, by means of that support of the six-factored sacrifice and through the jhāna of loving-kindness, is reborn in the Brahmā-world," he said, concluding his teaching while encouraging the brahmin.
The rest of all the verses has a meaning that is already evident. And from here onwards, it is according to the method previously stated.
The commentary on the Māgha Sutta within the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā* known as the *Paramatthajotikā*, is completed. 6.
The commentary on the Sabhiya Sutta.
Thus have I heard: this is the Sabhiya Sutta. What is its origin? It is that very account which has been told in its introduction (nidāna).
Furthermore, in the sequence of the commentary on the meaning, that which is similar to what precedes should be understood according to the method already explained.

However, regarding that which is new, we shall explain it while setting aside those words whose meaning is obvious. "In the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka feeding-place": "Bamboo Grove" refers to that pleasure grove.
It was called by that name because it was indeed surrounded by bamboos and an eighteen-cubit wall, provided with gate-towers and watchtowers, and was blue-hued and delightful;
therefore, it is called "Veḷuvana" (Bamboo Grove). Furthermore, they gave fodder for squirrels there, and thus it is called "Kalandakanivāpa" (Squirrel-Food).
"Kalandaka" refers to black squirrels. It is said that formerly, a certain...
The king, having come there for the purpose of a pleasure excursion in the park, fell asleep during the day, intoxicated by liquor.
His attendants, thinking "the king is asleep," departed here and there, enticed by flowers, fruits, and other such things.
Then, drawn out by the smell of the liquor from a certain hollow tree, a black snake emerged and came toward the king. Seeing it, [he...]
The tree deity, thinking, "I shall grant life to the king," came in the guise of a black dog and made a sound at the root of his ear.

The king woke up; the black snake had retreated. Seeing this, he thought, "My life has been given back by this black dog," and he established fodder for the black dogs there and caused a proclamation of safety to be made. Therefore, from that time on...
“Kalandakanivāpa” has become a conventional designation.
Regarding “of the wanderer Sabhiya”: “Sabhiya” is his name; he is called a “wanderer” (paribbājaka) by virtue of having undertaken the external form of renunciation.
Regarding “the deity who was formerly a blood relative”: she was neither his mother nor his father, but rather his mother.
Because he possessed an inclination toward their welfare like that of a father or a brother, that son of the gods was called "the deity who was formerly a blood-relative" (*purāṇasālohitā devatā*).
It is said that after the Blessed One Kassapa had attained final Nibbāna and the Golden Cetiya was established, three sons of good family went forth in the presence of the face-to-face disciples;
having taken meditation subjects suitable to their respective temperaments, they went to a border region.
They practiced the duties of a recluse in the forest retreats, and from time to time they went to the city to pay homage at the shrines and to listen to the Dhamma.
However, on another occasion, even though they announced their intention to remain in the forest for that long, they dwelt right there with negligence;
and even while dwelling thus, they did not attain any distinction. Then...
It occurred to them: “As we go for alms, we are still attached to life;
and one who is attached to life cannot attain the supramundane Dhamma. Even the death of an ordinary person is painful.
Come now, let us build a ladder, climb the mountain, and practice the ascetic life without regard for either body or life. They did accordingly.
Then, because they were endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), that great elder realized Arhatship together with the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiññā*) on that very day.
By means of his psychic power (*iddhi*), he went to the Himālayas, washed his face at Lake Anotatta, and wandered for alms in Uttarakuru.
Having finished his meal, he went again to another region, filled his bowl, and [took] water from Lake Anotatta.
Taking a tooth-stick made of *nāgalatā* creeper, he went to them and said: "Behold, friends, my power!
This alms-food has been brought from Uttarakuru, and this water and tooth-stick have been brought from the Himālayas.
Having consumed this, perform the duties of a recluse; in this way, I shall serve you always. When they heard this, they said:
“Venerable sir, you have accomplished your task; even a mere conversation with you is a distraction for us.
Do not come near us again. Being unable to persuade them by any means, he departed.
Then, after two or three days had passed, one of them became an Anāgāmī possessed of the five super-knowledges (pañca-abhiññā). He acted in exactly the same way, and the other...

Having been refused, he departed just as he had come. Having been refused, he exerted himself, but on the seventh day from the day he climbed the mountain, having failed to attain any distinction, he passed away and was reborn in the world of the gods.
On that very same day, the Elder Khīṇāsava attained final Nibbāna, while the Non-returner was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa heavens. As for the son of the gods, among the six sense-sphere heavens...

Having experienced divine success in both direct and reverse order, she passed away from the world of the gods during the time of our Blessed One and took rebirth in the womb of a certain female wanderer. It is said that she was the daughter of a certain kṣatriya;
her parents, thinking, "Let our daughter learn the various systems of thought," entrusted her to a certain wanderer.
They handed him over. One of his pupils, a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka), misconducted himself with her. She conceived a child by him.
Seeing that she was pregnant, the female ascetics (paribbājikā) expelled her. As she was going elsewhere, she gave birth on the way in a public hall (sabhā);
therefore, they gave him the name "Sabhiya. Sabhiya, too, having grown up, entered the wandering life of an ascetic.
Having gone forth and mastered various treatises, he became a great debater. Wandering throughout the whole of Jambudīpa due to his habit of engaging in debate,
and finding no rival debater equal to himself, he built a hermitage at the city gate and lived there,
teaching crafts to princes and others.
Then the Blessed One, having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, traveling by stages, arrived at Rājagaha and dwelt in the Bamboo Grove at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
However, Sabhiya did not know of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
Then that Suddhāvāsa Brahmā, emerging from meditative attainment, reflected, “By whose power have I attained this distinction? and [saw it was] during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Recalling those two companions who had practiced the duties of a recluse, he reflected: "One of them has attained final Nibbāna; where is the other now?

Perceiving that he had passed away from the world of the gods and been reborn in Jambudīpa, yet did not even know of the appearance of a Buddha, he thought, "Come, I shall direct him toward attending upon the Buddha.
Having formulated twenty questions, he went to his hermitage during the night.
Standing in the sky, he called out, “Sabhiya! Sabhiya! While sleeping, Sabhiya heard that voice three times;
having emerged and seen the radiance, he stood with palms joined in reverence. Then Brahmā said to him:
“I have brought twenty questions for your sake, Sabhiya; you should learn them. And whatever ascetic or brahmin asks you these questions—”
“He explains [the Dhamma]; you should lead the holy life in his presence. This was said with reference to this son of the gods:
“The questions of the deity who was formerly a blood-relative have been set forth. “Set forth” means they were stated merely as a summary, not by way of detailed analysis (*vibhaṅga*).
When this was said, Sabhiya grasped it all in a single utterance, following the sequence of the words. Then that Brahmā, although knowing of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, did not announce it.

However, with this intention—“The wandering ascetic, seeking the truth, will come to know the Teacher for himself, and he will realize the emptiness of the recluses and brahmins outside of this”—he spoke thus.
“O Sabhiya... [as before] ...you should practice. However, in the *Theragāthā*, while describing the legend (*apadāna*) of the Elder Sabhiya in the Catukkanipāta, they say:
“His mother, reflecting upon her own misconduct and feeling loathing for it, developed meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and was reborn in the Brahma-world;
it was by that Brahma-devatā that these questions were posed to him.”
"Those who... is now the summary and detailed enumeration of what is to be said.

"Ascetics and brahmins": by virtue of having gone forth and by worldly convention, they are both ascetics (*śramaṇa*) and brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*). "Possessing a retinue" means having a group. "Having a following" means teachers who claim, "We are omniscient.
"Teachers of groups" refers to those who, through instruction, interrogation, and so forth, [lead] a group consisting of both those who have gone forth and householders.
Teachers: "Known" means well-known; it is said they are famous and renowned. "Illustrious" means endowed with gain and a retinue.
"Founders of sects" means those who create the sectarian positions (diṭṭhitittha) which must be descended into and plunged into by those following their views.
"Esteemed as good by the many" means they are regarded by the multitude as "these are good men, holy persons."
“Seyyathidaṃ” (namely) is a particle used in this sense of “which are those three? “Pūraṇa” is his name; “Kassapa” is his clan-name.
It is said that he was born as a slave by birth, being born as the one who completed a hundred slaves; therefore they gave him the name “Pūraṇa.
But having fled and gone forth among the naked ascetics, he proclaimed his clan-name, saying, “I am Kassapa,” and claimed omniscience.
His name was Makkhali; because he was born in Gosālā, he is also called Gosāla.

It is said that he too was originally a slave, but having escaped, he went forth into homelessness and claimed omniscience. His name was Ajita; because of his fewness of desires, he wore a hair-blanket, and for that reason he is also called Kesakambala. He too claimed omniscience. His name was Pakudha.
*Kaccāyana* is his clan name (*gotta*). Because of his fewness of desires and his perception of living beings even in water, bathing, washing the face, and so forth were prohibited for him;
he too acknowledged omniscience. *Sañjaya* was his personal name, while *Belaṭṭha* was his father’s name;
therefore, he is called *Belaṭṭhaputta*. He too acknowledged omniscience. *Nigaṇṭha* is by way of his name as a renunciant, and *Nāṭaputta* is by way of his father’s name.
It is said: "Nātha" was the name of his father; he was the son of Nātha, thus "Nātaputta. He too claimed omniscience.
All of them had retinues of five hundred disciples each. "Those" refers to those six teachers.

"Those twenty questions" refers to those twenty questions. "Those" refers to those six teachers. "Do not succeed" means they do not accomplish [the goal]. "Anger" refers to the mind and mental factors.
"Turbidity" (*āvilabhāvaṃ*). "Hatred" (*dosa*) means a state of a corrupted mind; both of these are designations for anger (*kodha*) itself, distinguished as either mild or intense.
"Discontent" (*appaccaya*) means a lack of satisfaction; it is synonymous with "dejection" (*domanassa*). "They manifest" means they make known through bodily and vocal gestures;
they make [it] evident.

“Hīnāya” means for the state of a householder. For the state of a householder is called “inferior” (hīna) because, compared to renunciation, it is inferior in qualities such as virtue, or because it involves the pursuit of low sensual pleasures. “Uccā” means renunciation. “Āvattitvā” means having turned back.
“Kāme paribhuñjeyyaṃ” means I would enjoy sensual pleasures. Thus, even though he had made a claim to omniscience, [he would act] toward those who have gone forth...
He became [convinced] upon seeing his emptiness. And by means of the very reflections that had arisen, as he came and examined him again and again, it then occurred to Sabhiya the wanderer:
"This one too is a recluse," and "Those venerable ones too," and "A recluse, though young, is not to be despised," and so forth. In that context, the words "old" and so on—
The words are in the manner already explained. "Theras" means those who have attained stability in their own ascetic practice (*samaṇadhamma*). "Rattaññū" means "knowers of the jewel";
they are recognized even by the world through their own profession, saying, "We know the jewel that is Nibbāna," or they are those who are experts in many rains (*ratti*).
"Cirapabbajitā" means those whose going-forth has been long. "Na uññātabbo" means he should not be despised; he should not be held in low esteem.
"It should be understood by treating him as inferior"—this is what is meant. "He should not be despised" means he should not be held in contempt;
it is said that one should not take [his words] with the thought, "What will he know? 516.
