"Full of doubt, full of perplexity": Sabhiya, while exchanging greetings with the Blessed One, [perceived] thus the Blessed One’s excellence of form, which is indicated by his self-control and tranquility...
Honoring their omniscience and being free from arrogance, he said: "One who is doubtful, one who is perplexed.
In this context, he is "doubtful" (kaṅkhī) because of a doubt regarding the explanation of questions, thinking, "Would that I might receive an explanation of these questions?
He is "perplexed" (vecikicchī) because of perplexity, thinking, "What indeed is the meaning of this and that question? This refers to weak perplexity.
Or, because he is doubtful regarding the meaning of those questions, he is "one who doubts" (*kaṅkhī*);

searching with intense scrutiny, he merely suffers and is unable to reach a definitive conclusion, thus he is "one who is perplexed" (*vecikicchī*). "Desiring" (*abhikaṅkhamāno*) means longing intensely.
"One who brings an end to them" (*tesantakaro*) means one who brings an end to those questions. Showing that "only you can be thus," he said: "When asked a question by me... [etc.]"
“Give me an explanation. In this context, *pañhe me* means “in my question”; *puṭṭho* means “asked”;

*anupubbaṃ* means “in the sequence of the questions”; and *anudhammaṃ* means “placing the text in accordance with the meaning. *Byākarohi me* means “give me an explanation. 517. Regarding “from afar”:

it is said that he had come from a road of seven hundred yojanas, wandering here and there. Therefore the Blessed One said, “You have come from afar. Or, because he had come from the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Blessed One addressed him, saying, “You have come from afar.”

518. With this verse, "Ask," he invites [the Buddha] to the proclamation of omniscience (*sabbaññu-pavāraṇā*). Therein, *manasicchasi* means "you desire in your mind. *Yaṃ vatāhaṃ* means "whatever indeed I [desire]. *Attamano* means one whose mind is suffused with rapture, gladness, and joy.
*Udaggo* means uplifted in both body and mind. However, this word does not appear in all recensions. Now, by means of which phenomena...
Being pleased, he spoke thus to show them: “Delighted, born of joy and gladness.
(519) What was attained? What bowl? What was realized? “Gentle” (*sorata*) means well-pacified.

There is also the reading “*surata*,” which has the same meaning: well-restrained. “Tamed” (*danta*) means disciplined. “Awakened” (*buddha*) means fully awakened; that which is to be awakened by a Buddha.
In this way, Sabhiya, having formulated four questions for each verse,
asked twenty questions with five verses. The Blessed One, however, having formulated one question for each verse, answered them with twenty verses, culminating in the attainment of Arahatship.

520. In this context, because one whose defilements are destroyed is a bhikkhu in the ultimate sense, and he has attained Nibbāna, the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with "By the path" (*pajjena*) while answering the question: "What do they call a bhikkhu who has attained? Its meaning is as follows:
he who, by means of the path developed within himself, has gone to final Nibbāna—that is, has reached the Nibbāna of the destruction of defilements—and because he has gone to final Nibbāna...
And thus, having crossed over doubt, having abandoned both non-existence and existence— along with misfortune and prosperity, decline and growth,
annihilationism and eternalism, demerit and merit— and having dwelt in the dwelling of the Path, he is one for whom future becoming is exhausted;
such a person is worthy of these words of praise, "He is a bhikkhu."

521. However, because he is gentle (*sorata*) due to his state of being thoroughly ceased from misconduct and due to the pacification of various kinds of defilements (*kilesa*), the Blessed One spoke the answer to the second question by way of the passage beginning with “equanimous in all things” (*sabbattha upekkhako*) in order to demonstrate that meaning.
Its meaning is as follows: He who, in regard to all objects such as forms, “having seen a form with the eye, is neither glad... [nor dejected]... [and so forth].

One who is equanimous through the sixfold equanimity that proceeds thus, "not dejected," and who is mindful through mindfulness that has reached full development, does not harm, nor does he harm any being whatsoever—whether moving or stationary—in the entire world, in all the world.
Having crossed over the flood, he is "crossed"; having stilled evil, he is a "samaṇa" (ascetic); and by abandoning turbid intentions, he is "unclouded. Of him...

In this state, there are no longer any of the seven types of defilements— consisting of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, afflictions, and misconduct— which are crowded with living beings and range from gross to subtle.
Because he has thoroughly ceased all forms of misconduct through this abiding in equanimity, the fullness of mindfulness, and non-violence,
and because of this pacification of various defilements such as the floods (*ogha*), he is "tame" (*sorata*).

522. And because one whose faculties are developed becomes fearless, unshakable, and tamed, the Blessed One, in order to demonstrate this meaning, answered the third question with the verse beginning, "He whose faculties...
Its meaning is as follows: for one who, through the cultivation of the objective field, has applied the three characteristics—impermanence and so forth—to the six faculties, such as the eye;
and through the cultivation of mental impression (*vāsanā*), has infused them with the fragrance of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*).

And having grasped them, they have been developed; and just as they were developed internally through the cultivation of the internal range, so too externally throughout the entire world—wherever there is deficiency of the faculties or the possibility of such deficiency—they have been developed by way of non-covetousness and so forth.
Having thus become disillusioned, known, and penetrated this and the other, [he understands:]...

Desiring to die a death that is not untimely—desiring to die when the world, consisting of both the aggregates of one’s own continuity and the aggregates of the continuity of others, has reached its end—he awaits his time;
he looks forward to and honors the time of the exhaustion of life, and he does not fear death. As the Elder said:
“I have no fear of death, nor do I have attachment to life.”
“I do not long for death, nor do I long for life;
I await my time as a servant awaits his wages.
Thus, he whose faculties are developed is said to be “tamed,” meaning one who has developed his faculties in this way.

523. However, because one who is called a *buddha* is endowed with wisdom (*buddhi*) and has awakened from the sleep of the defilements (*kilesa*), he answered the fourth question with the verse beginning "Aeons" (*kappāni*) in order to demonstrate that meaning. In this context, "aeons" (*kappāni*) refers to craving and views.
For these are called "aeons" because they conceptualize in various ways (*vikappana*). "Having discerned" (*viceyya*) means having comprehended them through their nature of impermanence and so forth.
"Kevalāni" means all of them. "Saṃsāra" refers to that which is described thus:
"The uninterrupted succession of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as they proceed is called 'saṃsāra'."

Thus, having discerned this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is reckoned as the sequence of the aggregates and so forth, and that very cycle of existence—by this much he has stated insight (vipassanā) regarding the three rounds (vaṭṭa): namely, regarding karma and the defilements which are the roots of the aggregates, and regarding the aggregates themselves.
"Both passing away and rebirth" means having discerned and known both this passing away and rebirth of beings.
The meaning. By this, the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (*cutūpapātañāṇa*) is expressed.

"Free from dust, stainless, and purified" means it is free from dust because of the disappearance of the dust of passion and so forth, stainless because of the absence of blemishes, and purified because of the removal of impurities.

"Attained the destruction of birth" means Nibbāna has been attained. "That they call a Buddha"—that [one] by means of this supramundane insight, which is distinguished by the knowledge of passing away and rebirth...

Because of being endowed with wisdom (*buddhi*) and because of having awakened from the sleep of the defilements (*kilesa-niddā*) through this state of being free from dust (*vigata-rajas*), they call him "Buddha" because he has attained the destruction of birth (*jāti-kkhaya*) by means of that path.

Alternatively, "having discerned entire aeons" (*kappāni viceyya kevalāni*) refers to [the passage]: "In many aeons of dissolution and evolution (*saṃvaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa-kappa*), I was there," and so forth.
"Having investigated by way of method" is the meaning. By this, he states the first kind of knowledge (*vijjā*).

"Both sides of saṃsāra, namely death and rebirth"—that is, having investigated both this death and rebirth of beings by way of the method beginning with "These, indeed, venerable sirs, are beings..."—is the meaning.
By this, he states the second kind of knowledge. By what remains, he states the third kind of knowledge: through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*).

For indeed, there is both the state of being free from dust and the attainment of Nibbāna. Regarding the phrase "They call him a Buddha": they call that one a Buddha who is thus endowed with the wisdom that discerns the distinctions of the threefold knowledge (vijjā).
525. Having thus answered the questions stated in the first verse, [the author now explains] the meaning of the questions stated in the second verse as well:
because the supreme Brahmin—one who has attained the state of Brahmā, the state of excellence—is one who has cast out all evil, therefore that meaning...
By teaching through the verse beginning with "having banished" (*bāhitvā*), he answered the first question. Its meaning is as follows:

he who, having banished all evils by means of the fourth path, is "steadfast" (*ṭhitatto*)—the word used here being "steadfast" (*ṭhita*). And because he has banished evil, he is "stainless" (*vimalo*);
he has attained the stainless state, the state of a *brahma*, the supreme state, since the stains of the defilements that cause the distraction of concentration have been pacified.

Perfectly concentrated by means of the concentration of the supreme fruit, having transcended the cycle of existence by overcoming its causes, he is "one who has reached the goal" (kevalī) due to the completion of his task.
Because he is independent of craving and views, he is "unattached" (asita); and because he is unshaken by worldly conditions, he is called "such-like" (tādī).
Thus, he is truly worthy of praise; he is a Brahmā, he is a Brāhmaṇa.

526. However, because one is called a *samaṇa* due to having stilled evil, a *nhātaka* due to having washed away evil, and a *nāga* due to not performing sinful acts, he therefore answered three questions with three further verses in order to demonstrate that meaning.
Therein, "one who has stilled" (*samitāvī*) means one who stands having stilled the defilements by means of the Noble Path; thus is one called a *samaṇa*.
"Such a one is called a recluse (*samaṇa*). To this extent the question has been answered; the remainder is words of praise intended to generate great respect for that recluse in Sabhiya.

For he who is self-restrained (*samitāvī*)—by not producing rebirth through merit or evil, having abandoned merit and evil—is "dustless" (*viraja*) due to the disappearance of the dust [of defilement];
and having understood this world and the other world through [the contemplation of] impermanence and so forth...
He has transcended birth and death and becomes such a one.

Regarding the phrase "having bathed... the one who is washed": here, having bathed—that is, having washed away with the knowledge of the Path all evil states that are capable of arising by way of internal and external objects within the entire world of the sense-bases (āyatana), which is comprised of the internal and the external—[he is called "the one who is washed"].
Because he has washed away evil, he does not go through an eon among gods or humans who are fashioned by the fabrications of craving and views;
thus, "he is called a *nhātaka* (one who has washed)"—this is how the meaning should be understood.
Regarding the fourth verse as well: "He commits no sin whatsoever in the world," which means that in the world he does not commit even the slightest thing reckoned as evil.
"He commits no offense; he is called a Nāga because of suchness. To this extent the question has been answered;

the remainder is merely words of praise according to the previous method. For he who commits no offense—having abandoned through the Path that which was not abandoned—and having relinquished and cast off all yokes such as the yoke of sensual desire, all fetters consisting of the ten fetters, and all bonds, [remains] in every respect regarding the aggregates and so forth, by anything whatsoever...
“He is not stuck by attachment, he is liberated by the two kinds of liberation, and he is such-like.
(530) Having thus answered the questions stated in the second verse, regarding the questions stated in the third verse as well:
because “fields” (*khettāni*) refers to the sense bases (*āyatanāni*). As it is said: “This eye is the eye-base... this is a field.”
"Regarding the 'field of objects'": having conquered them—that is, having overcome them—or having discerned them by investigating and examining them as being impermanent and so forth;

[conquering] them entirely without remainder, and specifically the divine and human "Brahma-field" which serves as a basis for attachment—namely, the divine field consisting of the twelve bases (āyatana) and likewise the human field, and that which is the Brahma-field.
The six sense bases consist of the twelve bases, such as the eye-base and so forth; he should conquer or discern all of them.

Since that which is the root-binding of all fields—namely ignorance, existence, craving, and so on—he is liberated from that root-binding of all fields. Thus, because of having conquered or investigated these fields, he is called a "Conqueror of Fields" (khettajina); therefore...
With the verse beginning “Fields,” he answered the first question. In this regard, some say that “actions are the fields,” based on the statement:
“Action is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture. Furthermore, regarding the phrase “the divine, the human, and the Brahma-field”:
here, action leading to rebirth among the gods is “divine”; action leading to rebirth among humans is “human”; and action leading to rebirth among the Brahmas is—
They describe it as the "Brahma-field. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

However, because actions (kamma) are called "sheaths" (*kosāni*) due to their similarity to sheaths in the sense of being one's own property, and because one is skillful in the reaping—that is, the cutting off—of those [actions], the second question in the verse beginning with "Sheaths" (*kosāni*) is presented in order to demonstrate that meaning.

He explained it. Its meaning is as follows: having scrutinized, through both their objective sphere and function, the "treasuries" consisting of wholesome and unwholesome kamma—namely, the states of impermanence and so forth—by means of mundane and supramundane insight;

and specifically, having scrutinized the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome volition which serve as the basis for inclusion, as well as the nine types of sublime wholesome volition, both divine and human.
Having discerned the sheath of Brahma. Then, by means of this cultivation of the path, one is liberated from the fundamental bonds of all sheaths—namely, ignorance, existence, craving, and so forth.
Thus, because of the "reaping" of these sheaths, one is called "skilled" (*kusala*); and because of that state, one becomes "such-like" (*tādī*).
Alternatively, because they are similar to sword-sheaths in being the dwelling place of beings and phenomena, they are called "sheaths" (*kosāni*).
The three existences (bhava) and the twelve bases (āyatana) are to be understood. In this way, the application [of the term] should be made here.

Furthermore, since one is not called "wise" (paṇḍita) solely because he "understands" (paṇḍati), but rather is also called "wise" because he has approached what is pure (paṇḍara) and has resorted to the wisdom of investigation (pavicaya-paññā), therefore, in order to show that meaning:
With the verse beginning “Both,” he answered the third question. Its meaning is as follows: having discerned both internally and externally as impermanent and so forth;
“bright” refers to the sense bases (*āyatana*). For they are called thus because of their natural purity and by way of conventional usage.

Having discerned them through this practice, one whose wisdom is purified because the stains have been scrubbed away— (The remainder of the passage continues with the description of the practitioner who has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning.)
He is called a "paṇḍita" (wise man) because of being such; for he has gone beyond (*ito*) those white things by means of wisdom. The rest is words of praise for him.
Indeed, he has transcended the black and the white, reckoned as demerit and merit, and he is "such-like" (*tādī*); therefore he is praised in this way.
Furthermore, since "mona" is said to be knowledge—that wisdom, understanding, ... right view—by means of that knowledge...
It was said, "The sage is endowed [with this]. Therefore, demonstrating that meaning, he answered the fourth question with the verse beginning, "Of the non-existent and the existent.

Its meaning is as follows: having discerned with the knowledge of investigation (pavicaya-ñāṇa) within this entire world—both internally and externally—that phenomenon (dhamma) which is divided into the unwholesome and the wholesome, both the non-existent and the existent, [he understands] the phenomenon for him...
Having transcended—that is, having gone beyond—the sevenfold attachment consisting of the divisions of lust and so forth, as well as the twofold net consisting of the divisions of craving and views;
he is a *muni* because he is endowed with that investigative knowledge termed "silence.
"Worthy of worship by gods and humans" is a word of praise for him, for he is such because he is a *muni* whose taints are exhausted, [and thus] to gods and humans...
He is worthy of worship; therefore, he is thus praised.
Having thus answered the questions stated in the third verse, regarding the questions stated in the fourth verse as well:
since one who has gone by effecting the destruction of the defilements through the four knowledges of the paths is, in the ultimate sense, called a "Vedagu" (one who has attained knowledge).

And he who has, by means of that very cultivation of the path, analytically discerned through the aspects of impermanence and so forth the Vedas— which are regarded as weapons by all recluses and brahmins—
becomes free from lust for all those feelings, whether they arise conditioned by the Vedas or otherwise, having transcended all that Veda by abandoning desire and lust for it.
Therefore, demonstrating that meaning, he did not say "this is the answer," but rather answered the first question with the verse beginning "Now, having known" (*vedāni*).

Or, because one who has discerned the Vedas through the wisdom of investigation, and having abandoned desire and lust for them, proceeds having transcended all knowing (*veda*), he is one who has gone to, known, and transcended the Vedas—those things designated as "weapons. [This applies to] one who, regarding feelings (*vedanāsu*)...
One who is free from passion has also gone beyond and transcended those things known as feeling and perception; thus he is a "Vedagu" (one who has gone to the Vedas).
Therefore, in order to demonstrate this meaning, [the Buddha] did not say "this is the attainment," but answered the first question with this verse.
Furthermore, since in the second question "anuvidita" means "fully understood," and that [understanding] comes through having investigated *papañca*, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), [the Buddha]—
Having investigated and thoroughly understood, through the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, the conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) consisting of craving,
conceit, and views within one’s own internal continuum, as well as the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) conditioned by it— not only internally, but also externally as the root of disease,

and within the continua of others as the root of this disease of name-and-form, namely ignorance, becoming, and craving— or having investigated that very conceptual proliferation itself, by means of that...

Through cultivation, one is liberated from the root-bonds of all diseases—whether from the root-bonds of all diseases consisting of the divisions of ignorance (*avijjā*), existence-craving (*bhava-taṇhā*), and so forth, or from such conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) itself.
Showing this, he answered the second question with the verse beginning, "Having investigated" (*anuvicca*). Regarding the phrase, "And how is one possessed of energy?":
herein, it is because one who has desisted from all evils by means of the Noble Path [is so described].

Likewise, because of his abstention, he has transcended the suffering of hell and stands firm for the sake of no further rebirth in the future; thus, he is one whose dwelling is vigor (*vīriyavāsa*) and whose abode is vigor (*vīriyaniketa*).

Such a one, whose taints are exhausted, is worthy of being called "one who possesses vigor" (*vīriyavā*); therefore, demonstrating this meaning, he answered the third question with the verse beginning "Abstinent" (*virato*).
Furthermore, the phrases "exerting himself" (*padhānavā*), "the wise one" (*dhīro*), and "the poised one" (*tādī*) are words of praise for him.

For he is indeed "one possessed of striving" (*padhānavā*) by virtue of his striving for the path and jhāna; "wise" (*dhīra*) because of his capacity to destroy the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*); and "such-like" (*tādī*) because of his imperturbability.
Therefore, he is praised in this way. The rest should be explained by applying [the same logic].
Regarding the passage, “How indeed does one become a thoroughbred (*ājāniyo*)?”—it is because one who has abandoned all crookedness and fault is a knower of what is the right cause and what is not.
In the world, it is said that "a horse or an elephant is a noble breed," yet those faults have not been entirely abandoned in them;
however, for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), they have been abandoned.

Therefore, showing that such a person deserves to be called "noble" in the ultimate sense, he answered the fourth question with the verse beginning "Yassā... Its meaning is as follows: internally and externally...
Thus, for one whose fetters— reckoned as internal and external— are mown down, severed by the sword of wisdom,
and split asunder; whose roots of attachment— that which serves as the root for clinging, binding,
and non-transcending with respect to various objects— or rather, whose internal and external fetters such as lust and so forth are mown down.

And since attachments have their root in craving, he who is released from the bond that is the root of all attachments, or the bond which is the root of all attachments, is called an "Aryan" (ājāniya);
because of being such, he is "such-like" (tādi). 540. Having thus answered the questions stated in the fourth verse, [the commentary now addresses] those stated in the fifth verse as well, because...

That which grammarians describe as a "learned man" (*sottiya*) merely on account of their proficiency in the meditation on phonemes (*chandajjhāna*) is one who is a learned man only in conventional usage (*vohāramatta*).
However, the Noble One (*ariya*), through his great learning and his state of having flowed out from evil, is a learned man in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that meaning, he did not say "having attained," but answered the first question in the verse with the word "having heard. Its meaning is as follows:

—He who, in this world, having heard through the function of wisdom consisting of what is heard (*sutamayapaññā*), or having heard according to the tasks that ought to be performed, has directly known all phenomena conducive to insight by way of impermanence and so forth;

and having, by means of this practice, overcome both defilements and those things associated with defilements—whatever exists, whether blameworthy or blameless—he has attained the designation "the Overcomer" (*abhibhū*). Having heard all these phenomena...
Having directly known whatever is blameworthy and blameless in the world, they call him a learned Sottiya because he has overcome [all things].
And because he is free from doubt, liberated from the bonds of the defilements, and without distress through greed and the other fires in all respects regarding all phenomena—
such as the aggregates and the bases— they call that one who is free from doubt, liberated, and without distress...
He is called a "Sottiya" because he has, in every respect, become one whose evil has flowed out.

Furthermore, because he is worthy of being approached (*araṇīya*) by people who desire his welfare—meaning he is approachable—it is for this reason that, in order to show the qualities by which he is thus approachable, he answered the second question with the verse beginning, "Having cut... (Chetvā).

The meaning of this is as follows: having severed the four taints (*āsava*) and the two attachments (*ālaya*) with the sword of wisdom, the wise, learned, and discerning one, possessing the knowledge of the four paths, does not enter a womb by way of renewed existence;
he does not approach any mode of birth, nor the threefold perception consisting of sensual desire and the rest.
Having driven away—that is, having dispelled—the mire known as the strands of sensual pleasure, as well as the constructs of craving and views, [he is liberated].
He does not go even for another eon; thus, one endowed with qualities such as the cutting off of the taints (*āsava*) is called "Noble" (*ariya*).
Or, because he is far removed (*āraka*) from evil things and does not proceed in what is not the right way (*anaya*), he is noble;
showing this meaning as well, he answered the second question with this verse. For evil states such as the taints are considered "not the right way," and these have been abandoned by him.
“Cut off and expelled, he does not tremble because of them; thus they are far from him, and he does not dwell among them;
therefore, ‘evil states are far from him’—it is in this sense [that it is said]. ‘He does not dwell in what is unrighteous’—it is in this sense that he is called ‘noble’ (ariya).
Thus the construction here should be understood. Furthermore, ‘The wise man does not enter a womb-bed’—this, however,”
In this interpretation of the meaning, it is merely a word of praise.

Regarding the question, "How is he one who possesses conduct?"—since one who has attained what is to be attained through conduct deserves to be called "one who possesses conduct," the Blessed One, in order to demonstrate that, answered the third question with the verse beginning, "He who here... In that context, "he who here" means:
"Whoever in this teaching"—"in the practices" (*caraṇesu*) means in the fifteen qualities mentioned in the *Hemavata-sutta*, beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
The locative case is used here in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*). "One who has attained the attainment" (*pattipatto*) means one who has reached that which is to be reached.

What is meant is: "one who has attained *arahantship*, which is to be attained by reason of the practice, for the sake of the practice, and on account of the practice. "One who possesses the practice" (*caraṇavāso*) refers to one who, through these practices, has attained what is to be attained.
"He possesses conduct" (*caraṇavā*): to this extent the question is answered; the rest is words of praise for him.
For he who has reached attainment through his conduct is both skillful and clever, and at all times understands the Dhamma of Nibbāna.
Because his mind is constantly inclined toward Nibbāna, he does not cling anywhere to the aggregates and so forth. And with a mind liberated by the two kinds of liberation, "he has no aversions."

543. However, because one is called a *paribbājaka* (wanderer) through the wandering away from karma and so forth, he explained the fourth question with the verse beginning "Dukkhavepakkam" in order to demonstrate that meaning.
In this context, *vepakkam* is simply *vipāko* (result); that which has suffering as its result is *dukkhavepakkam*.
All karma within the three realms is so called because it generates the suffering of the process of existence (*pavatti*).
"Uddhaṃ" (above) refers to the past. "Adho" (below) refers to the future. "Tiriyaṃ vāpi majjhe" (or across in the middle) refers to the present. For that [present] is neither above nor below;
it is across, between both [past and future], and thus it is called "in the middle. "Paribbājayitvā" means having expelled or driven out.
"Pariññacārī" means one who moves about having delimited [reality] through wisdom. This, then, is the commentary on the previously unexplained terms.

This, however, is the interpretation according to the underlying intention: whatever karma exists that produces suffering—even if it is included within the three periods of time—he dries up all of it with the moisture of craving and ignorance by means of the Noble Path;

having expelled it by rendering it incapable of producing rebirth, and because he has thus expelled it, he is one who "courses in full understanding" (pariññacārī) due to his practice after having fully understood that karma.

And it is not only karma that he has abandoned; by means of the full understanding of abandonment, he has also fully understood these states—deceit, conceit, greed, and anger—and has brought name-and-form to its limit. "He has brought name-and-form to its limit" means he has excluded it; this is the sense. Because of his exclusion of these things—karma and the rest—they call him a "wandering ascetic" (*paribbājaka*). As for the phrase "one who has attained the attainment": [The remainder of the text follows: ...this is the meaning. Furthermore, "attainment" (*patti*) is the reaching of the goal; "attainment" is the act of reaching. It is called "attainment" because one reaches the goal through it. Or alternatively, "attainment" is the state of having reached. What is that? It is the Noble Path. Why is it called "attainment"? Because one attains it. By what means? By the Noble Path. This is his word of praise. 544.
Now, when Sabhiya was thus satisfied by the answering of the questions, [the Blessed One spoke] in the verses of exaltation beginning with "And those three," etc.
In these verses, *osaraṇāni* means places of resort, places of immersion, or bathing-places; the meaning is "views. Since these, together with the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*),...
Taking the sixty-two types of speculative views (diṭṭhigata) mentioned in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, there are sixty-three;
and because these are the doctrines (sita) and teachings (sattha) of the ascetics of other sects, they are to be pointed out by way of their exposition, not by way of their origin.

However, by way of their origin, there is this conventional designation, name, and expression consisting of the notions "woman" and "man," as well as that which arises through false reflections, oral traditions, and so forth.
The thought “one must become such a self” arises as a perverted perception in fools;

those [perceptions] arise depending on both [the body and the mind] and by way of them, not through the direct realization of a self. And the Blessed One, having disciplined and trained in these, has gone to the end of the flood, has gone to the darkness of the flood, and has transcended it.
There is also the reading “oghantaṃ agā,” meaning he has gone to the end of the floods.
Therefore he said: “Those three... [and so on] ...the state beyond darkness.

Following that, with reference to the end of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and to *nibbāna* as the further shore—because of the absence of suffering upon its attainment and because it is the opposite of that [suffering]—he said: “You have gone to the end;
you have gone to the further shore of suffering. Alternatively, the Blessed One is the one who has gone to the further shore, which is *nibbāna*.
Because he has gone [beyond], addressing him, he said: "You have reached the further shore, you have gone to the end of suffering. This is the connection here.
One who is perfectly awakened and awakened by himself is a *sammāsambuddha*. "I think of him as such" means "I think of him alone, and no other"—he speaks thus with great reverence.
"Possessor of radiance" means endowed with radiance through the dispelling of darkness even for others. "Possessor of wisdom" (*mutimā*)...
He is endowed with the wisdom of liberation capable of knowing that which is not dependent on others. "Of abundant wisdom" means of infinite wisdom;
here, omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is intended. "O makers of an end to suffering"—saying this, he addressed him.
"You have carried me across" means you have carried me across my doubt.
546–9. With the verse beginning "Yaṃ me," he speaks of performing an act of homage. In that context, "doubt" (kaṅkhita) is said with reference to the meaning based on the twenty questions;
for he was indeed doubtful regarding them. "In the paths of wisdom" (monapathesu) means in the paths of knowledge (ñāṇapathesu).
"Made free from reeds" (vinaḷīkata) means made devoid of reeds; it is said to mean "cut off. "O Nāga, of the Nāga"—this is one form of address, [and] of one [person].
The connection is with the phrase "rejoicing as it was spoken. "The teaching of the Dhamma" is the elliptical remainder of the text.
"All the gods" refers to those dwelling in the sky and those dwelling on the earth. "On Mount Nārada"—it is said that those two hosts of gods were also wise;
"they too rejoiced" expresses the offering of homage performed with complete faith.
Having heard the prophecy endowed with excellence, which was worthy of rejoicing, he raised his joined palms and said, "Homage to you!

He addressed him as "Purisājañña" (a thoroughbred among men), meaning one who is perfected in birth among men. He called him "Paṭipuggala" (the peerless person), meaning that you, the Buddha, are the counterpart [to all others] through the penetration of the Four Truths;
you are the Teacher through your instruction and your state of being a caravan-leader; and you are the Conqueror of Māra through your overcoming of the four Māras.
The Sage is the Buddha-Sage. "Bases" (*upadhī*) refers to the fourfold division of aggregates, defilements, sense-qualities, and volitional formations.

"Charming" (*vaggū*) means beautiful. "And in merits" (*puññe ca*) means you do not smear yourself with worldly merits by not performing them, or because there is no enjoyment of the fruit of those previously performed in the future;
or it refers to the smearing of craving and views caused by those [merits]. He pays homage to the Teacher while speaking thus.
Having grasped his ankles, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration.
"One who was formerly a follower of another sect" means one who was indeed a member of another sect. "Desires" means wishes for. "With uplifted minds" means with gratified minds.
Furthermore, "I have understood here the diversity of individuals" means that furthermore, I have understood here, regarding the probationary period for those of other sects...
"The diversity of individuals is known; it is not the case that everyone must undergo the probationary period. But by whom should one not undergo probation?
By those who are fire-worshipping ascetics (*aggiya-jaṭila*), by one born of the Sākiya clan, and by one who has come having discarded the [ascetic] marks.
Furthermore, even one who has come without discarding them, if they are endowed with the causes for the attainment of the path and its fruits—such as was the wanderer Sabhiya. Therefore:
The Blessed One said, “But for you, Sabhiya, there is no need for a period of probation (*parivāsa*) for the sake of fulfilling the practices of the sectarians;
it is known to me that you are one who seeks the goal and is endowed with the causes for the attainment of the paths and fruits.

Thus, granting him the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), he said, “Nevertheless, I have recognized here the diversity among individuals (*puggalavemattatā*). But Sabhiya, demonstrating his own earnestness, said:

He said, "If so, venerable sir. All of that and anything else of a similar nature has not been explained here because its meaning is obvious and because it follows the method already stated previously;
therefore, it should be understood according to what was explained before.
[End of] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Sabhiya-sutta of the Suttanipāta-ṭīkā is finished.
7. Commentary on the Sela-sutta:
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Sela-sutta. What is its origin? It is the very same that was stated in its introduction (nidāna). Also, in the sequence of the commentary on the meaning...
The portion that is similar to what has come before should be understood according to the method already explained.
However, regarding that which is new, we shall comment while setting aside those words whose meaning is obvious. "In Aṅguttarāpa": Aṅga itself is that country;
however, because it is not far from the waters (āpo) to the north of the Ganges, it is also called "Uttarāpa. Of which Ganges is it to the north?
"What is water? It is the Mahāmahī-Gaṅgā.
Herein, this is the description of that river from the beginning in order to clarify its manifestation: it is said that this Jambudīpa is ten thousand yojanas in extent.
Of that, an area measuring four thousand yojanas is submerged by water and is designated as the "ocean."
Humans dwell within an area measuring three thousand yojanas. Within that same extent of three thousand yojanas, the Himavat mountain stands established;
it is five hundred yojanas in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, and variegated by five hundred rivers flowing from all sides.
Therein, each lake measures fifty yojanas in length and breadth, fifty yojanas in depth, and is one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference.
In the commentary on the *Pūraḷāsa-sutta*, it is stated that seven great lakes, beginning with Anotatta, are established there.
Among them, Anotatta is surrounded by these five mountains: Sudassana Peak, Citrakūṭa, Kāḷakūṭa, Gandhamādana Peak, and Kelāsa Peak.
Therein, Sudassana Peak is made of gold and is two hundred yojanas in height.
The inner curve is shaped like a crow’s beak, situated so as to conceal that very lake. Citrakūṭa is composed entirely of jewels;

Kāḷakūṭa is made of collyrium; Gandhamādana-kūṭa is made of gold, its interior the color of green gram, covered with various kinds of medicinal herbs, and it stands blazing on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight like glowing embers. Kelāsa-kūṭa is made of silver.
All [the peaks] are equal in height and shape to Sudassana, standing so as to cover that very lake.
All of them rain by the power of the gods and the power of the nāgas, and rivers flow within them. All that water enters into Anotatta alone.
When the moon and sun move either to the south or to the north, they pass through the interval between the mountains.
They illuminate it when flowing straight, but they do not illuminate it when flowing crookedly; for that very reason, the designation "Anotatta" (Untroubled) arose for it.

Therein, bathing-places with charming stone slabs, free from fish and turtles, with water as pure as crystal, are well-prepared, where Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, those whose taints are destroyed, groups of seers, and devas, yakkhas, and others bathe.
And they sport in the pleasure gardens.
On its four sides there are four mouths—a lion’s mouth, an elephant’s mouth, a horse’s mouth, and a bull’s mouth—from which four rivers flow.
On the banks of the river issuing from the lion’s mouth, lions are most numerous.
There are elephants, horses, and bulls with the faces of elephants and so forth.
The river that issues from the eastern direction circles the Anotatta Lake three times clockwise;

without joining the other three rivers, it enters the great ocean by way of the eastern Himalayas, following a path frequented by non-humans. The same applies to the rivers issuing from the western and northern directions.
In the same way, having performed a circumambulation, they enter the great ocean by way of the western Himalayas and the northern Himalayas,
traveling along paths frequented by non-human beings. But the river that has issued from the southern direction, having performed three circumambulations,
travels sixty yojanas straight to the south across a rocky surface, strikes a mountain, and...

Emerging with a circumference of three *gāvutas*, the stream of water traveled sixty *yojanas* through the air and fell upon a rock named Tiyaṅgaḷa; the rock was split by the force of the water's impact.
There, a lotus pond named Tiyaṅgaḷā, measuring fifty *yojanas*, was formed. Having broken the bank of the pond and entered the rock, it [continued for] sixty...

It travels for sixty *yojanas*. Then, having pierced through the solid earth and gone sixty *yojanas* by way of a subterranean passage, it strikes the transverse mountain named Viñjha and flows forth as five streams resembling the five fingers on the palm of a hand.
Having circumambulated Anotatta three times to the right, the place where it flows out is called the "Āvaṭṭagaṅgā. It flows straight...

The place where it has traveled sixty yojanas over the surface of the rock is called the "Kanhagaṅgā" (Black Ganges). The place where it has traveled sixty yojanas through the air is called the "Ākāsagaṅgā" (Sky Ganges).
The area of fifty yojanas at the Tiyaggaḷa rock is called the "Tiyaggaḷapokkharaṇī" (Tiyaggaḷa Lotus Pond).
The place where, having broken the bank and entered the rock, it has traveled sixty yojanas is called the "Bahalagaṅgā" (Thick Ganges).
It is so called. In the place where it has gone sixty yojanas through a subterranean passage after breaking through the earth, it is called the "Ummangaganga.
After striking the transverse mountain named Viñjha, it flows forth in five streams;
in that place, it is called by five names: "Ganga, Yamuna, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī. Thus, these five great Ganges [flow] from the Himavat.
They arise. Among them, that which is this fifth earth is intended here as the "Great Earth Gaṅgā.
Because it is not far from those waters to the north of that Gaṅgā, that country should be understood as "Aṅguttarāpa.
In that country, among the Aṅguttarāpas.
"Traveling on a journey" means undertaking a trip. In this context, the Blessed One’s journeys are of two kinds: hurried journeys and unhurried journeys.
Among these, a hurried journey is traveling immediately upon seeing a person capable of spiritual progress even from afar;
this is to be seen in instances such as the Blessed One’s advance to meet Mahākassapa. For the Blessed One, while advancing toward him, reached him in a mere moment.
He traveled thirty *gāvutas* for the sake of subduing Āḷavaka, and thirty *yojanas* for the sake of Aṅgulimāla.
For the sake of Pukkusāti, however, he traveled forty-five *yojanas*; for Mahākappina, one hundred *yojanas*; and for Dhaniya, he traveled a distance of seven hundred *yojanas*.
This is called a "hurried journey. But by way of visiting villages, market towns, and cities in succession, through the practice of alms-gathering and so forth—
The journey of one who is favoring the world is called a "non-hurried wandering" (*aturitacārikā*); this is what is intended here.
While wandering in such a manner: "with a great community of monks" means with a multitude of ascetics, both great in number and great in virtue.
"With twelve hundred and fifty" means with twelve hundred and fifty monks; that is what is meant.
"Where... [he] arrived. Because of its abundance of market stalls (*āpaṇa*), that town received the name "Āpaṇa.

It is said that twenty thousand market fronts were laid out there. By whichever direction, path, or way that town of the Aṅguttarāpa kingdom was to be reached, he went by that way; he arrived, he went there. That—
"He reached the town" is what is meant.
"Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic": "Keṇiya" is by name, and "matted-hair ascetic" (jaṭila) means a forest-dweller (tāpasa).

It is said that he was a wealthy brahmin, but having undertaken the ascetic life for the sake of protecting his wealth, he gave a gift to the king, acquired a plot of land, and established a hermitage there.
Having established himself as the preceptor for a thousand families, he lived there.
It is said that even the single *tāla* tree in his hermitage produced a golden fruit day after day. During the day, he wore the saffron robes and bound his matted hair;
at night, however, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, he indulged in them as he pleased. Thus he was known as "the Son of the Śākyas."
This is an indication of his high birth. "He has gone forth from the Sakyan clan" is an indication of the fact that he went forth out of faith;
what is meant is that, unovercome by any loss and having abandoned that very clan while it was still undiminished, he went forth out of faith.
"But as for him... is the accusative case used in the sense of describing one who has become such; [it means] "of that venerable Gotama."
The meaning is as follows: "Kalyāṇa" means endowed with excellent qualities; that is to say, supreme. "Kittisaddo" (the sound of fame) refers simply to fame or the sound of praise.
Regarding the opening phrase, "Itipi so bhagavā," this is the construction: "That Blessed One is thus an Arahant, thus a Sammasambuddha...
[and so on]... thus a Bhagavā. This means "for such and such reasons. In that context:

The Blessed One is to be understood as "Arahant" for the following reasons: because of his remoteness (*ārakattā*); because of the destruction of enemies (*arīnaṃ*) and spokes (*arānaṃ*); because of being worthy (*arahattā*) of requisites and so forth; and because of the absence of secrecy (*rahābhāva*) in the performance of evil.

Firstly, he is an Arahant because of his remoteness (*ārakattā*), for he is remote from all defilements due to the total destruction of the defilements along with their latent tendencies by means of the Path. Furthermore, he is an Arahant because those enemies—the defilements—have been slain by him through the Path. Thus, regarding the enemies...

He is also an *arhat* because he has struck [the wheel]. This refers to the wheel of saṃsāra, which has ignorance, existence, and craving for its hub; which has the formative forces (*saṅkhāras*)—meritorious and so forth—as its spokes; which has aging and death as its rim;

and which has been yoked to the chariot of the three realms of existence by being pierced with the axle consisting of the origin of the taints (*āsava*), and which has been revolving since beginningless time.
Having established himself upon the earth of virtue with the feet of energy at the seat of enlightenment, he [struck it] with the hand of faith.

Having taken up the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma, he is an *arahant* because all spokes (of the wheel of existence) have been struck down (*hatā arā*), or because of the striking down of the spokes.

Furthermore, he is an *arahant* because he is worthy (*araha*) of the requisites such as robes and so forth, as well as of honor and respect, due to being the foremost among those worthy of offerings.
And just as in the world some fools, conceited in their own wisdom, commit evil deeds in secret for fear of ill-repute, this one does not do so.
He is called *arahaṃ* because he does not at any time perform evil deeds, even in secret.

And here it is said: “Because he has driven away (*āraka*) and slain (*hata*) the enemies that are the defilements, because he has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, and because he is worthy of the requisites and so forth—that sage is *arahaṃ*.”
“He does not commit evil deeds even in secret; therefore he is called an Arahant.
Because he has awakened to all truths both correctly and by himself, he is the “Perfectly Self-Awakened One” (Sammāsambuddha).

Because he is endowed with the most preeminent clear vision (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa), which are exceedingly purified, he is “One Perfect in Clear Vision and Conduct” (Vijjācaraṇasampanna). Because his going is beautiful, it is a “lovely state” (sugati).
He is the Sugata because he has gone well, gone perfectly, and gone rightly. He is the Knower of the World (*lokavidū*) because he has understood the world in every respect.

For that Blessed One understood, in all its aspects—from its intrinsic nature, its origin, its cessation, and the means to its cessation—the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāraloka*) divided into aggregates, bases, and so forth:
"The world is one: all beings subsist on nutriment. There are two worlds: name and form."
Three worlds are the three feelings. Four worlds are the four nutriments. Five worlds are the five aggregates of clinging.
Six worlds are the six internal sense bases. Seven worlds are the seven stations of consciousness.
Eight worlds are the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds are the nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds are the ten sense bases. Twelve worlds...
“The twelve sense-bases, the eighteen worlds, the eighteen elements”—in this way he understood the world of formations in every respect.
He knew the inclinations of beings, he knew their underlying tendencies, he knew their conduct, he knew their resolutions;

[he knew] those with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good disposition and those of bad disposition, those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct.
"Knowing beings who are capable and incapable" means he understood the world of beings in every respect.
Likewise, one *cakkavāḷa* (world-system) measures twelve hundred thousand, three thousand, and four hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth;
its circumference is three hundred and sixty thousand, ten thousand, and four hundred and fifty *yojanas*.
Therein—
two hundred thousand and forty nahutas;
this much, by its thickness, is reckoned as this Earth.
Four hundred thousand and eighty thousand [yojanas]— to this extent,
by its thickness, does the water rest upon the wind.
Nine hundred thousand [yojanas] the wind rises up into the sky.
"Sixty thousand [yojanas] indeed—this is the configuration of the world.
And herein, regarding its configuration in yojanas:
it plunges eighty-four thousand [yojanas] down into the great ocean.
Just as high as that is Sineru, the supreme mountain;
and by a measure half and half again of that, respectively,
the divine [palaces] are submerged and risen, variegated with various jewels.
Yugandhara, Īsadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana,
Nemindhara, Vinataka, and the great mountain Assakaṇṇa—
these are the seven great rocky peaks surrounding Sineru.
The abodes of the great kings, frequented by gods and yakṣas,
are on Mount Himavat, which is five hundred yojanas high and three thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks,
the city known as Nagavhayā has a trunk and circumference of three to five yojanas;
its trunk and branches extend fifty yojanas in every direction.
It is seven yojanas wide and rises to that same height.
It is by its power that Jambudīpa is made manifest;
it plunges eighty-two thousand [yojanas] deep into the great ocean.
“Right then, a mountain range of rock as high as the world-sphere (cakkavāḷa),
having encircled that entire world-sphere,
stands firm. Therein, the moon’s disk is forty-nine yojanas, the sun’s disk is fifty yojanas, and the realm of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa) is...
The realm of the asuras, the great Avīci hell, and Jambudīpa each measure ten thousand yojanas.
Aparagoyāna measures seven thousand yojanas, as does Pubbavideha; Uttarakuru measures eight thousand yojanas.
Furthermore, each of these great continents is surrounded by five hundred minor islands. All of this together constitutes a single world-system (cakkavāḷa). One...

The world-system (*lokadhātu*). Between the world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*) are the world-antarika hells. Thus, he knew by means of infinite Buddha-wisdom that there are infinite world-spheres and infinite world-systems;
in every way, he understood the world of space. Thus, because he has understood the world in every respect, the Blessed One is to be known as "Knower of the World" (*lokavidū*).
Because there is no one superior to him in his own qualities, he is "Incomparable" (*anuttara*).

He guides those who are to be tamed by means of various methods of discipline; thus, he is the "Charioteer of Men to be Tamed" (*purisadammasārathi*). He instructs and leads to final deliverance according to what is appropriate through the goals pertaining to this life, the life to come, and the ultimate goal;
thus, he is the "Teacher" (*satthā*). The mention of "gods and humans" is intended to define the highest limit [of his audience] and to identify those individuals who are capable [of being trained].

Furthermore, he instructs even the Nāgas and others in the worldly sense. Because he has awakened to everything that is to be known (*neyya*), he is "Awakened" (*buddha*) by virtue of the knowledge pertaining to liberation. Moreover, he is so called because:
"He is possessed of fortune (*bhagya*), he has shattered the defilements (*bhagga*), he is endowed with the [eight] fortunes (*bhaga*), and he is the distributor (*vibhattavā*) of them."
“The Blessed One has abandoned the going to rebirths; therefore, he is the Blessed One. This is the summary here;
however, these words are explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
“He [knows] this world”: that Blessed One [knows] this world. He now indicates what is to be said: “together with its devas,” and so forth.
This is according to the method explained in the *Kasibhāradvāja* and *Āḷavaka* suttas. He lies down himself, having become one who is not led by others.
"By direct knowledge" means by means of higher knowledge (*abhiññā*). "Having realized" means having made it manifest to direct perception.
"He proclaims" means he awakens, makes known, and reveals. He teaches the Dhamma... [pe] ...which is beautiful in the end; that Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, [teaches] the unsurpassed...

Even though he has abandoned the bliss of seclusion, he teaches the Dhamma. And whether he teaches it little or much, he teaches it in such a manner that it is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.

How so? For even a single verse, because of the all-excellence of the Dhamma, is good in the beginning by its first line, good in the middle by its second and third lines, and good in the end by its final line. A discourse with a single connection...

A discourse (*sutta*) is "good in the beginning" by way of its introduction (*nidāna*); it is "good in the end" by way of its conclusion (*nigamana*); and it is "good in the middle" by way of what remains in between.

A discourse with multiple thematic transitions (*anusandhi*) is "good in the beginning" by its first transition; it is "good in the end" by its final one; and it is "good in the middle" by the ones in between.

Furthermore, the entire Dhamma of the Dispensation is "good in the beginning" through the virtue that constitutes its own purpose, and [it is good in the middle and at the end] through serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), the paths (*magga*), and the fruits (*phala*).
It is beautiful in the middle and beautiful in the conclusion through Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is beautiful in the beginning through virtue and concentration;

beautiful in the middle through insight and the paths; and beautiful in the conclusion through the fruits and Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is beautiful in the beginning through the Buddha’s excellent awakening;
beautiful in the middle through the Dhamma’s being well-taught; and beautiful in the conclusion through the Saṅgha’s excellent practice. Having heard that...
It is "good in the beginning" because it leads to the full enlightenment that is to be attained by one practicing for suchness;
it is "good in the middle" because of the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha; and it is "good in the end" because of the enlightenment of a disciple.

Furthermore, it is "good in the beginning" because when heard, it brings about goodness even through the mere hearing, since it suppresses the hindrances and other defilements; and for one who practices it, it is good because it brings about the bliss of serenity and insight.

It is "beautiful in the middle" because it brings about what is beautiful even through the practice; and likewise, when one who has practiced thus reaches the completion of the fruit of practice, it brings about the state of suchness (*tādibhāva*), and thus it is "beautiful in the end" because it brings about what is beautiful even through the fruit of practice.

Furthermore, it is "beautiful in the beginning" due to the purity of its origin, as it originates from the Protector (*nātha*); it is "beautiful in the middle" due to the purity of its purpose (*attha*); and [it is beautiful in the end] due to the purity of its function (*kicca*).
It is "good in the ending. It should be understood that when teaching whether little or much, one teaches precisely in the manner of being "good in the beginning" and so forth.

Regarding such phrases as "with meaning and with phrasing," it should be understood that when teaching this Dhamma, one reveals both the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*) and the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*), illustrating them through various methods according to their respective excellence of meaning.

It is "with meaning" (*sāttha*) because it possesses the perfection of phrasing (*byañjana-sampatti*); it is "with phrasing" because it is endowed with the conjunction of words that reveal, clarify, explain, analyze, elucidate, and define the meaning.

It is "with meaning" due to the perfection of syllables, words, phrases, modes, etymologies, and definitions; it is "with phrasing" due to the profundity of the meaning and the profundity of penetration. It is "with meaning" through the profundity of the goal and the profundity of realization;

it is "with phrasing" through the profundity of the Dhamma and the profundity of the teaching. It is [so called] from the perspective of the analytical knowledge of meaning and the analytical knowledge of inspired speech.

It is "possessing the meaning" (*sāttha*) because it is the domain of the analytical knowledges of the Dhamma and of language; it is "possessing the phrasing" (*sabyañjana*) because it is to be understood by the wise and inspires confidence in those who resemble them.

It is "possessing the meaning" because it inspires confidence in the faithful; it is "possessing the phrasing" because it inspires confidence in worldly people. It is "possessing the meaning" because its intention is profound; it is "possessing the phrasing" because its words are clear.
It is "entirely complete" (*kevalaparipuṇṇa*) by virtue of its total perfection, as there is nothing further to be added.
It is pure because it is free from fault due to the absence of anything that must be removed.

It is the "holy life" (*brahmacariya*) because it is to be practiced by those who have become sublime and excellent through embracing the three trainings, and because it is the state of their conduct. Therefore, it is said: "He proclaims the Dhamma... which is beneficial in its meaning and phrasing... the holy life."
Furthermore, because he teaches with its basis and its origin, he teaches what is good in the beginning;
because he provides the correct meaning according to the capacity of those to be trained and employs reasons and examples, he teaches what is good in the middle;

and because he concludes with the attainment of faith by the listeners, he teaches what is good in the end. Teaching in this way, he proclaims the holy life (*brahmacariya*). And that [holy life] is through practice.

It is "possessing the meaning" (sāttha) because of its proficiency in realization; it is "possessing the phrasing" (sabyañjana) because of its proficiency in the tradition of the scriptures; it is "entirely complete" (kevalaparipuṇṇa) because it is endowed with the five aggregates of dhamma beginning with virtue;
it is "pure" (parisuddha) because it is free from defilements, functions for the sake of crossing over [saṃsāra], and is indifferent to worldly gain;
and it is so called because it is the conduct of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples who have become sublime (brahma) in the sense of being supreme.
It is called "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*); therefore, it is said: "He teaches the Dhamma...
he reveals the holy life. "It is good indeed" means it is excellent; what is meant is that it brings about welfare and brings about happiness.
"With a talk on the Dhamma" refers to one connected with the benefits of drinking [the Dhamma]. For this Keṇiya was waiting for the Blessed One's arrival in the evening.
He heard [the news]. Thinking, "It is shameful to go to see the Blessed One empty-handed;
even for those who abstain from eating at improper times, a drink is permissible," he had five hundred baskets well-prepared with jujube juice and set out.
As it is said in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka: "Then this thought occurred to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic: 'What..."
"Should I now cause [the food] to be taken away from the ascetic Gotama?"—all this should be understood.

Then the Blessed One addressed him with a discourse concerning the benefits of a lodging, as in the *Sekha-sutta* regarding the Sākiyans; with a discourse concerning the flavor of concord among three clansmen in the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove;
and with a discourse concerning the ten bases of talk regarding the monks of the Rathavinīta and Jātibhūma families.
Thus, with a discourse appropriate to that moment and connected with the benefits of drinking water, he demonstrated the merit of giving such a gift;
he incited them by directing them toward the further performance of similar meritorious deeds; he inspired them by generating enthusiasm;
and he gladdened them by exhorting them through the excellence of results both visible in this life and in the future. Therefore, he said:
“With a discourse on the Dhamma... [as before] ...he gladdened him. He, becoming even more deeply devoted to the Blessed One, invited the Blessed One;
and although the Blessed One declined three times, he finally consented. Therefore it was said: “Then Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic...
[as before] ...the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.”
But for what purpose did the Blessed One refuse? [It was because he thought: "Through his repeated requests, his merit will increase;
he will prepare a greater amount, and from that which is prepared for twelve hundred and fifty monks, it will reach sixteen hundred.
If it is asked, "Where would three hundred more come from?"—it was because even when the meal was not yet prepared, the brahmin Sela...
"He will go forth together with three hundred young men; seeing this, the Blessed One spoke thus.

"Friends and companions" (*mittāmaccā*) means friends and laborers. "Kinsmen and blood-relations" (*ñātisālohitā*) means those of common blood, such as sons, daughters, and other remaining relatives connected by birth from a single womb.
"By which" (*yena*) means because of which. "Mine" (*me*) means my. "Personal service" (*kāyaveyyāvaṭikaṃ*) means service performed with the body.
“He prepares a maṇḍalamāḷa” means he constructs a pavilion with a white canopy.
“Of the three Vedas” refers to the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda. “Together with the Nighaṇḍu and the Keṭubha” means including the Nighaṇḍu and the Keṭubha.
“Nighaṇḍu” is a treatise that elucidates synonyms for names, trees, and so forth. “Keṭubha” is the detailed exposition of ritual procedures.
The treatise for the benefit of poets; "together with the analysis of syllables" means for those who possess the analysis of syllables.

"Analysis of syllables" refers to phonology (*sikkhā*) and etymology (*nirutti*). Regarding "those for whom history is the fifth": having made the *Atharvaveda* the fourth, "history"—which consists of ancient narratives associated with such expressions as "Thus it was, thus it was"—is the fifth for them.

"Those for whom history (itihāsa) is the fifth. Of those for whom history is the fifth, one who studies and knows the *pada* [Vedic word-text] and the remaining grammar (*byākaraṇa*) is called a "reciter" (*padaka*) and an "exegete" (*veyyākaraṇa*).

One who is not deficient and is a complete practitioner in the *Lokāyata*—the treatise on caviling (*vitaṇḍavāda*)—and in the twelve-thousand-verse treatise on the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), is so described regarding the *Lokāyata* and the marks of a Great Man.
"Without decline" (*anavayo*); what is meant is that there is no decline (*avayo*). "Decline" refers to one who is unable to sustain those [qualities] either in meaning or in the text.
"Jaṅghāvihāra" means a walking-vihāra, which is for the purpose of refreshing the legs in order to dispel the fatigue produced by sitting for long periods;
what is meant is a journey that is not too long. "Anucaṅkamamāno" means while actually walking back and forth (*caṅkamamāno*). "Anuvicaramāno" means from here...
"And while wandering," [he arrived at] "the hermitage of Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic," meaning the dwelling-place of Keṇiya’s hermitage.

"A wedding" (*āvāha*) means the taking of a bride; "a marriage" (*vivāha*) means the giving away of a bride. "A great sacrifice" (*mahāyañña*) means a grand sacrificial rite. "The Lord of Magadha" (*māgadha*) means the ruler of the Magadhas.
Because he was endowed with a great army, he was called "Seniya. "Bimbī" means gold; therefore, because her complexion was like the finest gold, she was so named.
"Bimbisāra. He has been invited by me; that is, he has been invited by me.
Then the brahmin, because of his past meritorious deeds, upon hearing the word "Buddha," was as if sprinkled with the Deathless (amata).
Out of wonder, he said: "Sir Keṇiya, do you say 'Buddha'? The other, explaining it as it truly is, said: "'Buddha,' sir..."
“O Sela, I say so. Then, in order to strengthen his conviction, he questioned him again, and the other replied in the same way.
Thereupon, demonstrating how difficult it is even in hundreds of thousands of eons to hear the word “Buddha,” he said:
“Even this sound, namely ‘Buddha,’ is rare in the world. In this context, *yadidaṃ* is a particle; it means “that which is this,” as in “this which is [the Buddha].”
Then the brahmin, having heard the word "Buddha," thought, wishing to investigate whether he was truly a Buddha or merely one who has the name "Buddha," or he spoke thus:
"Indeed, [the signs] have appeared... [and so on] ...one who has drawn aside the veil.
In this context, "in the mantras" means in the Vedas. "It is said that a Tathāgata will arise"—thus the Suddhāvāsa devas [spoke] beforehand.
Having inserted the marks [of a Great Man] under the guise of Brahmins, they teach the Vedas, thinking:
"By following that, beings of great influence will come to know the Tathāgata. Therefore, in the past, the marks of a Great Man appeared in the Vedas;

however, after the Tathāgata had attained parinibbāna, they gradually disappeared, and thus they do not exist at present. "Of a Great Man" (mahāpurisa) means one who is great through qualities such as aspiration, the undertaking of vows, the acquisition of knowledge, and compassion.
"For a person. "Only two destinations" means only two final ends (*niṭṭhā*).

Now, although this word *gati* occurs in the sense of a division of existence in such passages as "Sāriputta, there are these five destinations," in the sense of a dwelling place in such passages as "The forest is the destination of wild beasts," in the sense of wisdom in such passages as "Thus possessing supreme intelligence," and in the sense of a state of dispersion in such passages as "gone to its destination," it should here be understood in the sense of a final end.
In this context, although a universal monarch (cakkavatti) possesses certain characteristics, a Buddha does not possess those very same ones.
Nevertheless, on account of their commonality of birth, they are said to be "those very same ones. Therefore it was said: "of one who is endowed with which [characteristics].
"If he dwells in the household" means if he lives in a house. "He becomes a universal monarch" refers to one endowed with four marvelous qualities.

He is a *rājā* (king) because he gladdens the world through the bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*). He sets the wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*) in motion; he turns [the wheel] by means of the four wheels of prosperity, and he causes others to turn by them as well.
Furthermore, he is a *cakkavatti* because in him there exists the turning of the wheels of postures for the benefit of others.
Here, "king" (*rājā*) is the general term, while "wheel-turner" (*cakkavatti*) is the specific qualification. He acts according to the Dhamma, thus he is "righteous" (*dhammika*).

The meaning is that he conducts himself according to the *ñāya* (the right method) and with equity (*sama*). Having obtained sovereignty through the *dhamma*, he has become a king; thus, he is a *dhammarāja*.

Alternatively, he is *dhammika* because he practices the *dhamma* for the welfare of others, and a *dhammarāja* because he practices the *dhamma* for his own welfare. He is *cāturanta* because he is the lord of the four quarters;
the meaning is that he is the lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans and adorned by the four kinds of continents. Internally, [he is the conqueror] of adversaries such as anger...
He is a "conqueror" (vijitāvī) because he has conquered all kings abroad. He is one who has "attained stability in his realm" (janapadatthāvariyappatta):
he has attained a state of permanence and steadfastness in his realm such that it cannot be shaken by anyone;
or else, the realm has attained stability under him—being free from anxiety, devoted to its own duties, immovable, and unshakable—and thus he is one who has attained stability in his realm.

“Seyyathidaṃ” is a particle; its meaning is “of these, which are they? The wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*), and so forth, up to the counselor-treasure (*pariṇāyakaratana*) as the seventh—these have been explained in all their aspects in the commentary on the *Ratana-sutta*.

Among them, this Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) conquers what is unconquered by means of the wheel-treasure, and he traverses the conquered realm at his pleasure by means of the elephant and horse treasures, and by means of the counselor-treasure...

He protects the conquered territory and experiences the pleasure of enjoyment through the remaining [treasures]. For him, the application of the power of exertion is fulfilled by means of the first [treasure];

the application of the power of abundance is fulfilled by means of the treasures of the elephant, the horse, and the householder; and the application of the power of counsel is fulfilled by means of the treasure of the counselor.
Through the treasures of the woman and the jewel, the fruit of the threefold application of power is realized. He experiences the pleasure of wealth through the treasures of the woman and the jewel.

The remaining [pleasures] consist of the bliss of sovereignty. It should be understood that, in particular, his first three [pleasures] are accomplished through the power of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa*);

the middle three through the power of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*); and the final one through the power of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*).
"More than a thousand" means exceeding one thousand. "Valiant" means those of a fearless nature. "Heroic in form" means having bodies resembling those of the sons of the gods.
Thus, some [explain it] in this way. However, the true nature here is as follows: "vīra" refers to supreme heroes;
"vīraṅga" is the limb of heroes, meaning that which is the cause of heroism, i.e., energy (*vīriya*). Those whose form (*rūpa*) consists of the limbs of heroes are "vīraṅgarūpā";
the meaning is that they are, as it were, bodies made of energy. "Crushers of enemy armies" means that if the enemy army should stand facing them, they crush it.
The intention is that he is capable of overcoming negligence. "By means of the Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the five precepts, beginning with "A living being must not be killed.

Regarding the statement, "He is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, who has uncovered the veil in the world," this means that in the world shrouded by the darkness of defilements—covered by the seven veils of greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, ignorance, and misconduct—he has uncovered those veils, and thus light has arisen all around him.
"Having offered and standing"—this refers to one whose covering is removed (*vivaṭṭacchado*). Here, by the first word, his worthiness for worship is expressed;

by the second, the reason for that, namely, that he is a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddho*); and by the third, it should be understood that his state of having the covering removed is stated as being due to his Buddhahood.
Alternatively, "one whose covering is removed and whose concealment is gone" (*vivaṭṭacchado*) means one who is devoid of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and devoid of concealment (*chadana*).
Thus, by the absence of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he is an *Arahant*, and by the absence of concealment (*chadana*), he is a *Sammāsambuddha*;

in this way, two causes are stated for each of the first two titles. Herein, the second intrepidity establishes the first [title], the first establishes the second, and the third and fourth establish the third.
Furthermore, the first is the "Dhamma-eye" (*dhammacakkhu*) and the second is the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakkhu*).
It should be understood that he accomplishes the third [eye], the all-seeing eye (*samantacakkhu*).
Now, desiring to go into the presence of the Blessed One, he said: "But where, sir... [etc. ...is the Perfectly Enlightened One?
Regarding the phrase "when it was thus spoken" and so forth: *yenesa* means "in whichever direction"; *nīlavanarājī* means a row of blue-colored trees.
The forest, it is said, was like a mass of clouds. Pointing out where the Blessed One was dwelling at that time, he said:
"Where, Sela, this line of dark-blue woods is. In this context, the phrase "he dwells there" (*so viharati*) is an ellipsis to be supplied;
or else, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. "Step by step" (*pade pade*) means near each step. By this, he prohibits hurried walking.

He states the reason, "For they are difficult to approach," meaning that because they are difficult to approach, therefore, "let my lords come in this manner. If one asks, "For what reason are they difficult to approach?
it is because they move alone like lions. For just as lions move alone due to the absence of any need for companions, so too do they out of a desire for seclusion.
With the words, "And when I... and so forth, he instructs those young brahmins in etiquette.
In that context, "do not dig up" means do not bring them forth; "do not speak" is what is intended. "Let them wait" means let them bide their time; the meaning is:
let them remain silent until the discourse reaches its conclusion.
"He investigated" means he searched. "For the most part" means he saw many and saw few. Then, as for those which he did not...
Seeing them, he spoke while pointing them out: "except for two. "He doubts" means he generates doubt or a longing, thinking, "O, would that I might see them!
"He is perplexed" means that searching here and there for them, he is distressed; he is unable to see them.
"He does not resolve" means that because of that perplexity, he does not reach a definitive conclusion. "He does not become confident" means...
Consequently, one does not attain confidence in the Blessed One, thinking, "This one possesses the complete marks.

Or rather, doubt (*kaṅkhā*) is said to be very weak uncertainty (*vimati*), while perplexity (*vicikicchā*) is middling; non-resolution (*anadhimuccanatā*) is strong, and through these three states, there is a state of turbidity in the mind due to lack of serene confidence (*asampasāda*).
“Kosohita” means concealed by the sheath of the prepuce. “Vatthaguyha” refers to the private organ. For the Blessed One’s private organ is like that of a noble elephant:
it is concealed by a sheath, golden-hued, and resembles the interior of a lotus.
Not seeing it because it was covered by his garment, and not perceiving its great extent because his tongue had gone inside his mouth, he [failed to see] those two characteristics.
He was full of doubt and perplexity. As for the phrase "of such a form," what kind of form is it? What need is there for us to say anything here?
This has already been stated by the Elder Nāgasena himself when questioned by King Milinda:
"It was difficult to do, venerable Nāgasena, that which was done by the Blessed One. Why so, Great King? [The Elder replied: "Because it created an occasion for shame among the great multitude."

“Venerable sir, he showed [the Buddha] to Brahmāyu the brahmin, to his pupil Uttara Bāvari, to the sixteen brahmins who were pupils of Bāvari, and to the three hundred young men who were pupils of the brahmin Sela.
“Great king, the Blessed One does not show what is hidden; the Blessed One shows a shadow, having fashioned it through supernormal power (iddhi) and clothed in a lower garment.”
“It shows only a shadow-form, girt with a waist-band and clothed in a robe, O Great King.
“But when the shadow-form is seen, is not the [body] itself seen, venerable sir? “Let that be, Great King. A being who could perceive it by seeing the heart-form would exist;
but the Perfectly Enlightened One would have to extract the flesh of the heart and show it to him. “You are clever, venerable Nāgasena.”

"Having bent down" means having drawn out. Herein, its length is indicated by the tracing along the ear-canal, its thinness by the tracing along the nostril-canal, and its breadth by the covering of the forehead; thus it should be understood.
