"Of the teachers and the teachers' teachers" means of both the teachers and the teachers' own teachers. "In his own praise" means in his own virtues.
554. "Paripuṇṇakāyo" means one whose body is complete due to its perfection in the [major] marks and because of having no deficiency in limbs or minor parts.

"Suruci" means one who possesses the splendor of a beautiful body. "Sujāto" means well-born, being perfectly formed through the excellence of height and girth, as well as the excellence of physical configuration.
"Cārudassano" means lovely to behold, producing no satiety even for those looking for a long time, and being free from repulsiveness and delightful.
“Of lovely appearance” (*cārudassano*) means one whose appearance is beautiful. Some, however, say: “‘Of lovely appearance’ means having beautiful eyes.
“Golden-hued” (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇo*) means having a complexion similar to gold. “You are eighty”—this is to be construed with all the preceding words.
“With very white teeth” (*susukkadāṭho*) means having teeth that are exceedingly white. For from the Blessed One’s teeth, rays of extreme whiteness stream forth like the rays of the moon.
Therefore he said: "You have very white teeth.
(555) Regarding the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), he spoke thus as a conclusion by way of a different expression, referring to the very same words already mentioned previously.
(556) Now, praising the Blessed One with those marks among them that were most pleasing to himself, he said:
“With clear eyes,” and so forth. For the Blessed One has clear eyes due to the perfection of the five-colored clarity; he has a beautiful face because his face resembles the full orb of the moon;

he is tall (*brahā*) due to the perfection of his height and girth; he is straight (*uju*) because of the straightness of his limbs like those of Brahmā; and he is majestic (*patāpavā*) because of his radiant splendor.
Furthermore, what was stated previously here is being praised by way of this method: “In the midst of the community of recluses.”
It is said again: "For one such as this shines thus. This same method applies to the following verse as well.

(557–8) "Possessing supreme beauty" means endowed with the highest physical splendor. "Of Jambusaṇḍa" means of Jambudīpa. He spoke thus while describing sovereignty through its manifestation; however, a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) is the lord of all four continents.
(559) "Kṣatriyas" refers to those of noble birth. "Bhojas" refers to those who possess wealth. "Kings" refers to whoever exercises rule. "Followers" refers to...
"Followers" refers to servants. "King of kings" means having become a king worthy of worship by other kings; the intended meaning is that he is a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
"Lord of men" means having become the sovereign ruler over humanity.
When this was said, the Blessed One [replied]: "Those who are Worthy Ones (*arahant*), Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*), when their own praises are being recited..."
Fulfilling Sela’s wish with the words, “I am a king,” he said, “I am a king. The intended meaning here is this:
O Sela, as for what you ask of me—“You ought to become a king, a wheel-turning monarch”—be at ease in that regard; for I am a king.
And even though I possess kingship, just as another king, though being a king, might rule over a hundred leagues, [so do I].

Whether it be two, three, four, or five hundred yojanas, or even a thousand yojanas, or even the extent of the four continents as a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), my domain is not limited in such a way. For I am the unsurpassed King of Dhamma;
from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci hell, and across immeasurable world-systems in the horizontal directions, I rule. As far as...

For existence is divided into categories such as the footless, the two-footed, and so forth, and I am the foremost among them. Indeed, there is no one who is my equal in virtue... [and so on] ...or in the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Thus, as a King of Dhamma, I turn the unsurpassed wheel by means of the unsurpassed Dhamma known as the factors of enlightenment—divided into the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth—through the wheel of command: "Abandon this; enter upon and dwell in that," and so forth.
“Moreover, monks, this is the noble truth of suffering,” and so forth; thus, by means of the Dhamma of the scriptures, it is indeed the Wheel of Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase “the wheel that cannot be turned back”: that wheel which is irreversible by any ascetic... [or] by anyone in the world.
Having seen the Blessed One thus revealing himself, Sela, filled with rapture and joy, for the sake of strengthening [his resolve]—
He spoke two verses beginning with, “Do you claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One? Therein, he asked:
“Who indeed is the general?”—asking who was the general that followed the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, who rules according to Dhamma.
At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was seated on the Blessed One’s right side, like a heap of gold.
Shining with glory as if [with] a crown, the Blessed One, demonstrating this, spoke the verse beginning with "set in motion by me.
Therein, "born after the Tathāgata" means born for the sake of the Tathāgata; the meaning is that he was born with the Tathāgata as the cause.
(564) Having thus answered the question, "Who indeed is the general?", regarding what Sela said—"Do you claim to be a Perfectly Awakened One?"—the Blessed One replied:

Desiring to make him free from doubt there, and wishing to make it known that "I do not claim to be the Buddha merely on the basis of my word, but rather for this reason I am the Buddha," he spoke the verse beginning with "That which is to be directly known.
In this context, "that which is to be directly known" refers to both clear knowledge (*vijjā*) and liberation (*vimutti*).
However, the truths of the path and the origin [of suffering] are, respectively, to be developed and abandoned; thus, by the mention of the cause...
However, because their fruits are established, their fruits—the truth of cessation and the truth of suffering—are indeed already stated.
For it is thus stated here: "that which is to be realized has been realized; that which is to be fully understood has been fully understood.

Thus, demonstrating both the fruit of the cultivation of the Four Truths and true knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti), he says: "Having awakened to what is to be awakened to, he is an Awakened One (Buddha)."
“I am born,” thus he establishes his Buddhahood by means of a logical reason.
Having thus manifested himself in a non-figurative sense, and in order to dispel the brahmin’s doubts regarding himself, he spoke three verses beginning with “In the Vinaya.
Therein, *sallakatta* means one who has extracted the seven arrows, such as the arrow of passion (*rāga*).
"Brahmabhūto" means having become supreme. "Atitulo" means having transcended the scale (*tula*), having transcended comparison; the meaning is that he is peerless.
"Mārasenappamaddano" means the crusher of the army of Māra, which is designated as the retinue of Māra in the passage beginning with "Lust is your first army" and ending with "and he despises others.
"Sabbāmitte" refers to the aggregates, defilements, formations, Death, the Son of the Devas, and other such Māras.
"Having brought all adversaries under his control" means having brought them into his own power. "Fearless from every quarter" means being without fear from any source.

568–70. When this was said, the brahmin Sela, at that very moment conceiving faith in the Blessed One and desiring to go forth, spoke these three verses beginning with "May your honors [grant me]," as was fitting for one whose supporting conditions had reached full maturity.
Being rightly exhorted: therein, one "of dark birth" (*kaṇhābhijātiko*) is one born into a low caste family such as the Caṇḍālas.

Then those young brahmins, likewise desiring to go forth, spoke this verse—“If this pleases you, sir”—just as those sons of good family who had previously performed meritorious deeds [had spoken] to him.
Then Sela, his heart filled with joy, showing them [the way], and requesting the going-forth, spoke the verse beginning with “O Brahmins.”
573. Then the Blessed One [explained] that because in the past, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Padumuttara, Sela had been the leader of those very three hundred men;

having built a monastic cell together with them and performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he experienced the prosperity of gods and humans in succession, and in his final existence, he became their teacher.

Having sacrificed, they were reborn; and that karma of theirs had matured for the ripening of liberation and served as the necessary condition (*upanissaya*) for their becoming "come-hither" monks (*ehibhikkhu*).
Therefore, ordaining them all through the *ehibhikkhu* going-forth, he spoke the verse beginning with "Well-expounded.
In this context, "visible here and now" (*sanditthika*) means directly perceptible. "Timeless" (*akālika*) refers to the arising of the fruit immediately following the path.

It is not a fruit to be attained at a later time. "Wherein" means for what purpose. For renunciation, which has the holy life of the path as its purpose, is not in vain for one who is diligent, free from lapses in mindfulness, and training in the three trainings. Therefore he said:
"Well-expounded... [and so on]... for one who trains."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One said, "Come, monks. They all, having taken up their bowls and robes, arrived through the air and paid homage to the Blessed One.
It was with reference to this attainment of the status of "come-hither monks" (ehibhikkhu) that the compilers of the Council said:
"Sela indeed received... [the rest] ...the full ordination."
“Having finished eating” means he had eaten. “With hand removed from the bowl” means with the hand taken away from the bowl; that is to say, his hand was withdrawn.

In this context, the word “having approached” (*upagantvā*) should be understood as a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*); otherwise, it would not be logical for him to sit down to one side after [merely] having finished eating.
574. "The fire-sacrifice is the chief," said the Blessed One, speaking thus as an expression of appreciation in accordance with Keṇiya’s own inclinations.
In this context, it is said that "the fire-sacrifice is the chief of sacrifices" because there is no sacrifice for the brahmins without the service of the sacred fire;
the meaning is that the fire-sacrifice is the best and the primary. Because it is the first to be recited by those studying the Vedas, the Sāvittī is [the chief] of the meters (*chandas*).
It is called the "mouth. Because he is the best among humans, the king is called the "mouth. Because it is the support and the refuge of rivers, the ocean is called the "mouth.
Because one recognizes the constellations by means of the moon's conjunction—thinking, "Today is Kattikā;
today is Rohiṇī"—and because it creates light and possesses a gentle nature, the moon is called the "mouth of the constellations. Because it is the foremost among those that burn...

The sun is called "the foremost of those that burn. But because they are the most preeminent among those worthy of offerings, specifically with reference to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha at that time, it is said:
"For those desiring merit, the Saṅgha is indeed the foremost of those who sacrifice.
By this, he shows that the Saṅgha is the gateway for the influx of merit.
576. He spoke this verse of self-proclamation, beginning with “That refuge. Its meaning is as follows: The Blessed One is possessed of vision through his five eyes;
because we went to that refuge on the eighth day from now, therefore, within seven nights, we have been tamed by your unsurpassed taming in your teaching. Oh, the power of your refuge!
577–8. After that, having praised the Blessed One with two verses, he requested a salutation with the third:
“These three hundred bhikkhus stand here with palms joined;
O Hero, stretch out your feet, so that the Nāgas may pay homage to the Teacher.”
The commentary on the Sela Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Paramatthajotikā, is completed. 8.
Commentary on the Salla Sutta.
580. *Animitta* is the Salla Sutta. What is its origin? It is said that the Blessed One had a certain lay follower as an attendant;
his son died, and overcome by grief for his son, he remained without food for seven days.
Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One went to his house and spoke this sutta for the purpose of dispelling his sorrow.
In this context, "signless" (*animitta*) means being devoid of a sign consisting of an action or a cause.
For instance, in cases such as, "When I prick my eye or raise my eyebrow, by that sign steal that goods," there is a sign consisting of an action or a cause;
it is not so with life. Indeed, it is impossible to obtain [the assurance]: "As long as I am doing this or that, you live."

"May I not die. Regarding "not known": for this very reason, it is impossible to know with certainty, either by way of the limit of the lifespan in a particular destiny, that "he must live for such a length of time or for such a length of time.
For while the lifespan of those in the realms of the Four Great Kings and so forth is limited, it is not so for mortals; thus, too, it is not known with certainty.
It is "difficult" because its mode of existence is dependent on numerous conditions; it is not easily maintained.
For it is dependent on inhalation, dependent on exhalation, dependent on the great primary elements, dependent on physical nutriment, dependent on heat, and dependent on consciousness.
Indeed, one does not live even if one stops breathing, nor does one live if one stops being conscious.
And among the four elements, first, through the provocation of the earth element, the body becomes rigid like a block of wood, similar to one bitten by a snake with a wooden mouth. As it is said:
"The body becomes rigid, as if bitten by a snake with a wooden mouth."
"By the provocation of the earth element, he becomes like a log at the mouth [of a river].
By the provocation of the water element, having reached a state of putrefaction, with his pus, flesh, and blood flowing away, he remains as nothing but bones and skin. As it is said:
"The body becomes putrid, like one bitten by a putrid-mouthed [insect]."
“By the provocation of the water element, he becomes like one with a putrid mouth.
By the provocation of the fire element, he burns all over as if cast into a pit of glowing embers. As it is said:
“The body becomes scorched, as if bitten by the mouth of a flame.”
“By the provocation of the fire element, he becomes as if at the mouth of a flame.
By the provocation of the air element, his joints and ligaments are severed, and he becomes like a skeleton being pulverized after being crushed with stones. As it is said:
“The body is cut asunder, as if pierced by the edge of a sword.”
"By the disturbance of the air element, he becomes like one with a sword in his mouth.
Thus, even when the elements are disturbed and the body is corrupted, one does not live.

But when those elements function equally, performing their respective functions such as mutual support, then life proceeds. In this way, life is dependent upon the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, during famines and similar crises, the loss of life among beings due to the cessation of food is indeed evident. Thus, life is dependent upon physical nutriment.
Likewise, when the kamma-born heat that digests what is eaten and drunk has been exhausted, beings who reach the end of their lives are also clearly evident.
Thus, life is dependent upon heat. But when consciousness has ceased, from the moment of its cessation onwards—
It is well known in the world that "life does not belong to beings. Thus, life is dependent upon consciousness.
Because its mode of existence is thus dependent on numerous conditions, it should be understood as fragile.
And it is "limited" (paritta), meaning small; compared to the life of the devas, it is like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass, lasting for only a moment of consciousness.
Or it is "limited" (paritta) by way of its absence in the upward direction. For even a being with an extremely long lifespan has lived by means of a past mind, but does not live and will not live;
he will live by means of a future mind, but does not live and has not lived; and he lives by means of a present mind, but has not lived and will not live. And this has been said:
“Life, the physical self, and all pleasure and pain—these are joined within a single moment of consciousness; the passing of a moment is swift.
Even those gods who remain for eighty-four thousand eons,”
“Indeed, even they do not truly live, being bound by two kinds of mental states.

And that life is joined with suffering; thus, although this life is signless, unrecognized, and characterized by hardship and meagerness, it is nonetheless associated with the suffering of contact with cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, as well as the suffering of formations, the suffering of change, and the suffering of suffering itself.
"Endowed. What is meant by this? Since such is the life of mortals, therefore, as long as that [life] has not reached its exhaustion, you should cultivate only the practice of Dhamma;
do not grieve for your son. 581. Or perhaps you might think: "Even though I protected my son with all available means, he has died; therefore..."
"Do not grieve even thus. For there is no means by which those who are born do not die; it is said that it is impossible for anyone to protect beings born from death by any means whatsoever.
Then, because he thought, "Venerable sir, having reached old age, death is indeed appropriate; my son was too young when he died," [he spoke].

Therefore he said: “Even having reached old age, they reach death; for such is the nature of living beings. This means that whether one has reached old age or not, there is no certainty regarding death.
Now, establishing this point by way of an illustration, he said: “Like ripe fruits,” and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:
Just as, when trees are heated by the sun’s rays from the time of sunrise onwards, the essence of the earth and the essence of water in ripe fruits proceed in this sequence—
from leaf to branch, from branch to trunk, and from trunk to root—
thus entering back into the earth itself from the root; whereas from the time of their descent [into the soil], they proceed from the earth back to the root.
From the root it ascends to the trunk; in this way, by successive stages, it further ascends to the branches, leaves, and sprouts.
As it thus ascends, when the fruit has reached full maturity, it does not enter the base of the stalk.
Then, as the base of the stalk is scorched by the heat of the sun, a feverish inflammation arises. Because of that, those fruits fall every morning at all times; because they fall every morning—
There is fear; the meaning is that there is fear of falling. Thus, for mortals who are born, there is constant fear of death.
For beings are like fruit on the verge of ripening.
Furthermore: “Just as for a potter... [the life of beings is]... their very livelihood. Therefore: “Both the young and... [are subject to] their final destination.”
Grasp it thus; and having grasped it thus, grasp it also in this way: "Death [overcomes] them... or kinsmen their kinsmen.
And because neither father protects his son, nor do kinsmen protect their kinsmen, therefore, even while they look on...
he is led away. Herein, this is the construction: even as the kinsmen are looking on, [he is led away] by various and manifold means, such as "O mother! or "O father! and so forth.
While mortals are still lamenting, one by one they are led away like a victim cow to the slaughter; see this, lay follower, how the world is without refuge.

587. In this regard, those such as the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas who are endowed with fortitude know that "the world is thus assailed by death and old age, and it is not possible for anyone to provide protection"; therefore, being wise, they do not...
They grieve having understood the course of the world; that is to say, having known this nature of the world, they do not grieve.
(Verse 588) But you, for whom there is no path... [you] lament. What is meant?
You do not know the path by which he came when he entered his mother’s womb, nor the path he went when he passed away from here and went elsewhere—for him, these two...
"Without seeing [the truth] before you, you lament in vain. But the wise, seeing and understanding the course of the world, do not grieve.
Now, in order to establish the pointlessness of the lamentation mentioned here in the phrase "you lament in vain," he says:
"If one were to lament... and so forth. In that context, *udabbaheti* means he would pull out, bear, or produce within himself.
The meaning is as follows: "Being deluded, he harms himself" means that, having become deluded, he afflicts himself.
"If one who is discerning were to do it" means that if such a person were to undertake any such matter, even a discerning person would lament it. 590.
Regarding the phrase "not by weeping," the construction here is as follows: "But no one [attains] peace of mind through weeping or through sorrow."
Furthermore, for one who weeps and laments, suffering arises even more intensely, and the body is afflicted by disfigurement and other such conditions.

591. "By that, the departed do not protect" means that by means of that lamentation, those who have passed away do not preserve themselves nor sustain themselves; it does not serve as a benefit to them. Therefore, lamentation is useless.

592. Not only is it useless, it brings about what is harmful. Why? Because, "not abandoning sorrow... [he] fell under its power. In this context, *anutthunanto* means grieving; *vasamanvagū* means having come under its power. 593.
Having thus shown both the uselessness and the harmful nature of sorrow, he now spoke the words beginning with "See others too," offering advice for the purpose of removing sorrow.
In that passage, *gamine* means one who is going, standing ready to depart for the next world.
This has been said. "While living beings here are still quivering" means while beings here are indeed trembling with the fear of death.
(594) "In whatever way" means in whatever manner they imagine, thinking, "He will be long-lived; he will be free from disease. Then it turns out quite otherwise than that;
thus, even one who was so imagined dies, and even becomes diseased. Such is this state of being separated.
"It exists as the opposite of what is conceived; see, lay follower, such is the nature of the world"—thus should the intended application here be understood.
"Having heard from an Arahant" means having heard such a teaching of the Dhamma from an Arahant.

"It is not possible for me [to have him back]" means that the deceased, fully understanding that "it is no longer possible for me to have him live again," has ceased his lamentation; this is what is meant.
597. Furthermore: “Just as one would extinguish a burning house... and so forth.

In this context, he should be understood as wise (*dhīra*) by virtue of his steadfastness (*dhiti-sampadā*), possessed of insight (*sapañña*) by virtue of his natural wisdom (*sābhāvikapaññā*), learned (*paṇḍita*) by virtue of his wisdom derived from extensive study (*bāhusaccapaññā*), and skillful (*kusala*) by virtue of his reflective nature (*cintakajātikatā*).
Alternatively, he may be associated with the wisdoms consisting of reflection, hearing, and cultivation (*cintāmayasutamayabhāvanāmayapaññā*).
598–9. Not only grief alone, but lamentation... [and so on] ...the dart within oneself. Therein, they long—that is, craving.
Mental distress (*domanassa*) is mental suffering. One should extract it; that is, pull it out.

"The dart" refers to this very thing, which is called a dart in the sense of being difficult to remove and in the sense of piercing inwardly, or it refers to the sevenfold dart previously mentioned, such as lust (*rāga*) and the rest. For in this regard—
"With the dart pulled out, the one with the dart pulled out... [etc. ...extinguished"—thus he concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship.
Therein, "unattached" means not dependent on craving or views. "Having reached" means having attained. The remainder is of plain meaning because it was already explained previously;
therefore, it is not commented upon here.
The commentary on the *Salla-sutta* in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, within the *Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā* known as the *Paramatthajotikā*, is finished. 9.
The commentary on the *Vāseṭṭha-sutta*.
"Thus have I heard": this is the Vāseṭṭha Sutta. What is its origin? It is precisely that which has been stated in its introduction (nidāna).
As for its commentary on the meaning, we shall provide it by following the established methods and explaining those words whose meaning is already clear.
"Icchānaṅgala" is the name of a village. Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Todeyya are honorific titles of wealthy brahmins. Pokkharasāti—
"Jāṇussoṇī" refers to the fortune-tellers. It is said that among them, one was born as a lotus in a lotus pond on the slopes of the Himālaya;
another ascetic, having taken that lotus and seeing a boy lying within it, raised him and presented him to the king.
Because he had lain in a lotus (*pokkhara*), they gave him the name "Pokkharasāti. [He occupied] a certain high position.
It was on account of this that he obtained the position of family priest known as Jāṇussoṇi, and by that alone he became renowned.
Why did all those other well-known and eminent brahmin mahāsālās reside at Icchānaṅgala? It was for the purpose of reciting and examining the Vedas.
At that time, it seems, there were brahmins who were experts in the Vedas in the Kosala country.
They would assemble in that very village for the purpose of reciting the Vedas and for the purpose of investigating their meaning.
For this reason, they too would come from their own villages of wealth and reside there from time to time.
"Of Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja" means of Vāseṭṭha and of Bhāradvāja. "This intermediate conversation" refers to that which [concerned] themselves...
They wandered about conversing in a manner consistent with their relationship as companions;
what is meant is that while they were in the midst of that conversation, another topic arose. "One of pure conception" (*saṃsuddhagahaṇika*) means one of pure womb;
the intention is that he was born from the very womb of a pure brahmin woman. This is as seen in such passages as "by a womb that ripens evenly," and so forth.
Indeed, the digestive fire (*udaraggi*) is called the "stomach" (*gahaṇī*). Here, however, it refers to the mother’s womb.

"As far as the seventh" means the mother’s mother, the father’s father, and so on in reverse order for seven generations. In this context, both the paternal grandfather and the paternal grandmother are "paternal grandparent" (*pitāmaha*);

likewise, both the maternal grandfather and the maternal grandmother are "maternal grandparent" (*mātāmaha*); and both the paternal and maternal grandfathers are simply "grandparents" (*pitāmahā*). Of these grandparents...

A *yuga* is a grandfather’s generation (*pitāmahayuga*). *Yugas* refer to the measure of a lifespan. This is merely a verbal expression; in actual meaning, however, a grandfather himself is the "grandfather’s generation.
"Not reviled" means not disparaged by anyone on account of his birth, [asking] "What is he?
"Not censured" means never before censured for defects in his birth. "Endowed with vows" means endowed with good conduct. "To inform" means to make known.
"To awaken" means to do so continuously; this is what is meant. "Āyāma" means "let us go. 600.
"Anuññātapaṭiññātā" means: "We have been authorized by our teachers as 'possessors of the threefold knowledge' (tevijjā), and we ourselves have acknowledged it"—this is the meaning.
"Asmā" means "we are. "Ubho" means both persons. "I" refers to Pokkharasāti.
"This young man is Tārukkha’s" means: "I am Pokkharasāti’s senior pupil and chief disciple;
this one is Tārukkha’s," he says with this intention, demonstrating both his own excellence and that of his teacher.
601. *Tevijjānaṃ* means "of those possessing the three Vedas. *Kevalino* means "those who have reached the ultimate goal. *Asmase* means "we are. Now...
Expounding that state of a Kevalin, he said: “From the word... [pe] ...similar. Therein, *jappeti* means in the Vedas.
*Kammunā* means by the tenfold wholesome path of action (*kusalakammapatha*). For previously, referring to the sevenfold bodily and verbal action, he said:
“Insofar as, sir, one is virtuous”; and referring to the threefold mental action, he said: “one who is endowed with vows (*vatasampanno*)”.
He said: "For one endowed with that is indeed perfected in conduct.
(602–5) Now, showing this by means of another statement, he said: "And I declare [one] by their karma.
"Beyond depletion" (*khayātīta*) means having transcended deficiency; the sense is "complete. "Having gone" (*pecca*) means having approached. "They revere" (*namassanti*) means they pay homage.

"The eye has arisen in the world": in this world of the darkness of ignorance, it has arisen having become an eye for the world by dispelling that darkness through the demonstration of goals pertaining to the present life and so forth.
Having thus praised [the Buddha], Vāseṭṭha made his request; and the Blessed One, including both individuals [in his response], said: "Of those..."
“I shall explain to you,” and so forth. Therein, “byakkhissam” means “I shall explain. Regarding “anupubbaṃ”: let alone the thought of [high] brahmins;
I shall explain to you in due order starting from insects, moths, grass, and trees—such is the intended meaning here to be understood.
For those young men are to be guided by such a detailed exposition. “Jātivibhaṅgaṃ” means...
The detailed exposition of birth (*jātivitthāra*). For "births are mutually distinct" means that the births of various living beings are distinct from one another and of diverse kinds.

607. Then, when the classification of the births of living beings was to be explained, [the Blessed One] began by first speaking of those not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*), saying, "Know them even among grasses and trees.
If one asks, "For what purpose? it is for the sake of making [the existence of] happiness known even in those things not clung-to. [This is] regarding those not clung-to...

For when a distinction between types is grasped, that [distinction] becomes more evident among derived (upādinnaka) things. In this context, "grasses" (tiṇa) are those with pith inside and bark outside;
therefore, palm trees, coconut trees, and the like are also included within the category of grasses. "Trees" (rukkha) are those with bark outside and pith inside.
"Grasses and trees" (tiṇarukkha) refers to both grasses and trees. He spoke thus—"even grasses and trees"—showing them by means of the plural form used for objects.
"Do you know? They do not claim it either, meaning they do not even claim, "We are grasses" or "We are trees.

Even though they do not claim that their characteristic is born of birth (*jātimaya*), their shape—which is indeed born of birth—is exactly like the grass and other things from which they themselves originated.
Why is this? Because births are distinct from one another; for the birth-class of grass is one thing, and the birth-class of trees is another. And among the grasses as well...
"The *tāla* species is one thing, the *nāḷikera* species is another"—thus it should be elaborated.

What does this illustrate? That which is distinct by way of species is apprehended as a distinction from other species even without one's own admission or the instruction of others. And if one were a brahmin by way of species, he too—his own...

If one were to be accepted as distinct from a khattiya, a vessa, or a suddaka without either a personal claim or the instruction of others, yet such a distinction is not accepted, therefore one is not a brahmin by birth.
Furthermore, this point will be revealed through verbal expression in the subsequent verse: "Just as among these various births... and so forth.

608. Having thus shown the distinctions among types of birth for those things not subject to clinging (*anupādinnā*), he says "Then insects," and so forth, in order to show that same distinction for those things subject to clinging (*upādinna*).
Therein, "insects" (*kīṭā*) means worms. "Moths" (*paṭaṅgā*) means moths themselves.
"Up to ants and termites" (*kunthakipillika*) means making the ant and the termite the limit; such is the meaning.
609. *Khuddaka* refers to the black scorpion and so forth; *mahallaka* refers to the mongoose and so forth.
For all of these are of many colors. 610. *Pādodara* means "belly-footed"; it is said that for them, the belly itself is the foot. Regarding *dīghapiṭṭhika*:

for snakes, from the head down to the tail-tip, there is only back; therefore they are called "long-backed. These too are of many kinds, distinguished by such varieties as the venomous snake (*āsīvisa*) and others.
611. "Aquatic" (*odaka*) means those born in water. "Fish" (*maccha*) refers to various species, distinguished by types such as the *rohitaka* (redfin) fish and others.

612. "Birds" (*pakkhī*) refers to winged creatures; for they are called "birds" because of the possession of wings (*pakkha*). "Those who go on foot" (*pattayāna*) are those who travel on feet. "Sky-goers" (*vihaṅgama*) are those who move through the air (*vehāsa*); these too are of many kinds, distinguished by types such as crows and others. 613.
Having thus shown the classification of the species of living beings that frequent land, water, and the sky, [the author] now, with whatever intention...

He showed it to him; and in order to reveal that, he spoke the verse beginning with “Just as in these. Its meaning should be understood in brief according to the explanation of the intended sense already stated previously.
However, as for what must be said here in detail, he himself shows it by saying “Not by the hair,” and so forth.
The application here is as follows: regarding what was stated, “Among humans there is no manifold mark consisting of birth,” it should be understood that it does not exist in this way.

That is to say: “Not by means of hair. For there is no fixed rule such as “Brahmins have such hair and Kshatriyas have such [hair],” in the manner seen with elephants, horses, deer, and so forth; according to this method, all [is explained].
It should be applied. The phrase "the mark is not based on birth, as it is in other births" should be understood as a conclusion to the very point already stated.

Its application is as follows: since there is no distinct mark based on birth among humans due to these [features] such as hair and so forth, therefore this should be understood: "among humans distinguished as Brahmins and so on, the mark..."

“Just as it is not so in other births. Now, even though such a distinction of birth does not exist, in order to show how this diversity—namely, that one is a brahmin or a kshatriya—has arisen, he spoke the verse beginning with “individually.
Its meaning is: this is established by birth alone, just like [the classification] of animals.
The diversity of shape regarding hair and so forth does not exist among humans within their own respective bodies, such as those of Brahmins and others.

Yet, even though this [physical diversity] is non-existent, that distinction consisting of various designations—such as "Brahmin" or "Kshatriya"—is spoken of among humans by way of conventional designation;
it is spoken of merely as a worldly convention.

619–625. Having thus refuted the argument of Bhāradvāja, the Blessed One now [proceeds] to refute the argument of Vāseṭṭha, on the grounds that if one were a brahmin by birth alone, then even one who has fallen away from right livelihood, virtue, and conduct would be a brahmin;
whereas the ancient brahmins as well as other wise men in the world do not accept his status as a brahmin. Therefore, for the purpose of upholding the argument of Vāseṭṭha:
Showing this, he spoke the eight verses beginning with “Whosoever among men. Therein, “cattle-herding” (gorakkha) means the protection of fields;
that is to say, agricultural work. For the earth is called “go,” and its various divisions are “fields.
“By various crafts” (puthusippena) refers to diverse crafts such as weaving and so forth. “Trade” (vohāra) means commerce. “By serving others” (parapessena) means...

“By performing services for others. “The profession of an archer” means one who lives by weapons; it is said to be the use of arrows and spears. “By the office of a domestic priest” means by the work of a *purohita*. 626.

Having thus established, both according to the Brahminical tradition and according to worldly convention, that one who has failed in livelihood, virtue, and conduct is not a Brahmin, [the author concludes]:
“This being so, one is not a Brahmin by birth, but rather one is a Brahmin by qualities. Therefore, wherever...”

"One born in a noble family who possesses virtue is a brahmin; this is the principle here"—having thus established this principle according to its meaning, he spoke again, clarifying that very same principle through words: "And I do not call one a brahmin.
Its meaning is as follows: I, however, [do not call a brahmin] merely one who is born anywhere among the four modes of birth, nor even specifically...
One who is born from a mother designated as "brāhmaṇī" is "born of the womb" (*yonija*) and "originated from the mother" (*mātisambhava*).
Furthermore, according to the method beginning with the phrase "well-born on both sides," the *yoni* (womb/source) is described by the brāhmaṇas as the path of pure origin for a brāhmaṇa;
and by the term "of pure descent through the womb" (*saṃsuddhagahaṇika*), the excellence of the mother is indicated. Because he is born and produced from that [mother], he is "born of the womb."
And it is said, "born of a mother. Yet even one who is born from a womb and born of a mother—I do not call him a brahmin merely by this fact of being born from a womb and born of a mother.
Why? Because he is called a "Bhovādi" (one who says "Ho, Ho! merely by the utterance of those words, provided he possesses something;
for he is distinguished from others who possess things only by that verbal address. But as for this person, though he may be born into any family whatsoever—

One who is "without possessions" (akiñcana) due to the absence of the encumbrances of lust and so forth, and who is "without grasping" (anādāna) through the relinquishing of all attachments—him, being without possessions and without grasping, I call a brahmin.
Why? Because he has "banished evil. Furthermore:
there are twenty-seven verses beginning with "having severed all fetters" (sabbasaṃyojanaṃ chetvā). Therein, "all fetters" (sabbasaṃyojanaṃ) means...
The tenfold fetter (*saṃyojana*). "He does not tremble" means he does not yearn through craving (*taṇhā*).

"I call him a brahmin" means that because he has transcended the snares of passion and the rest, he has gone beyond the snares (*saṅgātiga*); and because of the absence of all four bonds (*yoga*), he is disjoined (*visaṃyutta*)—this is the meaning.
628. "Naddhi" refers to anger (*kodha*) as it occurs in the state of striking; "varatta" refers to that which occurs in the state of binding.

Craving. Having cut through all this—the sixty-two bonds of views together with the sequence of underlying tendencies (anusaya) and the sequence of fetters (sandāna)—he stands having lifted the crossbar of ignorance;
because he has awakened to the four truths, he is "Awakened" (Buddha). This is the meaning of: "I call him a brahmin."

629. "Unangered" (*aduttha*): he who, remaining with a mind free from anger, endures verbal abuse through the ten bases of abuse, physical assault with hands and so forth, and binding with fetters and so forth;
because he is endowed with the power of patience, it is the "power of patience" (*khantībala*);
and because he is endowed with that very army of the power of patience which acts as a formation against repeated arising, it is the "army of powers" (*balānīka*).
The meaning is: "I call such a person a brahmin.

(630) "Vatantaṃ" means one endowed with the ascetic practices (*dhutavata*); "sīlavantaṃ" means one possessed of the fourfold purity of virtue; "anussadaṃ" means one who is free from swelling due to the absence of the excess of craving;
"dantaṃ" means one who is tamed through the subduing of the six sense faculties; and "antimasārīraṃ" means one whose physical body is the last, having reached the ultimate limit.
The meaning is: "I call him a brahmin. 631. "He who is not smeared":
in the same way, he who is not smeared by either of the two kinds of internal sense-desires, and who does not settle upon those desires—I call him a brahmin; this is the meaning. 632. "Of suffering":

of the suffering of the aggregates (*khandha*). "One who has laid down the burden": one who has set aside the burden of the aggregates, or is disconnected from the four yokes or from all defilements—I call him a brahmin; this is the meaning.
633. "Of profound wisdom" means endowed with wisdom that functions regarding the profound aggregates and so forth; one who is intelligent through the wisdom of the essence of the Dhamma;

one skilled in what is the path and what is not the path through expertise in discerning, "This is the way to a miserable destination, this is the way to a happy destination, this is the path to Nibbāna, this is not the path"; and one who has attained the supreme goal known as Arahantship.
The meaning is: "I call him a brahmin.
634. *Asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ* means not mingled, by way of the absence of mingling through seeing, hearing, conversation, enjoyment, and physical contact.
*Ubhayaṃ* means not mingled with either of the two, namely, with householders and with those who have gone forth. *Anokasārin* means one who wanders without a home or attachment.
The meaning is: "I call such a person a brahmin. 635.

*Nidhāya* means having laid aside or having set down. *Tasesu thāvaresu ca* means among those who are trembling due to the trembling of craving (*taṇhā-tāsa*), and among those who are stable due to the stability [brought about by] the absence of craving.
*Yo na hanti* means he who, through the removal of aversion toward all beings, has laid aside the rod.
The meaning is: "I call him a brahmin who neither kills anyone himself nor causes another to kill"—this is the sense.
(Verse 636) "Unopposed" (*aviruddha*) means that even toward the great masses of worldly people who are opposed by way of malice, he is unopposed due to the absence of malice;
and because he does not refrain from dealing blows to others even when a staff or a sword is not in his hand, he is [unopposed] among those who wield their own sticks (*attadaṇḍesu*).

Among people, one who has attained Nibbāna and laid down the rod—being free from grasping because of the absence of that grasping which seizes the five aggregates as "I" and "mine"—such a person, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin. (637) "Like a mustard seed on the point of an awl":
for whom these [defilements] such as lust and so forth, and this "slander" characterized by the smearing of others' virtues, are like a mustard seed on the point of an awl.
He has fallen away like a mustard seed that does not remain on the point of an awl;

thus he does not abide in the mind—this is what I call a brahmin, is the meaning. 638. *Akakkasaṃ* means not harsh. *Viññāpaniṃ* means making the meaning known. *Saccaṃ* means real. *Nābhisaje* means... [he does not revile].
One should not cause another to be provoked to anger by such speech. Only one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) would speak such words.
Therefore, the meaning is: "I call him a brahmin. 639.
Regarding garments, ornaments, and so forth, whether long or short; regarding gems, pearls, and so forth, whether small or large—according to their high or low value...
The meaning is: "Whosoever in this world does not take what is possessed by another, whether beautiful or ugly, him I call a brahmin.
(640) "Free from longing" means devoid of craving. "Detached" means detached from all defilements; the meaning is: "Him I call a brahmin. (641) "Attachment" means craving.
"Having known, free from doubt" means having understood the eight bases as they truly are, and [being free] from the eightfold basis of doubt...
"Free from doubt regarding doubt": the meaning is that he has plunged into and attained the Deathless, which is Nibbāna;
it is such a brahmin, O Brahmin, that I call [a true brahmin].
(642) "Both": the meaning is having abandoned both types of merit and evil. "Attachment": attachment consisting of the divisions of lust and so forth.

"He has transcended" (*upaccagā*) means he has gone beyond. "I call him a brahmin"—this is the meaning: one who is sorrowless through having transcended the sorrow that is the root of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*);

stainless because of the absence of the dust of passion and other defilements within; and pure because of being free from all afflictions. 643. "Immaculate" (*vimala*) means free from the impurities such as clouds. "Pure" (*suddha*) means free from afflictions. "Serene" (*vippasanna*) means one whose mind is clear and tranquil.

“Untroubled” means free from the turbidity of the defilements (*kilesa*). “With delight and becoming exhausted” means one whose craving for the three realms of existence has been completely destroyed;
that person, I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.
644. That bhikkhu who [crosses] this path of passion, this difficult ford of defilements, and this cycle of saṃsāra, [by means of] the four truths...
One who has transcended the delusion that fails to penetrate [reality], having crossed the four floods and reached the further shore;

one who meditates with the two kinds of jhāna, being unshaken due to the absence of craving, free from doubt due to the absence of skepticism, and extinguished through the extinction of defilements by not grasping at the objects of clinging—him, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin. This is the meaning.

645. The meaning is: "That person who, having abandoned both kinds of sensual pleasures in this world, goes forth as a homeless wanderer—I call him a brahmin, O Brahmin—meaning one whose sensual desire is utterly exhausted and whose existence is utterly exhausted.

646. [The meaning is: "He who, having abandoned craving with its six doors in this world, being disinterested in household life, goes forth as a homeless wanderer—I call him one whose craving and existence are utterly exhausted, because of the total exhaustion of craving and existence."
The meaning is: "I call him a brahmin.
(647) "Human bond" (*mānusaka-yoga*) refers to human lifespan as well as the fivefold strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

The same principle applies to the "divine bond" (*dibba-yoga*) as well. "He has transcended" (*upaccagā*): he who, having abandoned the human bond, has surpassed the divine, him [all four bonds]—by all four bonds.
The meaning is: "I call one who is disjoined [from defilements] a brahmin.
(648) *Rati* means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. *Arati* means weariness with dwelling in the forest. *Sītibhūta* means extinguished (*nibbūta*).
*Nirupadhi* means free from defilements (*nirupakkilesa*). *Vīra* refers to one who, having overcome this entire world of the aggregates (*khandhaloka*) of such a nature...
The meaning is: "I call him a brahmin who is steadfast and possessed of energy.
(649) "He who knows" refers to one who knows the passing away and rebirth of beings in all their aspects, having made them manifest;
him I call unattached due to his lack of clinging, a Sugata because he has gone well by means of the practice, [the knower] of the four truths...
The meaning is: "I call one a brahmin who is awakened by way of Buddhahood.

(650) "Of whom": of whom even these [beings], such as the gods, do not know the destination—I call him a brahmin who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) because of the destruction of the taints, and an *arahant* because of being far removed from the defilements (*kilesa*).
(651) "Before" refers to the past aggregates; "after" refers to the future; "in the middle" refers to the present. "Possession" (*kiñcana*)...
He who has no "possession" (kiñcana)—defined as the grasping of craving—in these states, him I call "possessing nothing" (akiñcana) because he is free from the possessions of lust and so forth;
by the absence of any grasping, I call him a "Brahmin" (anādāna). This is the meaning. 652.

He is a "bull" (usabha) because of his fearlessness and his resemblance to a bull; he is "excellent" (pavara) in the sense of being supreme; and [he is so called] through the perfection of his energy.

The meaning is: I call him a brahmin who is a hero because he has sought after the great aggregates of virtue and so forth; a great seer (*mahesi*) because he has transcended [the world]; a victor (*vijitāvin*) because he has conquered the three Māras;
a cleanser (*nhātaka*) because his defilements have been washed away; and an awakened one (*buddha*) because he has awakened to the Four Noble Truths. 653.
He who makes manifest and knows his former births, the heavens consisting of twenty-six classes of devas, and the fourfold...
"He sees the states of woe with the divine eye and has attained Arahantship, which is defined as the destruction of birth;
him, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin"—this is the meaning.
Having thus described the brahmin by way of his qualities, the Blessed One [addressed those] who hold the dogmatic adherence that "one is a brahmin by birth."
Showing that these people do not understand this mere conventional usage, and that their view is a wrong view, he spoke the two verses beginning with "For this is a designation.
Their meaning is as follows: "That which is fashioned as name and clan—'brahmin,' 'kshatriya,' 'Bhāradvāja,' or 'Vāseṭṭha'—this is merely a designation in the world;
it should be understood as being nothing more than a conventional expression and a formal definition."
Why? Because it has arisen from a combination and come about through consent;

for at the very time of its birth, it was fashioned and made so by his kinsmen and blood relations. If they had not fashioned it thus, no one, upon seeing anyone, would recognize them as "this is a brahmin" or "this is a Bhāradvāja."
655. Thus, this speculative view has been fashioned and has long lain dormant within those who do not understand;

it has long lain dormant in the hearts of beings who do not understand that "name and clan" are merely fashioned for the purpose of conventional usage. Because it lies dormant therein, they do not understand that name and clan.
They declare, "One becomes a brahmin by birth"; what is meant is that they speak thus without even knowing [the truth].

Having thus shown that those who form the dogmatic adherence that "one is a brahmin by birth" do not understand this mere conventional expression, and that their view is a wrong view, he now rejects the doctrine of birth in its literal sense.

Establishing the doctrine of karma, he spoke the verse beginning with "Not by birth," and so forth. Therein, in order to explain in detail the meaning of this half-verse—"By karma one is a brahmin, by karma one is a non-brahmin"—the passage beginning with "A farmer by his karma" was stated.
In that context, "by karma" means by the volitional action (cetanā-kamma) produced in the present through such acts as plowing.
659. "Seers of dependent origination" means those who see dependent origination thus: "By this condition, this comes to be.

"Skilled in the ripening of kamma" means they are proficient in the ripening of kamma, knowing that birth occurs by way of kamma even in families worthy of honor or contempt, and that other qualities of inferiority or excellence arise when inferior or superior kamma ripens. Thus they are skilled in the ripening of kamma.
660. Regarding the verse beginning with “By karma one turns,” the terms “the world,” “the generation,” and “beings” have one and the same meaning;
there is only a difference in the wording. Furthermore, by the first line here, the negation of this view—namely, that “there is a Brahmā, a Great Brahmā...
the best, the creator, the controller, the father of those who have been and those who will be”—is to be understood. For it is by karma that...
The world proceeds—that is, it arises—within those various realms of existence; who is its creator?

By the second [verse], he shows that although it has arisen through karma, even in its continued occurrence (*pavatti*), it proceeds solely by means of karma, distinguished as past or present, experiencing pleasure and pain and attaining states such as inferior or superior.
By the third [verse], he demonstrates that very same point...
He concludes: "Thus, in every respect, beings proceed bound by karma alone; they do not proceed otherwise.
With the fourth [simile], he clarifies that meaning through a comparison: "As the linchpin of a moving chariot.
Just as the linchpin is the binding factor for a moving chariot, and it does not move without being bound by it, so too for the world as it arises...
And karma is the bond for both what has arisen and what is proceeding; not being bound by it, one does not arise, nor does one proceed.
Now, since the world is thus bound by karma, [the Blessed One], showing the state of excellence through excellent karma, spoke the two verses beginning with "By austerity.
Therein, "by austerity" means by restraint of the sense faculties; "by the holy life" means by that which is based on the training.
By means of the noble conduct remaining to be practiced; by "restraint" (saṃyama), [meaning] virtue (sīla); by "taming" (dama), [meaning] wisdom (paññā).

By this action which has become sublime in its excellence, one becomes a brahmin. Why? Because this is the supreme brahminhood, and because it is said that this action is the highest state of being a brahmin. There is also the reading “brahmānaṃ,” the meaning of which is: "the divine" (brahmaṃ).
"He brings to" means he leads to the state of *brahmā*; it is said that he brings about, conveys, or bestows the state of *brahmā*.
In the second verse, "peaceful" (*santa*) means one whose defilements are stilled. "A *brahmā* and a *sakka*" refers to one who is both a *brahmā* and a *sakka*.
Such a person is not merely a brahmin, but is indeed both a *brahmā* and a *sakka* in the eyes of those who understand—the wise. Thus...
"Vāseṭṭha, know this"—this is what is meant. The remainder is exactly as previously explained.
Thus ends the commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta within the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Paramatthajotikā* commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*).
10. The Commentary on the Kokālika Sutta.
"Thus have I heard" refers to the Kokālika Sutta. What is its origin? The origin of this sutta will be made clear in the commentary on its meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*).
And the commentary on its meaning begins with "Thus have I heard," etc., in the manner already described. Then, "Now Kokālika... [and so forth].
But who was this Kokālika here, and why did he approach [the Buddha]? It is said:

This Kokālika, it appears, was the son of the merchant Kokālika in the city of Kokālika in the district of Kokālika; having gone forth, he resided in the very monastery built by his father under the name "Cūḷakokālika," and he was not a disciple of Devadatta. For that son of a brahmin was known as "Mahākokālika."
While the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, the two chief disciples,
traveling on a journey through the countryside together with about five hundred bhikkhus, desired to dwell in seclusion as the time for the rains retreat drew near.
Having dismissed those bhikkhus and taken their own bowls and robes, they reached that city in that country and [arrived at] that monastery.
They arrived there. Having exchanged greetings with Kokālika, they said to him:
"Friend, we shall dwell here for the three months of the rains; do not tell anyone. He consented, saying, "Very well.
When the three months had passed, on another day early in the morning, he entered the city and announced: "The two chief disciples have come here and are dwelling here."
“You did not know; no one even invited you with provisions. The city-dwellers asked, “Venerable sir, why did you not tell us?
“What was the use of telling you? Did you not see two monks staying there? Are they not the Chief Disciples?
They quickly assembled, brought honey-balls, garments, and other items, and placed them before Kokālika.
He thought: "The supreme disciples, being of the utmost fewness of desires, will not accept this gift once they know it has arisen through the instigation of a messenger.
Since they will not accept it, they will surely say, 'Give it to the resident monk. Well then, let me take this gift and go.
He did so. As soon as the elders saw him, they knew it had arisen through the instigation of a messenger and said, "These..."
Thinking, "These requisites belong neither to us nor to Kokālika," they refused them without saying, "Give them to the resident monk," and departed.
Because of this, Kokālika felt resentment, thinking, "How is it that they did not take them for themselves,
yet they would not even give them to me?"

They went into the presence of the Blessed One. And having performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, if the Blessed One did not himself go on a journey through the countryside, he would dispatch his chief disciples, saying: "Go forth, monks, on tour for the welfare of many people," and so forth.
This is the custom of the Tathāgatas. Now at that time, he was not himself desirous of going. Then...
He sent them out once again, saying, "Go, monks, wander on tour.
Wandering on tour together with about five hundred monks, they eventually arrived at that very city in that kingdom.
Recognizing the elders, the citizens prepared an offering along with the necessary requisites and constructed a pavilion in the center of the city.
They gave gifts and presented requisites to the elders. Having received them, the elders gave them to the Saṅgha of monks.
Seeing this, Kokālika thought: "In the past these were of few desires; now they have become overcome by greed and possessed of evil desires.
Although in the past they seemed like those of few desires, contented, and secluded, I think these are now of evil desires, proclaiming qualities they do not possess."
"…evil bhikkhus. Having approached them there, he said, "Friends, formerly you were as if few in desires, contented, and secluded;
but now you have become evil bhikkhus. Taking his bowl and robe, he departed immediately in great haste and, heading toward Sāvatthī, thought, "I shall report this matter to the Blessed One."
Having traveled by stages, he approached the Blessed One. This is how Kokālika came here;
for this reason he approached. Therefore it is said: "Then the bhikkhu Kokālika approached the Blessed One," and so forth.
Seeing him approaching in great haste, the Blessed One, having directed his attention, knew: "He wishes to revile the two chief disciples."
"He has arrived. Reflecting, "Is it possible to turn him back? he saw: "It is not possible; having offended against the Elders, he has come here;

he will certainly be reborn in the Paduma Hell. Even after seeing this, however, for the sake of clearing away the criticism of others who might say, "Even upon hearing that Sāriputta and Moggallāna were being reviled, he did not stop them," and in order to demonstrate the extreme gravity of reviling the Noble Ones, [he spoke].
He rejected [the request] three times by way of the method beginning with “Mā heva” (Do not say so). Therein, “mā heva” means “do not speak thus,” “do not say this.
“Pesalā” means those of lovely virtue. “Saddhāyiko” means one who causes faith to arise;
what is meant is that he brings about confidence. “Paccayiko” means one who causes conviction; what is meant is that he brings about the certainty that “this is indeed so.”
"Shortly after he had departed": as soon as he had gone, before long, his entire body became covered;
not leaving even a space the size of a hair-tip untouched, his whole body was completely overspread with pustules that had arisen by breaking through the bones.
In this regard, because of the power of the Buddhas, such karma does not reach fruition in the presence of the Buddhas.
He gave it; however, he gave it just as he had left the vicinity of sight. Therefore, not long after he had departed, boils broke out on him.
For this very reason it is said: "And not long after Kokālika had departed.
Now, if one asks why he did not remain right there, it was due to the power of karma. For karma for which the opportunity has been made ready must inevitably ripen; that [karma] was his.
He did not allow him to remain there. Being urged on by the power of his own karma, he rose from his seat and departed.
"Kaḷāyamattiyā" means the size of chickpeas; "beluvasalāṭukamattiyā" means the size of young *veluva* fruits. "Pabhijjiṃsu" means they burst open.
When they had burst open, his entire body became like a ripe jackfruit. With his limbs thus cooked, he met with ruin and disaster.
Having fallen [into the pit], overcome by suffering, he lay at the gateway of the Jeta Grove.
Then, people who had come one after another for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma saw him and said, "Shame on Kokālika! Shame on Kokālika! You have done what is improper;
you have met with ruin and disaster solely because of your own mouth. Hearing them, the guardian deities uttered cries of reproach, and the guardian deities...
By this means, a cry of reproach arose all the way up to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
At that time, a monk named Turū, who was Kokālika’s preceptor, had attained the fruit of non-returning and been reborn among the Suddhāvāsa deities.
Having emerged from his meditative attainment and heard that reproach, he also came and exhorted Kokālika.
It was for the purpose of generating a state of mental serenity toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
But he, instead of accepting her words, committed that very offense and, having passed away, was reborn in the Paduma Hell. Therefore it is said:
"Then the bhikkhu Kokālika, by that very affliction... having harbored resentment... etc.
Now, as for the phrase "Then Brahmā Sahampati": who is this Brahmā, and why did he approach the Blessed One and say this?

He was a monk named Sahaka in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa; having become a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), he was reborn among the Suddhāvāsa deities, where they know him as "Brahmā Sahampati. He [thought], "I shall approach the Blessed One..."
"I shall proclaim the Paduma Hell; then the Blessed One will explain it to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus, skilled in the continuity of discourse, will ask about the lifespan there, and the Blessed One, in explaining it, will reveal the danger in reviling the noble ones.
For this reason, he approached the Blessed One and said this. The Blessed One did exactly so, and another [bhikkhu] as well...
A bhikkhu asked. Being thus questioned, he said, "Just as with the bhikkhus," and so forth.
In that context, a "twenty-khārika" measure means: according to the Magadhan *pattha*, four *patthas* make one *pattha* in the kingdom of Kosala;
by that [Kosalan] *pattha*, four *patthas* make an *āḷhaka*; four *āḷhakas* make a *doṇa*; and four *doṇas* make a *mānikā*.
Four *mānikās* make one *khārī*; with that *khārī*, there are twenty *khāris*. "A cartload of sesame" (*tilavāha*) means a cart of sesame.

Regarding the "Avīci hell": there is no separate hell named Avīci; rather, it is a portion of Avīci itself where beings suffer according to the calculation of *abbuda* (swelling) that is called the "Avīci hell.
This same method applies to Nirabbuda and the others.

In this regard, the calculation of years should be understood as follows: just as one hundred times one hundred thousand is a *koṭi*, so too one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭis* is called a *pakoṭi*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is called a *koṭippakoṭi*;
one hundred times one hundred thousand *koṭippakoṭis* is a *nahuta*; one hundred times one hundred thousand *nahutas* is a *ninnahuta*; one hundred...
One hundred thousand *ninnahuta* make one *abbuda*; twenty times that is a *nirabbuda*. This same method applies everywhere.
Some, however, say: "These names were obtained there because of the variety of lamentations and the variety of karmic punishments";
others say: "These are merely cold hells."
The phrase "Furthermore" (*athāparaṃ*) is stated with reference to the composition of verses that illuminate specific details of that meaning.

For among the twenty verses recited according to the textual tradition, only this single verse beginning with "A hundred thousand" (*sataṃ sahassānaṃ*) illuminates the meaning already expressed; the remaining verses illuminate specific details.
Moreover, the two verses at the very end are not found in the text as determined in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Therefore, we said, "among the twenty verses."
663. Therein, "the axe" (*kuṭhārī*) refers to harsh speech, which is like an axe in the sense that it cuts oneself.

"It cuts" means that it chops away one's very own root, namely the roots of wholesome merit (*kusalamūla*). 664. "The blameworthy" (*nindiya*) means that which is to be censured. Or, "he who censures him who is praiseworthy" means that he reviles a person who is worthy of praise in the highest sense, by imputing to them evil desires and other such faults. "He gathers" (*vicināti*) means he accumulates. "Fault" (*kala*) means an offense. 665.

"This is a fault" (*ayaṃ kalī*) means this offense. "In dice" (*akkhesu*) means in the dice used for gambling. "Even with all his possessions and even with himself" (*sabbassāpi sahāpi attanā*)—means... [text fragment].
"With all one's own wealth and even with oneself" means together with everything that belongs to oneself.

"Among the Sugatas" refers to those named Sugatas—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—because they have gone well (*sugata*) and because they have gone to a beautiful state (*sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ*). "One who would corrupt the mind" means one who would defile the mind.
It is said that for such a person, this very corruption of the mind is the greater evil.

Why? Because [the lifespan] of a hundred thousand... [etc. ...is evil; because by the calculation of years that much time passes, during which time one who reviles the Noble Ones, having directed speech and mind toward evil, goes to hell and is cooked there—this is what is meant.
For this is, in brief, the measure of the lifespan in the Paduma Hell.

667. Now, by another method, in order to clarify this meaning—namely, "This indeed is the greater evil: that one should corrupt the mind toward the Sugatas"—the Blessed One said, beginning with "The speaker of untruth.
Therein, "a speaker of untruth" refers to one who speaks falsely by way of slandering the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
"Hell" refers to Paduma and the other hells. "And having gone there, they become equal" means that after departing from here, through rebirth in hell.
They become equal. "In the other world" means in the next life.

Furthermore: "He who [harms] one who is uncorrupted... Herein, one should be understood as "uncorrupted" due to the absence of mental corruption, "pure" due to the absence of the stain of ignorance, and "without blemish" due to the absence of evil desires. Or, because he is uncorrupted, he is pure; because he is pure...
"Of one who is without blemish"—thus it should be construed here.
(669) Having thus established that mental malice toward the Sugatas is a most grievous evil, he now spoke fourteen verses known as the "Verses on the Subject of What is Prohibited.
These, it is said, were spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna while exhorting Kokālika even as he was dying.
Some say they were spoken by Mahābrahmā. This enumeration beginning with “one who is devoted to the qualities of greed” is for the purpose of grouping them together with this sutta.
Therein, in the first verse, because it is designated as “qualities” (*guṇa*) or because it occurs many times, greed itself is “the quality of greed”;
this is a designation for craving (*taṇhā*). “Avadaññū” means one who does not know how to speak.
By not accepting the exhortation even of the Buddhas; "miserly" means by the fivefold miserliness;
"devoted to slander" means through the desire to cause a schism between the Chief Disciples. The rest is self-evident. This is what is meant:
"Friend Kokālika, whoever like you is devoted to the craving of greed, intent on the qualities of greed, faithless, stingy, ungrateful, and miserly..."

Devoted to slander, he reviles another person with his speech, even one who is not deserving of such abuse. Therefore, I call him "one with a foul mouth"—this refers to the triad of verses [beginning with] *mukhadugga*.
670. This is the explanation of the words not previously explained (*anuttānapada*):
*mukhadugga* means one with a foul mouth; *mukhavisama* means one with a distorted mouth; *vibhūta* means one devoid of truth; *alikavādi* means a speaker of falsehood.

An ignoble person, an untrue man, a destroyer of beings, a slayer of beings, one who causes the destruction of growth, a mere man, the lowest of men, a wretch, an ill-favored man, one born base from the Buddha, a base-born son.

(671) "You scatter dust" means you cast the dust of the defilements (*kilesa-raja*) upon yourself. "They fall into a pit" (*papatanti sobbhaṃ*). There is also the reading "papātaṃ," which has the same meaning. There is also the reading "papadaṃ," which means the Great Hell (*mahāniraya*).
672. *Eti hataṃ*: here, *ha* is a particle; *taṃ* refers to that wholesome or unwholesome kamma.
Alternatively, *hataṃ* means gone or entered; the sense is "accumulated. *Suvāmī* means "master" because of having performed that kamma.
For he indeed receives that kamma; it does not perish for him—this is what is meant. And because he receives it, therefore there is suffering.
The dull-witted... [and so on] ...the evildoer. 673.
Now, in order to reveal the suffering that the dull-witted person perceives, he says: "The place struck by iron spikes," and so forth.
Regarding this, first, the meaning of the first half-verse is as follows—with reference to that place struck by iron spikes:
The Blessed One said, "Monks, the wardens of hell inflict upon him a torture called the fivefold binding";

this applies here. And while he is being subjected to this, having been laid down right there upon the glowing iron ground, he encounters a heated iron stake with a sharp blade known as a *khila*, which is struck into him by the wardens of hell at five points. This...
It was spoken by the Blessed One with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) in the passage beginning, “They place a red-hot iron spike in his hand,” and so forth.

The subsequent half-stanza refers to what happens after he has been cooked there for many thousands of years and has reached the bank of the river of caustic water (*khārodaka-nadī*) in order to experience the remainder of his residual karma:
“They throw a red-hot iron ball into his mouth; they pour red-hot molten copper into his mouth.”
This was said; it was said with reference to that. In this context, "iron" (*ayo*) means metal. "Resembling a sugar-ball" (*guḷasannibhaṃ*) means having the shape of a *veluva* fruit.
Here, by the mention of "iron," copper is to be understood, and by the other term, an iron ball. "Appropriate" (*patirūpaṃ*) means corresponding to the specific action performed. 674.
In the verses following that, "for not pleasant" (*na hi vaggū*) refers to the hell-wardens who say things such as, "Seize them! Strike them! and so forth.

They do not speak sweet words. "They do not approach with a pleasant countenance" means they do not come forward with a cheerful expression; rather, it is said that they approach only bringing harm and ruin.
"They do not seek refuge" means they do not go to them as a shelter, a cave, or a resort; rather, it is said that they approach only to seize and kill.
"Hoti. "They lie upon spread embers" means that, having been made to ascend the mountain of embers, they lie for many thousands of years upon embers that have been spread out.
"A fire blazing all around" refers to a fire that is burning on all sides and ablaze in every direction.
"They enter" means that, having been cast into the Great Hell, they plunge within it. As for what is called the "Great Hell," it is that which is said to be "four-cornered."
When it is spoken [of], the eyes of those standing even a hundred *yojanas* away burst asunder.
675. "And being covered with a net" means that hunters, having enveloped them with iron nets, strike them like deer;
this is an unspoken karmic consequence for the divine messengers (*devadūta*). "As if entering blind darkness" means becoming truly blind by means of the production of blindness.
Because of its dense darkness, they go to the hell named Dhūmaroruva, which is designated as "Timisa" (Gloom).
It is said that there their eyes burst from smelling the harsh smoke; therefore, it is called "blind.
For it is spread out like a mist: the meaning is that that blinding gloom is spread out like a mass of mist.
“Vitthata” is also a reading [for this term]. This too is a mode of punishment not mentioned among the divine messengers.
676. Now, as for “made of iron”: this iron cauldron extends to the edge of the earth;
it is two hundred and forty-four thousand yojanas deep, filled level to the brim with molten iron. For they are cooked in those cauldrons for a long time.
"They are cooked for a long time" means they are roasted for a long duration. "In those resembling fire" means in those that are like fire. "Boiling up" means boiling over;
it is said that they are cooked while rising up and falling down again and again, like a mass of froth.
This should be understood in the same manner as described in the *Devadūta Sutta*.
677. *Pubbalohitamissāya*: in an iron cauldron mixed with pus and blood. *Tattha kinti*: "What there?"—that is, what is there?
*Yaṃ yaṃ disaṃ*: whichever direction, cardinal or intermediate. *Adhiseti*: he goes toward. There is also the reading *abhiseti*;
in that case, the meaning is that he clings to or leans against whichever direction. *Kilissati*: he is afflicted. There is also the reading *kilijjati*.
The meaning is that it becomes putrid. "Being touched" means being struck by that pus and blood. This too is a deed not mentioned among the messengers of the gods.
678. "In a dwelling of worms" means in the abode of worms. This too is simply the copper cauldron, which is called the "Feces Hell" in the *Devadūta Sutta*;
having fallen there, creatures with needle-like mouths pierce the skin and so forth, and devour the marrow of the bones.
“There is no shore to go to” means there is no shore to depart from. There is also a reading, “There is a shore,” which has the same meaning.

Here, the word “tīrava” is used to mean “the shore itself. Since all its sides are level—because the rim of that pot is tilted downward so that it is even on every side all around—it is therefore impossible to depart from it.
It is said that there is no shore. 679.
The Sword-Leaf Forest (*asipattavana*) is exactly as described in the *Devadūta Sutta*. For from afar it appears like a delightful mango grove;
then, out of greed, the denizens of hell enter it, whereupon leaves stirred by the wind fall upon them.
They cut off their limbs and members. Therefore it is said: “They enter it with their bodies completely severed. They enter it so that their limbs are thoroughly cut apart.
Having seized the tongue with a hook, they strike it repeatedly;
there, the hell-guardians [strike] those liars among the denizens of hell who have run with speed and fallen into the Forest of Sword-leaves.
Having pulled out the tongue with a hook, just as people spread raw hide upon the ground and beat it with thorns, so too they beat it;
having split it again and again with axes, they cut off each individual corner and strike it down.
As each corner is cut, it arises again and again. There is also a reading, "āracayāracayā," meaning "having dragged it along, having dragged it along."
This is the meaning. This too is a deed not mentioned by the divine messenger. 680. *Vetaraṇī*:
In the discourse of the divine messenger, this refers to the river described as "a great river of alkaline water. It is said that it appears filled with water like the Ganges.
Then, thinking, "We will bathe here; we will drink," the denizens of hell fall into it. [It is] with sharp edges and razor-sharp blades.
"Sharp-edged razor-edges" means it is said to have sharp edges like those of a razor.
It is said that on both banks of that river, from top to bottom, sharp-edged razors stand as if placed in a continuous row;
therefore, it is called "sharp-edged razor-edges. They approach that water with the hope of finding such sharp-edged razor-edges.
The meaning is: "they cling. And thus approaching, being impelled by their evil karma, the dull-witted fools fall there; this is the meaning. 681.
Regarding the phrase *sāmā sabalā*, it should be connected with the word *soṇā* that follows later.
What is meant is that tawny-colored and dark-colored *soṇā* (jackals) devour [them]. *Kākolagaṇā* means flocks of black crows. *Paṭigiddhā* means those who have become thoroughly greedy.
Having sacrificed, some say they are "great vultures. *Kulala* means birds of prey; some say this is the name for "hawks. *Vāyasa* refers to non-black crows.
This too is a deed not mentioned among the divine messengers (*devadūta*).

Furthermore, although some deeds mentioned there are not mentioned here, it should be understood that because they belong to the preceding or succeeding stages of these [deeds], they are effectively included as already stated.
682. Now, having shown this entire mode of existence in hell, he spoke the verse beginning with "Kicchā vatāyan" as an exhortation.
Its meaning is as follows: Alas, difficult indeed is this mode of existence here in hell, consisting of various kinds of karmic actions, which the person who commits evil deeds experiences.
Therefore, while there is still a remainder of life—that is, while the continuity of life still exists here in this world—[one should act accordingly].
Remaining steadfast, a person should be one who performs their duty by practicing wholesome qualities such as going for refuge;

and even while performing that duty, they should do so through constant application, not being negligent for even a moment nor falling into heedlessness—this is the commentary on the synthesis here. As for the remaining words mentioned previously...
Because it follows the method already stated and its meaning is self-evident, it is indeed easy to understand; therefore, no word-by-word commentary has been provided.
Thus ends the commentary on the Kokālika Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Paramatthajotikā* Khuddaka Commentary.
