11. Commentary on the Nālaka Sutta 685.

Regarding the *Nālaka Sutta*: what is its origin? It is said that after seeing a disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara practicing the way of the sage (*moneyya*), [the youth] desired such a state for himself; from that time forth, for a hundred thousand aeons...

Having fulfilled the perfections, the ascetic named Nālaka, the nephew of the sage Asita, on the seventh day after the Blessed One set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, questioned the Blessed One regarding the practice of the way of the Muni with two verses beginning with “This has been understood.
The Blessed One answered him in the manner beginning with “I shall explain the Muni-ship to you. However, when the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna...

When the Venerable Mahākassapa was compiling the Saṅgīti, he questioned the Venerable Ānanda regarding that very practice of the noble way (moneyyapaṭipadā) and the circumstances by which and when Nālaka was exhorted to question the Blessed One.
Desiring to make all of that clear and manifest, he spoke the twenty introductory stanzas beginning with “Ānandajāta,” and so forth. All of this is called the “Nālakasutta.”
In this context, "born of joy" means born of success and having reached growth. "Delighted" means satisfied. Alternatively, "born of joy" means gladdened;
"delighted" means possessed of mental happiness (*somanassa*). "Wearing clean garments" means wearing unstained clothes.

For the garments produced from the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) of the devas take on neither dust nor dirt. "Taking a cloth" refers here to what is called a "cloth" because it resembles a cloth.
Having cast aside the celestial garment that had been bestowed upon him; "Asita the seer" refers to the seer who received that name because of his dark-complexioned body;
"at his daytime abode" means at the place where he spent the day. The remainder is clear from the words themselves.
In terms of the connection, however—it is said that this man was the family priest of King Siha-hanu, the father of Suddhodana, and [he was also the priest] of Suddhodana himself.
Before his consecration, he was a master of the arts, but after his consecration, he became the royal chaplain.
Whenever he came to attend upon the king in the evening or morning, the king did not show him the same humble reverence as when he was a youth, but merely performed the salutation with joined palms.

It is said that this is the natural custom of the Śākya kings once they have attained the royal consecration. The chaplain, becoming disillusioned because of this, thought, "I shall go forth into the homeless life."
“Great King,” he said. The king, knowing his resolve, requested, “In that case, teacher, you must dwell in my very own park, so that I may see you frequently. He consented, saying, “So be it.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life, while being supported by the king and dwelling in the park itself, he performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas* and [attained] the eight...
He attained the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and the five supernormal powers (*abhiññā*).

From that time forth, having performed his meal duties at the royal court, he would go to one of the abodes such as the Himavat mountains or the realm of the Four Great Kings (*Cātumahārājika*) to spend the day in meditation.

Then, on one occasion, having gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and entered a jeweled celestial mansion (*ratnavimāna*), he sat upon a divine jeweled couch and experienced the bliss of concentration (*samādhisukha*).
Having enjoyed himself during the evening, he arose and stood at the door of his celestial mansion (vimāna).

Looking here and there, he made a gesture of waving his garment across the great street sixty yojanas wide, and uttering words of praise extolling the virtues of the Bodhisatta, he saw the gods headed by Sakka sporting about.
Therefore the Venerable Ānanda said: "Ānandajāte... [down to] ...divāvihāre."

686. Then, having seen the gods in this way... [omitted] ...on what account? Therein, "exultant" (*udagga*) means with the body uplifted. "Having made it a matter of the heart" (*cittim karitvāna*) means having shown respect. "In good form" (*kalyarūpa*) means in a state of joy. The rest has its meaning already explained. 687.

Now, the verses beginning with "Even when there was... have their connection already explained. As for the meaning of the words, first, in the initial verse: "The encounter" (*saṅgama*) means battle. "Victory of the Suras" means the victory of the gods (*devā*). To explain that in detail, this successive narrative (*anupubbikathā*) should be understood:
Sakka, it is said, was a resident of the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha.
Having been a young brahmin named Magha, the thirty-third best among men, he fulfilled the seven rules of conduct and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven together with his retinue.
Then the former gods, saying, "New divine sons have arrived;
we shall pay them honor," offered them celestial lotuses and invited them to share half of their kingdom. Sakka—
Dissatisfied with half the kingdom, he convinced his own assembly, and one day, when they were intoxicated by liquor and wine,
he seized them by their feet and hurled them to the base of Mount Sineru. There, at the foot of Sineru ten thousand yojanas below,
the Asura realm came into being, adorned with variegated *pāṭali* trees that concealed the *pāricchattaka* tree.
Then, having regained their mindfulness and no longer seeing the Tāvatiṃsa realm, they thought: "Alas! We have been ruined by our addiction to drink.
We shall not drink *sura* (liquor) anymore; we shall drink *asura* (non-liquor). We are no longer *surā*; we have now become *asurā*.
From that time forth, the designation "Asuras" arose for them, and they said: "Come now, let us wage war against the Devas!"

They climbed all around Sineru. Then Sakka, having attacked the asuras in battle and cast them back into the ocean once more, fashioned four statues of Indra identical to himself and stationed them at the four gates.
Thereupon the asuras thought, "This Sakka is indeed vigilant; he stands constantly on guard," and they returned to the city once again. Then...
The gods, proclaiming their own victory and waving their garments in the great street, played at the festival of the constellations.
Then Asita, being capable of recollecting forty aeons of the past and future, reflected: "Have these [gods] ever played in this manner before?
Upon reviewing it, he saw that this was the victory of the gods in the battle between the gods and the asuras, and he said:
“Even when there was a clash with the asuras,
and the gods were victorious while the asuras were defeated,
even then it was not like this, causing such horripilation.”
Even at that time, there was no such hair-raising joy. [The question is: "Having seen what marvel were the gods delighted?"—but today, having seen what marvel are the gods thus delighted?
In the second verse: *seḷenti* means they emit a sound of whistling from the mouth; *gāyanti* means they sing various kinds of songs;
*vādayanti* means they play sixty-eight thousand musical instruments; *phoṭenti* means they clap their hands. "I ask you" (*pucchāmi vo*).
Although he was capable of knowing [the answer] by reflecting within himself, he asked out of a desire to hear their words.
"Dwelling on the summit of Meru" means residing on the peak of Sineru. For at the bottom level of Sineru is the ten-thousand-yojana abode of the asuras;
at the middle level are the four great continents surrounded by two thousand minor islands; and at the upper level is another ten-thousand-yojana [expanse].
[He went] to the realm of the Thirty-three. Therefore, the gods are called "those who dwell upon the summit of Meru. "Mārisa" is an address to the gods;
it means they are free from suffering and free from affliction. 689.
Then, regarding the third verse spoken by the gods who were announcing that matter to him: "Bodhisatta" refers to a being capable of awakening.
The being worthy of attaining perfect enlightenment is the supreme jewel, the one who has become a most excellent treasure.

"Therefore we are delighted" means that for this reason we are joyful. For once he has attained Buddhahood, he will teach the Dhamma in such a way that both ourselves and other hosts of deities will reach the stage of those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*). And humans too, having heard his Dhamma...
It is said that their intention was this: "Those who will not be able to attain *parinibbāna* will perform acts of giving and so forth, and thus fill the world of the gods.
In that regard, although the two phrases "tuṭṭhā" and "kalyarūpā" are identical in meaning, [the text asks]:
"What wonder have the gods seen that they are so delighted? What has the host of gods done that they appear so exceedingly radiant?"
It should be understood that this was spoken for the purpose of answering these two questions.
Now, regarding the fourth verse spoken by those revealing the intention with which they were joyful at the birth of the Bodhisatta:
by the mention of "beings" (*satta*), gods and humans are included; by the mention of "creatures" (*pajā*), the remaining realms of existence are included.
Thus, by these two phrases, he demonstrates his preeminence even among all five realms of existence (*gati*).
For even among animals, such as lions and others who possess qualities like fearlessness and so forth, he surpasses them as well. Therefore, he is called "the supreme among beings" (*pajānamuttamo*).

Furthermore, among gods and humans, there are four types of persons, beginning with those practicing for their own benefit; among these, the one practicing for the benefit of both is the foremost person (*aggapuggalo*).
Because he is like a bull among men (*nara*), he is a "bull among men" (*narāsabha*). Therefore, those speaking his praise uttered these two words as well. 691.
In the fifth verse, *taṃ saddaṃ* means that sound of the speech uttered by the deities. *Avasarī* means he descended. *Tadā bhavanaṃ* means at that time, the abode. 692.
In the sixth verse, *tato* means immediately after the speech of Asita. *Ukkāmukheva* means just as in the mouth of a furnace.
"Mouse-mouthed" is what is meant. "Well-wrought by a skilled craftsman" means fashioned by a highly skilled goldsmith;
the intention is that it was heated while being worked by him. "Radiant" means shining brightly.
"Of the one called Asita" refers to the seer Kaṇhadevila, who was known by the second name Asita.
693. In the seventh verse, *tārāsabhaṃ* means "like a bull among the stars"; the intended meaning is "among the moons. *Visuddhaṃ* means free from defilements such as clouds and the like.
*Saradarivā* means "as if in the autumn season. *Ānandajāto* means "born of joy," having become joyful through the mere hearing [of the teaching].
*Alattha pītiṃ* means that upon seeing [the Buddha], he obtained joy once again.
694. Following that, in order to illustrate the constant honors being offered by the devas to the Bodhisatta, it is said in the eighth verse:
"With many spokes" means with many radii. "A thousand-fold circle" means endowed with a thousand circles made of red gold.
"The parasol" refers to the divine white parasol. "They hover about" means they fly up and down while fanning his body.
695. In the ninth verse, *jaṭī* means one who wears matted hair (*jaṭila*). *Kaṇhasirivhayo* means he who is called by the names *Kaṇha* and *Siri*.
It is said that they also call him and address him as *Sirikaṇha*; thus it is stated that they speak to him.
*Paṇḍukambale* means on a red blanket. And here, by virtue of the context, the word "prince" (*kumāra*) should be supplied, or it is an ellipsis.
It should be done. In the previous verse, the word "having seen" was used with reference to what had not yet come within the range of the hand;
here, however, it has come within the range of the hand and is being brought forward for the purpose of acceptance, therefore the word "having seen" is stated again.

Or else, the former [verse] refers to the attainment of the joy of seeing, as indicated by the words at the end of that verse, "he obtained abundant joy"; this [verse], however, refers to the act of acceptance, as indicated at the end by the words, "glad-minded..."
Because of the statement, "in the receiving [of the bowl]. The previous [passage] was related only to the prince, whereas this one is also related to the white parasol.

"Having seen" means having seen the white parasol—described in the passage "the gods held the parasol over his head"—being held over the prince's head like a gold coin upon a Gandhāra red blanket worth a hundred thousand [pieces]. Some, however, say: "This..."

They say this was said with reference to a human parasol; for just as the gods do, so too do humans approach the Great Man holding parasols, yak-tail whisks, peacock-feather fans, palm-leaf fans, and reed fans in their hands. Even though this is so, there is no special significance in that statement;
therefore, what has been stated above is better. Regarding "accepted," he accepted it with both hands. It is said that the seer...
They brought the prince forward to make him pay homage. Then his feet turned around and settled upon the head of the seer.
Having seen that marvel as well, he received him with a joyful heart and a mind uplifted.
In the tenth verse, "jigīso" means one who desires to conquer, one who seeks, searches for, or examines.
[He was] one who had reached the further shore of the marks and the mantras. Regarding the phrase *anuttarāyaṃ*: this one is unsurpassed.

It is said that when the wheels appeared on the soles of the Great Being’s feet as he approached him, the brahmin, following those [marks] and desiring to seek out the remaining marks, saw the perfection of all the marks; knowing, "Surely this one will become a Buddha," he spoke thus.
697. "Going to the formless" (*arūpagamana*) refers here to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the formless realm.
"He weeps with a wretched form" means that, recollecting his own rebirth in the formless realm and thinking, "I shall no longer be able to hear his teaching of the Dhamma," he becomes dissatisfied;
overcome by intense sorrow and born into a state of mental distress (*domanassa*), he sheds and pours forth tears.
There is also a reading, “garayati. But if his mind were inclined toward the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), why would it not arise there, such that he would weep in this way?
It is not that it would not arise; rather, due to unwholesomeness (akusalatā), he does not know this method.

If it is argued: “Even so, the arising of mental distress (domanassa) is improper for him, because it has been suppressed by the attainment,” we say no, because it has been suppressed [only temporarily].

It is just so. For defilements that have been eradicated by the development of the path do not arise; however, they may arise for those who have attained meditative absorption due to powerful conditions.
If it is asked: "Once the defilements have arisen, since their jhāna has been lost, how can there be a journey to the formless realm?

[The answer is: Because it is easily regained. For when defilements arise in one who has attained absorption, provided they do not fall into a state of gross transgression, [the jhāna] is merely subsided.
Furthermore, they attain that distinction with little difficulty through the force of their defilements;
thus, it is difficult to discern whether "these have fallen away from their distinction," and such is this case. [He thought:
"If there will be no obstacle for the prince, will there indeed be no obstacle for this prince?"
698. "This one does not appear inferior"—this means he is neither inferior nor limited. This is said with reference to his state of Buddhahood, which is to be explained in the following verse. 699.

"This one will attain the pinnacle of perfect enlightenment"—this refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). For it is called "perfect enlightenment" (*sambodhi*) because it awakens correctly through its non-erroneous nature;
and it is called "the pinnacle" (*agga*) because it is the supreme among all knowledges due to the absence of any obstruction whatsoever. "He will touch [it]"—that is, he will realize it.
He will attain it. "One who sees with supreme purity" means one who sees Nibbāna; for that [Nibbāna] is supremely pure because of its absolute purity.
"Of one whose life is widespread" means his life is widespread. "The holy life" (brahmacariya) refers to the Teaching (sāsana).
700. "Within these fourteen days" means within those very days; it is said to be prior to the attainment of full enlightenment.

[The word] *hoti* [is used]. *Na sossanti na suṇissaṃ* means "they will not hear, nor shall I hear. *Asamadhurassa* means "of one with unequalled energy" (*asamavīriyassa*). *Aṭṭo* means "afflicted" (*āturo*).

*Byasanaṃ gato* means "one who has met with misfortune," having reached the destruction of happiness. *Aghāvī* means "suffering"; he says this specifically with reference to the arising of all mental distress (*domanassa*).
For he is afflicted by that mental distress. And because it is the destruction of his happiness, it is called "misfortune" (*byasana*), meaning the ruin of happiness. Thus it is said.
He becomes [afflicted]. And by that mental affliction (*aghabhūta*), he is himself afflicted (*aghāvī*).
"Having produced a vast [amount] through the fifteen" means having produced it extensively. Or rather, this is the reading: "having produced. "Departed" means gone forth.
Having thus departed, he lies with his own sister's son—his own nephew (*bhāgineyya*), the son of his own sister.

"Son" is what was said. "He incited him" means that, having recognized his own short lifespan and having understood through his own power that his younger sister’s son, the young brahmin Nālaka, had accumulated merit,
he went to his sister's house out of compassion for him— fearing that once he reached maturity he might fall into negligence— and asked, "Where is Nālaka?"

“Venerable sir, Bahi is playing outside. Having ordered, “Bring him here,” he immediately ordained him into the ascetic life of a forest-dweller (*tāpasa-pabbajjā*) and exhorted, instructed, and advised him.
How? He recited the sixteen verses beginning with: “‘Buddha’ is the sound…” and ending with “…the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
702. Therein, *yada parato* means when from beyond. *Dhammamaggaṃ* refers to the path to the supreme Dhamma, which is Nibbāna.
The path, or the supreme Dhamma together with its practice, which is Nibbāna. "In him" means in his presence. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). 703.

"By one who is composed in the seventeen ways" means by one who is established in that state; the intention is that when there is the attainment of concentration through the suppression of defilements at that time, one is possessed of a mind whose defilements are suppressed and which is concentrated. "To one who sees the supreme purity in the future."

Because he had seen that "this Nālaka will, in a future time, behold the supremely pure Nibbāna in the presence of the Blessed One," that seer was described by this method as "one who will see the supremely pure [Nibbāna] in the future. By him, who will see the supremely pure [Nibbāna] in the future.
"One who has accumulated a store of merit" means one who has performed a collection of merit starting from the time of Padumuttara Buddha onwards.

He waited, expecting [the Teacher]. He "lived as a resident" means that after going forth, he lived in the guise of an ascetic. "With his sense-faculties guarded" means having guarded the faculty of hearing.
It is said that from then on he did not submerge himself in water, thinking:
"If I enter the water, my faculty of hearing might be destroyed; consequently, I would be excluded from hearing the Dhamma."
704. Having heard these eighteen [reports], Nālaka, while living thus, gradually heard of the Blessed One’s attainment of enlightenment;

and when the Wheel of Dhamma had been set in motion by the Blessed One at Bārāṇasī, he heard the sound arising from the turning of the wheel of the Supreme Victor, according to the manner of: “The Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the Blessed One!
Truly, that Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has appeared! and so forth.

Having heard what was announced by deities who had come wishing for his welfare, and having gone there and seen the "bull among seers" (isinisabha) while the deities were making a clamor of silence (*moneyyakolāhala*) for seven days, he went to Isipatana on the seventh day with the intention:
"Nālaka will arrive; I shall teach him the Dhamma. He sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat.
Having seen the Blessed One, who resembles a bull among men, that bull among sages; "Pasanna" means having become clear-minded at the very moment of seeing him.
"Moneyyasettha" means the supreme wisdom; it is said to be the knowledge of the Path (maggañāṇa).
"Samāgate asitāvhayassa sāsaneti" means when the time for the instruction of the sage Asita had arrived. Therefore—“When he opens the path of Dhamma...”
"Go then, and having thoroughly inquired about the [proper] conduct, practice the holy life under that Blessed One"—thus was he instructed; and this is that very time.
Therefore it is said: "When [the teaching] of the one named Asita had arrived. The rest here is self-evident.
This, then, is the commentary on the introductory verses.
705. Regarding the two verses of inquiry: "This is known by me" means this has been understood by me. "Just as it is" means unerringly.

What is the intention? That which Asita, having known that "this prince will touch the pinnacle of perfect enlightenment," said to me—"When you hear from afar the cry 'Buddha,' he who has attained perfect enlightenment will reveal the path of Dhamma"—that very thing has been realized by me.
Having seen the Blessed One today as a witness, one understands the word of Asita "exactly as it is. *Taṃ* means "therefore" (*tasmā*);

*taṃ* refers to that. "One who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena" means, according to the method stated in the Hemavata Sutta, one who has reached the further shore of all phenomena by way of the six aspects.
"706. To one who has entered the homeless life": to one who has entered the state of homelessness; the meaning is "to one who has gone forth. "Seeking the way of alms-gathering":
to one who is seeking the way of alms-gathering practiced by the Noble Ones (ariya), which is undefiled.
"Moneyya": that which belongs to the sages (munis). "The supreme state": the supreme practice. The rest here is self-evident.
707. Thus questioned, the Blessed One explained the way of the sage’s conduct (*moneyyapaṭipadā*) in the manner beginning with, “I shall declare the sage’s conduct to you.
In this context, *upaññissaṃ* means “I shall cause to be known,” which is to say, “I shall reveal” or “I shall explain.
Regarding the phrase *dukkaraṃ durabhisambhavaṃ*, it is said that it is difficult to perform, and when being performed, it is difficult to bring about—that is, difficult to endure.
This, however, is the intended meaning here: "I might prescribe this moneyya for you if it were easy to perform or easy to master;

but since it is so difficult to do and hard to master—because one must practice it from the time one is still a worldling by not giving rise to a defiled mind—it is thus. For indeed, [it was taught] by only one Buddha to only one person.
“The disciple both practices and achieves it.
Thus, the Blessed One, demonstrating the difficulty of the state of a sage (*moneyya*) and its hard-to-attain nature, inspired Nālaka with zeal;
wishing to explain it to him, he said: “Come, I shall declare it to you; steady yourself and be firm.”
In this context, *handā* is a particle used in the sense of determination. *Te naṃ pavakkhāmīti*: "I shall declare that to you"—that is, I shall declare that moneyya (monkhood) to you.
*Santhambhassūti*: "Be firm"—support yourself with the pillar of energy capable of performing difficult deeds.
*Daḷho bhavāti*: "Be steadfast"—be firm through unremitting exertion capable of enduring what is hard to overcome. What?

Is it said? Because you have accumulated a store of merit, therefore, being resolutely determined, I shall declare to you that *moneyya*, which, though difficult to perform and hard to achieve; stand firm, be steadfast.
(708) Thus, desiring to speak of the practice of *moneyya*—the supreme austerity—he [addresses] Nālaka regarding his standing firm and state of steadfastness.
Having thus enjoined [the listener], he first spoke the half-verse beginning with “samānabhāgaṃ” to demonstrate the abandoning of the defilements associated with village life.
In that context, “samānabhāgaṃ” means an equal portion, being uniform, identical, and without distinction.
“Akuṭṭhavanditaṃ” refers to both reviling and veneration.
Now, demonstrating the means by which that [state] is made equal, he spoke the half-verse beginning with “mental malice. Its meaning is as follows:
when reviled, one should guard against mental malice; being honored, one should walk without being puffed up;
even when honored by a king, one should not fall into agitation, thinking, “He honors me.”
709. Now, demonstrating the abandoning of the defilements connected with the forest, he spoke the verse beginning with “High and low. Its meaning is as follows:

Even in a grove designated as a forest, various kinds of objects—high and low according to whether they are desirable or undesirable—manifest and come within the range of the eye and the other senses;
and these, moreover, are like flames of fire in the sense that they produce feverish burning. Just as...
Or, just as when a forest is burning, flames of various kinds— some high, some low— issue forth,

being both with smoke and without smoke, blue, yellow, and red, small and large; even so, in the forest, objects of various kinds issue forth, high and low, according to the distinctions of lions, tigers, humans, non-humans, and the cries of various birds,
as well as flowers, fruits, sprouts, and so on— objects that are terrifying, delightful, and provocative of aversion.
They were also subject to delusion. Therefore he said: "High and low things issued forth, like crests of fire in the forest.

And while these high and low objects were thus issuing forth, whatever women—whether they were natural forest-dwellers or wood-gatherers and the like who had gone on a stroll through the park and woods—beheld the Sage in private and sought to seduce him with laughter, talk, smiles, weeping, ill-clad garments, and so forth; [they all failed].
"May those women not seduce you; may those women not entice you. What is meant is: "Act in such a way that they do not seduce you.
(710–11) Having thus shown the Blessed One the method of practice both in the village and in the forest, he now [teaches] the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*).

Showing this, he spoke two verses beginning with “Abstaining from sexual intercourse. Therein, “having abandoned desires, both high and low” means having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure—both the beautiful and the unattractive—that remain apart from sexual intercourse. For by abandoning those, the abstinence from sexual intercourse becomes perfectly accomplished.
Thus he said: “Having abandoned desires, both high and low. This is the intended meaning here. [He then speaks] “Unopposed,” and so forth.
However, these words are spoken for the purpose of showing the perfection of the abstention from taking life, which was stated in the passage: "One should not kill, nor cause to be killed.
Herein, this is the brief commentary: one who is free from hostility toward living beings belonging to the faction of others, and free from attachment toward those belonging to one's own faction;
and who, because all beings—whether trembling or stationary—are possessed of craving and free from its absence, desire to live and do not desire to die.
By desiring happiness and being averse to suffering, one removes aversion toward them through the identification with oneself, thinking, "As I am, so are these";
and by identifying with others, thinking, "As these are, so am I," one removes attachment to oneself.
Thus, having abandoned both attachment and aversion in these two ways, [one remains] through the aversion to death.
"Making oneself the standard of comparison, one should not kill any living beings— whether moving or stationary— among those creatures, by means of such methods as acting with one's own hand,
nor should one cause them to be killed by means of such methods as giving orders.
(712) Thus, by way of abstaining from sexual misconduct and abstaining from taking life, his morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is briefly explained.

Having spoken thus, and having shown restraint of the sense faculties by means of the verses beginning with "having abandoned sensual desires," he now speaks the verse beginning with "and having abandoned craving" in order to show purity of livelihood.
Its meaning is as follows: that craving which, having obtained one thing, desires a second;
having obtained two, a third; and having obtained a hundred thousand, desires even more than that—such is craving for objects not yet obtained.
Because one desires, it is called "desire" (*iccha*); and there is also this greed (*lobha*) which is the longing for objects already acquired.

Having abandoned both that desire and greed—in whatever [condition] the worldling is attached, and in whatever requisite such as robes the worldling remains stuck, bound, and fastened by those desires and greed—having abandoned both of these for the sake of the requisites, [one maintains] purity of livelihood.
Being possessed of vision by not contradicting [reality] with the eye of knowledge, one should practice this way of the sage (moneyyapaṭipadā).

For practicing in this way, one would cross over this "hell"—which is designated as hell in the sense of being difficult to fill, and which consists of craving for requisites that is the cause of wrong livelihood;
or rather, it is said that one would cross over by means of this practice.

713. Having thus shown the purity of livelihood by way of the abandoning of craving for requisites, he now speaks the verse beginning with "With a belly not too full" (*ūnūdaro*), demonstrating the virtue of moderation in the use of requisites by way of knowing the proper measure in food, and the path of practice following that, leading up to the attainment of Arahatship.
Its meaning is as follows: regarding the requisites such as robes and so forth, obtained through righteous and equitable means—
Regarding food, while taking it:
"Having eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;
this is sufficient for a well-disposed dwelling for a bhikkhu of resolute mind."

In the manner described, he should have a belly that is not full; it is meant that his belly should not be distended like a bellows filled with air, and he should avoid sloth and torpor caused by the indigestion of food.

Even while having a non-full belly, he should be moderate in eating, knowing the proper measure regarding food, with his intake of food delimited by reflecting on its virtues and defects according to the formula beginning, "Not for sport... and so forth.

Thus, even while being moderate in food, one should be of few desires by way of the fourfold fewness of desires through the ascetic practices regarding requisites (*paccaya-dhutaṅga*), the mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), and spiritual attainment (*adhigama*).
Indeed, a bhikkhu who has entered the practice of monasticism (*moneyya-paṭipadā*) must absolutely be thus of few desires.
In that regard, contentment with each individual requisite by means of the three kinds of contentment is "fewness of desire regarding requisites" (*paccaya-appicchatā*).
"Desire for the ascetic practices" (*dhutaṅgappicchatā*) is the lack of desire for others to know one as "an ascetic practitioner," even while being one who actually possesses the ascetic practices.

"Desire for the scriptures" (*pariyattiappicchatā*) is the lack of desire for others to know one as "one of great learning," even while being one who is indeed learned, as was the case with the Elder Majjhantika.
"Desire for realization" is the lack of desire for others to know, "This wholesome state has been realized by me," even while being one who is indeed endowed with realization.
"Not wishing 'May others know me' is the desire for little in what has been attained (*adhigamappicchatā*).

And that should be understood as being prior to the attainment of *arahantship*, for this is the path for the sake of attaining *arahantship*. Thus, one who has few desires, having abandoned the greed of craving through the path of *arahantship*, should be free from greed.
For one who is thus free from greed is always without longing due to the absence of desire; he is desireless and extinguished (*nibbuto*) by means of that [desirelessness]."

Beings are tormented by desire, like those afflicted by hunger and thirst, remaining unsatisfied; one becomes desireless through that very desire, and by being desireless, one is free from craving, free from affliction, and attains supreme satisfaction.
Thus, by being free from craving, one is extinguished (*nibbuto*), with all the fevers of the defilements (*kilesa*) stilled—this is how the sequence of the application should be understood here.

714. Having thus explained the practice leading up to the attainment of Arahantship, he now speaks two verses beginning with "He, having wandered for alms," while describing the undertaking of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) and the proper conduct regarding lodgings for a bhikkhu who has entered upon that very practice and reached the culmination of attaining Arahantship.
Therein, "he, having wandered for alms" means that the bhikkhu, having gone on his alms-round, has performed the duty of eating.
"Or having done so. "Let him approach the edge of the forest" means he should go to the forest itself, avoiding the diversions of household life.
"Established at the foot of a tree" means either standing at the foot of a tree. "Having approached a seat" means either having gone to a seat; that is to say, having sat down.
"The Sage" (muni) is one who has entered upon the practice of sagehood (moneyya). And here, [the phrase] "having wandered for alms" refers to...

By this, the practice of eating only almsfood (*piṇḍapātika-aṅga*) has been stated. However, since one who is a superior alms-food eater is necessarily one who wanders for alms in regular order, eats at a single sitting, eats from a single bowl, and does not accept food after the meal has begun, and since he also undertakes the practices of wearing only three robes and using rag-robes, these six [practices] are also already included.
By the phrase "he should frequent the edge of the forest," the practice of dwelling in the wilderness (*āraññika-aṅga*) is stated.
It is said: by the phrase “established at the foot of a tree,” the tree-root-dweller’s practice (*rukkhamūlika-aṅga*) is indicated;

by the phrase “having gone to his seat,” the sitter’s practice (*nesajjika-aṅga*) is indicated. Furthermore, because they follow in sequence, the open-air-dweller’s practice (*abbhokāsika-aṅga*), the any-bed-user’s practice (*yathāsanthatika-aṅga*), and the charnel-ground-dweller’s practice (*sosānika-aṅga*) are also implicitly stated.
Thus, with this verse, he explained the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) to the Elder Nālaka.

715. “That wise one intent on meditation” means that he is intent upon and devoted to meditations by way of producing unarisen meditation, and by way of adverting to, entering, resolving upon, emerging from, and reviewing arisen meditation.
“Wise” (*dhīra*) means endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*). “May he delight at the edge of the forest” means he should find joy in the forest;
it is said that he should not find joy in a monastery settlement near a village. “He should meditate at the foot of a tree, gladdening himself.”

One should not only be devoted to mundane *jhāna*, but rather, right there at the foot of that tree, one should meditate, greatly delighting oneself with supramundane *jhāna* associated with the path of stream-entry and the rest.

For it is only by means of supramundane *jhāna*—through the attainment of the ultimate consolation—that the mind is exceedingly satisfied, and not by anything else. Therefore, he said: "greatly delighting oneself. Thus, by this verse...
Because he was absorbed in jhāna, [the Buddha] spoke of his delight in forest dwellings and remote lodgings, as well as of Arahantship.
716. Now, having heard this teaching on the Dhamma, the Elder Nālaka set out for the forest edge;
yet even though he was without food, he was exceedingly eager to fulfill the path of practice. And it is not possible to perform the duties of a recluse while remaining without food. Thus...
For life does not proceed for one who performs [work]; rather, food should be sought by one who does not give rise to defilements—this is the principle here.

Therefore, the Blessed One, while teaching the duty of the alms-round with its culmination in the attainment of Arahantship, did so to show that although he must go for alms on successive days, he must nevertheless not give rise to defilements.
He spoke the six verses beginning with “Then, at the end of the night. Therein, “then” (*tato*) means after [the time] mentioned in the passage:
“Having wandered for alms, he should proceed to the edge of the forest. “At the end of the night” (*ratyā vivasāne*) means when the night has passed;

it is said to be on the second day. “He should proceed to the vicinity of a village” (*gāmantamabhihāraye*) refers to the conduct pertaining to the formal rules of discipline (*ābhisamācārika-vatta*).

Having cultivated seclusion for as long as it takes until the time for the alms-round, he should go to the village while attending to the meditation subject according to the method described in the section on the practice of "going and returning. He should not take delight in being invited;
that is, he should not welcome an invitation such as, "Venerable sir, please eat at our house," wondering, "Will they give or will they not? Will they give something good? and so forth.
"A monk who fulfills the practice [of the *paṭipadā*] should not delight in such a thought as 'Is he giving what is unattractive?
nor should he accept it. This is what is meant. However, if they take his bowl by force, fill it, and give it to him, he may consume it;
he should then perform the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), and the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is not violated. On that account, however, regarding that village...

One should not enter. Regarding "and from the village's offerings": even if they bring food to one who has already entered the village—even if it is brought by hundreds of people—one should not rejoice in that;
one should not accept even a single grain of rice from it, but should instead wander for alms strictly in regular order from house to house.
717. A sage does not, having approached a village, wander impulsively among families.
For that sage who has set out for the sake of wisdom, having gone to a village, he should not wander impulsively among families;

it is said that he should not fall into improper association with householders, such as impulsive grieving and the like. Having cut off idle chatter, he does not utter frivolous speech. "Having cut off chatter" means...
One should not speak words seeking food associated with light, indirect talk, hints, or gestures.

However, if one so desires, being ill, one may speak for the purpose of warding off that illness. Or, having made a formal request for lodging, one may speak in connection with light, indirect talk, or hints;
but if not ill, one should not say anything at all for the sake of the remaining requisites.
718–9. Regarding the meaning of this verse, *Alatthaṃ yadidaṃ*: when he has entered a village for alms, if he obtains even a small amount of anything, he thinks, "I have obtained this; it is good.
If he obtains nothing, he thinks, "I have not obtained anything wholesome," and he regards that too as "beautiful. Thus, through both gain and loss, he remains such—unperturbed.

Having offered [the gift], he returns to the tree; just as a man seeking fruit, having approached a tree, whether he obtains the fruit or not, goes on his way indifferent, unresisting, and neutral, so too, having approached a family, whether he obtains gain or not, he goes on his way remaining neutral.
This verse, "He with bowl in hand," is of plain meaning.
720. The connection with this verse, *uccāvacā*, is as follows:

Even though one has become accomplished in the practice of the alms-round (*bhikkhācāra-vatta*), one should not be satisfied with that alone, but should ascend the path of practice (*paṭipadā*). For the essence of the Dispensation (*sāsana*) is practice.
And this [practice] is "high and low" ... [etc] ... "liberation. Its meaning is: this path of practice is divided into the superior and the inferior.
Various high and low paths have been proclaimed by the Buddha-Samaṇa. For the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge is high;
the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge is low. The other two are high in one respect and low in another. Or else, the first alone is high, while the other three are low.
By means of either that high or that low practice, they do not go to the further shore twice over.
Alternatively, the reading is "duguṇaṃ," meaning that they do not reach Nibbāna twice by means of the same path. Why?
Because those defilements which have been abandoned by a particular path cannot be abandoned again. By this, he demonstrates the absence of the possibility of falling away.
This is not a single-fold release; furthermore, even this further shore is not something to be reached in only a single instance.
Why? Because all defilements are not abandoned by means of a single path. By this, he demonstrates that there is no attainment of Arahantship through that single path alone.
(721) Now, showing the benefit of the practice, he spoke the verse beginning with "yassa ca visatā. Its meaning is as follows:
for that bhikkhu who has practiced in this way, because [the defilements] have been abandoned by that practice, in terms of the state of the eight hundred modes of craving's wandering...

Because it has been seen through, craving no longer exists; for him who has cut off the stream of defilements, who has severed the stream, and who has abandoned both the wholesome and the unwholesome, having thus abandoned what is to be done and what is not to be done, not even the slightest fever born of lust or born of hatred is found. 722.
Now, having heard these verses, the mind of the Elder Nālaka arose thus: "If this much..."

“Moneyya is easy to do, not difficult; it can be fulfilled with little effort”—thinking thus, the Blessed One spoke again the words beginning with “I will point out moneyya to you,” showing that moneyya is indeed difficult to do.
In this context, *upaññissaṃ* means “I shall point out” (*upaññāpeyyaṃ*), which is to say, “I shall explain.
That which has the likeness of a razor’s edge is called “likened to a razor’s edge” (*khuradhārūpamo*).
"Bhaveti" means "should practice. What is the intended meaning? A monk practicing moneyya (the state of a sage) should conduct himself amidst the requisites by making the edge of a razor his simile.

Just as one licking a razor's edge smeared with honey protects his tongue from being cut, so too, while enjoying requisites obtained in accordance with the Dhamma, he should protect his mind from the arising of defilements; thus it is said.
It is so. For the Blessed One frequently speaks of being dependent on requisites, saying that it is not easy to obtain them by means of a pure method, nor to enjoy them without fault.
"Pressing the palate with the tongue, one should be restrained in the stomach": even by pressing the palate with the tongue, one should dispel craving for flavors, yet [not] by a defiled path.
Not indulging in arisen conditions, one should be restrained in eating.
(723) And one should be "unshrunken in mind": through constant cultivation of wholesome states and by acting with steadfastness, one's mind should not be indolent.
Furthermore, "one should not think too much": one should not engage in excessive reflection based on thoughts concerning relatives, the country, or immortality.

"Free from the stench of raw flesh, unattached, and devoted to the holy life": having become free from defilement, one should be independent of any state of existence through craving and views, and should indeed be devoted to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the entire teaching consisting of the three trainings.
724–5. "Of one who sits alone" means of one whose seat is secluded. And here, by way of the "seat," all postures (*iriyāpatha*) are implied. Since...
It should be understood that this means: "one should train in the state of oneness in all postures. The term *ekāsanassa* is a word in the dative case (the recipient).

And the phrase *samaṇūpāsanassa*: [this refers] either to the application to the cultivation of the thirty-eight objects of meditation which is to be attended upon by recluses (*samaṇa*), or to the very analysis of the thirty-eight objects of meditation which constitutes the attendance (*upāsana*) upon recluses. This too is indeed a word in the dative case.

It means "for the purpose of attending. Furthermore, it should be understood that here bodily seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is expressed by "sitting alone," while mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*) is expressed by "attending upon ascetics.
"Solitude is declared to be wisdom" (*ekattaṃ monamakkhātaṃ*): thus this is declared as "solitude is wisdom" by way of the seclusion of body and mind.
"If you should delight in being alone" (*eko ce abhiramissasi*): this, however, is a phrase that looks forward to the subsequent verse; "then... [the rest follows].
The connection with this [verse] is: "bhāhisī dasadisā" (you shall proclaim in the ten directions).
"Bhāhisī" means you will speak; you will make manifest. What is meant is that by cultivating this path, you will become renowned and well-known in all directions.
As for the meaning of the four lines beginning with "sutvā dhīrānaṃ" (having heard from the wise), it is as follows:

And when you proclaim your fame throughout the ten directions, having heard that report of those wise ones who meditate and have abandoned sensual desires, you should not fall into agitation because of it;
rather, you should further increase your sense of shame and faith.
Being moved by that report, you should generate faith, thinking, "This is the path leading to liberation," and proceed even further in that very practice.
"You should say: 'He is mine'; for if this is so, he becomes my disciple.

(726) "By means of the rivers": that which was said by me when saying, "One should cultivate shame and faith even more," and "Agitation should not be made"—know that by this illustration of the rivers, and its opposite in the case of the pools.
And you should know [the meaning] of *sobbhesu* and *padaresu*. *Sobbhesu* means in ravines; *padaresu* means in caves. How so?

"The small pools flow with noise, but the great ocean flows silently. For all small streams, including those classified as ravines, caves, and so forth, flow while making noise—that is, they go along agitated. But the great rivers, such as the Ganges and others, flow silently.

Thus, one who thinks, "I fulfill the state of a sage (moneyya)," becomes arrogant and lacks self-respect (*amāmaka*); however, one who possesses self-respect (*māmaka*), having generated moral shame (*hiri*) and faith (*saddhā*), remains humble in mind. 727–9.
Furthermore—regarding the passage beginning with "whatever is deficient... and ending with "...he is wise":

here it might be asked—if the fool is like a half-filled jar because of his noise, and the wise man is like a full lake because of his stillness, then why is the Buddha’s monk, being thus occupied with teaching the Dhamma, [not likewise noisy]...?
In connection with the phrase "having sacrificed, he speaks much," he recited the verse beginning with "Whatever the ascetic... Its meaning is as follows:
Whatever the Buddha-ascetic speaks in abundance—endowed with purpose, endowed with the Dhamma, and joined with what is beneficial—that is not out of agitation;
rather, knowing it, he teaches the Dhamma even if he were to teach for an entire day.

Having become free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). For all his verbal action follows after knowledge (*jñāna*). And while teaching in this way, knowing in various ways, "This is beneficial for him;
this is beneficial for him," he speaks much; it is not merely because of being a talkative person. The connection with the concluding verse:
thus, first of all, the Buddha-monk, endowed with omniscient knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), knowing—

He teaches the Dhamma; knowing, he speaks much. But as for the one who, through knowledge that partakes of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), knows the Dhamma taught by him, and being self-restrained, knowing, does not speak much—he is a sage worthy of silence; he is a sage who has attained silence.
Its meaning is this: knowing that Dhamma, having become self-restrained with a guarded mind, whatever he speaks...
Knowing that which does not bring welfare and happiness to beings, he does not speak much.
Such a person, practicing for the sake of *mona* (silence), is a sage (*muni*) worthy of *mona*, which is defined as the practice of sagely conduct.
Not only is he worthy of it, but furthermore, it should be understood that this sage has attained *mona*, which is defined as the knowledge of the path to *arahantship*.
He brought the teaching to its conclusion with the theme of arahantship.
Having heard this, the Elder Nālaka became moderate in his desires in three respects: in seeing, in hearing, and in questioning.
Indeed, at the conclusion of the teaching, he paid homage to the Blessed One with a mind full of faith and entered the forest, thinking again: "O, may I..."
He did not give rise to a state of restlessness, thinking, "May I see the Blessed One. This is his fewness of wishes regarding seeing.
Likewise, he did not give rise to a state of restlessness, thinking, "Oh, may I hear the teaching of the Dhamma again! This is his fewness of wishes regarding hearing.

Likewise, he did not give rise to a state of restlessness, thinking, "Oh, may I ask again about the practice of the way of the sage (moneyyapaṭipadā)! [This is his fewness of wishes regarding questioning.]
He understood this. This was his fewness of wishes regarding the question.
Being thus few in wishes, he entered a mountain foot and did not dwell for two days in a single grove;
he did not sit at the root of a single tree for two days; and he did not enter a single village for alms for two days. Thus...
Wandering from forest to forest, from tree to tree, and from village to village, he practiced the appropriate course of conduct and established himself in the supreme fruit.
Now, as for the monk who fulfills the practice of *moneyya* (monkhood) by making it rigorous, he lives for seven months;
by making it moderate, he lives for seven years; and by making it mild, he lives—

Sixteen years. He fulfilled this by taking the maximum limit; therefore, after staying for seven months, knowing that the life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*) was exhausted, he bathed, dressed, fastened his waist-band, and put on his double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*).
Facing the One of Ten Powers, he prostrated with the five limbs, raised his joined palms in reverence, and while still standing leaning against the Hiṅgulaka Rock, he said:
He attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue. Knowing that he had attained final Nibbāna, the Blessed One went there together with the community of monks;
having performed the funeral rites for the body, caused the relics to be collected, and established a shrine, he departed.
Thus ends the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the Nālaka Sutta of the Suttanipāta is finished.
12. Commentary on the Dvayatānupassanā Sutta:
“Thus have I heard” is the Dvayatānupassanā Sutta. What is its origin? This sutta originates from the Master’s own inclination.
The origin: The Blessed One taught this sutta out of his own internal inclination (*attajjhāsayena*). This is the summary here;
however, its detailed commentary will be made clear in the word-by-word explanation (*atthavaṇṇanā*) itself. In that regard, "Thus have I heard" and so forth are exactly as previously stated.
"In the Eastern Park" (*pubbārāme*) means in the monastery located to the east of the city of Sāvatthī. "In the Palace of Migāra’s Mother" (*migāramātupāsāde*)—here...
Because the laywoman Visākhā was established by her father-in-law, the merchant Migāra, in the position of a mother, she is called "Migāramātā" (Mother of Migāra).

A palace built for her by Migāramātā at a cost of nine koṭis, adorned with great festoons of jewels, was constructed with five hundred chambers on both the lower and upper levels, totaling one thousand gabled chambers. This...
"It is called the Migāramātupāsāda. In that Migāramātupāsāda.
"And at that time, the Blessed One" means at the time when the Blessed One was dwelling near Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery in the Migāramātupāsāda;
"on that Uposatha day" means on the day of the Uposatha.
This has been stated. Regarding the phrase "on the fifteenth": this is a statement that excludes all other Uposatha days by means of specifying the [specific] Uposatha day.

Regarding "on the night of the full moon": it is called "full" (*puṇṇāya*) because it is the fifteenth day and, by counting the days, is free from adventitious defilements such as clouds, and because it possesses the excellence of the night;
and it is called "the full-moon night" (*puṇṇamāya*) because the moon is completely full.
“Surrounded by the community of bhikkhus” means surrounded by the community of bhikkhus.
“He was seated in the open air” means he was seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the open space above, in the courtyard of Migāramātā’s Jewel Palace, in a place that was uncovered.
“Silent, silent” means exceedingly silent; or, from whichever direction he looked out, [he saw them all] silent.
Then, [he looked] at those who were silent, at those who were silent by word, and again at those who were silent by body.
Having surveyed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus—meaning the Saṅgha of bhikkhus numbering many thousands who sat surrounding him, all of whom were silent, silent—he [saw]:
"So many here are stream-enterers, so many are once-returners, so many are non-returners, and so many have insight meditation undertaken."
Having looked here and there in order to determine a suitable teaching of the Dhamma— thinking, "What kind of Dhamma-teaching is appropriate for this Saṅgha of bhikkhus?"—
he said: "Those wholesome states, bhikkhus," meaning those states which, by way of health, blamelessness, and desirable fruit.

And in the sense of being produced through skill, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) are wholesome (*kusala*), as are the teachings of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*) that illuminate them.
They are "noble" (*ariya*) in the sense of being accepted as leading to liberation; they are "leading out" (*niyyānika*) in the sense of leading away from the world;

and they are "leading to enlightenment" (*sambodhagāmina*) in the sense of going toward *arahantship*, which is designated as enlightenment. "For you, monks... [and so on]... for the sake of hearing these..."
"Monks, what is the proximate cause, what is the reason, what is the purpose for you to hear those wholesome states... leading to enlightenment?

For what aim do you listen to those teachings?"—this is what is meant. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of knowing, as it really is, the two kinds of phenomena": here, *yāvadeva* is a term used to define a limit or to establish a restriction. There are two parts.
"These are pairs": "pair" (dvaya) itself is "pairness" (dvayatā); [the phrase means] "of those pairnesses. There is also a reading "dvayānaṃ" (of the pairs).

"For the sake of knowledge as it really is" means for the sake of non-perverted knowledge. What is meant? This refers to that knowledge as it really is, termed insight, regarding phenomena established in two ways—such as the mundane and the supramundane—and it is for this purpose, and not beyond this.
For by means of hearing (savana), there is only this much; beyond that, the attainment of distinction comes through cultivation (bhāvanā).
As for the phrase "And what do you say regarding duality?"—here, if it were addressed to you, monks, the intended meaning would be: "And what, venerable sirs, do you say regarding duality?
However, the literal meaning of the words is: "And what do you say regarding the state of non-duality?"
(1) Then the Blessed One, demonstrating the state of duality, spoke thus: "This is suffering," and so forth.

Therein, regarding the four truths as a pair, this is one contemplation through the demonstration of a single mundane constituent of suffering—either together with its cause—as "this is suffering" and "this is the origin of suffering";
the other [contemplation] pertains to the supramundane second [constituent].

The second contemplation occurs through the vision of the cessation of the factors [of dependent origination] together with their means. Here, the first [contemplation] arises by means of the third and fourth purifications, while the second arises by means of the fifth purification.

Thus, for one who correctly contemplates the two-fold nature according to the method stated by the phrase "correctly contemplating the two-fold nature," there is mindfulness through non-separation from mindfulness, and through diligence consisting of physical and mental exertion.
"Of one who is ardent and regardless of body and life" refers to one who has sent forth his heart [in renunciation]. "To be expected" means it is to be desired.
"Final knowledge in this very life" means Arahantship within this very personal existence (*attabhāva*). Or, "if there is a residue of clinging, non-returning":
"residue of clinging" (*upādisesa*) refers to the remainder of the aggregates that are to be grasped by way of renewed existence; or, when that exists, the state of being a non-returner.
“He expects” indicates this. In that regard, although even the lower fruits belong to one who thus contemplates the dyad, he spoke thus in order to generate enthusiasm for the higher fruits.
“This he said,” and so forth, is the speech of the compilers of the collection. Therein, “this” refers to the aforementioned demonstration beginning with, “Those monks, bhikkhus.”

Now follows this demonstration of the composition of the verses to be recited, beginning with “Those who [know] suffering. These verses illuminate the meaning already stated because they elucidate the Four Noble Truths;

nevertheless, they are intended for those who prefer verse, for those who arrived later and were unable to retain what was previously said, for those who hope, “It would be excellent if he were now to speak,” and for those whose minds are distracted.

"Vuttā" means "it is said. It is called "the illuminator of the specific meaning" because, having shown both the non-possessor of insight (*avipassaka*) and the possessor of insight (*vipassaka*), it demonstrates for them the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*);
therefore, it is stated specifically for the purpose of showing that particular meaning. This same method applies to the subsequent verses as well.
(730) Therein, "wherein" (*yattha*) indicates *nibbāna*. For in *nibbāna*, suffering (*dukkha*) is completely brought to an end.
It ceases in every way; it ceases with its causes; and it ceases without remainder.
And that path—namely, the Eightfold Path.
"They are devoid of liberation of mind, and likewise liberation by wisdom"—here, the concentration of the fruit of Arhatship is the fading away of lust.

It should be understood that liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) is the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship through the fading away of ignorance (*avijjāvirāga*), and liberation by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*) is likewise.

Alternatively, the fruit of Arahantship attained by one of craving-temperament after suppressing defilements through the power of absorption meditation (*appanā-jhāna*) is liberation of mind through the fading away of lust (*rāgavirāga*);
whereas the fruit of Arahantship attained by one of view-temperament after producing merely access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*) and practicing insight (*vipassanā*) is [liberation by wisdom].

Through the fading away of ignorance, there is liberation by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*). Alternatively, with reference to sensual lust, the fruit of non-returning is liberation of mind through the fading away of lust (*rāgavirāgā cetovimutti*);

the fruit of arahantship is liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance in every respect. "For the making of an end" means for the purpose of bringing about the end of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
"Subject to birth and aging" means having approached birth and aging, or having come under the power of birth and aging; they are not liberated.
Birth and aging are to be understood in this very way. The rest here, from the beginning onwards, is already clear.
And at the conclusion of the verses, about sixty bhikkhus, having grasped that teaching and practiced insight (vipassanā), attained arahantship on that very seat.
And as it was here, so it was in all the sections.
(2) For this very reason, the Blessed One taught the contemplation of duality in its various modes by way of the method beginning with the words, “It may be by another way as well.

Therein, in the second section, “with the condition of acquisitions” means with the condition of kamma subject to taints (*sāsrava*). For here, it is kamma subject to taints that is intended by the term “acquisition” (*upadhi*).

“Through the remainderless fading away and cessation” means through cessation by means of the fading away of everything without exception, or cessation which is characterized as the fading away of everything without exception.

734. "With acquisitions as the cause" means with kamma as the condition. "Contemplating the origin of suffering from birth" means contemplating that "acquisitions" are the cause of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
The rest here is self-evident. Thus, this section also, having illuminated the Four Truths, is stated by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship. And just as this is so, so it is for all the sections.

(3) Therein, in the third section, "conditioned by ignorance" means conditioned by the ignorance that constitutes the accumulation of kamma leading to existence (*bhava*). However, "suffering" in all instances refers exclusively to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

735. "The cycle of birth and death" refers to birth as the arising of the aggregates, death as the dissolution of the aggregates, and the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) as the continuous succession of the aggregates.
"They go" means they proceed or arrive [there]. "This state and another state" refers to this human state...
And [it refers] to the state of being other nikāyas remaining from this. "Gati" means the state of being a condition.

736. "Ignorance wanes": for this is ignorance. "And those beings who have reached true knowledge (*vijjā*)," meaning those beings whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), having gone by piercing through the defilements with the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. The rest is of self-evident meaning.
(4) In the fourth section, "with volitional formations as condition" means with the conditions of meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations.
"Having known this danger" means: having known that this suffering has its condition in volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). "The stilling of all volitional formations" means:
by means of the knowledge of the path, there is the stilling—that is, the destruction and the capacity for the fruit—of all the aforementioned kinds of volitional formations.
"Of perceptions" refers to perceptions of sensual desire and so forth, [which are abandoned] by the path itself.
“Obstruction”: having known this as it truly is, meaning having known this destruction of suffering without error. “Perfect vision” means right seeing.
“Having fully understood” means having understood the conditioned as impermanent and so forth, and the unconditioned as permanent and so forth.
“The bond of Māra” refers to the round of existence in the three realms. The rest is self-evident.
(5) In the fifth section, "conditioned by consciousness" means conditioned by the formative volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*) that arises simultaneously with karma. 741.
"Free from hunger" means free from craving. "Parinibbūta" means he has attained final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna of the defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*). The remainder is self-evident.
(6) In the sixth section, "conditioned by contact" means conditioned by contact associated with the formative volitional consciousness.
Thus, instead of stating the name-and-form and the six sense-bases here in their sequential order, contact is mentioned.
For those [latter] are not associated with kamma because they are mixed with form; however, this suffering of the round might arise either from kamma or from states associated with kamma.
"Following the stream of existence" means following craving. "Having fully understood" means having understood by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*).
"Having known" means having known by means of the wisdom of the path of arahantship. "Delighting in peace" means delighting in Nibbāna by way of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"The realization of contact" means the cessation of contact. The rest is self-evident.
(7) In the seventh section, "conditioned by feeling" means conditioned by feeling associated with kamma. 744–5.
"Together with neither-pain-nor-pleasure" means together with that which is neither painful nor pleasant.

"Knowing this to be suffering" means knowing all this that is felt to be a "cause of suffering," or [knowing it as] suffering due to the suffering inherent in change and the suffering inherent in the state of ignorance.
"Having known": "subject to vanishing" means having the nature of perishing; "dissolving" means having the nature of crumbling away through aging and death.
"Touching again and again" means touching with the knowledge of arising and passing away. "They see its passing away" means seeing only its dissolution at the end.
"Thus one understands therein" means one understands those feelings in that way, or one understands the state of suffering therein.
"Of the destruction of feelings": beyond that, it means through the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*), there is the destruction of feelings associated with kamma.
The rest is self-evident. (8) In the eighth section, "conditioned by craving" means conditioned by the craving that constitutes the accumulation of kamma.
747. "Having known this danger, that craving is the origin of suffering": having known this danger in craving—that it is the origin of suffering. The rest is self-evident.
(9) On the ninth occasion, "with clinging as condition" means with the accumulation of karma as the condition for clinging. 748–9.

"Becoming" refers to resultant becoming (*vipākabhava*), the manifestation of the aggregates. "Once become, one encounters suffering" means that once born and come into existence, one undergoes the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
Regarding "death for one who is born," even though fools imagine, "once born, one encounters happiness," [it is not so].
Showing that even there it is nothing but suffering, he said: “For one who is born, there is death. The construction of the second verse is as follows:
having rightly understood through impermanence and so forth, the wise, by the destruction of clinging, having directly known the destruction of birth which is Nibbāna, do not go to further becoming.
(10) In the tenth section, "condition by undertaking" (*ārambha-paccaya*) means the condition of energy associated with kamma. 751.
"Liberation in non-undertaking" (*anārambhe vimutti*) refers to one who is liberated in non-undertaking, that is, in Nibbāna.
The rest is self-evident. (11) In the eleventh section, "nutriment condition" (*āhāra-paccaya*) means the nutriment condition associated with kamma. Another method: [it is] fourfold.

Beings are those who have approached form, those who have approached feeling, those who have approached perception, and those who have approached mental formations. Among these, beings in the elevenfold sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu) have approached form due to their indulgence in edible food.
Beings in the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu)—with the exception of the non-percipient beings—have approached feeling due to their indulgence in contact as nutriment.
Beings in the threefold immaterial realm (arūpadhātu) below that have approached perception due to their indulgence in the nutriment of mental volition produced by perception.
"At the peak of existence, beings go toward formations by means of the cultivation of consciousness-nutriment produced from formations.
Thus, it should be understood that whatever suffering arises, all of it has nutriment as its condition. 755.
"Health" is Nibbāna. "One who uses after reflecting" is one who uses [the requisites] having reflected upon the four conditions.
Having thus reckoned the world as "the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements," he dwells with the knowledge that it is "impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
"Established in the Dhamma" means established in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
"He does not enter into reckoning" means he does not fall into such designations as "god" or "human. The rest is self-evident.
(12) In the twelfth section, "the condition for wavering" (*iñjitapaccaya*) refers to the conditions for wavering caused by any of the following:

craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), views (*diṭṭhi*), karma (*kamma*), or the defilements (*kilesa*). "Having abandoned wavering" (*ejaṃ vossajja*) means having relinquished craving. "He restrains formations" (*saṅkhāre uparundhiya*) means having ceased karma and the formations associated with karma. The rest is self-evident.

(13) In the thirteenth section, "the wavering of one who is dependent" (*nissitassa calitaṃ*) means that for one who is dependent upon the aggregates through craving, or through craving, views, and conceit, there occurs a trembling of fear, as in the case of the gods in the *Sīhasutta*. The rest is self-evident.

(14) In the fourteenth section, “by means of forms” (*rūpehi*) refers either to form-existences (*rūpabhava*) or to form-attainments (*rūpasamāpatti*). “Formless” (*arūpā*) refers to formless existences (*arūpabhava*) or formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*). “Cessation” (*nirodha*) is *nibbāna*.

“Those who have abandoned death” (*maccuhāyino*) refers to those who have abandoned the death of physical mortality, the death of defilements (*kilesa*), and the death of the son of a god (*devaputta*); it is said that they are those who go having left behind all three kinds of death. The rest is self-evident.
(15) In the fifteenth section, he says “it” (*yaṃ*) with reference to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). For that is regarded by the world as permanent, beautiful, and pleasurable.
"This is true" refers to what has been contemplated, seen, and observed. "Tadamariyānaṃ" means "this belongs to the Noble Ones"; it is stated thus by eliding the nasalization and the letter *e*.
"Etaṃ musā" means that even though this was grasped as being permanent and so forth, it is false; it does not exist in such a way. Again, with reference to Nibbāna, he says "yaṃ.
For indeed, because of the absence of form, feeling, and so on, the world [regards] it as "this is false; it does not exist."
"Something" refers to that which has been closely contemplated. "This is the truth for the ignoble ones"—

this very thing is seen clearly with right wisdom as it truly is, according to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), as "truth" because it does not depart from its noble state characterized by the absence of defilements, its state of bliss characterized as the antidote to the suffering of the round of existence, and its state of permanence characterized as absolute peace.
762–3. *Anattani attamāninī*: one who conceives a self in what is not-self, that is, in name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
*Idaṃ saccanti maññati*: one conceives this name-and-form as "truth" by way of its being permanent and so forth. *Yena yena hi*:
by whatever [means], such as by way of form or feeling, they conceive [it] in the manner of "my form," "my feeling," and so on. *Tato taṃ*: from that, the mode of conceiving.
That name-and-form becomes otherwise. For what reason? Because it is false for him;
since it is false in the manner in which it was conceived, the meaning is that it therefore becomes otherwise. But why is it false?
Because it is of a deceptive nature and ephemeral; for whatever is ephemeral and has a limited manifestation is of a deceptive nature—that is, subject to destruction—and such is this [name-and-form].
"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). "The realization of the truths" (*saccābhisamaya*) means the awakening to the truths.
The rest is self-evident. (16) In the sixteenth section, he says "goes" with reference to the sixfold desirable object.

For that is what is contemplated as "this is happiness" by the world—including grasshoppers, fish, monkeys, and so forth—just as [grasshoppers contemplate] lamps, [fish] bait, and [monkeys] honeyed cakes. But for the Noble Ones (*ariya*), this is suffering.

This very thing has been well-seen by the Noble Ones with right wisdom, according to reality, as "this is suffering," in the manner beginning: "Sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful; they agitate the mind with their manifold forms. Again, he says "that" referring specifically to Nibbāna.
For that is contemplated as "suffering" by the world because of the absence of the strands of sensual pleasure. "That of the ignoble ones" means:
This very thing has been clearly seen as it really is with correct wisdom by the Noble Ones as "this is happiness," because it is the ultimate happiness of the Noble Ones.
765–6. *Kevalā* means without remainder. *Iṭṭhā* means desired or longed for. *Kantā* means dear. *Manāpā* means those that increase the mind's delight.
*Yāvatatthīti vuccatīti*: it is said that "as far as these six objects exist. The grammatical construction (*vacanabyatti*) should be understood accordingly.
*Ete* and *voti* here are merely particles.

767–8. "Happiness" (*sukha*) is seen by the Noble Ones as the complete cessation of identity-view (*sakkāya*). That is to say, the cessation of the five aggregates is seen as "happiness" by the Noble Ones;
what is meant is that it is Nibbāna. "This is contrary" means this is a reverse perspective.
"Passantānaṃ" means "of those who see," that is, of the wise (*paṇḍita*). Regarding the phrase "yaṃ paraṃ," here it refers to sense-objects (*vatthukāma*);
again, regarding "yaṃ paraṃ," here it refers to Nibbāna.
(Verses 769–71) "Passa" is an address to the listener. "Dhammaṃ" refers to the Dhamma of Nibbāna. "Sampamūḷhetthaviddasū" [means...]
The ignorant fools are utterly deluded herein. For what reason are they deluded? Darkness prevails for those who are shrouded; there is gloom for those who do not see.
For the fools, being shrouded by ignorance and enveloped by it, there is a darkness that produces blindness, by which they are unable to see the Dhamma of Nibbāna.
But for the wise, it is opened up; there is light as if for those who see. And for the wise...
For those who see with the wisdom-vision of true persons (*sappurisa*), Nibbāna becomes like a light revealed. "They do not perceive what is near;

these wanderers are unskilled in the Dhamma"—this refers to Nibbāna being "near" because it is to be attained immediately after one has delimited the mere fivefold skin [of the body] within one's own person, or because it is merely the cessation of one's own aggregates (*khandha*). Thus, it is near.
Even though it exists, people do not discern it; being like those lost on a path, they are unskilled in the nature of what is the path and what is not the path, or in the nature of truth.

In every respect, the craving for existence... [as before] ...is easily awakened to. In this context, "by those who have not entered Māra’s realm" means by those who have not entered the cycle of existence consisting of the three planes.
772. The connection with the final verse is: "Who indeed, other than Māra, would not know this which is so difficult to awaken to? Its meaning is as follows.
"Who else besides the Noble Ones is worthy to know the state of Nibbāna— that state which, having been rightly known through the fourth noble path,
they immediately become free from taints and attain final Nibbāna by the extinction of the defilements, or, having been rightly known and becoming free from taints,
they eventually attain final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue? Thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

"Attamanā" means with contented minds. "Abhinanduṃ" means they rejoiced. "Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ" means in this sixteenth discourse (veyyākaraṇa). "Bhaññamāne" means while it was being spoken. The rest is self-evident.

Thus, when each of the sixteen discourses was treated as consisting of sixty [verses], the minds of nine hundred and sixty monks were liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Sixteen times four...
Having established four [truths], sixty-four truths are taught here in various ways according to the needs of those to be trained.
This concludes the commentary on the *Dvayatānupassanā-sutta* from the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, within the *Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*.
It is concluded.
And the third chapter is finished according to the method of explaining the meaning; by name, it is called the Mahāvagga.
4. The Chapter of Eight Verses (Aṭṭhakavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Sensual Pleasures (Kāmasuttavaṇṇanā) 773.
"One who desires sensual pleasures... This is the Discourse on Sensual Pleasures. What is its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī...
A certain brahmin was plowing a field between Sāvatthī and Jetavana on the bank of the Aciravatī River, thinking, "I shall sow barley.
As the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, was entering for alms, he saw him; reflecting upon it, he perceived:
"The barley of this brahmin will perish. Then, reflecting further upon his [the brahmin's] excellence of supporting conditions...
