He saw the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for the fruit of stream-entry.
Reflecting on when he might attain it, he saw that it would be when [the people], overwhelmed by grief at the destruction of their crops, heard the teaching of the Dhamma. Then he thought:
"If I were to approach the brahmin right now, he would not think my advice worth hearing. For brahmins have diverse tastes; well then..."
“From this moment on, I shall take him under my care; thus, with a softened heart toward me, he will then listen to my advice.
Having approached the brahmin, he asked, “What are you doing, brahmin?
At that very moment, the brahmin thought, “The ascetic Gotama, though born of such a high lineage, is exchanging greetings with me,” and his mind became filled with confidence toward the Blessed One.
Having offered the oblation, he said, "Master Gotama, I am plowing my field; I shall sow barley. Then the Elder Sāriputta thought:
"The Blessed One has exchanged greetings with this brahmin, and Tathāgatas do not do so without cause or reason.
Come now, I too shall exchange greetings with him. Having thus reflected, he approached the brahmin.
In that same way, he extended a hospitable welcome. Thus did the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and the remaining eighty great disciples act.
The brahmin was exceedingly delighted.
Then one day, even though the harvest was failing, the Blessed One, having finished his meal, departed from Sāvatthī for Jetavana.
While traveling, he left the road, went into the presence of the brahmin, and said, "Your barley field is beautiful, brahmin.
"It is so, Master Gotama; it is beautiful. If it succeeds, I shall share some with you as well.
Then, at the end of four months, the barley was harvested. He thought, "I will reap it today or tomorrow."
While he was still making these anxious efforts, a great cloud arose and rained throughout the entire night.
The river Aciravatī overflowed its banks and swept away all the barley. Having spent the whole night in distress, the brahmin went to the riverbank at dawn;
seeing the total ruin of his crops, he was overcome by intense grief, thinking, "I am lost! How shall I live now?"
He caused it to arise. The Blessed One, too, on that very night at the time of dawn, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, knew:
"Today is the time for the brahmin’s teaching of the Dhamma. Having entered Sāvatthī for alms according to the practice of wandering monks, he stood at the door of the brahmin’s house.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, the brahmin thought: "The ascetic wishes to comfort me, who am overwhelmed by grief..."
Thinking, "Gotama has arrived," he prepared a seat, took up the bowl, and had the Blessed One sit down.
Although the Blessed One already knew, he asked the brahmin: "Brahmin, did you dwell with a corrupted mind?
"Yes, Master Gotama; my entire barley field was swept away by water. Then the Blessed One said: "No, brahmin..."
"One should feel grief when things go wrong and joy when they go well; for indeed, sensual pleasures both succeed and fail.
Having said this, and having understood what was suitable for that brahmin, he spoke this sutta by way of teaching the Dhamma.
Herein, we shall describe only the brief connection between the words, while the detailed exposition follows the method already stated in the Niddesa.
It is to be understood. And just as in this sutta, so it is in all subsequent suttas.
Therein, "desire" (*kāma*) refers to *vatthukāma*—the objects of desire consisting of agreeable forms and other phenomena belonging to the various planes.
"Of one desiring" (*kāmayamānassa*) means of one who wishes. "If that succeeds for him" (*tassa ce taṃ samijjhati*) means if that which is designated as desire succeeds for that being who desires it.
"If the basis succeeds" means, if he obtains it—that is what is meant. "Surely his mind is joyful" means his heart is filled with singular satisfaction.
"Having obtained" means having acquired. "A mortal" means a living being. "Whatever he desires" means that which he wishes for. 774.
"If for him who is desiring" means for that person who is longing for sensual pleasures, or who is striving through sensual desire.
"Chandajātassa" means one in whom craving has arisen. "Jantuno" means a living being. "Te kāmā parihāyanti" means if those sensual pleasures should diminish.
"Sallaviddhova ruppati" means then he is afflicted as if pierced by an arrow made of iron or other metals.
The summary meaning of the third verse is: But he who, through the suppression of desire and lust for these sensual pleasures therein...
Or by means of total eradication, he avoids it with his own foot as one would avoid the head of a snake.
That bhikkhu, having transcended the entire world, being mindful, overcomes craving—which is termed "clinging in the world. 776–8.
The summary meaning of the three following verses is this: whoever [avoids] this rice field and so forth...
Whether it be a field or a site such as a house, or wealth consisting of kahāpaṇas, or cattle and horses,
or women known as "female," or kinsmen and relatives such as father and mother, or other various desirable forms and so forth— the defilements,
which are termed "weakness," overpower, overcome, and crush that person who is greedily attached to them; for they lack the power of faith and the other [spiritual] powers.
Or, when that person is weak, the weak defilements overpower him; the meaning is that they overpower him because he is weak.

Then, while he is greedy for sense pleasures, guarding them and seeking after them, lions and other such manifest dangers, as well as the unmanifest dangers such as bodily misconduct and the like, crush him.
Thereafter, that person, overcome by those unmanifest dangers, experiences the suffering of birth and so forth.
It follows [the object] like water following a broken boat.

Therefore, by means of the cultivation of mindfulness directed to the body and so forth, a person, being constantly mindful, should avoid sensual pleasures—that is, all modes of defilement-sensual-desire regarding the objects of desire such as forms—by way of suppression and eradication.
Having thus abandoned those sensual pleasures, by means of the very path that effects their abandonment, [one abandons] even the fourfold...
One should cross the flood; one should be able to cross it.

Just as a person, having bailed out a boat heavy with water, would reach the far shore with ease by means of that lightened boat and go to the other side, even so, having bailed out the boat of the self which is heavy with the water of the defilements, one would reach the far shore by means of a lightened self, reaching the further shore of all phenomena.

"He would have attained Nibbāna; he would have gone for the attainment of Arahantship; he attains final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue"—thus he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the peak of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, both the brahmin and the brahmin lady were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The commentary on the Kāmasutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is finished. 2.
Commentary on the Guhaṭṭhakasutta.
779. *Satto guhāyam*: this is the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta. What is its origin?

It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja went to Kosambī to the royal park called Āvaṭṭaka on the bank of the Gaṅgā, desiring to sit for his midday rest in a cool place. For he used to go there even on other occasions.
This is according to the method explained in the commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta, regarding how the Elder Gavampati [attained] the Tāvatiṃsa realm through former practice.
There, having entered into meditative attainment at the cool foot of a tree on the bank of the Ganges, he sat for his midday rest.
King Udena, too, went that very day to the pleasure garden for recreation and spent most of the day there with dancing, singing, and other such diversions.
Having played in the park, intoxicated by drink, he lay down with his head in the lap of one woman.
The other women, thinking "the king is asleep," rose up and were gathering flowers, fruits, and so forth in the park;
seeing the Elder, they established a sense of shame and modesty, restrained one another saying "do not make a sound," and approached him quietly, paid homage, and [stood] before the Elder.
They sat down surrounding him. The Elder, having emerged from meditative absorption, taught them the Dhamma;
they, being delighted, said, "Excellent, excellent! and listened.
A woman sitting with the king's head on her lap became jealous of them, thinking, "These women are playing while leaving me behind," and [she struck] her thigh.
Having shaken the king, she awakened him. Upon waking, the king, not seeing the women of the harem, asked, "Where are these wretches?
She replied, "While you were occupied, they went away thinking, 'We will delight the ascetic. Enraged, he went toward the Elder.
When those women saw the king, some rose up, while others said, "Great King, [to one] who has gone forth..."
“Let us hear the Dhamma in his presence,” they said, and yet they did not rise. Becoming even more enraged by this, he failed to pay homage to the Elder and asked, “For what purpose have you come?
“For the sake of seclusion, Great King. He replied, “If you have come for the sake of seclusion, why do you sit here surrounded by a retinue of women?
Then he said, “Tell me about your seclusion. Although the Elder was confident, [he remained silent].
Thinking, "He does not ask this because he wishes to know," the Elder remained silent. The king thought, "If you do not speak, I will have you devoured by red ants!
He took a nest of red ants from an *aśoka* tree and scattered it over himself.
After wiping his body and taking another nest, he went toward the Elder. The Elder...
Thinking, “If this king were to offend against me, he would be headed for the states of misery,” he ascended into the sky by means of his supernormal power and departed out of compassion for him.
Then the women said, “Great King, when other kings see such a renunciant, they honor him with flowers, perfumes, and so forth...”
“They pay homage; you, however, have begun to attack him with a tambakipillika leaf and have set out to destroy the family lineage.
Realizing his own fault, he remained silent and asked the park-keeper, “Does the Elder come here on other days as well?
“Yes, Great King,” he replied. “In that case, inform me whenever he arrives. One day, when the Elder...
When he arrived, he reported this. The king also approached the Elder, asked him a question, and went for refuge with his life.
On the day [the Elder] was provided with a casket of red arsenic, however, the Elder came through the air, submerged again into the earth, and emerged within the Blessed One’s fragrant chamber.
The Blessed One, meanwhile, remained on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending.
While he was assuming the lion’s posture, seeing the Elder, he said, "Bhāradvāja, why have you come at an improper time?

The Elder replied, "Yes, Blessed One," and related the entire occurrence. Having heard this, the Blessed One said, "What will talk of seclusion avail one who is greedy for the strands of sensual pleasure?
and while still lying on his right side, [he spoke] to the Elder.
He spoke this sutta for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.

In this context, "beast" (*satta*) means one who is bound. "In the cave" (*guhāyaṃ*) means in the body. For the body is called a "cave" because it is the dwelling place of the wild beasts that are passion and the other defilements.
"Covered by much" (*bahunābhicchanno*) means covered by the extensive web of defilements such as passion. By this, the internal bondage is indicated.
It has been said: "They stand by means of lust and the other [defilements]. A "man" (*nara*) is a sentient being (*satta*). "Plunged into delusion" (*mohanasmim pagāḷho*):
"delusion" (*mohana*) refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), for therein gods and humans are deluded; having become submerged within them. By this, the external bond is described.
"For such a one is far from seclusion": such a person as that is distant from the three kinds of seclusion, beginning with physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).
"Far from seclusion, not near. For what reason? "For sensual pleasures in the world are indeed not easy to abandon"—this means that because sensual pleasures in the world are not easily abandoned.
Having thus established in the first verse that "one such as this is far from seclusion," [the text proceeds] again regarding beings of such a kind...
Revealing the nature of things (*dhammatā*), he spoke this verse: “With craving as their source” (*icchānidāna*). Therein, “with craving as their source” means having *taṇhā* as their cause.
“Bound by the pleasure of existence” (*bhavasātabaddha*) means bound to the pleasure of existence consisting of pleasant feeling and so forth. “Hard to release” (*duppamuñca*):

those phenomena which serve as the basis for the pleasure of existence, or the beings bound therein with craving as their source, are difficult to liberate. “Not by another’s release” (*na hi aññamokkha*) means not by another...
And they are not able to release them. Or rather, this is a statement of the reason:
those beings are difficult to release. Why? Because they cannot be released by another. But if they were to be released, they would be released by their own power;
this is its meaning. "Looking back or forward" means looking back toward or forward toward sensual pleasures in the future or the past. These very sensual pleasures...
They long for either past sensual pleasures or those of the present; that is, they yearn with powerful craving for both these two types—past and future.
Furthermore, the connection between these two phrases and the following line, “‘They are hard to release, for there is no other liberation,’” should be understood;
otherwise, it would not be clear what they do or what has been done by those who long while looking back [at the past].

781–2. Having thus established in the first verse that "such [beings] are far from seclusion," and having revealed in the second verse the natural disposition (*dhammatā*) of such beings, he now speaks the verse beginning with "greedy for sense pleasures" (*kāmesu giddhā*) to reveal their performance of evil deeds.
Its meaning is as follows: those beings are greedy for sense pleasures due to craving for enjoyment, because they are intent upon seeking them out and so forth.

They are "confused" because they have fallen into delusion; they are "bewildered" due to their lack of understanding and their stinginess, and because they do not accept the words of the Buddha and others, they are "uncultivated.

Established in the unevenness of bodily disorder and so forth, brought to the suffering of death at the end of life, they lament, "What shall we become when we pass away from here? Since this is so, therefore one should train... [etc. ...do not be.
"Be steadfast. In this context, "one should train" means one should undertake the three trainings. "Right here" means in this very teaching. The rest is self-evident.
Now, showing the misfortune that befalls those who do not act accordingly, he spoke the verse beginning with "I see.
In this context, "I see" means I perceive with the fleshly eye and so forth. "In the world" refers to the realms of misery and so on. "Trembling" means...

"Quivering here and there": this refers to this generation, this collection of beings. "Overcome by craving" means overcome or dominated by craving; the intended sense is that they have been cast down by it.
"In states of existence" (bhavesu) means in the realms of sensual existence and so forth. "Lowly men" are those whose actions are base.
"Lamenting in the mouth of death" means they wail when the time of death has arrived at the mouth of the Ender. "Those who have not transcended craving."

"Not free from craving. "In various states of existence" (*bhavābhavesu*) means in the realms of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth. Alternatively, "in various states of existence" (*bhavābhavesu*) means in existences and non-existences; that is to say, in repeated births. 784.
Now, since those who are not free from craving thus quiver and prattle, [the Buddha], exhorting them toward the subduing of craving—
He recited the verse beginning with “mamāyite. Therein, “mamāyite” means in an object grasped as “mine” through craving, views, and the conceit of “mine-ness.
“Passatha” (Behold! he said, addressing the listeners. “Etampi” (This too) refers to this very danger (*ādīnava*). The rest is self-evident. 785.
Thus, having shown the gratification (*assāda*) here by means of the first verse, and the danger by the four following verses, now—

In order to show the means of escape (*nissaraṇa*), the benefit of that escape (*nissaraṇānisaṃsa*), and by all these [verses] to show the danger (*ādīnava*), the degradation (*okāra*), and the defilement (*saṃkilesa*) of sensual pleasures (*kāma*),
he now spoke the two verses beginning with "In both extremes" (*ubhosu antesu*) in order to show the benefit of renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
Therein, "in both extremes" (*ubhosu antesu*) refers to the two limits consisting of contact (*phassa*) and the origination of contact (*phassasamudaya*), and so forth.
"Having removed desire" means having removed desire-and-lust (*chanda-rāga*). "Having fully understood contact" means:

having fully understood by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*) the entire range of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), namely, contact such as eye-contact and so forth; or, following from contact, all immaterial phenomena associated with it; and, by way of their bases, doors, and objects, all material phenomena as well. "Not greedy after" refers to form and the other [sense-objects].
"Unattached to all phenomena. Not doing what one censures oneself": not performing that which one condemns within oneself.
"The wise one is unstained by what is seen or heard":
such a wise one, endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*), is not stained by even one of the two stains regarding phenomena seen or heard. Like space, he is unsullied and has attained ultimate purity.
786. As for the verse beginning with "He fully understands perception," this is the summary of its meaning:

Not only contact, but also perception—divided into the categories of sensual perception and so forth—and having fully understood name-and-form through the three kinds of full understanding according to the method previously explained by way of following perception, he would cross over even the fourfold flood by means of this practice; thereafter, he...

Having crossed the flood by abandoning the stains of craving and views regarding the grasping of craving and views, the sage whose taints are exhausted is "one whose arrow is pulled out" because he has extracted the arrows of passion and the rest;
being vigilant through the attainment of the fullness of mindfulness— or having been vigilant in the preliminary stage— he,
having become one whose arrow is pulled out by that practice of vigilance, [abandons] the distinctions of his own and others' personal existences.
He did not wish for this world or the next; rather, with the cessation of his final consciousness, being without clinging, he attained Parinibbāna like a fire gone out.
Thus, establishing the guide of the Dhamma, he brought the teaching to its conclusion by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship.
He did not produce any further path or fruit through this teaching, because it was taught for one whose taints were exhausted.
The commentary on the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta from the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā within the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Paramatthajotikā, is completed. 3.
Commentary on the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta.
787. *Vadanti ve duṭṭhamanā*—this refers to the *Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka-sutta*. What is its origin? First, regarding the origin of the opening verse:
following the pattern of the *Muni-sutta*, the heretics, unable to endure the gain and honor arising for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, dispatched the female wanderer Sundarī.
She was indeed the most beautiful woman in the land, a female wanderer dressed in white garments.
She had bathed well, was well-dressed, and was adorned with garlands, perfumes, and ointments.
Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, she departed from Sāvatthī at the time when the residents of Sāvatthī were leaving the Jeta Grove, and she proceeded toward the Jeta Grove.
When asked by people, "Where are you going? she replied, "To the ascetic Gotama and his disciples."
Having said, "I am going to delight him," she wandered about at the gate-tower of the Jeta Grove.
When the gate-tower of the Jeta Grove was closed, she entered the city; then, returning to the Jeta Grove at dawn, she moved about near the Gandhakuṭi as if searching for flowers.
And when people who had come to attend upon the Buddha asked her, "For what purpose have you come? she replied:

When questioned, she said whatever came to mind. When half a month had thus passed, the heretics took her life, placed her on the bank of the ditch, and at dawn, crying out "We do not see Sundarī!", they raised a clamor and informed the king.
With his permission, they entered Jetavana and, as if searching, [found her] from the place where she had been laid.
Having lifted him up, placed him upon a bier, and carried him into the city, they raised a great outcry.
All of this is to be understood according to the method already set forth in the Pāḷi.
On that day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, [saw]: "Today the heretics will incur infamy..."

Knowing that [the people] were about to give rise [to such thoughts], and thinking, "Lest the great multitude, having believed them and provoked their hearts against one like me, should head toward the states of misery," he closed the door of the Fragrant Chamber and remained inside it; he did not enter the city for alms.
But when the monks saw the door closed, they entered just as they had before. When the people [saw] the monks...
Having seen him, they reviled him in various ways. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having reported that matter to the Blessed One, said:
"Venerable sir, a great scandal has been raised by the sectarians; it is not possible to live here. Jambudīpa is vast; let us go elsewhere.
When the scandal had arisen even there, [the Blessed One asked]: "Ānanda, where will you go? [He replied]: "Elsewhere..."
“...the Blessed One to the city. Then the Blessed One said, “Wait, Ānanda; this sound shall last for only seven days.

After the passing of seven days, it will fall upon those very people by whom this infamy was created,” and having spoken thus, he recited this verse, beginning with “They indeed say,” for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the Elder Ānanda.
In that context, "they speak" means they revile the Blessed One and the community of monks.

"Some with malicious minds, and others even though [knowing] the truth" means: some with corrupt hearts; some who, while perceiving it as such, were followers of other sects (tīrthikas) with corrupt hearts;
and those who, having heard their words, believed them—this is the intended meaning of "even though [knowing] the truth. And "the dispute has arisen"—this...
"An outburst of abuse has arisen; the sage does not approach it": because he is a non-doer and because he is unshakable, the Buddha-sage does not approach it.
Therefore, "for this sage there is no thicket anywhere": for that reason, it should be understood that this sage has no thicket of lust and so forth anywhere at all.
Having spoken this verse, the Blessed One asked the Elder Ānanda, “Ānanda, when monks are thus reviled and disparaged, what do they say? “Nothing at all, Blessed One.
“Ānanda, one should not remain silent everywhere thinking, ‘I am virtuous. For in the world, people do not recognize one who does not speak out, especially when mixed with fools.”
Having said, "He is wise," [the Blessed One] spoke this verse—"The speaker of untruth goes to hell"—for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, saying, "Ānanda, let the monks thus rebuke those people.
The Elder, having learned it, said to the monks, "People should be rebuked by you with this verse. The monks did so. Wise people...
They remained silent. The king, having dispatched his royal officers everywhere, had those scoundrels apprehended who had given bribes to the sectarians to have him murdered;
having learned the facts of the matter, he rebuked the sectarians.
When people saw the sectarians, they struck them with clods of earth and showered them with dust, saying, "They have brought infamy upon the Blessed One."
The Elder Ānanda saw this and informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One spoke this verse to the Elder: “For one’s own view...
[etc. ...one might speak.
Its meaning is as follows: regarding this view of the sectarians—that by killing Sundarī, [the blame would fall upon] the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans—
“Having proclaimed dispraise, we shall accept the honor obtained by this means”—how could such a person overcome that view?
On the contrary, he returns to that very same company of sectarians, being unable to transcend that view.
Or, how could one who holds views such as eternalism ever transcend his own view by means of that very desire for such a view?
He was won over by that view and inclination and became settled in it;
moreover, while himself performing those views as completed, he would speak exactly as he knew them to be perfect.
Then, after seven days had passed, the king had that corpse discarded and went to the monastery in the evening.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, she said: "Venerable sir, surely when such glory had arisen, it should have been announced to me as well.

When this was said, the Blessed One replied: "Great king, it is not fitting for noble ones to announce to others, 'I am virtuous and endowed with special qualities. Then, regarding that occasion, he spoke the verse beginning: "He who [proclaims] his own virtues..."
He spoke the remaining verses.

Therein, "virtuous qualities" (*sīlavatāni*) refers to the precepts such as the *Pātimokkha*, as well as the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) such as dwelling in the forest. "Unasked" (*anānupuṭṭho*) means not having been questioned.
"He proclaims" (*pāvāti*) means he speaks. The wise call that "ignoble quality" (*anariyadhamma*) which one proclaims about oneself even when unasked.
When one speaks of oneself in this way, the wise declare that such a claim is "un-Ariyan. 790. *Santo*:
He is peaceful (*santo*) through the subsiding of defilements such as lust; likewise, he is "one whose self is extinguished" (*abhinibbutatto*).
*Itiha*: Not boasting about his virtues means not praising himself regarding his moral conduct by such methods as "I am endowed with virtue," nor for the sake of virtue...
It is said: "one who does not utter speech that refers to oneself.
"The wise call that the noble Dhamma" means that the Buddhas and others, who are skilled in the aggregates and so forth, declare that absence of self-praise to be "the noble Dhamma.
"In whom there is no inflation anywhere in the world" means that in that one whose taints are destroyed, the seven types of inflation, such as lust and the rest, do not exist anywhere in the world.
The connection is that those skilled [in the Dhamma] say of that non-praising [of one's own virtues], "This is the noble Dhamma.

(791) Having thus shown the practice of one whose taints are destroyed, he now spoke—"fabricated and conditioned"—showing to the king the practice of the sectarian followers of wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika-titthiya*).
Therein, "fabricated" (*pakappita*) means thoroughly imagined (*parikappita*). "Conditioned" (*saṅkhata*)...
Conditionally constructed. "Of whom" means of whichever theorist. "Dhammas" means views. "Placed before" means made foremost.
"Exist" means they are found. "Not purified" means not cleansed. "Whatever benefit he sees in himself, he relies upon that as a fluctuating, dependent peace":
whoever has these views as dhammas placed before him, which are unpurified and exist, he—
Because such a person perceives within himself the benefits of that view—
both the worldly benefits such as honor and the transcendental benefits such as a distinguished rebirth—
he remains dependent upon both those benefits and the view itself, which is characterized as "fickle, dependent, and conventional" (kuppapaṭiccasanti). Due to that dependence, he...
One might exalt oneself or disparage others by means of qualities or faults that do not exist.
(792) And for one who is thus dependent, there are "fixations on views" (*diṭṭhīnivesā*)... [and so on] ... "and he grasps at phenomena.
In this context, "fixations on views" refers to the fixations on views characterized by the insistence that "this alone is the truth. For they cannot be easily transcended.
They do not exist. Regarding the phrase "having discerned and grasped among phenomena" (*dhammesu niccheyya samuggahītaṃ*):

because it proceeds by having discerned and adhered to various phenomena that have been grasped among the sixty-two types of views, it is said that "one does not transcend one's own adherence" (*na hi svātivattā*).
Therefore, regarding the lines "therefore a person, amidst those adherences, discards and takes up phenomena": since one does not transcend one's own [adherence], [the text continues].

Therefore, regarding those very same fixations on views, a person rejects and adopts, abandons and grasps various doctrines—such as the goat-vow, cow-vow, dog-vow, the five-heat penance, the mountain-climb, the leap-off, the squatting posture, the exertion, and the bed of thorns—as well as various [other matters] such as teachers, Dharma-expositions, and assemblies;
it is said that he is like a forest monkey, which seizes this or that branch. Thus rejecting and adopting...
And because of an unsettled mind, one might produce fame or infamy for oneself or for another, even through qualities that do not exist.
But he who is "shaken off" (*dhona*)—because he is endowed with the wisdom that shakes off all faults such as those inherent in all views—for that shaken-off one...
[as follows] ...he is "unattached. What is meant? One who is "shaken off" by virtue of possessing the quality of being shaken off; that is, one for whom all evil has been shaken off.
For the Arahant, there is no view constructed regarding any part of the world or regarding various states of existence. By the absence of such a view,
and having abandoned both the deceit and the conceit by which sectarian teachers go to that wrong course— concealing the evil karma they themselves have committed—
the one who is cleansed (dhona) [is freed] from what [source] among the faults such as lust?
Wherewith could he be reckoned—whether in this present life or in the future—in the various destinations such as the hells?
He is "without resort" (*anūpaya*), for he is without resort due to the absence of both craving and views, which are the two resorts.
But he who has a resort because of the presence of those two is indeed a resort... [as it continues] "...all views right here."

In this context, "clinging" (*upāya*) refers to being dependent on craving and views. One "enters into discourse regarding phenomena" means that one enters into discourse concerning various phenomena, such as saying, "He is lustful," or "He is hateful.
"How could one speak of the one who is without clinging? means:

by the abandoning of craving and views, how could one speak of the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), who is without clinging, using any passion or hatred, saying "He is lustful" or "He is hateful"? How could one speak of him in such a way?
The intention is this: since he is thus beyond reproach, why would he be like the followers of other sects who conceal their faults?
"He has neither self nor non-self" means that he possesses neither the view of a self (*attadiṭṭhi*) nor the view of annihilation (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*);
furthermore, for him there is no grasping or releasing known as "self" or "non-self. If one asks why they do not exist, it is because he has eradicated them.

"All views right here": because he has, in this very life, shaken off, abandoned, and dispelled every course of views with the wind of knowledge, the Teacher brought the discourse to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship. Having heard this, the king, being delighted, paid homage to the Blessed One and departed.
The commentary on the *Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka-sutta* in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, part of the *Paramatthajotikā* commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*), is completed. 4.
The commentary on the *Suddhaṭṭhaka-sutta*.
795. "I see it as pure"—this is the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta. What is its origin?
It is said that in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, a certain householder living in Bārāṇasī went to a border district with five hundred carts for the purpose of acquiring goods.
There, having formed a friendship with a forest-dweller and given him a gift, [he departed].
He asked, "Friend, have you ever seen the heartwood of sandalwood before?
When he replied, "Yes, sir," he entered the sandalwood forest with him, filled all the carts with the heartwood of sandalwood,
and said to that forest-dweller, "Friend, when you come to Bārāṇasī, you should bring some heartwood of sandalwood with you."
He went to Bārāṇasī itself. Then, at a later time, that forest-dweller also took some choice sandalwood and went to his house.
Upon seeing him, he offered him every form of hospitality;
then, in the evening, having had the sandalwood ground and filled a casket with it, he said to his own servant, "Go, my good man, and return after you have bathed."
He sent him to the bathing place. Now at that time, there was a festival in Bārāṇasī.

Then the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, having given alms early in the morning, dressed themselves in clean clothes in the evening and, taking garlands, perfumes, and other offerings, went to pay homage to the Great Cetiya of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Seeing them, the forest-dweller asked, "Where is this great multitude going?"
He asked, "To the monastery for the purpose of worshipping the cetiya. Having heard this, he went there as well.

There, seeing people making various kinds of offerings to the cetiya with yellow orpiment, red arsenic, and other substances, and knowing how to create no artistic design himself, he took that sandalwood and [applied it] over the golden bricks of the Great Cetiya to the extent of a bronze bowl.
He drew a mandala. Then, at the time of sunrise, the rays of the sun rose up there.
Seeing this, he gained confidence and made a resolution: "Wherever I am reborn, may such rays as these rise from my chest.
Having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Rays rose from his chest, and the moon’s orb—
The circle of his chest shone brilliantly, and they recognized him as the divine son Candābha.

Having spent an interval between Buddhas by traversing the six celestial worlds in both forward and reverse order through that excellence, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a family of great brahmin householders when our Blessed One had appeared; likewise, upon his chest—

A circle of rays appeared resembling the orb of the moon. On the day of his naming ceremony, after the auspicious rites had been performed, the brahmins saw that circle and, being struck with wonder, exclaimed, "This prince possesses the marks of merit and prosperity," and thus they gave him the name Candābha.
When he reached maturity, the brahmins took him, adorned him, dressed him in a crimson tunic, and placed him in a chariot.

Having hoisted it up and worshipped it, thinking, "This is Mahābrahmā," they wander through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, proclaiming: "Whoever beholds Candābha obtains fame, wealth, and the like, and in the life to come goes to heaven.
Wherever they go, people say: "O sirs, this is indeed the one named Candābha; whoever beholds him obtains fame, wealth, heaven, and so forth."
They arrived one after another, and the entire Jambudīpa trembled. The brahmins did not grant audience to those who came with empty hands;
they granted audience only to those who had brought a hundred or a thousand [pieces of gold].
Thus, wandering about while taking up the moon’s radiance, the brahmins eventually reached Sāvatthī.

At that time, the Blessed One, having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, arrived at Sāvatthī by stages and was dwelling there in Jeta’s Grove, teaching the Dhamma for the welfare of many people. Now, Candābha, upon reaching Sāvatthī, became as inconspicuous as a small river lost in the ocean;
even when his name "Candābha" was mentioned, no one recognized him. In the evening, he [approached] a great multitude of people...
Seeing him going toward Jetavana taking garlands, perfumes, and other offerings, [the people] asked, "Where are you going?
They replied, "A Buddha has appeared in the world; he teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of many beings. We are going to Jetavana to hear it.
Hearing their words, that brahmin, surrounded by his own group, went right there as well. And the Blessed One, in his regard for him—
At that time, he was seated upon the excellent Buddha-throne in the Dhamma Hall.
Canda approached the Blessed One, exchanged sweet greetings, and sat down to one side; at that very moment, his light vanished.
For no other light can prevail within eighty cubits of the Buddha’s radiance. He thought, "My light..."
"I am ruined! Having said this, he rose from his seat and, having risen, began to depart.
Then a certain man said to him, "Sir Candābha, are you going because you are afraid of the ascetic Gotama?
"I am not going because I am afraid," he replied, "but rather because light does not appear to me due to his splendor. Thereupon, he sat down once again in front of the Blessed One.
Having observed from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair the perfection of his physical radiance, marks, and other qualities, [he thought]: "The ascetic Gotama is of great power;
because a mere slight light arose in my breast, the brahmins have taken me and wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
Yet, such is the pride of the ascetic Gotama, who is endowed with such a perfection of excellent marks."

"Surely this Teacher of gods and humans must be endowed with extraordinary qualities," he thought, and with a heart overflowing with serene confidence, he paid homage to the Blessed One and requested the going-forth. The Blessed One commanded a certain elder, "Ordain him.

Having ordained him, the elder taught him the meditation subject of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcakkhandha-kammaṭṭhāna*). He [the newly ordained monk] applied himself to insight (*vipassanā*).
Having begun his practice, he attained arahantship before long and became renowned as "Candābha Thera.
Regarding him, the monks raised this discussion: "Friends, did those who saw Candābha obtain fame or wealth, go to heaven, or attain purification simply by that seeing of forms through the eye-door?"
The Blessed One spoke this sutta on that occasion.
Therein, first, the meaning of the initial verse is as follows: Monks, purity does not come from such a [physical] appearance.
Rather, it is impure due to being defiled by the *kilesas* (defilements); because the diseases of the *kilesas* have not departed, the Brahmin Candābhā remains truly diseased.
Or, having seen something else of such a kind, a foolish person caught up in wrong views claims: "I see that which is pure, supreme, and healthy;
by means of that vision, which is reckoned as a view, a person attains purification.
Claiming thus, and knowing that vision to be "supreme," while observing purity in that vision, he regards that vision as "knowledge of the path."
He believes it; however, that is not the knowledge of the Path. Therefore he said the second verse: "If purity comes through what is seen.

(796) Its meaning is this: if, by means of that "seeing" known as the sight of forms, a person attains purification from the defilements, or if by that knowledge he abandons the suffering of birth and so forth—this being the case, [he would be relying] on a path of impurity other than the Noble Path.
Thus it follows that he is purified while still possessing acquisitions (*upadhi*) such as lust;
yet one of such a kind is not truly purified. Therefore, "it is his view that makes him speak thus":
that very view declares of him, "This one is a holder of wrong view," and they speak accordingly—following the lead of that view—in such ways as "the world is eternal," and so forth.

797. “He is not a brahmin” is the third verse. Its meaning is as follows: He who is a brahmin because he has banished evil (bāhitapāpa) is a brahmin whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), having attained the destruction of taints through the Path.

Apart from the knowledge of the Noble Path, he does not regard as an auspicious sign (abhimaṅgala) what is merely considered such by others—namely, visible forms (diṭṭha) known as sounds (suta), virtue (sīla) characterized by non-transgression, or vows (vata) such as the elephant-girdle and so forth.
He did not say that purity comes through the wrong knowledge that arises regarding perceived objects such as the earth and so forth.
The rest was spoken for the purpose of praising this brahmin. For he is unsullied by all merit within the three realms and by all evil;

because those have been abandoned, he has "abandoned self" (*attañjaha*)—that is, because the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*) or any grasping whatsoever has been abandoned—and [he is free] from the formative activities of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and the rest.
"One who does not act here is called 'one who does nothing' because of his non-doing. Therefore, praising him in this way, he said:

'Unstained by both merit and evil, having abandoned the self, and doing nothing here—a brahmin does not seek purity from anything else. It should be understood that all of this is connected with the first line."

798. Having thus stated that a brahmin does not declare purification from another source, he now spoke this verse beginning with "Having abandoned the former" to show that those proponents of views who claim purification from another source do not lead to Nibbāna because of their failure to abandon that view.

Its meaning is as follows: although they are proponents of purification from another source, because they have not abandoned that particular view, there remains for them the grasping and the releasing [of objects].
Having abandoned the former Teacher and others by means of that [craving], they rely upon another;

pursued and overcome by craving—which is designated as "movement" (ejā)—they do not cross over the attachment consisting of the divisions of lust and so forth. Not crossing over that, they grasp and let go of various phenomena, just as a monkey grasps one branch and lets go of another.
799. The connection with the fifth verse: He who was described as “for views indeed lead him astray when he speaks thus,” that very person, having himself undertaken...
In this context, *sayam* means by oneself. *Samādāya* means having taken up. *Vatāni* refers to the vows, such as the elephant-vow and others.

*Uccāvacaṃ* means higher and lower, or inferior and superior, ranging from one teacher to another teacher and so forth. *Saññasatto* means attached to perceptions, such as the perception of sensual pleasure and the like.

"He has clung" (*laggo*). "And having fully understood the Dhamma through the knowledges" (*vidvā ca vedehi samecca dhamman*): the Arahant, possessing ultimate knowledge, has fully realized the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the four knowledges of the paths. The rest is self-evident. 800.
"He who has become detached from all phenomena—whatever is seen, heard, or sensed—he is one of vast wisdom. (*sa sabbadhammesu visenibhūto, yaṃ kiñci diṭṭhaṃ va sutaṃ mutaṃ vā ti so bhūripañño*)
One whose taints are destroyed has become "free from the army" (visenibhūta) by virtue of standing firm after having destroyed Māra’s host regarding all phenomena—whether seen, heard, or sensed.
"Seeing him thus" means seeing one who is thus pure in vision. "Moving about uncovered" means moving about having become uncovered through the disappearance of the veil of craving and so forth.
"Who in this world could conceptualize him? means by what [means]...?

In this world, someone might conceptualize by means of craving-conceptualization or view-conceptualization; or [they do not so conceptualize] because those [defilements], such as lust and the rest, have been abandoned as previously described.
This is the connection and the meaning of the verse beginning with "They do not conceptualize" (na kappayanti).

Furthermore: being such as they are, they neither conceptualize nor prioritize the two types of conceptualization and the two types of prioritizing, because they have attained ultimate and absolute purity.
They do not say that the view of non-action and eternalism—which is itself not ultimate purity—is "ultimate purity.

Regarding the phrase "he releases the knot of grasping that is tied": because it grasps the fourfold [aggregates] beginning with form, the "knot of grasping" is tied and bound within one's own mental continuum;
having released it, meaning having severed it with the sword of the Noble Path. The rest is self-evident.
802. The verse beginning with *sīmātigo* was spoken as a teaching based on the example of a single individual.
Its connection, however, is similar to that of the preceding [verse], and it should be understood together with the following explanation of its meaning:

Furthermore, such a person of vast wisdom, because he has transcended the four boundaries of the defilements (*kilesa-sīmā*) and because he has banished evil, is a brahmin; for one who has become thus...
Furthermore, he has nothing grasped—meaning nothing adhered to—whether known through the knowledge of others' minds or of past lives, or seen with the fleshly eye or the divine eye.
Because of the absence of sensual lust, he is not one who lusts after passion;

because of the absence of lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, he is not attached to dispassion. Thus, for one such as this, there is nothing grasped here that could be designated as "this is another."
"There is not" [is the end]; thus he concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship.

The commentary on the Sutta Nipāta, within the *Paramatthajotikā*, the sub-commentary on the Minor Collections (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*), is finished. Specifically, the commentary on the *Suddhaṭṭhaka-sutta* is completed.

5. Commentary on the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta 803. Regarding "Paramaṃ" as "among views," this refers to the *Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta*. What is its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, various non-Buddhist teachers gathered together and, each proclaiming his own view, declared: "This is supreme; this is the highest. [The Blessed One then addressed them: "Monks, there are these eight views... and so forth. Thus arose the *Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta*. As for the meaning of the title: "paramaṃ" means "supreme"; "diṭṭhīsu" means "among views. Therefore, it is called the *Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta* because it teaches that among the eight views, the view of self is the supreme. This is the meaning of the title. Now, regarding the exposition of the meaning: first, the summary of the meaning should be understood. Herein, the Blessed One taught the eight views by way of three methods: by way of the basis, by way of the person, and by way of the fruit. Among these, the first method is shown by the passage beginning: "Monks, there are these eight views. The second method is shown by the passage beginning: "In this world, monks, some ascetic or brahmin. The third method is shown by the passage beginning: "If he holds such a view, he declares: 'This is the supreme, this is the highest, this is the best, this is the finest. Of these, the first method is explained by the words: "Monks, there are these eight views. The second method is explained by the words: "In this world, monks, some ascetic or brahmin. Having quarreled, saying, "This is the ultimate [nature]," they reported it to the king. The king had many people born blind assembled and commanded, "Show them the elephant.
The king’s men, having gathered the blind men and laid the elephant down before them, said, "Look!
They each touched one part of the elephant. Then the king—
When asked, "Tell me, sir, what is an elephant like? he who touched its trunk replied, "It is just like a plow-pole, Great King.
Those who touched its tusks and other parts rebuked him, saying, "Do not speak falsely before the king, sir!
and they said, "It is just like a pillar," and so forth. Having heard all this, the king said, "Such is your [knowledge]..."
“Enough! he said, and dismissed the heretics. A certain alms-collector, having learned of this occurrence, reported it to the Blessed One.

On that occasion, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, just as those born blind, not knowing an elephant, grasped various parts of its body and fell into dispute, so too do the heretics [dispute] regarding the Dhamma pertaining to liberation.”
Having said, "Not knowing, they grasp at various views and dispute," he spoke this sutta for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.
Therein, "dwelling supreme among views" means dwelling according to one's own respective view, having grasped it as "this is supreme.
"He makes that which is beyond superior" means he makes his own teacher and so forth the best. "Inferior" refers to others than those.
"He says 'all'" means that, setting aside his own teacher and others, he says of all others besides them, "These are inferior.
Therefore, "he has not transcended disputes" means for that reason he has indeed not transcended quarrels over views.
The meaning of the second verse is as follows: And being thus not transcendent, regarding what is seen, heard, or the rules of conduct and vows—among these...
In the objects of experience, he perceives within himself—conceived as a self characterized by arisen views—the kind of benefit previously described.
Having adhered to that very benefit through his own view, thinking, "This is supreme," he regards everything else, such as other teachers and so forth, as inferior.
The meaning of the third verse: And for one who sees in this way, whatever else there is dependent upon his own teacher and so forth—
One sees another teacher and so forth as inferior; the wise say that such seeing is indeed a fetter—it is called a "bond.
Because it is precisely this [seeing], therefore a bhikkhu should not rely upon, nor adhere to, what is seen, heard, or sensed, or to rules and observances (sīlabbata). This is what is meant.

806. The meaning of the fourth verse: Not only should one not rely on what is seen, heard, and so forth, but furthermore, one should not construct (*kappayeyya*), that is, should not produce, even further and further views regarding the world. Of what kind?

That which is constructed by means of knowledge or by virtue and observances—that is, by knowledge such as the knowledge of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-ñāṇa*) and so forth, or by virtue and observances.

One should not construct such a view. Not only should one not construct a view, but furthermore, one should not represent oneself as equal to others on account of birth and other such bases, nor should one think of oneself as inferior or superior.
The meaning of the fifth verse is this: for by thus not constructing a view and not forming such conceits, having abandoned the self and not grasping at it—
Or, having abandoned what was previously grasped here, one who does not grasp another [view] does not provide a twofold support for that aforementioned type of knowledge.
And by not providing it, he indeed does not become a partisan among beings divided by various views;
being one whose nature is not to go according to desire and so forth, he does not adopt anything at all from among the sixty-two views.
“He does not rely on views”—this means he does not return to them.
Now, in order to praise that one who has exhausted the taints (khīṇāsava), as described in this verse, the Teacher spoke three verses beginning with “For whom both ends... (*yassūbhayante*).
Therein, “both ends” refers to the categories previously mentioned, such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth. “Aspiration” (*paṇidhi*) is craving (*taṇhā*).

“From existence to existence” means for the sake of repeated becoming. “Either here or beyond” means either in this present state of selfhood and so forth, or in another future state of selfhood and so forth.
“In the seen” means by way of purification through what is seen; the same method applies to what is heard and so forth. “Perception” refers to the view that gives rise to such perception.
“Even their doctrines are not concealed” means that even the sixty-two types of speculative views are [held by them as] “this alone is...”.
"Truth alone is real, the other is vain"—thus it was not accepted [by others]. "One who has gone to the further shore does not return, such a one":
having reached the further shore of Nibbāna, he does not return again to the defilements abandoned by each respective path; and he is "such a one" (tādī) in five ways. The rest is self-evident.
Thus ends the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.
The commentary on the Paramatthaka Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
6. Commentary on the Jarā Sutta (Sutta 811):
"Alas, short indeed is life. What is its origin? At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.
Having spent the rains retreat, he reflected upon those signs for wandering through the countryside— such as providing for the health of the Buddhas,
the promulgation of training rules not yet arisen, the taming of those to be trained, and the telling of Jātaka tales and other discourses on such occasions—
and having considered these, he set out on a journey through the country. Wandering by stages, he eventually reached Sāketa in the evening.

Having arrived, he entered the Añjana Grove. The inhabitants of Sāketa, hearing of this, thought, "It is now the wrong time to see the Blessed One," yet as the night was turning into dawn, they took flowers, perfumes, and other offerings and went into the presence of the Blessed One.

Having performed acts of worship, veneration, and friendly greeting, they stood surrounding him until the time for the Blessed One’s entry into the village; then the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, [entered].
He entered for alms. A certain wealthy brahmin from Sāketa, having come out from the city, saw him at the city gate.
Upon seeing him, he felt a surge of affection for his son and, lamenting, "I have not seen you, my son, for a long time," went forward toward him.
The Blessed One informed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, this brahmin is doing as he wishes."
"Let him do so; he should not be prevented.

Then the brahmin, like a cow longing for her calf, came forward and embraced the Blessed One on all sides—before, behind, to the right, and to the left—saying, "I have seen you after a long time, my son! We have been apart for a long time!"
But if he were not permitted to do so, his heart would break and he would die.
He said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, I alone am capable of providing alms for the monks who have come with you; please show favor to me alone.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. The brahmin [took] the Blessed One’s bowl...
Taking it, he went ahead and sent word to the brahmin woman: "My son has arrived; a seat should be prepared.
Having done so, she stood watching for his arrival; seeing the Blessed One right in the middle of the street, maternal affection arose within her.
"I have not seen you for a long time, my son! she cried, and taking him by the feet, weeping, she led him into the house and honored him with due respect.
He fed them. When the brahmin had finished eating, he set aside his bowl. The Blessed One, knowing what was suitable for them, taught the Dhamma;
at the conclusion of the teaching, both of them became stream-enterers. Then they requested the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, as long as the Blessed One dwells in dependence on this city, alms should be accepted only from our own house."
The Blessed One rejected their request, saying, "Buddhas do not go to only one fixed place in this manner.

They said, "In that case, venerable sir, please wander for alms together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, but after you have finished your meal right here and taught the Dhamma, please return to the monastery. Out of compassion for them, the Blessed One did so.
People addressed the brahmin and the brahmin lady as "the father of the Buddha" and "the mother of the Buddha.
That family also received the name "the Buddha-family.
The Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One: "I know the parents of the Blessed One; but why [do you not acknowledge these]?"
They say, "I am the mother of the Buddha; I am the father of the Buddha. The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, for five hundred births in succession, both the brahmin woman and the brahmin man have been my mother and father;
for five hundred births they were my elder siblings, and for five hundred births they were my younger siblings. It is out of this former affection that they speak," and he spoke this verse:
“Whether through former association or by present benefit,
such affection arises for one, just as a lotus grows in the water.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Sāketa for as long as he desired, set out again on his journey and arrived back at Sāvatthī.

That brahmin and his wife, having approached the monks and heard a suitable discourse on the Dhamma, reached the further path and attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue.
In the city, the brahmins gathered together, saying, "We shall honor our kinsman. The lay followers who were stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners [also gathered].
The female lay disciples also gathered together, thinking, "We shall honor our fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
Having placed them all upon the Kambala gabled house, they escorted them out of the city while making offerings of garlands, perfumes, and other honors.
On that very day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, perceived their state of final Nibbāna.

Knowing that "if I go there, many people will attain realization of the Dhamma upon hearing the teaching," and having understood this, he took his bowl and robe, came from Sāvatthī, and entered the cremation ground itself.

When the people saw him, they thought, "The Blessed One has come wishing to perform the funeral rites for his parents," and after paying homage, they stood by. The citizens, meanwhile, were honoring the gabled pavilion.
Having brought [the remains] to the cremation ground, they asked the Blessed One: “How should noble lay disciples be honored?
With the intention that “these should be honored in the same manner as those beyond training (asekha) are honored,” the Blessed One spoke this verse, illustrating their status as Asekha Munis:
“Those sages who are non-violent and always restrained in body go to the deathless state, having gone to which they do not grieve.
Having surveyed that assembly, he spoke this sutta, teaching the Dhamma appropriate for that very moment.
In this context, "Truly short indeed is this life" means: "Truly, this life of human beings is short and limited, both by its brevity of duration and its brevity of essence.

This is according to the method stated in the *Sallasutta*. "One dies even before a hundred years" means one dies even during the stage of the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth, prior to reaching a hundred years.
"After exceeding [a hundred years]" means having passed beyond a hundred years. "One also dies through old age" means one dies even because of aging.

812–6. *Mamāyita*: because of the object of what has been treated as "mine. They know that which exists as inseparable (*vinābhāvasanta*) as being "the inseparability of the existent" (*santavinābhāva*), meaning this is precisely the inseparability of that which exists;
it is stated that it is not possible for it to exist without inseparability. *Māmaka*:
one who has come to be reckoned as "my lay follower" or "my bhikkhu," or one who treats the Buddha and other such objects as "mine. *Saṅgata*: come together, previously seen.

“Beloved” means made dear. “Only the name will remain as that which can be expressed” means that the entire collection of phenomena, such as form and so forth, is abandoned, and only a mere name remains for the purpose of reckoning and speaking, such as “Buddharakkhita” or “Dhammarakkhita.
“Sages” refers to sages whose taints are exhausted. “Seers of security” refers to those who see Nibbāna.
817. This seventh verse was spoken for the purpose of showing the appropriate course of conduct in a world afflicted by death.
In that context: *patilīnacarassa* means one who wanders having made the mind withdrawn from this and that;

*bhikkhuno* refers to either a noble ordinary person (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) or one in training (*sekkha*). Regarding the phrase *sāmaggiyamāhu tassa taṃ, yo attānaṃ bhavane na dassaye*: they say that it is fitting for him who does not display himself in existence.

One who practices in this way would not show himself in existence, whether in the various realms such as hell and so forth. For it is with the intention that "in this way he shall be liberated from this death" that [the Buddha spoke].
Now, in order to praise him who has been thus described as one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) by the words "he would not show himself in existence," [the following is said]:
He spoke three verses following this. Therein, "in all things" (*sabbattha*) means in the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*).

Regarding the phrase "namely, what is seen, heard, sensed, or thought" (*yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutaṃ mute su vā*), the connection should be understood as follows: "In regard to these things—namely, what is seen, heard, or among those things that are sensed—the sage (*muni*) is not defiled.
The one who has shaken off [defilements] (*dhona*) does not, by means of that, conceive [notions], namely, regarding what is seen or heard.

Regarding the phrase "or in respect of the mute [dhammas]": here too, the connection should be understood in this way: by means of that basis, namely the discourse on what has been seen (*diṭṭhasutta*), he does not conceive;
or he does not conceive in respect of the mute dhammas. For it is said: "He neither lusts nor is dispassionate.

He does not lust like foolish worldlings (*bālaputhujjana*), nor is he dispassionate like noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) or those in training (*sekkha*); rather, this is because of the exhaustion of lust (*rāga*).

“It goes by the designation ‘dispassion’ (virāga). The remainder is clear everywhere. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was the realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Jarāsutta of the Suttanipāta-ṭīkā is finished.
7. Commentary on the Tissa-metteyya-sutta.
821. "For one devoted to sexual intercourse": this is the Tissa-metteyya-sutta. What is its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was at Sāvatthī...
While they were staying there, two companions named Tissa and Metteyya went to Sāvatthī.
Seeing a great crowd of people heading toward the Jeta Grove in the evening, they asked, "Where are you going?
Then, when they replied, "A Buddha has appeared in the world; he teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of many people, so we are going to the Jeta Grove to hear it," [the two friends followed].

Thinking, "We too shall hear it," they went there. Having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, who teaches the Dhamma that is never in vain, they sat within the assembly and reflected: "It is not possible for one remaining in the midst of a household to fulfill this Dhamma.
Then, when the great multitude had departed, they requested the Blessed One for the going-forth. The Blessed One said, "Ordain them," and [instructed] another...
He commanded a bhikkhu. That bhikkhu, having ordained him and given him the meditation subject of the "five aggregates of clinging" (tacapañcaka), began to depart for the forest dwelling.
Metteyya said to Tissa, "Friend, the preceptor is going to the forest;
let us go as well. Tissa replied, "Enough, friend; I desire to see the Blessed One and hear the Dhamma; you go on."

He did not go. Metteyya, having gone with his preceptor and practicing the duties of a recluse in the forest, attained Arahantship before long together with his teacher and preceptor. Tissa’s elder brother also passed away from illness.
Upon hearing this, he went to his own village; there, his relatives enticed him and caused him to disrobe. Metteyya also—

Having returned to Sāvatthī together with his teacher and preceptor, the Blessed One, having completed the rains retreat, set out on a journey through the countryside and eventually arrived at that village.
There, Metteyya paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, there is a lay friend of mine in this village; please wait for a moment out of compassion."
Having entered the village, he brought him into the presence of the Blessed One; standing to one side, he asked the Blessed One a question for his sake using the first verse.
As the Blessed One was explaining it to him, he spoke the remaining verses. This is the origin of this sutta.
In that context, "one devoted to sexual intercourse" means one engaged in the practice of sexual union. "Thus" (*iti*) means "in this way. "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment.
"Tissa" was the name of that elder; for he was indeed known by the name Tissa. "Metteyya" was his clan (gotta), and it was precisely by way of his clan that he became well-known.
Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhuppatti*: "Two companions named Tissa and Metteyya. "Vighātaṃ" means affliction (*upaghāta*).
"Brūhi" means explain. "Mārisa" is a term of endearment; he is described as being "free from suffering" (*nidukkha*).
"Having heard your instruction" means having heard your word. "I shall train in seclusion"—this he says while requesting a teaching on the Dhamma concerning a companion;
however, that companion is already one who has completed his training. 822. "Or else the instruction perishes":

both kinds of instruction—the scriptural (pariyatti) and the practical (paṭipatti)—are lost. "Or else" (*vāpi*) is merely for the purpose of completing the meter. "This is ignoble in him": in that person, this is ignoble, namely, this wrong practice.
823. "Having previously wandered alone" means having formerly dwelt alone, either by way of what is termed renunciation or by way of abandoning the company of a group.
"Like a carriage that has gone astray in the world, they call him a base worldling"—this refers to a person who has fallen away from the path;
just as a carriage such as an elephant-vehicle that is untrained mounts uneven ground, breaks its rider, and falls into a precipice.
Thus, by ascending the uneven path of bodily misconduct and so forth, one falls into the hells and other realms; and by the destruction of one's welfare, one falls into the abyss of birth and so on.
Therefore, they say that such a person is like a swaying vehicle—lowly—and call them a worldling (*puthujjana*).
(824–5) "Fame and renown" refers to gain, honor, and praise. "In the past" means in the state of having gone forth. Or, it may mean "it declines."

For him who has fallen away from that [training], both that fame and that reputation diminish. "Seeing this also" means seeing both the previous existence of fame and reputation and their subsequent decline.

"One should train to abandon sexual intercourse" means one should train in the three trainings. For what reason? Because sexual intercourse must be abandoned; it is for the sake of abandoning sexual intercourse.
This has been said. For he who does not abandon sexual intercourse, such a person is possessed of [unwholesome] thoughts... [as before]... "Therein, 'overcome' means endowed with.
"'The reproach of others' refers to words of censure from preceptors and others. "'Becomes dejected' means becomes dispirited. 826. The verses following this have an obvious connection.
Among them, "wounds" refers to bodily misconduct and so forth. These...
For they are called "weapons" in the sense that they cut both oneself and others.
And among these, one who has been specifically reproved performs only the weapon of false speech when saying, "For this reason I have left the Order. Therefore it was said:
"This indeed is his great snare; he plunges into the transgression of lying. In this context, *esa khvassa* means "this indeed is his."
"Great bog" means a great bond. If one asks what it is: it is when one plunges into false speech; that plunge into lying should be understood as the "great bog.

"The dull-witted one wallows about": performing such acts as the killing of living beings and experiencing the suffering resulting therefrom, while also engaging in the pursuit and protection of wealth, he wallows like one who is utterly deluded.
828–9. “Having understood this danger, the Sage [considered] what comes before and after here”:

from the verse beginning with “Whatever fame and renown one had before, even that diminishes for him,” the Sage, having understood the danger here in this teaching between what precedes and what follows—that is, between the state of being a recluse and the state of falling away—[saw] this as the supreme among the Noble Ones. This is what is meant.
The practice of seclusion is the supreme [practice] of the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas; therefore, the intention is that one should train in seclusion alone.

"One should not think oneself superior because of that" means that one should not, on account of that seclusion, think of oneself, "I am superior," nor should one become arrogant because of it—this is what is meant.
830. "Of one who is solitary" means of one who is secluded, being devoid of bodily misconduct and so forth.

"The world, clinging to sensual pleasures, envies him who has crossed the flood"—beings attached to objective sensual pleasures envy that one who has crossed the four floods, just as debtors envy one who is free from debt.
Thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, Tissa...
Having attained the fruit of stream-entry, he later went forth and realized arhatship.
Thus ends the commentary on the Tissa Metteyya Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Paramatthajotikā* commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*).
8. The Commentary on the Pasūra Sutta 831.
"Purity is found right here" is the Pasūra Sutta. What is its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, there was a wandering ascetic named Pasūra, a great debater.
He thought: "I am the foremost in debate throughout the entire Jambudīpa; therefore..."
"Just as Jambudīpa has the renown of the Rose-Apple Tree, so it is fitting that mine should also become such.
Having made a branch of the rose-apple tree his banner, and encountering no opposition throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī.
There, having prepared a mound of sand at the city gate and hoisted the branch upon it, he proclaimed: "Whoever is capable of engaging in debate with me..."
"Let him break this branch," he said, and entered the city. A great crowd of people stood surrounding that spot.
At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, having finished his meal, was departing from Sāvatthī.
Seeing them, he asked many village boys, "What is this, children? and they told him everything.
“Very well then, lift it up yourselves and break it with your feet, and say, ‘Let him who seeks debate come to the monastery!
Having said this, he departed.
The wanderer, having wandered for alms and finished his meal, returned; seeing that the branch had been lifted up and broken, he [thought]:
“Who had this made? he asked. When it was replied, “By Sāriputta, the disciple of the Buddha,” he became delighted and thought, “Today let the wise behold my victory and the defeat of the ascetic!
Having entered Sāvatthī to summon those who examine questions and those who investigate causes, he wandered through the streets, crossroads, and marketplaces, [saying], “Of the ascetic Gotama...”
“Those of you who wish to hear the wisdom and eloquence in the debate with the Chief Disciple, please come forth! he proclaimed.
Thinking, “We shall hear the words of the wise,” many people went out, both those who were faithful in the Teaching and those who were not.
Then Pasūro, surrounded by a great crowd, went to the monastery, reflecting on such things as, “When this is said, I will say this.”
He arrived. The Elder, thinking, "Let there not be loud noise, great clamor, and a crowd of people in the monastery," prepared a seat at the gateway of the Jetavana and sat down.
The wanderer approached the Elder and said, "O you who have gone forth, you have caused my Jambudhvaja to be broken!"
He said, "Yes, wanderer. When this was said, he replied, "Let there be some exchange of conversation with us, sir.
When the Elder had accepted, saying, "Let there be, wanderer," he said, "Ask, ascetic; I shall answer.
Then the Elder said to him, "Wanderer, which is more difficult: the question or the answer?"
“Sir, what is difficult about answering a question? For anyone can answer whatever they are asked.
When this was said, the wanderer thought, “This monk is a man of great character;
he makes me break a branch where there is no tree,” and with a mind full of wonder, he questioned the Elder.
“What is desire for a man? “Resolve and lust are desire for a man,” the Elder replied.
Having heard this, the wanderer conceived a hostile attitude toward the Elder and, wishing to claim victory over him, said:
“But, sir, you do not say that the manifold and variegated objects of sense are desire for a man? “Indeed, wanderer, I do not so say. Then the wanderer—
After having him give his word three times, [the monk] addressed the questioners, saying, "Gentlemen, listen to the fault in the ascetic’s doctrine," and said:
"Sir, renunciant, do your fellow celibates dwell in the forest?
"Yes, wanderer, they dwell there. "While dwelling there, do they entertain thoughts such as sensual thoughts?"
“Yes, wanderer, ordinary people think impulsively. “If that is so, from where would their status as recluses come?
Are they not householders who enjoy sensual pleasures? Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“Those various beautiful things in the world are not truly sensual pleasures;”
"You speak of sensual desire as the passion of intention;
yet by entertaining unwholesome thoughts,
even a bhikkhu will become a consumer of sensual pleasures."
Then the Elder, pointing out the fault in the wanderer’s doctrine, said:
"Wanderer, do you not say that desire for a man is passion of intention (*saṅkapparāga*), but rather that it is a variegated and manifold object? "Yes, sir, I do," he replied.
Thereupon, the Elder made him admit this three times, saying: "Listen, friend, to the wanderer..."
Having addressed him with the words, "In debate, there are faults," he asked: "Friend Pasūra, does your teacher exist? "Yes, ascetic, he exists.
"Does he see a visible object cognizable by the eye, or does he indulge in objects such as sounds? "Yes, ascetic, he indulges in them.
"If that is so, from where does his status as a teacher come? Is it not true that..."
“Thus he becomes a householder enjoying sensual pleasures. Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“Those indeed are the ‘sensual pleasures’ which are the various beautiful things in the world;
you do not call the passion of intention ‘sensual pleasure.’”
Beholding delightful forms,
hearing delightful sounds,
smelling delightful fragrances.
Tasting delightful flavors and experiencing delightful touches,
you will become a teacher who indulges in sensual pleasures.
When this was said, the wanderer, rendered speechless, thought: "This renunciant is a great debater; having gone forth under him, I shall train in the science of debate.
He entered Sāvatthī, sought alms and robes, and entered Jeta’s Grove.
There he saw Lāḷudāyin, who possessed a golden complexion, whose body was well-proportioned, and who was pleasing in every aspect of his physical form.
Having seen him and considering, "This bhikkhu is one of great wisdom and a great debater," he went forth in his presence.
Having defeated him in debate, he departed from that very sectarian fold while still wearing the same religious garb.
Then, thinking, "I shall engage in debate with the ascetic Gotama," he made a proclamation in Sāvatthī in the same manner as before, surrounded by a great multitude, [saying], "Thus, the ascetic..."
Saying such things as, "I shall refute Gotama," he went to the Jeta Grove.
A deity dwelling at the gate-tower of the Jeta Grove, thinking, "This man is not a fit vessel," bound his mouth shut. He approached the Blessed One and sat there like one who was mute.
People, thinking, "Now he will ask a question! Now he will ask a question! kept looking toward his face.
“Speak, sir Pasūra! Speak, sir Pasūra! they cried out with loud and great clamor. Then the Blessed One, saying, “What will Pasūra say?
spoke this sutta for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the assembly gathered there.
As for the first verse therein, this is the summary: these proponents of various views, referring to their own respective views—
"They proclaim, 'Purity is found right here,' and they do not say that purity lies in other teachings.
This being so, many ascetics and brahmins— relying on their own teachers and the like, and speaking of purity by saying "This doctrine is beautiful"—
become attached to individual truths such as "The world is eternal" and so forth.
832. And thus established—“Those who desire debate,” is the verse.
Therein, “burning the fool mutually with one another” means that these two people, each thinking “this one is a fool, this one is a fool,” burn the other as a fool; they view him as a fool.
“They speak, relying on others, in a dispute of words” means that, relying on others such as teachers and so forth, they speak in mutual quarrel.
“Desiring praise, claiming to be skilled”—meaning both [parties], desiring praise, perceive themselves thus: “We are speakers of what is skillful, speakers of wisdom. 833.
And among those speaking in this way, one is necessarily—“engaged in the talk,” as the verse says.
Therein, “engaged in the talk” means striving for contentious discussion. “Seeking praise, he meets with ruin” means his own praise...
Desiring [to win], even before the conversation begins, he becomes one who wavers in doubt and is frustrated, thinking in such a manner as, "How indeed shall I refute him?
