When his argument has been rejected—meaning when the debate has been dismissed by those who examine the question with such statements as, "Your statement is devoid of meaning," or "Your statement is devoid of phrasing"—he becomes angry at that censure; thus, when his argument has been rejected...
He becomes angry when criticism arises. "Seeking faults" means searching only for the faults of others.
(Verse 834) Not only does he become angry, but furthermore, regarding the verse beginning with "Whatever they say of him":
therein, "they call it deficient" means they say it is deficient in both meaning and phrasing; "he laments" means because of that [deficiency].
Thus he raves with such thoughts as, "Another [idea] was adverted to by me. He grieves means that he grieves concerning such things as, "His victory.
He laments, "He has surpassed me," means that he raves even more intensely in the manner of, "He has surpassed me in debate," and so forth.
835. Regarding the phrase "these disputes among recluses" (*samaṇesu*), here "recluses" (*samaṇā*) refers to the outside wanderers (*bāhiraparibbājakā*).

"In these there is striking and counter-striking" (*etesu ugghāti nighāti hoti*): in these doctrines, by way of victory and defeat, one reaches the striking (*ugghāta*) and counter-striking (*nighāta*) of the mind;
thus one becomes a striker and a counter-striker. "One should cease from talk" (*virame kathojjaṃ*): one should abandon quarreling. "There is no one who is not slain" (*na haññadatthatthi*).
“Gain through praise”: for here there is no meaning other than gain through praise. 836–7.

The meaning of the sixth verse: Since there is no purpose in being slain other than gain through praise, therefore, even while receiving the highest gain, one is either praised by holding the view that “this is beautiful,” or one adheres to that doctrine.
Having proclaimed [his victory] in the midst of the assembly, he then laughs, attaining either satisfaction or showing his teeth with a grin, and he becomes puffed up with pride.
For what reason? Because, having attained that state of victory, he has become as proud as he was;
thus, regarding one who is thus puffed up, there is the verse beginning "And for one who is puffed up... Therein, "He speaks with pride and overweening pride" means this person indeed...
Not understanding that "exaltation" is a ground for affliction, he speaks only of conceit (*māna*) and overweening pride (*atimāna*).
Having thus shown the fault in that doctrine, [the Blessed One] now spoke the verse beginning with "The hero," not accepting his position.
Therein, "by royal food" (*rājakhādāya*) means by royal provisions, that is, by food and wages; "in the face of an assailant" (*abhigajjame*).

"They seek a rival hero"—this shows that just as one seeking a rival hero approaches while roaring, so too does one who holds a particular view approach another who holds a particular view. "Go right where he is"—go to where that rival hero of yours is.
"There is nothing at all here for fighting"—that is to say, whatever kind of defilement there might be for the sake of battle, that [does not exist here].
It shows that [the defilements] did not exist previously, but were abandoned right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
The remaining verses have a self-evident connection. 839–40. Therein, *vivādayanti* means they dispute. *Paṭisenikattā* means one who acts in opposition.
*Visenikatvā* means having destroyed the army of the defilements (*kilesasena*). *Kiṃ labhetha* means what rival will you find? *Pasūra* refers to that wanderer (*paribbājaka*).
"He addresses": "Of those who have nothing here" means of those who have nothing here.
"With discursive thought" means while thinking such thoughts as, "Will there be victory for me?

"Having come together with the Pair in union with the Shaker" means having entered into a state of union with the Buddha, who has shaken off the defilements. "For you will not be able to go along with him."
"Just as jackals and the like cannot go even a single step with lions and the like, having taken hold of the same yoke, nor can they achieve the state of taking the yoke together;
so too, you will not be able to do so. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus ends [the commentary] in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the Pasūra Sutta in the Suttanipāta-ṭīkā is finished.
9. Commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.
842. "Having seen craving... This is the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta. What is its origin? At one time the Blessed One was at Sāvatthī.
While dwelling there, at the time of dawn, he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye.

Seeing that the brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya, a resident of the town of Kammāsadhamma in the Kurus, together with his wife, possessed the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship, he immediately departed from Sāvatthī and went there.
He sat down in a certain grove not far from Kammāsadhamma, emitting a golden radiance.
As he was rinsing his mouth, Māgaṇḍiya, who had gone there at that very moment for the same purpose, saw a golden radiance and wondered, "What is this?
Looking here and there, he beheld the Blessed One and became delighted.
It is said that his daughter was of golden complexion; many princes and others sought her hand as brides, but they did not obtain her. Such was the brāhmaṇa’s conviction.
He thought, "I shall give this to a recluse who is of the same golden complexion as myself. Upon seeing the Blessed One, he conceived the thought, "This man is of the same complexion as my daughter;
I shall give it to him. Therefore, as soon as he saw him, he was delighted.
He went home in haste and said to his wife, "Madam, madam! I have seen a man of the same complexion as our daughter..."
“He has been seen; adorn the girl, and we shall give her to him.
While the brahmin woman was bathing the girl with scented water and adorning her with garments, flowers, ornaments, and the like, the time for the Blessed One’s almsround arrived.
Then the Blessed One entered Kammāsadhamma for alms.
Taking their daughter by the hand, they went to the place where the Blessed One was seated.
Not seeing the Blessed One there, the brahmin woman looked here and there and saw a grass mat spread out at the spot where the Blessed One had been sitting.
By the power of the Buddhas’ resolve, both the seating place and the footprints remain undisturbed. She said to the brahmin: “This—”
“Brahmin, is that a grass mat? “Yes, madam. “In that case, Brahmin, our purpose for coming here will not be accomplished.
“And why not, madam? “Look, Brahmin, at how orderly this grass mat is;
it has not been used by one who indulges in sensual pleasures. The Brahmin said, “Madam, while we are seeking auspiciousness, do not bring inauspiciousness!”

“He did not speak,” she said. Again, the brahmin woman, wandering here and there, saw the Blessed One’s footprint and said to the brahmin, “Is this his footprint? “Yes, lady,” he replied. “Look, brahmin, at this footprint;
this being is not attached to sensual pleasures. When asked, “How do you know this, lady? she spoke, demonstrating the power of her own knowledge:
For one who is angry, the footprint is crouched;
for one who is malicious, it is dragged along;
for one who is deluded, it is pressed down suddenly.
“This is such a state for one who has removed the veil.
Now, while their conversation was still unfinished, the Blessed One, having completed his meal, arrived at that very grove.
Upon seeing the Blessed One’s form, adorned with excellent marks and encircled by a fathom-wide radiance, the brahmin lady—
He said to the brahmin, “Brahmin, was this seen by you? “Yes, lady,” he replied. “The task of his arrival will not succeed at all;
it is impossible that one such as this would enjoy sensual pleasures.
Even as they were speaking thus, the Blessed One sat down upon a grass mat. Then the brahmin, taking his daughter with his left hand and his water-pot...
Taking her by the right hand, he approached the Blessed One and said, "O renunciant, you are golden-hued and this maiden is likewise;
she is a fitting match for you. I give her to you as a wife for the sake of raising offspring.
Having spoken thus, he went before the Blessed One and stood there desiring to offer her. The Blessed One, without addressing the brahmin, [turned] away toward another direction.
As if conversing with her, he spoke this verse: “Having seen her, craving... The meaning of this is as follows:

Having created various forms at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree and having seen Māra’s daughter who had approached with longing, there was not even a mere desire in me for craving, discontent, or passion regarding sexual union; what indeed is this of hers?
"Having seen the girl's form filled with urine and excrement, one would not wish to touch her even with one's feet;
how much less would one live with her?
Then Māgaṇḍiya said, "Those called 'renunciants' indeed renounce human desires and go forth for the sake of divine desires."
He spoke the second verse in order to ask: "This one does not even desire divine pleasures; this too is a woman-jewel—what indeed could be his view?
Therein, "If such a jewel" refers to the divine woman-jewel;
"not a woman" refers to his own daughter. "What is his way of views, virtue, and life? refers to his view and his virtue.
"Vow and life. "You speak of rebirth; what kind of rebirth do you speak of for yourself? 844.
The two verses following this are clearly connected because they proceed by way of a response to a question.
Among them, the summary meaning of the first verse is as follows: "Māgaṇḍiya, regarding those sixty-two types of speculative views..."
Having investigated thoroughly, it is not grasped, does not exist, and is not found that one says, "This alone is the truth;

all else is vain. Why is that? Because, seeing the danger in views and not grasping at any view, I have discerned the truths and seen only Nibbāna—designated as "inner peace"—by virtue of the subsiding of lust and other defilements within.

845. The brief meaning of the second verse: These "views" (*diṭṭhigata*) are called "determinations" (*vinicchaya*) because they have been grasped after being determined by various beings, and they are called "constructed" (*pakappita*) in the sense that they are fashioned by their own respective conditions.
You, O Sage, having not grasped those phenomena of views, abide in internal peace—this is the meaning.
“You say, ‘Tell me, how has that state been proclaimed by the wise? How has it been revealed by the wise? (846).
Then the Blessed One, showing the means by which that state was revealed by the wise—along with its opposite—uttered the verse beginning with “Not by view.
In that context, by the words “not by view” and so forth, [he excludes] views, learning, the eight attainments, knowledge, and external rules and observances.

He rejects [the view]. Regarding the word *āha* (he says) used here in the phrase "one who speaks of purity" (*suddhimāha*), it should be understood that this meaning—"I do not speak of purity through views"—is to be applied by joining that word with the negative particle *na* throughout all instances and thereby forming a masculine nominative.
And just as it is here, so it is in the subsequent sections as well. In that context, "not by non-view" (*adiṭṭhiyā nāha*) refers to right view consisting of ten bases.

"I do not speak without [these]. Likewise, "without learning" means without hearing the ninefold [scripture]. "Without knowledge" means without the knowledge that accords with the truth regarding the deeds performed.
"Without virtue" means without the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "Without vows" means without the vows of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).
"Nor even by one of these" should be understood as: "I do not speak even by means of any one of these, such as mere views," and so forth. And having relinquished these...
"Having assisted": having abandoned the former states belonging to the dark side, such as wrong view and so forth, by means of their total eradication;
and having assisted the latter states belonging to the bright side, such as right view and so forth, by attaining non-identification with them.

"Being peaceful, he does not yearn for existence through dependence"—by this practice, being peaceful through the subsiding of lust and other defilements, [he remains] regarding the eye and the other sense bases.
The intention is that he would be capable of not seeking or aspiring for even a single state of existence without depending on any phenomenon whatsoever;
this is his internal peace.
When this was said, Māgaṇḍiya, failing to perceive the meaning of the words, recited the verse beginning with "If indeed... (no ce kira). In that regard:
"Seen" and so forth are exactly as previously explained. However, he spoke regarding those things belonging to the dark side (kaṇhapakkhiya) in both instances.
The word *āha* (said) should be construed with the particle *nocekira*, and thus the meaning should be understood as: "If indeed he did not say it, and if indeed he did not speak it.
*Momuhaṃ* means utterly deluded, or that which causes delusion. *Pacenti* means they know.
848. Then the Blessed One, rejecting the question based on that view, spoke this verse: "And relying on a view...

The meaning of this is as follows: Māgaṇḍiya, you who ask again and again while relying on a view have fallen into such delusion regarding those very speculative views you have grasped; and from this [I say] by me...

"Whether from the perspective of what has been stated regarding internal peace, from the perspective of practice, or from the perspective of the teaching of the Dhamma, you do not perceive even the slightest sign of consistency;
for that reason, you view this Dhamma through delusion.
(849) Having thus demonstrated Māgaṇḍiya’s fall into dispute due to his confusion regarding those things thus grasped, [the text now proceeds] to others among them...
And showing his own freedom from dispute regarding phenomena due to being devoid of delusion, he spoke this verse: “The same, the superior.
Its meaning is as follows: whoever thus conceives by means of the threefold conceit or by means of a view, he would dispute because of that conceit, that view, or that person.
But one such as we, who does not waver in these three ways, is the same.
"Neither superior" (*visesī*) means he does not possess [such a state]; "nor inferior" (*na ca hīno*) is the remaining portion of the reading.

Furthermore: "Truth is 'he'... is the verse. Its meaning is as follows: such a person—one who has abandoned pride and views, one like me who is a *brāhmaṇa* by virtue of having cast out evil and so forth—what could he say, "This alone is the truth," regarding what object? What basis would he have for such a claim?
For what reason or by what cause would one say, "My [view] is true, yours is false," or with what pride, view, or person would one dispute?

In one such as I, whose taints are destroyed, there is no conceiving of equality through the occurrence of the thought "I am equal," nor any conceiving of inequality through the occurrence of the other two states; therefore, among those who are equal and so forth, by what...?
"One should engage in debate and counter-argue. Is it not the case that such a person is described by the verse beginning with "Having abandoned his home" (okaṃ pahāya)?
851. Therein, "having abandoned his home" means having discarded the dwelling-place (*oka*) of consciousness—namely, form, bases, and so forth—by abandoning desire and lust for them.
"Wandering without a home" (*aniketasārī*) means not wandering according to craving toward the signs of form, homes, and so forth. "Not making [a home] in the village..."

"A sage who avoids intimacy" means one who does not form intimate ties with householders in the village. "Empty of sensual pleasures" means being detached from all sensual desires due to the absence of longing and lust for them.
"Not looking forward [to future existence]" means not bringing about the production of a new personal identity in the future.
"How should he not engage in dispute with people? means that he should not speak contentious speech with others. Such a person—
—The verse beginning with "yehi vivitto.
(852) Therein, "yehi" means by which views. "Vivitto vicareyya" means he should wander empty [of them].

"Na tāni uggayha vadeyya nāgo" means that an "elephant" (nāga)—according to the method of the phrase "he does not come back" (*āguṃ na karoti*) and so forth—having grasped those views, does not speak [of them].
One should not speak thus. "Jalambuja" refers to a water-born lotus with a thorny stalk growing in water known as "jala";

this is what is meant by "paduma. Just as that lotus is unsullied by water and mud—just as that lotus remains untainted by both water and mud—so too the sage who speaks of peace (*santivādo*) is free from greed;
thus, the sage who speaks of inner peace is free from the state of craving.

“Unattached. “Untainted by both kinds of desire and by the world” means that he is untainted by the two types of clinging—namely, to both the two kinds of sensual pleasure and to the world beginning with the states of deprivation (apāya).
853. Furthermore: “Nor a master of knowledge” (na vedagū), etc. Therein, “nor a master of knowledge who is a dogmatist” (na vedagū diṭṭhiyāyako):
one such as I, a master of the four paths, is not a dogmatist; nor does he go along with dogmatic views, nor does he regard them as essential.
The meaning of the words here is as follows: he who goes (*yāti*) is a goer (*yāyaka*); by way of the instrumental case, one who goes by means of views is "one who goes by views" (*diṭṭhiyāyaka*).
Alternatively, by way of the genitive case in the sense of the accusative, one who goes toward views is also "one who goes by views. He does not approach conceit through wisdom;
that is, he does not approach conceit even through wisdom consisting of the analysis of the liberated form and so forth. For he is not made of that, because of his [lack of] craving and views.
He is made of that and has that as his supreme resort; however, this one is not like that.

"Not to be led by action nor by learning" means he is not to be led by action such as the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and the like, nor by learning such as purification through what has been heard (*sutasuddhi*) and the like.
"He is not led into abodes" means that because both types of leading have been abandoned, he is not led into any abodes of craving or views (*taṇhā-diṭṭhi*). And of him—
Regarding such a person, there is the verse beginning with "one who is detached from perception" (saññāviratta).

Therein, "detached from perception" means one for whom perceptions of sensual desire and so forth have been abandoned through meditation preceded by the perception of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saññā*).

By this term, the one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*) who is a follower of serenity (*samatha-yānika*) is intended. "Liberated by wisdom" (*paññā-vimutta*) refers to one [liberated] through meditation preceded by insight (*vipassanā*).
"For one liberated from all defilements through meditation"—by this, the "dry-insight practitioner" (sukkha-vipassaka) is intended.
"Those who have grasped perception and views wander about, clashing with one another in the world":

those who have grasped perceptions such as sensual perception and so forth—these are especially householders, for whom sensual pleasures are the primary concern—and those who have grasped views—these are especially those who have gone forth.
"Legal disputes arise as they wander about, clashing with one another. Whatever else remains unsaid here should be understood according to what has already been stated.
At the conclusion of the teaching, both the brahmin and the brahmin woman went forth and attained arahantship.
Thus ends [the commentary] in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta of the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
10. The commentary on the Purābheda Sutta. 855.
"How shall he see?"—this is the Purābheda Sutta. What is its origin? This sutta and the five that follow it...

The general origin of the *Kalahavivāda*, *Cūḷabyūha*, *Mahābyūha*, *Tuvaṭaka*, *Attadaṇḍa*, and *Sammāparibbājanīya* suttas has been explained according to the method already stated. However, as for their specific origin:

just as on that great occasion, in order to teach the Dhamma in a way suitable for deities of lustful temperament, he had himself questioned by a manifested Buddha and then spoke the *Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta*.
Thus, at that very time, having known the thoughts of the deities who had conceived the thought, "What indeed should be done before the breaking up of the body?",
and for the sake of favoring them, he brought a manifested Buddha accompanied by a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty monks through the air;
having caused him to question himself [on their behalf], he spoke this sutta.

Therein, regarding the question first: "How does he appear? asks concerning higher wisdom (*adhipañña*); "How is his virtue? asks concerning higher morality (*adhisīla*); and "Is he at peace? asks concerning higher consciousness (*adhicitta*). The remainder is self-evident.

In the response, however, the Blessed One, without answering higher wisdom and the others by way of their specific forms, [answered] by way of the very pacification of those defilements which, through the radiance of higher wisdom and the rest, are called "at peace.
Thus, in accordance with the inclinations of the various deities, he spoke of that very pacification.

Illuminating [this meaning], he spoke the verses beginning with “one who is free from craving. Therein, the connection for the first eight verses should be understood through this verse, “Him I call one who is at peace”;
thereafter, they are connected by the final phrase of all [the verses], “he indeed is called ‘peaceful’.”

And according to the method of commentary by way of word-by-word analysis (*anupada-vaṇṇanā*): "One whose craving has long since been destroyed" means one who has abandoned craving even before the breaking up of the body.
"Not dependent on the prior limit" means not dependent on the prior limit divided into the past time and so forth.
"Not to be reckoned by the middle" means that even in the present time, he is not to be reckoned as "attached" and so forth. For him, there is nothing placed before.
Because that Arahant lacks the two types of preoccupation, there is nothing to be placed before him in the future;
therefore, I call him "peaceful. Such is the application of the terms here that should be understood. This same method applies everywhere.
From this point on, however, we shall provide only an explanation of the difficult words (*anuttānapada*) without showing the grammatical construction (*yojana*).
857. "Not disheartened" means not being dejected by various failures to obtain [what one desires]. "Not boastful" means having a nature that does not boast of one's virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
"Free from fidgeting" means being devoid of hand-fidgeting and the like. "Speaking with deliberation" means speaking words after having reflected with wisdom (*mantā*).
"Not agitated" means being free from restlessness (*uddhacca*). "He indeed is restrained in speech" means he is self-controlled in his speech and speaks words free from the four faults.

858. "Free from longing" (*nirāsatti*) means devoid of craving. "Seeing seclusion in contacts" (*vivekadassī phassesu*) means he sees the seclusion of selfhood and so forth within present contacts such as eye-contact and the rest. "And not led by views" (*diṭṭhīsu ca na nīyati*) means he is not led by any of the sixty-two views. 859.

"Withdrawn" (*paṭilīna*) means having departed from passion and the other [defilements] due to their abandonment. "Not fraudulent" (*akuha*) means not deceiving by means of the three bases of hypocrisy.

"Not covetous" (*apihālu*) means one whose nature is free from coveting; what is meant is that he is devoid of the craving of aspiration. "Not miserly" (*amaccharī*) means free from the five kinds of stinginess.
"Free from immodesty" means being devoid of bodily immodesty and so forth. "Not loathsome" means not to be shunned because of his perfection in virtue and other qualities;
he is unctuous, pleasing, and agreeable. "And not intent on slander" means unfit for the act of slandering which should be avoided in two ways.
(860) "Not greedy for acquisitions" means free from intimacy with craving toward the strands of sensual pleasure that serve as the objects of desire. "Gentle" means by means of gentle [speech].
He is endowed with bodily actions and so forth. "Eloquent" means he is endowed with eloquence regarding the scriptures, inquiry, and realization.
"Not having faith" means he does not place faith in anyone else regarding the Dhamma he has realized for himself.
"He does not become dispassionate" means that because he has become dispassionate through the destruction of lust, he does not now [need to] become dispassionate [further].
861. “He does not train out of desire for gain” means he does not train in the Suttantas and so forth with the aspiration for gain.
“Unopposed by craving and not greedily attached to flavors” means that, being unopposed due to the absence of conflict, he does not fall into greed for the root-flavors and so forth of craving.
862. “Equanimous” means endowed with the sixfold equanimity. “Mindful” means possessed of the mindfulness of body-contemplation and so forth.
863. "Dependence" (*nissaya*) refers to dependence on craving and views. "Having known the Dhamma" means having understood the Dhamma through such aspects as impermanence and so forth.
"Independent" means thus independent of those dependencies. By this, he demonstrates that apart from the knowledge of the Dhamma, there is no absence of dependencies;
[this applies] "for existence or non-existence," meaning for eternalism or annihilationism.

864. "I call him 'one who is stilled'"—I speak of one such as this, described by each individual verse, as being "stilled. "He has crossed over the clinging"—he has crossed over this great craving, which is termed "clinging" (visattikā) because of its state of being attached and so forth.
865. Now, praising that very one who is stilled, he said: "He has no sons," and so forth. In this context, "sons" refers to the four types beginning with those born of one's own loins.
Furthermore, it should be understood that here the term "sons" and so on is used to denote the acquisition of sons and the like.
These do not exist within him, or because of their absence, sons and the like do not exist.

(866) "By which the worldlings, as well as recluses and brahmins, might speak of him"—by which fault, such as passion and so forth, all worldlings, including gods and humans, as well as recluses and brahmins outside of this [teaching], might say of him: "He is lustful" or "he is hateful."
They might speak. "That is not set before him" means that those faults such as lust (*rāga*) are not set before that Arahant;
therefore, "he is not led by what is spoken," meaning for that reason he does not waver amidst words of censure. 867.
"He does not speak of superiors" means that, including himself among those who are distinguished, he does not, out of a sense of excessive pride (*atimāna*), think, "I am distinguished."

He does not speak. This same method applies to the other two [cases]. "He does not go to what is allowable" (*kappaṃ neti akappiyo*): such a person does not go to either of the two kinds of what is allowable. Why?
Because he is "unallowable" (*akappiyo*), which means it is said that his allowance has been abandoned.

868. "His own" (*sakaṃ*) means that which is claimed as "mine" and thus appropriated. And "he does not grieve over what is non-existent" (*asatā ca na socati*): that is, over what is non-existent and so forth.
“He does not grieve; he does not pursue phenomena. This means that among all phenomena, he does not proceed by way of desire and the like.
“He is indeed called ‘the Peaceful One’”—thus, referring to such a supreme person as “the Peaceful One,” he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, one hundred thousand million deities attained Arahantship.
There is no counting of those who have attained stream-entry and so forth.
Thus ends the commentary on the Purābheda Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, within the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā.
11. Commentary on the *Kalahavivāda-sutta* (Discourse on Quarrels and Disputes) 869.
*Kuto pahūtā kalahā vivādā*: This is the *Kalahavivāda-sutta*. What is its origin?
This too arose during that same Great Assembly for certain individuals whose minds were concerned with the question: "From what, indeed, do the eight things beginning with quarrels proceed?"
In order to reveal the Dhamma to the deities, he had himself questioned by a manifested Buddha in the same manner as before;
thus, because it stands there according to the sequence of questions and answers, all the verses have a clearly evident connection.
However, the commentary on the non-obvious words (*anuttānapada*) of these [verses] should be understood as follows: "From what source do quarrels and disputes arise?"—quarrel (*kalaha*).
And from where are these—their preliminary stage and quarrel—born? From where have lamentation, sorrow, and stinginess arisen?
From where have pride, arrogance, and slander arisen? "All those"—that is, all eight of these defiled states.
"Tell me that indeed"—tell me this matter which I have asked.
"Speak! I entreat you, sir"—for the particle *iṅgha* has the sense of entreaty. 870.
"Born from the basis of what is dear" means born from the object that is dear; the grammatical justification for this is already stated in the *Niddesa*.
By the phrase "quarrels and disputes joined with stinginess," it is shown that quarrels, disputes, and so forth arise not only from the basis of what is dear, but also from stinginess.
This demonstrates the condition. It should be understood that all these phenomena are spoken of here under the heading of quarrels and disputes.
Just as there is stinginess regarding these things, so too is there malicious speech regarding disputes. Therefore he said: "And malicious speech among those who have fallen into dispute.

(871) Regarding the verse: "From what source in this world do dear things arise, and from what source do the cravings that wander through the world come forth?"—it is because "dear things abound in quarrels."
Those who are mentioned here—whence in this world do they arise as objects of affection?
And not only those who are dear, but also those such as the kṣatriyas and others who wander about driven by greed, wandering about overcome by greed; whence does that greed of theirs arise?
Thus he asks two matters with a single question. "Hope and fulfillment": hope, and the success of that hope.
"And those which are for a man’s future life" means those things which exist for a man’s future life; what is meant is that they are his final resorts (*parāyana*).
This too is a single question.
872. "Having greed as their source" means having the types of greed beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) as their source. And "those which wander about through lust" means those which...
Kṣatriyas and others wander about due to greed; thus, since their greed also has desire as its source, [the text] answers both meanings together.

"From this source" means precisely "from the source of desire. Furthermore, the grammatical derivation of the words "kutonidānā kutonidānā" should be understood according to the method explained in the Sūciloma Sutta.

873. *Vinicchayā* refers to the determinations of craving and views. Or, regarding those states which have been spoken of by the ascetic: whatever other unwholesome states associated with anger and so forth, or similar unwholesome states, have been spoken of by the Buddha-ascetic—“from where have they arisen?

874. *Tamūpanissāya pahoti chando*: depending upon that pleasant or painful feeling—that is, depending upon the agreeable or disagreeable state known as the basis for both [pleasure and pain]—desire arises by way of the aspiration for union or separation. To this extent, “desire”...
“Now, from what cause does this arise in the world?”—this question has been answered. “Having seen both dissolution and existence in forms” means having seen both decline and arising among forms.

“A person makes a determination in the world” means that in the world of the states of woe and so forth, this person, for the sake of acquiring wealth, makes a determination of craving such as “I have gained a self,” and likewise makes a determination of views according to the same method.

It performs [its function]. Furthermore, the reasoning (*yutti*) here is exactly as stated in the *Niddesa*. To this extent, the question, "And from where have the determinations (*vinicchaya*) arisen?
has been answered. 875.
"These states (*dhammā*) also exist only as a dyad": these states, such as anger and so forth, exist only when there is the dyad of the pleasant and the unpleasant.
They are capable of arising; and their arising has already been explained in the *Niddesa*. To this extent, the third question has also been answered.
Now, showing the means for abandoning doubt for one who might still be skeptical regarding these questions thus answered, he said:
"One who is doubtful should train for the path of knowledge," that is, for the sake of attaining the knowledge and vision of knowledge.
"It should train in the three trainings"—this is what is meant. For what reason? Because the teachings were proclaimed by the ascetic after having known them.
Indeed, it was only after knowing them that the Buddha-ascetic proclaimed the teachings; there is no ignorance regarding the teachings on his part.

However, one who does not know them due to a lack of knowledge in himself would not understand them, but this is not due to a fault in the teaching. Therefore, for one who is full of doubt, [the path] is for the sake of knowledge.
"Train yourself, having understood the teachings proclaimed by the ascetic.
(876–7) "From what source do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?"—here, "the pleasant and the unpleasant" refers specifically to the feelings of pleasure and pain.
"They do not come into being"—that is, these do not exist. "Both non-existence and existence"—tell me the meaning of this.
"Yatonidānaṃ" (from what source) refers to that same matter: the non-existence and existence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. Here, a change of gender has been made [in the compound].
This is what is meant: "Tell me thus: from what source is this matter—the non-existence and existence of the pleasant and the unpleasant?
And here, the views of non-existence and existence have the non-existence and existence of the pleasant and the unpleasant as their objective basis.
Thus, *vibhava* and *bhava* should be understood according to their meaning. For it is stated in the exposition of the answer to this question:

"The view of existence (*bhavaditthi*) has contact as its source; the view of non-existence (*vibhavaditthi*) also has contact as its source. "From this source" means having contact as its source. 878.
"When what is absent do they not touch?"—when what has passed away do the five contacts, beginning with eye-contact, no longer touch?

879. “Dependent on name-and-form” means dependent on associated name and on the form of the physical basis and the object. “When form has vanished, contacts do not touch” means that when form has passed away, the five kinds of contact do not touch.

880. “How for one who has attained? means how for one who has practiced [the path]. “Form vanishes” means form ceases, or it would no longer exist. “Pleasure and pain” refers specifically to agreeable and disagreeable form. 881.
“Neither percipient nor non-percipient” means that for one who has thus attained such that form vanishes, he is no longer percipient even by way of natural perception (*pakatisaññā*).
"Not percipient of the contrary" means he is not one who possesses a contrary or distorted perception, nor is he insane or deranged.
"Nor non-percipient" means he is not devoid of perception, such as one who has attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*) or a non-percipient being (*asaññasatta*).

"Nor percipient of the sublime" means he is not even one who has transcended perception in the manner described by the formula beginning with "completely transcending perceptions of form" (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 265; Vibhaṅga 602).

One who has not attained the formless jhānas does not [perceive] it thus. For one who has become thus composed, thinking "form vanishes," without remaining in that state of perception-perceivedness and so forth, there is what was said: "When his mind is thus concentrated...

he directs his mind toward the attainment of the base of infinite space. For one who has become thus composed and possesses the path of the formless, form vanishes. It is rooted in perception (*saññā-nidāna*).

"Indeed, for one who has practiced thus, even though they have abandoned the 'proliferations of conceptualization' (*papañca-saṅkhā*), it is shown that the proliferations of craving and views (*taṇhā-diṭṭhi-papañca*) rooted in that perception (*saññā*) remain unabandoned.
(882–3) "To this extent alone, some wise ones here say there is purification for a *yakkha*; or is there something else?"

"They say 'just this much'": he asks whether the wise recluses and brahmins here claim that purity for a being is supreme only up to this point, or whether they speak of something else beyond this formless attainment as superior. "Some say even this much is the supreme":
some recluses and brahmins who hold to eternalism and consider themselves wise claim that even this much is the supreme purity.
"But some among them speak of a 'time'": some among those very people, being annihilationists (*ucchedavāda*), speak of annihilation as a "time.
"Those who speak of the wholesome regarding the residueless" means those who, while being proponents of the wholesome, [speak] regarding the state without residue (*anupādisesa*).
"And having known these as dependent": and having known these holders of views as being dependent upon the views of eternalism and annihilationism.
"Having known. "Having known the supports, that sage is one who investigates": having known the supports, that wise Buddha-sage is an investigator. "Having known, he is liberated":
having known the Dhamma regarding suffering, impermanence, and so forth, he is liberated. "He does not come together for further becoming": he does not come together again for repeated rebirth;
thus he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching...
The realization was exactly as described in the Purābheda Sutta.
Thus ends the commentary on the Kalahavivāda Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā.
12. Commentary on the Cūḷabyūhasutta 885–6.
*Sakaṃsakaṃdiṭṭhiparibbasānā*: This is the Cūḷabyūhasutta. What is its origin?

This too arose during that same great assembly [of the Tāvatiṃsa devas], when [Sakka] thought: "All these proponents of views say, 'We are of excellent character. Are they indeed of excellent character?"

This was spoken by the Buddha—having, in the same manner as before, caused himself to be questioned by an emanated Buddha—in order to clarify that matter for certain deities who had conceived the thought: "Do these beings establish themselves solely in their own view, or do they also adopt other views?
In this context, the first two verses are indeed verses of inquiry. Among them, the phrase *sakaṃsakaṃdiṭṭhiparibbasānā* means "clinging to their respective own views."
"Abiding under the sway of their own views, they dispute, each claiming to be skilled.
Having grasped a firm hold on the power of their respective views, they profess, "We are the skilled ones," and speak individually and separately; they do not speak as one.
"He who knows thus has known the Dhamma; he who denies this is incomplete"—this refers to that very view. He who knows in such a manner [is one who has truly understood].
He understood the Dhamma. But they say that one who opposes this is inferior. "Foolish" means inferior; "unskilled" means ignorant. 887–8.
Now there are three verses of response. These stand by restating with the second half the meaning already stated in the first half.
Because of this expansion (*byūha*) and because it is shorter than the subsequent sutta, this sutta is called the "Cūḷabyūha" (The Shorter Expansion).
It receives its name. In that context, "another's doctrine" means another's view (*diṭṭhi*).
"All are indeed fools"—the intention is that, such being the case, all these people are indeed fools. For what reason?
Because "all these are steeped in views," they are neither purified nor cleansed by their own views. "Those of pure wisdom, skillful, and wise" are not purified nor cleansed by their own views.
If they are indeed defiled, yet they possess purified wisdom, are skillful, and are possessed of intelligence;
or alternatively, there is a reading: "But if they are purified by their own view. Its meaning is:
if they are purified by their own view, possessing purified wisdom, being skillful and possessed of intelligence—then, such being the case, not even one among them... [is to be found].
He does not possess inferior wisdom. Why is that? Because their views are held with such firm conviction, just as those of others are.

Regarding the verse beginning "Nor do I say this is so": the summary of the meaning is this—I do not say that what those two pairs of people have mutually called each other a "fool" is true. Why is that? Because all of them [regard] their own [view].
They held the view: "This alone is the truth; all else is vain. And for that reason, they regarded others as "fools.
In this context, there are two readings: both "tathiyan" and "kathivan. 890.
Regarding the verse of inquiry, "yamāhu": some say that which is the truth of views is "tathiya."

891. Regarding the verse of response, "For there is one truth": the one truth is either cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*magga*). "In which people do not dispute" means that when people understand that truth, they would not dispute among themselves.

"They praise it themselves" means they speak of it by themselves. 892. Regarding the verse of inquiry, "Why indeed": "proponents" (*pavādiyāse*) refers to those who argue. "Or do they follow their own reasoning? (*udāhu te takkamanussaranti*) means:
do those proponents merely follow their own logic? 893. Regarding the verse of response, "Not so": "Except for perception, [they are] permanent" means setting aside mere perception (*saññāmattena*).
"Perceptions grasped as permanent": having formulated reasoning regarding views means having generated merely one's own wrong intentions (*micchā-saṅkappa*) toward those views.
Since, however, those who generate thought (*vitakka*) regarding views also generate [specific] views, it is therefore stated in the *Niddesa*:
"They generate, they produce, destinations of views (*diṭṭhigata*)," and so forth.

894–5. Now, in order to show the perversion of those proponents of views who, while these various truths do not exist, merely rely on ratiocination, the Blessed One spoke the verses beginning with “In what is seen, in what is heard. Herein, “the seen” means the seen;
the intention is “purification through the seen. This same method applies to the heard and so forth. And “relying on these, one sees celestial mansions” refers to these phenomena of views.

Even one who, relying on a celestial mansion (vimāna) characterized by purity, looks down upon others with contempt, stands within that judicial determination of views and, laughing aloud, says, "The other is a fool and unwholesome.
Thus, even such a beholder of a celestial mansion, standing within that determination of views, becomes filled with satisfaction and laughter, and speaks thus:
"The other is inferior and ignorant. This being so, there follows the verse beginning with "By whichever... (yeneva).
In this context, *sayamattānā* means "himself [as] self. *Vimāneti* means "he reviles.
*Tadeva pāvā* means he speaks that very same word, [expressing] a view, or [speaking of] that person.
The meaning of the verse beginning with *atisāradiṭṭhiyā* is as follows: He [acts] thus by means of that excessive view which exceeds the [true] characteristic (*lakkhaṇātisārini*).
It is full, swollen, and he is intoxicated by that view and conceit, thinking, "I am complete, I am a Kevalin.
Thus, possessing the conceit of being complete, he himself mentally consecrates himself, thinking, "I am wise. Why?
Because that view of his has become so fully established.
897. The connection and meaning of the verse beginning with *parassa ce*—and what more?

Furthermore, he who, standing in judgment, laughs and says, "The other is a fool, unskilled," if by that speech of the other he becomes inferior while being addressed by him, then he himself becomes inferior in wisdom along with him; he too becomes inferior in wisdom together with him. He too...
For indeed, one calls him a "fool. Yet his word is not authoritative; he himself, however, is a master of knowledge (*vedagu*) and wise.
This being the case, there is no fool whatsoever among the ascetics (*samaṇa*). For all of them are wise according to their own desire.
The connection and meaning of the verse beginning with *aññaṃ ito* is as follows: "But if he himself is a master of knowledge and wise... [the rest of the verse continues].
"Is there any fool among the recluses? When this has been said, someone might ask, "Why? To that it is replied:
Because those who profess a doctrine other than this, having missed and failed to reach the path of purity, are incomplete;
thus do the various sectarian teachers speak individually—those who profess a view other than this, who have missed and failed to reach the path of purity.
"And they are not solitary" (akevalino ca te)—this means that various sectarian teachers speak thus. But why do they speak in this way? Because they are "delighted by their own views";
that is to say, because they are delighted by their own respective views.
899–900. And being thus delighted, [the verse begins: "In this very world, purity... and so forth. Therein, "in one's own system" (sakāyane) means in one's own path.

"Those who speak firmly" means those of firm speech. And thus, among those speakers of firm speech, whichever sectarian (tīrthika) speaks firmly regarding his own doctrine, thinking "Who here is a fool?

might burn others; in brief, regarding his own domain—whether characterized as eternalism or annihilationism, or in detail, divided into nihilism, theism, causality, determinism, and so forth—he [speaks] firmly, thinking "This alone is the truth."
When speaking here of another as a "fool" according to one's own view, whom could one rightly regard as such in accordance with the Dhamma?
For according to his own standard, would not everyone else be wise and well-practiced?

This being the case, by speaking of another as a fool who possesses impure qualities, he brings about his own lack of intelligence; yet that other person, in turn, speaks of him: "This one is a fool and possesses impure qualities."
One would bring strife upon oneself. Why? Because, according to his own view, everyone is indeed wise and indeed well-practiced.
901. Thus, having taken a stand on a decision in every respect, one brings about dispute in the world by exalting oneself;
having taken a stand on a particular view, and having measured for oneself the Teacher and others, he brings about even greater dispute. In this way, regarding these decisions...
"Having known the danger and having abandoned all conceptual determinations by means of the Noble Path, a person does not create a conflict in the world"—
thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, there occurred a realization (abhisamaya) similar to that described in the *Purābheda Sutta*.
The commentary on the Cūḷabyūha Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, within the *Paramatthajotikā* commentary on the Minor Works, is completed. 13.
Commentary on the Mahābyūha Sutta.

902. As for this *Mahāvyūha-sutta*: what is its origin? This too arose during that same great assembly, in order to reveal the meaning to certain deities who had conceived the thought, "Do these who are entangled in views receive only reproach from the wise, or do they also receive praise?
[The Buddha spoke] by means of a manifested Buddha, in the manner previously described.
This was said after having questioned oneself. In that context, "they lead on" (*anvānayanti*) means they lead along (*anu ānayanti*), bringing [the matter] forward again and again.
Now, because those proponents who follow views (*diṭṭhigatika-vādino*), asserting "only this is the truth," sometimes and in some places obtain praise;
and as for that fruit of their doctrine known as praise, it is trifling for the sake of the pacification of lust and the other defilements.
It is not capable [of achieving its aim], so what need is there to mention the second fruit, which is blame?
Therefore, in order to demonstrate this point, he first uttered this verse of response: "For this is little and not enough for equanimity; I declare two fruits of dispute," and so forth.
Therein, "the two fruits of dispute" refers to blame and praise, or alternatively, victory and defeat and things of that nature.
"Seeing even this" means: having seen this disadvantage in the fruit of dispute—that "blame is indeed undesirable, and praise is not sufficient for one's welfare.
"Beholding the secure ground free from dispute" means: seeing Nibbāna, the ground free from dispute, as "secure.
Thus, not disputing in this way, [he recites] the verse beginning with "Whatever conventions... Therein, "conventions" (*sammutiyo*) refers to views (*diṭṭhiyo*). "Ordinary folk" (*puthujja*)...

“Arising from the world of ordinary persons. “How could he approach a means?”—in the sense of something to be approached, how could he approach even a single phenomenon among form and the rest, or for what reason would he approach it?
“Not forming a conviction regarding what is seen or heard”—meaning not feeling affection for purity based on what is seen or heard. 905.
But those outside of this [tradition] have the verse beginning with “Virtue is supreme. Its meaning is: conceiving that virtue alone is “supreme,”...
Some venerable ones who hold virtue as supreme declare that purity comes through mere restraint;
having undertaken vows such as the elephant-like conduct and others, they remain established in them.
Being led by existence and clinging to existence, they say, "Purity shall come from this very teacher's view," and furthermore, being proponents of skillfulness, they speak thus: "We are skillful."
906. "And among those who are supreme in virtue, whoever has practiced accordingly—if he passes away," etc. The meaning of this is as follows:
if, having passed away from that state of virtue and observance, he either becomes dissatisfied with others or fails to achieve his goal, he then falters;
having failed in that work consisting of virtue and observances, or in the work consisting of the formative forces of merit, he trembles. And it is not only...
He trembles; moreover, he yearns for, prattles about, and longs for that purification through rules and observances.

How is this so? It is like a caravan-leader who has fallen away while traveling from his home. Just as one traveling away from home, having fallen away from his caravan, might long for either his home or his caravan.
907. Thus, for those who hold virtue to be supreme, the noble disciple’s cause for penetration is expressed in the verse beginning: “Having abandoned all rules and observances.
In this context, “all that is blameworthy and blameless” refers to all unwholesome states and mundane wholesome states.

“Not desiring this purity or impurity” means not desiring this so-called purity, consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure and the like, nor this so-called impurity, consisting of the unwholesome and the like.
“One who is detached should practice for purity; one should practice detached from impurity. “Without grasping at peace” means without adopting [wrong] views.

(908) Thus, having shown the failure of those outsiders who speak of purification through restraint despite being supreme in mere morality, and having shown the practice of the Arahant who has abandoned both rules and observances, he now shows another way in which outsiders speak of purification, beginning with: “Depending on that...”

He spoke this verse. Its meaning is as follows: There are other recluses and brahmins as well who, depending on either Amarāpanta—which they loathe—or one or another of the views such as purification through seeing, and being "upward-leapers" due to their view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi), proclaim, praise, and speak of purity while remaining unsatiated by craving for various states of existence.

909. Thus, while those who have not abandoned craving continue to praise purity, even for one who might imagine themselves to have attained purity, because they have not abandoned craving, there will indeed be repeated yearnings as they long for this or that object in various states of existence;
this is the intended meaning. For craving, when cultivated, only increases craving. And it is not only...
"Chattering" (*jappitāni*) refers to the quivering (*pavedhitaṃ*) that occurs regarding things fashioned by one's own imaginings;

what is meant is that there is also a quivering due to craving and views regarding those objects fashioned by oneself. However, because he is free from craving for various states of existence (*bhavābhava*), there is for him no future passing away and re-arising;
"where would he chaffer with his own [craving]?"—this is the connection of this verse.
The remainder is exactly as stated in the *Niddesa*.

910–11. The verse beginning with “Yamāhu” (*Yamāhū*) is a question-verse. Now, since not even a single doctrine here is true, but they speak merely out of their own views, he spoke this response-verse beginning with “Sakañhi” to demonstrate that point.
In this context, "conventional designation" (*sammuti*) refers to a view.

912. Thus, while these [teachers] proclaim their own doctrine as complete, yet speak of another's doctrine as "inferior," for anyone among them—[the verse begins]: "If, by disparaging another... The meaning of this is: if...
On account of censuring another, one would become inferior; no one at all would excel among those who teach the Dhamma, nor would anyone be supreme.
Why is that? Because many speak of the Dhamma to others, yet they all speak firmly of their own Dhamma as being superior.
(913) Furthermore: "The honoring of the True Dhamma" is the verse. Its meaning is this: and as for how those sectarians praise [themselves]...
Their own bodies [are their authority], and their worship of the True Dhamma proceeds in that same manner. For they honor the Teacher and the rest exceedingly.
In that regard, if those [views] were authoritative, then all doctrines would be true.
Why? Because their purification is purely subjective; it is not established elsewhere, nor is it established in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). It is merely the grasping of a view within oneself.
For that is the case for those whose intellects are led by others.
Or alternatively, regarding the one who is the opposite—the *brāhmaṇa* because he has cast out evil—there is this verse: "The *brāhmaṇa* has no mind to be led by others.
Its meaning is as follows: for the *brāhmaṇa*, because [the truth] has been well-seen in the manner of "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and so forth...
There is no knowledge to be led by another; nor is there anything grasped after having determined among the phenomena of views, "This alone is the truth.
For that reason, he has transcended quarrels over views, and he does not regard any other phenomenon as superior apart from the foundations of mindfulness and the like.
915. The connection and meaning of the verse beginning with "I know" (*jānāmi*) are as follows: Thus, first of all, the ultimate brahmin does not regard any other phenomenon as supreme.

However, other sectarians—though they claim to know and see by means of such things as the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittañāṇa*), and though they say, "I know, I see, and it is exactly so"—yet they maintain that purity comes through their own views. Why is this? Because...
If even one among them has seen it—if indeed he has seen the matter as it truly is by means of that knowledge of others' minds and so forth—what has been accomplished for him by that seeing?
Has the full understanding of suffering (*dukkha-pariññā*) been achieved, or perhaps one of the other factors such as the abandoning of its origin (*samudaya-pahāna*)?
For in every respect, those sectarians speak of purity through something entirely different, having bypassed the Noble Path (*ariya-magga*).
Having surpassed those other sectarians, the Buddhas and others speak of purity in quite another way.
This is the connection and the meaning of the verse beginning with “The man who sees” (passaṃ naro).
Furthermore, that person who has seen by means of the knowledge of others' minds and so forth—that seeing man shall see name-and-form (nāmarūpa); having seen it, he shall know nothing beyond this.

Name-and-form are not eternal, nor are they pleasant, nor are they otherwise. One who sees thus—whether he perceives much or little name-and-form as eternal and pleasant—does not attain purity through such a view; for the wise do not say that purity comes by such means.
917. As for the verse beginning with *nivissavādī*, the connection and the meaning are as follows: even though there is no purity through that view...
One who asserts with dogmatic conviction, "I know, I see, and it is exactly thus," or one who, relying on that very vision,
proclaims the purity of their view and asserts with dogmatic conviction, "This alone is the truth"— such a person is not easily disciplined,
for they hold fast to that view which has been thus preconceived and constructed. Indeed, he remains attached precisely to whatever teacher or doctrine he has relied upon.
Speaking of the beautiful, speaking of purity, thinking of himself, "I am one who speaks of what is pure and sees what is pure," he saw it there exactly as it was;
he saw it precisely without distortion according to his own view.
The intention is that he saw it exactly as that view functions, and did not wish to see it otherwise.
918. Thus, among the sectarians who hold such fabricated views as foremost, there is the verse: “The brahmin does not enter into reckoning” (*na brāhmaṇo kappam upeti saṅkhaṃ*).
Therein, *saṅkhaṃ* means by reckoning; the sense is “having known. Nor is he one whose bond is knowledge (*napi ñāṇabandhū*);

that is, one who has not formed bonds of craving or wrong view through the knowledge of meditative attainments and so forth. The analysis (*viggaha*) therein is: “nor is there any bond made by his knowledge for him,” hence *napi*.

*Ñāṇabandhu*. "Conventional designations" (*sammutiyo*) refers to conventional views (*diṭṭhisammutiyo*). "Arising among the many" (*puthujāti*) means arising among ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*).
"They grasp them as 'I'" (*uggahaṇanti maññeti*): others [grasp] "I," meaning it is said that others grasp those conventional designations.

919. Furthermore: "Having cast off the bonds," etc., is the verse. Therein, "one who does not grasp" (*anuggaho*) is one devoid of grasping; he has no grasping, thus he is "one who does not grasp" (*anuggaho*); or, he does not grasp, thus he is "one who does not grasp."
920. Furthermore: "And what more? Such a one as he—regarding past taints," and so forth.
Herein, "past taints" refers to defilements arising with reference to past forms and so on. "New" refers to defilements arising with reference to present forms and so on.
"Not led by desire" means he does not proceed by way of desire and the like. "Not reproaching himself" means not reproaching himself on account of what has been done or left undone.

921. Thus, the verse begins: "And he who reproaches himself for non-self in all phenomena. Therein, "in all phenomena" (*sabbadhammesu*) refers to the sixty-two types of views (*diṭṭhidhamma*), categorized as "whatever is seen," and so forth.
"With burden laid down" (*pannabhāro*) means one whose burden has fallen away. "He does not construct" (*na kappeti*) means he is not one who constructs (*na kappiyo*);

the meaning is that he performs neither of the two kinds of construction (*kappa*). "Not yet stilled" (*nūparato*) refers to the ordinary person, the virtuous worldling, and those in training (*sekkhā*).
He is not even one who possesses cessation (uparati). "Not one who desires" (na patthiya) means he is free from craving; for craving "desires" (patthiyati), thus it is called "desire" (patthiyā);
since he has no such desire, he is "not one who desires" (na patthiya). The rest is already clear in various places and so has not been stated here.
Thus he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship; at the conclusion of the teaching, [the result] was similar to what was described in the Purābheda Sutta.
Thus there was this realization.
The commentary on the Mahāvyūha Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
14. Commentary on the Tuvaṭaka Sutta.
922. "I ask you"—this is the Tuvaṭaka Sutta. What is its origin?
This too arose during that same great assembly for the sake of certain deities who had conceived the thought, "What indeed is the practice for attaining Arahatship? regarding that very matter.

This was spoken by having himself questioned by the emanated Buddha in the same manner as before. Therein, regarding the first verse, the question "I ask" (*pucchāmi*) is analyzed according to the categories such as the inquiry for the revelation of what has not been seen. "Kinsman of the Sun" (*ādiccabandhu*) means the kinsman by lineage of the Sun. "Seclusion and the state of peace" (*vivekaṃ santipadañca*) means both seclusion and the state of peace.
