"For what reason did he see [it], and how did he become one who sees its occurrence?"—
this is what is meant. Then, because the Blessed One, seeing in such a way as to suppress the defilements, attains final nibbāna by becoming one who sees their occurrence,
he therefore revealed that matter by means of various modes to that assembly of deities for the sake of abandoning the defilements.
Addressing [the bhikkhus], he spoke five verses beginning with: “The root of the conceptual proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā).
Therein, first, the summary meaning of the opening verse is as follows: because they are reckoned as “proliferation,” they are indeed “conceptual proliferations” (papañca-saṅkhā).
Ignorance and the other defilements are the root of that; and all that proceeds as the thought “I am” is the root of that conceptual proliferation.
"He obstructs the mind. This means: whatever cravings (*taṇhā*) might arise within him, he should train himself by constantly being mindful to remove them;
having established mindfulness, he should train himself.
Thus, first of all, having taught the discourse connected with the three trainings (*tisikkhā*) according to the peak of Arahantship by means of the first verse alone, [the Buddha spoke].
Furthermore, in order to teach by way of abandoning conceit (*māna*), he spoke the verse beginning with “whatever.
Therein, “whatever phenomenon one might recognize within oneself” means that one might know some personal quality of one’s own, such as being born into a high-born family;
or “even externally” means that one might know the qualities of one's teachers or preceptors. “One should not take strength from that” means—
One should not take pride in that quality. 925.
Now, showing the method for not doing so, he spoke the verse beginning with "Better not by that. Its meaning is as follows:
one should not, on account of that conceit, imagine oneself to be "superior," or "inferior," or even "equal"; and by those...
One should not remain conceptualizing oneself by way of such modes as "I have gone forth from a high-born family," while being filled with various qualities such as noble birth and the like.
Having thus taught by way of the abandoning of conceit, he now teaches by way of the pacification of all defilements with the words, "Internally indeed... (Ajjhattameva).
He spoke this verse. In this context, "he pacifies within himself" means he should pacify all defilements, such as lust and so forth, within his own self.
"A bhikkhu should not seek peace from another" means that, setting aside the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, he should not seek peace by any other means.
"From where could there be anything discarded? means: how indeed could there be anything discarded?
927. Now, demonstrating the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*) of one whose taints are destroyed and who is inwardly calmed, he spoke this verse beginning with "Just as in the middle.

Its meaning is as follows: just as there is no wave in the middle of the great ocean—that middle being reckoned as the interval between the upper and lower parts, measuring four thousand *yojanas*, situated amidst the mountain ranges—or in the very center of the ocean;
He is born, yet he remains steadfast and unshakable; in this way, one who is unshaken and whose taints are exhausted should remain firm and unshakable amidst gains and the like.
Such a monk should not allow any excess of passion and the rest to arise anywhere.
Now, rejoicing in this teaching of the Dhamma which has been taught with the pinnacle of Arahatship as its goal, [he reflects] upon that Arahatship...
The created Buddha, asking about the first way of practice, spoke this verse beginning with “He proclaimed. In this context, “he proclaimed” (*akittayi*) means he explained.
“One whose eyes are opened” (*vivaṭacakkhu*) means one endowed with the five eyes that are opened and unobstructed.

“The Dhamma realized by himself” (*sakkhidhamma*) refers to the Dhamma known through his own direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) and personally witnessed. “The removal of perils” (*parissayavinaya*) means the dispelling of dangers. “The way of practice” (*paṭipadaṃ*).
"Speak" means: now speak of the practice (*paṭipatti*). "Venerable Sir" (*bhaddante*)—he said this while addressing the Blessed One, meaning "May it be well with you.
Alternatively, it is said: "Speak of your auspicious, beautiful practice (*paṭipadā*).
"The Pātimokkha or else concentration"—by this he asks, having divided that very practice. Or, by the word "practice," he refers to the Path (*magga*).
He asks. By means of the other [questions], he asks about virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*).

929–30. Then, because the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) is the protection of virtue, or because this teaching being taught in this sequence is suitable for those deities, the Blessed One [explained] the path of practice beginning from the restraint of the sense faculties.

The passage beginning with “With the eyes” is commenced in order to show this. Therein, “with the eyes he should not be fickle” means that he should not be fickle with his eyes by way of looking at things that ought not to be seen and so forth.
“He should shut his ear against village talk” means that he should close his ear against frivolous chatter (*tiracchānakathā*).
“Against contact” means against the contact of disease. “And he should not long for existence” means for the purpose of dispelling that contact.
One should not long for existence in the realm of sense-desires (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, nor should one tremble at fears.

That is to say, one should not tremble at fears such as lions, tigers, and the like, which serve as conditions for that contact; or rather, one should not be agitated by the remaining objects of the nose-faculty and the mind-faculty.
In this way, the complete restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) is described. Or else, [it is described] through the preceding [methods] as the restraint of the faculties...
Having shown this, he demonstrates by means of it: "One dwelling in the forest should not tremble upon seeing or hearing something terrifying.

(931) "Having obtained, one should not make a store": having obtained any of these things, such as food and so forth, in accordance with the Dhamma, one should not make a store, reflecting: "For one dwelling in a forest lodging, these are always difficult to obtain."

932. “A meditator should not be fickle with his feet” means he should be devoted to meditation and not be restless in his gait. “He should abstain from remorse and not be negligent” means he should dispel remorse such as that concerning the hands and so forth;

and herein, he should not be negligent by virtue of performing his duties with thorough care. 933. “Laziness, deceit, laughter, and play” refers to sloth, deceit, laughter, and physical or mental play.
“With adornment” means together with bodily decoration. 934–7. “Atharvan” refers to the employment of Atharvanic mantras. “Dreams” refers to the science of dream interpretation. “Signs” refers to...
He does not practice the examination of jewels and so forth; he would not employ them. "Crying out" (*viruta*) refers to the vocalizing of deer and other animals.
"Slander" (*pesuṇiya*) means backbiting. Regarding "buying and selling," he should not engage with his five fellow practitioners either through deception or through the pursuit of profit.
"A monk should not utter reproach" means that, by not producing the defilements that cause reproach within himself...

One should not cause reproach from other recluses and brahmins. One should not become attached to the village; that is, one should not become attached to the village through socializing with householders and the like.
One should not chatter to people out of a desire for gain; that is, one should not address people out of a longing for profit.
"Engaged" means being occupied with robes and so forth, or employed for their sake.
"938–9. *Mosavajje na nīyethā* means one should not be led away into speaking falsehoods. *Jīvitena* means by way of livelihood. *Sutvā rusito bahuṃ vācaṃ, samaṇānaṃ vā puthujanānan*ti:

having heard much offensive speech from others—whether from those ascetics or from other common people such as kṣatriyas and so forth—one is provoked or irritated. *Na paṭivajjā* means one should not retaliate."
One should not speak back. What is the reason? For the virtuous do not act as adversaries. 940.

"And having understood this Dhamma" means having known all this Dhamma as it has been described. "Discerning" means discerning. "Knowing that there is peace" means knowing that *nibbāna*—the pacification of lust and the other defilements—is peace. 941.

If one asks, "For what reason does he not become negligent?"—it is because of the verse beginning, "For he is a conqueror. In that context, "conqueror" refers to [one who has conquered] form and the other aggregates.

"Overcomer. "Unconquered" means not overcome by those [defilements]. "He saw the Dhamma, immediate and beyond mere speculation" means he saw the Dhamma that is directly evident and not based on hearsay.
"Always training while paying homage" means one should train in the three trainings while always paying homage.
The rest is clear everywhere.
However, herein, by means of such passages as "not fickle with the eyes," the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) is shown;

by such passages as "of food and drink," the morality of utilizing requisites through the rejection of hoarding (*sannidhi*) is shown; by means of sexual misconduct, intoxicants, slander, and so forth, the morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (*pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla*) is shown;

by such passages as "divination, dreams, and bodily marks," the morality of purity in livelihood (*ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla*) is shown; and by the phrase "he should be a meditator" (*jhāyī assa*), [the morality of right concentration is shown].
By the phrase "Discern things, O bhikkhus," concentration is indicated; by "Always train in mindfulness," wisdom is indicated;

and again, by the summary "Then, in seats and beds, a bhikkhu should dwell in quietude and not indulge in sleep," etc., the assistance, hindrance, inclusion, and avoidance regarding virtue, concentration, and wisdom are stated.
Thus the Blessed One, having explained the complete course of practice for the created being, brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the realization occurred exactly as described in the Purābheda Sutta.
[End of] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Tuvaṭaka Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* is finished.
15. Commentary on the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. 942.
The Attadaṇḍa Sutta begins with the words: “Fear has arisen from the stick of oneself. What is its origin? It is that which follows the *Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta*.
When the origin [of the dispute] was being told, the quarrel of the Sākiyas and Koliyas over water was described. Knowing this, the Blessed One thought, "Relatives are quarreling;
come now, I shall restrain them," and standing between the two armies, he spoke this sutta. Therein, the meaning of the first verse is as follows:
whatever fear there is for the world, whether pertaining to the present life or the future life—
"All that has arisen—this fear born of the staff of self—has arisen because of one's own misconduct.
Even though this is so, "behold the people in their strife"; behold these people, such as the Sakyans and others, who are in mutual conflict, harming and oppressing one another.
Having thus rebuked those people who were hostile and practicing wrongly, [the Blessed One] demonstrated his own right practice.
In order to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in him, he said: “I shall proclaim the sense of urgency, just as it was realized by me.
The intention is that this was previously realized by the Bodhisatta himself.
Now, showing the manner in which he was moved to such urgency, he spoke the verse beginning with “phandamānaṃ. Therein:
"Trembling" means shaking due to craving and other such factors. "In waterless" means in a place lacking water.
"Seeing them mutually hostile" means seeing various beings who are at variance with one another. "Fear entered me" means fear has taken possession of me.
(944) "The world is entirely without essence" means that, beginning with the hells, the world all around is without essence, being devoid of any permanent substance or the like.
"All directions tremble" means all directions are shaken by impermanence. "Seeking a dwelling for myself" means seeking protection for oneself.
"I saw no place where I could rest" means I did not see any place that was not overrun by old age and the like. 945.
"When [youth] had come to its end," and "seeing this, weariness arose in me," means precisely at the conclusion, the final limit, of youth and so forth.
Seeing beings whose minds were struck down, obstructed by old age and other such afflictions that lead to destruction, aversion arose in me. Then, regarding the phrase "the dart here":
it means the dart of passion and so forth among these beings. "Residing in the heart" means residing in the mind.
If one asks, "Of what power is this dart?"—it is answered by the verse beginning, "By which dart one is pierced. Therein, "all directions... [and so on].
"It runs" means it runs toward all directions of misconduct, as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions.
"Having extracted that very dart, he neither runs nor sinks" means that having pulled out that very dart, he does not run toward those directions, nor does he sink in the four floods.
Even while beings are afflicted by such a dart of great power—therein the trainings are sung: which...

“In the world, they are called ‘attachments’ (gadhitāni)”: this is a verse. Its meaning is as follows: those five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) in the world which, because they are craved for the sake of acquisition, are called “attachments”;
or, because they have been practiced for a long time, they are called “attachments.
In that regard, various trainings such as elephant-training and so forth are explained or mastered as their means. Behold how far...
This world is heedless; therefore, a wise clansman should not be attached to those [pleasures] or intent upon those trainings.
On the contrary, having become disillusioned with all sensual desires through the vision of impermanence and so forth, he should train solely for his own Nibbāna.
Now, showing how one should train for the sake of Nibbāna, he said, "One should be truthful," and so on. Therein—
"Truthful" means endowed with truth in speech, truth in knowledge, and truth in the Path. "Free from slander" means one who has abandoned slander.
"Deceit" means stinginess. 949.

"He should overcome sleep, sloth, and torpor"—that is, he should master these three states: drowsiness, physical laziness, and mental laziness. "With a mind bent on Nibbāna" means one whose mind is inclined toward Nibbāna.
950–51. *Sāhasā* refers to the performance of reckless acts, such as those arising from the temperament of lust and so forth, on the part of one who is intoxicated.
*Purāṇaṃ nābhinandeyya*: one should not delight in past forms and so forth. *Nave*: in the present. *Hiyyamāne*: in that which is perishing. *Ākāsaṃ na sito siyā*:
one should not be dependent upon space; that is, one should not be dependent upon craving (*taṇhā*). For craving is called "space" because it provides space for forms and other objects.
952. If it is asked, “For what reason should one not be attached to space?”—the verse begins with, “I call it greed. Its meaning is as follows:
I indeed call this craving, which is designated as “space,” “greed” (*gedha*) because it greedily clings to forms and so forth; I declare it to be “greed.
Furthermore, in the sense of carrying away, it is called a “flood” (*ogha*), and in the sense of rushing toward, it is called “rushing” (*ājava*); [thinking] “this is mine, this is... [it is said].
I call it "craving" (*jappanā*) because of its nature as yearning; "the object" (*ārammaṇa*) in the sense of being difficult to let go of; and "quivering" (*pakampana*) because it causes trembling.
And this mire of sensual desire (*kāmapaṅka*) is called "difficult to cross" because it is an impediment to the world and because it is hard to transcend.
When it is said, "One should not be dependent on space," if one asks, "What is this 'space'? [it refers to the cessation of craving].
"I call it greed" (gedhaṃ brūmi). In this way, the connection of that verse should be understood. Therein, the construction of the words is as follows: "I call the sky 'greed'.
Likewise, that which is called the "great flood," I call that; I call it "coming and going" (ājavaṃ), I call it "longing" (jappanaṃ), I call it "trembling" (pakampanaṃ);
and that which is the "mire of sensual desire" (kāmapaṅko) in the world with its devas, so difficult to cross—I call that.
953. Thus, this sequence beginning with "greed" leads to the verse: "Not dependent on space, having transcended all truths. Its meaning is as follows:
Having not overstepped the three kinds of truths previously mentioned, the one who has attained sagehood (*moneyya*) and is reckoned a sage stands upon the ground of Nibbāna, the Brahmin.
Indeed, such a person, having relinquished all sense-bases (*āyatana*), is called "the Peaceful One" (*santo*).

954. Furthermore: "He indeed is wise... This verse [is as follows]. Therein, "having known the Dhamma" means having known the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) by way of their impermanence and so forth.
"He conducts himself rightly in the world" means that by abandoning the defilements that cause improper conduct, he conducts himself rightly in the world.

955. And likewise: "He who here does not long for desires... This verse [is as follows]. Therein, "attachment" (*saṅga*) refers to the sevenfold attachment; "he who has transcended it" means he does not covet it.
956. Therefore, regarding one who wishes to be such as this among you, I say: "That which was before... and so forth.
In this context, "that which was before" refers to the defilements that arise with reference to past formations, as well as past karma. "Let there be nothing for you afterwards" means:
let there be no "something"—namely, lust and other defilements—that would arise with reference to future formations.
“If you do not grasp at the middle” means if you do not grasp even at present phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
(957) Having thus shown the attainment of *arahantship* by saying, “you will wander in peace,” he now spoke the following verses by way of praising the *arahant*.
Therein, in the verse beginning with “all,” “possessed of ‘mine’” (*mamāyita*) refers to the act of making something one’s own; “my... [the rest of the sentence follows].
"‘This’" refers to an object that has been grasped. "And he does not grieve over what is non-existent" means that he does not grieve due to causes that do not exist, due to reasons that are absent.
"He does not waste away" means that he does not undergo decay.
958–9. Furthermore: "For whom there is nothing," etc. Therein, "anything" (*kiñcana*) refers to any class of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
And what more?—the verse beginning with "not harsh" (*aniṭṭhurī*). Therein, "not harsh" means free from envy (*anissukī*).
Some read it as "not cruel" (*aniddhurī*). "Even-minded everywhere" (*sabbadhī samo*) means equal in all respects; the intended meaning is that he is equanimous. What is being said?
When asked about that person who does not grieve, thinking "I have nothing," I call that unshakable individual "not harsh."
“Not greedy, unshaken, equal in all respects”—this, I say, is the fourfold benefit in that person. 960.
And what more? The verse beginning with “of the unshaken one. Therein, “conditioned thing” (*nisaṅkhata*) refers to any formation whatsoever among the formations of merit and so forth.
For it is called a “conditioned thing” because it is conditioned by others (*nisaṅkhariyati*) or because it conditions itself (*nisaṅkharoti*).

"Various undertakings" (*viyārambhā*) refers to various undertakings such as the formative volitions of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). "He sees security everywhere" means he sees only fearlessness in all places. 961.

Regarding the verse beginning with "Seeing thus, not among equals...": therein, "he does not speak" means that by way of conceit—such as "I am equal"—he does not speak of himself even among equals, nor among those who are inferior or superior.
"Neither takes up nor rejects" refers to anything among [the aggregates] such as form (*rūpa*).
He does not grasp at the Dhamma; he does not relinquish it. The rest is clear everywhere.

Thus he brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred Sākiyan princes and Koliyan princes went forth by means of the "Come, monk" formula.
Taking them with him, the Blessed One entered the Great Forest.
The commentary on the Attadaṇḍa Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Paramatthajotikā, is completed. 16.
Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta.
962. *Na me diṭṭho* is the Sāriputta-sutta; it is also called the "Thera-pañha-sutta.
What is its origin? The origin of this sutta begins with the elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja raising into the air a bowl made from a sandalwood casket that he had received from a merchant of Rājagaha.
The taking of a bowl by means of psychic power; the prohibition of psychic powers for disciples regarding that matter;
the desire of the heretics to perform a miracle together with the Blessed One; the performance of the miracle; the Blessed One’s journey to Sāvatthī; the pursuit of the heretics;
King Pasenadi’s approach to the Buddha in Sāvatthī; the manifestation of the Kaṇḍamba tree; and [the events] for the sake of the four assemblies’ victory over the heretics.
The prevention of the Blessed One’s desire to perform miracles; the performance of the Twin Miracle;
the Blessed One’s journey to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven after performing that miracle; his preaching of the Dhamma there for three months;
and his descent from the world of the gods to the city of Saṅkassa at the request of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera—these are the episodes, interspersed with Jātaka stories.

Having been honored by the devas of the ten thousand world-systems, the Blessed One descended into the city of Saṅkassa by way of a central staircase made of jewels and stood upon the landing of the stairs,
saying: “Those wise ones who are devoted to meditation, who delight in renunciation and tranquility;”
"Even the gods envy those mindful ones who have attained perfect enlightenment"—
this was said in reference to this verse from the *Dhammapada*. However, when the Blessed One was standing upon the staircase,
the Venerable Sāriputta paid homage to him first, followed by the Bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, and then the rest of the multitude.
There the Blessed One thought: "In this assembly, Moggallāna is renowned as foremost in psychic power, Anuruddha for the divine eye, and Puṇṇa for his skill in preaching the Dhamma;
however, this assembly does not know Sāriputta to be foremost by virtue of any such quality.
What if I were to make Sāriputta known by way of the quality of wisdom? Then [he addressed] the Elder...
He asked questions. The Elder answered every question posed by the Blessed One—whether concerning the questions of worldlings, those of trainees, or those of those beyond training.

Then the people recognized him as "the foremost in wisdom. Thereupon the Blessed One, thinking, "Sāriputta is not only now the foremost in wisdom, but was also the foremost in wisdom in the past," related a Jātaka story.
More than a thousand years ago, there lived at the foot of a mountain a thousand seers who subsisted on forest roots and fruits.
A sickness befell their teacher, and attendants were attending to him. The eldest pupil said, "I will bring suitable medicine;
attend to the teacher with diligence," and departed for the path of men. Even before he had returned, the teacher—
He passed away. Thinking, "He will pass away now," his pupils asked him about meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Referring to the attainment of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti*), he said, "There is nothing.
The pupils concluded, "The teacher has no further realization. Then, the senior pupil returned with medicine and, seeing that he had passed away, [proceeded to act].
He asked the teacher, “Have you asked anything? [The other replied,] “Yes, we have asked. [The teacher] said, “There is nothing. This meant that nothing had been attained by the teacher.
By saying, “There is nothing,” the teacher proclaimed the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*);
thus, the teacher is to be honored.
“Even if a thousand fools were gathered together and they cried out for a hundred years,
a single wise man is better.”
“He who understands the meaning of what has been spoken.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One had related the Jātaka, the Venerable Sāriputta, for the sake of his five hundred co-resident bhikkhus, asked about suitable lodgings, alms-resorts, moral conduct, observances, and so forth, saying: “I have not seen since then...”
Beginning with this verse of praise, “In the past...,” he spoke eight verses. Explaining that meaning, the Blessed One spoke the remaining verses thereafter.
In that context, “prior to this” means prior to his descent here at Saṅkassanagara. “Vagguvado” means one of beautiful speech. “Tusitā... [and so forth].
"Come from the Tusita" means he has come from the Tusita realm because he descended from the Tusita body into his mother’s womb;

he is "a leader of a group" (*gaṇī*) because he is a teacher of a group. Alternatively, in the sense of being contented, he has come to the leader of the gods known as the Tusitas; or, he has come to the leader of the host of Arahants in the Tusita realm.
In the second verse, "as it appears to the world with its devas" means that just as it appears to the world with its devas, so too to human beings.
"It is seen. Or, "as it is seen": it is seen truly and without error as one who possesses the eye; thus, he is the "One with the Supreme Eye" (*uttamacakkhu*).
"The One" (*eko*) means alone by virtue of his renunciation and so forth. "Bliss" (*rati*) refers to the bliss of renunciation (*nekkhammarati*) and so forth.
Regarding the third verse, "of the many bound here": "here" refers to the many disciples, such as the *khattiyas* and others. Disciples...
Because their livelihood is dependent upon teachers, they are called "bound.

Regarding the phrase "one comes with a question": it means one who has need comes with a question; or, it refers to the coming of those who have need for the sake of a question, or the coming for the sake of a question.

In the fourth verse, "vijigucchato" means being repelled by birth and so forth. "Rittamāsanaṃ" means a secluded bed or seat. It should be connected as follows: "or in mountain caves," meaning one should resort to a secluded seat in mountain caves.
966. In the fifth verse, *uccāvacesu* means among those that are low and high. *Sayanesu* refers to lodgings such as monasteries (*vihāra*) and so forth.

*Kīvanto tattha bheravā* means how many causes of fear are there therein? There is also a reading *kuvanto*, which has the meaning "moaning" (*kūjanto*), but it does not connect with what precedes or follows.
In the sixth verse, "how many perils" (*katī parissayā*) means how many calamities. "The direction not yet gone to" (*agataṃ disaṃ*) refers to Nibbāna;

for it is "not yet gone to" because it has never been reached before, and it is called a "direction" (*disā*) because it is to be pointed out as such. Therefore it is said, "the direction not yet gone to.
"One should overcome" (*abhisambhaveyya*) means one should master. "In a remote place" (*pantamhi*) means in a secluded or peripheral location.

In the seventh verse, *kyāssa byappathayo assu* means "what would his modes of speech be," that is, what would his words be like. In the eighth verse, *ekodi nipako* means "one-pointed-minded and wise.

Thus, after the Venerable Sāriputta had praised the Blessed One with three verses, the Blessed One—being questioned in five verses for the sake of his five hundred disciples regarding lodgings, alms-resorts, moral conduct, observances, and so forth—explained that matter.
He began the response by way of the verse beginning with “vijigucchamānassa” (for one who is disgusted) in order to explain it. Therein, first, the meaning of the initial verse is as follows:

O Sāriputta, for a bhikkhu who desires full awakening—who is disgusted with birth and so forth, and who resorts to empty seats and beds—whatever is comfort, whatever is a pleasant dwelling, whatever is in accordance with the Dhamma, and whatever is the Dhamma itself.
"I shall declare that to you as I understand it, just as one who understands would speak; thus do I say.
(971) In the second verse, *pariyantacārī* means "one who walks within the boundaries," walking within the four boundaries consisting of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
*Ḍaṃsādhipātānaṃ* refers to tawny flies and other flies; for other flies descend from here and there and bite.
Therefore, they are called "calamities. "From human contacts" means from the contacts of thieves and the like. 972.

In the third verse, those called "adherents of other doctrines" (paradhammikā) include all outsiders, excluding those who follow the same doctrine (sahadhammika). "Seeking what is wholesome" (kusalānuesī) means searching for wholesome states (kusaladhamma). 973.
In the fourth verse, "from the contact of affliction" (ātaṅkaphassena) means from the contact of disease. "Cold and heat" (sītaṃ uṇhaṃ) refers to both cold and heat.
"Though touched by them in many ways": although he is touched by those various forms such as afflictions and the like; "without a home" (*anoka*):
being a place where no room is found for volitional formations, consciousness, and so forth.
Having thus answered the question regarding the meaning of "the bhikkhu who feels revulsion," etc., by means of these three verses, [the author proceeds].
Now, answering the question asked in the manner beginning with “What would be his modes of speech? he says: “He would not commit theft,” and so forth.
In this context, “he touches” means he would experience. Regarding the phrase “he should know whatever turbidity of mind there may be”:
whatever turbidity of the mind he should recognize, all that he should dispel, thinking, “This belongs to the side of the dark.”
"Having dug up even their root, he stands firm": having dug up even that root of those anger and conceit which begins with ignorance, he would stand firm.
"Surely you, sir, will overcome them": thus, while overcoming the pleasant and unpleasant, one would overcome them by one means alone;
the intention is that one should not exert effort laxly in this regard.
976. "Having placed wisdom foremost" means having made wisdom the precursor. "Possessing noble joy" means being endowed with noble rapture (*pīti*).
"One should endure the four states of lamentation" means one should endure those things subject to lamentation that are mentioned in the immediately following verse.
977. "What indeed shall I eat? means what shall I consume? "Or where shall I eat? means in what place shall I eat? [This is] suffering.
"Alas, who will sleep best tonight? I have slept in suffering; where shall I sleep tonight on my arrival?
These are the four thoughts: two dependent on almsfood and two dependent on lodgings.
"Wandering without a home" means wandering without obstructions and wandering free from craving.
"At the proper time" means at the time for alms-food, having obtained food designated as alms-food; or at the time for robes, having obtained clothing designated as robes;
the intention is "righteously and justly. "He should know moderation" means he should know the measure both in receiving and in using.
"Here" refers to the Teaching (*sāsana*), or it may simply be a particle. "For the sake of contentment" means for the sake of satisfaction.

"What is meant is that he should know the proper measure for this purpose. "He is guarded in those" means that the bhikkhu is guarded regarding those requisites. "One of restrained conduct" means one who dwells in self-restraint;

what is meant is that his modes of deportment are protected, and the doors of his body, speech, and mind are guarded. There is also the reading "yatacārī," which has the same meaning. "Rusito" means provoked; what is meant is that he is struck or disturbed.
979. "Devoted to jhāna" means devoted to jhāna by way of producing what has not yet arisen and by way of cultivating what has already arisen.
"Having attained concentration by undertaking equanimity" means having produced the equanimity of the fourth jhāna, his mind is concentrated.

"He cuts off the tendency toward discursive thought and remorse" means he cuts off discursive thought (*takka*) such as sensual thoughts, and the "abode of that discursive thought" (*takkāsaya*) such as perceptions of sensuality, as well as physical remorse (*hatthakukkucca*) and so forth.
And one should cut off remorse. 980.
"Being reproved by words, the mindful one rejoices": being reproved by the words of preceptors and others, one should, being mindful, rejoice in that reproof.
"One should let loose speech that is wholesome": one should utter speech arising from knowledge.
"Not excessively" means that one should not utter speech that exceeds the proper time or transgresses the limits of moral conduct (*sīla*).
"For the sake of worldly talk" means for the purpose of conversation concerning people. "One should not intend" means one should not give rise to the volition (*cetana*) [to speak].
981. "Furthermore" means now, even beyond this point. "The five stains" refers to the five stains beginning with lust for form (*rūpa-rāga*).
"For those who, being mindful, train for the sake of discipline"—meaning that one, having established mindfulness, should train in the three trainings for the purpose of disciplining oneself.
For by training in this way, one may overcome passion regarding forms... [and so on] ...regarding contacts, and not otherwise. 982.
Then, as he trains for their discipline, he proceeds in due order with the verse beginning, "In these things... Regarding that:
"In these" means in form and the other [aggregates]. "At the proper time, examining the Dhamma rightly":
that bhikkhu, at the time described by the method beginning with "when the mind is agitated, it is the time for concentration," examines all conditioned phenomena by way of impermanence and so forth.
"Becoming unified, he shall dispel the darkness": he, with a one-pointed mind, [dispels] all...
One should destroy the darkness of delusion and the rest; there is no doubt about this. The remainder is clear everywhere.

Thus the Blessed One brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred bhikkhus attained Arahantship, and there was a penetration of the Dhamma by thirty koṭis of gods and humans.
[End of] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Sāriputta-sutta of the Suttanipāta is finished.
And the fourth section is completed according to the method of explaining the meaning; it is known by the name the Aṭṭhakavagga.
5. Pārāyanavagga: Commentary on the Introductory Verses (Vatthugāthāvaṇṇanā) 983.
"The delightful city of the Kosalans" is the introductory verse for the Pārāyana-vagga. As for the origin of these verses: it is said that in the past...
There was a certain master carpenter living in Bārāṇasī who was peerless among his own teachers;

he had sixteen disciples, and each of them had a thousand pupils. Thus, these seventeen thousand and six hundred masters and pupils all made their livelihood depending on Bārāṇasī, and having gone near a mountain, they took trees right there.
Having completed various types of palaces and constructed a raft, they brought it to Bārāṇasī on the Gaṅgā;
if the king was in need, they would construct and give him a palace of one story... up to... seven stories.
If not, they sold them to others as well and supported their wives and children. Then one day, their teacher said, "It is not possible..."
Thinking, "It is difficult to maintain one's livelihood constantly by the work of a carpenter, for this kind of labor is arduous in old age," he addressed his pupils:
"Sons, Udumbara and the others, bring me trees with little sapwood. Having agreed, saying "Very well," they brought them.
He had a wooden bird constructed from them, and having entered its interior, he [set up] a machine...
He filled it. Like Supaṇṇarāja, the king of birds, the wooden bird leaped into the air, soared above the forest, and descended in front of his pupils.
Then the teacher said to his students: "Dear ones, by making such wooden vehicles as these, it is possible to seize the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa.
You too, dear ones, make these; having seized the kingdom, we shall live."
“It is suffering to live by the craft of carpentry. Having done so, they informed their teacher.
Then the teacher said to them, “Dear sons, which kingdom shall we take? “The kingdom of Bārāṇasī, Teacher,” they replied. “Enough, dear sons; do not let this please you.
For even if we were to take that, we would still be called ‘the Carpenter King’ and ‘the Carpenter Heir-Apparent,’ and thus the name of carpenter would persist.”
"We shall not escape; Jambudīpa is vast. Let us go elsewhere.
Then, with their wives and children, they mounted wooden carts, equipped themselves with weapons, and set out toward the Himavat.
Having entered a certain city in the Himavat, they presented themselves at the very residence of the king. There they...
Having taken the kingdom, they consecrated their teacher as king. He became known as King Kaṭṭhavāhana.
Because he had seized it, that city also received the name “Kaṭṭhavāhana City,” and likewise the entire kingdom.
King Kaṭṭhavāhana was righteous, as were the crown prince and the sixteen ministers appointed to the positions of counselors.
Sissā. That kingdom, being sustained by the king through the four bases of sympathy, became exceedingly prosperous, flourishing, and free from calamity.
Both the city-dwellers and the country-folk felt great affection for the king and his retinue, saying, "We have obtained an excellent king;
we have obtained an excellent royal assembly."
Then one day, merchants from the Middle Country, having taken their wares, arrived at the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana;
and taking gifts, they saw the king. The king asked them everything, including where they had come from.

He placed those woolen cloths inside the caskets and had ivory-workers fashion the outside of each casket so that they resembled lac-balls. Then he placed all eight lac-balls into boxes.
Having wrapped it in cloth and sealed it with the royal seal, he dispatched his ministers with the instruction, "Give this to the King of Bārāṇasī.
He also sent a letter stating, "This gift should be inspected in the middle of the city by you, surrounded by your ministers.

In the royal courtyard, having broken the seal, removed the wrapping, and opened the casket, he saw eight balls of lac.

The ivory casket opened a gap and became divided into two parts. Seeing a blanket within it, he opened the others as well, and it was exactly the same everywhere.
Each individual blanket was sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width.
When the blankets were spread out, the royal courtyard appeared as if illuminated by the radiance of the sun. Having seen this, the great multitude—

Having had it written down and placed inside a casket made of the seven precious gems, he placed that gem-casket in a casket made of gems;
the gem-casket in one made of masāragalla stone; the masāragalla-casket in one made of ruby; the ruby-casket in one made of gold; the gold-casket in one made of silver;
the silver-casket in one made of ivory; the ivory-casket in one made of heartwood; and the heartwood-casket in a chest.
Having placed it inside, wrapped the chest in cloth, and sealed it, he had a magnificent elephant fashioned with a golden banner,
adorned with golden ornaments, and covered with a net of gold; having prepared a couch upon it and placed the chest on the couch,
while a white parasol was held aloft and all manner of perfumes, flowers, and the like were offered in worship, accompanied by the sound of all musical instruments—
Having had the road decorated for as far as the boundaries of his own kingdom by those singing hundreds of hymns of praise, he went there himself.
Standing there, he sent gifts to the neighboring kings with the message: "Gifts should be sent in this manner by those who wish to honor him.
Upon hearing this, those kings came out to meet him along the road as far as Kaṭṭhavāhana’s [territory].
They led [the casket] as far as the boundary of the kingdom.
Having heard this, Kaṭṭhavāhana also came along the opposite road and, honoring it in the same manner, had it enter the city.
Then, having assembled his ministers and the citizens, he removed the wrapping cloth in the royal courtyard and opened the casket.
Having seen the casket within the chest, he gradually opened all the nested caskets;
then, seeing the inscription upon the golden plate, he became joyful, thinking, "After a hundred thousand aeons, my friend has sent me this most rare jewel of a gift.
Delighted, he thought, "Indeed, we have heard what was never heard before: 'A Buddha has arisen in the world! What if I were to go and [see] the Buddha?'"
Thinking, "I shall go forth and hear the Dhamma," he addressed his ministers: "It is said that the jewels of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha have appeared in the world;
what do you think should be done? They replied, "Your Majesty, you remain right here;
we shall go and find out the news."

Then sixteen ministers, accompanied by a retinue of sixteen thousand, paid homage to the king and departed, saying, "If a Buddha has appeared in the world and we cannot see him again, and if he has not appeared, we shall return.
But the king's nephew, having bowed to the king afterwards, said, "I too shall go. "My dear," [the king replied], "you must find out whether a Buddha has appeared there..."
"Come back again and inform me," he said. Having agreed, saying "Very well," he departed.
They all traveled, staying for only one night at every place, until they reached Bārāṇasī. But before they had even arrived, the Blessed One passed away into parinibbāna.
While wandering throughout the entire monastery, wondering "Who is the Buddha? Where is the Buddha?", they saw the personal disciples and questioned them.
They announced to them, "The Buddha has attained final Nibbāna. They lamented, "Alas! Having come from such a great distance, we did not even obtain the sight of him.
Then they asked, "Venerable sir, was there any instruction given by the Blessed One?
"Yes, lay followers, there was: one should be established in the three refuges, the five precepts should be undertaken, and [the eightfold path] endowed with eight factors..."
“The Uposatha day must be observed, alms must be given, and one must go forth into homelessness.
Having heard this, they all went forth, setting aside that nephew who was a minister. Taking the *paribhogadhātu* (relics of use), the nephew set out toward the kingdom of Kaṭṭhavāhana.
“Relics of use” refers to such things as leaves from the Bodhi tree, robes, and so forth; however, in this case, it was the Blessed One’s water-strainer (*dhammakaraṇa*).
Taking with him one elder who was a bearer of the Dhamma and a bearer of the Vinaya, he departed.
Traveling by stages, he reached the city and informed the king, "A Buddha has arisen in the world and has also attained final Nibbāna," and he related the instruction given by the Blessed One.
The king approached the elder, heard the Dhamma, and having caused a monastery to be built and a shrine to be established, [he brought] a Bodhi tree...

Having taken refuge in the Three Jewels and established himself in the five constant precepts, he observed the eightfold Uposatha, practiced giving and other virtues, and upon living out his full lifespan, was reborn in the world of the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
Those sixteen thousand as well went forth into homelessness; after their deaths as ordinary worldlings (puthujjana), they became the retinue of that very king.
Having spent one interval between Buddhas in the world of the gods, even before our Blessed One had appeared,
he passed away from that celestial realm and was born as the son of the family priest of King Pasenadi’s father, named Bāvarī.
Endowed with three marks of a Great Man and having mastered the three Vedas, he occupied the position of family priest upon his father’s death.
He stood there. The remaining sixteen thousand and more were also reborn right there in Sāvatthī in brahmin families.
Among them, sixteen—the senior pupils—learned their craft in the presence of Bāvari, while the other sixteen thousand did so in the presence of those very same teachers;
thus they all came together once again. King Mahākosala also passed away.
Then they consecrated Pasenadi in the kingdom. Bāvari became his chaplain as well.
The king gave Bāvari the wealth bestowed by his father as well as other riches; for in his youth, he had learned his craft from him alone.
Then Bāvari announced to the king: "I shall go forth, Great King. "Teacher, while you remain..."
“My father stands [in his place]; do not go forth,” he said. “Enough, Great King; I shall go forth,” he replied.
Unable to stop him, the king requested, “Go forth in the royal park, which is my place of audience, this very evening.
Having taken the ascetic’s going-forth together with sixteen thousand disciples, the teacher entered the royal park.
The king served his preceptor with the four requisites; he went to attend upon him both evening and morning.
Then one day, the students said to their teacher: "Living near a city is indeed a great hindrance.
Teacher, let us go to a secluded place where people do not frequent; living in a remote lodging is of great benefit to those who have gone forth."
The teacher accepted, saying, “Very well,” and informed the king.

The king, having tried to dissuade him three times and being unable to do so, gave two hundred thousand kahāpaṇas and commanded two ministers: “Wherever this group of seers wishes to dwell, there you must build a hermitage and provide it.
Then the teacher, surrounded by sixteen thousand and one hundred and sixty ascetics, [set out].
Being assisted by his ministers, he departed from the northern country toward the southern country.

Having requested, "Go and bring my maidservant," another brahmin arrived, having been sent.

Thinking, "This is such a state," they reached the conclusion that the Buddha was omniscient.

(1020) Therein, “the city of Magadha” (*māgadhaṃ puraṃ*) means Rājagaha, the city of Magadha; this is the intended meaning.
“The Pāsāṇaka Cetiya” was formerly a place of residence for deities atop a great rock; however, when the Blessed One appeared, it became a monastery (*vihāra*).
Thus, by that same former designation, it is called "the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya.
