"The head and the striking of the head. Then the Blessed One, explaining them to him, spoke this verse: "Ignorance is the head.
In that regard, because ignorance—which consists of non-knowing regarding the Four Truths—is the head of saṃsāra, therefore...

He said, “Ignorance is the head. And because the knowledge of the path to Arahatship— being endowed with faith, mindfulness, concentration, the desire for action, and energy that are co-nascent with itself—
overcomes that head by reaching the state of a single flavor and a single purpose among the faculties, he therefore said, “Knowledge is that which strikes down the head,” and so forth.
1034-8. Then, having heard this explanation of the question, he was stiffened by the great rapture that arose;
the meaning is that he attained a state of non-depression and an upliftedness of body and mind. Having fallen [prostrate], he spoke this verse: “Bāvarī.
Then the Blessed One, feeling compassion for him, spoke the verse beginning with “Sukhito. And having spoken thus to Bāvarī—
And thus he made the invitation of the Omniscient One. Therein, "of all" means of the sixteen thousand without exception.

"Therein the Tathāgata was questioned" means that at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, or there in the assembly, or when they had invited him, Ajita asked the first question. The rest is evident throughout all the verses.
The commentary on the introductory verses of the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* within the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*), is completed. 1.
Commentary on the *Ajitasutta*.
1039. Regarding that question, *nivuto* means "concealed. *Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsī* means "What do you say is the defilement of this world?
1040. *Vevicchā pamādā nappakāsatī* means "Because of stinginess and negligence, it does not shine forth.
For stinginess does not allow one's virtues such as generosity to manifest, and negligence [prevents] virtues such as moral discipline. *Jappābhilepanaṃ* means...
Craving (taṇhā) is like the monkey’s ointment; it is the smearing of a monkey upon this world. "Suffering" (dukkha) refers to the suffering consisting of birth and so forth. 1041.
"Streams flow everywhere" means that in all the sense-bases, such as forms and so on, the streams of craving and the like flow forth.
"What is the obstruction? asks what the hindrance or protection for them is. "Speak of restraint" (saṃvaraṃ brūhi) refers to that which is designated as their obstruction.
"Tell me of restraint. By this, he asks about abandonment with remainder.
"By what are these streams blocked?"—by what phenomenon are these streams blocked and cut off? By this, he asks about abandonment without remainder.
"Mindfulness is their warding off"—this refers to those engaged in insight (vipassanā), examining the courses of wholesome phenomena.
"When there is mindfulness, there is the warding off of those streams. "I call it the restraint of the streams"—the intention here is that I call that very mindfulness the restraint of the streams.
"By wisdom they are shut off"—by means of the path-wisdom which accomplishes the penetration of impermanence and so forth regarding forms and other objects, these streams are completely shut off.
1043. Regarding the verse of the question, "And wisdom," the summary meaning should be understood as follows:
"Where do all these cease—the wisdom mentioned by you, the mindfulness, and that remaining name-and-form? Being asked this question of mine, please explain.
1044. However, in the verse of the answer, since wisdom and mindfulness are included under the very names [of those categories], therefore...
These have not been stated separately. This is the summary of the meaning here:
Ajita, when you asked me this question, "Where does this [consciousness] cease?", I am telling you that where name-and-form cease without remainder, there I say it ceases;
for with the cessation of each respective consciousness, this [consciousness] ceases right here, neither before nor after.
It is obstructed. It ceases right here with the cessation of consciousness; through the cessation of consciousness, its cessation occurs. What is meant is that it does not transcend that.
At this point, the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) has been elucidated by the phrase "suffering is his great terror," as well as those...

By the phrase "the streams," the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) is indicated; by "they are closed off," the truth of the path (*maggasacca*); and by "it ceases without remainder," the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*).

Thus, although he had heard the four truths, because he had not yet attained the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*), he again asked about the practice of those in training and those beyond training, and uttered the verse beginning with "And those who have discerned the Dhamma. In that context, "those who have discerned the Dhamma" (*saṅkhātadhammā*) means...
"Phenomena examined by way of impermanence and so forth" is a designation for the Arahants.
"Those in training" refers to the remaining noble persons who are still practicing the training in virtue and the other perfections. "Many" means numerous beings and people.
"Tell me, being asked, their conduct, O wise one"—that is, being asked by me regarding those who are both in training and beyond training, you, being wise and learned, explain their practice.

1046. Now, because all defilements must indeed be abandoned by one in training (sekha), beginning with the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), the Blessed One shows the path of training through the half-verse beginning with "In sensual pleasures" (kāmesu). Its meaning is as follows:
regarding the basis, "in sensual pleasures," one should not covet them with the defilement of desire, while abandoning bodily misconduct and other factors that cause turbidity of the mind.

"By mind one should not be turbid. However, because the adept (*asekha*), having thoroughly examined all conditioned phenomena and so forth by way of impermanence and the rest, is skilled (*kusala*) regarding all things;

and because, being mindful through the foundations of mindfulness such as mindfulness of the body, he has attained the state of a monk (*bhikkhu*) due to the destruction of the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and other defilements, and thus wanders as a wanderer in all postures—it is for this reason that he is called "skilled" in the half-stanza.
He shows the way of practice for one beyond training (*asekhapaṭipadā*). The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One brought the teaching to its conclusion with the pinnacle of arahantship;
at the conclusion of the teaching, Ajita was established in arahantship together with his thousand disciples, and the eye of Dhamma arose in many thousands of others as well.
Simultaneously with the Venerable Ajita’s attainment of arahantship, the deerskins, matted hair, bark garments, and so forth of himself and his thousand disciples vanished.
All of them, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power and with hair two finger-breadths long, became "Come, monk" bhikkhus;
they sat down with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to the Blessed One.
The commentary on the Ajita-sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is completed. 2.
The commentary on the Tissa-metteyya-sutta.
1047. *Kodhasantussito* refers to the *Tissametteyyasutta*. What is its origin? The origin of all suttas is indeed dependent upon a question.
For those brahmins, having been invited by the Blessed One with the words, "Being granted the opportunity, ask whatever you wish," each asked about his own doubt.
And as each was questioned, the Blessed One gave them an explanation. Thus, these [suttas] are likewise dependent upon questions.
These should be understood as discourses (*suttāni*).
However, when the Ajita-question was concluded with the words, "How observing the world does the King of Death not see him?", Mogharāja began to ask this question.
Knowing that "his faculties have not yet reached full maturity," the Blessed One—
“Stay, Mogharāja; let another ask,” he replied, declining. Then Tissa Metteyya, asking about his own doubt, spoke the verse beginning with “From anger.
In that context, *kodha santussito* means: who here is satisfied? *Iñjitā* refers to the fluctuations of craving and views.
*Ubhantaṃ abhiññāya* means having directly known both extremes. *Mantā na lippati* means he is not smeared by wisdom.

1048–9. Explaining this meaning, the Blessed One spoke the two verses beginning with “kāmesu. Therein, “brahmacariyavā in regard to sensual pleasures” means one who leads the holy life for the sake of sensual pleasures;
what is intended is that, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, he is endowed with the holy life of the Path.
By this much, he shows contentment; by the words “free from craving” and so forth, he shows imperturbability.

In this context, "having understood, he is extinguished" means that having investigated phenomena by way of their impermanence and so forth, he is extinguished through the extinction of lust and the other defilements.
The remainder is self-evident, as it follows the method already explained in various places.
Thus, the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating specifically in Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, this brahmin as well—
He established himself in Arahatship together with a thousand pupils, and the Dhamma-eye arose in many thousands of others.
The rest is exactly as before.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Tissa-metteyya Sutta of the Suttanipāta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Puṇṇaka Sutta (1050):
"Unshaken" is the Puṇṇaka Sutta. This too was spoken after first rejecting Mogharāja in the same manner as before.

In that context, "one who sees the root" means one who sees the unwholesome roots and so forth. "Sages" (isayo) refers to those with matted hair named *isi*. "Sacrifice" (*yañña*) refers to the object to be given.
"They prepared" (*akappayiṃsu*) means they sought after it.
"Hoping" (*āsīsamānā*) means longing for form and so forth. "This state" (*itthattaṃ*) means longing for this very condition of existence.

The meaning is that they desired the state of being human and so forth. "Seated upon old age" means dependent on old age. And here, by way of old age, all the suffering of the round (*saṃsāra*) is expressed.
By this, it is shown that being dependent on the suffering of the round and not being liberated from it, they performed [their sacrifices]. 1052. Regarding the passage:
"O Blessed One, were those who were heedful in the path of sacrifice able to cross over birth and old age, O Venerable Sir?"—here...
"The path of sacrifice is indeed the sacrifice itself. This is what is meant: "I hope that by being diligent in the sacrifice and performing it, you have transcended the suffering of saṃsāra.
(1053) "They pray" means they long for the acquisition of form and so forth. "They praise" means [they say] "well-sacrificed, well-given," and so on.
They praise sacrifices and so forth according to their own method. "They long for" means they utter speech for the sake of obtaining forms and other such objects.

"They offer oblations" means they give. "They long for sensual pleasures based on gain" means that, depending on the acquisition of forms and other objects, they repeatedly long for sensual pleasures themselves, saying, "O, may these be ours," and thus they increase craving therein.
This has been said. "Devoted to sacrifice" means those who are intent upon sacrifice. "Stained by the lust for existence":

thus, being stained by the very lust for existence through these [desires] such as longings, or having become stained by the lust for existence while performing these longings and so forth, they did not cross over; they did not transcend the suffering of the cycle of birth and so on.
1054–5. "Then who else? means: then now, who else has crossed over? "Having reflected" means: having investigated with knowledge.
"Far and near" means both distant and close; that is to say, the bodies of others and one's own body, and so forth, are both distant and close.
"Smokeless" means free from the smoke of bodily misconduct and the like. "Untroubled" means free from the troubles of passion and the like.
"He has crossed over" means that such an Arahant has crossed over birth and old age. The rest here is self-evident.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating specifically in Arhatship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, this brahmin also established himself in Arhatship together with his thousand disciples, and the Dhamma-eye arose in many hundreds of others.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Puṇṇaka-sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Paramatthajotikā, is completed. 4.
Commentary on the Mettagū-sutta.

1056. "I ask you" refers to the Mettagu Sutta. Therein, "I consider you a master of knowledge (vedagu) and one who has developed the self (bhāvitatta)" means: "I consider you thus—a master of knowledge and one who has developed the self.
1057. "You do not ask": here, *a-* is a particle used merely for filling the meter; the meaning is simply "you ask. "I shall declare how they understand" means:
I shall explain in the same way that one who understands explains. "They originate with acquisition (upadhi) as their source."
"From suffering": from the substrate (upadhi) rooted in craving and so forth, the various sufferings such as birth and the rest arise.
Thus, regarding the sufferings that arise from the substrate as their cause, there is the verse beginning with "He who indeed is unwise.

Therein, "one who understands" means one who knows the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) by way of their impermanence and so forth. "One who contemplates the origin of suffering" refers to the cause of birth for the suffering of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭadukkha).
“Contemplating ‘the acquisitions’ (*upadhī*): [means] contemplating them as such. 1059.

“And grief and lamentation” (*sokapariddavañca*) means both sorrow (*soka*) and lamentation (*parideva*). For it is said, “this Dhamma is known by you”: just as beings know it, so too is this Dhamma known by way of its manifestation.
1060–61. “I shall proclaim the Dhamma to you”: the Dhamma of Nibbāna and the Dhamma of the practice leading to Nibbāna.
I shall teach those to you. "In this very life" (*diṭṭhe dhamme*) means in the phenomena such as suffering that are seen, or in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Not based on hearsay" (*anītiham*) means directly perceived by oneself. "Having understood which" (*yaṃ viditvā*) means having understood that phenomenon by way of such methods as "all conditioned things are impermanent.
"And that I rejoice in" (*tañcāhaṃ abhinandāmi*) refers to that teaching of yours which illuminates the aforementioned nature of phenomena.
"I long for that word; and I rejoice in that supreme Dhamma.
(1062) "Above, below, across, and in between": here, "above" refers to the future time, "below" to the past time, and "across and in between" to the present time.
Having dispelled both delight and attachment toward these...
Regarding "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) among these—namely, craving, the settling of views, and the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*)—drive them away;
having driven them away, do not abide in existence (*bhava*). This being so, one would not abide in either of the two kinds of existence.

Thus, first, is the connection of the word *panudja* in this interpretation of the meaning as "drive away" (*panudehi*); however, in the case of "having driven away" (*panuditvā*), [the connection is as follows:]...

The connection is simply this: "it does not persist in existence" (*bhave na tiṭṭhati*). What is meant is that, having dispelled these consciousnesses which are the abodes of delight (*nandinivesana-viññāṇa*), it would not persist in either of the two kinds of existence (*bhava*).
1063–4. Having dispelled these and not persisting in existence, he is described by the verse beginning "one who dwells thus" (*evaṃvihārī*). Therein, "right here" (*idheva*)...
"In this very teaching, in this very existence. Regarding the phrase "well-proclaimed by Gotama is that which is without substrate (*anūpadhika*)," here "without substrate" refers to *nibbāna*.
Addressing the Blessed One with reference to that, he said: "Well-proclaimed by Gotama is that which is without substrate.
(1065) "He abandoned not only suffering alone—those as well... is the verse. Therein, "firmly" (*aṭṭhitaṃ*) means with earnestness.
"Or always. "I shall pay homage to him"—therefore, I pay homage to him. "Having approached" means having gone near. "O Nāga"—he spoke thus addressing the Blessed One. 1066.

Now, although the Blessed One was already known by that brahmin as one who had "surely abandoned suffering," the Blessed One, without allowing himself to be drawn into that [identification], spoke to the person who had abandoned suffering as an instruction, saying: "That which, O brahmin..."
He spoke this verse. Its meaning is as follows: That which you would know by direct realization—namely, that "this one is a brahmin because he has warded off evil;

he is a master of knowledge (vedagu) because he has gone by means of the Vedas; he is a possessor of nothing (akiñcana) due to the absence of any belongings; and he is unattached to sense pleasures and states of existence because he is not clinging to them"—you should know him thus.
For certainly he has crossed this flood; he has reached the further shore, free from all harshness and doubt.

1067. Furthermore: "And what more?"—this refers to the verse beginning with *vidvā ca yo*. Therein, *idha* means in this teaching or in this personal existence (*attabhāva*). *Visajja* means having relinquished. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught even this sutta by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma exactly as described above.
[End of] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the Mettagū-sutta of the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
5. Commentary on the Dhota-sutta (Verses 1068–1069).
"I ask you" refers to the Dhota-sutta. Therein, "I desire speech" means I long for speech.

"One should train for one’s own Nibbāna" means that one should train in the higher morality and other practices for the sake of extinguishing one's own lust and other defilements. "From me" means from my own mouth.

(1070) When this was said, Dhota, being delighted, spoke the verse beginning with "I see," praising the Blessed One and requesting the resolution of his doubts. Therein, "I see in the world of gods and men" means: I see.
"In the world of gods and humans. "I shall revere him"—that is, I shall revere such a one as him. "Release"—that is, cause [me] to be released.
Then the Blessed One, showing that the resolution of doubt is indeed dependent upon oneself by way of crossing the flood, spoke the verse beginning with "I am not.
Therein, "I will not endure" means I will not endure, I will not be able; I—

"I shall strive"—this is what is meant. "For the sake of liberation" means for the purpose of being liberated. "Doubt" (*kathaṃkathi*) means having uncertainty. "Cross over" (*taresī*) means you should cross over.
When this was said, Dhota, being even more uplifted in mind, spoke the verse beginning with "Instruct me, O Brahmā," while praising the Blessed One and requesting his instruction.
In that context, "Brahmā" is a term for the supreme; by it, he addresses the Blessed One.
Addressing him, he said: "Instruct me, O Brahmā. "The dhamma of seclusion" means the dhamma of Nibbāna, which is the seclusion from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
"Without falling into affliction" means without undergoing various forms of distress. "Tranquil right here" means being composed right here. "Unattached" means independent.
The two verses following this are exactly as they were recited in the *Mettagu Sutta*; for there it says simply "the Dhamma."
"Peace here"—this is the distinction. In the third verse as well, the first half is according to the method already stated;
in the second half, "saṅga" means a place of attachment, that is to say, clinging. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating specifically in Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma just as previously described.
The commentary on the Dhātusutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Paramatthajotikā, is completed. 6.
The commentary on the Upasīvasutta.
1076. “I am alone,” refers to the Upasīva Sutta. Therein, “the great flood” means a great flood.
“Independent” means not dependent upon either a person or a phenomenon. “I am not able” means I am not capable.
“An object” means a support. “Dependent upon which” means dependent upon which person or phenomenon.

1077. Now, because that brahmin was an attainer of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) yet did not know its peaceful support (*nissaya*), the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with “Nothingness” (*ākiñcañña*), showing him both that support and the further path of deliverance (*niyyānapatha*).
Therein, “beholding” (*pekkhamāno*) means having mindfully entered and emerged from that attainment of the base of nothingness.
"Seeing by way of impermanence and so forth. "Relying on 'there is nothing'" means taking as an object that attainment which occurs with the thought, "There is nothing whatsoever.
"Cross the flood" means: from that point onward, cross over the fourfold flood by means of insight (vipassanā) as it arises accordingly.
"With doubts" means with hesitations (vicikicchā). "Behold the destruction of craving at nightfall" means: look upon the total exhaustion of craving.
"Day and night, having made Nibbāna manifest, look! By this, he describes his dwelling in happiness in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).

Now, having heard "having abandoned sensual pleasures," and perceiving that he himself has abandoned sensual pleasures by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), he recited the verse beginning with "in all.
Therein, "having left behind," they imagine [something else] other than that; [it refers to] the sixfold attainment (*samāpatti*) below that.

"Having abandoned. "He goes to the supreme among the liberations through perception": he goes to the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), which is the highest among the seven liberations through perception.
"Would he remain there, not following after?"—the questioner asks whether that person would remain there in the Brahma-world of the base of nothingness without passing away.
Then the Blessed One, acknowledging that his stay would last for only sixty thousand eons, spoke the third verse.
1080. Having thus heard of his standing there, [the Buddha], now asking about his state of eternalism or annihilationism, spoke the verse beginning with "tiṭṭhe ce.
Therein, "pūgam pi vassānaṃ" means many, countless years; the sense is a multitude or heap.
There is also the reading "pūgam pi vassāni," wherein, by a change of case-ending, the genitive case becomes the nominative case.
The meaning should be stated as "many things to be done" (*pūga* means many for this). Alternatively, they also read "groups" (*pūgāni*), but the former reading alone is entirely superior.

"Right there he would become cool" (*tattheva so sīti siyā*): the intention is that this person, right there in the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), being liberated from various sufferings, would attain a state of coolness; having reached Nibbāna, he would remain eternal.
"Does he conceive of consciousness as being such-and-such?"—this asks whether one who is of such a kind would attain final nibbāna without clinging;
"or does his consciousness [persist]?"—this asks whether there might even be rebirth-linking for him.
Then the Blessed One, without falling into either annihilationism or eternalism, spoke regarding the noble disciple who has arisen therein:
Demonstrating parinibbāna without clinging, he spoke the verse beginning with “Just as a flame. Therein, “goes to its end” means it reaches its cessation.
“Does not enter into reckoning” means it does not enter into conventional designation such as “it has gone to such-and-such a direction.
“Thus the sage is liberated from the name-body”: thus, the sage in training who has arisen there is by nature already liberated from the form-body even before that.
Having attained liberation there by producing the fourth path, and because the Dhamma-body has been fully understood,
he is liberated even from the mental body; being one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) with taints destroyed, he goes to the goal known as final Nibbāna without clinging,
and no longer enters into such reckoning as "a khattiya" or "a brahmin," and so forth.
1082. Now, having heard the words "he has passed away," and not correctly discerning their meaning, he recited the verse beginning with "Has he set?
Its meaning is as follows: "Has he truly set, or does he not exist;
or rather, by virtue of eternity, is he healthy and of an unchanging nature? Thus, O Sage, please explain this clearly to me. For what reason? Because—
"For this Dhamma is known to you.
(1083) Then the Blessed One, demonstrating that he could not be described in such a way, spoke the verse beginning with "Of him who has gone to rest.

Therein, "of him who has gone to rest" means of one who has attained final nibbāna through non-clinging. "There is no measure" means there is no measure of form and so forth by which [he might be defined]. By what...
"One would call him by that" means one would speak of him by means of that passion (rāga) and so forth. "In all phenomena" means in all phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha) and others.
The rest is clear everywhere.

Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta precisely with the pinnacle of Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) exactly as previously described.
The commentary on the Upasīva Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is completed. 7.
Commentary on the Nanda Sutta.
1084–5. *Santi loke* is the *Nandasutta*. Therein, the meaning of the first verse is as follows:
regarding the people in the world—kṣatriyas and so forth—the [opponents] say, "There are sages (*munis*)," referring to the Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, and others.

To this they ask, "How so? Do they call such a person a sage endowed with knowledge because he has arisen through knowledge such as the knowledge of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-ñāṇa*)? Such a one...
Now they ask: "Do they speak thus, or rather, do they arise with a life characterized by various kinds of coarse existence?
The Blessed One, rejecting both of these, spoke the verse beginning with "Not by view" (*na diṭṭhiyā*) to show who a sage (*muni*) is.
Now, in order to remove doubt regarding the doctrine of those who say that purity comes "by view and so forth," he speaks the verse beginning with "Whosoever these... (*ye kecime*).
He asks. Therein, "in various ways" means by means of such things as curiosity and auspicious rites.
Therein, "living restrained" means dwelling protected by their own respective views. Then, demonstrating to him the absence of purity in that way, the Blessed One spoke the second verse (1088–90).
Having thus heard that "they did not cross over," he now asks, "Whosoever these may be," desiring to hear about those who have crossed over.
Then the Blessed One spoke the third verse, showing that by means of one who has crossed the flood, those who have crossed over birth and old age are likewise shown.
Therein, *nivutā* means covered, enveloped, or shrouded. *Yesīdha* means "among whom here. And here, *su-* is merely a particle.

*Taṇhaṃ pariññāya* means having fully understood craving through the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*). The rest is clear everywhere because it follows the method already explained previously.

Thus the Blessed One brought the teaching to its conclusion precisely at the pinnacle of arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, Nanda, rejoicing in the words of the Blessed One, recited the verse:
“I rejoice in this. And here too, as previously mentioned, there was a realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya).
The commentary on the Nanda Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Paramatthajotikā, is completed. 8.
Commentary on the Hemaka Sutta.
1091–4. *Ye me pubbe* is the Hemaka Sutta. Therein, *ye me pubbe viyākaṃsu* means those such as Bāvari and others who previously explained their own views to me.
*Huraṃ Gotamasāsanā* means prior to the teaching of Gotama.
*Sabbaṃ taṃ takkavaḍḍhanaṃ* means all that is an increase of discursive thoughts such as sensual desire. *Taṇhānigghātanaṃ* means the destruction of craving.
It is the destruction of craving. Then the Blessed One, explaining that Dhamma to him, spoke these two verses beginning with “Herein.

Therein, “those who, having known this, are mindful”—this refers to those who, by way of such methods as “all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” have gradually come to know the deathless state of Nibbāna, being mindful through the foundations of mindfulness such as the contemplation of the body. “Completely extinguished in this very life” (diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā)—

Because they have known the Dhamma, because they have seen the Dhamma, and because they are completely extinguished through the extinction of lust and the other defilements. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta with the pinnacle of Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as before.
From the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Hemaka Sutta in the Suttanipāta-ṭṭhakathā is finished.
9. Commentary on the Todeyya Sutta:
1095. "In whom [are] desires... This is the Todeyya Sutta. Therein, as for the question "What is his liberation like?", it refers to what kind of liberation he possesses.
"He should be desired" is what he asks. Now, showing that there is no other liberation for him, the Blessed One spoke the second verse.
Therein, "there is no other liberation for him" means that for him there is no liberation other than this.
Thus, although it has been stated that "the destruction of craving alone is liberation," one who does not perceive that meaning [might think], "one who is without hope..."
"Does he [live] with a thirst for existence?"—thus he asks again. Therein, "does he fashion through wisdom" means:

does he, by means of knowledge such as the knowledge of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-ñāṇa*), fashion a fabrication of craving (*taṇhā-kappa*) or a fabrication of views (*diṭṭhi-kappa*)? Then the Blessed One, explaining that to him, spoke the second verse.
Therein, "in sensual pleasure and in existence" means: in both sensual pleasures (*kāma*) and in existence (*bhava*). The rest is clear in every respect.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta also by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma just as before.
Thus ends the commentary on the Todeyya Sutta in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Paramatthajotikā* commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*).
10. Commentary on the Kappa Sutta 1099.
“In the midst of the stream” refers to the Kappa Sutta. Therein, “in the midst of the stream” means in the midst of *saṃsāra*, because there is no discernment of a prior or subsequent limit.
“While it stands” means while it is standing. “As this, and not another” [is the end].
"May it be" means: "May this suffering not arise again.
(1101–2) Then the Blessed One, explaining that matter to him, recited three verses. Therein, "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*) is the opposite of possession (*kiñcana*).
"Without grasping" (*anādāna*) is the opposite of grasping (*ādāna*); what is meant is the subsiding of both possession and grasping.
"Anāparanta" means without a further limit, being devoid of any counterpart; "supreme" is what is meant.
"They are not followers of Māra" means they are not those who walk in Māra’s path, his attendants, or his disciples. The rest is clear everywhere.

Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating specifically in Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma identical to that of the previous occasion.
The commentary on the Kappa-sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Paramatthajotikā, is completed. 11.
The commentary on the Jatukaṇṇi-sutta.
1103–4. Having heard the *Jatukaṇṇi-sutta*. Therein, “Having heard that the Hero is one who does not desire desires”:

having heard of the Buddha, the Hero, who does not desire desires because he has no longing for sensual pleasures, according to the method beginning with “Thus indeed is the Blessed One”; “I have come desiring the Desireless”:
I have come to question the Blessed One, who is free from desire (*nikkāma*). “Born together with the eye”: born together with the eye of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
"Just as it is, so it is. When [the Blessed One] said this, [Sela], requesting again, said: "Tell me. For even if one were to ask a thousand times, one would speak;
how much more so twice? "Possessing splendor, by splendor"—meaning endowed with splendor, having overcome [others] by splendor.
"That Dhamma which I might know here as the complete abandoning of birth and aging"—meaning that Dhamma which is the state of the abandonment of birth and aging, may I know it right here.
1105–7. Then the Blessed One, explaining that Dhamma to him, spoke three verses.
Therein, "having seen renunciation as security" means having perceived both Nibbāna and the path leading to Nibbāna as "security.
"Grasped" means grasped by way of craving and views. "Or rejected" means it should be cast off; that is to say, it should be released.
"May it not exist for you" means: may it not be yours. "Possession" (kiñcana) refers to the possession of passion and so forth; may that also not exist for you.
"Past" refers to the defilements arisen with reference to past formations. "O Brahmin," the Blessed One addresses Jaṭukaṇṇī.
The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta also by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma just as before.
Thus ends the commentary on the Jatukaṇṇi Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā.
12. The Commentary on the Bhadrāvudha Sutta (1108–9).
"Leaving the dwelling-place" (*okañjaham*) means leaving behind attachment (*ālaya*). "Severing craving" (*taṇhacchidam*) means severing the body of craving.
"Unshakable" (*anejam*) means unswayed by the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*). "Leaving behind delight" (*nandiñjaham*) means leaving behind the longing for future forms and so forth.
For craving is indeed one alone, though it is described here in various ways by way of praise. "Kappañjahaṃ" means abandoning the two kinds of *kappa*.

"Abhiyāce" means I entreat most earnestly. "Sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito" means that having heard the Blessed One’s words, O Naga, many people will depart from here—from this Pāsāṇaka Cetiya; such is the intended meaning. From the provinces...
“Gathered” (*saṅgatā*) means assembled here from various regions such as Aṅga and so forth. “Explain” (*viyākarohi*) means teach the Dhamma.
Then, teaching the Dhamma in accordance with his disposition, the Blessed One spoke two verses.

Therein, “craving for grasping” (*ādānataṇhā*) refers to the craving for seizing and taking up forms and so forth; it is what is called “craving as clinging” (*taṇhūpādāna*). For whatever one grasps in the world...
Among these various types of grasping, such as restlessness and so forth, whatever they grasp, by that very means Māra follows the person;
that is, by way of the production of kamma-formations conditioned by clinging, the Māra of the rebirth-linking aggregates follows that being.
Therefore, they understand; that is, one who knows formations through their impermanence and other characteristics understands this danger regarding the being of grasping.

Thus beholding: seeing this generation clinging within the realm of death; that is, seeing this generation clinging to the objects of grasping—form and so forth—in the sense of being taken up, and seeing it stuck in the entire world within the realm of death.

Or alternatively, seeing this generation clinging to persons who are themselves attached to grasping, and because of that attachment to grasping, seeing this generation stuck in the realm of death and unable to transcend it.
"Thus, seeing this, one should not produce anything whatsoever in the entire world"—the remainder is clear everywhere.
In this way, the Blessed One taught even this sutta with the pinnacle of Arahantship itself. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as before.
[End of] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the Bhadrāvudha-sutta of the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
13. Commentary on the Udaya-sutta 1112–3.
"They meditate" refers to the Udaya-sutta. Therein, "liberation through final knowledge" (*aññāvimokkha*) means liberation that has been thoroughly contemplated through the power of wisdom (*paññā*).

He asks. Then the Blessed One, because Udaya was an attainer of the fourth jhāna, spoke two verses to show him the liberation through higher knowledge (*aññāvimokkha*) in its various aspects by way of the jhāna he had attained. Therein, regarding "the abandoning of sensual desire":
that which is the abandoning of sensual desire for one producing the first jhāna—that too I call liberation through higher knowledge.
In this way, all the phrases are to be construed.
"Purified by equanimity and mindfulness" means purified by the equanimity and mindfulness of the fourth jhāna.

"Preceded by the reasoning on phenomena" refers to the liberation of Arahatship attained by one who, having stood in that liberation of the fourth jhāna, has practiced insight (vipassanā) upon the factors of that jhāna.

He says this because, for the liberation of arahantship, the analytical reflection on the Dhamma (*dhammatakkapurejava*)—consisting of right intention and other factors associated with the path—is a precursor.
Therefore he says: "preceded by analytical reflection on the Dhamma. Regarding the phrase "the breaking up of ignorance":

we call this very same liberation through final knowledge "the breaking up of ignorance" by way of figurative designation, because it arises depending upon Nibbāna, which is itself termed the "breaking up of ignorance."
1115–6. Having heard that Nibbāna described by the statement on the breaking up of ignorance, he asks, "By the abandoning of what is it said to be?
and thus utters the verse beginning with "What is its fetter? (*Kiṃsu saṃyojano*). Therein, "What is its fetter?

(*Kiṃsu saṃyojano*) means "What is its fetter? (*Kiṃ saṃyojano*). "Investigation" (*vicāraṇaṃ*) means the cause for wandering. "By the abandoning of what" (*kissassa vippahānena*) means "by the abandoning of what named thing."
“By the complete relinquishing of the Dhamma. Then the Blessed One, explaining that matter to him, recited the verse beginning with “Bound by delight.
Therein, “of thought” (*vitakkassa*) means that his thought consists of sensual thoughts and so forth.
Now, asking about the path to that Nibbāna, he recited the verse beginning with “How for one who is mindful” (*kathaṃ satassā*). Therein—

"Consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) refers here to formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*). Then, while explaining the path to him, the Blessed One spoke this verse beginning with "Internally" (*ajjhattañca*).
Therein, "being thus mindful" (*evaṃ satassa*) means being thus mindful and clearly comprehending (*sampajāna*). The rest is clear everywhere.
In this way, the Blessed One taught even this discourse culminating in Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as before.
The commentary on the Udaya Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā, known as the *Paramatthajotikā*, is completed. 14.
Commentary on the Posāla Sutta.

1119–20. *Yo atītan* refers to the *Posāla-sutta*. In that context, "he who points out the past" means the Blessed One who points out for himself and for others the various types of the past, such as "even one birth," and so forth. "One whose perception of form has become clear" (*vibhūtarūpasaññissa*) means one who has transcended the perception of form.

"One who abandons the entire body" (*sabbakāyappahāyino*) means one who abandons the entire aggregate of form by way of its specific abandonment (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*), and thus one for whom rebirth-linking into the existence of form has been abandoned.
The intention [is as follows]: "One who sees that 'there is nothing at all'" means one who sees "there is nothing at all" through insight into the absence of consciousness;
it refers to one who has attained the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). "I ask about the knowledge of Sakka":
addressing the Blessed One as "Sakka," he says, "I ask about the knowledge of that person; what kind of knowledge is to be asked about? "How is he to be led? [ends the passage].
"How is he to be led? How is higher knowledge to be produced in him?
Then the Blessed One, having manifested his own unimpeded knowledge regarding such a person, spoke two verses to explain that knowledge.
Therein, "The Tathāgata, fully knowing all stations of consciousness" refers to [his knowledge] by way of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
"There are seven [beings] by way of rebirth-linking"—thus the Tathāgata directly knows all the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

"He knows one who is staying" means he knows this person who is staying by way of the formative forces of karma (*kamma-abhisaṅkhāra*), [knowing]: "In the future, this one will have such a destination.
"Liberated" means intent upon the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) and so forth. "Having that as one's resort" means being composed of that.
“Having known the origin of nothingness” means having known the formative volitional activity (kamma-abhisaṅkhāra) that produces the base of nothingness, thinking, “How is this an impediment?
“Delight is a fetter” means having known that whatever delight there is therein—consisting of attachment to the formless—that too is a fetter.
“Then one sees with insight therein” means having emerged from that attainment of the base of nothingness.

One contemplates that attainment by way of its impermanence and so forth. "This knowledge is true for him" means that this knowledge of Arahantship, which arises in due sequence for that person who is thus practicing insight, is unerring. "Vusīmato" means for one who has lived the holy life.
The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta also by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma just as before.
Thus ends the commentary on the Posāla Sutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
15. Commentary on the Mogharāja Sutta 1123.
"Twice I asked" refers to the Mogharāja Sutta. Therein, "twice" means two times.
For he previously asked the Blessed One twice at the conclusion of both the Ajita Sutta and the Tissa Metteyya Sutta.
But the Blessed One, waiting for the ripening of his faculties, did not explain it to him. Therefore he said: "Twice, Sakka, I asked.

And as for the words, "Up to three times, O Goddess, he explained; so have I heard": this means that when questioned up to three times on a matter consistent with the Dhamma, the Blessed One—the Seer who has become a pure deity, the Perfectly Enlightened One—explained it; thus have I heard. [This occurred] right there on the banks of the Godhāvarī River.
It seems he heard it thus. Therefore he said: “I have heard him declare.
(1124) “This world” refers to the human world. “The other world” refers to everything remaining after setting that aside.

“Together with the devas” refers to everything remaining after setting aside the Brahma-world, including both the devas by birth and those recognized as devas; or else, this phrase “the Brahma-world together with the devas” [is used].
The phrase beginning with “in the world” (*loke*) is merely an illustration of the method; by this, the entire world described in such a manner should be understood.

1125. “Thus, one who has seen the excellent” (*abhikkantadassāvī*): thus, he shows [the Buddha] as one who sees the supreme, capable of perceiving the underlying intentions, inclinations, destinies, final goals, and so forth, of the world including its devas.

1126. “Behold the world as empty” (*suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu*): either by way of observing what proceeds according to its determined course, or by way of contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as void.
"See the world as empty for two reasons; uproot the view of self"—that is, having eradicated the personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating precisely in *arahantship*. And at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma exactly as described above.
The commentary on the Mogharāja Sutta within the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā is completed. 16.
The commentary on the Piṅgiya Sutta.
1127. *Jiṇṇohamasmi* (I am old), the Piṅgiya Sutta. Regarding that:
"I am old, weak, and my complexion is faded"—it is said that this brahmin was overcome by old age and one hundred and twenty years of birth;
he was weak such that when he thought, "I will place my foot here," he placed it elsewhere, and his former skin-color had perished. Therefore he said: "I am old, weak, and my complexion is faded."
"May I not perish, bewildered, along the way"— may I not, having failed to realize your Dhamma, perish midway through ignorance.
"The complete abandoning of birth and aging right here"— right here at your feet, O Pāṣāṇaka Cetiya,
explain to me that Dhamma of Nibbāna which I might come to know as the complete abandoning of birth and aging.

1128. Now, because Piṅgiya spoke the verse beginning with “I am old” due to his concern for the body, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with “Having seen those afflicted among forms” in order to bring about the abandonment of attachment to the body.

In this context, “among forms” (*rūpesu*) means on account of form, with form as the condition. “Afflicted” (*vihaññamāne*) means being tormented by such things as karmic retribution and legal punishments. “They suffer among forms” (*ruppanti rūpesu*).
And by means of eye diseases and so forth, people are afflicted and oppressed solely because of form (rūpa).
Having heard the practice described by the Blessed One thus, up to the stage of Arahatship, Piṅgiya—
failing to attain any distinction due to his weakness from old age— again praised the Blessed One with this verse beginning "The four quarters," and [delivered] the teaching.
He requested [instruction]. Then the Blessed One, showing him the path of practice leading up to Arhatship, spoke the verse beginning with "Taṇhādhipanne.
The rest is clear everywhere.
This sutta, too, the Blessed One taught culminating specifically in Arhatship. And at the conclusion of the teaching, Piṅgiya [attained] the fruit of Non-returning.
He established himself there. It is said that from time to time he thought:
"My uncle Bāvari does not obtain such a teaching of diverse eloquence for me to hear. Because of that distraction caused by affection, he was unable to attain Arahatship.
However, his thousand disciples, the jaṭilas, all attained Arahatship, and they all wore robes and bowls produced through supernormal power (iddhimaya).
"Come, bhikkhu, be one.
The commentary on the Piṅgiya Sutta, within the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*,
the *Paramatthajotikā* Khuddaka Commentary, is finished.
Commentary on the Verses of Praise for the *Pārāyana*:
Following this, the compilers of the collection, extolling the teaching, said: "This the Blessed One spoke," and so forth. Therein, "this he spoke" means he spoke this *Pārāyana*.
"Of the sixteen attendants" refers to [the disciples] together with Piṅgiya, who was an attendant of Bāvari.
"Of the sixteen attendants of the Buddha, the Blessed One"—that is, "of the sixteen attendants.

And they were brahmins. Therein, the sixteen assemblies sat six yojanas in front, six behind, six on the left side, and six on the right side; thus, in a straight line, they extended for twelve yojanas. "Requested" means...
"Knowing the purpose for which they requested [it]" means knowing the meaning of the text (*pāḷi*).
"Knowing the Dhamma" means knowing the text. Having thus assigned this designation to this discourse on the Dhamma, they spoke, praising the names of those brahmins:
"Ajita, Tissa Metteyya... [and so forth]... approached the Best of Buddhas."
1131–7. In this context, "endowed with conduct" (*sampannacaraṇa*) means endowed with the virtue of the Pātimokkha and so forth, which serves as the foundation for the state of Nibbāna.

"Sage" (*isi*) refers to a great seer (*mahesi*). The rest is self-evident. Following that, "they practiced the holy life" (*brahmacariyam acariṃsu*) means they practiced the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*).
Therefore, it is called "the Way to the Beyond" (*pārāyana*); that is to say, it is the way (*ayana*) to that which is the beyond (*pāra*), namely Nibbāna.
Commentary on the Verses of the Pārāyanānugīti 1138.

This is the connection for those who will sing the Pārāyana in accordance with it: when the Pārāyana was taught by the Blessed One, sixteen thousand matted-hair ascetics attained arahantship, and there was a realization of the Dhamma for the remaining fourteen crores of gods and humans.
It happened thus. For this was said by the ancients:
“Then, at the delightful Pāsāṇaka, in the assembly of the Pārāyana, the Buddha brought fourteen koṭis of beings to the Deathless.”
When the teaching of the Dhamma was concluded, the people who had come from here and there reappeared in their own respective villages, towns, and so forth, through the power of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One also returned to Sāvatthī, surrounded by many thousands of bhikkhus, including sixteen personal attendants. There, Piṅgiya paid homage to the Blessed One and said: "I am going..."
“Venerable sir, please announce the appearance of the Buddha to Bāvari; for I have given him my word.
Then, having been granted permission by the Blessed One, he went to the banks of the Godhāvarī by means of his psychic power (*ñāṇagamana*) alone, and proceeded on foot toward the hermitage.
As the brahmin Bāvari sat watching the road, he saw from afar [the sage] free from matted hair and carrying a water-pot, appearing in the guise of a monk (*bhikkhu*).
Seeing him approaching, he reached the conclusion: "A Buddha has arisen in the world. When he had arrived, Bāvarī asked him:
"Is it true, Piṅgiya, that a Buddha has arisen in the world? "Yes, brahmin, he has arisen;
he is sitting at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya teaching us the Dhamma, and I shall teach it to you. Thereupon, Bāvarī, with great honor...
Having honored him along with his retinue, he prepared a seat. Sitting there, Piṅgiya said, "I shall sing in accordance with the Pārāyana," and so forth.
In this context, "I shall sing in accordance" (*anugāyissaṃ*) means I shall sing in accordance with what was sung by the Blessed One.

"Just as he saw" (*yathāddakkhi*) means just as he himself saw through the direct realization of truth (*saccābhisambodha*) and through his uncommon knowledge (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*). "Free from desire" (*nikkāmo*) means one who has abandoned desire. There is also a reading, "one who exerts effort" (*nikkamo*), meaning one who possesses energy (*vīriyavā*).
The purpose has emerged from the side of the unwholesome. "Nirvana" means being devoid of the forest of defilements, or indeed, being devoid of craving.
By the words "for what reason would he speak falsely? he shows that those defilements by which one might speak falsely have been abandoned by him.
By this, he generates enthusiasm in the brahmin for listening.
1139–41. *Vaṇṇūpasañhitaṃ* means endowed with qualities (*guṇūpasañhitaṃ*). *Saccavhayo* means one who is possessed of the name "Buddha," which is a designation used in accordance with truth.
*Brahme* is an address to that brahmin. *Kubbanakaṃ* means a small grove.
*Bahupphalaṃ kānanam āvaseyya* means one might come to dwell in a forest filled with various kinds of many fruits and so forth. *Appadassaṃ*... [text fragment]... means not visible.
"Bāvari and others" refers to those of limited wisdom. "The great ocean" refers to a vast mass of water such as Lake Anotatta and so forth.
(1142–4) "Those who were before" means those who existed previously. "The dispeller of darkness" means one who sits dispelling darkness.
"Of vast discernment" means one whose banner is knowledge. "Of vast intelligence" means one of expansive wisdom. "Visible here and now, timeless" means the fruit which is to be personally realized.
Nor is it a fruit to be attained at a later time. *Anītika* means free from the calamity of the defilements (*kilesa*). 1145–50.

Then Bāvarī spoke two verses beginning with “What indeed [is it] from that? Thereupon Piṅgiya, demonstrating that he was not separated even for a moment from the Blessed One, said “I am not from that,” and so forth. “I see him with my mind as with my eye”—that...
"I see the Buddha with my mind as if with my eye. "Worshipping, I pass the night" means that I spend the night while indeed worshipping him.
"In that very direction I am bowed" shows that in whichever direction the Buddha is, in that very direction I too am bowed—leaning toward him, inclined toward him.

1151. *Dubbalathāmakassa* means one who has little stamina; or alternatively, it refers to one who is weak and has a corrupted foundation (*dutthāmaka*), that is, one deficient in strength and energy.
"Therefore the body does not move" means that because of that very weakness and lack of stamina, the body does not go, or it does not go toward where the Buddha is.
There is also the reading *na pareti*, which has the same meaning. *Tattha* means "in that [regard]"—namely, regarding the Buddha.
"In the presence. "Intending" means by way of forming an intention. "Intent upon that" shows that he is joined to, devoted to, and dedicated to that which is the Buddha.
"Lying in the mire" means lying in the mud of sensual desire (*kāma*). "Islands leaping from island to island" refers to [seeking refuge] from one teacher after another.
"I went there. Then I saw the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having thus held such a wrong view, as I was wandering about, I then beheld the Buddha at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya.
At the conclusion of this verse, having understood the ripening of the faculties of both Piṅgiya and Bāvari—
While remaining right there in Sāvatthī, the Blessed One emitted a golden radiance. Piṅgiya, who was sitting and praising the Buddha’s qualities to Bāvari, saw that radiance and asked, "What is this?
Looking around, he saw the Blessed One as if standing right before him and announced to the brahmin Bāvari, "The Buddha has arrived! The brahmin rose from his seat and joined his palms in reverence.

Having taken hold [of the bowl], he stood there. The Blessed One, having emitted a radiance and revealed himself to the brahmin, and perceiving what was suitable for both of them, addressed Piṅgiya alone and spoke this verse beginning with "Just as it was with Vakkali.
Its meaning is as follows: just as the Elder Vakkali was devoted to faith, and through the predominance of faith attained Arahantship—
He attained it. Just as Bhadrāvudha was among the sixteen, and just as Āḷavī Gotama was, even so you too should release your faith.

Then, resolving through faith and undertaking insight meditation by way of the method beginning with "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent," you will go to the further shore of the realm of death, which is Nibbāna; thus, [the Buddha spoke] by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship.
He brought the teaching to its conclusion. At the conclusion of the teaching, Piṅgiya was established in Arahatship, while Bāvarī was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala).
Furthermore, five hundred disciples of the brahmin Bāvarī became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna). 1154–5.
Now, Piṅgiya, expressing his own faith, spoke the verse beginning with "This is even more... (*esa bhiyyo*). In that context, *paṭibhānavā* means...

He is endowed with the analytical knowledge of inspired ingenuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). "Having directly known the supreme gods" means having understood the qualities that make one a supreme god.
"The low and the sublime" means he knows all categories of phenomena that make oneself or another a supreme god; this is what is meant.
"Of those who acknowledge themselves as doubters" means of those who, while still being in doubt, claim, "We are free from doubt."
"Unshakable" means unshakeable by lust and the other defilements. "Imperturbable" means unagitated and subject to no change.
With these two terms, he speaks of Nibbāna. "I shall surely go" means that I will certainly go to that Nibbāna-element without residue.
"I have no doubt in this" means that I have no uncertainty regarding this Nibbāna. "Bear me thus as one whose mind is resolute."
Piṅgiya said, “In this very way, you too should release your faith.

Having generated faith within himself through this exhortation of the Blessed One, and having been liberated by means of that very faith as his primary vehicle, he spoke to the Blessed One, declaring his own devotion to faith:
“Thus, O one whose mind is resolute, remember me. This is the intended meaning here: “Just as you have spoken to me...”
"In this very way, you should remember Adhimutta.
Thus ends the commentary on the Soḷasabrāhmaṇasutta in the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, which is part of the Paramatthajotikā Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā.
The fifth chapter is concluded according to the method of explaining the meaning; by name, it is called the Pārāyana-vagga.
Concluding Statement.
And to this extent, that which was said—
“Having paid homage to the Three Jewels, the most worthy of veneration,
[this work] in the Khuddakanikāya, by one who has abandoned minor misconduct... — [is completed].
“Taught by the Lord of the World, who seeks to ferry the world across, we shall now provide a commentary on the meaning of that *Sutta Nipāta*.

Herein, the commentary on the meaning of the *Sutta Nipāta*—which comprises five sections beginning with the *Uraga-vagga*, and consists of seventy distinct discourses beginning with the *Uraga-sutta*—is hereby completed. Thus it is said:
“Whatever merit has been gained by me through composing this commentary on the meaning of the *Sutta Nipāta*,
out of a desire for the preservation of the True Dhamma— by the power of that merit,
may there quickly [be attainment] in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.”
"May this people attain growth, increase, and abundance.
(From the measure of the scriptures, there are forty-four recitation sections.
By [the one] adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy, and endowed with a multitude of virtues such as virtue, conduct, speed, and gentleness...

To the Great Poet, the foremost of debaters who spoke with propriety and eloquence; who was endowed with the analytical discernment of wisdom capable of penetrating and fathoming both his own tradition and the traditions of others;
who possessed unimpeded radiance of knowledge regarding the Teacher’s Dispensation—the Three Piṭakas with their commentaries—divided into various branches of study;

who was a great expounder whose sweet, noble, and graceful speech issued forth from the bliss produced by perfection of composition; and who was adorned with qualities such as the six supernormal powers and the analytical knowledges.

This is the commentary on the Sutta Nipāta, titled *Paramatthajotikā*, composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa— a name bestowed upon him by his teachers— who was an ornament to the lineage of the Mahāvihāravāsī Elders,
who were lamps of the Elder tradition and possessed wisdom well-established in the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
May he remain in the world for as long as there are seekers of deliverance from the world,
showing to the sons of good family the method for the purification of wisdom—
so long as even the name "Buddha" exists for that one of pure mind who is like a mountain peak.
"In this world, the Great Seer acts for the World-Honored One.
The commentary on the Sutta Nipāta is finished.
